y.B: Subjective means based on personal feelings rather than the facts, and a decision could be subjective whether one member likes it or all of them do.
y.D: Superior means better, or higher in rank, but the sentence tells you everyone voted yes, which is about agreement rather than quality.

vr.q: She borrowed the first ______ of the encyclopaedia from the library.
vr.e: A volume is one book of a set, and an encyclopaedia comes in numbered volumes.

y.B: A charter is an official document setting out the rules or rights of a group, so it is not one of the books of an encyclopaedia.
y.C: Consensus means general agreement reached by a group, which is not a thing you can carry home from a library.
y.D: A trace is a tiny leftover sign that something was once there, far too small a word for a whole book.

vr.q: TANGIBLE most nearly means:
vr.e: tangible: touchable, concrete, real — something you could actually hold or point at.

y.A: Hopeful means full of hope, expecting something good, which is about how you feel rather than what you can touch.
y.C: Distant means far off, and something can be miles away and still be perfectly solid and touchable.
y.D: Imaginary means existing only in the mind, which is the opposite of tangible — a tangible thing is really there to hold.

vr.q: The narrow mountain road became ______ after the ice storm.
vr.e: Treacherous means dangerous and not to be trusted, which is what ice makes a narrow mountain road; rural, stable and spacious describe where the road is, not the danger.

y.A: Rural means out in the countryside, which this road may well be, but that says nothing about the ice or the danger.
y.B: Stable means steady and unlikely to shift or give way, and ice would make a road less stable, not more.
y.C: Spacious means roomy, with plenty of space, and the sentence has already called the road narrow.

vr.q: The movement fought for women's ______, or the right to vote.
vr.e: Suffrage is the right to vote, which the sentence defines outright with “or the right to vote”; consensus, a charter and prestige are not that right.

y.B: Consensus means general agreement in a group, and people can agree about something without anyone being allowed to vote on it.
y.C: A charter is an official document granting rights or setting out rules, so it is the paper rather than the right to vote itself.
y.D: Prestige means respect and high standing in other people's eyes, which is not something you exercise at a ballot box.

vr.q: One ______ of the contract requires payment within thirty days.
vr.e: A term here is one condition of a contract, which is what requires payment within thirty days; a trace, capital and volume are not conditions.

y.A: A trace is a small remaining sign that something was once there, not a rule written into an agreement.
y.C: Capital has more than one meaning — a country's main city, a big letter at the start of a name — and none of those is a condition written into a contract.
y.D: A volume is one book of a set, or an amount, or loudness, and none of those is a rule about paying within thirty days.

vr.q: Scientists tried to ______ the contamination back to its source.
vr.e: To trace is to follow something back to its source, which is exactly what the scientists tried to do; you cannot grant, cultivate or render contamination.

y.A: To grant is to give or allow something officially, and nobody hands out contamination.
y.B: To cultivate is to grow something or carefully build it up, like a crop or a friendship — the scientists wanted to follow the contamination back, not raise it.
y.C: Render means to make something become a certain way, as in rendering a room unusable, which is not a word for following a trail backwards.

vr.q: Her ______ reply arrived within five minutes.
vr.e: Prompt means quick, without delay, which is what a reply arriving within five minutes is; rigid, remote and static describe something else.

y.B: Rigid means stiff and unbending, and a reply could be rigid in tone and still take a week to arrive.
y.C: Remote means far away or out of the way, which is about distance, not about how quickly something came.
y.D: Static is about whether a thing changes at all, which says nothing about a reply arriving in five minutes.

vr.q: Play was ______ until the rain stopped.
vr.e: To suspend something is to halt it for a time, and play waits here until the rain stops.

y.A: To grant is to give or allow something officially, so granted play would be permitted play — but the sentence needs a word for play stopping while the rain falls.
y.B: To decline is to refuse something politely, or to go downhill, and you can refuse an invitation but not refuse play until the rain stops.
y.D: To evoke is to bring a feeling or a memory to mind, the way a smell can evoke a kitchen, so it is not a word for halting a game.

vr.q: Beth was ______ with the simple meal and asked for nothing more.
vr.e: Content here means satisfied, which is what asking for nothing more shows; static, capital and literal are not feelings.

y.A: Static is used of things rather than of feelings, so it is not a word for how Beth feels about her meal.
y.B: None of capital's meanings — a country's main city, a big letter at the start of a name — is a way of feeling about a meal.
y.D: Literal means taking words exactly as they are, with no figure of speech, so a person can be literal-minded but cannot be literal with a meal.

vr.q: The company needed more ______ to expand its business.
vr.e: Capital here means money to invest, which is what expanding a business needs; content, volume and a term are not money.

y.B: Content means satisfied, or else the things inside something, and being satisfied is not what a company needs in order to grow.
y.C: Volume means an amount, or loudness, or one book of a set, so it names a quantity of something rather than what pays for an expansion.
y.D: A term is one condition of an agreement, or a stretch of time like a school term, and neither is something a company needs more of to expand.

vr.q: STATIC most nearly means:
vr.e: static: not changing, motionless — The population remained static for several years.

y.B: Expensive means costing a lot of money, and static is about whether a thing changes, not what it costs.
y.C: Very social describes a person who loves company, and static is not about people at all.
y.D: Changing rapidly is the exact opposite of static, because something static stays as it is.

vr.q: To SUSPECT something means to:
vr.e: suspect: to think it may be true without being sure — She suspected the door had been left open. Said SUS-pect, it is a noun: the person thought to have done it.

y.A: Proving something false means showing for certain that it is not so, while suspecting is having a hunch with no proof either way.
y.C: Knowing something for certain means being sure, and suspecting is the step before that, when you think it may be true but cannot yet show it.
y.D: Forgetting about something is putting it out of your mind, whereas when you suspect something it is very much on your mind.

vr.q: Even after the first three attempts failed, she stayed ______ and tried once more.
vr.e: Resolute means determined and unwavering, and she tried once more after three failures.

y.A: Hesitant means holding back, unsure whether to go on, but she tried once more, which is the opposite of hanging back.
y.B: Careless means not taking care or attention, and the sentence says she failed three times, not that she was sloppy about it.
y.D: Distant means far away, or cool and unfriendly, and neither one describes someone who keeps trying.

vr.q: DUBIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: dubious: doubtful, unsure, suspicious about something — Jo was dubious about Amy's plan to bake a cake all by herself.

y.A: Loyal means faithful and sticking by someone, which is about who you stand with rather than whether you believe something.
y.B: Cheerful means happy and in good spirits, which has nothing to do with being dubious — that is about having doubts.
y.C: Certain means being completely sure, which is the opposite of dubious — someone dubious has doubts.

vr.q: The campaign set out to ______ the disease completely, leaving none of it behind.
vr.e: To eradicate something is to wipe it out entirely, and the campaign leaves none of the disease behind.

y.A: To suspend something is to stop it for a time, and anything stopped for a time can start again, while the campaign wanted none of the disease left at all.
y.B: To evoke is to bring a feeling or a memory to mind, the way a song can evoke a summer, so it is not a word for getting rid of something.
y.C: To grant is to give or allow something officially, and a disease is not something anyone hands out.

vr.q: CONSPICUOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: conspicuous: noticeable, obvious, easy to pick out — Jo's long chestnut mane was conspicuous among the other girls.

y.B: Ordinary means usual and nothing special, so an ordinary thing blends in, while a conspicuous one stands out.
y.C: Quiet means making little sound, and something can be completely silent and still be impossible to miss, like a bright red coat.
y.D: Hidden means out of sight, which is the opposite of conspicuous — you spot a conspicuous thing straight away.

vr.q: DISCRETION most nearly means:
vr.e: discretion: good judgment about what to say and when — Jo used great discretion when sharing her stories, never revealing which sisters they were about.

y.B: Wealth means having a great deal of money, and discretion costs nothing; it is about knowing what to say and when.
y.C: Speed is how fast something happens, and discretion is often the opposite, taking a moment before you speak.
y.D: Loud disagreement is the opposite of discretion — discretion is the quiet good sense to know what to say and when to say nothing.

vr.q: RETALIATE most nearly means:
vr.e: retaliate: respond with revenge, strike back — When Amy burned Jo's manuscript, Jo wanted to retaliate.

y.A: Remembering fondly means looking back on something warmly, which is closer to the word reminisce, while retaliating is hitting back.
y.C: Retreat means to back away or withdraw, which is the opposite of striking back; the two words only look alike because both begin with re-.
y.D: Repair means to mend something that is broken, and retaliating usually leaves things worse rather than mended.

vr.q: He had to ______ a yawn in the middle of the long speech.
vr.e: To stifle something is to hold it back or smother it, which is what he does with the yawn.

y.B: Unite means to join together into one, which is something people or groups do, not something you do to a yawn.
y.C: Retrieve means to fetch something back, the way a dog retrieves a ball, and he needed to hold the yawn in, not go and get it.
y.D: Cultivate means to grow or carefully build something up, and encouraging the yawn was the last thing he wanted.

vr.q: SUBSEQUENT most nearly means:
vr.e: subsequent: following later, coming after — The first meeting was short; subsequent ones ran for hours.

y.A: Motionless means not moving at all, which is about movement, while subsequent is about when something happens.
y.C: Not yet decided describes something still up in the air, closer to a word like pending, while subsequent simply means later.
y.D: Happening before is the opposite of subsequent, because subsequent events are the ones that come after.

vr.q: SUPERIOR most nearly means:
vr.e: superior: better or higher-ranking than something else — The second draft was superior in every way.

y.B: Lasting only briefly describes something temporary, like a passing shower; superior is about rank or quality, and says nothing about how long a thing lasts.
y.C: Equal means the same as something else, level with it — but superior means above it, better or higher in rank.
y.D: Below others in rank is what inferior means, and it is superior's opposite: the super- in superior points upwards.

vr.q: SUPPLEMENT most nearly means:
vr.e: supplement: add to or complete something that is not quite enough — She supplemented her notes with diagrams from the library book.

y.A: To hide something is to keep it out of sight, while to supplement it is to add something extra to what is already there.
y.B: To argue against something is to speak in opposition to it; supplementing it is helping it along by adding more.
y.D: Taking away entirely is the opposite of supplementing — a supplement adds to what is not quite enough, it never removes it.

vr.q: The evidence was too ______ to ignore; everyone could see the broken window.
vr.e: Tangible means solid and plain to see or touch, which a broken window everyone can see is; whimsical, subjective and remote describe evidence you cannot point at.

y.A: Whimsical means playful and fanciful, the way a made-up story is — but a broken window that everyone can see is solid and real.
y.B: Subjective means a matter of what someone believes rather than of what is there, and a broken window is there for anyone to look at.
y.C: Remote means far away or distant, and a broken window everyone can see is as close and as plain as evidence gets.

vr.q: The hikers sought ______ in a cabin when the storm became dangerous.
vr.e: A sanctuary is a place of safety, which is what a cabin becomes when a storm turns dangerous; consensus, volume and prestige are not shelters.

y.A: A consensus is a meeting of minds among a group, not a place — and what the hikers needed from the storm was somewhere safe to be.
y.B: Volume means how loud a sound is, or how much space something fills — neither is a thing you can shelter inside.
y.C: Prestige means the respect and admiration a person or place has earned, which does not keep anybody out of a storm.

vr.q: The teacher could not tell which story was true because the two accounts were ______.
vr.e: Conflicting means clashing rather than matching, which is why two accounts can leave a listener with no way to tell which story is true; prompt is about speed, unanimous means everybody agrees, and stationary is about staying still.

y.A: Prompt means quick, given without delay; two prompt accounts would simply arrive early and could still say exactly the same thing, so being quick is no reason for the teacher to be stuck.
y.B: Unanimous means agreed on by everybody, so unanimous accounts would match each other and the teacher would know at once which story to believe.
y.D: Stationary means staying in one place without moving, like a parked car; it describes where a thing sits, not whether two accounts agree.

vr.q: The doctor tried to ______ the worried child with a calm voice.
vr.e: To soothe is to calm someone, which is what a calm voice is for; to stifle, suspect or trace a worried child is not to comfort them.

y.A: To stifle something is to smother it or hold it back, so stifling a worried child would mean keeping her quiet rather than calming her down.
y.B: To suspect someone is to think they may have done something wrong, which is not what a doctor does with a calm voice.
y.D: To trace is to follow something's path, or to draw over its lines, and neither is a way of comforting anybody.

vr.q: A ______ student keeps working carefully even when a task is difficult.
vr.e: Diligent means carefully hardworking, which is what keeping at a difficult task shows; static, reckless and aloof are the opposite.

y.B: Static means making no progress and going nowhere, so a static student would be one who never gets any further — not one who keeps at a hard task.
y.C: Reckless means charging ahead without thinking about the danger, and this student is working carefully at something hard.
y.D: Aloof means keeping apart from other people and staying distant from them, which says nothing about how hard somebody works.

vr.q: The model ship took months of ______ work, with every tiny rope tied by hand.
vr.e: Painstaking means done with great care and attention to every detail, which is what tying every tiny rope by hand takes.

y.A: Hasty means done in a hurry, and work that takes months with every rope tied by hand is the opposite of hurried.
y.C: Careless means not taking care or attention, but tying every tiny rope by hand takes a great deal of care.
y.D: Brief means lasting only a short time, and this work took months.

vr.q: A referee has to stay ______ and judge only what actually happened.
vr.e: Objective means going by facts that can be checked rather than by feelings, and a referee judges only what actually happened.

y.A: Subjective means coming from inside one person's own head rather than from what actually happened, which is exactly what a referee must not do.
y.B: Feisty means lively and quick to fight back, which may be spirited but is not what keeps a referee fair.
y.D: Tangible means solid enough to touch or point at, which describes things themselves, not the way a person judges them.

vr.q: Which flavour tastes best is ______, because it depends on who you ask.
vr.e: Subjective means resting on personal opinion rather than on checkable fact, and this depends on who you ask.

y.A: Unanimous means everyone agreeing, but here people disagree — that is why it depends on who you ask.
y.B: Stationary is about a thing not budging from where it is, which has nothing to do with opinions about flavour.
y.C: Objective means going by what is actually so rather than by how you feel about it, and how a flavour tastes is only ever how it strikes you.

vr.q: The exercise bike stays ______ however hard its wheels are turning.
vr.e: Stationary means staying in one place, which the bike does even while its wheels spin.

y.B: Frequent means happening often, which is about how often something occurs, not about whether it stays in one place.
y.C: Unsteady means wobbly and likely to tip over, and nothing in the sentence says the bike wobbles at all.
y.D: Distant means far away from something else, and nothing here puts the bike far from anything — its wheels turn hard while it goes nowhere.

vr.q: Despite the storm, the bridge remained ______ and safe to cross.
vr.e: Stable means steady and safe to rely on, which is what a bridge that came through the storm is; static means unchanging, stationary means not moving, remote means far off.

y.A: Static means unchanging, and a thing can be perfectly unchanging and still not be safe — the sentence is praising the bridge for holding firm.
y.C: A stationary thing is one that never travels anywhere, which every bridge manages, storm or no storm; the point here is that it is still firm enough to cross.
y.D: Remote means far away, and the sentence is about the bridge surviving the storm, not about where it stands.

vr.q: The frozen image on the monitor was ______ for several seconds.
vr.e: Static means not changing, which is what a frozen image on a monitor is; social, prompt and spacious describe nothing about a frozen screen.

y.A: Social means having to do with being among other people, which a frozen picture on a screen has nothing to do with.
y.B: Prompt means quick and on time, but this image was stuck for several seconds, which is the opposite of quick.
y.D: Spacious means having plenty of room inside, which describes a room or a bag, not a picture that has stopped changing.

vr.q: The watchmaker examined the ______ gears, each tiny part fitting precisely.
vr.e: Intricate means made of many small parts fitting together, which is what tiny gears meshing precisely are; subjective, literal and remote say nothing about detail.

y.A: Subjective means based on someone's personal opinion, but gears are real parts, and the sentence is describing how detailed they are.
y.B: Literal means taking words exactly as they are said, with no figurative meaning behind them — it describes language, not gears.
y.D: Remote means far away, and the watchmaker had these gears right in front of him.

vr.q: The committee reached a ______ after everyone finally agreed.
vr.e: A consensus is agreement reached by everyone, which is what “everyone finally agreed” says; volume, prejudice and a trace are not agreements.

y.A: Volume means how loud something is, or how much space it fills, and neither is a thing a committee can reach.
y.B: Prejudice means an unfair opinion formed before you know the facts, which is not what a group arrives at when everyone finally agrees.
y.C: A trace is a tiny leftover sign that something was once there, not an agreement.

vr.q: The report tried to remain ______ by relying on measurable facts.
vr.e: Objective means based on facts rather than opinion, which is what relying on measurable facts is; conspicuous, rigid and literal are not the opposite of opinionated.

y.B: Conspicuous means standing out so that it is easy to notice, which is about being seen, not about sticking to the facts.
y.C: Rigid means stiff and unbending, like a metal bar or a strict rule, and a report built on measurable facts is meant to be fair rather than stiff.
y.D: Literal means keeping to the exact words rather than a figurative meaning — a report can be perfectly literal and still be full of opinion.

vr.q: In 'a remote possibility,' REMOTE means:
vr.e: remote: unlikely, barely possible — a remote possibility is one you would not bet on. Its everyday meaning is far away, and a distant chance is where this use comes from.

y.A: Remote can make a place sound lonely, but the word itself means far off — a remote possibility is far from likely, not dangerous.
y.C: Formal means proper and done by the rules, which is no part of what remote means.
y.D: Nearby is remote turned round the other way: remote means far away, and a remote possibility is a long way from happening.

vr.q: The camera's ______ design made it easy to carry.
vr.e: Compact means small and neatly packed, which is what makes a camera easy to carry; remote, tender and domestic say nothing about size.

y.A: Remote means far away, so it tells you where something is rather than how small and neatly packed it is.
y.C: Tender means gentle and soft-hearted, or sore when it is touched, and neither has anything to do with carrying a camera.
y.D: Domestic means to do with the home, or with your own country rather than abroad — not with how big a thing is.

vr.q: GRANT most nearly means:
vr.e: grant: to give or allow something — the opposite of refusing it.

y.B: To refuse is to say no, which is the exact opposite of granting something.
y.C: To borrow is to take something for a while and give it back, while to grant is to give it or to give permission for it.
y.D: To delay is to put something off until later, but granting it means saying yes to it.

vr.q: EXPLOIT most nearly means:
vr.e: exploit: to take advantage of someone or something, often unfairly.

y.A: To repair something is to fix what is broken, while to exploit it is to use it for your own gain, often unfairly.
y.C: To praise someone is to say good things about them; exploiting them is using them for what you can get out of them.
y.D: To ignore something is to pay it no attention at all, but exploiting it means making full use of it.

vr.q: DECLINE most nearly means:
vr.e: decline: to refuse or turn something down — the opposite of accepting it.

y.A: To repeat is to do or say something over again, which has nothing to do with turning an offer down.
y.B: To enlarge is to make something bigger — and decline, in its other meaning, is about getting smaller or weaker, which is nearer the opposite.
y.C: To accept is to say yes, and to decline is to say no, so this is the other way round.

vr.q: A few notes of that song can ______ a whole summer she had forgotten.
vr.e: To evoke something is to bring it to mind, and the notes call the summer back.

y.A: To measure something is to find out how big or how long it is, but the notes are bringing a memory back, not sizing it up.
y.B: To postpone something is to put it off until later, and a summer already gone cannot be put off — only called back to mind.
y.D: To destroy something is to wreck it, and the notes bring the forgotten summer back rather than ruining it.

vr.q: Early warnings helped ______ a larger disaster.
vr.e: To avert is to prevent something bad before it happens, which is what early warnings do; to provoke, inundate or dwindle a disaster is not to stop it.

y.A: To provoke is to stir something up on purpose, which is the opposite of what early warnings are meant to do.
y.B: To inundate is to flood or swamp something with far too much of it, so you could be inundated by a disaster but not inundate one.
y.C: To dwindle is to shrink away little by little, and it is something that happens on its own — you cannot dwindle a disaster.

vr.q: The agency decided to ______ the license after repeated violations.
vr.e: To revoke is to cancel something already granted, which is what repeated violations cost a license; to proclaim, acquire or commend it is not to take it away.

y.A: To proclaim is to announce something publicly, which is not what happens to a license after repeated violations.
y.B: To acquire is to get something for yourself, but here the agency is taking the license away rather than gaining one.
y.C: To commend is to praise someone for doing well, and repeated violations do not earn praise.

vr.q: A UTOPIA is:
vr.e: utopia: an imagined perfect society — a place arranged so well that nothing goes wrong. Its opposite, where everything has gone wrong, is a dystopia.

y.A: A legal decision is a ruling handed down by a court, and utopia is not a law word at all — it names an imagined place.
y.C: A utopia is imagined as a place where everything has been arranged perfectly, so nothing about it is dangerous.
y.D: A rural village is a small settlement out in the countryside; a utopia may be any size, and what makes it one is that it is imagined to be perfect.

vr.q: TREACHEROUS most nearly means:
vr.e: treacherous: dangerous or untrustworthy; an icy path and a false friend are both treacherous — The mountain track was treacherous after the storm.

y.A: Ordinary means usual and nothing out of the common way, but treacherous marks a thing out as dangerous or not to be trusted.
y.C: Safe and dependable is treacherous turned right around — a treacherous path, or a treacherous friend, is exactly the one you cannot rely on.
y.D: Quiet is about how much noise a thing makes, and something treacherous can be perfectly quiet while still being dangerous.

vr.q: CANDID most nearly means:
vr.e: Candid means openly saying what you really think, so honest and direct is the match; a candid friend is never secretive or polite but vague.

y.A: Hurried means done quickly and in a rush, but candid is about being open and truthful — you can be candid and take all the time you like.
y.B: Secretive means keeping things to yourself and not letting others know, which is the very opposite of being candid.
y.C: Polite but vague means softening your words until nobody can tell what you really think, while a candid person says plainly what she thinks even when it is awkward.

vr.q: THOROUGH most nearly means:
vr.e: Thorough work covers every part of the job, so leaving nothing out fits; a thorough search is the opposite of one done in a great hurry.

y.A: Friendly to strangers says how someone treats people, while thorough says how completely something is done — every part covered, nothing skipped.
y.B: Work done in a great hurry is rushed, and rushing is how things get missed; thorough work is the opposite, covering everything carefully.
y.D: Difficult to believe describes a far-fetched story, while thorough is about how completely a job has been done, not about whether anyone believes it.

vr.q: PLAUSIBLE most nearly means:
vr.e: A plausible excuse is one that could reasonably be true, so believable is right; plausible is the opposite of impossible.

y.A: Temporary means lasting only a short time, but plausible is about whether something could reasonably be true, not about how long it lasts.
y.B: Expensive means costing a lot of money, and a plausible excuse costs nothing — it is simply one that could be true.
y.C: Impossible means it could not happen at all, which is the opposite of plausible; a plausible story is one that easily could be so.

vr.q: TEDIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: A tedious chore drags on and wears you out with dullness, so long and boring fits; brief and lively is its opposite.

y.A: Hard to reach means far away or awkward to get to, like a shelf too high, whereas tedious describes a job that drags on and bores you.
y.B: Sudden and loud describes a bang or a crash, over in a moment, and a tedious job is the opposite — it drags on and on until it wears you out.
y.C: Brief and lively means short and full of energy, which is exactly what a tedious lesson is not.

vr.q: DISPUTE most nearly means:
vr.e: To dispute a call or a claim is to argue against it and say it is not right, so to argue against is the match; someone who disputes a decision is doing the opposite of agreeing quickly.

y.A: To promise again is to give your word a second time, but disputing is about challenging what someone has said, not pledging anything.
y.C: To agree quickly is to say yes at once, and someone who disputes a decision is refusing to go along with it.
y.D: To explain politely is to make something clear in a kind way, and you can explain something you completely agree with; disputing it means saying outright that it is wrong.

vr.q: SUPERFICIAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Superficial means staying on the surface, so a superficial cut or a superficial friendship is shallow rather than deep.

y.B: Ancient means very old, from long ago, but superficial is about depth — staying on the surface, like a superficial scratch.
y.C: Generous means giving freely to others, while superficial says how deep something goes; a superficial friendship is a shallow one, not a mean one.
y.D: Sturdy means strong and solidly built, but superficial means going no further than the surface, like a cut that barely breaks the skin.

vr.q: MEDIOCRE most nearly means:
vr.e: Mediocre means no better than middling, so only average fits; it is the opposite of clearly excellent.

y.A: Clearly excellent means very good indeed, and mediocre falls well short of that — middling, nothing special either way.
y.B: Very expensive means costing a lot, but mediocre is about quality being middling, and something mediocre can carry any price at all.
y.D: Extremely rare means hardly ever found, while mediocre things are everywhere — the word means no better than average.

vr.q: LENIENT most nearly means:
vr.e: A lenient teacher lets small things slide, so not strict; forgiving is the match, and strict and demanding is the opposite.

y.B: Difficult to please describes someone you can never quite satisfy, but a lenient teacher is easily satisfied and forgives small mistakes.
y.C: Strict and demanding means holding people to every rule and expecting a lot of them, while a lenient teacher lets small slips go.
y.D: Quick to anger means losing your temper easily, whereas lenient means going easy on people, which is a calmer sort of kindness.

vr.q: ADMIRABLE most nearly means:
vr.e: Something admirable earns real respect and praise, so worth praising fits; barely acceptable is nearly its opposite.

y.A: Strangely old-fashioned means belonging to a much earlier time, which tells you when something comes from; admirable tells you it deserves respect.
y.B: Unusually noisy is about how much sound something makes, but admirable is about deserving praise, and the quietest acts are often the most admirable.
y.C: Barely acceptable means only just good enough to get by, and something admirable is far more than that — it earns real respect.

vr.q: SKEPTICAL most nearly means:
vr.e: A skeptical listener is not convinced and wants proof, so doubting is right; trusting is the opposite attitude.

y.A: Sleepy means tired and ready for bed, but a skeptical listener is wide awake — she simply is not convinced yet.
y.C: Generous means quick to share what you have, while skeptical is about whether you believe something, not about what you hand out.
y.D: Trusting means taking what you are told as true without needing proof, which is the opposite of skeptical.

vr.q: Even though he wanted to keep arguing, Marcus had to ______ that his sister was right.
vr.e: To concede is to admit that someone else is right, which is what "had to" signals here; to deny or to insist that she was right would mean he never gave in.

y.B: To insist is to keep saying firmly that you are right and refuse to back down, but the sentence says Marcus had to give in.
y.C: To imagine is to picture something in your mind, and Marcus is not picturing anything here — he actually admits his sister was right.
y.D: To deny something is to say it is not true, and denying that his sister was right is exactly what he could no longer do.

vr.q: The principal stopped by our classroom to ______ the students for their hard work.
vr.e: To commend is to praise someone for what they have done, which is what hard work earns; to scold or to warn would be the opposite reaction.

y.A: To scold is to tell someone off for doing something wrong, and hard work deserves the opposite reaction.
y.B: To warn is to tell someone about trouble that may be coming, and the students had done well, so there was nothing to warn them about.
y.D: To replace is to put something new in the place of something else, and a principal pleased with the class is not swapping the students for others.

vr.q: Because her own brother was racing, Mia could not serve as a ______ judge.
vr.e: A neutral judge favors neither side, and Mia would naturally want her brother to win; having a brother in the race would not stop her from being patient, careful, or capable.

y.A: Careful means paying close attention so as not to make mistakes, and Mia could still do that; what her brother's racing takes away is her ability to favor neither side.
y.C: Patient means waiting calmly without getting annoyed, and having a brother in the race would not make Mia impatient — it would make her want him to win.
y.D: Capable means having the skill to do the job, and nobody says Mia cannot judge, only that she could not do it fairly this time.

vr.q: Ana shouted her answer before she had read the whole question — a ______ move she soon regretted.
vr.e: Hasty means done too quickly and with too little thought, which is exactly what answering before reading is; a patient or clever move would have been the opposite.

y.A: Clever means quick-witted and sharp, but answering before reading the whole question is the opposite of sharp, and Ana regretted it.
y.B: Patient means willing to hold back and wait without fretting, which is exactly what Ana was not — she shouted before she had finished reading.
y.D: Generous means open-handed, happy to give others what you have, and that has nothing to do with rushing an answer out too soon.

vr.q: Ms. Bell wrote a helpful ______ of my essay, naming both its strengths and its weaknesses.
vr.e: A critique is a careful judgement that weighs strong points against weak ones, which is what Ms. Bell wrote; an apology or an announcement judges nothing.

y.A: An announcement is a public notice telling people that something is happening, but Ms. Bell was weighing up the essay, not sharing news.
y.B: An invitation asks someone to come to something, and nobody is being invited here — the writing judges the essay.
y.C: An apology says sorry for something you did wrong, and Ms. Bell had nothing to be sorry for; she was giving a judgement on the essay.

vr.q: Her apology sounded ______; anyone could tell she truly meant it.
vr.e: Sincere means truly meant, which matches the clue that she really meant it; a sarcastic apology is one that is not meant at all.

y.B: Boastful means showing off about how good you are, which is not what an apology does at all.
y.C: Sarcastic means saying the opposite of what you really mean, often to mock, so a sarcastic apology is one that is not meant — and the clue says she truly meant it.
y.D: Confusing means hard to understand, but the sentence says anyone could tell how she felt, so nothing was unclear.

vr.q: Forgetting the tickets was a ______ that cost us an hour.
vr.e: A blunder is a careless mistake, and forgetting the tickets cost the group an hour; a bargain or a reward would be something good.

y.A: A reward is something good given to you for doing well, and forgetting the tickets cost the group an hour — nobody was rewarded for that.
y.C: A bargain is something you get for less than it is worth, a piece of good luck, and losing an hour is the opposite of a good deal.
y.D: A custom is something a group has always done, a tradition handed down, while forgetting the tickets was a one-off mistake.

vr.q: The judges ______ each photograph before choosing a winner.
vr.e: To scrutinize is to examine something very closely, which is how judges pick a winner; judges who ignored the photographs could not choose at all.

y.A: Framed means set in a border ready to hang, but the judges here are choosing which photograph wins, and that means looking hard at each one.
y.B: Purchased means bought, and judges in a contest choose a winner rather than paying for the entries.
y.D: Ignored means paid no attention to, and judges who ignored the photographs could never pick a winner.

vr.q: The coach said the plan had real ______ and was worth trying.
vr.e: Merit is real worth or value, so a plan with merit is worth trying; damage, delay, and silence would all be reasons to drop it.

y.B: Damage is harm done to something, which would be a reason to drop a plan rather than to call it worth trying.
y.C: Silence is the absence of sound, and a plan cannot contain silence — the coach is saying the plan has real worth.
y.D: Delay means being held up or made to wait, which would be a fault in a plan, not a reason to try it.

vr.q: A ______ athlete, Nia plays goalkeeper, midfield, and forward equally well.
vr.e: Versatile means able to do many different things well, which is what playing three positions equally well shows; clumsy and nervous name weaknesses, not range.

y.A: Clumsy means awkward, likely to trip or drop things, but playing three positions equally well is a compliment, not a complaint.
y.B: Solitary means alone or doing things by yourself, and Nia plays right across a team in three different positions.
y.D: Nervous means anxious and easily worried, and the sentence praises how much Nia can do, not how she feels before a match.

vr.q: FLAW most nearly means:
vr.e: A flaw is a weak spot or fault, like a crack in a bowl; a reward, a journey, and a promise have nothing to do with imperfection.

y.A: A reward is what you get for doing something well, a prize or a treat, whereas a flaw is something wrong with a thing — a crack or a weak spot.
y.B: A promise is something you pledge to do, but a flaw is a fault in a thing, like a chip in a bowl.
y.D: A journey is a trip from one place to another, and a flaw has nothing to do with travelling — it is an imperfection.

vr.q: TRIVIAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Trivial details are so small that they hardly matter, so unimportant is the match.

y.A: Expensive says how much something costs, but trivial says how much it matters, and a trivial detail is one hardly worth mentioning.
y.B: Noisy means making a lot of sound, while trivial means mattering so little that it can safely be passed over.
y.C: Frozen means turned to ice or held fast by cold, which has nothing to do with trivial, a word about small unimportant things.

vr.q: HARSH most nearly means:
vr.e: Harsh means rough or severe, as in a harsh winter or a harsh punishment; gentle is its opposite.

y.A: Gentle means mild and kind, the very opposite of harsh — a harsh winter or a harsh word is rough, not soft.
y.B: Curious means eager to find things out, but harsh describes something rough or severe, like a harsh punishment.
y.C: Damp means slightly wet, and although a winter can be damp, harsh means severe and hard to bear rather than merely moist.

vr.q: APPROVE most nearly means:
vr.e: To approve something is to judge it good and agree to it, so to accept as good fits; to argue against it is the opposite.

y.A: To argue against something is to speak out and say it is wrong, which is the opposite of approving it.
y.B: To forget entirely is to let something slip out of your mind, but approving is an active decision that something is good.
y.D: To repeat aloud is to say something over again, and you could repeat a plan aloud without approving of it at all.

vr.q: PRUDENT most nearly means:
vr.e: A prudent choice is a careful, sensible one that avoids needless risk, so careful and wise is right; bold and reckless is its opposite.

y.A: Loud and talkative describes how much noise a person makes, but prudent is about thinking ahead, and a quiet person and a chatty one can both be prudent.
y.C: Rich and famous is about money and being well known, while prudent describes how carefully someone thinks before acting.
y.D: Bold and reckless means rushing in without weighing the risk, which is the opposite of prudent.

vr.q: SHODDY most nearly means:
vr.e: Shoddy goods are put together cheaply and badly, so poorly made fits; carefully built is the opposite.

y.A: Expensive means costing a lot of money, and something shoddy is usually cheap rather than costly; shoddy is about how badly a thing is made, not its price.
y.B: Brightly colored means having strong, vivid colors; shoddy is about the quality of the work, and a badly made thing can be any color at all.
y.D: Carefully built means put together with attention so that it lasts, which is the exact opposite of shoddy.

vr.q: FLATTER most nearly means:
vr.e: To flatter is to pile on more praise than is deserved, often to get something; to blame unfairly is the opposite kind of remark.

y.B: To blame unfairly is to accuse someone of a fault that is not theirs, whereas to flatter is the opposite kind of remark: praise laid on thicker than the person has earned.
y.C: To arrive early is to turn up before the time set; flatter has nothing to do with time, and means to praise someone more than they deserve.
y.D: To explain clearly is to make something easy to understand; to flatter is to praise someone far beyond what is deserved, often to get something out of them.

vr.q: CONDEMN most nearly means:
vr.e: To condemn something is to declare that it is very wrong, so to strongly disapprove is the match; praising and celebrating point the other way.

y.A: To celebrate loudly is to make a noisy show of joy over something good, while to condemn is to declare that something is very wrong — the two point in opposite directions.
y.C: To praise quietly is still to say good things about something; condemning is declaring it wrong, which is the reverse.
y.D: To repair something carefully is to mend what is broken, but to condemn is to say in words that something is very wrong, which mends nothing.

vr.q: Ravi tends to ______ when he tells the story, so the fish he caught grows another foot longer every time.
vr.e: To exaggerate is to make something sound bigger than it really was, which is why the fish keeps growing with every telling.

y.B: To apologize is to say sorry for something you did, and Ravi is not saying sorry — he is making the fish bigger with every telling.
y.C: To whisper is to speak very softly; the trouble with Ravi is not how loudly he tells the story but that he makes it bigger than it really was.
y.D: To hesitate is to pause because you are not sure, and Ravi never pauses — he simply adds another foot to the fish.

vr.q: We were told not to ______ about our victory, no matter how proud we felt.
vr.e: To boast is to brag about your own success, exactly what proud winners were warned against; complaining and grumbling are what a losing team might do.

y.B: To grumble is to complain in a low, muttering way, which is what an unhappy person does; these winners were proud, so the warning was about bragging.
y.C: To chatter is to talk quickly and lightly about small things, but the warning here is about crowing over a win, which is bragging rather than idle talk.
y.D: To complain is to say out loud that you are unhappy about something; a proud winning team has nothing to complain of, which is why they were warned about bragging instead.

vr.q: Their plan was ______; one hard question and it fell apart.
vr.e: Flimsy means weak and easily broken, so a plan that collapses at the first hard question is flimsy; sturdy is its opposite.

y.A: Lengthy means long, going on and on; a plan can be long and still collapse, so length is not what failed here — weakness is.
y.B: Generous means willing to give freely, which describes a person's kindness rather than whether a plan can stand up to one hard question.
y.C: Sturdy means strong and solidly made, and this plan fell apart at the first hard question, so it was the opposite of sturdy.

vr.q: Before repairs began, an expert came to ______ the damage.
vr.e: To assess damage is to judge how bad it is before deciding what to do; an expert would not be sent for to ignore or enjoy it.

y.A: To enjoy something is to take pleasure in it, and nobody sends for an expert to take pleasure in damage — they send for someone to judge how bad it is.
y.B: To cause something is to make it happen, but the damage had already happened before the expert arrived, so his job was to judge it, not create it.
y.C: To ignore something is to take no notice of it on purpose; an expert called in before repairs begin is there to look closely, not to look away.

vr.q: Her excuse was ______: she had a doctor's note for that morning.
vr.e: A valid excuse is one that really holds up, and a doctor's note is solid proof; untrue would mean the opposite.

y.A: Hilarious means extremely funny, and a doctor's note is what makes an excuse hold up — nothing about it is a joke.
y.C: Untrue means false, and the doctor's note is exactly what shows her excuse was genuine, so untrue is the opposite of what the sentence tells you.
y.D: Hidden means put out of sight, and she produced a doctor's note, so her excuse was shown openly rather than concealed.

vr.q: Spending his whole allowance on one poster now seems ______ to Theo, who has nothing left for the class trip.
vr.e: Foolish means showing poor judgement, and Theo can now see that the poster was a bad use of his money; a wise choice would have left him enough for the trip.

y.A: Generous means giving freely to other people; Theo spent the money on a poster for himself, and the point is that it left him short, not that he gave anything away.
y.C: Wise means showing good judgement, and Theo now has nothing left for the class trip, so his choice turned out to be the opposite of good judgement.
y.D: Cheerful means happy and in good spirits; Theo may well feel gloomy, but the word here has to describe his decision, not his mood.

vr.q: The ______ shopper compared prices at three stores before buying.
vr.e: A shrewd shopper judges value cleverly, which is why she checked three stores first; a careless shopper would have taken the first price offered.

y.A: Generous means ready to give away what you have, which is a fine quality but not the one on show here: comparing prices at three stores is judging value sharply.
y.B: Sleepy means drowsy and ready for bed, and a shopper who visits three stores before buying is wide awake and thinking hard.
y.C: Careless means not paying attention, but this shopper paid a great deal of attention, checking three stores before she spent her money.

vr.q: After years of service, the librarian was ______ of the town's highest honor.
vr.e: To be worthy of an honor is to deserve it, and years of service is exactly what earns one.

y.A: Jealous means wanting what somebody else has, or fearing you will lose what is yours; the librarian is the one being given the honor, so there is nobody for her to envy.
y.C: Guilty means having done something wrong, and years of service is the opposite — it is what earns an honor rather than what deserves blame.
y.D: Afraid means frightened; the sentence is about deserving the town's highest honor, not about being scared of it.

vr.q: The young pianist won wide ______ after her first concert.
vr.e: Acclaim is loud public praise, the natural result of a successful first concert; blame would follow a failure instead.

y.A: Silence is the absence of sound or of comment, and a successful first concert wins loud public praise, which is the opposite of nobody saying anything.
y.B: Confusion means being muddled and not understanding, but her concert was a success, and what a success earns is public praise rather than puzzlement.
y.D: Blame is being held responsible for something that went wrong, which follows a failure; this pianist's first concert was a triumph.

vr.q: SUPERIOR most nearly means:
vr.e: A superior is the person above you in rank, the one you answer to, like a boss: the new firefighter asked her superior before taking the truck out. As a describing word, superior means higher in rank or better in quality.

y.B: Rival means someone you compete against, usually at your own level; a superior is not against you but above you.
y.C: Superstar starts with super- just like superior, but a superstar is a very famous performer or player, not the person in charge of you.
y.D: Teammate names someone at your own level who works beside you; a superior is the person above you, who gives the orders.

vr.q: SUSPECT most nearly means:
vr.e: To suspect something is to doubt or distrust it, and sometimes to believe something without proof: Maya suspected the email offering a free phone, so she deleted it.

y.A: Arrest is what police may do later, taking a person away; to suspect someone is only to doubt them, with no proof yet.
y.C: Inspect looks like suspect, but it means to look at something closely, the way a guard inspects a bag.
y.D: Trust is the opposite: if you trust someone you believe them, and if you suspect them you doubt them.

vr.q: BLUNDER most nearly means:
vr.e: A blunder is a big, careless mistake: calling the new coach by the wrong name in front of the whole team was an embarrassing blunder.

y.A: Apology is what you might give after a blunder, saying you are sorry; the blunder is the mistake itself.
y.C: Trick means something done on purpose to fool someone; a blunder is not planned at all, it is a careless mistake.
y.D: Wonder rhymes with blunder, but a wonder is something amazing, like a giant waterfall, not a careless mistake.

vr.q: BRISKLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Briskly means quickly and with lots of energy: when the coach blew her whistle, the players jogged briskly back to the line.

y.A: Bravely starts and ends like briskly, but it means with courage; a brave person can still walk slowly.
y.B: Lazily is the opposite: a lazy walker drags along, and a brisk walker moves fast and full of energy.
y.C: Nervously means in a worried way; someone moving fast may look hurried, but briskly means lively and energetic, not afraid.

vr.q: COMMEND most nearly means:
vr.e: To commend someone is to praise them for doing something well: the mayor commended the lifeguard for spotting the swimmer in trouble.

y.A: Command looks almost like commend, but to command is to give an order, the way a captain commands the crew.
y.B: Mend is hiding inside commend, but to mend something is to fix it, like mending a torn sleeve.
y.D: Thank is also something kind to say, but you thank someone for a favor they did for you; you commend someone for doing a job well, even when it was not for you.

vr.q: CONCEDE most nearly means:
vr.e: To concede is to admit that something is true, or that you have lost, usually after holding out against it: when the last votes were counted, the losing candidate conceded and congratulated the winner.

y.B: Apologize means to say you are sorry; someone who concedes may also apologize, but to concede is to admit the other side is right or has won.
y.C: Argue is the opposite: you argue while you still think you are right, and you concede when you finally admit you are not.
y.D: Conceal starts the same way as concede, but it means to hide something.

vr.q: CRITIQUE most nearly means:
vr.e: A critique is a careful review of a piece of work that points out what is strong and what could be better: the film club wrote a critique of the movie's music and its ending.

y.A: Draft means an early, rough version of a piece of work; a critique is a judgment of the work, not the work itself.
y.C: Summary means a short retelling of what a story or article says; a critique goes further and judges how good it is.
y.D: Technique also ends in -ique and comes up in art class, but a technique is a way of doing something, like a brush stroke, not a judgment of finished work.

vr.q: ELOQUENT most nearly means:
vr.e: Eloquent means expressive and well-spoken, able to speak or write in a clear and powerful way: Abraham Lincoln's eloquent Gettysburg Address is only about 270 words long.

y.A: Elegant looks a little like eloquent, but it means graceful and stylish, the way a dancer moves or a fancy gown looks.
y.C: Loud describes how much sound a voice makes; eloquent is about using words well, and a speaker can be eloquent in a quiet voice.
y.D: Tongue-tied is the opposite: a tongue-tied person cannot get the words out, and an eloquent one uses them with skill.

vr.q: INFAMOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Infamous means well known for something bad, the same as notorious: the Grinch is infamous for trying to steal Christmas.

y.A: Admired is the opposite: an admired person is well known for something good, and an infamous one for something bad.
y.B: Important is tempting because infamous people are well known, but infamous says their fame comes from something bad, not that they matter.
y.D: Unknown is the trap hidden in the in- at the start: infamous does not mean not famous; it means famous for the wrong reasons.

vr.q: MERIT most nearly means:
vr.e: Merit is worth, a good quality that deserves praise: the judges said the great merit of Lena's poem was its surprising last line.

y.A: Effort is how hard someone tries; a lot of effort can still produce work with little merit, because merit is how good the work is.
y.B: Luck is good fortune that comes by chance; merit is a good quality that earns praise, not something that just happens to you.
y.C: Mercy looks a little like merit, but mercy is kindness shown to someone you could have punished.

vr.q: NEUTRAL most nearly means:
vr.e: A neutral person or country does not take sides in an argument or a war, so it can be fair to both: Switzerland stayed neutral in both World Wars.

y.B: Kind means gentle and caring; a kind person can still take one side in an argument, but a neutral person takes neither side.
y.C: Loyal pulls the other way: a loyal fan sticks with one side, while a neutral person refuses to pick a side at all.
y.D: Natural looks like neutral, but it means made by nature, the way a lake or a forest is natural.

vr.q: RELINQUISH most nearly means:
vr.e: To relinquish something is to surrender it, giving it up or letting it go even if you would rather keep it: after three years as champion, Aunt Rosa finally had to relinquish her title to a younger player.

y.A: Lend means to let someone use something for a while and then get it back; when you relinquish something, you give it up.
y.B: Relish starts like relinquish, but to relish something is to enjoy it very much.
y.C: Share means to let others have part of something while you keep some too; to relinquish it is to give the whole thing up.

vr.q: SCRUTINIZE most nearly means:
vr.e: To scrutinize is to examine something very closely and carefully, looking at every detail: the jeweler scrutinized the diamond under a magnifying glass, searching for the tiniest scratch.

y.B: Notice means to see something, often just in passing; to scrutinize something is to study it on purpose, closely and for a long time.
y.C: Scribble starts with the same scr- sound, but to scribble is to write or draw quickly and messily.
y.D: Skim is the opposite: to skim a page is to read it fast for the main idea, and to scrutinize it is to read every word with care.

vr.q: SELDOM most nearly means:
vr.e: Seldom means rarely, hardly ever, only once in a long while: it seldom snows in Miami, so the flurries of January 1977 made the news.

y.A: Never is too strong: something that seldom happens does happen, just not often, while never means not at all.
y.C: Briefly means for a short time, which is about how long something lasts; seldom is about how often it happens.
y.D: All the time is the opposite: something that happens all the time happens constantly, and something that seldom happens is rare.

vr.q: SINCERE most nearly means:
vr.e: Sincere means honest and heartfelt, really meaning what you say: Ben's sincere thank-you note told his aunt exactly why he loved the book she had sent.

y.A: Cheerful means happy and bright; a smile can be cheerful without being sincere, and a sincere smile can even be sad.
y.C: Polite means having good manners; you can be polite without meaning a word of it, but being sincere means you truly mean it.
y.D: Sorry is tempting because people often talk about a sincere apology, but sincere means really meaning what you say, whether you are saying sorry or thank you.

vr.q: VERSATILE most nearly means:
vr.e: Versatile means able to do many different things or be used in many ways, which makes a person or a tool flexible: a scarf is versatile, since it can keep you warm, hold back your hair or wrap a gift.

y.A: Busy means having lots to do; a versatile person is able to do many kinds of things, even on a quiet day.
y.C: Limited is the opposite: something limited can do only a few things, and something versatile can do many.
y.D: Vertical looks a little like versatile, but it means standing straight up and down, like a flagpole.

vr.q: Although Coach Dunn lets her assistant coaches run most of the team's practices, they are still her ____, and on game day every decision is hers.
vr.e: Although sets up a turn: the assistants run practices, yet every game-day decision is still the coach's, so they work under her. A subordinate is a person who is lower in rank and takes direction from someone above.

y.A: Adversaries looks a little like advisers, which assistant coaches are, but it means opponents, and nothing in the sentence says the assistants are against their own coach.
y.B: Equals would share the decisions, but every game-day decision is hers alone; letting them run practices does not make them her equals, which is the turn although signals.
y.D: Superiors are people above you in rank, so if the assistants were her superiors, the game-day decisions would be theirs, not hers.

vr.q: Although Bruno's soccer team lost every game that season, Coach Bell called their effort ____ and praised them for never giving up.
vr.e: Although turns from the losses to the coach's praise, and never giving up is something to be proud of. Admirable means deserving respect and praise.

y.B: Hopeless fits a team that lost every game, but the coach praised the effort, and although tells you the effort was something good despite the losses.
y.C: Mediocre means only average, which might describe a losing record, but nobody praises an effort for being ordinary.
y.D: Tedious means long and boring, and a losing season can feel that way, but the coach was praising the players, not complaining about how dull the games were.

vr.q: The birthday cake Bria baked for her coach tasted wonderful, but it looked plain until she ____ it with frosting roses and a ring of fresh strawberries.
vr.e: But turns from how the cake tasted to how it looked: it looked plain until she added roses and strawberries on top. To adorn something is to decorate it so it looks prettier.

y.B: Cultivated means grew or tended, the way a gardener grows roses and strawberries, but these roses were made of frosting, and nothing was growing on the cake.
y.C: Seasoned means flavored with salt or spices, but the cake already tasted wonderful; the problem that but points to was how it looked.
y.D: Stripped means took things off, which would leave the cake even plainer, the opposite of adding roses and strawberries.

vr.q: In the first round of the tennis tournament, Amara's ____ was her best friend, Dalia; the two girls hugged at the net and then spent an hour trying their hardest to beat each other.
vr.e: The second half says what the blank means: two players trying their hardest to beat each other. An adversary is an opponent, the person you play or fight against.

y.B: Ally means someone on your side who helps you, which a best friend usually is, but in this match the two girls were trying to beat each other.
y.C: Partner is the player on your own side in a doubles match, but partners play together, and these two girls were trying their hardest to beat each other.
y.D: Umpire is the official who calls the points in a tennis match, but an umpire does not play, and these two girls spent an hour trying to beat each other.

vr.q: With only six practice balls for twenty players, Coach Castro had to ____ them carefully, giving one ball to each group of three or four.
vr.e: The words after the comma say what the coach did: she handed out the few balls, one to each group. To allocate is to give out or set aside things for a certain use.

y.B: Borrow means get something from someone else for a while, which might solve having too few balls, but the sentence says what she did with the six she had: gave one to each group.
y.C: Collect means gather things in, the opposite direction from giving one ball to each group.
y.D: Scrutinize means examine very closely, and carefully goes well with it, but looking hard at the six balls would not give one to each group.

vr.q: Unlike Dmitri, who stirred the cocoa powder into his milk so slowly that it stayed in lumps, Cassie whisked hers ____, and in under a minute it was smooth.
vr.e: Unlike sets Cassie against slow, lumpy stirring, and smooth cocoa in under a minute means quick, energetic whisking. Briskly means in a quick, lively way, full of energy.

y.B: Feebly means weakly, with no strength behind it, and weak whisking would leave lumps too, not smooth cocoa in under a minute.
y.C: Lazily is how Dmitri stirred, slowly and without effort, but unlike says Cassie did the opposite.
y.D: Seldom is about how often something happens, not how fast, and whisking only once in a while would never make the cocoa smooth in under a minute.

vr.q: Because Coach Duncan wanted a ____ answer rather than a polite one, Bianca told him the truth: the new drills were boring, and half the team had stopped trying.
vr.e: Rather than a polite one tells you the coach wanted the plain truth, and Bianca gave it, even though it was not pleasant to hear. Candid means honest and direct, saying what you really think.

y.A: Bashful means shy, and a shy answer comes out quiet and careful, but Bianca said the hard truth straight out.
y.C: Flattering means full of praise meant to please, which is closer to the polite answer the coach did not want, and boring drills are not praise.
y.D: Vague means unclear, but Bianca was perfectly clear: the drills were boring, and half the team had stopped trying.

vr.q: The league's new safety rule ____ every player to wear a mouth guard; anyone who showed up without one had to sit on the bench.
vr.e: The part after the semicolon shows the rule left no choice: without a mouth guard, a player sat on the bench. To compel is to force someone to do something.

y.A: Advised means gave advice, and advice can be ignored without trouble, but a player without a mouth guard had to sit on the bench.
y.C: Forbade means ordered someone not to do something, and rules often forbid things, but a rule that forbade mouth guards would not bench the players who came without one.
y.D: Permitted means allowed, which leaves each player free to choose, but this rule left no choice: no mouth guard, no game.

vr.q: With a broken griddle, batter that ran out after ten pancakes, and a smoke alarm that went off twice, the class pancake breakfast turned into a ____.
vr.e: The sentence lists what went wrong, one thing after another, and a smoke alarm going off twice is embarrassing too. A fiasco is a complete and embarrassing failure.

y.A: Feast means a big meal with plenty of food, but the batter ran out after only ten pancakes.
y.C: Tradition means something done the same way year after year, and the sentence never says that; it lists what went wrong this time.
y.D: Triumph means a great success, the opposite of a broken griddle, too little batter and a smoke alarm going off twice.

vr.q: When Abby forgot her library books for the third week in a row, she had to ____ her turn to choose the class read-aloud, and the turn went to Caleb instead.
vr.e: Forgetting her books three weeks running brought a penalty: her turn went to someone else. To forfeit is to lose or give up something as a penalty.

y.A: Earn means get something by doing well, but forgetting her library books three weeks in a row is not doing well, and the turn went to Caleb.
y.B: Enjoy means have fun with something, but Abby never got to use her turn at all; it went to Caleb instead.
y.D: Repeat means do again, but Abby did not take her turn even once, because it went to Caleb instead.

vr.q: Unlike the sturdy plastic cups in Cora's school cafeteria, which bounce when they fall, the antique teacups at her class tea party were so ____ that a single bump could crack one.
vr.e: Unlike sets the teacups against cups that bounce when they fall, and a cup that a single bump could crack is easily broken. Frail means weak and easily hurt or broken.

y.A: Costly means expensive, which is a reason to be careful with a cup, but a high price is not what lets a single bump crack it.
y.B: Elegant means graceful and fancy, which antique teacups may well be, but fanciness is not what makes a cup crack at a single bump.
y.D: Stable means steady and not likely to fall or break, which describes the plastic cups that bounce, and unlike sets the teacups against them.

vr.q: Mr. Brennan is usually strict about late homework, but this time he was ____ and let Arjun turn in his report on Monday without losing any points.
vr.e: But turns away from usually strict, and letting the report come in late with no penalty shows how. Lenient means not strict; easygoing and merciful about rules and punishments.

y.A: Furious means very angry, and an angry teacher would take points off, but Arjun lost none.
y.C: Punctual means on time, which matches the topic of lateness, but it describes someone who arrives on time, and the late one here was Arjun's report.
y.D: Rigid means stiff and unbending about rules, the usual strict Mr. Brennan, while the word but signals that this time he acted differently.

vr.q: While most of the team hurried to the bus after practice, Diego liked to ____ on the field, kicking a ball around until the coach called his name twice.
vr.e: While sets Diego against the teammates who hurried off; he stayed on the field so long that the coach had to call him twice. To linger is to stay around longer than expected.

y.A: Depart means leave, which is what the rest of the team did; while sets Diego apart from them, and he stayed on the field.
y.C: Scramble means rush about in a hurry, like the teammates hurrying to the bus, but Diego took his time.
y.D: Vanish means disappear, but Diego stayed in plain sight, kicking a ball until the coach called him twice.

vr.q: Coach Diaz's instructions for the new play were ____: one simple drawing in plain pencil, three numbered steps, and a single short sentence telling each player what to do.
vr.e: The colon gives examples of how easy the instructions were to follow: one simple drawing, numbered steps, a short sentence for each player. Lucid means clear and easy to understand.

y.A: Colorful means full of bright colors, which a drawing might make you think of, but this one was in plain pencil; the examples show how simple the instructions were.
y.B: Elaborate means worked out in great detail, with many parts, but one simple drawing, three steps and a single short sentence for each player are the opposite of detailed.
y.D: Mysterious means hard to understand or explain, the opposite of a simple drawing and numbered steps.

vr.q: Dina was sure Axel had bumped her elbow out of ____, hoping to make her spill her batter and lose the baking contest, but he had only slipped on a puddle of spilled milk.
vr.e: The words after the comma say what Dina believed: that he wanted her to spill and lose. Malice is a wish to hurt someone on purpose.

y.A: Clumsiness is what really happened, a slip on spilled milk, but the blank is what Dina wrongly believed, and but tells you the truth was different from her belief.
y.B: Goodwill means wishing someone well, and nobody hopes to make a person spill and lose out of good wishes.
y.D: Suspicion is what Dina felt about Axel, but the blank names the reason she imagined for his bump: hoping to make her lose.

vr.q: Cyrus was the best hitter on his baseball team, but his fielding was only ____: he caught the easy balls and missed most of the hard ones.
vr.e: The colon shows fielding that was neither great nor terrible: the easy catches made, the hard ones missed. Mediocre means only average, nothing special.

y.A: Dreadful means terrible, but a player who catches every easy ball is not terrible; only says his fielding was ordinary.
y.B: Flawless means without a single mistake, but he missed most of the hard balls, and the sentence sets his fielding below his hitting.
y.D: Superior means better than others, the way his hitting was, but his fielding missed most of the hard balls, and only marks it as a step down.

vr.q: In class, Daria was so ____ that she went along with whatever her group decided, even when she had a better idea, but on the basketball court she shouted plays and took every big shot.
vr.e: The first half shows her giving in to her group even when she knew better, and but sets the bold basketball player against that. Meek means gentle and quick to give in to others.

y.A: Feisty means bold and full of fight, which fits Daria on the basketball court, but in class she went along with whatever her group decided.
y.C: Stubborn means refusing to give in, but Daria gave in even when she had a better idea.
y.D: Talented means very skilled, which may fit her basketball, but the blank describes how she acted in class, and being skilled is not why she went along with her group.

vr.q: At first, Chloe's guess that the oven was far too hot sounded silly, but it seemed much more ____ once Desmond noticed that the dial had been bumped up to 500 degrees.
vr.e: But turns away from sounded silly, and the bumped dial is evidence that her guess was right. Plausible means seeming likely to be true; believable.

y.A: Dubious means doubtful and hard to trust, which is how the guess sounded at first; but and the bumped dial tell you it became easier to believe, not harder.
y.C: Plentiful looks like plausible but means in large amounts, and a guess cannot become more plentiful.
y.D: Ridiculous means silly, which repeats how the guess sounded at first; but tells you the dial changed that.

vr.q: When fans from the other team began to tease him, Brady had to ____ his temper, taking a deep breath and walking away instead of yelling back.
vr.e: The words after the comma show what he did: breathed deeply and walked away instead of yelling. To restrain something is to hold it back or keep it under control.

y.A: Cultivate means help something grow, the way a farmer grows crops, and a temper that grew would end in yelling, the very thing Brady avoided.
y.B: Lose, in the phrase lose his temper, means getting angry and blowing up, but Brady breathed deeply and walked away instead of yelling.
y.D: Reveal means let others see, but walking away instead of yelling back kept his anger hidden, not shown.

vr.q: Strawberries cost so much in winter that Ava's family ____ buys them then; they get them maybe once or twice, for a birthday cake, and wait until summer for the rest.
vr.e: Once or twice all winter is not very often, and the high price explains why. Seldom means not very often; rarely.

y.A: Always means every time, but the family buys strawberries only once or twice all winter.
y.B: Eagerly means with excitement, which is how many people feel about strawberries, but the blank is about how often the family buys them, and the high price keeps that to once or twice.
y.C: Never means not even once, but the family does buy strawberries once or twice in winter, for a birthday cake.

vr.q: After the noisy school carnival, the empty park by the lake felt wonderfully ____: the water was smooth as glass, and the only sound was a duck paddling past.
vr.e: The colon gives examples of a peaceful place, smooth water and almost no sound, and wonderfully says the quiet felt good after all the noise. Serene means calm and peaceful.

y.A: Gloomy means dark and sad, and an empty park might sound lonely, but wonderfully tells you the quiet felt good, not sad.
y.B: Rowdy means noisy and wild, like the carnival, but the park after it was so quiet that a paddling duck was the only sound.
y.D: Stagnant describes water that does not flow and has gone stale, but smooth as glass here means calm, a duck was paddling through it, and nobody calls stale water wonderful.

vr.q: When Alma claimed she could make ice cream in ten minutes by shaking a small bag of milk and sugar inside a bigger bag of ice and salt, her brother Dev was ____ until he tasted the creamy result.
vr.e: Until he tasted it tells you his mind changed: before tasting, he did not believe her surprising claim. Skeptical means doubtful and not easily convinced.

y.A: Credible means believable, which describes a claim, not the person listening to one; it was Alma's claim that had to be believable, and Dev who doubted it.
y.B: Delighted is how he probably felt once he tasted the creamy result, but until tells you the blank is how he felt before that.
y.C: Gullible means quick to believe anything, but Dev needed to taste the proof before he believed her.

vr.q: Over winter break, with the fish staying at Ms. Abbott's house and the filter switched off, the water left in the class tank stopped moving and grew ____, cloudy and stale-smelling.
vr.e: The sentence describes the water: it stopped moving and turned cloudy and stale. Stagnant means not flowing or moving, and often stale.

y.A: Fragrant means sweet-smelling, but the water was stale-smelling.
y.B: Luminous means glowing with light, but the water had turned cloudy.
y.D: Turbulent means moving roughly, churning and splashing, but the water had stopped moving altogether.

vr.q: Anika's first draft of her history report was ____; it listed the dates of the battles but never explained why the war began or how it changed people's lives.
vr.e: The second half shows a report that stayed on the surface: dates, but no causes and no effects. Superficial means only on the surface, not deep or thorough.

y.A: Biased means unfairly favoring one side, but nothing says the report took sides; its problem is that it explained nothing.
y.B: Inaccurate means full of mistakes, but nothing says the dates were wrong; what the draft missed was any explanation.
y.D: Thorough means complete and leaving nothing out, but this draft left out why the war began and how it changed lives.

vr.q: Shelling three pounds of peas one pod at a time was so ____ that Camila started counting the pods out loud just to stay awake.
vr.e: So … that links cause and effect: the job was so long and boring that she had to work to stay awake. Tedious means long, slow and boring.

y.A: Messy means making a mess, which shelling peas can do, but a mess is not what makes someone count pods just to stay awake.
y.C: Tender, said of food, means soft and easy to chew, as fresh peas can be, but a job is not tender, and softness does not make anyone fight to stay awake.
y.D: Tidy means neat and orderly, and a careful job can be tidy, but neatness does not make anyone count pods just to stay awake.

vr.q: The softball game was called off when a ____ swept across the field, bending the trees and blowing the tarp right off the dugout roof.
vr.e: Bending trees and a tarp blown off a roof are examples of a very strong wind. A tempest is a violent, windy storm.

y.A: Drizzle is light, gentle rain, far too weak to bend trees or blow a tarp off a roof.
y.B: Fog is a cloud close to the ground that makes it hard to see, and it can stop a game, but fog comes with almost no wind.
y.C: Stampede is a herd of animals running wildly, and it could sweep across a field, but it does not bend trees or blow a tarp off a roof.

vr.q: Before the health inspector's visit, the cafeteria workers gave the kitchen a ____ cleaning, scrubbing every shelf, every oven rack, and even the bottoms of the tables.
vr.e: Every shelf, every oven rack and even the bottoms of the tables show that nothing was skipped. Thorough means complete and careful, leaving nothing out.

y.A: Careless means not paying attention, but workers who remembered even the bottoms of the tables were paying very close attention.
y.B: Hasty means hurried, and a visit coming soon might suggest a rush, but a hurried cleaning would not reach even the bottoms of the tables.
y.C: Partial means covering only part, but they scrubbed every shelf and every oven rack.

vr.q: The temperature in Ivan's bedroom stayed static all night, so he ____.
c: got a shock from his fuzzy blanket
kicked his blanket off at midnight
never added or kicked off a blanket
pulled on a second blanket at midnight
vr.e: Static means not changing. The room never got warmer or colder all night, so Ivan never added a blanket or kicked one off.

y.A: Got a shock from his fuzzy blanket mixes up the two meanings of static: a temperature that stays static is unchanging and has nothing to do with electric shocks.
y.B: Kicked his blanket off at midnight would follow if the room had warmed up, but static means the temperature did not change.
y.D: Pulled on a second blanket at midnight would follow if the room had cooled off, but static means the temperature stayed the same.

vr.q: Kira is striving to learn a hard piano piece for the family's New Year's party, so every evening she ____.
c: never even lifts the piano lid
already plays it without a slip
bangs the keys as hard as she can
vr.e: To strive is to work hard to reach a goal. Kira has not mastered the piece yet, so striving means practicing it again and again.

y.B: Never even lifts the piano lid is what someone who had given up would do, the opposite of striving.
y.C: Already plays it without a slip reads strive as succeed; she is still striving, working hard toward a goal she has not reached yet.
y.D: Bangs the keys as hard as she can mixes up strive with strike, which means hit; striving to learn a piece means working hard at it.

vr.q: Leah's vet said one brand of cat food was superior to all the others, so Leah ____.
c: fed her cat twice a day
bought that brand from then on
picked the brand with the biggest bag
vr.e: Superior means better or higher in quality. If the vet said one brand was better than all the others, Leah would buy that brand.

y.A: Fed her cat twice a day says nothing about which brand she chose, so it does not follow from what the vet said.
y.B: Never bought that brand again is what Leah would do if the vet had called the brand worse than the others, the opposite of superior.
y.D: Picked the brand with the biggest bag reads the super in superior as super-sized; superior means better, not bigger.
