vr.q: In the family's holiday mystery game, Kai was the chief suspect, so the other players ____.
c: asked him to solve the case
passed around a bowl of popcorn
vr.e: A suspect is the person believed to be guilty. Players who think Kai did it would keep a close eye on him.

y.A: Crossed him off their lists is what players do with someone they believe is innocent, the opposite of a suspect.
y.B: Asked him to solve the case mixes up the suspect with the detective, the player who solves the mystery.
y.D: Passed around a bowl of popcorn may happen at a game night, but it does not follow from Kai being the suspect.

vr.q: The way Isaac cared for his grumpy old cat was admirable, so his grandmother ____.
vr.e: Admirable means deserving praise. Care that is admirable earns praise, so his grandmother praised him.

y.B: Fed the cat its supper does not follow from Isaac's care being admirable; the word so asks what his grandmother did because of it.
y.C: Saluted him like a sailor mixes up admirable with admiral, a navy officer; admirable means worth praising.
y.D: Scolded him sharply for it is how someone reacts to shameful behavior, the opposite of admirable.

vr.q: Jun wanted to adorn his grandmother's birthday cake, so he ____.
c: told her how much he loved her
vr.e: To adorn something is to decorate it to make it prettier. Sugar flowers on top make a cake prettier.

y.A: Cut it into ten slices gets the cake ready to eat, but it does not make it prettier, which is what adorn means.
y.B: Scraped off all the frosting makes the cake plainer, the opposite of adorning it.
y.C: Told her how much he loved her mixes up adorn with adore, which means love; to adorn is to decorate.

vr.q: At family game night, Jasper's adversary in charades was Grandma, so he ____.
c: tried his best to beat her
asked her advice on every clue
vr.e: An adversary is an opponent, the one you play against. With Grandma on the other side in charades, Jasper tried his best to beat her.

y.B: Cheered for her every guess is what a teammate would do, but an adversary is the player you are trying to beat.
y.C: Asked her advice on every clue mixes up adversary with adviser, someone who gives advice; an adversary plays against you.
y.D: Wished her a happy anniversary mixes up adversary with anniversary, which only looks like it; an adversary is an opponent.

vr.q: Grandma allocated what was left of the pumpkin pie, so ____.
c: she ate all of it herself
it had a flaky golden crust
she found it behind the milk
vr.e: To allocate something is to give it out, setting a share aside for each person or use. Grandma gave out what was left of the pie, so each cousin got a slice.

y.A: She ate all of it herself keeps the pie instead of giving it out, the opposite of allocating it.
y.C: It had a flaky golden crust describes the pie, but the word so asks what allocating it led to.
y.D: She found it behind the milk reads the locate inside allocate as find; to allocate the pie is to give it out in shares.

vr.q: Because of Ian's blunder with the oven timer, the holiday cookies ____.
vr.e: A blunder is a careless mistake. Of the four endings, only burnt cookies show that something went wrong with the timer.

y.A: Were shaped like stars is about the cookie cutters, not the timer, and the words because of ask what Ian's mistake with the timer caused.
y.C: Were mixed in a blender mixes up blunder with blender, a word one letter away; a blunder is a careless mistake.
y.D: Came out perfectly golden is what careful work with the timer would bring, the opposite of a blunder.

vr.q: Kofi stirred the pot of hot cocoa briskly, so ____.
c: he poured it into red mugs
the powder mixed in right away
lumps of powder sat at the bottom
vr.e: Briskly means quickly and with energy. Fast, lively stirring mixes the cocoa powder in right away.

y.A: The cocoa turned icy cold reads briskly as chilly, like a brisk wind; stirring briskly means stirring fast, not making it cold.
y.B: He poured it into red mugs tells what came next, but the word so asks what stirring briskly did to the cocoa.
y.D: Lumps of powder sat at the bottom is what slow, lazy stirring would leave, the opposite of stirring briskly.

vr.q: Jonah's big sister is always candid, so when he asked about his new haircut, she ____.
c: asked him to vote for her
said it looked a little crooked
mocked it in front of his friends
vr.e: Candid means honest and direct, saying what you really think. A candid sister tells Jonah plainly that his haircut is a little crooked, without flattering him or making fun of him.

y.A: Asked him to vote for her mixes up candid with candidate, someone running in an election; candid means honest and direct.
y.C: Mocked it in front of his friends is teasing, not candor; being candid means telling him honestly what you think, not making fun of him.
y.D: Said only sweet, flattering things sugarcoats the truth, the opposite of being candid.

vr.q: At the end of puppy class, the trainer commended Lucas, so on the ride home he ____.
c: fell asleep in the back seat
sulked and stared out the window
vr.e: To commend is to praise. Being praised by the trainer would make Lucas smile all the way home.

y.B: Fell asleep in the back seat might happen after any long class, but it does not follow from being commended.
y.C: Mended the puppy's chewed leash reads the mend inside commend as repair; to commend someone is to praise him.
y.D: Sulked and stared out the window is how someone feels after being scolded, the opposite of being commended.

vr.q: At the holiday dinner, Grandma compelled every cousin to take a turn at the sink, so Lydia ____.
c: ate a second slice of pie
raced to wash the most plates
took her turn, though she grumbled
skipped her turn since it was optional
vr.e: To compel is to force. Grandma made every cousin take a turn, so Lydia took hers even though she did not want to.

y.A: Ate a second slice of pie does not follow from being made to take a turn at the sink; the word so asks what Grandma's rule made Lydia do.
y.B: Raced to wash the most plates mixes up compel with compete; Grandma made everyone take a turn, which is a rule, not a contest.
y.D: Skipped her turn since it was optional reads compel as invite; to compel is to force, so the turn was not optional.

vr.q: Down to his king and one pawn against Jin, Grandpa Lou conceded the game, so he ____.
vr.e: To concede a game is to give up and admit the other player has won. Having conceded, Grandpa Lou congratulated Jin.

y.A: Claimed the winner's prize reads concede as if it meant succeed or win; Grandpa gave up the game, so the prize was not his.
y.C: Kept on playing until bedtime is what someone who refused to give up would do, the opposite of conceding.
y.D: Bragged about his clever moves mixes up conceded with conceited, which means too proud; to concede is to give up.

vr.q: Jamal asked Grandpa to critique his model sailboat, so Grandpa ____.
c: named its strong and weak points
glanced at it and said it was fine
vr.e: To critique something is to judge it carefully, noting what is good and what could be better. That is what Grandpa did when he named the boat's strong and weak points.

y.A: Fixed the broken mast himself repairs the boat instead of judging it; a critique says what is good and what needs work.
y.B: Bought him a brand-new sailboat does not follow from being asked to judge the model; the word so asks what Grandpa did when asked for a critique.
y.D: Glanced at it and said it was fine is a quick look, the opposite of a careful critique that notes strengths and weaknesses.

vr.q: When Dad called the ball out of bounds in the backyard soccer game, Isla disputed his call and ____.
c: asked Dad what the score was
insisted the ball had stayed in
vr.e: To dispute something is to argue against it. Disputing Dad's call means saying it was wrong: the ball had stayed in.

y.A: Agreed it had rolled out accepts the call, the opposite of disputing it.
y.B: Passed out orange slices mixes up dispute with distribute, which means hand out; to dispute a call is to argue against it.
y.C: Asked Dad what the score was does not argue with the call at all, so it is not what disputing it means.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Aunt June's toast at last year's holiday dinner was so eloquent that this year the family ____.
c: begged her to give it again
set a timer to keep it short
asked someone else to give it
asked her to wear the same dress
vr.e: Eloquent means able to speak in a powerful, moving way. A toast that eloquent makes everyone want to hear another one.

y.B: Set a timer to keep it short reads eloquent as long-winded; an eloquent speaker is powerful and moving, and nobody wants to cut that short.
y.C: Asked someone else to give it is what a family does after a muddled toast, the opposite of an eloquent one.
y.D: Asked her to wear the same dress mixes up eloquent with elegant, which describes how someone looks; eloquent is about how someone speaks.

vr.q: Ines's first try at a gingerbread house was a fiasco, so she ____.
c: gave up and bought one instead
showed it off to the neighbors
threw a party with music and dancing
vr.e: A fiasco is a complete and embarrassing failure. After a try that went that badly, Ines gave up and bought one.

y.A: Used red and green icing describes the house, but the word so asks what she did because the try went so badly.
y.C: Showed it off to the neighbors is what a proud success would bring, the opposite of a fiasco.
y.D: Threw a party with music and dancing mixes up fiasco with fiesta, a party; a fiasco is a complete failure.

vr.q: Liam's family rule says that whoever skips a chore forfeits dessert, so after Liam skipped his on Sunday, he ____.
c: got to choose the pie flavor
saved his slice of pie for Monday
vr.e: To forfeit something is to lose it as a penalty. Under the rule, skipping his chore cost Liam his dessert.

y.B: Forgot what his chore was mixes up forfeit with forget; to forfeit dessert is to lose it as a penalty.
y.C: Got to choose the pie flavor is a reward, the opposite of forfeiting dessert.
y.D: Saved his slice of pie for Monday reads forfeit as put off; to forfeit dessert is to lose it, so there was no slice left to save.

vr.q: The tiny ornament Lucy bought at the holiday market was so frail that she ____.
c: wrapped it in her soft scarf
said it looked dull and pale
paid for it with a ten-dollar bill
vr.e: Frail means weak and easily broken. An ornament that breaks easily needs to be wrapped in something soft.

y.A: Tossed it in her backpack is how you carry something sturdy, the opposite of frail.
y.C: Said it looked dull and pale mixes up frail with pale, which rhymes with it; frail means easily broken.
y.D: Paid for it with a ten-dollar bill tells how she bought it, which does not follow from the ornament being frail.

vr.q: Because her packing for the holiday trip was hasty, Josie ____.
c: did not pack a single thing
vr.e: Hasty means done too quickly, without enough care. Packing in a hurry is how a toothbrush gets left behind.

y.A: Packed the tastiest snacks mixes up hasty with tasty, which only rhymes with it; hasty means hurried.
y.B: Remembered every last thing is what slow, careful packing would bring, the opposite of hasty.
y.D: Did not pack a single thing goes too far; hasty packing is still packing, only done in a hurry, so something gets forgotten, not everything.

vr.q: Lulu, the goat next door, is infamous on our street, so whenever she slips out of her pen, the neighbors ____.
c: know she is three years old
have no idea whose goat she is
come out to cheer and take pictures
vr.e: Infamous means well known for something bad. Neighbors who know the goat's bad reputation rush to protect their gardens when she gets out.

y.B: Know she is three years old is a fact about the goat, but it does not follow from her being infamous, and the word so asks what the neighbors do.
y.C: Have no idea whose goat she is takes the in at the start of infamous to mean not, as if the word meant unknown; infamous means well known for something bad.
y.D: Come out to cheer and take pictures is how people greet someone famous for something good, but infamous means famous for something bad.

vr.q: Because Grandma Iris is lenient about bedtime when the cousins visit for the holidays, they ____.
c: never go to bed at all
are in bed by eight sharp
each get five dollars to spend
vr.e: Lenient means not strict. A grandmother who is lenient about bedtime lets the cousins stay up late, though they still go to bed.

y.A: Never go to bed at all goes too far; lenient means not strict, so bedtime comes later, not that there is no bedtime.
y.B: Are in bed by eight sharp is what a strict bedtime looks like, the opposite of lenient.
y.D: Each get five dollars to spend reads lenient as generous with money; lenient means not strict about rules.

vr.q: After the holiday dinner, the guests lingered at the table, so Leo ____.
c: never washed the dishes at all
found the platters bare in minutes
vr.e: To linger is to stay longer than expected. With the guests still at the table, the dishes had to wait, so Leo washed them late.

y.A: Had the dishes done early would follow if the guests had hurried off, the opposite of lingering.
y.C: Never washed the dishes at all reads linger as stay forever; guests who linger stay longer than expected, but they do leave, so the dishes just got done late.
y.D: Found the platters bare in minutes reads linger as lunge, a quick grab forward; lingering guests take their time.

vr.q: Aunt Lily's recipe card for her holiday stuffing was so lucid that Joel ____.
c: baked a pie for dessert too
made it right on the first try
won the family raffle that night
called her five times with questions
vr.e: Lucid means clear and easy to understand. A card that clear let Joel make the stuffing right the first time.

y.A: Baked a pie for dessert too has nothing to do with how clear the card was, so it cannot be what the clear card led to.
y.C: Won the family raffle that night mixes up lucid with lucky; lucid means clear, and a clear recipe has nothing to do with a raffle.
y.D: Called her five times with questions is what a confusing card would cause, the opposite of a lucid one.

vr.q: In the family's holiday play, Kwame's character was full of malice: on stage he ____.
c: tried to ruin the town feast
vr.e: Malice is a wish to hurt someone on purpose. A character full of malice would try to spoil things for others, like the town feast.

y.A: Wore a tall black hat describes his costume, but the colon promises something that shows his malice.
y.C: Brought gifts to every family is what a kind character would do, the opposite of one full of malice.
y.D: Played silly pranks for laughs reads malice as harmless mischief; malice is a wish to hurt, and it is not done for laughs.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The town's holiday fireworks show was mediocre this year, so Jesse ____.
c: called it the worst show ever
vr.e: Mediocre means only average, neither very good nor very bad. A mediocre show earns a shrug and a word like okay.

y.B: Raved about it for weeks is what an amazing show would get, but mediocre means only average.
y.C: Watched it from the rooftop tells where he watched it, which does not follow from how good the show was.
y.D: Called it the worst show ever goes too far; mediocre means so-so, not terrible.

vr.q: Ivy's new kitten is meek, so when the old tomcat hissed at her, she ____.
c: licked her fur sleek and shiny
hissed back and stood her ground
vr.e: Meek means gentle, timid, and quick to give in. A meek kitten backs away from a fight instead of standing up to it.

y.B: Purred loudly in Ivy's lap does not answer the hiss; the word when asks what the kitten did right after the tomcat hissed.
y.C: Licked her fur sleek and shiny mixes up meek with sleek, which describes smooth fur; meek means timid and quick to give in.
y.D: Hissed back and stood her ground is what a bold kitten would do, the opposite of meek.

vr.q: At the holiday craft fair, the judges found merit in Lena's bird feeder, so they ____.
c: laughed at how funny it looked
vr.e: Merit is the quality of deserving praise, a real strength. Judges who found merit in the bird feeder rewarded it with a ribbon.

y.A: Told her to start over is what judges say when they find nothing good, the opposite of finding merit.
y.C: Measured how tall it was could happen at any judging, but it does not follow from finding merit; the word so asks what the judges did because they found it good.
y.D: Laughed at how funny it looked mixes up merit with merry, which means jolly; merit means good qualities that deserve praise.

vr.q: Grandpa Joe stayed neutral in the family's vote between the beach and the mountains, so he ____.
c: did not vote for either place
begged everyone to pick the beach
said the mountains felt more natural
vr.e: Neutral means not taking either side. Staying neutral, Grandpa Joe did not vote for the beach or the mountains.

y.A: Booked the train tickets does not follow from staying neutral; the word so asks what not taking a side meant for his vote.
y.C: Begged everyone to pick the beach takes a side, the opposite of staying neutral.
y.D: Said the mountains felt more natural mixes up neutral with natural and picks a side; staying neutral means not taking either side.

vr.q: Jade's guess that the scratching in the attic was a squirrel seemed plausible, so Dad ____.
c: said she had to be right
climbed up to look for one
said it could not possibly be
vr.e: Plausible means likely to be true, believable, though not certain. A guess that seems likely is worth checking, so Dad climbed up to look.

y.A: Said she had to be right goes too far; plausible means likely, not certain, which is why Dad went up to check.
y.C: Clapped for her clever guess reads the plaus in plausible as applause; a plausible guess seems likely to be true, which is a reason to check it.
y.D: Said it could not possibly be treats the guess as unbelievable, the opposite of plausible.

vr.q: Lars loved his bedroom, but he relinquished it to his new baby sister and ____.
c: moved his things into the den
kept his bed right where it was
got a new bike for his birthday
vr.e: To relinquish something is to give it up, often when you would rather not. Lars gave up the room he loved and moved his things into the den.

y.A: Shared the room with her reads relinquish as share; to relinquish the room is to give it up completely.
y.C: Kept his bed right where it was means he held on to the room, the opposite of relinquishing it.
y.D: Got a new bike for his birthday has nothing to do with giving up the room, so it does not continue the sentence.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: All through the holiday concert, Keiko restrained her giggles, so ____.
c: nobody heard a peep from her
she slept through the second half
the whole row turned to stare at her
vr.e: To restrain something is to hold it back. Keiko held back her giggles the whole time, so nobody heard a sound from her.

y.A: The concert ended at eight would be true however Keiko behaved, so it does not follow from her holding back her giggles.
y.C: She slept through the second half reads the rest inside restrain as sleep; to restrain her giggles is to hold them back.
y.D: The whole row turned to stare at her is what would happen if she let her giggles out, the opposite of restraining them.

vr.q: After a hike in the woods, Jake scrutinized his dog's fur, so he ____.
c: missed the tick behind its ear
scrubbed it with soap and water
spotted a tiny tick behind its ear
vr.e: To scrutinize is to examine very closely. Looking that carefully at the fur is how Jake found such a tiny tick.

y.A: Gave it a crunchy treat does not follow from looking closely at its fur; the word so asks what the close look turned up.
y.B: Missed the tick behind its ear is what a quick glance would do, the opposite of scrutinizing.
y.C: Scrubbed it with soap and water reads scrutinize as scrub, which only starts the same way; to scrutinize is to examine closely.

vr.q: Kaito seldom sees his cousins from Osaka, so when they visited for New Year's, he ____.
c: made a snowman in the yard
noticed how much they had grown
met them for the very first time
treated it like any other weekend
vr.e: Seldom means rarely, not very often. Seeing his cousins so rarely, Kaito noticed how much they had changed since last time.

y.A: Made a snowman in the yard could happen on any winter day, but it does not follow from how rarely he sees his cousins.
y.C: Met them for the very first time reads seldom as never; seldom means rarely, so he had seen them before.
y.D: Treated it like any other weekend is how it feels to see someone often, the opposite of seldom.

vr.q: Grandma Lin is usually serene in the kitchen, but with a houseful of holiday guests this year she ____.
c: snapped at anyone near the stove
smiled and chatted with every guest
hummed softly as she basted the turkey
vr.e: Serene means calm and peaceful. But says this year was different: instead of staying calm, Grandma Lin got frazzled and snapped at people.

y.A: Wore her red holiday sweater describes her clothes, while the word but asks for a change from being serene.
y.C: Smiled and chatted with every guest reads serene as serious and looks for a change to friendly; serene means calm, and a calm cook can smile and chat, so that is no change.
y.D: Hummed softly as she basted the turkey is serene all over again, and the word but says this year was different.

vr.q: Ike's thank-you to Aunt Kim for the knitted sweater was sincere; he ____.
c: wrote it on fancy cream paper
never smiled once as he said it
secretly planned to give it away
vr.e: Sincere means honest and meant from the heart. Ike's thanks were sincere because he really did love the sweater.

y.A: Wrote it on fancy cream paper reads sincere as formal; fancy paper does not make thanks sincere, meaning them does.
y.C: Never smiled once as he said it reads sincere as serious or solemn; sincere means meaning what you say, and you can mean it with a smile.
y.D: Secretly planned to give it away means his thanks were fake, the opposite of sincere.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Jude was skeptical when his little sister said their cat could open the fridge, so he ____.
c: warned Mom to lock the fridge
asked her to show him the trick
vr.e: Skeptical means doubtful, not ready to believe something. A skeptical brother asks to see it for himself.

y.A: Gave the cat a treat does not follow from doubting the story; the word so asks what his doubt made him do.
y.B: Scolded her for telling lies goes too far; skeptical means doubtful, not sure the story is false.
y.C: Warned Mom to lock the fridge means he believed the story, the opposite of being skeptical.

vr.q: The water in Lola's turtle tank had grown stagnant, so she ____.
c: said it was as fresh as spring water
vr.e: Stagnant water is still and stale because it has not moved or been changed. The fix is to change it for fresh water.

y.A: Named the turtle Kiwi does not follow from the water going stale; the word so asks what she did about the water.
y.B: Chipped ice off the top reads stagnant as frozen; stagnant water is still and stale, not ice.
y.D: Said it was as fresh as spring water is the opposite of stagnant, which means still and stale.

vr.q: Uncle Kip's cleaning before the holiday guests arrived was superficial, so ____.
c: dust still hid under the couch
he set out fake plastic flowers
vr.e: Superficial means only on the surface, not deep or thorough. A surface-only cleaning wipes what shows and leaves dust where nobody looked.

y.A: Every corner sparkled is what a deep, thorough cleaning would bring, the opposite of superficial; the super in superficial does not mean super good.
y.B: Not one thing got cleaned goes too far; a superficial cleaning does clean the surface, it just misses what lies underneath.
y.D: He set out fake plastic flowers mixes up superficial with artificial, which means fake; superficial means only on the surface.

vr.q: Untangling the strings of holiday lights was so tedious that Kayla ____.
c: yawned and put on some music
vr.e: Tedious means long, slow, and boring. A job that tedious makes you yawn and look for something to pass the time.

y.A: Called the lights ugly mixes up tedious with hideous, which sounds a lot like it; tedious means long and boring.
y.B: Finished it in a minute describes a quick, easy job, the opposite of a tedious one.
y.C: Plugged them in right away does not follow from a slow, boring job; the words so tedious that ask what the dullness made her do.

vr.q: A tempest swept through on the night before Thanksgiving, so in the morning Luis ____.
c: found ants all over the porch
found branches all over the yard
found the yard just as he left it
vr.e: A tempest is a violent, windy storm. Winds that strong break branches and scatter them across a yard.

y.A: Set the table for twelve is part of getting ready for Thanksgiving, but the word so asks what the storm left behind.
y.B: Found ants all over the porch reads the pest inside tempest as bugs; a tempest is a violent storm.
y.D: Found the yard just as he left it is what a calm night would bring, the opposite of a tempest.

vr.q: Liv gave her shaggy dog a thorough brushing, so ____.
c: the dog yelped and ran off
burrs still hid in its tail
not a single tangle was left
vr.e: Thorough means complete and careful, leaving nothing out. A thorough brushing gets out every tangle.

y.A: It was time for dinner does not follow from the brushing; the word so asks what a thorough brushing left behind.
y.B: The dog yelped and ran off reads thorough as rough, a word hiding inside it; thorough means careful and complete, not rough.
y.C: Burrs still hid in its tail is what a quick, careless brushing would leave, the opposite of thorough.

vr.q: Grandma Lupe's old cast-iron pan is versatile: she ____.
c: got it as a wedding gift
fries, bakes, and roasts in it
vr.e: Versatile means able to be used in many different ways. A pan that fries, bakes, and roasts is versatile.

y.A: Writes poems about it reads the verse inside versatile as poetry; versatile means able to be used in many ways.
y.B: Uses it only for eggs keeps the pan to one job, the opposite of versatile.
y.C: Got it as a wedding gift tells where the pan came from, but the colon promises something that shows how many ways she uses it.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: ADORN most nearly means:
vr.e: To adorn something is to decorate it by adding pretty things to it: we adorned the classroom door with paper snowflakes.

y.A: Admire starts like adorn and also goes with beautiful things, but to admire something is to look at it and like it, while to adorn it is to add the decorations yourself.
y.C: Polish also makes a thing look nicer, which is the trap, but polishing means rubbing it until it shines; adorning means adding something pretty, like ribbons or lights.
y.D: Strip is the opposite: to strip a wall is to take everything off it, and to adorn it is to put decorations on.

vr.q: MALICE most nearly means:
vr.e: Malice is the wish to hurt someone on purpose, the same thing as spite: he tore up her drawing out of pure malice.

y.A: Envy is a bad feeling too, but it means wanting what someone else has; malice means wanting to hurt them.
y.B: Kindness is the opposite: a kind person wants good things for others, and a person full of malice wants them hurt.
y.C: Mischief is naughty fun, like hiding your brother's shoes as a joke; malice is meant to hurt, which makes it much meaner.

vr.q: LINGER most nearly means:
vr.e: To linger is to stay somewhere longer than you need to, slow to leave: we lingered at the beach until the sun went down.

y.A: Chat means to talk in a friendly way; people often chat while they linger, but to linger is to stay on, slow to leave.
y.B: Hurry is the opposite: someone who lingers is slow to leave, and someone who hurries rushes off.
y.C: Lunge sounds a little like linger, but to lunge is to jump forward suddenly, the way a dog lunges at a ball.

vr.q: ALLOCATE most nearly means:
vr.e: To allocate is to decide how much of something each person or job gets, and hand it out: the teacher allocated two markers to each table.

y.B: Calculate means to work out an answer with math; you might calculate how big each share should be, but to allocate is to hand the shares out.
y.C: Collect goes the other way: collecting gathers things in from everyone, while allocating hands them out, a share to each.
y.D: Spend means to pay money out for things; to allocate is to decide ahead of time how much each person or job will get.

vr.q: FORFEIT most nearly means:
vr.e: To forfeit is to lose something or give it up as a penalty: a team that does not show up for a game forfeits it.

y.A: Cheat means to break the rules to get ahead; a team caught cheating may have to forfeit, but forfeiting is the losing that comes after.
y.B: Forget starts with the same sound as forfeit, which is the trap; to forget is to not remember, while to forfeit is to lose something as a penalty.
y.D: Postpone means to put a game off until another day; a forfeited game is not played later, it is simply lost.

vr.q: COMPEL most nearly means:
vr.e: To compel is to force someone to do something, whether they want to or not: the pouring rain compelled us to move the picnic indoors.

y.A: Allow means to let someone do something if they choose; compel means to make them do it, with no choice.
y.B: Compete looks almost like compel, but it means to try to win against others, as in a race.
y.D: Invite means to ask someone to come, and they can say no; when you compel someone, they cannot say no.

vr.q: RESTRAIN most nearly means:
vr.e: To restrain is to hold someone or something back and keep it under control: Dad restrained the puppy on its leash when a squirrel ran past.

y.B: Punish means to make someone suffer for doing wrong; restraining only holds someone back, and nobody has to have done anything wrong.
y.C: Release is the opposite: you release a dog by letting go of its leash, and you restrain it by holding on.
y.D: Strain is hiding inside restrain, which is the trap; to strain is to pull very hard, or to pour something through a sieve, not to hold something back.

vr.q: STAGNANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Stagnant water is still: it does not flow, so it just sits in one place and often turns green and smelly, like an old puddle in the shade.

y.A: Flowing is the opposite: a flowing river keeps moving, and stagnant water just sits.
y.B: Frozen is tempting because a frozen pond does not ripple or flow either, but frozen means turned to ice; stagnant water is liquid water that just lies in one place.
y.C: Shallow means not deep, and a stagnant puddle may be shallow, but stagnant is about water that does not move, however deep it is.

vr.q: MEEK most nearly means:
vr.e: A meek person is quiet and gentle and goes along with what others want instead of arguing: the meek boy let everyone else choose a seat first and took the one left over.

y.A: Bold is the opposite: a bold person speaks up and takes charge, while a meek one stays quiet and goes along.
y.C: Sleek rhymes with meek, but it means smooth and shiny, like a seal's wet fur.
y.D: Tiny comes from picturing a meek little mouse, but meek describes how someone acts, quiet and gentle, not how big they are; a huge dog can be meek.

vr.q: FRAIL most nearly means:
vr.e: Frail means weak and easily hurt or broken: the baby bird was so frail it could barely lift its head.

y.A: Afraid sounds a little like frail, but it means scared; a frail person is weak and may not feel afraid at all.
y.B: Elderly means old; frail people are often elderly, which is the trap, but frail means weak and easily hurt, and a young child who has been very sick can be frail too.
y.C: Pale means having little color in your face; a frail person may look pale, but frail means weak, not pale.

vr.q: SERENE most nearly means:
vr.e: Serene means calm and peaceful: the lake was serene at sunrise, without a single ripple.

y.B: Lonely means sad from being alone; a serene beach may have nobody on it, but serene is about feeling peaceful, not sad.
y.C: Scenic sounds like serene and is used about the same lakes and mountains, but scenic means pretty to look at, not calm.
y.D: Serious starts like serene, but it means thoughtful and not joking; a serious face can be worried or stern, not peaceful.

vr.q: LUCID most nearly means:
vr.e: Lucid means clear and easy to understand: her lucid directions got us to the party without one wrong turn.

y.A: Brief means short; a lucid explanation can be long, as long as it is easy to follow.
y.C: Lucky starts with the same letters, which is the trap, but lucky means having good things happen by chance.
y.D: Polite means having good manners; a lucid answer is one that is easy to understand, whether it is polite or not.

vr.q: FIASCO most nearly means:
vr.e: A fiasco is a complete and embarrassing failure: the school play was a fiasco when the curtain fell down and the lights went out.

y.A: Accident is something bad that happens by chance, like a spill; a fiasco is a whole plan or event that goes completely wrong.
y.C: Fiesta sounds like fiasco, which is the trap; a fiesta is a party or festival, the kind of event you hope will not turn into a fiasco.
y.D: Prank is a trick played as a joke, on purpose; a fiasco can be funny to watch, but it is a real failure that nobody wanted.

vr.q: TEMPEST most nearly means:
vr.e: A tempest is a violent storm with strong winds: the tempest tore branches off the trees and rattled every window.

y.A: Breeze is a wind too, but a gentle one; a tempest is a wild, violent storm.
y.B: Drought is weather of a different kind, a long time with little or no rain; a tempest brings fierce wind and often rain.
y.D: Temperature starts with the same sounds as tempest and is a weather word too, which is the trap; temperature is how hot or cold it is.

vr.q: ADVERSARY most nearly means:
vr.e: An adversary is the person or team you are playing or fighting against: in the chess final, her adversary was last year's champion.

y.A: Anniversary ends with the same sounds as adversary, which is the trap; an anniversary is the date each year when something happened, like a wedding.
y.C: Referee is in the game too, but a referee keeps it fair and is on nobody's side; an adversary is the one you are playing against.
y.D: Teammate is the opposite: a teammate is on your side, and an adversary is on the other.

vr.q: HASTILY most nearly means:
vr.e: Hastily means quickly and in a rush, often too fast to be careful: he dressed so hastily that his shirt was inside out.

y.A: Busily means in a busy way, with lots to do; you can work busily all day at a calm, steady pace, but hastily means rushing, often too fast to be careful.
y.B: Carefully is the opposite: work done hastily is rushed, and work done carefully takes its time to get things right.
y.C: Happily starts and ends like hastily, which is the trap; it tells how someone feels, not how fast they move.

vr.q: CAUTIOUSLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Cautiously means carefully, watching out for danger: the deer stepped cautiously out of the woods, its ears turning at every sound.

y.A: Boldly is the opposite: a bold person charges ahead without worrying, while someone acting cautiously checks for danger first.
y.C: Curiously starts and ends like cautiously, which is the trap; it means wanting to find something out, and a curious cat is not always a careful one.
y.D: Quietly means without much noise; a cautious person is often quiet too, but cautiously means watching out for danger, and you can do that while talking.

vr.q: Although the outlaw Wade Rourke was almost never seen by anyone, he was ____ across the whole territory, and every family had heard about the stagecoaches he had robbed.
vr.e: Although signals a turn: he was hardly ever seen, yet everyone knew of him, for robbing stagecoaches. Infamous means well known for something bad. The in- does not mean “not” here: an infamous outlaw is famous, for the wrong reasons.

y.A: Beloved means dearly loved, but nobody loves a man for robbing stagecoaches; the stories made him well known, not loved.
y.C: Invisible just repeats “almost never seen” instead of turning against it, as although requires, and the stories prove that people knew all about him.
y.D: Obscure means hardly known at all, which is what you pick if you read infamous as “not famous”; it agrees with “almost never seen” and ignores the stories every family had heard.

vr.q: Even after the rain began, Ulysses was not about to ____ the front-row seat he had waited two hours to get; he simply pulled up his hood and stayed.
vr.e: Not about to means he refused to. He pulled up his hood and stayed, so what he refused to do was give the seat up. Relinquish means to give up or let go of something.

y.A: Guard means to protect and keep, which is just what he did; with not in front of it, the sentence would say he was ready to leave, but he pulled up his hood and stayed.
y.B: Occupy means to sit in or fill a place, which he kept doing; read with not, it would mean he was giving the seat away, the reverse of staying under his hood.
y.D: Reserve means to save a place ahead of time, but he already had the seat; the question was whether he would give it up once the rain began.

vr.q: Although Victor often stumbles over his words at the dinner table, on the debate stage he is ____, speaking smoothly and persuasively.
vr.e: Although sets up a turn: at dinner he stumbles, but on stage he speaks smoothly and persuasively. Eloquent means able to speak well and convincingly.

y.A: Awkward fits stumbling over his words at dinner, but although says the debate stage is different.
y.C: Silent cannot be right when the same sentence says he is speaking, smoothly and persuasively.
y.D: Talkative means talking a lot, not talking well, and a person can chatter all day and still stumble; it misses the turn from stumbling to speaking smoothly.

vr.q: In one old fairy tale, a princess pricks her finger on a spindle and falls into a ____ that lasts a hundred years, until a prince's kiss wakes her.
vr.e: The clue is wakes: you wake from sleep, so the princess fell into a long, deep sleep. Slumber means sleep.

y.A: Fever is the body running hot when you are ill; nothing says she is sick, and you do not wake from a fever with a kiss.
y.B: Panic is sudden, wild fear, which keeps a person wide awake; it is not something you wake from a hundred years later.
y.C: Puddle takes falls into literally, as if she tripped into water, but a puddle does not last a hundred years, and no kiss wakes you from one.

vr.q: Because deer kept eating the lettuce in his garden, Yusuf's grandfather built a tall fence to ____ them.
vr.e: Because tells you the fence answers a problem: deer eating the lettuce. A fence built for that keeps them away. Deter means to discourage or stop someone from doing something.

y.A: Befriend means to make friends with, but the deer were the problem eating his lettuce, and a tall fence keeps animals away, not close.
y.C: Feed would give the deer food, but they were already eating his lettuce, and that was the problem the fence was built to solve.
y.D: Tame means to make a wild animal gentle and used to people, and a fence does nothing of the kind; it only keeps animals out.

vr.q: Since the ice cream truck had already turned the corner, Uma's shouting and waving were ____; the truck kept going.
vr.e: Since gives the reason: the truck was already around the corner, so no one in it could see or hear her. Futile means useless, having no chance of success.

y.B: Polite is about manners, and the truck being gone says nothing about her manners; it only says whether the shouting could work.
y.C: Rude means impolite, and nothing about a truck turning the corner makes shouting rude; since gives the reason the shouting could not work.
y.D: Silent contradicts the sentence itself: shouting is the opposite of silent.

vr.q: The sailors knew they were in great ____: the storm had cracked the mast, water was pouring in, and the nearest harbor was a day away.
vr.e: The colon lists what was happening: a cracked mast, water pouring in, help a day away. Peril means serious danger.

y.A: Demand, in “in great demand,” means wanted by many people, but the colon lists dangers at sea, not people who want something.
y.C: Shape, in “in great shape,” means in good condition, but a ship with a cracked mast is in very bad condition.
y.D: Spirits, in “in great spirits,” means cheerful, but the colon lists dangers, and none of them would cheer a sailor.

vr.q: In the 1800s, many Americans worked for years to ____ slavery, and they finally got their wish in 1865, when the Thirteenth Amendment ended it throughout the United States.
vr.e: The second half says what they wanted: they got their wish when slavery was ended. Abolish means to end something completely, by law.

y.B: Debate means to argue about something, and arguing was not their wish; their wish came true only when the amendment ended slavery.
y.C: Record means to write something down, and nobody works for years just to write slavery down; their wish was for it to end.
y.D: Reform means to change something to make it better, but these people wanted slavery gone, and their wish came true when it was ended.

vr.q: Wesley's grandpa and his old dog take walks that are hardly ____ these days; the two of them stop to rest at every bench along the way.
vr.e: Hardly means almost not. Stopping to rest at every bench makes the walks slow, so they are hardly brisk. Brisk means quick and full of energy.

y.B: Leisurely means slow and relaxed, which is exactly what the walks are; it would fit without hardly, but hardly makes the blank what the walks are not.
y.C: Noisy has nothing to do with resting at benches; the part after the semicolon tells you how fast they go, not how loud they are.
y.D: Restful fits resting at every bench, but hardly says the walks are not the blank, so picking it means reading the sentence as if hardly were not there.

vr.q: Vaughn felt certain his paper airplane would fly the farthest, and he made a ____ with Zoe: the loser would give the winner a week of desserts.
vr.e: The colon explains the blank: each one puts something at stake, and the loser pays the winner. A wager is a bet.

y.A: Apology means saying sorry, but nothing has gone wrong yet; Vaughn expects to win.
y.B: Guess fits feeling certain who would win, but a guess has no prize for the winner and no cost for the loser, and the colon describes both.
y.C: Toast, when you make one, means raising a glass and saying something kind about someone; the colon describes a prize for the winner instead.

vr.q: A northern mockingbird can ____ the songs of many other birds, and some even copy the sounds of car alarms and squeaky wheels.
vr.e: Even copy tells you the blank is already a kind of copying, and car alarms and squeaky wheels are surprising examples of what it copies. Mimic means to imitate.

y.A: Hush means to make something quiet, and a bird that copies songs adds them rather than quieting them.
y.B: Ignore means to pay no attention, but even copy needs a blank that is already a kind of copying.
y.C: Interrupt means to break in while someone else is singing or talking; even copy tells you the bird repeats the songs instead.

vr.q: Unlike the green valley below it, the top of the old volcano was ____: bare black rock where not a single plant could grow.
vr.e: Unlike sets the top against the green valley, and the colon describes it: bare rock where nothing grows. Barren means unable to grow plants.

y.B: Fertile means rich enough to grow plenty of plants, which describes the green valley, not the top that unlike sets against it.
y.C: Snowy would make the top white, but the colon says bare black rock.
y.D: Tropical means hot and full of lush plants, and the colon says not a single plant could grow there.

vr.q: When Zeke first worked the handle of the old pump, only a trickle came out, but a moment later a ____ of water burst from the spout and soaked his shoes.
vr.e: But signals a change from only a trickle, and water that bursts out and soaks his shoes is a rush. A torrent is a fast, powerful flood of water.

y.A: Mist is a spray of tiny drops floating in the air, far too light to burst from a spout and soak his shoes.
y.B: Puddle is water lying still on the ground; it might be what the water made afterward, but a puddle does not burst out of a spout.
y.C: Ripple is a small wave moving across still water, like the rings a pebble makes in a pond; it does not burst from a spout and soak anyone's shoes.

vr.q: Vikram knew that one more late assignment could ____ his place on the honor roll, so he finished his science project a day early.
vr.e: So links the two halves: he worked ahead because a late assignment could cost him his place. Jeopardize means to put something in danger.

y.A: Delay means to put off until later, but he already had his place; the worry was losing it, not getting it later.
y.B: Earn means to get something by working for it, but a late assignment is not good work; he hurried because lateness could cost him his place.
y.C: Improve means to make better, but turning work in late lowers a grade, which is why he finished early.

vr.q: Unlike the fine, powdery sand on the beach, the sand Zion scooped from the creek bed was ____, full of gritty bits as big as grains of rice.
vr.e: Unlike sets the creek sand against fine, powdery sand, and gritty bits as big as rice finish the picture. Coarse means rough and made of large grains.

y.A: Brown is the color of the sand, but unlike sets it against fine, powdery sand, so the blank is about how big and gritty the grains were.
y.C: Silky means smooth and soft, like the fine, powdery beach sand that unlike sets this sand against.
y.D: Sticky means gluey, clinging to things; the sentence is about how big and gritty the grains are, not whether they cling.

vr.q: Bats fly as well as many birds do, but unlike birds, bats ____.
vr.e: Unlike birds asks for something bats do and birds do not. Bats are mammals, and a bat mother nurses her babies with milk from her own body, as every mammal mother does; birds do not nurse their chicks.

y.A: Lay eggs in a nest is what birds do, so it cannot be how bats are unlike birds; bats give birth to live babies.
y.C: Can fly through the air is true of bats, but birds fly too, so it is not a difference, and unlike asks for one.
y.D: Have feathers on their wings describes birds; a bat's wings are thin skin, so this is neither true of bats nor a difference.

vr.q: Since arguing with the referee was futile, the coach ____.
c: sat down and let the game go on
made the referee change the call
vr.e: Since gives the reason: arguing could not change anything. Futile means useless, so a sensible coach stops arguing and lets the game go on.

y.A: Won the argument easily cannot follow from futile, which means arguing had no chance of working.
y.B: Argued even louder than before keeps doing the useless thing; futile gives a reason to stop, not to shout more.
y.D: Made the referee change the call means the arguing worked, the opposite of futile.

vr.q: From across the gallery, the painting looked as smooth as a photograph, but up close it ____.
c: showed a lighthouse by the sea
was made of thousands of tiny dots
looked just as real as a photograph
vr.e: But turns from how the painting looked far away to how it looked up close, so the ending must be different from smooth. Thousands of tiny dots are the opposite of a smooth photograph.

y.A: Hung in a golden frame is true from any distance, so it is not what changed when you came close.
y.B: Showed a lighthouse by the sea tells what the painting is of, which is the same from across the room and up close.
y.D: Looked just as real as a photograph repeats the first half, while the word but promises that something changed up close.

vr.q: The new puppy had hardly ever been away from its mother; on its first night alone in Yara's house, it ____.
c: acted as though nothing had changed
vr.e: Hardly ever means almost never: the puppy was used to its mother always being there, so a first night without her would upset it. Whimpering all night follows.

y.B: Was used to sleeping alone reads hardly ever as if it meant often; a puppy almost never away from its mother has never slept alone.
y.C: Slept soundly from the start is how a puppy used to being alone might act, but this one had hardly ever left its mother.
y.D: Acted as though nothing had changed ignores hardly ever; for this puppy, a night without its mother was a very big change.

vr.q: Because the hillside behind the farm was barren, Yael's goats ____.
c: grazed on thick grass all day
ate hay carried up from the barn
vr.e: Because tells you the goats' meals follow from the hillside being barren, which means nothing grows there. With no grass to eat, they ate hay carried up from the barn.

y.A: Napped under tall trees needs trees, and nothing grows on a barren hillside.
y.B: Nibbled the hillside clover needs plants growing on the hillside, and a barren hillside grows nothing.
y.C: Grazed on thick grass all day is the opposite of barren, which means nothing grows.

vr.q: BENEVOLENT most nearly means:
vr.e: Bene means “good,” and a benevolent neighbor wishes other people well, so kind and generous is the match; being strict about rules is a different quality entirely.

y.A: Strict about rules means insisting that every rule be kept exactly, which is a different quality from benevolent — bene means "good", and a benevolent person wishes others well, strictly or not.
y.C: Noisy and restless describes someone who cannot sit still or stay quiet, while benevolent is about wishing other people well, and a quiet person can be just as kind.
y.D: Quick to forget things means forgetful, having a poor memory; benevolent is about goodwill toward other people, not about what you can remember.

vr.q: MALICIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: The prefix mal- means “bad,” so a malicious rumour is spread on purpose to hurt someone — meaning to do harm.

y.B: Extremely tired is what exhausted means, but malicious comes from mal-, "bad", and describes someone who means to do harm, however rested that person is.
y.C: Difficult to lift means heavy, and malicious describes an intention to hurt somebody, which has no weight at all.
y.D: Brightly colored means full of strong, vivid colors; malicious is not about how a thing looks at all, but about meaning to do harm on purpose.

vr.q: DEJECTED most nearly means:
vr.e: De- means “down” and ject means “thrown,” so a dejected player walks off the field thrown down — low in spirits.

y.A: Highly organized means keeping everything tidy and in order, but dejected is a feeling — de- means "down" and ject means "thrown", so it means low in spirits.
y.B: Very wealthy means having a great deal of money, while dejected describes spirits thrown down, which happens to rich and poor alike.
y.C: Wide awake means alert and not at all sleepy, and you can be wide awake and downhearted at the same moment.

vr.q: ABRUPT most nearly means:
vr.e: An abrupt stop or an abrupt answer comes with no warning at all, so sudden fits; lengthy is closer to its opposite.

y.A: Colorful means full of bright colors, or lively and vivid, and abrupt is about something happening with no warning, which has nothing to do with how it looks.
y.B: Polite means having good manners, and an abrupt answer is close to the opposite — so short and unexpected that it can seem rude.
y.C: Lengthy means long and drawn out, which is the opposite of abrupt: begun or finished all at once, with no warning.

vr.q: OBSTRUCT most nearly means:
vr.e: Ob- means “against” and struct means “build,” so to obstruct a road is to put something in the way — to block it.

y.A: To polish is to rub something until it shines, whereas obstruct is built from ob- "against" and struct "build", so it means putting something in the way.
y.B: To measure is to find out how big or how long something is, but to obstruct a road is to put something across it so that nothing can get past.
y.D: To invite is to ask somebody to come, and to obstruct is the reverse — standing in the way so that nothing can come through.

vr.q: RETRACT most nearly means:
vr.e: Re- means “back” and tract means “pull,” so a cat retracts its claws and a writer retracts a statement — both take back.

y.A: To write down is to put words on paper, whereas retract is re- "back" and tract "pull", so a writer who retracts a statement pulls it back after it has already been written.
y.C: To shout loudly is to say something at great volume, but retracting is about withdrawing what you said, not about how loudly you said it.
y.D: To repeat often is to say the same thing again and again, which is the opposite of retracting it — pulling it back in, the way a cat pulls in its claws.

vr.q: CREDIBLE most nearly means:
vr.e: The root cred means “believe,” as in credit and incredible, so a credible witness is a believable one.

y.A: Costly means expensive, and credit may be what makes you think of money, but the root cred means "believe", so a credible witness is one you can believe.
y.B: Recent means happening not long ago, while credible is about whether an account can be believed, and an old account can be every bit as believable as a new one.
y.C: Crowded means full of people, and credible describes a witness or a story you can believe, which is not a matter of numbers.

vr.q: NOVICE most nearly means:
vr.e: Nov- means “new,” so a novice is someone new to an activity — a beginner, whatever else she may also be.

y.A: A volunteer is somebody who offers to help without being paid, and a novice may well be a volunteer too, but nov- means "new", so the word itself says only that she is new to the thing.
y.C: A leader is the one who guides everybody else, and nov- means "new", so a novice stands at the other end — new to the activity and still learning it.
y.D: A stranger is somebody you do not know, but a novice may be perfectly familiar to you and still be new at the activity, which is all the word claims.

vr.q: SURPLUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Sur- means “over,” so a surplus is what is left over once everyone has enough — an extra amount, the exact opposite of a shortage of supplies.

y.A: A serious mistake is a bad error, and surplus comes from sur- "over", meaning what is left over, which is not a mistake at all.
y.B: A short delay is a little wait before something happens, but a surplus is about amount rather than time — it is what remains once everyone has enough.
y.D: A shortage of supplies is having too little of something, and a surplus is exactly the reverse: more than is needed.

vr.q: VERDICT most nearly means:
vr.e: Ver- means “truth” and dict means “speak,” so a verdict is what the jury speaks at the end of a trial; the speeches and the stories all come before it.

y.A: A lawyer's long speech is an address to the court arguing one side, and the verdict is ver- "truth" and dict "speak" — what the jury speaks once all the speeches are done.
y.C: A written promise is a contract or pledge set down on paper, whereas a verdict is spoken aloud at the end of a trial to settle the matter.
y.D: A witness's story is testimony, an account of what that person saw, and it is evidence heard before the verdict rather than the verdict itself.

vr.q: The team watched the little robot ______ and waited for its lights to reappear.
vr.e: Sub- means “under,” so to submerge is to go down under the water, which is why the crew has to wait for the lights to come back into view.

y.A: To assemble is to put the parts of something together, or to gather in one place, but this robot is already built — the crew is waiting for lights that have sunk out of sight beneath the water.
y.B: To announce is to make something known out loud, but the robot is doing something rather than saying something, and lights that have to reappear tell you it has gone down under the water.
y.C: To apologize is to say sorry, and a robot has nothing to be sorry for; the crew waiting for its lights to reappear tells you it has gone down under the water.

vr.q: The bats slept in a cool ______ chamber the cavers reached only after an hour’s climb down.
vr.e: Sub- means “under” and terra means “earth,” so a subterranean chamber lies underground at the bottom of a long climb; bats would not sleep in a flooded one.

y.A: Transparent means clear enough to see straight through, like glass, and this chamber is described by how far down it lies, not by what you can see through it.
y.B: Portable means easy to carry from place to place, and a stone chamber an hour's climb below ground is the last thing anybody could pick up and carry.
y.D: Flooded means filled or covered with water, and although caves can flood, this chamber is simply a cool one deep underground, where the bats can sleep dry.

vr.q: Announcing the winner before the last runner had finished turned out to be ______: the trophy had to be handed to someone else.
vr.e: Pre- means “before,” so something premature happens too early; the announcement was clearly not harmless, since the trophy had to change hands.

y.B: Impossible means it could not happen at all, but the announcement plainly did happen — the trouble was that it happened too early.
y.C: Harmless means doing no damage, and this announcement did do damage, since the trophy had to be taken back and handed to somebody else.
y.D: Traditional means done a certain way for many years because that is the custom, and there is nothing customary about naming a winner before the race has finished.

vr.q: It is rude to ______ your grandmother in front of guests, even when you are sure she is wrong.
vr.e: Contra- means “against” and dict means “speak,” so to contradict is to speak against what someone has just said — which is what makes it rude here.

y.A: Imitate means to copy the way someone speaks or moves; the clue "even when you are sure she is wrong" is about arguing with what she said, not about copying her.
y.B: Praise means to say out loud how good someone is, which is a kind thing to do in front of guests, not the rude thing the sentence needs.
y.D: Congratulate means to tell someone you are glad about their success or good luck, and nobody would call that rude.

vr.q: The ______ of a whole week at the beach kept the twins cheerful all through exam season.
vr.e: Pro- means “forward” and spect means “look,” so a prospect is something you look forward to; a penalty or a disappointment would not keep anyone cheerful.

y.A: A penalty is a punishment for breaking a rule, and a punishment waiting for you would not keep anyone cheerful through exam season.
y.B: A disappointment is the flat feeling you get when something you hoped for does not happen, but the twins are cheerful precisely because the beach week is still ahead of them.
y.C: A burden is a heavy load that weighs you down, and a week at the beach is the opposite of a weight on your shoulders.

vr.q: Because the harvest was so large, the country was able to ______ tons of rice to its neighbors.
vr.e: Ex- means “out” and port means “carry,” so to export rice is to carry it out of the country to buyers elsewhere.

y.B: Postpone means to put something off until later, but the large harvest let the country send its rice to its neighbors, not delay anything.
y.C: Memorize means to learn something by heart so you can say it without looking, and you cannot memorize tons of rice.
y.D: Inherit means to receive money or property from someone after they die, which is not how a country sends its harvest abroad.

vr.q: The jeweler offered to ______ our initials on the inside of the ring.
vr.e: Scrib and script mean “write,” so to inscribe initials on a ring is to write or carve them into it.

y.A: Rehearse means to practice a play, a speech, or a piece of music before performing it, and the jeweler is not practicing anything — he is cutting initials into the ring.
y.C: Predict means to say what will happen before it happens, and the jeweler is putting initials on the ring rather than foretelling anything.
y.D: Swallow means to send food or drink down your throat, which has nothing to do with marking initials inside a ring.

vr.q: Workers set out barrels to ______ traffic around the flooded street.
vr.e: Di- means “aside” and vert means “turn,” so to divert traffic is to turn it aside — here, around the flooded street.

y.A: Flatten means to press or knock something flat, and the barrels are there to send the cars a different way, not to squash them.
y.B: Applaud means to clap to show you like something, and traffic at a flooded street needs steering, not applause.
y.D: Purchase means to buy, and the workers are steering traffic around the flood, not paying for it.

vr.q: One strong kick was enough to ______ the swimmer all the way to the far wall.
vr.e: Pro- means “forward” and pel means “drive,” so to propel the swimmer is to drive her forward to the far wall.

y.A: Forgive means to stop being angry with someone for what they did, which is not something a kick can do to a swimmer.
y.B: Dissolve means to break up and spread right through a liquid until it disappears, the way sugar does in water, and a swimmer crossing a pool does no such thing.
y.D: Measure means to find out how big or how far something is, but the kick did not find out the distance — it drove her along it.

vr.q: Ms. Reyes asked Dev to speak up, because his answer was barely ______ at the back of the room.
vr.e: Aud means “hear” and -ible means “able to be,” so audible means able to be heard — which is why Dev is asked to speak up.

y.A: Edible means safe to eat; it ends in -ible just as audible does, but edible is about food while audible is about what can be heard.
y.B: Grateful means thankful, which tells you how Dev feels rather than whether the back of the room could hear him.
y.C: Portable means able to be carried about easily, like a portable radio, but Ms. Reyes is asking about how well Dev can be heard.

vr.q: EJECT most nearly means:
vr.e: E- means “out” and ject means “throw,” so to eject is to throw or force something out — the opposite of joining it together.

y.A: To measure carefully is to find out exactly how big or how much something is, while eject is about throwing something out, not sizing it up.
y.B: To join together is to fasten two things into one, which is the reverse of eject, where the e- means out.
y.D: To praise loudly is to say aloud how good someone is, and eject has nothing to do with approval — only with forcing something out.

vr.q: SPECTACLE most nearly means:
vr.e: Spect means “look,” so a spectacle is something people stop to look at — a remarkable sight, not a sound.

y.A: A long journey is a trip from one place to another, but spect means look, so a spectacle is something worth stopping to look at, wherever you are.
y.B: A quiet whisper is speech so soft you can barely hear it, and a spectacle is something you see rather than something you hear.
y.C: A small mistake is something done wrong, while a spectacle is a sight that makes people stare.

vr.q: MANUSCRIPT most nearly means:
vr.e: Manu means “hand” and script means “write,” so a manuscript is the author’s own written text, before any printing happens.

y.A: A musical instrument is something you play, like a violin or a flute; manu means hand and script means write, so a manuscript is writing, not music.
y.C: A printed poster is made by a machine and pasted up for everyone to read, whereas a manuscript is the author's own text as she wrote it, before any printing.
y.D: A spoken speech is words said aloud to an audience, but script means write, so a manuscript sits on the page rather than in the air.

vr.q: RUPTURE most nearly means:
vr.e: Rupt means “break,” as in erupt and interrupt, so a rupture in a pipe is a break in it.

y.A: A loud cheer is a shout of approval from a crowd, which is only noise; a rupture is something breaking, as in erupt and interrupt.
y.C: A warm welcome is the friendly greeting you give someone who arrives, while a rupture is something splitting or breaking apart.
y.D: A long delay means being kept waiting, which is about time, but a rupture is about something breaking, like a burst pipe.

vr.q: AVERT most nearly means:
vr.e: A- means “away” and vert means “turn,” so you avert your eyes by turning them away.

y.B: To sing along is to join in with the words of a song, which is something you do with your voice, while a- means away and vert means turn, so averting your eyes is turning them away.
y.C: To count again is to go back over a total to check it, and avert has nothing to do with numbers — it means turning away.
y.D: To gather up is to collect things together into one place, which brings them toward you, while avert turns something away.

vr.q: MAGNITUDE most nearly means:
vr.e: Magn- means “great,” as in magnify, so the magnitude of an earthquake is how great it is.

y.A: A bad habit is something you do over and over without thinking about it, while magn- means great, so magnitude is about how great something is.
y.B: A soft sound is a faint one, but magnitude does not name a sound at all — it names how great a thing is, like the magnitude of an earthquake.
y.D: A short pause is a brief stop, which is about time, whereas magnitude is about size.

vr.q: FLUENT most nearly means:
vr.e: Flu means “flow,” as in fluid, so fluent speech flows easily; the word is about talking, not about running, lifting, or drawing.

y.A: Being able to run very fast makes you swift or speedy; flu means flow, and it is a fluent speaker's words that flow, not her feet.
y.B: Being able to lift heavy loads makes you strong, while fluent describes words coming out smoothly, not muscles.
y.C: Being able to draw neatly makes you a careful artist, but fluent is about speech that flows easily, not about a steady hand.

vr.q: VACANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Vac means “empty,” as in vacuum and vacate, so a vacant seat has nobody in it — the opposite of crowded.

y.B: Crowded means packed full of people, which is the opposite of vacant — vac means empty, as in vacuum.
y.C: Expensive means costing a lot of money, but a vacant room is simply an empty one, and an empty room can be cheap or costly.
y.D: Noisy means full of sound, while vacant is about whether anyone is there at all, and an empty hall is usually the quiet one.

vr.q: She had forgotten to mention the party, so she squeezed it into a ______ after she had already signed her name.
vr.e: Post- means “after” and script means “write,” so a postscript is added after the letter is finished and signed; a preface would come first instead.

y.A: A preface is the short introduction at the front of a book, before the main text, so a preface comes first while she added her note after signing.
y.B: A caption is the line of words printed under a picture to explain it, not something you squeeze onto the end of a letter.
y.C: A heading is the title at the top of a page or section, so it goes first, but she remembered the party only after she had signed her name.

vr.q: The dentist used a small tool to ______ the loose tooth.
vr.e: Ex- means “out” and tract means “pull,” so to extract the loose tooth is to pull it out.

y.A: Assemble means to fit parts together to build something, which is the reverse of what the dentist does in pulling a tooth out.
y.C: Translate means to put what someone said or wrote into another language, and the tooth is being pulled, not put into words.
y.D: Inflate means to fill something with air until it swells, like a balloon, while the dentist is drawing the tooth out rather than pumping it up.

vr.q: The whale rose to the surface to ______ a spray of air and water.
vr.e: Ex- means “out” and pel means “drive,” so to expel the spray is to drive it out of the blowhole.

y.A: Borrow means to take something for a while meaning to give it back, and the whale is pushing the spray out, not taking anything.
y.B: Gather means to collect things together and bring them in, whereas the whale is driving the spray out of its blowhole.
y.D: Invent means to make something that never existed before, but air and water already exist and the whale is simply blowing them out.

vr.q: The radio tower can ______ a signal for a hundred miles.
vr.e: Trans- means “across” and mit means “send,” so the tower sends a signal across a hundred miles.

y.A: Sharpen means to give something a fine point or edge, the way you sharpen a pencil, and a tower is not putting a point on its signal.
y.C: Decorate means to make something look prettier by adding things to it, which is not what a radio tower does with a signal.
y.D: Swallow means to send food or drink down your throat, which if anything is the opposite of sending a signal out across a hundred miles.

vr.q: The hospital needed a ______ receptionist, because half the families who came in spoke only Spanish.
vr.e: Bi- means “two” and lingua means “language,” so a bilingual receptionist can speak with the Spanish-speaking families as well as the English-speaking ones; being punctual or courteous would not solve that problem.

y.B: Courteous means polite and well mannered, and however polite the receptionist is, politeness alone will not let her understand a family speaking Spanish.
y.C: Punctual means always on time, which is a fine quality but no help when half the families speak a language the receptionist does not.
y.D: Reliable means you can count on someone to do what she promised, but the receptionist could turn up faithfully every day and still not understand the families who speak only Spanish.

vr.q: The sign warns drivers to stop for any ______ in the crosswalk.
vr.e: Ped means “foot,” so a pedestrian is a person travelling on foot — exactly who a crosswalk is meant for.

y.A: A delivery truck is a vehicle that brings goods to people's doors, but ped means foot, and a crosswalk is painted for people crossing on foot.
y.B: A chimney is the tall shaft above a fireplace that lets smoke out through the roof, and no chimney ever stood in a crosswalk.
y.C: A textbook is a book you study a subject from, so it is not something a sign would tell drivers to stop for.

vr.q: The Romans built a stone ______ across the valley, and the city’s fountains ran for the first time.
vr.e: Aqua means “water” and duct means “lead,” so an aqueduct leads water into the city, which is why the fountains could finally run.

y.B: An archway is a curved opening you walk or ride through, and although an aqueduct is often carried on rows of arches, an archway by itself brings no water to the fountains.
y.C: A monument is a statue or structure built to keep the memory of a person or an event alive, and admiring one would never make the fountains run.
y.D: A furnace is a closed chamber where a fire burns to heat a building or melt metal, so it gives the city heat rather than the water it needed.

vr.q: A single lantern was enough to ______ the whole tent.
vr.e: Lumin means “light,” as in luminous, so to illuminate the tent is to light it up.

y.B: Flatten means to press or squash something flat, which is not what a lantern does to a tent.
y.C: Translate means to put words into another language, and a lantern gives light, not words.
y.D: Purchase means to buy, so a lantern can be purchased but it cannot purchase anything itself.

vr.q: Her second jump was so long that it seemed to ______ the school record.
vr.e: Sur- means “above,” so to surpass the school record is to go beyond it — her jump was longer than the old best.

y.A: Postpone means to put something off until later, but her jump had already happened, and what it did was go beyond the old record.
y.B: Borrow means to take something for a while meaning to return it, and a record is not lent out — it is beaten.
y.D: Describe means to say in words what something is like, and the jump did not talk about the record, it went past it.

vr.q: CHARTER most nearly means:
vr.e: To charter a bus, boat or plane is to rent it for your group's own use for a while: the orchestra chartered a plane to fly all ninety players to the concert.

y.A: Buy means to pay for something and own it for good; when you charter a boat or a bus, you only rent it for a while.
y.B: Map is the trap in the look of the word: charter begins with chart, which is a kind of map, but to charter something is to rent it.
y.D: Steer is what someone does to guide a boat or bus once they are aboard; to charter it is to rent it in the first place.

vr.q: CONFLICT most nearly means:
vr.e: A conflict is a fight or serious disagreement between people, groups or countries: the conflict between the two neighbors began over a fence and lasted for years.

y.B: Peace is the opposite: peace is what you have when a conflict is over.
y.C: Plot comes from reading class, where a story's conflict is part of its plot; the plot is all the events, and the conflict is the struggle at the center of them.
y.D: Solution is how a conflict or problem gets settled; it is what ends a conflict, not the conflict itself.

vr.q: STOCK most nearly means:
vr.e: A stock is a supply of something kept ready to use or sell: before the storm, the family built up a stock of batteries, candles and bottled water.

y.A: Customer means a person who buys from a store; the stock is the goods the store keeps on hand for its customers to buy.
y.B: Delivery is the bringing of goods to a place; a delivery can add to a store's stock, but the stock is the supply kept on hand.
y.C: Shock looks almost like stock, with one letter changed, but a shock is a sudden, upsetting surprise.

vr.q: TENDER most nearly means:
vr.e: Tender means gentle and loving: Grandpa gave the newborn lamb a tender pat on the head. It can also mean sore, or soft enough to chew easily.

y.B: Grateful means thankful; a grateful smile thanks someone for something, while a tender smile is gentle and loving.
y.C: Proud means pleased about what someone has done; a parent can feel proud and tender at once, but proud does not mean gentle.
y.D: Slender rhymes with tender, but it means thin, the way a young tree has a slender trunk.

vr.q: TERM most nearly means:
vr.e: A term is a word or phrase with a special meaning, often in one subject: allegro is a music term that tells the players to go fast. A term can also be a stretch of time, like a school term.

y.A: Letter is a single symbol of the alphabet; a term is a whole word or phrase.
y.B: Team looks almost like term, with only one letter different, but a team is a group of players.
y.C: Test is tempting because students take tests at the end of a school term, but here a term is a word, not an exam.

vr.q: TRACE most nearly means:
vr.e: To trace something is to track it by following the marks or clues it left behind: the hikers traced the deer's footprints through the snow to a stream.

y.A: Race is hiding inside trace, but to race is to run as fast as you can to beat someone.
y.C: Trade looks almost like trace, but to trade is to swap one thing for another.
y.D: Trap goes with hunting, which is where tracking happens, but to trap an animal is to catch it, while to trace it is to follow its trail.

vr.q: VOLUME most nearly means:
vr.e: A volume is a book, often one book in a set: Grandma's recipes fill three thick volumes, one each for soups, breads and desserts. Volume can also mean loudness, or an amount of space.

y.A: Author means the person who writes a book; a volume is the book itself.
y.C: Chapter is one part inside a book; a volume is a whole book, often one of a set.
y.D: Speaker is where your mind goes if you know volume as loudness, the thing you turn up, but a speaker is the machine the sound comes out of.

vr.q: AUDIBLE most nearly means:
vr.e: Audible means loud enough to be heard: the ticking of the old clock was audible from the hallway.

y.A: Can be seen is what visible means; visible ends in -ible like audible, but audible is about hearing, not seeing.
y.B: Can be eaten is what edible means, another -ible word; the aud- in audible, as in audio, is about hearing.
y.D: Sounds like music is tempting because aud- also starts the word audio, but an audible sound is any sound that can be heard, even a sneeze.

vr.q: CONTRADICT most nearly means:
vr.e: To contradict is to deny what someone said by saying the opposite: when Sam said the movie started at seven, his sister contradicted him and said it was eight.

y.A: Agree is the opposite: to agree is to say someone is right, and to contradict them is to say they are wrong.
y.C: Interrupt means to cut in while someone is talking; you can contradict a person without interrupting, by waiting your turn and then saying the opposite.
y.D: Predict ends in -dict, as contradict does, but to predict is to say what will happen in the future.

vr.q: DIVERT most nearly means:
vr.e: To divert something is to redirect it, turning it aside from the way it was going: the farmers dug a ditch to divert water from the river to their fields.

y.A: Dive is hiding inside divert, but to dive is to jump headfirst into water.
y.C: Keep going is the opposite: something that keeps going stays on its path, and something that is diverted is turned off it.
y.D: Block the way means to stop anything from getting through; workers may block the way on a flooded road and divert the cars, but diverting means sending them another way.

vr.q: EXPORT most nearly means:
vr.e: To export goods is to send them to another country to sell: Brazil exports more coffee than any other country in the world.

y.A: Grow is what a farm does to raise crops; growing food is not the same as sending it to another country to sell.
y.B: Explore starts with ex- like export, but to explore is to travel around a place to discover it.
y.D: Pack in boxes is one step in getting goods ready to ship, but to export them is to send them to another country to sell.

vr.q: INSCRIBE most nearly means:
vr.e: To inscribe is to write or carve words onto something so that they last, the way you would engrave them: the builders inscribed the year 1925 on the cornerstone of the library.

y.A: Describe ends in -scribe too, but to describe something is to tell what it is like.
y.C: Erase is the opposite: to erase words is to rub them out, and to inscribe them is to write or carve them in.
y.D: Polish is something you might do to a trophy or a stone sign after it is carved, rubbing it until it shines; it puts no words on it.

vr.q: LAVISH most nearly means:
vr.e: Lavish means far more generous or fancy than is needed: the movie star's lavish house had six kitchens and its own bowling alley.

y.A: Crowded means full of people; a lavish party might be crowded, but lavish describes the rich, fancy way it is done.
y.C: Festive means cheerful and full of holiday spirit; a simple picnic can be festive without being lavish, which means far more than is needed.
y.D: Stingy is the opposite: a stingy person gives as little as possible, and a lavish one gives far more than is needed.

vr.q: PREMATURE most nearly means:
vr.e: Premature means too early, happening before the right time: a premature baby is born weeks before the date it was expected.

y.B: Grown-up is the meaning of mature, the word hiding inside premature, but the pre- in front turns it around: premature means too early, before something is ready.
y.C: Planned is a guess from the pre- at the start, which means before; premature does mean before, but before the right time, not planned ahead.
