y.D: Tiny is tempting because premature babies are often very small, but premature means too early, not small.

vr.q: PROPEL most nearly means:
vr.e: To propel something is to push or drive it forward: a squid propels itself by squirting a jet of water out of its body.

y.A: Lift means to raise something up; to propel it is to push it forward.
y.B: Protect starts with pro- like propel, but to protect something is to keep it safe.
y.D: Steer means to guide which way something goes, like turning a boat's wheel; the push that moves it forward is what propels it.

vr.q: PROSPECT most nearly means:
vr.e: A prospect is a chance or possibility that something will happen in the future: the prospect of a three-hour car ride with no snacks made the cousins groan.

y.B: Memory looks back at the past; a prospect looks ahead, at something that might happen.
y.C: Miner comes from the other meaning, since to prospect is to search the ground for gold, but a prospect is a chance of something to come, not a person who digs.
y.D: Respect ends in -spect like prospect, but respect means admiring and honoring someone.

vr.q: RECONCILE most nearly means:
vr.e: To reconcile is to make peace and become friends again after a fight: Mom helped the twins reconcile by having each one listen to the other's side of the story.

y.A: Argue is the opposite: people argue during a fight, and they reconcile when the fight is over and they are friends again.
y.B: Say sorry is often part of making up, but you can apologize and still not be friends; to reconcile is to make peace and be friends again.
y.D: Think again is a guess from the re- at the start, which can mean again; reconcile is not about thinking twice but about making peace.

vr.q: SUBMERGE most nearly means:
vr.e: To submerge something is to put it completely under water or another liquid: to find the leak in a bike tube, submerge it in a tub and watch for bubbles.

y.A: Merge is hiding inside submerge, but to merge is to join together, the way two lanes of traffic merge into one.
y.C: Splash is what happens at the top of the water when something hits it; something submerged has gone all the way under.
y.D: Swim means to move through water using your arms and legs, often at the top; to submerge is to go or put something completely under.

vr.q: SUBTERRANEAN most nearly means:
vr.e: Subterranean means underground, below the surface of the earth: subterranean tunnels let subway trains run beneath the busy streets of the city.

y.A: Overhead is the opposite: something overhead is up above you, and something subterranean is down below the ground.
y.B: Rocky is tempting because the terr- in subterranean means earth or ground, but rocky ground is full of stones; subterranean means under the ground.
y.D: Underwater is the trap in the sub-, which does mean under; but the terr- part means earth, so subterranean means under the ground, not under water.

vr.q: The school concert's ____ ending, when the power went out without warning in the middle of the second song, left the whole choir standing in the dark.
vr.e: Without warning, in the middle of a song, tells you the ending was sudden and nobody expected it. Abrupt means sudden and unexpected.

y.B: Elaborate means carefully worked out with many parts, like a big planned finale, but this ending was a power cut in the middle of a song.
y.C: Gradual means happening slowly, a little at a time, but the power went out all at once, without warning.
y.D: Scheduled means planned ahead of time, but the power went out without warning in the middle of a song.

vr.q: Blake used to drop almost every pass in gym class, but after a summer of practice he became ____ at catching, snagging even the wildest throws with one hand.
vr.e: But turns from dropping passes to snagging even the wildest throws one-handed, which takes real skill. Adept means very skilled at something.

y.B: Awkward describes Blake before the summer, when he dropped almost every pass; but tells you he changed.
y.C: Mediocre means only average, but snagging even the wildest throws with one hand is far better than average.
y.D: Nervous is how someone might feel after dropping passes in front of the class, but a nervous catcher does not snag the wildest throws with one hand.

vr.q: The ____ owner of the corner bakery gives every unsold loaf to the food pantry at closing time and sends free muffins to the fire station each Friday.
vr.e: Both examples show someone giving to others and asking nothing back. Benevolent means kind and generous, wanting to do good for others.

y.B: Greedy means wanting to keep everything for yourself, the opposite of giving bread and muffins away.
y.C: Impulsive means acting suddenly without thinking, but this owner gives at closing time every day and every Friday, a planned habit, not a whim.
y.D: Malicious means wanting to hurt others, and giving food to a pantry and a fire station helps them.

vr.q: Delaney's claim that she had run the mile in under seven minutes was ____, because Coach Abrams had timed her with a stopwatch from start to finish.
vr.e: Because gives the reason: the coach timed her from start to finish, so the claim can be trusted. Credible means able to be believed; trustworthy.

y.A: Boastful means bragging, and a fast mile can sound like a brag, but because points to the stopwatch, which shows the claim was simply true.
y.B: Creative looks like credible and is also praise, but creative means full of new ideas, and a stopwatch time is not an idea.
y.D: Dubious means doubtful and hard to trust, but a coach's stopwatch is good proof, so the claim was easy to believe.

vr.q: When her soufflé sank into a flat puddle just minutes before her grandparents arrived for dinner, Bea looked so ____ that her brothers hurried over to cheer her up.
vr.e: A ruined dish just before the guests arrive is a big disappointment, and her brothers rushed to cheer her up, so she looked sad. Dejected means sad and without hope after a disappointment.

y.B: Delighted means very happy, and a happy person does not need cheering up, least of all after a soufflé sinks.
y.C: Determined means firmly set on doing something, but brothers hurry to cheer up someone who is sad, not someone full of fight.
y.D: Serene means calm and untroubled, and nobody rushes over to cheer up someone who is perfectly calm.

vr.q: Most of the recipe was easy, but stirring the thick peanut butter into the oats forced Chen to ____ real effort, leaning his whole weight on the spoon.
vr.e: But turns from the easy parts to the hard one, and leaning his whole weight on the spoon shows him putting in effort. To exert is to use strength or effort; to try hard.

y.B: Exhale looks like exert and means breathe out, which hard work can make you do, but you cannot breathe out effort.
y.C: Inhale means breathe in, and hard stirring can leave you out of breath, but you cannot breathe in effort; Chen was putting effort out, into the spoon.
y.D: Restrain means hold back, but leaning his whole weight on the spoon is the opposite of holding back.

vr.q: Instead of sharing the candy from her birthday party, Carmen ____ it in a shoebox under her bed and ate one piece a night for two months.
vr.e: Instead of sharing, she kept a big supply hidden under her bed and made it last two months. To hoard is to collect and hide away a large supply.

y.A: Devoured means ate quickly and greedily, but she ate only one piece a night, and the candy lasted two months.
y.B: Displayed means set out for people to see, but a shoebox under the bed is where you hide something, not show it off.
y.D: Relinquished means gave up or let go of, but Carmen kept every piece for herself and ate one a night for two months.

vr.q: Daisy's ____ decision to toss a whole handful of chili flakes into the soup, without tasting it first or checking the recipe, left her whole family gulping water.
vr.e: Without tasting first or checking the recipe means she acted without stopping to think. Impulsive means acting suddenly, without thinking first.

y.A: Cautious means careful, and a careful cook would taste first and check the recipe, the two things Daisy skipped.
y.B: Generous goes with handful, as in a generous handful, but it describes an amount, and nothing kind came of a decision that left her family gulping water.
y.D: Spicy describes the soup after the chili went in, but the blank describes Daisy's decision, and a decision cannot taste hot.

vr.q: Millions of tiny yeast cells ____ the jar of sourdough starter on Chef Castillo's counter, living and multiplying as they feed on the flour she adds each day.
vr.e: Living and multiplying in the jar says what the yeast does there: it lives in it. To inhabit a place is to live in it.

y.A: Desert, as a verb, means leave a place for good, which has nothing to do with dessert, and the yeast stays in the jar, living and multiplying.
y.B: Exhibit ends like inhabit but means show to the public, and nobody puts yeast cells on show; they live in the jar.
y.D: Sweeten means make sweeter, which sounds like cooking, but sourdough tastes sour, and the sentence is about the yeast living in the jar.

vr.q: When the school garden was paved over for a parking lot, the fifth graders ____ its loss in poems so sad that the principal read one aloud at the assembly.
vr.e: Poems so sad that the principal read one aloud show deep sadness about the garden. To lament is to express deep sadness or regret about something.

y.A: Commended means praised, and poems often praise things, but nobody praises losing a garden in poems that sad.
y.B: Ignored means paid no attention to, but children who write poems about the garden are paying it plenty of attention.
y.D: Predicted means said ahead of time what would happen, but the garden had already been paved over when they wrote.

vr.q: The referee showed Dante a red card for a ____ tackle, saying he had kicked the other player on purpose, long after the ball was gone.
vr.e: The referee explains the red card: the kick was on purpose and aimed at a player, not the ball. Malicious means meaning to cause harm or hurt on purpose.

y.A: Benign means harmless and gentle, but a kick aimed at a player long after the ball was gone was meant to hurt.
y.B: Clumsy means awkward, and a clumsy tackle is usually an accident, but the referee said Dante kicked the player on purpose.
y.D: Skillful means done with great skill, but kicking a player long after the ball is gone takes no skill and earns a red card.

vr.q: Since Benji was a ____ in the kitchen who had never used an oven by himself, his aunt stood beside him the whole time and read each step aloud.
vr.e: Since gives the reason his aunt stayed close: he had never used an oven by himself. A novice is a beginner, someone new to an activity and not yet skilled.

y.A: Chef means a skilled cook who runs a kitchen, and a chef has used an oven thousands of times; Benji had never used one by himself.
y.B: Critic means someone who judges food or art, but judging is not why his aunt read him each step; he had never used an oven by himself.
y.D: Veteran means someone with years of experience, but Benji had never used an oven by himself.

vr.q: The tall boy sitting in front of Ada at the basketball game ____ her view of the court, so she had to lean left and right to see the players.
vr.e: So gives the result: she had to lean around him to see, because he was in the way. To obstruct is to block or get in the way of something.

y.A: Observed looks like obstructed but means watched or noticed, and a boy watching the game is not what made Ada lean left and right.
y.C: Scrutinized means examined very closely, but studying the court would not block it, and Ada had to lean around the boy just to see.
y.D: Widened means made wider, the opposite of a view she had to lean around to see.

vr.q: At only eleven, Dominic was already swimming faster than the high school team's best racers, and newspapers called him a ____.
vr.e: An eleven-year-old who beats the best high school swimmers has amazing talent for his age. A prodigy is a young person with amazing talent.

y.A: Mascot means a person or animal chosen to stand for a team, which a young kid near a high school team might be, but Dominic was racing them, and winning.
y.B: Novice means a beginner, and he is young, but a beginner does not beat a high school team's best racers.
y.D: Spectator means someone who watches, but Dominic was in the pool racing, not in the stands.

vr.q: Brooke's ____ at the net made her the most feared player in the volleyball league: she could leap higher than anyone and block almost any spike.
vr.e: The colon explains why other teams feared her: she could out-leap everyone and block almost any spike. Prowess means great skill or ability.

y.A: Inexperience means not having done something much, and a player new to the net would not block almost any spike.
y.B: Malice means wanting to hurt others, and feared can suggest a mean player, but the colon says why they feared her: her leaping and blocking.
y.C: Nervousness is a feeling of worry, and a nervous player is the one who fears others, not the one everyone fears.

vr.q: Grandma Dora's little kitchen was so ____ that every visitor smiled: a cast-iron stove, a wall of hand-painted plates, and a butter churn she still used on Sundays.
vr.e: Every detail is old-fashioned, a cast-iron stove and a butter churn, and the visitors' smiles show it was charming. Quaint means charming in an old-fashioned way.

y.A: Dreary means dull and gloomy, and old things can seem that way, but every visitor smiled.
y.B: Grand means large and impressive, but the kitchen was little, and its charm came from old-fashioned things, not from size.
y.D: Trendy means in the latest style, but a cast-iron stove and a butter churn are about as old-fashioned as a kitchen gets.

vr.q: Avery and Brynn's ____ over who would be team captain grew so loud that Coach Delgado had to step between them and send them to opposite ends of the gym.
vr.e: It grew so loud that the coach had to separate them, so it was an angry argument. A quarrel is an angry argument between people.

y.A: Cheer is a loud, happy shout from a team or a crowd, but a coach does not send cheering players to opposite ends of the gym.
y.B: Consensus means agreement among everyone, and nobody has to separate two players who agree.
y.C: Election is how many teams choose a captain, by voting, but an election does not need a coach to step between two players.

vr.q: When Cole learned that the class hamster had not escaped after all, he had to ____ his announcement that it was lost, and he apologized for scaring everyone.
vr.e: The hamster was never lost, so Cole had to take back what he had said, and he said sorry for the scare. To retract is to take back something you said or wrote.

y.A: Confirm means say that something is true, but his announcement turned out to be false.
y.B: Inscribe means write or carve words onto something, like a name on a trophy, but writing down a false announcement would not take it back.
y.C: Retrace looks like retract but means go back over the same path, as you retrace your steps to find something, and that is not what you do to a mistaken announcement.

vr.q: Asher was so nervous before the championship swim meet that he ____ touched his breakfast; he took one bite of toast and pushed the plate away.
vr.e: One bite and then the plate pushed away: he ate almost nothing. Scarcely means almost not at all; barely.

y.A: Hungrily means with a big appetite, but he took one bite of toast and pushed the plate away.
y.B: Nearly touched would mean he came close but never touched it at all, and he did take one bite.
y.D: Seldom means not often, which counts many times, but this was one breakfast on one morning.

vr.q: Ever since she got sick after eating clams at the beach, Delia has ____ seafood, ordering pasta even at her favorite fish restaurant.
vr.e: Getting sick gave her a reason to stay away from seafood, and ordering pasta at a fish restaurant shows her avoiding it on purpose. To shun is to avoid someone or something on purpose.

y.A: Craved means wanted very badly, the opposite of ordering pasta at a fish restaurant.
y.B: Sampled means tried a little, but she orders pasta even where seafood is the specialty.
y.C: Shelled looks like shunned and goes with seafood, because to shell shrimp or clams is to take them out of their shells, but that is handling seafood, not staying away from it.

vr.q: The team ordered thirty water bottles but had only twenty-two players, so Coach Dixon gave the ____ to the girls' team practicing next door.
vr.e: Thirty bottles for twenty-two players leaves eight extra, and those were what the coach gave away. A surplus is an amount left over after what is needed is used.

y.A: Capital means money used to start or run something, but the coach gave away bottles, not money.
y.B: Shortage means not enough, but thirty bottles for twenty-two players is more than enough.
y.D: Total means the whole amount, all thirty bottles, but the team kept twenty-two for its own players.

vr.q: On picture day, Aiden arrived with his shirt untucked, his collar crooked, and his hair sticking up in every direction, and his ____ appearance sent the photographer hunting for a comb.
vr.e: An untucked shirt, a crooked collar and wild hair are examples of a messy look, and the comb was meant to fix it. Unkempt means messy and not cared for, especially hair or clothes.

y.A: Dejected means sad and discouraged, and a face can look that way, but the sentence is about his shirt, collar and hair, and a comb does not fix a sad face.
y.B: Elegant means neat and stylish, the opposite of an untucked shirt and wild hair.
y.D: Unknown means not known, but the photographer could see exactly what Aiden looked like; the problem was how messy he was.

vr.q: The county fair judges tasted all twelve pies twice before announcing their ____: Bryce's blueberry pie had won first prize.
vr.e: What follows the colon is the judges' decision about the contest. A verdict is a decision or judgment, like a ruling.

y.A: Appetite means how hungry you are, which tasting twelve pies twice might well change, but the colon tells you what the judges decided, not how hungry they were.
y.B: Prospect means the chance that something will happen in the future, but the judges had finished tasting, and Bryce's pie had already won.
y.C: Recipe means the directions for making a dish, but the judges announced who won, not how to bake a pie.

vr.q: To get the last bits of burnt cheese off the pan, Calvin scrubbed it ____, pressing down with both hands until his arms were tired.
vr.e: Pressing down with both hands until his arms were tired shows great force and energy. Vigorously means with lots of force and energy.

y.A: Lightly means with very little force, but he pressed down with both hands.
y.B: Seldom means not often, which counts how many times, but this was one long scrubbing that went on until his arms were tired.
y.D: Vividly looks like vigorously but means brightly or clearly, as in vividly colored, and it says nothing about how hard he scrubbed.

vr.q: Celeste ____ her lacrosse stick like an expert, using it to scoop up the ball, slip past two defenders, and fire a shot in one smooth motion.
vr.e: Using the stick to scoop, dodge and shoot in one smooth motion shows a tool handled with skill. To wield something is to handle a tool or weapon with skill.

y.A: Adorned means decorated, as players sometimes do with colored tape on their sticks, but decorating a stick does not scoop up a ball or fire a shot.
y.B: Fumbled means handled clumsily and dropped, the opposite of one smooth motion.
y.C: Shielded rhymes with wielded but means protected, and you shield something to keep it safe, not to scoop up a ball and fire a shot with it.

vr.q: The ____ point guard fooled the defense again and again, looking left before passing right and pretending to shoot before slipping the ball to a teammate.
vr.e: Every example is a trick: a fake look, a fake shot. Wily means full of clever tricks for fooling others.

y.A: Candid means honest and direct, saying plainly what you think, but this guard fooled the defense with a fake look and a fake shot.
y.B: Generous fits passing the ball to a teammate, but the passes are not the point; every example shows the guard tricking the defense.
y.C: Stingy means unwilling to give or share, but this guard kept slipping the ball to a teammate, and every example is a trick, not a refusal to share.

vr.q: Devon brought great ____ to the school cooking club: she arrived early to every meeting, tried every recipe at home, and begged the teacher for extra assignments.
vr.e: Arriving early, cooking at home and begging for more all show great eagerness. Zeal means great energy and eagerness for something.

y.A: Caution means care to avoid danger, which matters in a kitchen, but arriving early and begging for extra assignments show eagerness, not carefulness.
y.B: Prowess means great skill, and the sentence never says how well Devon cooked; it shows how eager she was.
y.C: Recklessness means not caring about danger, and a kitchen has hot ovens and sharp knives, but nothing Devon did was risky; arriving early and asking for more work is eagerness.

vr.q: Nadia's team of ocean scientists chartered a ship for the summer, so in September they had to ____.
c: draw a chart of the bay
give it back to its owner
sell it to a fishing company
vr.e: To charter a ship is to hire or rent it for a time. A rented ship belongs to someone else, so when the summer was over the team had to give it back.

y.A: Draw a chart of the bay mixes up charter with chart, a kind of map, and renting a ship gives no reason to draw one.
y.C: Sell it to a fishing company treats charter as buy, but a chartered ship is only rented, so it was never theirs to sell.
y.D: Start their very first voyage skips in September; the team had the ship all summer, so September was the end of their time with it, not the start.

vr.q: The class trip to watch the rocket launch conflicted with Maya's piano recital, so she ____.
c: had to miss one of them
had time to rest in between
played piano at the launch pad
vr.e: When two events conflict, they clash, usually by happening at the same time. Maya could not be in two places at once, so she had to miss one.

y.B: Had time to rest in between would be true if the two events came at different times, but conflicted means they clashed.
y.C: Played piano at the launch pad reads conflicted as joined together, but two events that clash cannot be combined into one.
y.D: Practiced her piece every night is something she might do anyway, so it does not follow from the two events clashing.

vr.q: Petra trained for her first ocean swim race with real discipline: she ____.
c: wore a bright red swim cap
swam laps every morning without fail
vr.e: Discipline is self-control: making yourself keep training even when you would rather not. Swimming laps every morning without fail shows it.

y.A: Wore a bright red swim cap tells what she looked like, not how she trained, so it shows no discipline.
y.B: Was born a natural swimmer is talent, which a person is given, while discipline is self-control a person shows by working.
y.C: Stayed up late every night shows a lack of self-control, the opposite of training with discipline.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Nico built his robot to be a domestic helper, so most days you would find it ____.
c: on a ship far out at sea
vr.e: Domestic means having to do with the home and household. A domestic helper works in people's homes, so you would find it in a family's kitchen.

y.B: In a busy shoe factory is a place of work but not a home, and a domestic helper works in a household.
y.C: Under a moon base's dome picks up the dome at the start of domestic, but the word means having to do with the home.
y.D: On a ship far out at sea is about as far from a home as a robot could be, the opposite of domestic.

vr.q: Omar's team exploited Jupiter's strong gravity, so their spacecraft ____.
c: picked up speed as it swung past
vr.e: To exploit something is to use it to your advantage. The team used Jupiter's pull like a slingshot, so the spacecraft picked up speed as it swung past.

y.A: Exploded near Jupiter mixes up exploit with explode; using the planet's pull helped the spacecraft, it did not blow it up.
y.B: Kept far away from Jupiter is the opposite: to exploit the planet's gravity, the spacecraft had to fly close enough to use it.
y.C: Landed on Jupiter to explore mixes up exploit with explore, and Jupiter is a giant ball of gas with no solid surface to land on.

vr.q: Because Marisol's ocean lab received a large grant, her team ____.
c: had to sell its only boat
had to pay it all back by May
was told to stop all its research
could afford a new underwater camera
vr.e: A grant is money given to pay for something, and it does not have to be paid back. With a large grant, the team could afford a new underwater camera.

y.A: Had to sell its only boat is what a lab short of money might do, but a grant gave the lab money.
y.B: Had to pay it all back by May treats the grant as a loan, but a grant is money given, not lent, so nothing is paid back.
y.C: Was told to stop all its research is the opposite of a grant, which gives help instead of taking it away.

vr.q: The kitchen on Captain Paz's research ship was well stocked, so the crew ____.
c: had to catch fish to eat
could not open the stuck door
vr.e: Stocked means filled with a supply of things. A kitchen well stocked with food means the crew never ran short.

y.B: Had to catch fish to eat is what a crew with an empty kitchen would do, but well stocked means it was full of food.
y.C: Could not open the stuck door mixes up stocked with stuck; the sentence is about what the kitchen held.
y.D: Found every pot sparkling clean describes a tidy kitchen, but stocked means full of supplies, not clean.

vr.q: Penny did not know the term the aquarium guide used, so she ____.
c: asked him what the word meant
checked how warm the water was
explained the word to her friends
asked how many weeks it would last
vr.e: A term is a word or name for something. Penny did not know the word the guide used, so she asked him what it meant.

y.B: Checked how warm the water was has nothing to do with a word she did not know.
y.C: Explained the word to her friends skips did not know; she could not explain a word she had never heard.
y.D: Asked how many weeks it would last treats term as a stretch of time, like a school term, but here it is a word the guide used.

vr.q: Nora traced the seahorse from a photo in her science book, so her drawing ____.
c: was twice as big as the photo
was hung on the classroom wall
was blank where the seahorse had been
had the very same outline as the photo
vr.e: To trace a picture is to copy its outline by drawing over it, often through thin paper. So Nora's drawing had the same outline as the photo.

y.A: Was twice as big as the photo could happen to a drawing made by eye, but tracing copies the outline at the very same size.
y.B: Was hung on the classroom wall might happen to any drawing, so it does not follow from tracing.
y.C: Was blank where the seahorse had been mixes up traced with erased; tracing adds lines, it does not rub them out.

vr.q: The storm's arrival was so abrupt that Owen's team of beach scientists ____.
c: had spent the morning counting crabs
watched the clouds build all afternoon
ran for shelter with their gear still out
vr.e: Abrupt means sudden and unexpected. A storm that arrives that suddenly leaves no time to pack, so the scientists ran for shelter with their gear still out.

y.A: Saw a volcano erupt offshore mixes up abrupt with erupt; the sentence is about how suddenly the storm arrived.
y.B: Had spent the morning counting crabs tells what they did before the storm, so it does not follow from how suddenly it came.
y.C: Watched the clouds build all afternoon fits a storm that came on slowly, the opposite of an abrupt one.

vr.q: Because Priya was adept at repairing robots, the science team ____.
c: adopted a robot as a pet
kept her away from the robots
asked her to fix their broken rover
showed her how to hold a screwdriver
vr.e: Adept means very skilled. A team with a broken rover would ask its most skilled repairer, Priya, to fix it.

y.A: Adopted a robot as a pet mixes up adept with adopt; the sentence is about how well Priya repairs robots.
y.B: Kept her away from the robots is what a team would do with someone clumsy, the opposite of adept.
y.D: Showed her how to hold a screwdriver treats her as a beginner, but someone adept already knows the tools well.

vr.q: The singing humpback whale was audible through the hull of the research boat, so Mila ____.
c: had no idea a whale was near
could only see it from the deck
stopped her work to listen closely
vr.e: Audible means loud enough to be heard. Because the whale's song could be heard inside the boat, Mila stopped to listen.

y.A: Covered her ears in pain reads audible as painfully loud, but it only means loud enough to be heard.
y.B: Had no idea a whale was near would follow if the song could not be heard, but audible means Mila could hear it.
y.C: Could only see it from the deck reads audible as visible, but audible is about hearing, not seeing.

vr.q: Because Nkem was a benevolent inventor, she ____.
c: wore a white lab coat every day
spent her money on a giant yacht
vr.e: Benevolent means kind and generous, wanting to do good for others. A benevolent inventor would give her water pumps away to help people.

y.B: Built robots for violent fights sees violent in the end of benevolent, but the word means kind, not violent.
y.C: Wore a white lab coat every day tells what she wore, which has nothing to do with being kind.
y.D: Spent her money on a giant yacht is what a selfish inventor might do, not one who wants to do good for others.

vr.q: Oscar said that the moon makes its own light, and Pia contradicted him by ____.
c: adding that it glows like a lamp
writing down exactly what he said
vr.e: To contradict someone is to say the opposite of what they said. Oscar said the moon makes its own light, so Pia contradicted him by saying it only reflects sunlight.

y.A: Pointing at the full moon says nothing against what Oscar claimed, so it does not contradict him.
y.B: Adding that it glows like a lamp backs up what Oscar said, so it agrees with him instead of saying the opposite.
y.D: Writing down exactly what he said is taking dictation, not saying the opposite of what he said.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Because Pilar's report of a new kind of glowing jellyfish was credible, the scientists ____.
c: decided to cook it for dinner
laughed it off as a tall tale
set out to find it themselves
gasped at how amazing it sounded
vr.e: Credible means able to be believed. Since the scientists believed Pilar's report, they set out to find the jellyfish themselves.

y.A: Decided to cook it for dinner mixes up credible with edible, which means safe to eat.
y.B: Laughed it off as a tall tale is what people do with a story they do not believe, the opposite of credible.
y.D: Gasped at how amazing it sounded reads credible as incredible, but credible means believable, not amazing.

vr.q: Ola looked dejected as she walked out of the science fair, so her friends ____.
c: asked why she was thrown out
asked what had made her so happy
watched her slides on a projector
vr.e: Dejected means sad and discouraged, often after a disappointment. When a friend looks dejected, you try to cheer her up.

y.B: Asked why she was thrown out mixes up dejected with ejected; the word tells how she felt, not that anyone threw her out.
y.C: Asked what had made her so happy fits a smiling face, but dejected means she looked sad and discouraged.
y.D: Watched her slides on a projector could happen at any science fair, so it does not follow from how she looked.

vr.q: Nell's town diverted the muddy stream that ran into the oyster beds, so now the oysters ____.
vr.e: To divert something is to turn it aside from the way it was going. With the muddy stream turned away from the oyster beds, the oysters live in cleaner water.

y.B: Are buried in thick mud would happen if the stream still ran into the beds, but diverting it turned the mud away.
y.C: Dive deeper into the bay mixes up divert with dive, and oysters stay fixed in one place anyway.
y.D: Grow in many different colors mixes up divert with diverse, which means varied.

vr.q: Pavel exerted himself throughout the long spacewalk, so afterward he ____.
c: needed a long rest and a meal
exited the space station for good
headed straight to the exercise bike
vr.e: To exert yourself is to use a lot of strength and effort. Working that hard on a long spacewalk would leave Pavel needing rest and food.

y.A: Pulled on his space suit happens before a spacewalk, but the sentence asks what came afterward.
y.C: Exited the space station for good mixes up exert with exit, which means leave.
y.D: Headed straight to the exercise bike fits someone with energy to spare, but exerting himself on the spacewalk would have worn him out.

vr.q: Norway exports much of the salmon raised along its coast, so ____.
c: experts must cook all of it
people in many countries eat it
vr.e: To export is to send goods to other countries to sell. Because Norway exports its salmon, people in many other countries eat it.

y.A: It never leaves Norway is the opposite of export, which means sending goods out to other countries.
y.B: Experts must cook all of it mixes up exports with experts; the sentence is about where the salmon is sold.
y.C: Norway buys salmon from abroad describes importing, bringing goods in, the opposite direction from exporting.

vr.q: Pedro hoarded every shark tooth he found on the beach, so by the end of summer ____.
c: each of his friends had one
he had boarded a fishing boat
a jar of them sat hidden in his closet
he was still hunting for his first one
vr.e: To hoard is to collect a large supply of something and hide it away. Pedro kept every tooth he found, so by the end of summer a jar of them sat hidden in his closet.

y.A: Each of his friends had one would follow from sharing the teeth, but hoarding means keeping every one hidden away.
y.B: He had boarded a fishing boat mixes up hoarded with boarded, which means got on.
y.D: He was still hunting for his first one reads hoard as search for, but Pedro found teeth and kept every one.

vr.q: Paloma's impulsive lab partner usually ____.
c: waits for the teacher to say go
jumps in without reading the steps
vr.e: Impulsive means acting suddenly without thinking first. An impulsive lab partner jumps into an experiment before reading the steps.

y.A: Impresses every judge mixes up impulsive with impressive; the sentence is about how the partner acts, not how good the work is.
y.B: Plans every step with care is the opposite of impulsive, which means acting without thinking first.
y.C: Waits for the teacher to say go is patient and careful, the opposite of impulsive.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Thousands of seabirds inhabit the rocky island, so when Oren's research team landed, they ____.
c: saw the birds only passing through
vr.e: To inhabit a place is to live there. With thousands of seabirds living on the island, its ground was covered with their nests.

y.B: Heard nothing but the wind reads inhabit as abandon; an island where thousands of seabirds live is full of their noise.
y.C: Learned the island was theirs mixes up inhabit with inherit, which means to receive something someone left you.
y.D: Saw the birds only passing through treats them as visitors, but to inhabit a place is to live there.

vr.q: When Otto inscribed the brass bell from the old ship, he ____.
c: carved a short poem into its side
scraped off all of its old letters
vr.e: To inscribe is to write, carve, or engrave words on something. Otto inscribed the bell by carving a short poem into its side.

y.A: Described it to a friend mixes up inscribe with describe; inscribing puts words onto the bell itself.
y.B: Polished it until it shone works on the bell's metal but adds no words, and inscribing means writing or carving words.
y.D: Scraped off all of its old letters takes words away, the opposite of inscribing, which puts them on.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Marta's grandfather often laments that city lights now hide most of the stars, so when he looks up at night he ____.
c: misses the stars he saw as a boy
cheers at how bright the city has become
vr.e: To lament is to express deep sadness or regret. Sad that city lights hide the stars, Marta's grandfather misses the ones he saw as a boy.

y.A: Laminates his old star charts mixes up laments with laminates, which means seals in clear plastic.
y.B: Explains how streetlights work only gives facts, while lamenting means showing deep sadness or regret.
y.D: Cheers at how bright the city has become is glad about the lights, the opposite of lamenting what they hide.

vr.q: The judges were lavish with their praise for Naomi's ocean-cleaning robot, so she ____.
c: asked them what was wrong with it
vr.e: Lavish means very generous, more than needed. When judges are lavish with praise, they say many kind things, so Naomi glowed with pride.

y.A: Built it from old cans tells how she made the robot, which happened before the judging, not because of it.
y.B: Won a costly gold trophy treats lavish as fancy and expensive, but what was lavish here was the praise, kind words.
y.D: Asked them what was wrong with it fits judges who said little that was kind, the opposite of lavish praise.

vr.q: Pablo's computer caught a malicious program, one that ____.
c: was written to wreck his files
broke because of a simple mistake
vr.e: Malicious means meaning to cause harm on purpose. A malicious program is written to do damage, like wrecking someone's files.

y.A: Made his computer run faster would be a helpful program, the opposite of a malicious one.
y.C: Shared delicious cookie recipes hears delicious in malicious, but the two words mean very different things.
y.D: Broke because of a simple mistake is harm by accident, but malicious means harm done on purpose.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Since Ophelia was a novice at using the big telescope, the astronomer ____.
c: showed her how to focus it
pointed it at an exploding star
turned off the lights in the dome
let her run the night's work alone
vr.e: A novice is a beginner who is new to something and not yet skilled. A beginner at a big telescope first needs to be shown how to focus it.

y.B: Pointed it at an exploding star links novice to nova, the name for a star that suddenly blazes up, but a novice is a beginner.
y.C: Turned off the lights in the dome might happen on any night, so it does not follow from her being new.
y.D: Let her run the night's work alone is how you would treat an expert, the opposite of a novice.

vr.q: Drifting seaweed obstructed the propeller of Noor's underwater robot, so the robot ____.
c: built a nest out of the seaweed
stalled until a diver cut it free
glided on as if nothing were there
vr.e: To obstruct is to block or get in the way. Seaweed caught in the propeller kept it from turning, so the robot stalled.

y.A: Obeyed every command picks up the ob- of obey; seaweed gives no orders, it gets in the way.
y.B: Built a nest out of the seaweed mixes up obstructed with constructed, which means built.
y.D: Glided on as if nothing were there is what the robot would do if the seaweed drifted past, but obstructed means it blocked the propeller.

vr.q: The launch of Parker's model rocket was premature: ____.
c: its glue had not dried yet
it had sat on the pad for weeks
it was the smallest rocket there
vr.e: Premature means happening too early, before the right time. Launching before the glue had dried was too soon.

y.A: It was built by adults sees mature, grown-up, inside premature, but the word means too early.
y.C: It had sat on the pad for weeks makes the launch late, the opposite of premature.
y.D: It was the smallest rocket there treats premature as small, but the word is about time, meaning too early.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Because Malik is a physics prodigy, ____.
c: he sells rocket toys in a shop
he is already in college at twelve
he has taught college for fifty years
vr.e: A prodigy is a young person with amazing talent. A physics prodigy might already be in college while still a child.

y.A: He has never studied physics fits a beginner, but a prodigy has amazing talent in the subject.
y.B: He sells rocket toys in a shop hears product in prodigy, but a prodigy is a gifted young person, not something sold.
y.D: He has taught college for fifty years describes a grown expert, but a prodigy is a young person.

vr.q: Moana showed the class how a squid propels itself by squirting water out through a tube, which lets it ____.
c: change color to match the sand
vr.e: To propel something is to push or drive it forward. The squid's jet of water pushes it along, so it can zoom through the sea.

y.A: Drive other fish away mixes up propels with repels, which means pushes something else away.
y.B: Sink slowly to the seafloor means going nowhere under its own power, the opposite of being propelled forward.
y.D: Change color to match the sand is something a squid can do, but squirting water is not what lets it.

vr.q: Mira kept talking about the prospect of seeing the space station pass overhead, so she ____.
c: stayed up late to watch for it
felt sad that she had missed it
told everyone how it had looked
vr.e: A prospect is the chance that something will happen in the future. Excited by the chance of seeing the station, Mira stayed up late to watch for it.

y.B: Felt sad that she had missed it treats the chance as already gone, but the station was still to come that night.
y.C: Told everyone how it had looked treats the sighting as over, but a prospect is something that has not happened yet.
y.D: Inspected it through a microscope mixes up prospect with inspect, and no microscope could show a station high in the sky.

vr.q: Because of his prowess at steering the submarine, Miguel ____.
c: was chosen to pilot the dive
bumped the submarine into the dock
vr.e: Prowess is great skill or ability. Miguel's great skill at steering made him the one chosen to pilot the dive.

y.A: Stood at the ship's prow picks out prow, the front of a ship, but prowess means great skill.
y.B: Prowled the ship at night mixes up prowess with prowl, which means to sneak around.
y.D: Bumped the submarine into the dock is what an unskilled pilot might do, the opposite of someone with prowess.

vr.q: Odette thought the fishing village was quaint, with its ____.
c: broken windows and piles of trash
vr.e: Quaint means charming in an old-fashioned way, like a scene from a storybook. Flower-lined stone cottages make a village quaint.

y.A: Shiny glass towers are modern, while quaint means charming in an old-fashioned way.
y.C: Busy highways and parking lots are new and noisy, not the storybook, old-time charm that quaint means.
y.D: Broken windows and piles of trash make a place run-down, but quaint means old in a charming way.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Because of their quarrel over the robot design, Nasir and Opal ____.
c: raced their robots for a trophy
finished the design in record time
vr.e: A quarrel is an angry argument. After quarreling over the design, Nasir and Opal both went home feeling upset.

y.A: Dug stones from a quarry mixes up quarrel with quarry, a place where stone is dug out of the ground.
y.C: Raced their robots for a trophy is a contest, which can be friendly, but a quarrel is an angry argument.
y.D: Finished the design in record time fits partners who agreed, but a quarrel is an angry argument, not a reason to work faster.

vr.q: Mateo and Olivia, who had argued over their volcano model, reconciled by ____.
c: asking the teacher for new partners
vr.e: To reconcile is to become friends again after a fight. Apologizing and shaking hands is how Mateo and Olivia made peace.

y.A: Having the same fight again reads the re- of reconcile as again, but to reconcile is to end a fight and make peace.
y.B: Recycling the volcano model mixes up reconcile with recycle; the word is about the two friends, not the model.
y.D: Asking the teacher for new partners splits them up, but to reconcile is to become friends again.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Before driving away, Neel's model rover retracted its long arm, so the arm ____.
c: folded in close to its body
pulled rocks to it like a magnet
vr.e: To retract something is to pull it back in. When the rover retracted its arm, the arm folded in close to its body.

y.A: Dropped off onto the sand treats retract as remove, but the arm was pulled back in, not lost.
y.C: Stuck straight out in front is the opposite of retracted; the arm was pulled in, not reached out.
y.D: Pulled rocks to it like a magnet mixes up retract with attract, which means to draw something toward you.

vr.q: By noon the tide pool Marcus was watching held scarcely any water, so the little crabs ____.
c: were washed away by big waves
vr.e: Scarcely means almost not at all. With barely any water left in the pool, the crabs hid under damp seaweed to keep from drying out.

y.B: Swam laps in deep water needs a full pool, but scarcely any water means almost none.
y.C: Ran from a scary seagull hears scary in scarcely, but the word tells how much water was left.
y.D: Were washed away by big waves needs a lot of water, the opposite of scarcely any.

vr.q: Most fish shun the sea anemone, but a clownfish ____.
c: makes its home among the anemone's tentacles
vr.e: To shun something is to stay away from it on purpose. But tells you the clownfish does the opposite of most fish: it makes its home among the anemone's tentacles.

y.A: Basks in the sunshine mixes up shun with sun; the sentence is about keeping away from the anemone.
y.B: Is stunned by its sting mixes up shun with stun, and a clownfish's slimy coat keeps the anemone from stinging it.
y.C: Keeps well away from it is what most fish do, and but says the clownfish is different.

vr.q: Ngozi submerged her toy boat in the bathtub, so for ten minutes the boat ____.
c: floated on top of the water
was wiped with a damp cloth
vr.e: To submerge something is to put it completely under water. Ngozi put her toy boat all the way under the bathwater, so it stayed under instead of floating.

y.A: Sat in a dry drawer keeps the boat out of the water, the opposite of submerging it.
y.C: Floated on top of the water is what a toy boat usually does, but submerged means held completely under.
y.D: Was wiped with a damp cloth only gets it a little wet, while submerging puts it all the way under water.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The nests of the ants Nyla studies are subterranean, so to look inside one she ____.
c: peels back the bark of a log
digs carefully down into the dirt
vr.e: Subterranean means underground, beneath the surface of the earth. To see inside an underground nest, Nyla has to dig down into the dirt.

y.A: Climbs into the treetops is where she would go for a nest high above the ground, the opposite of subterranean.
y.B: Dives deep under the sea takes the sub- of submarine to mean under water, but subterranean means under the ground.
y.C: Peels back the bark of a log looks inside wood, but subterranean nests are below the ground.

vr.q: On sunny days, Milo's solar-powered boat made a surplus of electricity, so he ____.
c: stored the extra in a battery
painted the boat a bright yellow
was surprised when the boat sank
vr.e: A surplus is an amount left over after what is needed has been used. Milo's boat made more power than it needed, so he stored the extra in a battery.

y.A: Had to paddle home is what a shortage of power would cause, the opposite of a surplus.
y.C: Painted the boat a bright yellow has nothing to do with having extra electricity, so it does not follow from the surplus.
y.D: Was surprised when the boat sank mixes up surplus with surprise; the word tells how much power the boat made.

vr.q: Because the grounds of the old observatory were unkempt, Max and the other volunteers ____.
c: found no grass left at all
set up their telescopes right away
vr.e: Unkempt means messy and not cared for. Grounds left overgrown and untidy meant the volunteers had to mow and weed all day.

y.A: Were rude to visitors mixes up unkempt with unkind; the word describes the grounds, not anyone's manners.
y.C: Found no grass left at all reads unkempt as not kept, as if the lawn were gone, but unkempt grounds are still there, just overgrown and messy.
y.D: Set up their telescopes right away fits grounds that were already neat, but unkempt grounds needed work first.

vr.q: Dr. Mei gave her verdict on the injured sea turtle: ____.
c: it could return to the sea
it would rain later that week
she had not decided anything yet
sea turtles can live a long time
vr.e: A verdict is a decision or judgment made after looking at the facts. Dr. Mei's verdict was her decision that the turtle was well enough to return to the sea.

y.B: It would rain later that week is a guess about the weather, not a judgment about the turtle.
y.C: She had not decided anything yet means there was no verdict, but a verdict is the decision itself.
y.D: Sea turtles can live a long time is a fact about all sea turtles, not a decision about this injured one.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Because Malia stirred the salt into the water vigorously, ____.
c: it took all afternoon to dissolve
vr.e: Vigorously means with lots of force and energy. Stirring hard and fast helps salt dissolve quickly.

y.A: She weighed it exactly is careful and exact, which is rigorous, a different word from vigorous.
y.B: She wore safety goggles is a good lab habit, but it does not follow from how hard she stirred.
y.D: It took all afternoon to dissolve fits slow, gentle stirring, the opposite of stirring vigorously.

vr.q: Nils wields the space station's robotic arm, so when a supply ship arrives, he ____.
c: uses the arm to catch it
yields the job to someone else
watches it drift past the window
vr.e: To wield a tool is to handle and use it with skill. Since Nils is the one who handles the robotic arm, he uses it to catch the ship.

y.A: Welds it to the station mixes up wield with weld, which means to join metal using heat.
y.C: Yields the job to someone else mixes up wield with yield, which means to give way to another.
y.D: Watches it drift past the window leaves the arm unused, but wielding the arm means using it.

vr.q: Pearl's film showed just how wily the octopus was: it ____.
c: posed as a deadly sea snake
had no tricks to escape enemies
fought a shark with its strong arms
vr.e: Wily means full of clever tricks for fooling others. Pretending to be a deadly sea snake is a clever trick that fools hungry fish.

y.A: Swam into the wild sea mixes up wily with wild, and swimming in the sea shows no trick at all.
y.C: Had no tricks to escape enemies is the opposite of wily, which means full of clever tricks.
y.D: Fought a shark with its strong arms shows strength, not trickery, and wily is about fooling others.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Because of her zeal for astronomy, Nina ____.
c: had a natural gift for math
sold her telescope at a yard sale
vr.e: Zeal is great energy and eagerness for something. Nina was so eager about astronomy that she went stargazing every clear night.

y.A: Had a natural gift for math is talent, something a person is born with, while zeal is eagerness.
y.B: Watched seals at the aquarium mixes up zeal with seal, the sea animal.
y.C: Sold her telescope at a yard sale is what someone bored with astronomy might do, the opposite of zeal.

vr.q: UNKEMPT most nearly means:
vr.e: Unkempt means messy and not looked after, especially hair or clothes: after a week of camping, his hair was unkempt and full of pine needles.

y.A: Lost is a guess from hearing un-kept inside unkempt, as if something had not been kept; but unkempt means untidy and uncared for, the way hair looks when nobody has brushed it.
y.C: Neat is the opposite: neat hair is brushed and in place, while unkempt hair is tangled and messy.
y.D: Unkind starts the same way, which is the trap; unkind describes how someone treats people, while unkempt describes how someone or something looks.

vr.q: WILY most nearly means:
vr.e: Wily means clever at tricking others to get what you want: the wily fox pretended to be asleep until the hens wandered close.

y.A: Fierce describes a dangerous animal too, like a fierce wolf, but it means violent and ready to attack; a wily fox wins with tricks, not by fighting.
y.B: Honest is the opposite: an honest person tells the truth, while a wily one is full of tricks.
y.D: Wild looks almost like wily, which is the trap; wild means not tame, while wily means clever at tricking.

vr.q: INHABIT most nearly means:
vr.e: To inhabit a place is to live in it, to occupy it: frogs and turtles inhabit the pond behind our school.

y.A: Abandon is the opposite: to abandon a house is to leave it for good, and to inhabit it is to live in it.
y.B: Explore means to travel through a place to learn about it; explorers visit a place, but the people and animals that inhabit it live there.
y.C: Inherit looks a lot like inhabit, which is the trap; to inherit is to receive something from a family member, often after that person dies.

vr.q: LAMENT most nearly means:
vr.e: To lament is to feel and show deep sadness about something lost, often out loud: the whole town lamented the old oak tree that the storm knocked down.

y.A: Apologize means to say you are sorry for something you did; to lament is to show sorrow about a loss, even one that was nobody's fault.
y.B: Comment ends like lament, and both can be done out loud, but to comment is just to say what you think about something.
y.D: Rejoice is the opposite: to rejoice is to be full of joy, and to lament is to be full of sorrow.

vr.q: SHUN most nearly means:
vr.e: To shun someone or something is to stay away from it on purpose: after the bee stung him, Leo shunned the flower bed for the rest of the summer.

y.B: Stun rhymes with shun, but to stun someone is to shock or daze them, the way a loud bang can; to shun someone is to keep away from them.
y.C: Tease is another unkind way to treat someone, but teasing is making fun of them, and shunning is staying away from them.
y.D: Welcome is the opposite: you welcome someone by greeting them warmly, and you shun them by keeping away.

vr.q: EXERT most nearly means:
vr.e: To exert strength or effort is to put it to work, to apply it: she exerted all her strength to twist the stuck lid off the jar.

y.B: Exit looks like exert because both start with ex-, but to exit is to go out of a place.
y.C: Measure goes with force too, which is the trap; you can measure how hard someone pushes, but to exert force is to do the pushing.
y.D: Relax is the opposite: when you exert yourself you work hard, and when you relax you rest.

vr.q: HOARD most nearly means:
vr.e: To hoard is to collect and store away a big supply, often secretly and more than you need: the squirrel hoarded acorns in a hollow log.

y.A: Board rhymes with hoard, but to board is to get on a bus, a train, a plane, or a ship.
y.B: Share is the opposite: someone who hoards keeps everything for later, and someone who shares gives some away.
y.C: Steal means to take what belongs to someone else; a hoarder may be greedy, but the things being hoarded can be all their own.

vr.q: WIELD most nearly means:
vr.e: To wield a tool or a weapon is to hold it and use it: the chef wielded a huge wooden spoon to stir the soup.

y.A: Drop is the opposite: to wield a sword is to grip it and use it, and to drop it is to let it fall.
y.C: Sharpen goes with swords and knives, which is the trap; you sharpen a blade to get it ready, and you wield it when you use it.
y.D: Yield rhymes with wield, but it means to give way or give up, as when a driver yields to another car.

vr.q: IMPULSIVE most nearly means:
vr.e: An impulsive person acts on a sudden wish without stopping to think about what might happen, which can be reckless: in an impulsive moment, she jumped into the cold lake with all her clothes on.

y.A: Excited means full of eager feeling, and an excited person may act on impulse, but impulsive means acting without thinking, excited or not.
y.B: Impressive looks a lot like impulsive, which is the trap; impressive means so good that people admire it.
y.C: Patient is the opposite: a patient person can wait and think things over, while an impulsive one acts on the spot.

vr.q: QUAINT most nearly means:
vr.e: Quaint means charming in an old-fashioned way: we stayed in a quaint little cottage with lace curtains and a creaky gate.

y.B: Modern is the opposite: modern things are new and up to date, and quaint ones are pleasantly old-fashioned.
y.C: Quiet looks like quaint, and a quaint village may well be quiet, which is the trap, but quaint is about charm, not noise.
y.D: Shabby means old and worn out in an ugly way, like a coat full of holes; quaint means old-fashioned in a sweet, charming way.

vr.q: ADEPT most nearly means:
vr.e: Adept means very skilled, expert at something: she is so adept at juggling that she can keep four balls in the air.

y.A: Adopted looks like adept, which is the trap; an adopted child is one who joined a family through adoption.
y.B: Clumsy is the opposite: a clumsy person drops things, and an adept one handles them with skill.
y.C: Eager means wanting very much to do something; a beginner can be eager without being adept, which means already very good at it.

vr.q: QUARREL most nearly means:
vr.e: A quarrel is an angry argument: the twins had a quarrel over who got the top bunk.

y.B: Competition is trying to beat others, as in a spelling bee, and nobody has to be angry; a quarrel is an angry fight in words.
y.C: Conversation is people talking together, which a quarrel is too, but a quarrel is angry and a conversation can be perfectly friendly.
y.D: Insult is one rude remark that hurts someone's feelings; a quarrel may be full of insults, but a quarrel is the whole angry argument.

vr.q: ZEAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Zeal is great eagerness and energy for something you believe in: she cleaned up the park with such zeal that she filled six bags of trash.

y.A: Anger is a strong feeling too, but it means being mad; zeal is strong eagerness for something you care about.
y.B: Boredom is the opposite: a bored person has no interest at all, and zeal is a great, eager interest.
y.D: Talent is being naturally good at something; zeal is wanting it badly, and a beginner can have plenty of zeal and very little talent.

vr.q: PRODIGY most nearly means:
vr.e: A prodigy is a young person with an amazing talent, a young genius: the eight-year-old prodigy played the violin like a grown-up star.

y.A: Beginner is nearly the opposite: a beginner is just starting to learn, while a prodigy is already amazing while still young.
y.C: Product starts with the same letters, which is the trap; a product is something made to be sold, like a toy or a box of cereal.
y.D: Student is anyone who is learning, and many prodigies are students, but a prodigy is a young person with a rare and amazing gift.

vr.q: PROWESS most nearly means:
vr.e: Prowess is great skill or ability, especially in a sport or a battle: the goalie's prowess kept every shot out of the net.

y.A: Luck is good things happening by chance; prowess is great skill, so a win that comes from prowess is earned, not lucky.
y.B: Pride is the good feeling you get from doing well; a person with prowess may feel pride, but prowess is the skill itself.
y.C: Progress looks like prowess, both starting with pro and ending in ss, but progress means moving forward or getting better over time.

vr.q: SCARCELY most nearly means:
vr.e: Scarcely means only just, or almost not at all: the fog was so thick that she could scarcely see the house next door.

y.B: Completely is the opposite: if you can see something completely, you see all of it, and if you can scarcely see it, you see almost nothing.
y.C: Nearly means almost, and the two are easy to mix up: if you nearly won, you did not win; if you scarcely won, you did win, but only just.
y.D: Scarily looks like scarcely, which is the trap; scarily means in a frightening way.

vr.q: VIGOROUSLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Vigorously means with a lot of strength and energy: she shook the paint can vigorously until the colors mixed.

y.A: Gently is the opposite: you pat a kitten gently, but you scrub a muddy pan vigorously.
y.B: Loudly is about noise; a vigorous scrub can be quite quiet, because vigorously means with strength and energy.
y.D: Victoriously starts and ends like vigorously, which is the trap; it means like a winner, and you can play vigorously and still lose.

vr.q: The museum's new exhibit shows ____ life long ago: a kitchen hearth with an iron pot, a spinning wheel, and a wooden cradle by the bed.
vr.e: The examples decide it: a hearth, a spinning wheel and a cradle are all things in a home. Domestic means having to do with the home and family. It can also mean inside your own country, as in a domestic flight, but every example here comes from a home.

y.B: Military means having to do with soldiers and war, and there is not a weapon or a uniform in the exhibit, only things from a house.
y.C: Nautical means having to do with ships and sailors; a hearth, a spinning wheel and a cradle belong in a home, not on a ship.
y.D: Political means having to do with government and voting, and the exhibit shows cooking, spinning and a baby's bed.

vr.q: Because Zara and Yasmin both missed their old friendship, they decided to ____ and put their silly argument behind them.
vr.e: Because gives the reason: they missed being friends, so they made up. Reconcile means to become friends again after a disagreement.

y.A: Celebrate means to have a party for something happy, but the girls had not made up yet; missing a friend is a reason to make peace first.
y.B: Compete means to try to beat someone, which has nothing to do with missing a friend.
y.C: Complain means to say you are unhappy about something, which would keep the argument going instead of putting it behind them.

vr.q: Winston's own birthday parties had always been simple picnics in the park, but his cousin's party was ____, with a chocolate fountain, a magician, and pony rides.
vr.e: But turns away from simple picnics, and the examples show how far: a chocolate fountain, a magician and pony rides. Lavish means rich, generous and costly.

y.A: Dull means boring, and a party with a magician and pony rides is the opposite of boring.
y.B: Humble means simple and plain, like Winston's picnics, the very thing but sets the cousin's party against.
y.D: Rushed means hurried, but the examples are about how fancy the party was, not how fast it went.

vr.q: In the old Greek legend, the giant wooden horse left outside the gates of Troy was really a ____: Greek soldiers were hiding inside it.
vr.e: Really tells you the horse was not what it seemed, and the colon gives the example: soldiers hidden inside. A ruse is a trick meant to fool someone.

y.A: Gift is what the people of Troy were fooled into thinking it was; really tells you the truth was different.
y.B: Monument is a statue built to honor someone, and soldiers hiding inside it show it was built to fool, not to honor.
y.D: Stable is a building for horses, which fits the word horse but not a wooden horse with soldiers hiding inside, waiting to attack.

vr.q: Because the old doctor had cared for three generations of families and never turned anyone away, the whole town came to ____ her.
vr.e: Because gives the reason: a lifetime of caring for everyone earns deep respect. Revere means to respect and admire deeply.

y.A: Envy means wanting what someone else has, and caring for every family is not a reason to be jealous.
y.B: Fear means being afraid, but a doctor who never turned anyone away gave the town nothing to fear.
y.C: Pity means to feel sorry for someone, but nothing in the sentence is sad; a lifetime of caring for everyone earns respect, not sorrow.

vr.q: On the first warm Saturday of spring, the park was anything but ____: children crowded every swing, and families spread blankets across the grass.
vr.e: Anything but means not at all. A park full of children and families is not at all empty. Desolate means empty, lonely and bleak.

y.A: Crowded echoes the sentence's own words, children crowded every swing, and that is the trap: anything but turns the blank into what the park was not.
y.C: Lively is exactly what the crowded park was, but anything but means the park was not the blank, so picking it means skipping those two words.
y.D: Popular describes a park that crowds come to, which this one was; anything but needs a word for what it was not.

vr.q: Although the choir sang in perfect harmony at the concert, its rehearsals were full of ____, with singers arguing over every song.
vr.e: Although turns from perfect harmony to something different, and singers arguing over every song shows what. Discord means disagreement, the opposite of harmony.

y.A: Applause is clapping for something you enjoyed, and singers arguing over every song were not clapping for one another.
y.C: Harmony is the word from the first half, and although says the rehearsals were different from it.
y.D: Triumph is a great success, and rehearsals spent arguing over every song were no success.

vr.q: Instead of competing against each other at the science fair, Vivian and Willa decided to ____ and build one big project about bees together.
vr.e: Instead of turns away from competing, and together finishes the thought. Collaborate means to work together.

y.A: Argue means to disagree out loud, the opposite of building one project together.
y.C: Compete is the very thing instead of rules out.
y.D: Withdraw means to pull out of the fair, but they stayed in and built one big project.

vr.q: Although Vera had hoped her summer job at the art museum would be thrilling, most of her days were spent on ____ tasks like dusting picture frames and counting brochures.
vr.e: Although tells you the job turned out different from thrilling, and the examples, dusting and counting, are dull chores. Mundane means ordinary and dull.

y.A: Dangerous would make the job thrilling, which although says it was not; dusting frames is not risky.
y.B: Exotic means strange and from far away, the kind of job she dreamed of, not the dusting and counting she got.
y.C: Glamorous means exciting and full of style, the job she hoped for; although says what she got was different.

vr.q: For the young violinist Yolanda, playing a solo at the famous concert hall was the ____ of her career; nothing she did afterward ever topped it.
vr.e: The second half explains the blank: nothing afterward ever topped it, so it was the very top. Pinnacle means the highest point.

y.A: Footnote means a small, unimportant detail, but a moment nothing she did afterward ever topped was the biggest moment of her career, not a small one.
y.B: Intermission is a short break in the middle of a show, and a break is not the high point that nothing afterward could top.
y.D: Souvenir is an object you keep to remember a place, and the solo was an event, not a keepsake.

vr.q: In the old story, the furious king decided to ____ the dishonest knight, ordering him to leave the kingdom and never come back.
vr.e: The words after the comma define the blank: ordering someone to leave and never come back. Banish means to send someone away as a punishment.

y.A: Applaud means to clap for someone, which an angry king does not do for a dishonest knight.
y.C: Boo means to shout your dislike, the way a crowd boos a bad call; it does not order anyone to leave the kingdom and never come back.
y.D: Pardon means to forgive and let someone off, but the king was angry and sent the knight away for good.

vr.q: In Aesop's fable, the ____ fox flatters the crow and asks to hear her sing, and when the vain bird opens her beak, her piece of cheese falls straight to the fox.
vr.e: The example shows the fox fooling the crow with false praise to get the cheese. Cunning means clever at tricking others.

y.A: Careless describes the crow, who opens her beak without thinking; the fox's plan is carefully worked out.
y.B: Clumsy means awkward and likely to drop things, but it is the crow that drops the cheese, and the fox's plan works perfectly.
y.D: Timid means shy and easily frightened, but the fox boldly talks the crow out of her cheese.

vr.q: Dozens of volunteers rushed to the beach because news of the stranded whales' ____ had reached the town.
vr.e: Because tells you the news is why the volunteers rushed to help, and stranded means stuck on the beach, a dangerous fix for a whale. Plight means a difficult or dangerous situation.

y.A: Escape would mean the whales had already gotten free, and then no one would need to rush to the beach.
y.B: Migration is a long seasonal journey, but stranded whales are stuck on the sand, going nowhere.
y.D: Safety would mean the whales were already out of danger, and then nobody would need to rush to the beach.

vr.q: Without enough sunlight, the tomato plants on the shady side of the house could never ____, no matter how often Wyatt watered them.
vr.e: Never flips the sentence: without sunlight, the plants could never do well, however much water they got. Flourish means to grow strong and healthy.

y.B: Freeze is about cold weather, but the sentence is about too little sunlight, and watering has nothing to do with freezing.
y.C: Hibernate is what some animals do in winter, sleeping for months; the problem here is plants getting too little light.
y.D: Wilt is what plants without enough light might do, but never flips the blank: the sentence says what the plants could never do, so it needs the opposite of wilting.

vr.q: The snow leopard is so ____ that even people who live in its mountains almost never see one, and some call it the mountain ghost.
vr.e: So … that links cause and effect: people almost never see it because it is so hard to find. Elusive means hard to find or catch.

y.A: Aggressive means quick to attack, and an animal that attacked people would be seen, not called a ghost.
y.C: Enormous means very large, and a very large animal would be easier to spot, not harder.
y.D: Friendly means glad to be around people, and a friendly animal would come close enough to be seen, not hide like a ghost.

vr.q: Long before refrigerators were invented, families who wanted to keep meat from spoiling ____.
c: left it out in the warm sun
vr.e: Long before refrigerators means the answer has to be something people could do without one. Salting and smoking are old ways of keeping meat from spoiling.

y.A: Ate it a month later says nothing about keeping it fresh; meat left alone for a month spoils, and the sentence asks how they stopped that.
y.C: Stored it in the freezer skips long before refrigerators were invented; a freezer needs the same cold machine, which did not exist yet.
y.D: Left it out in the warm sun would make meat spoil faster, the opposite of keeping it.

vr.q: Because the plight of the stray cats in her neighborhood worried her, Ursula ____.
c: chased them out of her yard
raised money for the animal shelter
vr.e: Plight means a hard or dangerous situation. Worrying about the cats' plight is a reason to help them, and raising money for a shelter helps.

y.A: Chased them out of her yard would make their hard situation worse; worry about their plight is a reason to help them, not drive them off.
y.B: Bought herself a new bicycle has nothing to do with the cats, so because has nothing to connect it to.
y.C: Laughed at their silly tricks treats the cats as funny, but plight means they were in trouble, which is what worried her.

vr.q: Most of the composer's music was loud and stormy, but her final piece ____.
c: was written during a long winter
crashed with drums and booming horns
vr.e: But promises a change from loud and stormy, so the ending must be the opposite: quiet and gentle.

y.A: Was played by an orchestra could be said of her stormy music too, so it is no change, and but needs one.
y.C: Was written during a long winter tells when she wrote it, not how it sounded, so it does not turn against loud and stormy.
y.D: Crashed with drums and booming horns is loud and stormy all over again; but says the last piece was different.

vr.q: Yvette had never been on a boat before, so on the ferry ride across the bay she ____.
c: told tales of her past voyages
was amazed by everything she saw
felt bored by the familiar sights
vr.e: Never been on a boat means the ferry ride was her first, so everything was new to her; being amazed by it all follows.

y.A: Steered like an old sailor needs years on boats, and she had never been on one.
y.B: Told tales of her past voyages reads never as if it were often; she had no past voyages to tell about.
y.D: Felt bored by the familiar sights cannot be right on a first trip, because nothing on it was familiar yet.

vr.q: Because there is no air to breathe on the moon, astronauts who walk there ____.
c: fly kites in a gentle breeze
take deep breaths of fresh air
vr.e: Because there is no air to breathe, astronauts have to bring their own. Every other ending would need air on the moon.

y.B: Leave their helmets at home is the one thing they cannot do; with no air outside, the helmet is part of the sealed suit that holds the air they breathe.
y.C: Fly kites in a gentle breeze needs moving air, and the moon has no air to move.
y.D: Take deep breaths of fresh air is exactly what no air to breathe rules out.

vr.q: FRUGAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Frugal describes someone who spends carefully and avoids waste, so wasting money is its opposite; being frugal says nothing about how much money a person was born with or about giving it away.

y.A: Being eager to give money away is being generous, while frugal describes someone careful about what she spends, which is a different quality altogether.
y.B: Being born into great wealth is about how much money you start with, but frugal is about how carefully you spend it, and rich and poor people alike can be frugal.
y.C: Being quick to waste money is the exact opposite of frugal, since a frugal person spends carefully and tries never to waste anything.

vr.q: INQUISITIVE most nearly means:
vr.e: An inquisitive person asks questions and wants to find things out; fear, boasting, and refusing to change are different traits altogether.

y.A: Being quick to boast about winning is showing off after a victory; an inquisitive person is not showing anything off, she is asking questions because she wants to find things out.
y.C: Being unwilling to change plans is stubbornness, keeping to what you already decided; inquisitive is about wanting to know more, which has nothing to do with plans.
y.D: Being frightened by new places is fear of the unfamiliar, and an inquisitive person feels the opposite about anything new — she wants to go and find out about it.

vr.q: ARROGANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Arrogant means having too high an opinion of yourself — the opposite of shy, and unrelated to forgiving or to being careful.

y.A: Being shy around strangers means feeling small and quiet with people you do not know, which is the reverse of arrogant — an arrogant person thinks very highly of herself.
y.B: Being quick to forgive means letting a wrong go easily; arrogant is about how high an opinion you hold of yourself, which is a different thing altogether.
y.C: Being careful with details means checking the small things closely; arrogant describes a swollen opinion of yourself, and a careful person need not have one.

vr.q: STERN most nearly means:
vr.e: A stern teacher looks and sounds serious and expects the rules to be kept; gentleness, cheerfulness, and hesitation all point the other way.

y.A: Gentle and forgiving means soft with people and quick to let a fault go, and a stern teacher is the opposite — she means the rule to be kept.
y.C: Unsure and hesitant describes someone holding back because she does not know what to do; a stern person is not hesitating at all, she is being firm.
y.D: Cheerful and chatty means bright and full of talk, and stern is the grave, serious face that makes a room go quiet.

vr.q: DILIGENT most nearly means:
vr.e: A diligent worker keeps at a job carefully and steadily, so giving up quickly and working carelessly are its opposites; sharing is a different trait.

y.B: Careless in a hurry means rushing and letting mistakes through; diligent means the opposite, working steadily and taking the care the job needs.
y.C: Quick to give up means dropping a task as soon as it gets hard, and a diligent worker is exactly the one who stays with it.
y.D: Unwilling to share is about holding on to what is yours; diligent describes how hard and steadily you work, which is a different thing entirely.

vr.q: EARNEST most nearly means:
vr.e: Earnest means you truly mean what you say and say it seriously, which rules out joking, rudeness, and boredom.

y.A: Joking and playful means treating things lightly, for fun; earnest is the opposite — an earnest person means every word she says.
y.B: Bored and distant describes someone whose mind has drifted away, and an earnest person is the one who cares most about what is being said.
y.C: Angry and rude is about a hot temper and bad manners; earnest says only that you are serious and truly mean it, and you can be earnest quite politely.

vr.q: INDIGNANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Indignant is the particular anger you feel when something is unjust. Delight, curiosity, and worry are not anger at all.

y.A: Delighted means filled with pleasure, and indignant is anger — the particular anger you feel when something is unfair.
y.C: Curious means wanting to find out about something; indignant is not a question at all, it is anger at unfairness.
y.D: Worried means uneasy about what might happen next, and indignant is not unease at all — it is the anger you feel when something is unfair.

vr.q: ENVIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: An envious person looks at what someone else has and wishes it were hers, so being glad about another's good luck is the opposite feeling; fear and pride are different feelings altogether.

y.A: Being afraid of new people is shyness, and envious is not fear at all — it is wanting what somebody else has.
y.B: Being glad about other people's good luck is the very opposite of envious; an envious person wishes that luck had been hers instead.
y.D: Being proud of your own success is about what you have done yourself, and envious is about looking at what somebody else has and wanting it.

vr.q: ENTHUSIASTIC most nearly means:
vr.e: An enthusiastic helper throws herself into the job because she is genuinely excited about it, which rules out boredom, cool calm, and polite distance.

y.A: Being bored by the whole idea means it does not interest you, and enthusiastic is the opposite — brimming with interest.
y.B: Calm and very careful describes someone taking her time and weighing each step, and enthusiastic is about eagerness instead — how keen you are, not how slowly you go.
