y.D: Polite but distant means being pleasant while keeping your feelings back; an enthusiastic helper holds nothing back, she throws herself in.

vr.q: CAUTIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: A cautious driver slows down before a blind corner, so cautious is the opposite of taking chances or rushing, and it says nothing about being friendly.

y.A: Friendly to strangers is about being warm with people you do not know; cautious is about watching for danger, and you can easily be both at once.
y.B: Willing to take chances means running the risk and hoping it turns out, which is exactly what a cautious person will not do.
y.C: Quick and impatient means rushing because waiting annoys you, and cautious means slowing down on purpose so that nothing goes wrong.

vr.q: Even after his cousins offered to pay him back the next day, Marcus refused to lend a single dollar, and the family found his ______ behavior hard to forgive.
vr.e: “Hard to forgive” marks the word as criticism, and refusing a loan that would be repaid the next day costs him nothing — so the praising words thrifty, frugal, and practical (all meaning wise with money) cannot fit; only stingy, which means mean about giving, does.

y.A: Frugal means careful and sparing with money, and it is praise; the family is not praising Marcus, and refusing a loan he would have back the next day saves him nothing.
y.B: Practical means sensible and down-to-earth about how things really work, and there is nothing sensible about refusing to lend a dollar the cousins would have handed straight back.
y.C: Thrifty is praise too — it means making your money go a long way by not wasting it, and nothing here was going to be wasted, since the cousins would have paid him back.

vr.q: Nobody saw who took the last cupcake, but the ______ grin Rico wore when the empty plate was found told everyone exactly who had.
vr.e: The grin that gives him away shows he got the cupcake by quiet trickery, which is what sly means; honest is the opposite, gracious describes warm manners, and someone who is puzzled has not just pulled off a trick.

y.B: Honest means truthful and open, but Rico is hiding what he did and the grin gives him away; sly means getting something by quiet trickery.
y.C: Puzzled means not understanding something, and Rico understands perfectly well what became of the cupcake — that is why he is grinning.
y.D: Gracious means warm and well-mannered, and Rico's grin is not good manners; it is the look of someone pleased with a trick he has got away with.

vr.q: The inventor's claims were ______: she said the new battery might last an hour longer, not that it would change the world.
vr.e: Claiming only an extra hour rather than changing the world keeps her claims small and unexaggerated, which is what modest means here; boastful and grand describe exactly the big claims she avoids, and her careful wording is the opposite of reckless.

y.A: Reckless means charging ahead without thinking what could go wrong, and the inventor is doing the careful opposite — claiming only what she is sure of.
y.B: Boastful means talking up how good you are, and the inventor does the reverse — she deliberately keeps her claim small.
y.C: A grand claim is a huge, sweeping one, and hers was deliberately small — one extra hour, not changing the world.

vr.q: When the rest of the team stopped speaking to Priya after the missed penalty, Dana walked home with her as she always had; nobody who knew Dana was surprised at how ______ she was.
vr.e: Standing by a friend when everyone else turns away is faithfulness, which is what loyal means; the sentence is not about bragging, about being liked by the crowd, or about running out of patience.

y.A: Popular means liked by a great many people, and the sentence is not about how many people like Dana — it is about her standing by the one friend everyone else dropped.
y.C: Boastful means going on about how good you are, and Dana says nothing about herself; she just keeps walking Priya home.
y.D: Impatient means quickly annoyed at having to wait; nobody is waiting for anything here, and walking Priya home is faithfulness, not irritation.

vr.q: His advice was accurate but so ______ that it stung: “Your essay is dull, and you never checked the spelling.”
vr.e: “Stung” rules out gentle and tactful, and the quoted remark names two specific faults, which rules out vague; blunt means honest in a way that spares no feelings.

y.A: Gentle means soft and careful of people's feelings, and his advice stung, so it was anything but gentle; blunt means saying the truth without softening it.
y.B: Vague means unclear and short on detail, and he named two exact faults — the dull writing and the unchecked spelling — so his advice was the opposite of vague.
y.C: Tactful means telling the truth in a way that spares the other person's feelings, and his remark spared none, which is what made it sting.

vr.q: Nobody had asked Mr. Odile to drive two hours with the costumes the cast had forgotten, and the cast was so ______ that they made him a card and clapped when he walked in.
vr.e: Making a card and clapping for someone who drove two hours unasked is a show of thanks, which is what grateful means; annoyance and indifference would show no thanks at all, and nothing about the drive puzzles them.

y.A: Puzzled means confused and unable to work something out; nothing confuses the cast here — they know exactly what Mr. Odile did and are thanking him for it.
y.B: Indifferent means not caring one way or the other, and a card and applause are what people do when they care very much.
y.D: Annoyed means mildly cross, and the cast has nothing to be cross about — the forgotten costumes were their own fault and he put it right.

vr.q: The assembly opened with a ______ minute of silence for the school's founder, and even the youngest students stopped fidgeting.
vr.e: A minute of silence that makes small children go still is grave and dignified, which rules out festive, playful, and casual.

y.A: Playful means full of fun and games, and this is the moment even the fidgeters go still; solemn means grave and serious.
y.C: Casual means easy-going and informal, the way you are with friends, and a minute of silence for the school's founder is as formal as an assembly gets.
y.D: Festive means cheerful in the way a party or a holiday is, and this silence is a mark of respect, which is grave rather than merry.

vr.q: Ms. Ortiz did not excuse the late homework, but her voice was so ______ that Danny came away feeling understood rather than scolded.
vr.e: “Feeling understood rather than scolded” rules out severe and mocking, and indifference would leave him feeling nothing; sympathetic means sharing in how someone else feels.

y.A: Indifferent means not caring either way, and an indifferent voice would have left Danny feeling nothing at all rather than understood.
y.B: Severe means harsh and stern; Ms. Ortiz did hold him to the rule, but she did it in a kind voice, and severe describes a voice that is not kind.
y.C: Mocking means making fun of someone, and nobody is laughing at Danny — he comes away feeling understood.

vr.q: The box of old camp photographs left Grandma smiling and ______, saying again and again how much she missed those summers by the lake.
vr.e: She is smiling and speaking fondly of what she misses, which rules out bitter and anxious; nothing is being waited for, so not impatient. Nostalgic is exactly this fond longing for the past.

y.B: Impatient means fed up with waiting, and Grandma is not waiting for anything; she is looking back at summers that are already over.
y.C: Anxious means worried about what might happen, and her feeling points backwards to the lake summers she misses, not forwards to anything to fear.
y.D: Bitter means sour and angry over something that went wrong, and she is smiling as she remembers, so her feeling is fond rather than sour.

vr.q: By the last mile of the hike Ana had stopped chattering altogether, and her answers came out in a ______ mumble.
vr.e: Falling silent and mumbling at the end of a long hike shows worn-out tiredness, which is what weary means; a cheerful or playful hiker would still be talking, and nothing on the trail has alarmed her.

y.A: Cheerful means bright and in good spirits, and Ana has gone quiet and is mumbling, which is what being worn out looks like at the end of a long walk.
y.C: Playful means in the mood for fun and games, and someone in that mood would still be chattering; Ana has stopped altogether.
y.D: Alarmed means suddenly frightened by something, and nothing on the trail has frightened Ana — she is simply worn out.

vr.q: BOASTFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: A boastful person keeps announcing how good he is; complaining, fear, and generosity are unrelated traits.

y.B: Always complaining about others is grumbling and faultfinding, and a boastful person's subject is not other people at all — it is himself.
y.C: Being very generous with money means giving it away freely, and boastful says nothing about money; it is about how a person talks about himself.
y.D: Being easily frightened by noise is being jumpy or timid, and a boastful person is not shrinking from anything — he is announcing how good he is.

vr.q: GRACIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Gracious describes warm good manners, the direct opposite of coldly rude, and it has nothing to do with confusion or humor.

y.A: Wildly funny is about making people laugh, which is humor rather than manners, and gracious is about how warmly and politely you treat people.
y.B: Being confused by simple things means struggling to understand, and gracious has nothing to do with how quickly you understand — it is about kind good manners.
y.D: Coldly rude is meeting someone with no warmth at all, and gracious is its exact opposite — warmth and good manners.

vr.q: RESENTFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: Resentful is the sour anger left behind by treatment you think was unfair; gratitude is its opposite, and eagerness and puzzlement are not anger.

y.B: Being eager to begin a task is keenness, wanting to get started, while resentful is a sour, angry feeling that looks back at something already done to you.
y.C: Grateful means thankful for a kindness, and resentful is its opposite — the bitterness left behind when you feel you were treated unfairly.
y.D: Being puzzled by a new rule means not understanding it, and a resentful person understands the rule perfectly well — she just feels she was treated unfairly and stays angry about it.

vr.q: MELANCHOLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Melancholy is a low, lingering sadness, so humor, energy, and alertness all miss it.

y.A: Extremely funny is about making people laugh, and melancholy is a low, lingering sadness — the furthest thing from laughter.
y.C: Wide awake is about being alert rather than sleepy, and melancholy describes a mood; you can feel melancholy wide awake or half asleep.
y.D: Full of energy describes someone bursting to get going, and melancholy is a quiet, heavy sadness that slows a person down.

vr.q: GRIM most nearly means:
vr.e: Grim describes something stern and cheerless; hopeful, silly, and welcoming are all the opposite in feeling.

y.A: Warm and welcoming is how a friend greets you at the door, and grim is the opposite — hard, cheerless and forbidding.
y.B: Silly and light means playful and not serious, while grim is heavy and severe, the look on a face when the news is bad.
y.C: Bright and hopeful means expecting things to turn out well, and grim is the opposite in feeling — hard, cheerless and gloomy to look at.

vr.q: APOLOGETIC most nearly means:
vr.e: Apologetic means showing that you regret something you did; pride, anger, and curiosity carry no regret.

y.B: Being proud of a win is pleasure in something you did well, and apologetic is the opposite feeling — regret for something you did badly.
y.C: Being curious about a plan means wanting to know more about it, and apologetic carries no question in it at all, only sorriness for a fault.
y.D: Being angry at a rule is temper aimed at the rule, and an apologetic person is not angry; she is admitting she was in the wrong.

vr.q: SCORNFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: Scorn is contempt, so scornful means treating something as beneath you — the opposite of admiring, and unrelated to helpfulness or uncertainty.

y.B: Eager to help describes someone quick to pitch in, which says nothing about scorn — scorn is the cold feeling that a thing is beneath you.
y.C: Admiration is looking up to someone and thinking well of them, which is the exact opposite of scorn — a scornful person looks down.
y.D: Being unsure of the answer is doubt, which is about not knowing something; scorn is about looking down on a thing as not worth your respect.

vr.q: DEFIANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Defiant means openly standing against an order, the opposite of obedient; amusement and gratitude are different feelings entirely.

y.A: Easily amused means quick to find things funny, which is about laughing, not about standing up to an order.
y.B: Grateful means full of thanks for something you have been given, and someone defiant is refusing rather than thanking.
y.D: Quietly obedient means doing as you are told without any fuss, which is the very opposite of defiant — defiance is refusing out loud.

vr.q: Though the whole town praised her invention, Maya stayed ______, insisting that her science teacher deserved as much credit as she did.
vr.e: She insists on sharing the credit, which rules out smug, and insisting aloud is not timid; she plainly cares, so not indifferent. Humble means not thinking too highly of yourself.

y.A: Timid means shy and easily frightened, but Maya insists out loud that her teacher deserves the credit, and insisting takes nerve rather than shyness.
y.C: Indifferent means not caring one way or the other, and Maya plainly cares a great deal — she insists her teacher be given credit.
y.B: Smug means pleased with yourself and showing it, and Maya does the reverse — she hands the credit to her teacher.

vr.q: After the win, Trent's grin was ______, and he reminded everyone yet again that he had predicted the score exactly.
vr.e: Reminding everyone “yet again” of his own correct prediction is self-satisfied, not gracious; he is neither sorry (apologetic) nor worried (anxious) after winning.

y.A: Gracious means being kind and generous about other people, especially when you have won, and Trent does the opposite by reminding everyone of his own cleverness.
y.D: Apologetic means looking sorry, as though you wished you had not done something, and Trent is enjoying himself far too much for that.
y.C: Anxious means worried, and Trent has just won and is reminding everyone that he called the score.

vr.q: The kitten's ______ streak showed the moment she batted every pencil off the desk and darted away with her tail high.
vr.e: Knocking pencils down harms nobody, so vicious (cruel) is far too strong; she is causing trouble, so not obedient, and darting off tail-high is not timid. Mischievous means playfully naughty.

y.A: Obedient means doing what you are told, and a kitten who sweeps every pencil off the desk is doing the opposite of what she is told.
y.B: Vicious means cruel and meaning to cause harm, which is far too strong for a kitten knocking pencils about for fun.
y.D: Timid means shy and easily scared, but this kitten darts off with her tail high, which is the swagger of a confident cat.

vr.q: Two goals behind at half time, Coach stayed ______, telling the players the comeback was still theirs for the taking.
vr.e: He encourages the team, which rules out gloomy and furious, and “still theirs for the taking” shows he is sure rather than uncertain; optimistic means expecting things to turn out well.

y.A: Gloomy means low-spirited and expecting the worst, and the coach tells his players the comeback is still theirs, which is expecting the best.
y.B: Furious means extremely angry, and the coach is encouraging his players rather than raging at them.
y.D: Uncertain means not knowing which way things will go, but "still theirs for the taking" is said with confidence, not with doubt.

vr.q: Ravi had been certain he had failed the audition, so when the cast list went up with his name on it, he sat down on the steps looking utterly ______.
vr.e: Seeing his name after expecting the worst lifts a weight off him, which is what relieved means; alarm, annoyance, and disappointment would all follow bad news, not good.

y.B: Disappointed is what you feel when something you hoped for does not happen, and Ravi's name is on the list, so the hoped-for thing did happen.
y.C: Alarmed means suddenly frightened by something bad, and finding out you have been cast is good news, not a fright.
y.D: Annoyed means mildly cross at something irritating, and there is nothing to be cross about when you have been cast after expecting to fail.

vr.q: Rather than saying the painting was ugly, Nina gave a ______ reply, praising its colors before suggesting one change.
vr.e: “Rather than saying it was ugly” and the praise that comes first rule out blunt and rude, and she says nothing about herself, so not boastful; tactful means honest without wounding.

y.A: Blunt means saying exactly what you think without softening it, which is precisely what Nina avoided by praising the colors first.
y.B: Boastful means showing off about yourself, and Nina says nothing about herself at all — she is talking about the painting.
y.C: Rude means openly disrespectful, and Nina goes out of her way to be kind about the painting before she suggests a change.

vr.q: The old dog was ______, nudging Nora's hand until she petted him and then settling his head in her lap.
vr.e: He seeks Nora out for petting, so he is not indifferent, and resting his head in her lap shows trust, which rules out hostile and fearful; affectionate means showing fondness.

y.B: Hostile means unfriendly and ready for a fight, and a dog who settles his head in your lap is doing the opposite of picking one.
y.C: Indifferent means not caring either way, but this dog nudges Nora's hand until she pets him, so he cares very much.
y.D: Fearful means frightened and expecting to be hurt, and a dog who feels that way shrinks back rather than pushing his head into someone's hands.

vr.q: With the results due any minute, Dev chewed his sleeve and kept checking the clock; he was plainly ______, certain the news would be bad.
vr.e: Being “certain the news would be bad” is worry, not boredom, and the sleeve-chewing and clock-watching rule out relaxed and delighted; anxious means uneasy about what is coming.

y.B: Relaxed means calm and free of worry, and someone chewing his sleeve and watching the clock is the opposite of calm.
y.C: Bored means having nothing interesting to occupy you, but Dev is not short of something on his mind — he is certain the news will be bad.
y.D: Delighted means filled with joy, and Dev expects bad news, which is nobody's idea of a delight.

vr.q: The review was sharply ______, listing every flaw in the play and praising almost nothing.
vr.e: Listing every flaw and praising almost nothing rules out admiring and cheerful, and the word “sharply” rules out neutral; critical here means fault-finding.

y.A: Neutral means taking neither side, but a review that lists every flaw and praises almost nothing has plainly taken a side.
y.B: Cheerful means bright and good-humoured, which is not how a review reads when it finds fault with everything in the play.
y.D: Admiring means full of praise for something, and this review praises almost nothing.

vr.q: BLUNT most nearly means:
vr.e: A blunt person says what they think in a plain, direct way, even if it stings: when Ava asked how her drawing of a horse looked, her blunt little brother said it looked more like a dog. A blunt knife or pencil is one that is not sharp.

y.A: Blurry looks a little like blunt, but it means fuzzy and hard to see clearly; blunt words are very clear, sometimes too clear.
y.C: Loud is about how much noise a voice makes; a blunt remark can be whispered, because blunt means plain and direct, not noisy.
y.D: Polite is the opposite: a polite person softens hard news, and a blunt person says it straight out.

vr.q: DELIBERATELY most nearly means:
vr.e: Deliberately means on purpose, not by accident: Mira deliberately wore one striped sock and one spotted sock for Crazy Sock Day.

y.A: Rudely means in an impolite way; people often do rude things on purpose, but deliberately only means on purpose, and you can do a kind thing deliberately too.
y.B: In secret means without anyone knowing; you can do something deliberately right in front of everyone.
y.D: By accident is the opposite: a thing done by accident was not meant, and a thing done deliberately was.

vr.q: FICKLE most nearly means:
vr.e: Fickle means quick to change your mind or your loyalty, again and again: the fickle weather turned from sunshine to hail and back to sunshine before lunch.

y.A: Always loyal is the opposite: a fickle person's loyalty does not last, and they may switch sides without warning.
y.B: Hard to please describes a picky person who is seldom satisfied; a fickle person may be pleased one minute and change their mind the next.
y.D: Quick to forget describes a forgetful person; a fickle person remembers what they liked yesterday but has simply changed their mind.

vr.q: GLIMMER most nearly means:
vr.e: A glimmer is a faint, flickering light, like a twinkle, or a tiny bit of something such as hope: down by ten points at halftime, the team still had a glimmer of hope.

y.A: Darkness is the other end from a glare: darkness has no light at all, and a glimmer is a small, faint light.
y.B: Glare is a harsh, blinding light, like the sun bouncing off a car windshield; a glimmer is faint and soft.
y.D: Whimper rhymes with glimmer, but a whimper is a soft, sad cry, like a puppy's; you hear it, and a glimmer is a light you see.

vr.q: GRATEFUL most nearly means:
vr.e: Grateful means thankful, glad about something someone did for you: the town was grateful to the volunteers who filled sandbags before the flood.

y.A: Generous describes the giver, someone who likes to give and share; grateful describes the person who receives and says thank you.
y.B: Graceful looks almost like grateful, but it means moving in a smooth and lovely way, like a dancer or a swan.
y.C: Hopeful also ends in -ful and names a good feeling, but hopeful means expecting good things to come, while grateful means thankful for what already came.

vr.q: LOYAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Loyal means faithful, always on the side of a person, team or cause: the town stayed loyal to its baseball team through twenty losing seasons.

y.B: Fickle means nearly the opposite of loyal, so it cannot be the answer; a loyal fan stays with a team through good seasons and bad.
y.C: Friendly means kind and pleasant to people; you can be friendly to everyone, but being loyal means sticking with one person, team or cause.
y.D: Royal rhymes with loyal, but it means having to do with a king or queen.

vr.q: MODEST most nearly means:
vr.e: Modest means humble, not bragging about yourself: the modest astronaut talked more about her team than about her own spacewalk.

y.A: Cheerful means happy and bright; a cheerful winner can still boast, but a modest one plays down what she did.
y.C: Modern starts with mod- like modest, but modern means new and up to date.
y.D: Proud is the opposite here: a proud winner shows off, and a modest one plays down what she did.

vr.q: NOSTALGIC most nearly means:
vr.e: Nostalgic means missing the past, with a sweet, sad longing for the way things used to be: at the reunion, the old teammates grew nostalgic, trading stories about the season they won the championship.

y.A: Old-fashioned describes things made in an old style, like a typewriter; nostalgic is a feeling of longing for the past, not a way something looks.
y.C: Studying history means learning facts about the past; being nostalgic means missing a time you remember, with a bittersweet feeling.
y.D: Eager for tomorrow points the other way: it looks ahead with excitement, while nostalgic looks back with longing.

vr.q: RENOVATE most nearly means:
vr.e: To renovate a building is to repair it and fix it up so it is like new again: the school renovated its gym over the summer, putting in a new wooden floor and brighter lights.

y.A: Innovate looks almost like renovate, but to innovate is to invent new ways of doing things, not to fix up an old building.
y.B: Inspect means to look a building over carefully to find what is wrong; to renovate it is to do the work of fixing it up.
y.C: Relocate starts with re- as renovate does, but to relocate is to move to a new place.

vr.q: SLY most nearly means:
vr.e: A sly person or animal is clever in a sneaky, secret way: the sly raccoon waited until the campers were asleep, then pried open their cooler.

y.A: Fierce means wild and ready to attack; a fierce animal comes at you openly, while a sly one sneaks around you.
y.B: Greedy means wanting more than your share; a sly fox may be greedy for the hens, but sly describes its sneaky cleverness, not its appetite.
y.C: Shy looks like sly, with one letter changed, but a shy person is quiet and nervous around others.

vr.q: SOLEMN most nearly means:
vr.e: Solemn means very serious and dignified, with no joking: the courtroom was solemn as the judge stood up to read her decision.

y.A: Bored means tired of something dull; a bored face can look as unsmiling as a solemn one, but solemn means serious and dignified, not uninterested.
y.B: Lonely is a trap in the sol- at the start, which looks like solo, meaning alone; solemn means serious, not alone.
y.D: Sunny is a trap from sol-, as in solar, and sunny also means cheerful, the opposite of solemn.

vr.q: STINGY most nearly means:
vr.e: A stingy person hates to spend or give, even when they should, the kind of person people call cheap: the stingy king kept his gold locked away while his people went hungry.

y.B: Generous is the opposite: a generous person loves to give and share, and a stingy one holds on to every penny.
y.C: Rich means having lots of money; a stingy person may be rich or not, because stingy is about refusing to spend or give, not about how much you have.
y.D: Stringy looks almost like stingy, but it means long, thin and tough, like stringy celery.

vr.q: SYMPATHETIC most nearly means:
vr.e: A sympathetic person understands and cares when someone else is in trouble: when Jonah broke his arm, his sympathetic friends carried his books all week.

y.B: Pathetic is hiding inside sympathetic, but pathetic means weak or sad in a way that makes people pity you.
y.C: Patient means able to wait calmly; a good nurse is patient and sympathetic, but sympathetic means caring about someone's trouble.
y.D: Symmetrical starts with sym- like sympathetic, but symmetrical means the same on both sides, like a butterfly's wings.

vr.q: WEARY most nearly means:
vr.e: Weary means very tired, worn out by long work or effort: after unloading the moving truck all day, the whole family was weary.

y.A: Careful is what wary means, a look-alike with one letter missing; weary means tired, not watchful.
y.B: Hungry is how you might also feel after a long, hard day, but hungry means wanting food, and weary means worn out.
y.C: Teary rhymes with weary, but it means about to cry, with tears in your eyes.

vr.q: When the swan hissed and flapped her wings at his canoe, Henry quickly paddled away from her nest to ____ her, and she soon folded her wings and swam off.
vr.e: Henry gave the swan what she wanted, space around her nest, and she calmed down. Appease means to calm someone by giving in to them.

y.B: Feed means to give food, and Henry gave the swan none; he calmed her by moving away from her nest.
y.C: Provoke means to stir up or annoy, but the swan folded her wings and swam off, so she grew calmer, not angrier.
y.D: Scrutinize means to look at something very closely, but Henry paddled away from the swan instead of moving in for a closer look.

vr.q: Even though it was his first camping trip, Felipe was so ____ that he ignored the ranger's advice and told everyone he already knew more about the woods than anybody there.
vr.e: Felipe acts as if he knows more than everyone, even the ranger, though he has never camped before. Arrogant means thinking you are more important or smarter than others and looking down on them.

y.B: Cautious means careful to avoid danger, and a careful first-time camper would listen to the ranger's advice, not ignore it.
y.C: Humble means not thinking you are better than others, the opposite of telling everyone you know more than anybody there.
y.D: Inquisitive means eager to ask questions and learn, but Felipe would not even listen to the ranger, let alone ask anything.

vr.q: Because anyone who can hear thunder is probably close enough to be struck by lightning, ____ campers head for shelter at the first rumble instead of waiting for the rain to start.
vr.e: Thunder means lightning may be close enough to be dangerous, so careful campers take shelter right away. Cautious means careful to avoid danger or mistakes.

y.B: Energetic means full of energy, and how lively the campers feel has nothing to do with the danger of lightning.
y.C: Reckless means not caring about danger, and reckless campers would be the ones who stay out until the rain starts.
y.D: Weary means tired, and tired campers might want to rest, but the reason the sentence gives is the danger of lightning, not being worn out.

vr.q: When a fox comes near its nest, a killdeer will ____ droop one wing as if it were broken and cry out, pretending to be hurt so that the fox follows it away from the eggs.
vr.e: The killdeer is pretending, so it droops its wing on purpose to trick the fox. Deliberately means on purpose, not by accident.

y.A: Accidentally means by mistake, but a bird that is pretending to be hurt is acting on purpose.
y.C: Painfully would mean the wing really hurts, but the sentence says the killdeer is only pretending to be hurt.
y.D: Silently means without a sound, but the killdeer cries out while it droops its wing.

vr.q: When the neighbors' oak tree grew tall enough to shade Hattie's garden, it began to ____ her tomato seedlings of the sunlight they needed, and they grew thin and pale.
vr.e: The tree's shade kept away the sunlight the seedlings needed, so they grew weak. Deprive means to take away something that is needed.

y.A: Assure means to promise or make certain, but shade does not make sure the seedlings get sunlight; it blocks it.
y.B: Cultivate means to grow and care for plants, but the oak's shade left the seedlings thin and pale, which is the opposite of caring for them.
y.C: Cure means to make well by getting rid of a sickness, and sunlight is something the seedlings needed, not a sickness.

vr.q: Grandpa Femi is a ____ birdwatcher: for fifty years he has written down every bird he sees, and he has never once missed the town's winter bird count.
vr.e: Fifty years of notes and never missing a count show how committed he is. Devout means deeply religious, or very committed and faithful to something, as Grandpa Femi is to his birds.

y.A: Casual means relaxed and not very serious about something, but a casual birdwatcher would not keep a record for fifty years without missing a count.
y.C: Fickle means always changing your mind or your interests, the opposite of sticking with one hobby for fifty years.
y.D: Nostalgic means missing the old days, but the sentence shows a man still out counting birds every winter, not longing for the past.

vr.q: Most of the campers treated the fire-safety lesson as a joke, but Evan was ____ about it: he took careful notes, asked thoughtful questions, and checked that every last ember was out before bed.
vr.e: But sets Evan apart from the joking campers, and his notes, questions and care show he took the lesson to heart. Earnest means sincere and serious.

y.A: Bored means tired of something dull, but a bored camper would not take careful notes or ask thoughtful questions.
y.C: Playful describes the campers who treated the lesson as a joke, and but tells you Evan was different.
y.D: Superficial means only on the surface, without real thought, but careful notes and thoughtful questions show Evan thought hard about the lesson.

vr.q: The campers had to ____ by noon, because the only ferry to the island campground left the dock at 12:15 and would not come back until Sunday.
vr.e: To catch a ferry that leaves at 12:15, the campers had to get on board before it left. Embark means to board a ship, or to set out on something new.

y.A: Anchor means to hold a boat in place with an anchor, which is a job for the ferry's crew, not for passengers trying to catch it.
y.B: Disembark means to get off a ship, the opposite of what the campers needed to do before the ferry left.
y.D: Linger means to stay behind longer than you need to, and anyone who lingered would miss the only ferry.

vr.q: Although the rest of her family groaned about getting up so early, Flora was ____ about the whale-watching trip: she had packed her binoculars the night before and was waiting by the door at five.
vr.e: Although tells you Flora felt differently from her groaning family, and packing early and waiting by the door show how excited she was. Enthusiastic means full of eager excitement and interest.

y.A: Dejected means sad and discouraged, which might fit the groaning family, but Flora was packed and waiting by the door.
y.B: Drowsy means sleepy, which fits the early hour, but someone waiting by the door at five is wide awake and ready.
y.D: Reluctant means not wanting to, which describes the groaning family, and although says Flora was different.

vr.q: Ezra could name every bird in the forest just by its song, and his little brother felt ____ as he listened, wishing he could do the same.
vr.e: His brother wanted Ezra's skill for himself. Envious means wanting what someone else has, such as their things or their success.

y.B: Generous means happy to give and share, but the little brother was not giving anything; he wanted something.
y.C: Stingy means unwilling to share or spend, but nothing here is about keeping things to himself; the little brother wished he had Ezra's skill.
y.D: Superior means better or higher, but it was Ezra who had the skill, so his brother had no reason to feel better than him.

vr.q: Mountain weather in spring can be so ____ that Gwen packs both sunscreen and a winter hat: a sunny morning may turn to sleet by lunch and back to sunshine an hour later.
vr.e: The weather keeps changing without warning, from sun to sleet and back again. Erratic means not steady or regular; unpredictable.

y.B: Frigid means freezing cold, which fits the sleet but not the sunny morning or the sunscreen.
y.C: Mild means gentle and pleasant, which fits the sunny morning but not the sleet that follows it.
y.D: Stable means steady and not likely to change, the opposite of weather that flips from sunshine to sleet and back.

vr.q: Instead of fighting a hungry seal, an octopus will usually try to ____ it, squirting a cloud of dark ink and jetting away while the seal is confused.
vr.e: Instead of fighting, the octopus uses a clever trick and a quick getaway to escape. Evade means to escape or avoid, often by being quick or clever.

y.A: Attack means to start a fight, which is exactly what instead of fighting rules out.
y.B: Chase means to run after something, but the octopus jets away from the seal, not toward it.
y.D: Invade sounds like evade, but it means to enter a place by force, not to escape.

vr.q: Unlike campers who buy brand-new gear for every trip, Grandpa Hector is ____: he has used the same patched tent for thirty years and saves every leftover for the next day's lunch.
vr.e: Unlike tells you he does the opposite of buying new things, and patching his tent and saving leftovers show he wastes nothing. Frugal means careful with money and things; not wasteful.

y.B: Impulsive means acting on a sudden wish without thinking, like campers who buy new gear for every trip, not a man who has kept one tent for thirty years.
y.C: Wasteful means using up or throwing away more than you need, the opposite of saving every leftover.
y.D: Wealthy means rich, but the sentence tells how carefully he uses what he has, not how much money he has.

vr.q: Fiona grew ____ when she saw a boy carving his initials into the bark of an ancient redwood, and she marched over to tell him that he was hurting the tree.
vr.e: Carving into the ancient tree was wrong, and Fiona was angry enough to march over about it. Indignant means angry because of something unfair or wrong.

y.A: Delighted means very pleased, and nobody who cares about trees is pleased to see one carved up.
y.B: Indifferent looks like indignant, but it means not caring, and Fiona cared enough to march over and speak up.
y.D: Meek means quiet and timid, someone who goes along with things, but Fiona marched over and spoke up.

vr.q: Holly is so ____ that every nature walk with her takes twice as long: she stops to ask the guide the name of each wildflower and why moss grows on some rocks but not on others.
vr.e: Holly keeps stopping to ask questions because she wants to learn. Inquisitive means eager to learn and ask questions; curious.

y.A: Bored means not interested, the opposite of a girl who wants to know the name of every wildflower.
y.B: Hasty means in too much of a hurry, but a hasty walker would make the walk shorter, not twice as long.
y.D: Sluggish means slow-moving, which fits the walk taking twice as long, but the colon says the reason is her questions, not slowness.

vr.q: Gideon's plans for the summer were ____: although he had never camped for more than one night, he meant to hike the entire 200-mile trail along the mountain ridge.
vr.e: Hiking 200 miles when you have never camped more than one night is a very big goal. Lofty means very high, or grand and ambitious, as Gideon's plans were.

y.A: Cautious means careful to avoid danger, but a careful planner would not jump from one night of camping to a 200-mile hike.
y.C: Modest means small and not showy, the opposite of a plan to hike an entire 200-mile trail.
y.D: Realistic means sensible and likely to work, but although warns that this plan is far beyond anything he has done.

vr.q: On some summer nights, the breaking waves at certain beaches are ____: tiny living things in the water flash blue light whenever the water is stirred up.
vr.e: The colon explains the blank: the waves flash with blue light. Luminous means giving off light; bright and glowing.

y.A: Frigid means freezing cold, and the colon explains the waves with flashing light, not with cold.
y.C: Opaque means letting no light through, almost the opposite of waves that flash with their own blue light.
y.D: Sweltering means uncomfortably hot, which might describe a summer night, but the colon explains the waves with flashing light, not with heat.

vr.q: While they waited at the trailhead for the ranger, members of three hiking clubs that had never met began to ____, swapping trail stories and passing around bags of snacks.
vr.e: Swapping stories and sharing snacks with people from the other clubs is mixing with them. Mingle means to mix with others and get to know them, as people do at a party.

y.A: Depart means to leave, but they were still waiting for the ranger and trading stories.
y.C: Quarrel means to argue, but swapping stories and sharing snacks is friendly, not an argument.
y.D: Scatter means to spread out in different directions, but trading stories and snacks brings people together.

vr.q: Freya is a gifted ____: speaking at the town meeting without a single note, she argued so clearly and movingly for saving the wetland that she won over the whole room.
vr.e: The words after the colon show Freya's gift: speaking so well to a crowd that she won everyone over. An orator is a skilled public speaker.

y.A: Editor is someone who checks and fixes writing, but Freya's gift showed when she spoke aloud without any notes.
y.B: Listener is someone in the audience, but Freya was the one giving the speech.
y.D: Writer is someone whose gift is putting words on paper, but Freya spoke without a single note, which is what an orator does.

vr.q: The rangers wanted to learn which trail visitors liked best, so they took a ____ at the visitor center, asking everyone who came in to name a favorite.
vr.e: Asking everyone to name a favorite is a way of collecting opinions. A poll is a survey of people's opinions or votes.

y.A: Break means a short rest, and resting would not tell the rangers which trail people liked best.
y.B: Hike fits the phrase took a, and rangers do hike, but a hike would not collect anyone's favorite trail.
y.C: Photo means a picture, and a picture cannot tell the rangers what visitors think.

vr.q: Hank, our old beagle, hates getting his paws wet, so on rainy mornings he steps out the back door ____, pausing on the mat to look back at his warm bed.
vr.e: Hank hates wet paws, and pausing to look back at his bed shows he does not want to go. Reluctantly means without really wanting to; unwillingly.

y.A: Briskly means quickly and with energy, which does not fit a dog who stops on the mat to look back at his bed.
y.B: Enthusiastically means with eager excitement, the opposite of a dog who hates getting his paws wet.
y.C: Playfully fits many dogs, but Hank hates the rain, and looking back at his bed is not play.

vr.q: When a strong gust caught Elif's kite at the top of the hill, it began to ____, climbing higher and higher until it was only a tiny speck against the clouds.
vr.e: The words after the blank describe it: climbing higher and higher. Soar means to fly or rise high into the air.

y.A: Decline means to go down or grow less, the opposite of a kite climbing higher and higher.
y.B: Hover means to stay in one spot in the air, but the kite kept climbing until it was a speck.
y.D: Tangle is a common kite problem, but a tangled kite comes down, and this one kept rising.

vr.q: Ranger Hazel usually joked with the campers, but when she found a cooler of food left open where bears could reach it, her face turned ____, and she told everyone firmly that the rule had no exceptions.
vr.e: But signals a change from joking, and telling everyone firmly that the rule had no exceptions is serious and strict. Stern means serious and strict.

y.A: Puzzled means confused, but she knew exactly what was wrong and said so firmly.
y.B: Sheepish means embarrassed about your own mistake, but someone else left the cooler open, and she was the one setting them straight.
y.D: Whimsical means playful and full of fun, which fits a ranger who usually joked, but the word but tells you her mood changed when she found the cooler.

vr.q: In the play Hugo wrote for the campfire show, the lion ruled the forest as a ____: he took food from the smaller animals whenever he pleased and roared at anyone who dared to complain.
vr.e: The lion uses his power cruelly, taking from the weak and frightening anyone who objects. A tyrant is a cruel ruler who uses power unfairly.

y.A: Beggar means someone who asks others for food or money, but this lion did not ask; he took whatever he pleased.
y.B: Benefactor means someone who kindly gives help or money to others, but this lion took from the smaller animals instead of giving.
y.C: Subordinate means someone of lower rank who follows another's orders, but the lion was the one ruling the forest.

vr.q: Each night, the lighthouse keeper's long ____ began at sunset: until dawn, she stayed awake in the lantern room, keeping the great lamp burning so that passing ships could steer clear of the rocks.
vr.e: The keeper stayed awake all night to keep watch and keep the ships safe. A vigil is a time of staying awake to watch or guard.

y.A: Errand means a short trip to get or do something, but the keeper stayed in the lantern room all night.
y.B: Nap means a short sleep, the opposite of staying awake until dawn.
y.C: Tempest means a violent storm, which a lighthouse might face, but the blank names what the keeper herself did each night: stay awake and keep watch.

vr.q: While the rest of the group digs for beetles and scorpions, one meerkat stands guard on a rock, staying ____ and giving a sharp alarm call the moment it spots an eagle overhead.
vr.e: The meerkat on guard watches carefully and warns the others the instant danger appears. Vigilant means carefully watching for danger; alert.

y.A: Distracted means thinking about something else, but this meerkat spots the eagle the moment it appears.
y.B: Playful means full of fun, but standing guard and calling out a warning is a serious job.
y.D: Weary means worn out, and a worn-out guard would be slow to notice an eagle, not quick to call out.

vr.q: To appease her grumbling crew, who were sick of eating dry biscuits, Captain Rosa ____.
c: pretended she could not hear them
promised them a feast on the next island
vr.e: To appease people is to calm them by giving them what they want. The crew wanted better food, so a promised feast would calm them.

y.A: Cut their meals in half would make the hungry crew even angrier, the opposite of appeasing them.
y.B: Checked the ship's compass has nothing to do with the crew's complaint, and to appease them she had to answer it.
y.C: Pretended she could not hear them leaves the crew as upset as before; to appease people you give them what they want, not ignore them.

vr.q: Unlike the arrogant leader of the expedition, the young mapmaker Talia ____.
c: knew the name of every river
shared the credit with her crew
bragged that she had found it all
vr.e: Arrogant means acting more important than others and looking down on them. Unlike a leader like that, Talia was humble and shared the credit with her crew.

y.A: Drew maps of the coast is simply her job, and it does not show how she differed from a proud, boastful leader.
y.B: Knew the name of every river mixes up arrogant with ignorant, which means not knowing things; arrogant means too proud.
y.D: Bragged that she had found it all is just what an arrogant person does, but the word unlike says Talia was different from the leader.

vr.q: When Quinn leaned over the rope to touch an old painting, the museum guard was blunt: he ____.
c: told Quinn plainly to step back
pushed Quinn roughly away from it
hinted gently that Quinn might move
mumbled so softly Quinn heard nothing
vr.e: A blunt person speaks in a very direct, plain way, even if it stings. A blunt guard would simply tell Quinn to step back, without softening it.

y.B: Pushed Quinn roughly away from it reads blunt as rough, the way a blunt object hits hard; a blunt person is plain and direct with words, not rough with hands.
y.C: Hinted gently that Quinn might move is polite and roundabout, the opposite of blunt.
y.D: Mumbled so softly Quinn heard nothing reads blunt as unclear, as if it meant blurry; a blunt remark is plain and easy to understand.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Ravi was cautious as he carried the museum's ancient glass vase to its new case, so he ____.
c: tossed it from hand to hand
shook so hard he nearly dropped it
stopped to admire its painted patterns
vr.e: Cautious means careful to avoid danger or mistakes. Someone cautious with a precious glass vase holds it with both hands so it cannot fall.

y.B: Tossed it from hand to hand takes a foolish risk, the opposite of being cautious.
y.C: Shook so hard he nearly dropped it reads cautious as frightened; a cautious person stays calm and careful, and nearly dropping the vase is just the mistake caution avoids.
y.D: Stopped to admire its painted patterns mixes up cautious with curious, which means eager to look and learn; cautious means careful to avoid danger.

vr.q: On his map of ancient Egypt, Sami had deliberately drawn the Nile very wide, so when his teacher asked why, he ____.
c: asked for an eraser to fix his mistake
said it showed the river's yearly flood
vr.e: Deliberately means on purpose, not by accident. Because Sami drew the Nile wide on purpose, he had a reason ready: it showed the river's yearly flood.

y.A: Pointed at the pyramids does not answer why the Nile was so wide, which is what the teacher asked.
y.B: Said his pencil had slipped would explain an accident, but deliberately means Sami drew it that way on purpose.
y.C: Asked for an eraser to fix his mistake treats the wide river as an accident, but Sami drew it that way on purpose.

vr.q: Because months at sea had deprived the sailors of fresh fruit, many of them ____.
c: sang songs on deck at night
vr.e: To deprive someone of something is to take away something they need. Sailors deprived of fresh fruit for months got scurvy, a sickness that comes from going too long without fresh fruit and vegetables.

y.B: Ate an orange every day reads deprived as if it meant provided; sailors deprived of fresh fruit had none to eat.
y.C: Stayed strong and healthy is what plenty of fresh fruit would bring, the opposite of being deprived of it.
y.D: Sang songs on deck at night could happen on any voyage, but it does not follow from losing the fruit they needed.

vr.q: Rhea's grandmother is devout, so on their trip to Rome she ____.
c: lit a candle in every church
played tricks on the tour guide
skipped every church on the tour
vr.e: Devout means deeply religious and faithful. Even on vacation, a devout grandmother makes time for her faith, such as lighting a candle in every church she visits.

y.A: Ate huge plates of pasta mixes up devout with devour, which means to eat hungrily; devout means deeply religious.
y.C: Played tricks on the tour guide mixes up devout with devious, which means sneaky; devout means deeply religious and sincere.
y.D: Skipped every church on the tour is what someone who did not care about religion might do, the opposite of devout.

vr.q: Ruth is a diligent volunteer at the history museum, so when she was asked to label the old coins, she ____.
c: knew each coin's age at a glance
vr.e: Diligent means hardworking and careful. A diligent volunteer takes the time to check every label twice.

y.A: Liked the gold ones best tells which coins she enjoyed, not how hard or carefully she worked.
y.C: Left half of them unlabeled is what a lazy helper would do, the opposite of diligent.
y.D: Knew each coin's age at a glance mixes up diligent with intelligent; diligent means hardworking and careful, not quick-minded.

vr.q: Tobias's offer to guide the lost tourists back to their hotel was earnest: he ____.
c: led them right to the door
asked them to pay him first
had lived in town all his life
vr.e: Earnest means sincere and serious, truly meaning what you say. Tobias meant his offer, so he led the tourists right to their hotel door.

y.A: Was only joking with them is the opposite of earnest, which means he truly meant what he said.
y.C: Asked them to pay him first sees the word earn inside earnest, but earnest means sincere, not paid.
y.D: Had lived in town all his life shows he knew the way, not that he truly meant his offer.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Thea embarked on a two-month sled journey across Greenland in May, so in June she was ____.
vr.e: To embark is to set out on a journey. Thea set out in May on a two-month trip, so in June she was somewhere out on the ice.

y.A: Already back home would be true only if May were when her journey ended, but to embark is to set out, and a two-month journey begun in May is still going in June.
y.B: Still packing her sled reads embarked as only planned; to embark is to actually set out, so by June she had already left.
y.D: Teaching her dogs to bark picks out the bark inside embark, but to embark is to set out on a journey.

vr.q: Rory was enthusiastic about the museum's new drawing class, so he ____.
c: was the first to sign up
vr.e: Enthusiastic means full of eager excitement and interest. Rory was so eager about the class that he was the first to sign up.

y.B: Used pencils and charcoal tells what he drew with, not how eager he was to take the class.
y.C: Skipped it to play outside is what someone with no interest would do, the opposite of enthusiastic.
y.D: Drew better than the teacher mixes up being eager with being skilled; enthusiastic means full of excitement, not talented.

vr.q: Sven was envious of the Roman coin in Theo's collection, so he ____.
c: wished he had one like it
was too nervous to touch it
was glad his friend owned it
vr.e: Envious means wanting what someone else has. Sven wanted a coin like Theo's for himself.

y.A: Asked how old it was shows he was curious about the coin, not that he wanted it for himself, which is what envious means.
y.C: Was too nervous to touch it mixes up envious with nervous, which only sounds like it; envious means wanting what someone else has.
y.D: Was glad his friend owned it is the opposite of envious; an envious person wants the thing instead of being happy for its owner.

vr.q: The little train up the mountain was erratic: it ____.
c: came at a different time each day
vr.e: Erratic means not steady or regular, changing without warning. An erratic train keeps no steady schedule; it comes at a different time each day.

y.A: Always left at exactly nine describes a steady, regular train, the opposite of erratic.
y.B: Had stopped running for good reads erratic as broken down; an erratic train still runs, just never at steady times.
y.D: Climbed past three tall waterfalls tells where the train went, not when it came, and the key to erratic here is its timing.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Captain Rowan's ship evaded the pirates by ____.
vr.e: To evade is to escape or avoid someone, often by being quick or clever. Slipping away into the fog let the ship escape the pirates.

y.B: Surrendering to them at once means giving up and being caught, but to evade the pirates is to get away from them.
y.C: Loading barrels of fresh water is a chore on any voyage and does nothing to help the ship get away.
y.D: Storming aboard the pirate ship attacks the pirates head-on, the opposite of evading them, and it mixes up evade with invade.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Sana is so fickle about vacation plans that last summer she ____.
c: chose the same beach as always
vr.e: Fickle means changing your mind often. A fickle traveler keeps switching plans, so Sana changed her mind four times.

y.A: Packed a jar of pickles only sounds like fickle; fickle means changing your mind often.
y.C: Complained about every hotel describes someone picky and hard to please; fickle means changing your mind often.
y.D: Chose the same beach as always shows someone who sticks with one choice, the opposite of fickle.

vr.q: Rania was frugal during her train trip across Italy, so she ____.
c: wrapped her bags in bubble wrap
refused to pay her share of the taxi
vr.e: Frugal means careful with money and not wasteful. Packing her own lunches saved Rania money without being unfair to anyone.

y.B: Wrapped her bags in bubble wrap mixes up frugal with fragile, which means easy to break; frugal means careful with money.
y.C: Dined at the fanciest restaurants spends money freely, the opposite of frugal.
y.D: Refused to pay her share of the taxi is being stingy, not frugal; a frugal traveler saves money but still pays what she owes.

vr.q: The museum's tomb exhibit was lit by a glimmer of light, so Silas ____.
c: had to squint to find his way
felt his way in total darkness
shielded his eyes from the glare
vr.e: A glimmer is a faint flicker of light. With so little light in the tomb room, Silas had to squint to find his way.

y.A: Liked the gold masks best tells which objects he enjoyed, and the word so asks what the dim light made him do.
y.C: Felt his way in total darkness reads glimmer as no light at all, but a glimmer is a faint light, just enough to see by if you squint.
y.D: Shielded his eyes from the glare reads glimmer as a dazzling glare, but a glimmer is a faint light, far too weak to dazzle anyone.

vr.q: Tariq felt grateful as he stepped off the long, bumpy flight, so he ____.
c: thanked the pilot on his way out
vr.e: Grateful means feeling or showing thanks. Glad to have landed safely after a long, bumpy flight, grateful Tariq thanked the pilot.

y.A: Tucked his passport away is something any traveler does, and it shows no thanks to anyone.
y.B: Twirled like a ballet dancer mixes up grateful with graceful, which means moving smoothly; grateful means thankful.
y.C: Grumbled about the bumpy ride is what an ungrateful passenger would do, the opposite of grateful.

vr.q: Sofia felt indignant when the museum's label gave a professor all the credit for the dinosaur bones, because ____.
c: the label was printed in gold
she wanted to dig up bones too
she thought he truly deserved it
her grandmother had found them first
vr.e: Indignant means angry about something unfair. Sofia's grandmother found the bones first, so giving all the credit to someone else was unfair.

y.A: The label was printed in gold is a detail about how the label looked, not anything unfair that would make her angry.
y.B: She wanted to dig up bones too picks out the dig inside indignant, but indignant means angry about something unfair.
y.C: She thought he truly deserved it would make her pleased, not indignant; she could only be angry if the credit was unfair.

vr.q: Because Quentin is so inquisitive, the guide at the science museum ____.
c: gave him a quiz at the end
never heard a single word from him
vr.e: Inquisitive means eager to learn and quick to ask questions. Quentin asked so many questions that the guide answered dozens of them.

y.A: Wore a bright red jacket describes the guide's clothes, which have nothing to do with how curious Quentin is.
y.B: Gave him a quiz at the end hears quiz in inquisitive, but the word means eager to ask questions, not to take a test.
y.D: Never heard a single word from him fits a boy with no questions at all, the opposite of inquisitive.

vr.q: Tomas had lofty hopes for the tiny history museum in his town: he ____.
c: only hoped it would stay open
wanted to sleep up in its loft
dreamed it would become world famous
vr.e: Lofty means very high, or grand and ambitious. Tomas's lofty hopes were grand ones: he dreamed the tiny museum would become world famous.

y.A: Visited it every Sunday tells what Tomas did, not what grand hopes he had for the museum.
y.B: Only hoped it would stay open is a small, modest hope, the opposite of a lofty one.
y.C: Wanted to sleep up in its loft picks out the loft inside lofty, but lofty hopes are grand ones, not hopes about an attic room.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: When the other climbers laughed at their leader's plan, Reid was loyal: he ____.
c: was the son of a great king
had the warmest boots of all
vr.e: Loyal means faithful and supportive to a person or group. When the others laughed at their leader's plan, loyal Reid stood up for her.

y.B: Laughed the loudest of all joins in mocking the leader, the opposite of being loyal to her.
y.C: Was the son of a great king mixes up loyal with royal, which means belonging to a king or queen; loyal means faithful.
y.D: Had the warmest boots of all tells what he wore, not how he stood by his leader.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The deep-sea creatures in the museum's dark aquarium room were luminous, so visitors ____.
c: could barely see them at all
could spot them without a lamp
vr.e: Luminous means giving off light, bright and glowing. Creatures that glow can be seen even in a dark room, without a lamp.

y.A: Counted hundreds of them mixes up luminous with numerous, which means many; luminous means glowing.
y.B: Could barely see them at all fits creatures that give off no light, the opposite of luminous.
y.D: Bought cookies shaped like fish could happen at any museum shop and does not follow from creatures that glow.

vr.q: At the museum's opening night, Ruby mingled with the guests, so by the end of the evening she ____.
c: had talked to no one at all
had lost one of her earrings
vr.e: To mingle is to mix with other people, moving around to talk with many of them. By mingling all evening, Ruby met almost everyone at the party.

y.B: Had danced to every song is something to do at a party, but mingling means moving around and talking with many guests, not dancing.
y.C: Had talked to no one at all is what someone who kept to herself would do, the opposite of mingling.
y.D: Had lost one of her earrings could happen at any party and does not follow from mixing with the guests.

vr.q: When reporters praised Selma for finding the long-lost shipwreck, she was modest: she ____.
c: said she had simply been lucky
said no one else could have done it
said her camera was the latest model
vr.e: Modest means not boastful about what you have done. Instead of bragging about her find, modest Selma said she had simply been lucky.

y.A: Showed them her diving mask does not tell how she spoke about her find, which is what being modest is about.
y.C: Said no one else could have done it is boasting, the opposite of modest.
y.D: Said her camera was the latest model mixes up modest with modern, which means new; modest means not boastful.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Catching the smell of pine trees on the trail, Aunt Tamar grew nostalgic, so she ____.
c: talked only of her plans for next year
told stories of her childhood camping trips
vr.e: Nostalgic means feeling a bittersweet longing for the past. The smell of pine reminded Aunt Tamar of camping as a child, so she told stories of those trips.

y.A: Checked her watch shows nothing about the past, and the word so asks what her longing for the past made her do.
y.B: Kept blowing her stuffy nose picks out the nos at the start of nostalgic, as if the word were about her nose; nostalgic means longing for the past.
y.C: Talked only of her plans for next year looks ahead to the future, the opposite of feeling nostalgic about the past.

vr.q: Long before microphones were invented, a great orator had to ____.
c: speak in a loud, clear voice
connect each telephone call by hand
vr.e: An orator is a skilled public speaker. Without microphones, a great orator had to speak in a loud, clear voice so that a whole crowd could hear.

y.A: Wear a tall silk hat is about clothing, and nothing about giving a speech required it.
y.B: Sit quietly and listen is what the crowd does; an orator is the one giving the speech.
y.D: Connect each telephone call by hand mixes up orator with operator, a person who once connected phone calls; an orator gives speeches.

vr.q: On the last night of the trip, the tour guide took a poll, so Tara ____.
c: said which city she liked best
argued with the guide for an hour
vr.e: A poll is a survey that asks people for their opinions or votes. When the guide took a poll, Tara got to say which city she liked best.

y.A: Had no say in anything would happen if the guide decided everything alone, but a poll asks everyone for an opinion.
y.B: Jumped into the hotel pool mixes up poll with pool, a word one letter away; a poll is a vote or survey.
y.D: Argued with the guide for an hour treats a poll as a debate, but a poll simply collects what each person thinks.

vr.q: Saul had joined his family's castle tour reluctantly, yet by the end he ____.
c: was bored and ready to leave
lost his ticket on the way out
won a prize in the castle raffle
vr.e: Reluctantly means without really wanting to. Saul did not want to go on the tour, and the word yet shows that by the end he had changed his mind and loved it.

y.B: Was bored and ready to leave would follow if he had joined eagerly; since he joined reluctantly, yet points to a change for the better.
y.C: Lost his ticket on the way out hears luck in reluctantly and reads it as bad luck; reluctantly means without wanting to, so yet points to a change in how he felt.
y.D: Won a prize in the castle raffle hears luck in reluctantly, but reluctantly means without wanting to and has nothing to do with luck.

vr.q: The city renovated its crumbling old library, so today it ____.
c: is a shiny new glass tower
stands on the other side of town
looks as grand as when it was new
still has a leaky roof and broken windows
vr.e: To renovate a building is to fix up the old building and make it better. After the city renovated the crumbling library, today it looks as grand as when it was new.

y.A: Is a shiny new glass tower reads the nov in renovate as brand new; renovating fixes up the old building, it does not replace it with a new one.
y.B: Stands on the other side of town mixes up renovate with relocate, which means to move; renovating fixes a building where it stands.
y.D: Still has a leaky roof and broken windows means nothing was fixed, the opposite of renovating the library.

vr.q: In the old Greek legend, the army finally got inside the walls of Troy with a sly plan: they ____.
c: were too shy to come near
smashed down the gates by force
marched right up to the main gate
hid soldiers in a giant wooden horse
vr.e: Sly means clever in a sneaky, secret way. Hiding soldiers inside a wooden horse was a sneaky trick that fooled the people of Troy.

y.A: Were too shy to come near mixes up sly with shy; a shy army would never have gotten inside the walls, and sly means sneaky and clever.
y.B: Smashed down the gates by force is a plain show of strength, not a sneaky trick, so it is not sly.
y.C: Marched right up to the main gate is open and direct, the opposite of a sly, secret plan.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: As Tessa's hot-air balloon soared, the farms below ____.
c: were planted with rows of corn
vr.e: To soar is to fly or rise high into the air. As the balloon rose higher and higher, the farms below looked tinier and tinier.

y.A: Grew closer and closer is what Tessa would see if the balloon were sinking, the opposite of soaring.
y.C: Stayed exactly the same size is what she would see if the balloon only hovered in one place; soaring means rising high.
y.D: Were planted with rows of corn describes the farms, not how they looked as the balloon rose, and the sentence asks what changed.

vr.q: At the old palace, the changing of the guard is a solemn ceremony, so as the guards march, they ____.
c: joke and wave at the crowd
sob and wipe away their tears
keep their faces still and serious
vr.e: Solemn means very serious and dignified, not cheerful or playful. In a solemn ceremony, the guards keep their faces still and serious.

y.A: Take turns marching alone mixes up solemn with solo, which means alone; solemn means serious and dignified.
y.B: Joke and wave at the crowd is playful, the opposite of solemn.
y.C: Sob and wipe away their tears reads solemn as sad; solemn means serious and dignified, so the guards keep calm, still faces.

vr.q: Captain Sadie was stern with her new sailors, so they ____.
c: worked at the back of the ship
worked at the front of the ship
laughed and joked with her all day
vr.e: Stern means serious and strict. A stern captain expects to be obeyed, so her sailors obeyed her orders at once.

y.B: Worked at the back of the ship mixes up two meanings: the stern of a ship is its back end, but a captain who is stern is strict.
y.C: Worked at the front of the ship also treats stern as a part of the ship, and gets even that wrong, since a ship's front is its bow; a captain who is stern is strict.
y.D: Laughed and joked with her all day fits an easygoing captain, the opposite of a stern one.

vr.q: Quincy was stingy, so when the tour guide passed around a tip jar at the end of the day, he ____.
c: asked the guide where to eat
kept every coin in his pocket
had spent all his money already
vr.e: Stingy means unwilling to spend or give, even when you should. A stingy traveler keeps his money to himself instead of tipping the guide.

y.A: Dropped in a generous tip is what a generous person would do, the opposite of stingy.
y.B: Asked the guide where to eat does not answer what he did with the tip jar, which the word so asks about.
y.D: Had spent all his money already would mean he could not give, but stingy means he could have given and chose not to.

vr.q: When Rafael got seasick on the ferry, one sympathetic sailor ____.
c: laughed at his pale green face
complained about the mess he made
brought him water and a cool cloth
vr.e: Sympathetic means showing understanding and care for someone in trouble. A sympathetic sailor would help seasick Rafael feel better.

y.A: Ran laps around the deck mixes up sympathetic with athletic, which only rhymes with it; sympathetic means caring about someone's trouble.
y.B: Laughed at his pale green face makes fun of Rafael's trouble, the opposite of being sympathetic.
y.C: Complained about the mess he made blames Rafael instead of caring about his trouble, the opposite of sympathetic.

vr.q: Unlike his father, who had been a tyrant, the young king ____.
c: lived in the very same castle
jailed anyone who disagreed with him
vr.e: A tyrant is a cruel ruler who uses power unfairly. The word unlike tells us the young king was different from his father: he treated his people fairly.

y.A: Was short and slight mixes up tyrant with giant; a tyrant is a cruel ruler, not a very tall person.
y.C: Lived in the very same castle shows how the two kings were alike, but unlike asks how the son was different.
y.D: Jailed anyone who disagreed with him is just what a tyrant does, so it would make the son like his father, not unlike him.

vr.q: After a long vigil on the ship's deck, Rosalind ____.
c: was stuffed from the big feast
could barely keep her eyes open
had drawn a new map of the coast
vr.e: A vigil is a time of staying awake to keep watch. After staying awake on watch for so long, Rosalind could barely keep her eyes open.

y.A: Felt fresh and well rested would follow a long sleep, the opposite of a vigil, which means staying awake to keep watch.
y.B: Was stuffed from the big feast treats a vigil as a holiday party, perhaps because vigils are often held on the night before a holiday; the vigil is the staying awake to keep watch, not the meal.
y.D: Had drawn a new map of the coast is a different job from a vigil, which is staying awake to keep watch.

vr.q: At the museum, the guard at the front door was vigilant, unlike the guard at the back door, who ____.
c: wore a cap with a gold badge
spoke softly and kindly to all
spotted every visitor who came in
vr.e: Vigilant means carefully watching for danger or trouble. The guard at the back was not vigilant like the one at the front, so he never noticed the open window.

y.A: Wore a cap with a gold badge describes his uniform, not how carefully he watched, which is what unlike asks about.
y.C: Spoke softly and kindly to all mixes up vigilant with violent; vigilant means watchful, so the back guard differed by not watching.
y.D: Spotted every visitor who came in describes a watchful guard, but unlike says the back guard was not vigilant like the front one.

vr.q: After two weeks of touring gardens, Stella had grown weary of them, so when her father suggested one more, she ____.
c: cheered and raced to the car
groaned and asked for the beach
asked if its old bridge was safe
vr.e: Weary means very tired, and to be weary of something is to be tired of it. After two weeks of gardens, Stella was tired of them and wanted something different.

y.A: Put on her favorite sweater picks out wear inside weary, but weary means tired, not anything about clothes.
y.B: Cheered and raced to the car is what someone eager for more castles would do, the opposite of being weary of them.
y.D: Asked if its old bridge was safe mixes up weary with wary, which means careful and watchful; weary means tired.

vr.q: BIASED most nearly means:
vr.e: Biased means unfair because it leans toward one side instead of treating both sides the same: a biased coach gives the best positions to her favorite players, whatever anyone else does at practice.

y.A: Lenient means easygoing about the rules; a lenient teacher goes easy on the whole class, while a biased one favors some students over the others.
y.B: Mistaken means wrong about something; a person can be mistaken without favoring anyone, but biased means leaning unfairly toward one side.
y.C: Strict means firm about the rules; a strict teacher can still treat everyone the same, while a biased one favors one side.

vr.q: CONSENSUS most nearly means:
vr.e: A consensus is an agreement reached by a whole group: after a long talk, the garden club's consensus was to plant beans along the fence.

y.B: Dispute means an argument or disagreement, the opposite of the agreement a consensus is.
y.C: Permission is what consent means, the word that looks like consensus; consent is given by one person, but a consensus is an agreement shared by a whole group.
y.D: Poll means a survey or vote that asks many people what they think; a poll can show that a group disagrees, while a consensus means the group agrees.

vr.q: INDUSTRIOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Industrious means hardworking, busy and getting a lot done: the industrious members of the bike club fixed six flat tires and oiled every chain in one afternoon.

y.B: Industrial looks like industrious, but it means having to do with factories and making goods, like an industrial part of town full of warehouses.
y.C: Lazy is the opposite: a lazy person avoids work, and an industrious one works hard and gets a lot done.
y.D: Successful means having done well or reached a goal; hard work can lead to success, but industrious describes the hard work itself, not how things turn out.

vr.q: INTRICATE most nearly means:
vr.e: Intricate means complex, made of many small parts carefully connected to one another, like the threads of a spider's web.

y.A: Breakable means easy to break; an intricate thing may need gentle handling too, but intricate means it has many small parts carefully connected.
y.C: Simple is the opposite: a simple design has only a few parts, and an intricate one has many small parts carefully connected.
y.D: Tiny means very small; an intricate thing has many small parts, but the whole of it can be big, like an intricate quilt that covers a bed.

vr.q: PROMINENT most nearly means:
vr.e: Prominent means famous and important, well known to many people; it can also describe something that stands out, like a prominent tower that can be seen from every street.

y.B: Permanent looks a lot like prominent, but it means lasting forever, the way a permanent marker does not wash off.
y.C: Promising starts like prominent, but it means likely to do well in the future; a prominent person is already important and well known.
y.D: Wealthy means rich; many prominent people are wealthy, but prominent means well known and important, which is not about money.

vr.q: STABLE most nearly means:
vr.e: Stable means steady, not likely to wobble, fall or suddenly change: before stacking books on a new shelf, push on it to check that it is stable.

y.A: Capable means able to do something well; the word able hides at the end of stable, but stable means steady and not likely to fall.
y.B: Heavy means weighing a lot; a heavy thing can still tip over if it is tall and narrow, so heavy and stable do not mean the same.
y.C: Stale looks like stable with one letter missing, but it means old and no longer fresh, like stale bread.

vr.q: Lamar's first sketch of the treehouse was just a box with a roof, but his final plan was far more ____, with a rope ladder, a trapdoor, two windows, and a pulley for hauling up snacks.
vr.e: But sets the final plan against a plain box with a roof, and the plan adds a ladder, a trapdoor, windows and a pulley. Elaborate means worked out in great detail, with many parts.

y.A: Compact means small and tightly packed, but the final plan added parts instead of squeezing the treehouse into less space.
y.C: Hasty means done too quickly and without care; the quick, plain sketch came first, and the final plan, with all its added parts, shows more care, not less.
y.D: Modest can mean plain or not large, which fits the first sketch, a box with a roof; but tells you the final plan was different.

vr.q: Last year the stage crew mostly sat backstage and chatted, but this year's crew members are so ____ that in one month they have built a castle wall, painted three backdrops, and sewn twelve costumes.
vr.e: But turns from a crew that sat and chatted to members who built, painted and sewed in just one month. Industrious means hardworking and busy, getting a lot done.

y.A: Cautious means careful to avoid danger or mistakes, and being careful does not explain how the crew got so much done in one month.
y.C: Inquisitive means curious and full of questions; curious crew members might ask a lot about the play, but asking questions does not build a castle wall.
y.D: Weary means very tired; the crew might feel weary after all that work, but being tired is not what made them get so much done.

vr.q: Kendra wanted the art club's painting contest judged without ____, so before the judges came in, she covered the name and age of each painter with a sticky note.
vr.e: Hiding who painted each picture keeps the judges from deciding ahead of time that some painters, such as the youngest, will do worse. Prejudice is an unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts, often against a whole group of people.

y.A: Consensus means agreement reached by a whole group, and a sticky note over a name does nothing to stop the judges from agreeing with one another.
y.B: Discretion means good judgment about what to say or do, and Kendra wanted the judges to use good judgment, not to judge without it.
y.C: Merit means worth or quality, which is exactly what the judges should look at; hiding the names makes them judge each painting on its merit.

vr.q: The paper wings on Lorenzo's first glider drooped as soon as he let go, so he cut new wings from cardboard ____ enough to stay perfectly straight.
vr.e: The paper wings drooped, so the new ones had to be stiff enough to stay straight. Rigid means stiff and unbending, not able to flop or flex.

y.A: Frail means weak and easily broken, and wings cut from frail cardboard would droop just as the paper ones did.
y.B: Opaque means not letting light through; cardboard is opaque, but blocking light does nothing to keep a wing from bending.
y.D: Rigorous looks like rigid, but it means very careful and demanding, like a rigorous test; it describes work or rules, not cardboard.

vr.q: Although the school paste was cheaper, Kalani's dad said wood glue was the ____ choice for her craft-stick bridge, since it would hold the joints firm long after paste had cracked.
vr.e: Although tells you the glue cost more, and since gives the reason to choose it anyway: it holds far better than paste. Superior means higher in quality, better than the others.

y.A: Frugal means careful not to spend or waste money, and the cheaper paste would be the frugal choice; although tells you the glue was not the cheap one.
y.B: Inferior means lower in quality, the opposite of what the sentence says about wood glue, which holds long after paste has cracked.
y.C: Mediocre means only average, but the dad chose the glue because it holds far better than paste, which is praise, not a shrug.

vr.q: Javier's newsletter article comparing the garden club's two scarecrows was biased, so it ____.
c: found fault with both of them
praised only the one he had made
was printed on bright green paper
