vr.e: Biased means unfairly favoring one side over another. A biased article leans toward one scarecrow, here the one Javier made himself, instead of judging both the same way.

y.A: Praised both of them equally is what a fair article would do; biased means favoring one side, not treating both the same.
y.B: Found fault with both of them reads biased as harsh, but an article that is hard on both scarecrows still treats them the same; biased means favoring one.
y.D: Was printed on bright green paper tells how the article looked, but the word so asks what being biased made it say.

vr.q: Izzy's woodworking club had a consensus about which bench design to build, so ____.
c: the club meets on Friday afternoons
almost everyone wanted the same design
the members argued about it for a month
vr.e: A consensus is a general agreement reached by a whole group. If the club had a consensus about the bench, almost every member wanted the same design.

y.A: One teacher gave them permission mixes up consensus with consent, which means permission from one person; a consensus is an agreement shared by the whole group.
y.B: The club meets on Friday afternoons tells when the club gathers, but the word so asks what having a consensus meant.
y.D: The members argued about it for a month is what happens when a group cannot agree, the opposite of a consensus.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Leon inferred that the bean seedlings were thirsty when he ____.
c: was told so by the club leader
hinted to Kiana that she should water them
vr.e: To infer is to work out what is meant or true from clues. Drooping leaves are a clue, and from them Leon worked out that the seedlings needed water.

y.A: Flipped a coin to decide treats infer as a blind guess; to infer is to work something out from clues, and a coin gives no clue about the plants.
y.C: Was told so by the club leader means someone said it outright; when you infer, nobody tells you, and you work it out from clues yourself.
y.D: Hinted to Kiana that she should water them is implying, sending a hint to someone else; to infer is to be the one who reads the clues.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The trowel from the garden club's shed was inferior to the one Jordan brought from home, so ____.
c: it hung on a hook by the door
it dug faster than his own trowel
its thin blade bent in the hard soil
vr.e: Inferior means lower in quality. The trowel of lower quality is the one that bends when it meets hard soil.

y.A: It had a shorter handle reads inferior as smaller, but inferior means lower in quality, not in size.
y.B: It hung on a hook by the door tells where the trowel was kept, but the word so asks what being inferior led to.
y.C: It dug faster than his own trowel is what a superior tool would do, the opposite of inferior.

vr.q: The friendship bracelet Jada chose to make at craft club had such an intricate pattern that ____.
c: it fit only around her pinky
it took her all week to finish
she finished it in a single recess
it used only three strands of thread
vr.e: Intricate means very complicated, with many small parts carefully connected. A pattern with that many small knots and twists takes a long time to make.

y.A: It fit only around her pinky reads intricate as tiny; the parts of an intricate pattern are small, but the bracelet itself can be any size.
y.C: She finished it in a single recess is what would happen with a simple pattern, the opposite of an intricate one.
y.D: It used only three strands of thread describes a plain pattern with few parts; an intricate pattern has many small parts carefully connected.

vr.q: Isabel did a painstaking job of measuring the boards for the birdhouse her club was building, so ____.
c: her fingers were sore for a week
each board fit exactly in its place
each board came out an inch too long
each board came out an inch too short
vr.e: Painstaking means done with great care and attention to every detail. Measuring with that much care makes each board the right size, so it fits exactly where it belongs.

y.A: Her fingers were sore for a week reads the pain in painstaking as hurting, but painstaking means very careful, not painful.
y.C: Each board came out an inch too long is what careless, hurried measuring would cause, the opposite of painstaking work.
y.D: Each board came out an inch too short is another mistake careless measuring makes; painstaking measuring gets every board right.

vr.q: Julian's grandmother is a prominent member of the town garden club, so ____.
c: few members have ever heard of her
everyone in the club knows her name
everyone notices her bright yellow hat
she may become a great gardener someday
vr.e: Prominent, said of a person, means important and well known. A prominent member of a club is one whose name everyone there knows.

y.A: Few members have ever heard of her is what would follow if she were unknown, the opposite of prominent.
y.C: Everyone notices her bright yellow hat would make her conspicuous, easy to notice; prominent adds importance, being well known for who she is.
y.D: She may become a great gardener someday mixes up prominent with promising, which means likely to do well in the future; a prominent member is already important and well known.

vr.q: Before the cardboard boat race at Joaquin's school, the judges gave every boat a rigorous inspection, so they ____.
c: failed every boat after one glance
had picked the winner ahead of time
checked every seam and strip of tape
waved every boat through without looking
vr.e: Rigorous means extremely careful, thorough and demanding. A rigorous inspection looks at every part of every boat, down to each seam and strip of tape.

y.A: Failed every boat after one glance is strict without being careful; a rigorous inspection is thorough, and one glance is not.
y.B: Had picked the winner ahead of time reads the rig in rigorous as rigged, meaning fixed by cheating; rigorous means careful and thorough.
y.D: Waved every boat through without looking is what careless judges would do, the opposite of a rigorous inspection.

vr.q: The table Kieran built for the chess club is stable, so ____.
c: players can lean on it safely
it is kept in the school library
its legs are held on with staples
it tips over when anyone leans on it
vr.e: Stable means steady, not likely to tip, wobble or fall. A table that holds steady under the players' elbows is safe for them to lean on.

y.B: It is kept in the school library tells where the table stays, but the word so asks what being stable means for the players.
y.C: Its legs are held on with staples mixes up stable with staple, a word one letter away; stable means steady and not likely to tip.
y.D: It tips over when anyone leans on it describes a wobbly table, the opposite of a stable one.

vr.q: The caterpillar Luz found in the garden club's flower bed was stationary all morning, so ____.
c: it inched slowly up the stem
Luz could sketch it without rushing
it crawled quickly across the garden
Luz drew it on her best writing paper
vr.e: Stationary means not moving, staying in one place. A caterpillar that stayed still all morning made an easy model, so Luz could take her time sketching it.

y.A: It inched slowly up the stem is still moving, only slowly; stationary means not moving at all.
y.C: It crawled quickly across the garden is the opposite of stationary, which means staying in one place.
y.D: Luz drew it on her best writing paper mixes up stationary with stationery, which means paper for writing letters.

vr.q: Imani's report on the garden club's pumpkins was entirely subjective, so ____.
c: it was pinned up beside the door
it never wandered off its subject
it listed the weight of each pumpkin
it said which pumpkins she liked best
vr.e: Subjective means based on personal feelings, taste or opinion. When a report is entirely subjective, it tells what the writer likes, not facts anyone could check.

y.A: It was pinned up beside the door tells where the report hung, but the word so asks what being subjective meant for what it said.
y.B: It never wandered off its subject reads subjective as staying on a subject, but subjective means based on personal feelings or taste.
y.C: It listed the weight of each pumpkin gives facts anyone can check on a scale, which would make the report objective, the opposite of subjective.

vr.q: ORATOR most nearly means:
vr.e: An orator is a person who gives speeches, usually a skilled public speaker: the orator spoke so well that the whole crowd rose and cheered.

y.A: Listener is the opposite role: an orator is the one speaking, and the listeners are the audience.
y.B: Operator looks a lot like orator, which is the trap; an operator is someone who runs a machine or answers calls.
y.D: Writer works with words too, but on paper; an orator speaks to an audience out loud.

vr.q: POLL most nearly means:
vr.e: A poll is a survey: you ask many people the same question and count their answers. Our class poll showed that most of us wanted pizza at the party.

y.A: Debate is people arguing for different sides of a question; a poll does not argue, it asks many people and counts what they say.
y.B: Pole sounds exactly like poll, which is the trap; a pole is a long stick, like a flagpole.
y.C: Rumor is a story passed from person to person that may not be true; a poll collects real answers from people and counts them.

vr.q: MINGLE most nearly means:
vr.e: To mingle is to mix together, or to move around a crowd chatting with different people: at the party, the parents mingled while the kids played tag.

y.A: Dance is another thing people do at parties, which is the trap; to mingle is to move around and mix with the crowd, talking to different people.
y.B: Gossip is talk about other people's private business; people may gossip while they mingle, but to mingle is to mix with a crowd.
y.D: Mumble looks a bit like mingle, but it means to speak so quietly and unclearly that others cannot understand.

vr.q: EVADE most nearly means:
vr.e: To evade is to escape or keep away from something, often by being clever or quick: the rabbit evaded the fox by darting into its burrow.

y.A: Catch is what the other side is trying to do: the fox tries to catch the rabbit, and the rabbit evades it.
y.C: Invade rhymes with evade, which is the trap; to invade is to march into a place to take it over.
y.D: Vanish means to disappear completely; someone who evades a chaser is still there, just out of reach.

vr.q: SOAR most nearly means:
vr.e: To soar is to fly or rise high into the air: my kite soared high above the beach on the strong wind.

y.A: Dive goes the other way: a bird that dives plunges straight down, and one that soars rises high.
y.B: Flap is something wings do, which is the trap; to flap is to move wings up and down, while to soar is to fly high.
y.D: Roar rhymes with soar, but it means to make a loud, deep sound, like a lion.

vr.q: APPEASE most nearly means:
vr.e: To appease someone is to calm them down by giving them what they want, to satisfy them: Dad appeased the crying baby with her favorite blanket.

y.A: Annoy is the opposite: annoying someone makes them more upset, and appeasing them calms them down.
y.B: Applaud starts the same way and also pleases people, but to applaud is to clap to show you liked something.
y.C: Ignore is another way to deal with someone upset, but ignoring means paying no attention, while appeasing means giving them what they want so they settle down.

vr.q: EMBARK most nearly means:
vr.e: To embark is to set off or begin, especially on a journey, often by getting on a ship or plane: the explorers embarked on a long voyage across the sea.

y.B: Embarrass starts with the same letters, which is the trap; to embarrass someone is to make them feel foolish in front of others.
y.C: Pack is something you do to get ready for a trip; to embark is to actually set off.
y.D: Return is the other end of the trip: you embark when you set out, and you return when you come back.

vr.q: DEPRIVE most nearly means:
vr.e: To deprive someone of something is to keep it from them or take it away, to deny it to them: the barking dog deprived the whole street of sleep.

y.B: Depart starts like deprive, which is the trap; to depart is to leave, like a train departing the station.
y.C: Provide is the opposite: to provide food is to give it, and to deprive someone of food is to keep it from them.
y.D: Punish is a near miss, since taking away a treat can be a punishment, but to deprive is only to keep something from someone, and it need not be a punishment at all.

vr.q: ERRATIC most nearly means:
vr.e: Erratic means changing in ways nobody can predict, with no steady pattern: the fly's erratic path around the kitchen made it impossible to swat.

y.A: Dramatic rhymes with erratic, but it means full of excitement or strong feeling, like the dramatic ending of a movie.
y.B: Mistaken is a guess from error, a word that starts like erratic; mistaken means wrong, but erratic means unpredictable, and something erratic is not always wrong.
y.C: Steady is the opposite: a steady beat keeps the same pattern, and an erratic one keeps changing.

vr.q: VIGILANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Vigilant means watchful and alert, always on the lookout for danger: the lifeguard stayed vigilant, scanning the water every few seconds.

y.B: Brave is another quality a good guard has, which is the trap; brave means not afraid, while vigilant means always watching.
y.C: Nervous means worried and jumpy; a vigilant lifeguard watches carefully for danger but can stay perfectly calm.
y.D: Violent looks a lot like vigilant, but it means using force to hurt people or things.

vr.q: LOFTY most nearly means:
vr.e: Lofty means very high, rising far above: lofty mountains towered over the valley. Lofty goals are high goals too.

y.B: Lovely starts and ends like lofty, which is the trap; lovely means beautiful, and a lofty tower can be ugly.
y.C: Short is the opposite: a lofty tower rises high, and a short one barely reaches the treetops.
y.D: Steep means sloping sharply, like a hill that is hard to climb; a lofty mountain is very high, and a small hill can be steep.

vr.q: DEVOUT most nearly means:
vr.e: Devout means deeply faithful, especially to a religion; you can also be a devout fan of a team: he is a devout fan who has not missed a home game in five years.

y.A: Devious looks almost like devout, which is the trap; a devious person is sneaky and full of tricks, nearly the opposite of a sincere, devout one.
y.B: Doubtful is the opposite: a devout believer is sure and steady in her faith, and a doubtful one is unsure.
y.D: Greedy is a guess from devour, which looks like devout; devour means to eat hungrily, but devout means deeply faithful.

vr.q: LUMINOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Luminous means giving off light, glowing or shining: the luminous stars on my bedroom ceiling glow after I turn out the lamp.

y.A: Dim is the opposite: a dim light is weak and faint, and a luminous one glows brightly.
y.C: Hot is tempting because campfire coals glow, but luminous is about light, not heat; a glow-in-the-dark sticker is luminous and stays cool.
y.D: Numerous ends like luminous, but it means many in number, like the numerous ants at a picnic.

vr.q: VIGIL most nearly means:
vr.e: A vigil is a time of staying awake, often all night, to keep watch or to pray: Mom kept a vigil by my bed the night I had a high fever.

y.A: Nap is the opposite: a nap is a short sleep, and a vigil is staying awake to keep watch.
y.B: Party is a gathering for fun; people sometimes gather for a vigil too, but a vigil is quiet and serious, a time to keep watch or to remember someone.
y.C: Visit starts like vigil, and you might visit a sick friend, but a visit can be short; a vigil means staying awake and watching, often through the night.

vr.q: TYRANT most nearly means:
vr.e: A tyrant is a ruler who uses power in a cruel, unfair way, or anyone who bosses others around cruelly: the tyrant in the story made the villagers work day and night.

y.B: Giant ends like tyrant, and either one can be the scary character in a story, but a giant is a very large person; a tyrant is a cruel ruler of any size.
y.C: Rebel is someone who fights against a ruler, often against a tyrant, so a rebel is on the other side.
y.D: Servant is the opposite: a servant takes orders, and a tyrant gives harsh ones.

vr.q: RELUCTANTLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Reluctantly means not wanting to do something but doing it anyway: he reluctantly turned off the game and started his homework.

y.A: Angrily means in a mad way; a reluctant person may grumble, but reluctantly only means not wanting to, and you can be reluctant without being angry at all.
y.B: Luckily shares the luc sound inside reluctantly, which is the trap; luckily means by good luck.
y.C: Politely means with good manners; you can agree politely and still be glad to, while reluctantly means not wanting to.

vr.q: DILIGENTLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Diligently means working hard and carefully, without giving up: she practiced her spelling words diligently every night before the test.

y.B: Intelligently ends with the same sounds as diligently, which is the trap; it means in a smart way, and being smart is not the same as working hard.
y.C: Late tells when someone works, like after dark; diligently tells how, with steady effort, at any hour.
y.D: Lazily is the opposite: a lazy worker does as little as possible, and a diligent one keeps at it.

vr.q: Over the summer, Uriel's family worked to ____ the old farmhouse: they patched the roof, replaced the broken windows, and painted every room.
vr.e: The colon lists the work: patching, replacing and painting. That is fixing an old building up. Renovate means to repair something and make it like new.

y.A: Explore means to look around a place you do not know, but the colon lists repairs the family made, not rooms they looked through.
y.B: Inherit means to receive something from someone who has died; it might be how they got the farmhouse, but it is not the work the colon lists.
y.C: Inspect means to look something over carefully, but the colon lists work done with tools, patching, replacing and painting, not just looking.

vr.q: Grandpa Walter is hardly ____: he has eaten the same breakfast, two eggs and toast, every morning for forty years.
vr.e: Hardly means almost not at all. Eating the same breakfast for forty years shows he never changes his mind, so he is hardly fickle. Fickle means changing your mind often.

y.B: Hungry fits the word breakfast, but the sentence is about eating the same thing for forty years, which shows how steady he is, not how hungry.
y.C: Loyal fits a man who has stuck with one breakfast for forty years, but hardly turns the blank into what he is not.
y.D: Predictable describes Grandpa exactly, and that is the trap: hardly means the blank is what he is not, so it needs the opposite.

vr.q: The cabin was pitch dark, but as Yohan's eyes adjusted, he noticed a faint ____ of light under the door.
vr.e: But turns from pitch dark to something he could see, and faint says it was small. Glimmer means a faint, flickering light.

y.A: Blaze is a big, bright fire, much too strong to be called faint, and it would have lit the whole cabin.
y.B: Echo is a sound that bounces back, but he noticed it with his eyes, and the sentence says of light.
y.D: Shadow goes with pitch dark, the part but turns away from; a shadow is where light is missing, not something faintly shining.

vr.q: Although many scientists doubted Alfred Wegener when he first said, in 1912, that the continents slowly drift across Earth's surface, his idea would eventually ____.
vr.e: Although sets up a turn: doubted at first, but in the end the idea won out. Prevail means to win out or be accepted after a struggle.

y.A: Collapse goes with the doubting scientists, but although promises the opposite of how it started.
y.C: Vanish would mean the idea disappeared, which is what the doubters expected, not the turn although signals.
y.D: Wander borrows the drifting continents from the sentence, but an idea that wanders is not one that wins out.

vr.q: Valeria had looked pale and nervous all morning, but when the judges announced her name as the winner, her face was suddenly ____.
vr.e: But and suddenly signal a change from pale and nervous, and winning makes a face light up. Radiant means glowing with happiness.

y.A: Furious means very angry, and nothing about winning makes a face angry.
y.B: Pale is how Valeria looked all morning, and but and suddenly say her face changed.
y.D: Weary means worn out, and hearing that you won does not wear you out; but and suddenly point to a happy change.

vr.q: When Yuki stirred a drop of black paint into the bright red, it turned a darker ____, closer to the color of cherries.
vr.e: The sentence explains itself: the paint became closer to the color of cherries. Hue means a color, or a shade of a color.

y.B: Scent is a smell, and adding black paint changes how the paint looks, not how it smells.
y.C: Texture is how something feels to the touch, and one drop of paint changes the color, as the end of the sentence says.
y.D: Volume is how much space something fills, and one drop hardly changes that; the sentence is about color.

vr.q: Rather than throw out the whole class constitution, the students voted to ____ it by adding one new rule about sharing art supplies.
vr.e: Rather than tells you they did not throw it out, and adding one new rule shows what they did instead: changed it a little. Amend means to change or correct a rule or document.

y.A: Abolish means to end something completely, which is the throwing out that rather than rules out.
y.C: Memorize means to learn by heart, but adding a rule changes the constitution rather than committing it to memory.
y.D: Sign means to write your name on it, which adds no rule; adding a rule changes what the document says.

vr.q: Zack is ____: when his older sister told him spaghetti grows on trees, he asked Dad if they could plant some in the backyard.
vr.e: The example shows Zack believing an obvious joke. Gullible means easily fooled.

y.A: Generous means happy to give and share, which has nothing to do with believing a silly story.
y.C: Selfish means caring only about yourself, but nothing in the example is about sharing or keeping things; it shows Zack believing a joke.
y.D: Skeptical means doubting what you are told, the opposite of a boy who believes spaghetti grows on trees.

vr.q: In many kingdoms long ago, a ruler's ____, an official order that everyone had to obey, was read aloud in the streets.
vr.e: The words after the blank define it: an official order that everyone had to obey. An edict is an official order from someone in power.

y.A: Ballad is a song that tells a story; it might be sung in the streets, but no one has to obey a song.
y.B: Diary is a private journal of someone's days, not an order read aloud for everyone to obey.
y.D: Legend is an old story handed down, not an order from a ruler.

vr.q: After the long, dry summer, the town's reservoir was nearly empty, so everyone hoped the autumn rains would ____ it.
vr.e: So links the problem, a nearly empty reservoir, to what the town hoped for: rain to fill it back up. Replenish means to fill up again.

y.A: Clean means to wash away dirt, but the trouble was that the reservoir was nearly empty, not dirty; it needed more water.
y.B: Measure means to find out how much there is, and rain cannot do that; the town needed water, not a number.
y.C: Pollute means to make dirty, which no town hopes for; the problem was that the water was low, not dirty.

vr.q: Uncle Ulric's chili is famous for its fiery spices, but the soup he made for my sick sister was ____, with no pepper or spice at all.
vr.e: But turns away from fiery spices, and no pepper or spice at all describes the flavor. Bland means mild, without much taste.

y.B: Boiling is about how hot the soup was, while no pepper or spice at all is about how it tasted.
y.C: Fiery is the word for the chili, and but says the soup was different.
y.D: Frozen soup would be a block of ice, and no pepper or spice at all describes the soup's flavor, not how cold it was.

vr.q: Because the novel was far too long to read aloud in one class, Ms. Vance read only a short ____ from its first chapter.
vr.e: Because gives the reason: the whole book was too long, so she read a small part of it. An excerpt is a short passage taken from a longer piece of writing.

y.A: Biography is a book about a real person's life, not a short piece taken out of a novel.
y.B: Epilogue is a short section at the very end of a book, and the sentence says the passage came from the first chapter.
y.D: Glossary is the list of hard words and meanings at the back of a book, not part of the story's first chapter.

vr.q: The race could not ____ until every runner was standing behind the starting line; the officials waited for the last few stragglers.
vr.e: Could not … until tells you the race had to wait for something: every runner at the starting line. What waits for the starting line is the start. Commence means to begin.

y.B: Conclude means to end, and a race ends at the finish line, not the starting line.
y.C: Pause means to stop for a moment, but a race that has not started yet has nothing to pause.
y.D: Relocate means to move to a new place, but the officials were waiting for runners, not for a new spot.

vr.q: The ____ actor refused to eat lunch with the rest of the cast and demanded that his name be printed twice as large as theirs on every poster.
vr.e: The examples show an actor who thinks he is more important than everyone else. Pompous means self-important and showy.

y.A: Calm means quiet and relaxed, but the examples are not about staying relaxed; demanding a bigger name shows he thinks he matters more than everyone else.
y.B: Nervous means worried, but nothing here shows worry; demanding a bigger name shows he thinks he is better than the rest.
y.D: Shy could explain eating lunch alone, but a shy actor would never demand that his name be printed twice as large as everyone else's.

vr.q: Because the salt water in the shallow dish slowly evaporated over the weekend, by Monday only a white ____ of salt crystals was left on the bottom.
vr.e: Because tells you the water went off into the air as it evaporated, and the salt could not go with it. Residue means what is left behind after the rest is gone.

y.A: Bubble is a pocket of air inside a liquid, and the liquid was gone; what was left was solid crystals.
y.B: Droplet is a single drop of water, and the water had all evaporated; what was left was salt.
y.C: Mist is a cloud of tiny water drops in the air, and the water had gone; what was left lay on the bottom of the dish.

vr.q: Many spiders spin webs to catch insects, but a jumping spider ____.
c: has eight legs like other spiders
vr.e: But promises a difference from spinning webs to catch insects, so the jumping spider must catch them another way: it pounces on them.

y.A: Spins a large sticky web is what many spiders do, and but says the jumping spider is different.
y.B: Lives in gardens and homes says where it lives, not how it catches insects, which is what but turns against.
y.D: Has eight legs like other spiders tells how it is the same, when but asks for a difference.

vr.q: Since the rice tasted bland, Usha ____.
c: added a pinch of salt and pepper
vr.e: Bland means without much flavor, so the sensible next step is to add some: a pinch of salt and pepper.

y.A: Ate it with a smile does not follow from since; tasting bland is a reason to fix the rice, not a reason to smile.
y.B: Said it was too spicy is the opposite of bland, which means the rice had hardly any taste at all.
y.C: Complained it was too salty is wrong for the same reason: bland rice has too little flavor, not too much.

vr.q: Although the folk singer never learned to read music, she ____.
c: lived in a small mountain town
read each new song from sheet music
vr.e: Although sets up a surprise: you might expect someone who cannot read music to make little of it, yet she wrote songs people loved.

y.B: Could not play any instrument goes along with not reading music instead of against it, and although needs a surprise.
y.C: Lived in a small mountain town is about where she lived, which has nothing to do with reading music, so although has nothing to turn on.
y.D: Read each new song from sheet music contradicts the first half, since she never learned to read music.

vr.q: An ostrich cannot fly away from danger; instead, it ____.
c: runs away on its long legs
hides in a nest high in a tree
vr.e: Cannot fly rules out escaping through the air, so the ostrich must escape on the ground, and it runs fast on its long legs.

y.A: Flies off to safety reads cannot as can; the sentence says flying is the one thing an ostrich cannot do.
y.C: Has feathers like other birds is true, but it does not follow from being unable to fly; instead asks what the ostrich does when it cannot fly.
y.D: Hides in a nest high in a tree would mean getting up there, which a bird that cannot fly cannot do.

vr.q: Because the library's air conditioner broke on the hottest day of the year, the librarian ____.
c: closed early for the winter holidays
vr.e: Because tells you the ending answers the problem: a broken air conditioner on the hottest day. Opening the windows lets in a breeze to cool the room.

y.A: Turned up the heat would make a hot library hotter, the opposite of what the problem needs.
y.C: Handed out wool blankets is what you do when people are cold, not on the hottest day of the year.
y.D: Closed early for the winter holidays is about a winter break, while the problem is a broken air conditioner on the hottest day of the year.

vr.q: DISCRETION most nearly means:
c: the power to decide for yourself
a rule that must always be followed
vr.e: When a trip is “left to the principal's discretion,” she has the power to decide; a rule that must be followed is the opposite of leaving a choice to someone.

y.B: A loud and public complaint is an outcry or a protest; discretion points the other way, at quietly being trusted to make the choice yourself.
y.C: A rule that must always be followed leaves nobody any choice, and discretion is exactly the opposite — it is what you have when the choice is left up to you.
y.D: A careful written record is a log or a register, but discretion is not something written down; it is the freedom to decide.

vr.q: UNANIMOUS most nearly means:
c: agreed to by every single member
decided by one person in charge
put off until a later meeting
vr.e: A unanimous vote is one in which everyone agrees. The look-alike word is anonymous, which means the name is not known.

y.B: A decision made by one person in charge is a decree, an order given from the top; unanimous means every single member agreed, not just the one in charge.
y.C: Putting something off until a later meeting is postponing it, which is about when the decision is made, not about how many people agreed.
y.D: Kept secret from every member is not what unanimous means — that word, with a u, means every single member agreed. You may be thinking of anonymous, which does not mean secret either: there the thing is out in the open and only the name behind it is unknown.

vr.q: CONSPICUOUS most nearly means:
c: acting in a sneaky, guilty way
vr.e: A conspicuous stain is one everyone sees at once. Suspicious (sneaky) and conscientious (careful) are the two look-alike words that do not mean the same thing.

y.A: Someone extremely careful about details in their work, because they want it done properly, is conscientious — the word that looks and sounds like this one; conspicuous is about being easy to see.
y.B: Something kept carefully out of sight is hidden, which is the opposite of conspicuous — a conspicuous thing is right there where you cannot miss it.
y.D: Acting in a sneaky, guilty way is suspicious, another look-alike word; something conspicuous simply stands out where everyone notices it, with no guilt about it at all.

vr.q: BENIGN most nearly means:
vr.e: A benign remark or a benign old dog does no harm; none of the other choices carries the idea of harmlessness.

y.B: Large and very heavy is massive or bulky, and size has nothing to do with benign — a huge old dog can be perfectly benign.
y.C: Quick and noisy describes how something moves and sounds, while benign describes whether it can do you any harm.
y.D: Sharply critical of others means finding fault with people, which is the opposite of benign — a benign remark hurts nobody.

vr.q: PREDICAMENT most nearly means:
c: a hard spot to get out of
a promise made in front of a crowd
a guess about what will happen next
a long delay before an event
vr.e: Being locked out in the rain with no phone is a predicament — a situation you cannot easily escape. The look-alike word is prediction, a guess about the future.

y.B: A promise made in front of a crowd is a pledge or a vow, but a predicament is trouble you are stuck in, not something you promised.
y.C: A guess about what will happen next is a prediction, the look-alike word; a predicament is the fix you are already in.
y.D: A long delay before an event is a wait or a postponement, which is about time passing, while a predicament is a difficulty you cannot easily get out of.

vr.q: REMINISCE most nearly means:
c: to remind someone of a chore
to plan carefully for next year
to talk fondly about times gone by
vr.e: To reminisce is to look back and share memories, the way grandparents do about their childhood; reminding, apologizing, and planning all point at the present or future.

y.A: To remind someone is to make them think of something they still have to do, while to reminisce, which looks similar, is to look back at the past for pleasure.
y.B: To apologize is to say sorry for something you did wrong, and reminiscing is simply sharing stories about the past, with no fault in it.
y.C: To plan carefully for next year looks forward to what has not happened yet, and reminiscing looks the other way, back at what already has.

vr.q: WANE most nearly means:
c: to get smaller little by little
vr.e: Interest that wanes fades bit by bit, the way a waning moon shrinks each night; its partner word wax means to grow.

y.B: To break apart suddenly is to shatter, but waning is slow and gradual, the way the moon loses a sliver each night.
y.C: To stay exactly the same is to remain constant, but something that wanes is changing all the while by growing less.
y.D: To grow larger and brighter is to wax, wane's partner word; wane is the shrinking half of the pair.

vr.q: LITERAL most nearly means:
c: spoken in a very loud voice
having to do with books and authors
taking words in their exact meaning
vr.e: The literal meaning of “raining cats and dogs” would be actual animals falling from the sky. Literary, the look-alike word, is about books.

y.A: Spoken in a very loud voice is about how something is said, not about what the words mean, and literal is entirely about meaning.
y.B: Having to do with books and authors is literary, the look-alike word with two r's; literal has one r and means taking words exactly as they stand.
y.D: Full of colorful comparisons describes figurative language, which is the opposite of literal — the literal meaning is the plain one, with no comparison in it.

vr.q: SUBORDINATE most nearly means:
vr.e: In “cost was a subordinate concern,” cost mattered less than the main issue; something subordinate ranks below, never above or equal.

y.B: Being in charge of everyone else makes you superior, and a subordinate is the one ranked below, not above.
y.C: Exactly equal in rank means neither one stands above the other, but subordinate always means lower than something else.
y.D: Needed more than anything else is essential, and subordinate says the opposite — that this concern matters less than the main one.

vr.q: COMPACT most nearly means:
c: spread out over a wide area
vr.e: A compact kitchen fits everything into a small area; compact says nothing about softness, single use, or wide spread.

y.A: Used only one time is disposable, which is about how often you use a thing, not about how much room it takes up.
y.C: Made of very soft material is about what a thing is made of, while compact is about how tightly it is packed into a small space — a compact kitchen can be full of soft things.
y.D: Spread out over a wide area is the opposite of compact, which means everything gathered neatly into a small space.

vr.q: Starting a bakery takes more ______ than most people expect: ovens, rent, and flour must all be paid for before the first loaf is sold.
vr.e: Capital is the money and resources needed to start or run a business, which is exactly what the ovens, rent, and flour require.

y.A: A trace is a tiny amount of something, or a mark it leaves behind, which is the opposite of the large sum ovens and rent cost.
y.B: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, like a wildlife sanctuary, and a new bakery needs money rather than shelter.
y.D: A conflict is a fight or a disagreement, and this sentence is about what must be paid for before the first loaf is sold, not about anyone quarrelling.

vr.q: Mr. Alvarez graded the ______ of each essay — the ideas and the evidence — rather than the neatness of the handwriting.
vr.e: Here content means what is inside the essay — the ideas and the evidence — rather than how much was written (volume); this is a different meaning from “content with her meal,” which means satisfied.

y.A: Volume can mean how much there is of something — how many pages an essay runs to — and Mr. Alvarez is grading the ideas inside it, not the amount.
y.B: Discipline is training yourself to keep at something and behave well, which is a habit a person has, not something written inside an essay.
y.C: Stock is the supply of goods a shop keeps ready to sell, so it has nothing to do with the ideas and evidence in an essay.

vr.q: Our science teacher wrote the ______ “habitat” on the board and asked us to explain what it names.
vr.e: A term is a word or expression used for something — a different meaning from a school term or the terms of a contract.

y.A: A riddle is a puzzling question meant to be guessed at, but "habitat" is not a puzzle — it is a word with a settled meaning.
y.B: A rumor is a story passed from person to person that may well not be true, and "habitat" is a word from science, not gossip.
y.D: A custom is something a group has long been in the habit of doing, like a holiday tradition, and "habitat" is a word, not a practice.

vr.q: Grandma keeps the first ______ of the old encyclopedia, the one covering A through C, beside her chair.
vr.e: A volume is one book of a set; “the one covering A through C” rules out the loudness and the amount meanings.

y.B: A verdict is the decision reached at the end of a trial, which has nothing to do with a book beside Grandma's chair.
y.C: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, such as a bird sanctuary, and an encyclopedia is a set of books, not a refuge.
y.D: Stock is the supply of goods a shop keeps to sell, so a shop might hold a stock of encyclopedias, but one book of the set is a volume.

vr.q: When the storm knocked out the power, the fire department ______ assistance to every family on the block, delivering water and blankets before midnight.
vr.e: To render assistance is to give it, which is exactly what delivering water and blankets describes; refusing or suspending help would mean the opposite, and to eradicate something is to wipe it out completely.

y.A: Suspended means stopped for a while with the idea of starting again later, but the fire department did not pause its help — it carried water and blankets out that same night.
y.B: Eradicated means wiped out completely, the way a disease can be eradicated; help given to families is handed over, not destroyed.
y.C: Refused means said no and would not do it, which is the opposite of a crew delivering water and blankets to every family before midnight.

vr.q: The museum applied for a ______ from the city and used the money to repair its leaking roof.
vr.e: A grant is a sum of money given for a purpose; “used the money” shows this is the noun, not the verb “to grant permission.”

y.A: A warning tells you trouble may be coming so you can get ready for it; a warning from the city would not have paid for a new roof.
y.B: A custom is a way of doing something that people have kept up for years, like a birthday custom — it is a habit, not money a museum can apply for.
y.C: A verdict is the decision a jury or a judge reaches at the end of a trial, and nobody is being judged here; the museum was given money.

vr.q: Because no ferry ran on Sundays, the team had to ______ a boat to reach the island for the tournament.
vr.e: To charter a boat or a bus is to hire it for private use — the verb sense, not the city charter that is a founding document.

y.B: Stifle means to smother something or hold it back, the way you stifle a yawn in class; you can stifle a laugh, but you cannot stifle a boat.
y.C: Eradicate means to get rid of something completely, like eradicating the weeds from a garden — the team needed to hire a boat, not destroy one.
y.D: Suspect means to think something may be true before you have proof; the team's problem is not a doubt about the boat, it is having no boat at all.

vr.q: Ticket sales began to ______ in the third week, dropping from four hundred a night to barely fifty.
vr.e: The numbers fall from 400 to 50, so decline here means to go steadily down, not to turn down an invitation.

y.A: Retaliate means to strike back at someone who has hurt you first, but ticket numbers are not paying anybody back — they are simply falling.
y.B: Cultivate means to tend something so that it grows, the way a gardener tends a row of beans; sales going from four hundred to fifty are shrinking, not growing.
y.C: Strive means to try hard at something, which says nothing about numbers falling from four hundred to fifty.

vr.q: The vet spoke in a ______ voice and moved slowly, and the frightened kitten stopped shaking.
vr.e: Tender here means gentle and kind, which is what calms the kitten; the sore-to-the-touch meaning of tender would not describe a voice.

y.A: Domestic means having to do with the home — domestic chores, a domestic cat — so it can describe a household, but not the sound of someone's voice.
y.C: Tangible means solid enough to touch, like a receipt you can hold in your hand; a voice can be heard but never touched, and it is the vet's kindness that calms the kitten.
y.D: Restless means unable to keep still or settle down, which is how the frightened kitten was — the vet is the opposite, moving slowly and speaking gently.

vr.q: The old radio crackled with so much ______ that we could not make out a single word of the weather report.
vr.e: Static is the crackling noise that blocks a radio signal — a noun, and a different meaning from static as “not changing.”

y.A: A trace is a tiny bit of something left behind, like a trace of mud on the floor; what fills this radio is a loud crackling, which is the opposite of a tiny bit.
y.C: Conflict means a fight or a clash between people or ideas, and a radio crackling on a shelf is making a noise, not having an argument.
y.D: Rust is the reddish-brown flaking that grows on old iron when it gets wet; rust can ruin a radio, but it is something you see, not the crackle you hear.

vr.q: EXPLOIT most nearly means:
c: to take unfair advantage of someone
vr.e: An employer who exploits workers profits from them by paying unfairly; praising, repairing, and handing over involve no unfair use.

y.A: Repairing something with care is mending or restoring it, which leaves a thing better than you found it; someone who exploits people is using them for his own gain instead.
y.C: Praising someone in public is complimenting or commending them, which is treating them well; exploiting them is treating them unfairly.
y.D: Handing something over willingly is surrendering or giving it up, and the giving is your own choice; exploiting is taking advantage of someone who has no such choice.

vr.q: STRIVE most nearly means:
c: to wait for someone else to act
to try hard over a long time
vr.e: To strive for a goal is to keep making real effort toward it; each of the other choices describes not making that effort.

y.A: Waiting for someone else to act is being passive and leaving the work to others, while striving is effort you make yourself.
y.B: Wandering with no plan is roaming or drifting, going wherever you happen to end up; someone who strives is heading somewhere on purpose.
y.D: Giving up quickly is quitting, which is exactly what striving is not — you strive by keeping at something even when it is hard.

vr.q: DISCIPLINE most nearly means:
c: a talent a person is born with
a piece of unexpected good luck
vr.e: The discipline to practice every day is trained control over your own behavior, not a mood, a natural gift, or luck.

y.A: A sudden burst of anger is an outburst, or losing your temper — a feeling that takes hold of you; discipline is the steady self-control that stops feelings taking hold.
y.B: A talent a person is born with is a gift, something you have without working for it; discipline is trained, which is the whole point of the word.
y.D: A piece of unexpected good luck is a stroke of fortune that arrives by chance; discipline is built on purpose, a little at a time, and chance has nothing to do with it.

vr.q: FEISTY most nearly means:
c: polite and quiet in a crowd
vr.e: A feisty puppy barks boldly at a much larger dog — full of spirit and unwilling to back down.

y.B: Shy and easily frightened is timid, and a timid puppy backs away from a bigger dog rather than barking boldly at it, which is what a feisty one does.
y.C: Polite and quiet in a crowd is reserved or well-mannered; feisty describes someone spirited and ready to stand up for herself, which is rarely quiet.
y.D: Slow and always sleepy is sluggish, and it takes energy to square up to a much larger dog; feisty is full of that energy.

vr.q: PROMPT most nearly means:
vr.e: A prompt reply arrives right away, so prompt is about speed; care, repetition, and group size are different ideas.

y.A: Done by a large group is collective work, everybody's effort together; prompt tells you how soon something happened, not how many people did it.
y.B: Done again from the start is repeated; a prompt reply is a quick one, and a reply can be quick the very first time it is sent.
y.C: Done very carefully is meticulous; prompt is about being quick, and you can be prompt and sloppy, or slow and careful.

vr.q: CULTIVATE most nearly means:
c: to grow and care for over time
to cut down and clear away
vr.e: Farmers cultivate crops and people cultivate friendships — both mean tending something so it develops; cutting down is closer to the opposite.

y.B: Cutting down and clearing away is clearing or felling, which takes a growing thing away; cultivating is the opposite, keeping it growing.
y.C: Copying exactly is imitating or duplicating; cultivating a friendship or a garden means building it up over time, with nothing copied from anybody.
y.D: Buying in large amounts is stocking up; a farmer who cultivates a field works the soil and raises the crop rather than buying it ready-made.

vr.q: DOMESTIC most nearly means:
c: built a very long time ago
having to do with the home
vr.e: Domestic chores are household chores and a domestic animal is one kept at home; the other choices all point away from the home.

y.A: Coming from somewhere outside your own country is what foreign means, and foreign is domestic's opposite — domestic points at home, whether that is your house or your own country.
y.B: Living wild in the forest is being wild or feral; a domestic animal is the tame one kept at home, which is the other end of the same scale.
y.C: Built a very long time ago is ancient; domestic tells you something belongs to the home and says nothing at all about its age.

vr.q: RETALIATE most nearly means:
c: to strike back after being harmed
to go back and fetch something
to say sorry and make peace
vr.e: A team that trips a player after being tripped retaliates. Retrieve (fetch) and retreat (pull back) are the look-alike words.

y.B: Moving away from danger is retreating, and retreat looks a lot like retaliate at the start; retaliating means hitting back rather than backing off.
y.C: Going back to fetch something is retrieving it — a dog retrieves a ball — and retrieve is the look-alike word; retaliating is something you do back to a person, not something you go and get.
y.D: Saying sorry and making peace is apologizing and forgiving, the gentlest way a quarrel can end; retaliating is the harshest, striking back at whoever harmed you.

vr.q: Two coaches told Nadia the record was out of reach, but she remained ______ and trained every morning anyway.
vr.e: “Trained every morning anyway” shows she held firmly to her purpose, which is what resolute means; the other three say nothing about determination.

y.A: Whimsical means playful and full of odd little fancies that change from moment to moment; Nadia training every single morning is steady, which is the opposite of whimsical.
y.B: Literal means sticking to the plain, exact meaning of words rather than picture-language; it describes how a person reads or speaks, not how firmly she holds to a goal.
y.C: Subordinate means lower in rank, placed under somebody else's authority; the sentence is not about Nadia's rank, it is about her refusing to give up on the record.

vr.q: The class had plenty of theories about the missing mascot but no ______ proof — no photograph, no footprint, nothing they could point to.
vr.e: Tangible proof is solid evidence you can touch or point to, which is exactly what the missing photograph and footprint would have been.

y.A: Unanimous means agreed on by everybody, with nobody against it; the class could all agree on a theory and still have no photograph and no footprint.
y.C: Remote means far away — a remote farmhouse, or a remote chance, meaning a very slight one — but what the class lacks is proof solid enough to point to, not proof from somewhere distant.
y.D: Benign means harmless and kindly, the way a benign smile does nobody any damage; proof is either there or missing, and that is not a question of harm.

vr.q: A classroom rule that punishes every mistake can ______ the very curiosity the teacher hopes to build.
vr.e: To stifle something is to smother or hold it back, and a rule that punishes every mistake crushes the curiosity the teacher wants; cultivating curiosity would grow it instead, exploiting means using something unfairly for your own gain, and nothing here is being measured.

y.A: Exploit means to use someone or something unfairly for your own gain; the rule in the sentence is crushing curiosity, not making a profit from it.
y.B: Measure means to find out how much or how big something is; a rule that punishes every mistake is not measuring curiosity, it is snuffing it out.
y.C: Cultivate means to tend something so that it keeps growing, which is what the teacher hopes to do with curiosity — the rule does the reverse.

vr.q: The general finally learned that his most trusted messenger had been ______ all along, quietly carrying the battle plans to the enemy.
vr.e: Treacherous here means disloyal — betraying the trust placed in him — a different sense from a treacherous mountain road. Conspicuous is ruled out by “quietly.”

y.B: Compact here means packed neatly into a small space, like a compact kitchen — a size or a shape, which says nothing about whether a person can be trusted.
y.C: Conspicuous means easy to notice, standing out so that everyone sees you; this messenger worked quietly, which is why nobody caught him for so long.
y.D: Literal means taking words at their exact, plain meaning; a messenger can be literal-minded and still be perfectly loyal, so it says nothing about carrying plans to the enemy.

vr.q: The offer sounded ______ to Mom: a free bicycle for anyone who simply forwarded the message to ten friends.
vr.e: Something dubious is doubtful and not to be trusted, which is how an offer that seems too good to be true sounds; the other three say nothing about doubt.

y.A: Static means staying the same without changing, and as a noun it is the crackle that spoils a radio; neither one describes an offer that sounds too good to be true.
y.B: Unanimous means agreed on by everyone, with nobody disagreeing; only Mom is judging this offer, and what she feels about it is doubt.
y.D: Compact means packed tightly into a small space; the sentence is about how believable the offer is, not about how much room it takes up.

vr.q: The umpires had to ______ the game in the fourth inning, and both teams waited under the bleachers until the lightning had passed.
vr.e: To suspend something is to stop it for a while, which is what umpires do when lightning arrives; extending, announcing, or repeating the game would all keep it going. Suspend can also mean to hang something up.

y.A: Extend means to make something longer or stretch it out, so extending the game would add to it; the lightning made the umpires stop it instead.
y.C: Announce means to tell everybody something openly; the umpires probably did announce their decision, but the word for halting the game while the storm passes is not announce.
y.D: Repeat means to do something over again from the beginning; the teams are waiting under the bleachers for the same game to carry on, not to start afresh.

vr.q: The injured owl was carried to a bird ______ outside town, where volunteers fed it by hand until it was strong enough to hunt again.
vr.e: A sanctuary is a safe place where something is protected, which is what a refuge for hurt birds is; a laboratory is for experiments, a boundary is a line, and a predicament is a situation rather than a place.

y.A: A boundary is the line where one piece of land ends and the next begins; an owl cannot be carried to a line and fed by hand there.
y.B: A laboratory is a room fitted out for experiments and testing; the volunteers are feeding the owl until it can hunt again, which is looking after it, not experimenting on it.
y.C: A predicament is a difficult spot you are stuck in, and the injured owl was certainly in one — but a predicament is a situation, not a place anyone can carry a bird to.

vr.q: By noon there was not a ______ of snow left on the field; the grass was green and dry from one end to the other.
vr.e: A trace is the tiny amount left behind, so “not a trace” means none at all, which fits grass that is green and dry from end to end. Trace can also mean to copy a drawing through thin paper.

y.A: A verdict is the decision reached at the end of a trial; snow melting off a field is weather, and there is nothing for anyone to decide.
y.C: Volume means how much of something there is — it can also mean loudness, or one book of a set; here the word needed is for the tiniest bit left behind, which is what a trace is.
y.D: A custom is something people have done the same way for years, like a family custom at Christmas; snow on a field is weather, not a habit.

vr.q: After the third sandwich went missing from the counter, Dad began to ______ that the new puppy was not as innocent as she looked.
vr.e: To suspect is to start believing something is true before you have proof, which is what the missing sandwiches lead Dad to think about the puppy; he is not telling anyone, he is far from certain, and he plainly has not forgotten.

y.A: Forget means to let something slip out of your mind, and Dad has done the opposite — three missing sandwiches are very much on it.
y.B: Announce means to tell people something openly; Dad is only beginning to think the puppy is guilty, and he has not declared it to anyone.
y.C: Guarantee means to promise something for certain, and Dad is nowhere near certain — he has a hunch, a puppy, and three missing sandwiches.

vr.q: SUFFRAGE most nearly means:
vr.e: Suffrage is the right to vote: in 1893 New Zealand became the first country to give women suffrage in its national elections.

y.A: Paying taxes is a duty of citizens, as voting is, but suffrage is the right to vote, not money paid to the government.
y.C: Great suffering is the trap in the suff- at the start, which looks like suffer; suffrage has nothing to do with pain.
y.D: Running for office means trying to be elected yourself; suffrage is the right to cast a vote for someone.

vr.q: CAPITAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Capital is money or wealth, especially money used to make more money: a bank lends capital to farmers so they can buy seed and tractors. A capital is also the city where a state's or country's government meets.

y.A: Caption starts with cap- like capital, but a caption is the line of words printed under a picture.
y.B: Country comes from the other meaning, a capital city, but even that meaning names a city, the place where a government meets, not a whole country.
y.D: Tax is money people must pay to the government; capital is money or wealth that a person or business owns and puts to work.

vr.q: CONSENT most nearly means:
vr.e: Consent is permission, saying yes to what someone else wants to do: you need the owner's consent before you fish in a private pond.

y.A: Contest looks a lot like consent, but a contest is a competition, such as a spelling bee.
y.C: Promise is saying that you yourself will do something; consent is saying that someone else may.
y.D: Request is the asking, as when you ask a farmer whether you may fish in his pond; consent is the yes that answers it.

vr.q: CONSPICUOUS most nearly means:
vr.e: Conspicuous means easy to see or notice, standing out so that it is obvious: the tall white lighthouse was conspicuous from miles out at sea.

y.A: Curious ends in -ous and sounds a little like conspicuous, but curious means eager to know about things.
y.B: Invisible is the opposite: something invisible cannot be seen at all, and something conspicuous is impossible to miss.
y.D: Suspicious sounds almost like conspicuous, but suspicious means making people think something is wrong; a conspicuous thing simply stands out.

vr.q: CONTENT most nearly means:
vr.e: To be content is to be satisfied, happy with what you have and not wanting more: the puppy was content to lie in the sunny spot on the porch all afternoon.

y.A: Confident looks a little like content, but it means sure of yourself and your abilities.
y.B: Excited means stirred up and eager for something to happen; a content person is calm and satisfied with things as they are.
y.D: Sleepy is how a content cat may look, curled up after a meal, but sleepy means ready to fall asleep, and content means satisfied.

vr.q: ELABORATE most nearly means:
vr.e: Elaborate means worked out in great detail, with many parts: the elaborate sandcastle had towers, bridges, a moat and tiny windows made of shells.

y.A: Celebrated looks a little like elaborate, but it means famous and praised by many people.
y.C: Secret means kept hidden; an elaborate plan may also be secret, but elaborate means it has many detailed parts.
y.D: Simple is the opposite: a simple sandcastle is one plain mound, and an elaborate one has many detailed parts.

vr.q: PREJUDICE most nearly means:
vr.e: A prejudice is a bias, an unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts, often against a whole group of people: Jackie Robinson faced prejudice when he became the first Black player in modern Major League Baseball in 1947.

y.B: Justice ends the same way as prejudice but means nearly the opposite: justice is fairness, and a prejudice is an unfair opinion.
y.C: Rumor means a story passed around that may not be true; a prejudice is an unfair opinion about people, formed before knowing them.
y.D: Verdict is the decision a judge or jury reaches at the end of a trial, after hearing the facts; a prejudice is a judgment made before the facts.

vr.q: REMOTE most nearly means:
vr.e: Remote means distant, far away from towns and people: the lighthouse keeper's island was so remote that the mail boat came only once a month.

y.B: Mountainous means full of mountains; many remote places are in the mountains, but remote means far from towns and people, wherever the place is.
y.C: Nearby is the opposite: a nearby store is close at hand, and a remote one is far away.
y.D: Scenic means having beautiful views; a remote spot may be scenic, but remote means far away, pretty or not.

vr.q: RENDER most nearly means:
vr.e: To render is to give or provide something, such as help or a service: the doctor in the crowd rendered first aid to the runner who had fallen at the finish line.

y.A: Borrow means to take something for a while and then give it back; to render is to give or provide.
y.C: Hinder sounds a little like render but means getting in someone's way, almost the reverse of rendering help.
y.D: Wonder sounds a little like render, but to wonder is to be curious about something.

vr.q: SKEPTICAL most nearly means:
vr.e: A skeptical person is hard to convince and wants proof before believing something: when her brother said he had seen a bear in the backyard, Lily was skeptical and asked to see a photo.

y.A: Eager to learn describes a curious person; a skeptic also asks questions, but out of doubt, wanting proof before believing.
y.B: Hard to please describes a picky person who is seldom satisfied; a skeptical person is hard to convince, not hard to please.
y.D: Slow to understand describes someone who has trouble following an idea; a skeptical person understands it fine but doubts that it is true.

vr.q: SUSPEND most nearly means:
vr.e: To suspend something is to hang it from above so that it dangles: the museum suspended a whale skeleton from the ceiling of its great hall. Suspend can also mean to stop something for a while.

y.A: Decorate is what you might be doing when you hang streamers or lights, but decorate means to make something look nicer, while suspend means to hang it.
y.C: Spend is hiding inside suspend, but to spend is to use up money or time.
y.D: Suspect looks almost like suspend, but to suspect someone is to doubt them or think they did something wrong.

vr.q: ABIDE most nearly means:
vr.e: To abide by a rule or a decision is to obey it and do what it says: the two teams agreed to abide by whatever the coin toss decided.

y.A: Break is the opposite: to break a rule is to disobey it, and to abide by it is to obey it.
y.B: Decide rhymes with abide, but to decide is to make up your mind; abiding is following what was decided.
y.C: Explain is what a referee or a teacher may do with a rule, telling what it means; to abide by a rule is to obey it.

vr.q: APPRENTICE most nearly means:
vr.e: An apprentice is a learner who works beside an expert to learn a trade: after high school, Leo became an apprentice to a carpenter and built real staircases beside her.

y.A: Customer means someone who comes into a shop to buy; an apprentice works in the shop to learn the trade.
y.B: Inventor means a person who makes up new things; an apprentice is learning how to do work that experts already know.
y.D: Owner means the person a shop belongs to, often the expert who does the teaching; the apprentice is the learner.

vr.q: INTREPID most nearly means:
vr.e: Intrepid means fearless and adventurous, very brave: Amelia Earhart was an intrepid pilot who flew alone across the Atlantic Ocean in 1932.

y.B: Curious means eager to find things out; an explorer may be curious and intrepid, but intrepid means fearless, not full of questions.
y.C: Famous means known by many people; an explorer can become famous for being intrepid, but intrepid means fearless, not well known.
y.D: Rapid ends in -pid like intrepid, but rapid means very fast.

vr.q: TENACIOUSLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Tenaciously means holding on firmly and not giving up, stubbornly: Ruth practiced the hard piano piece tenaciously, every day for a month, until she could play it without a mistake.

y.A: Loosely is the opposite: a loose grip lets go easily, and a tenacious one holds on.
y.C: Tediously looks a little like tenaciously, but it means in a long, boring way.
y.D: Tenderly starts with ten- too, but it means gently and lovingly.

vr.q: Milk snakes have no venom and would rather slither away than bite, so Esme's father told her that the one in the woodpile was ____ and could stay.
vr.e: A snake with no venom that would rather slither away is harmless, so it could stay. Benign means harmless and gentle.

y.B: Enormous means very large, and the snake's size has nothing to do with having no venom or slithering away.
y.C: Malicious means wanting to hurt others, but a snake that would rather slither away than bite means no harm.
y.D: Venomous means having a poisonous bite, but the sentence says milk snakes have no venom.

vr.q: A snowshoe hare's white winter coat hides it in the snow, but when the snow melts early, a white hare on the brown ground becomes ____, and a hungry lynx can pick it out from far away.
vr.e: But turns from hidden to easy to see: a white hare on brown ground stands out. Conspicuous means easy to notice; obvious.

y.A: Camouflaged means hidden by matching the background, which is true in the snow, but the sentence turns to what happens once the snow melts.
y.C: Nocturnal means active at night, and that has nothing to do with a lynx picking the hare out from far away.
y.D: Vigilant means watchful, but the sentence is about how easily the hare is seen, not how well it watches.

vr.q: Halfway across the creek, Eli found himself in a ____: the next stepping-stone was too wobbly to stand on, and the one he had just left had rolled into the water behind him.
vr.e: The colon describes the trouble: Eli could go neither forward nor back. A predicament is a difficult situation that is hard to get out of.

y.A: Dispute means an argument between people, but no one argues in this sentence; Eli's trouble was being stuck.
y.B: Hurry means a rush, but the colon explains a problem with the stones, not a need for speed.
y.D: Puddle fits the creek, but Eli was stuck on a stone in the middle, which is a tricky situation, not a little pool of water.

vr.q: Forty years after their first hike together, Gloria and Hal returned to the canyon rim and began to ____ about that trip, smiling as each of them remembered a different part of the story.
vr.e: They are looking back on a hike from forty years ago and enjoying the memory. Reminisce means to remember and talk about the past.

y.A: Lament means to cry out in sorrow about a loss, but Gloria and Hal were smiling as they remembered.
y.B: Predict means to say what will happen in the future, but their first hike happened forty years earlier.
y.D: Worry means to feel nervous about what might happen, but they were smiling about something already in the past.

vr.q: Instead of naming its trails Trail 1, Trail 2, and Trail 3, the park chose ____ names such as Giggling Brook Path, Upside-Down Pine Loop, and Dragon's Sneeze Ridge.
vr.e: Instead of plain numbers, the park picked silly, made-up names that are fun to say. Whimsical means playful, fanciful and a little quirky.

y.A: Literal means exact and true to the real thing, but a brook cannot really giggle and no dragon sneezes on the ridge.
y.B: Ordinary describes Trail 1, Trail 2, and Trail 3, the plain names that instead of tells you the park did not choose.
y.C: Solemn means serious, and names like Dragon's Sneeze Ridge are anything but serious.

vr.q: Everyone agreed that the judge of the nature photo contest was ____: she gave first prize to her own grandson, even though most people thought his blurry picture of a heron was the worst one there.
vr.e: Giving first prize to her own grandson's blurry photo shows she unfairly favored him. Biased means unfairly favoring one side or person over another.

y.B: Neutral means not taking sides, the opposite of a judge who handed first prize to her own grandson.
y.C: Observant means quick to notice things, but a judge who looked closely would have seen how blurry the photo was.
y.D: Strict means holding everyone to high standards, but a strict judge would never reward the blurriest picture.

vr.q: Gus was ____ about the forecast of sunshine all weekend: dark clouds were already piling up over the mountains, so he packed his rain jacket anyway.
vr.e: The dark clouds made Gus doubt the sunny forecast, so he packed for rain. Dubious means doubtful or unsure about something.

y.A: Careless means not thinking ahead, but Gus packed a rain jacket just in case, which is the opposite of careless.
y.B: Confident means sure, but if Gus had trusted the forecast, he would not have packed his rain jacket.
y.C: Content means satisfied, which fits a sunny forecast, but the clouds and the rain jacket show that Gus did not believe it.

vr.q: Compared with the sturdy hiking boots Ella borrowed from her aunt, her own sneakers were clearly ____ on the rocky trail: they slipped on every wet stone and soon had a hole in one toe.
vr.e: The sneakers slipped and wore through, so they were worse than the boots. Inferior means lower in quality or rank.

y.A: Flawless means without a single fault, but these sneakers slipped on wet stones and got a hole.
y.C: Sturdy describes the borrowed boots, not the sneakers that slipped and wore through.
y.D: Superior means better, the opposite of sneakers that slipped and got a hole while the boots held up.

vr.q: When Dad said it was raining cats and dogs, five-year-old Emil took the words in their ____ meaning and ran to the window to look for falling pets.
vr.e: Emil thought real cats and dogs were falling, exactly as the words say. Literal means exact and word-for-word, the actual meaning of the words.

y.A: Exaggerated describes the saying itself, which stretches the truth to say the rain is heavy, but a boy who heard it that way would not look for falling pets.
y.B: Figurative is the meaning Dad intended, that it was raining very hard, but Emil went looking for real pets instead.
y.D: Secret means hidden, but Emil did not look for a hidden meaning; he took the plain words exactly as they were.

vr.q: Half Dome is one of the most ____ landmarks in Yosemite National Park: its huge rock face towers over the eastern end of Yosemite Valley.
vr.e: A huge rock face towering over a valley stands out and is well known. Prominent means standing out because of size or position, or important and well known.

y.A: Hollow means empty inside, but the colon is about how the rock towers over the valley, not what is inside it.
y.B: Modest means small or plain, and a huge rock face that towers over a valley is neither.
y.C: Obscure means little known or hard to see, the opposite of a giant landmark towering over a valley.

vr.q: The ranger's cabin was so ____ that it took Hamid two full days of hiking to reach it, and the nearest road was forty miles away.
vr.e: Two days of hiking and a road forty miles off show how far away the cabin is. Remote means far away from other places; distant and isolated.

y.A: Compact means small and tightly packed, and the size of a cabin does not explain why it took two days to reach.
y.B: Crowded means full of people, but a cabin forty miles from the nearest road would see very few.
y.D: Spacious means roomy inside, and the size of a cabin does not explain a two-day hike to get there.

vr.q: Gita's favorite ____ about the class camping trip takes only a minute to tell and always gets a laugh: she set up her tent in the dark and woke up to find it in the middle of the trail.
vr.e: The story is short, it is funny, and it really happened to Gita. An anecdote is a short, often funny, true story.

y.B: Critique means a careful judgment of what is good and bad about something, not a funny story about what happened to Gita.
y.C: Fable means a made-up story, often about talking animals, that teaches a lesson, but this one really happened to Gita on the trip.
y.D: Legend means an old story handed down for many years, but this one happened to Gita herself on the class trip.

vr.q: Most birds raise their own chicks, but the common cuckoo is ____: it sneaks its eggs into the nests of other birds and tricks them into raising its young.
vr.e: The cuckoo sneaks and tricks other birds into doing its work. Crafty means clever in a sneaky way; sly.

y.B: Devoted describes most birds, which raise their own chicks, and the sentence turns to how the cuckoo is different.
y.C: Helpless means unable to take care of yourself, but sneaking eggs into other nests and tricking other birds takes cleverness.
y.D: Sincere means honest and meaning what you say, and a bird that tricks others into raising its young is the opposite.

vr.q: Deer ____ salt so strongly that in winter they often wander onto roads to lick up the salt spread there to melt the ice.
vr.e: Wanting salt badly enough to walk onto roads for it is a very strong wish. Crave means to want something very strongly.

y.B: Dread means to fear something that is coming, but the deer go looking for the salt instead of fleeing from it.
y.C: Ignore means to pay no attention, but deer that wander onto roads to lick up salt are paying close attention to it.
y.D: Shun means to keep away from on purpose, but these deer walk right onto roads to get the salt.

vr.q: Even though a sign beside the waterfall clearly told visitors to stay behind the railing, two teenagers chose to ____ it and climbed out onto the slippery rocks.
vr.e: Even though tells you they did the opposite of what the sign said, openly breaking the rule. Defy means to openly refuse to obey.

y.B: Enforce means to make others follow a rule, which is a ranger's job, not something the rule-breakers did.
y.C: Heed means to pay attention to a warning and follow it, the opposite of climbing out onto the rocks.
y.D: Respect means to treat a rule as something that matters, but climbing past the railing shows they did not.

vr.q: During the long drought, the river began to ____ until it was little more than a trickle running between dry stones.
vr.e: With no rain, the river got smaller and smaller until only a trickle was left. Diminish means to become smaller or less.

y.B: Freeze is something rivers do in bitter cold, but a drought is a long time without rain, and the river ended as a trickle between dry stones, not as ice.
y.C: Submerge means to go under water, but here the water itself was disappearing and leaving the stones dry.
y.D: Thaw means to melt from ice back into water, which would give the river more water, not leave a trickle between dry stones.

vr.q: The baby robins pushed one another aside, stretched their necks, and opened their beaks wide, chirping ____ the moment their mother landed on the edge of the nest with a worm.
vr.e: Pushing, stretching and opening wide show chicks that can hardly wait to be fed. Eagerly means in a way that shows you can hardly wait.

y.A: Calmly means in a quiet, relaxed way, but chicks pushing one another aside are anything but calm.
y.C: Reluctantly means without wanting to, but these chicks were stretching toward the worm.
y.D: Sleepily does not fit chicks that are pushing, stretching and chirping the moment food arrives.

vr.q: In 1925, ____ teams of sled dogs and their drivers raced through blizzards to carry medicine to Nome, Alaska, where many children were sick with a dangerous disease.
vr.e: Racing through blizzards to bring medicine to sick children was brave and noble. Gallant means brave and noble, or very polite and kind.

y.A: Cowardly means easily scared, but these teams raced straight through blizzards.
y.B: Frail means weak and easily hurt, but these teams were strong enough to race through blizzards.
y.D: Selfish means caring only about yourself, but the teams faced the storms to help sick children in a faraway town.

vr.q: Fatima had friends in both cabins and did not care which one got more, so the counselors trusted her to be ____ when she divided the last bag of marshmallows between them.
vr.e: Fatima did not favor either cabin, so the counselors could trust her to share fairly. Impartial means treating all sides equally and fairly.

y.A: Biased means unfairly favoring one side, but Fatima did not care which cabin got more.
y.B: Hasty means too quick and careless, which no one would trust a person to be when sharing something out fairly.
y.D: Unanimous means agreed on by everyone in a group, and one girl dividing marshmallows cannot be unanimous by herself.

vr.q: The beavers' new dam ____ the flow of the stream, and within a few weeks the water had backed up into a wide, still pond.
vr.e: A dam blocks the stream, so the water slows down and piles up into a pond. Impede means to slow down or block something.

y.A: Drained means let the water run out, but here the water piled up into a pond instead of running away.
y.C: Measured means found out how much there was, and measuring a stream would not make its water back up.
y.D: Propelled means pushed forward, the opposite of what a dam does when it makes a stream back up into a still pond.

vr.q: Elephants seem to ____ when a member of their family dies: they gather quietly around the body and gently touch it with their trunks, sometimes for hours.
vr.e: Staying quietly by the body and touching it gently look like sadness at a loss. Mourn means to feel or show deep sadness after a loss.

y.A: Forget means to stop thinking about something, but elephants that stay beside the body for hours have not put it out of their minds.
y.C: Rejoice means to feel great joy, and nothing about a quiet gathering around a dead family member is joyful.
y.D: Wander means to roam without a plan, but these elephants stay in one place around the body.

vr.q: When the pond first froze, the ice was so clear that Finn could watch fish swimming beneath it, but after a heavy snowfall it was so ____ that he could see nothing below.
vr.e: After the snow, no light got through to show the fish, so Finn saw nothing at all. Opaque means not letting any light through, so you cannot see through it.

y.A: Glassy means smooth and clear like glass, which describes the ice before the snowfall, not after.
y.C: Slippery is true of most ice, but being slippery would not stop Finn from seeing the fish.
y.D: Stagnant means still and not flowing, which can describe pond water, but stillness would not stop Finn from seeing through the ice.

vr.q: When the heat wave dried up the creek, the wildlife rescue center put out a ____ to the town, begging neighbors to leave shallow bowls of water in their yards for thirsty birds.
vr.e: Begging the neighbors for help is an urgent, heartfelt request. A plea is an urgent request, an appeal for help.

y.A: Complaint means saying you are unhappy about something, but the center was begging for help, not grumbling.
y.B: Forecast is a weather word that fits the heat wave, but a forecast tells what the weather will do; it does not beg anyone for help.
y.C: Grant means money given for a special purpose, but the center was not offering anything; it was begging the neighbors for help.

vr.q: The new trail map showed the waterfall on the wrong side of the river, so the park printed corrected copies to ____ the error before the summer hikers arrived.
vr.e: Printing maps with the waterfall in the right place fixes the mistake. Rectify means to fix a mistake or put something right.

y.A: Ignore means to pay no attention, but printing corrected copies is the opposite of ignoring a mistake.
y.B: Inscribe means to write or carve words onto something, but the park printed new maps to remove the mistake, not to set it down.
