y.C: Notice means to see or become aware of something, but the park had already noticed the error; the new copies were printed to fix it.

vr.q: The arrowhead Emeka found in the riverbank turned out to be a ____ more than a thousand years old, left behind by people who hunted in the valley long ago.
vr.e: The arrowhead is something people made and left long ago that has lasted until today. A relic is an object that survives from long ago.

y.A: Fossil means the remains or traces of a plant or animal preserved in rock, but an arrowhead was made by people, not by a living thing turning to stone.
y.B: Pebble means a small, smooth stone shaped by water, but this arrowhead was made and left behind by people.
y.D: Replica means a modern copy of something old, but this arrowhead really was left behind long ago.

vr.q: In the desert, rain is ____: some years only a few light showers fall, with months of dry weather in between.
vr.e: Only a few showers with months in between means very little rain, spread far apart. Sparse means thinly spread out, with only a few here and there.

y.A: Constant means happening all the time, but desert rain comes only now and then, with months of dry weather between.
y.B: Lavish means given in great amounts, the opposite of a few light showers a year.
y.C: Refreshing may be how desert rain feels, but the colon is about how little rain falls, not how it feels.

vr.q: Lichens cling ____ to bare mountain rock, holding on through howling winds, freezing nights, and blazing sun for hundreds of years.
vr.e: Holding on through wind, cold and heat for centuries means never letting go. Tenaciously means holding on firmly and not giving up.

y.A: Briefly means for a short time, but these lichens hold on for hundreds of years.
y.B: Loosely means not tightly, and a loose hold would never last through howling winds.
y.C: Occasionally means only now and then, but the lichens hold on the whole time, through every wind, night and blazing day.

vr.q: Cher Ami, a pigeon that carried messages for the American army in World War I, showed great ____: although he was shot in the chest and badly hurt in one leg, he kept flying and delivered his message.
vr.e: Flying on through a battle after being badly wounded took great courage. Valor means great courage, especially in battle.

y.A: Cowardice means being too afraid to face danger, the opposite of a bird that kept flying after being shot.
y.B: Malice means wanting to hurt others, and nothing in the sentence shows the pigeon wanting to hurt anyone; it shows him pushing on while hurt.
y.D: Weakness fits how badly he was hurt, but he kept flying anyway, which shows courage, not weakness.

vr.q: Because the big bulldog that naps by the door of Wanda's music shop is benign, customers ____.
c: pat it on the way in
ask Wanda to chain it up
wonder why it sleeps so much
use the side door to avoid it
vr.e: Benign means harmless and gentle. Customers can safely pat a dog that will not hurt anyone.

y.B: Ask Wanda to chain it up is what people want done with a dangerous dog, and benign means this dog is harmless.
y.C: Wonder why it sleeps so much has nothing to do with being harmless, so it does not follow from because.
y.D: Use the side door to avoid it treats the dog as something to fear, the opposite of benign.

vr.q: The mural Ximena painted on the side of the bakery is so conspicuous that ____.
c: drivers see it from far away
it has won every town art prize
Ximena has to show people where it is
the police want to know who painted it
vr.e: Conspicuous means easy to see or notice. A mural that stands out that much catches drivers' eyes from far away.

y.B: It has won every town art prize is about how good the mural is, but conspicuous is about how easy it is to see.
y.C: Ximena has to show people where it is describes a mural that is hard to notice, the opposite of conspicuous.
y.D: The police want to know who painted it mixes up conspicuous with suspicious, which means looking as if something is wrong.

vr.q: The town let families cultivate the empty lot behind the fire station, and by August the lot ____.
c: held a show of local art
was full of beans and squash
had a new bench and a birdbath
vr.e: To cultivate land is to grow crops on it and care for them. A lot the families cultivated all summer would be full of vegetables by August.

y.A: Held a show of local art mixes up cultivate with culture; to cultivate land is to grow plants on it.
y.B: Was covered in tall weeds is what happens to a lot nobody tends, the opposite of cultivating it.
y.D: Had a new bench and a birdbath could be true of any park and says nothing about growing anything.

vr.q: Zahra used discretion when she told the conductor about the spinach in his teeth: she ____.
c: pointed at it during the concert
laughed about it with the audience
talked it over with the whole orchestra
vr.e: Discretion means good judgment about what to say and who should hear it. Whispering backstage told the conductor without embarrassing him.

y.B: Pointed at it during the concert shows his mistake to the whole hall, the opposite of the care that discretion means.
y.C: Laughed about it with the audience would embarrass him in public, which discretion is careful to avoid.
y.D: Talked it over with the whole orchestra mixes up discretion with discussion, and spreads the news instead of keeping it quiet.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Yosef was dubious that the parade would go on in such heavy rain, so he ____.
c: called the town hall to check
studied a map of the parade route
planned to sneak a ride on a float
vr.e: Dubious means doubtful or unsure. Because Yosef doubted the parade would happen, he checked before going.

y.A: Bought a new raincoat gets him ready to stand in the rain and watch, which only makes sense if he were sure the parade would go on; dubious means he doubted it.
y.C: Studied a map of the parade route mixes up dubious with studious, which means fond of studying.
y.D: Planned to sneak a ride on a float mixes up dubious with devious, which means sneaky.

vr.q: The neighborhood volunteers set out to eradicate the graffiti on the park wall, so they ____.
c: added their own names to it
took photos of it for the paper
scrubbed until none of it was left
vr.e: To eradicate something is to wipe it out completely. Scrubbing until none was left got rid of every bit of the graffiti.

y.A: Added their own names to it makes more graffiti, the opposite of wiping it out.
y.B: Painted over just one corner leaves most of the graffiti there, and eradicate means getting rid of all of it.
y.C: Took photos of it for the paper keeps a record of the graffiti instead of removing it.

vr.q: Although Zuri's character in the town play is feisty, in the final scene she ____.
c: sits down to a huge feast
quietly does as she is told
talks back to the bossy king
wears a crown of paper roses
vr.e: Feisty means bold and full of spirit. Although sets up a surprise, and for a feisty character the surprise is quietly doing as she is told.

y.A: Sits down to a huge feast mixes up feisty with feast, and nothing about it is a surprise.
y.C: Talks back to the bossy king is just what a feisty character would do, so it ignores although, which promises a surprise.
y.D: Wears a crown of paper roses says nothing about her spirit, so although has nothing to turn against.

vr.q: Five minutes before the curtain rose, Wendell found himself in a predicament: ____.
c: he knew every line by heart
the zipper on his costume had broken
he could predict how the play would end
the audience was quietly taking its seats
vr.e: A predicament is a difficult situation that is hard to get out of. A broken zipper minutes before the show is that kind of trouble.

y.A: He knew every line by heart is good news, the opposite of being in a predicament.
y.C: He could predict how the play would end mixes up predicament with predict; a predicament is a tough spot, not a guess.
y.D: The audience was quietly taking its seats happens before every show and is no trouble at all.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: When the oldest members of the town band met for lunch, they reminisced about ____.
c: whether to order soup or salad
the parades they played in long ago
the tiniest drums sold in shops today
the songs they would learn in the spring
vr.e: To reminisce is to remember and talk about times gone by. The old band members looked back on parades from long ago.

y.A: Whether to order soup or salad is a choice about right now, and to reminisce is to look back on the past.
y.C: The tiniest drums sold in shops today picks up the mini inside reminisce, but the word is about looking back, not about small things or about today.
y.D: The songs they would learn in the spring looks ahead to the future, the opposite of looking back.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Veda, the conductor, was resolute about ending the concert by nine, so when the crowd begged for one more song, she ____.
c: let the crowd vote on it
wore a long red concert gown
thanked them and said good night
settled an argument between two players
vr.e: Resolute means firmly determined and not changing your mind. Veda had decided to end by nine, so she ended by nine.

y.A: Let the crowd vote on it hands the choice to others, as someone unsure of her plan might; resolute means her mind was made up.
y.B: Wore a long red concert gown describes her clothes, which have nothing to do with how she answered the crowd.
y.D: Settled an argument between two players mixes up resolute with resolve, as in to resolve a quarrel; resolute means firmly decided.

vr.q: When the band on the float behind them kept playing over their song, Wiley's drummers retaliated by ____.
c: tuning their drums before the song
vr.e: To retaliate is to strike back at someone who has done something to you. The drummers answered the noise with even more noise of their own.

y.A: Stopping to let them finish lets the matter go, the opposite of striking back.
y.B: Marching away from the noise mixes up retaliate with retreat, which means to move back.
y.D: Tuning their drums before the song gets the drums ready, which does nothing to pay the other band back.

vr.q: For Vanessa, the art room was a sanctuary, so whenever the lunchroom got too loud, she ____.
c: slipped in to draw in peace
hid in the coat closet instead
vr.e: A sanctuary is a safe, peaceful place to go for shelter. The quiet art room was where Vanessa could escape the noise.

y.A: Fed the class hamster thinks of animal sanctuaries, but here the sanctuary is a calm place for Vanessa herself.
y.C: Hid in the coat closet instead goes somewhere else to escape the noise, but a sanctuary is the safe place you go to, and hers was the art room.
y.D: Complained to the lunch monitor leaves the art room out entirely, so it does not follow from the room being her sanctuary.

vr.q: Unable to stifle his excitement when his name was called for the solo, Xavier ____.
c: forgot the words to his song
let out a whoop the whole hall heard
vr.e: To stifle a feeling is to hold it back. Xavier could not hold his excitement in, so it burst out as a loud whoop.

y.A: Felt too stiff to move mixes up stifle with stiff; to stifle a feeling is to hold it in.
y.B: Nodded calmly and sat down is what someone who could hold in his excitement would do, but Xavier was unable to.
y.C: Forgot the words to his song has nothing to do with holding his excitement back or letting it out.

vr.q: In Yolie's painting, the trees are subordinate to the bright red barn, so the trees ____.
c: are just as bold as the barn
were painted on a summer day
are small and pale in the distance
vr.e: Subordinate means lower in rank or importance. Trees that matter less than the barn are painted small and pale so the barn stands out.

y.A: Hide most of the barn would make the trees more important than the barn, the opposite of subordinate.
y.B: Are just as bold as the barn makes the trees its equal, but subordinate means less important.
y.C: Were painted on a summer day tells when, which does not follow from the trees being less important.

vr.q: When the town gave sixteen-year-olds suffrage, Umar, who had just turned sixteen, ____.
c: joined a march for the right to vote
cast his first vote for mayor that fall
vr.e: Suffrage is the right to vote. Once sixteen-year-olds had it, Umar could vote for mayor.

y.A: Flew into a rage reads the rage at the end of suffrage as anger, but the word means the right to vote.
y.B: Felt miserable all fall mixes up suffrage with suffer; suffrage has nothing to do with pain.
y.C: Joined a march for the right to vote is what he would do if he did not have that right yet, but the town had just given it to him.

vr.q: Wanting to give Grandma a tangible gift for her birthday, Xiu ____.
c: sang her a song over the phone
vr.e: Tangible means real enough to touch. A knitted scarf is a gift Grandma can hold and wear.

y.B: Danced the tango for her mixes up tangible with tango, and a dance cannot be held in your hands.
y.C: Asked her what she wanted does not give her anything yet, so it is not a tangible gift.
y.D: Sang her a song over the phone gives her something to hear, not something to touch, the opposite of tangible.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The old wooden stairs up to the theater's attic were treacherous, so the stage manager ____.
c: sent the youngest actor up for props
roped them off until they were repaired
vr.e: Treacherous means dangerous, often in a way that is hard to see. Stairs that could give way had to be closed off until they were repaired.

y.A: Painted them a cheerful yellow makes the stairs look nicer but does nothing about the danger.
y.B: Searched the attic for treasure mixes up treacherous with treasure; treacherous means dangerous.
y.C: Sent the youngest actor up for props is what you would do with stairs you trusted, the opposite of treacherous.

vr.q: The town choir's choice of a song for the holiday concert was unanimous, so ____.
c: only the director had a say
no one knew who had picked it
no singer asked for a different one
a coin toss broke the tie between songs
vr.e: Unanimous means agreed on by everyone. If every singer agreed, no one asked for a different song.

y.A: Only the director had a say takes the un at the start of unanimous to mean one person, as in unicycle; unanimous means all of one mind, so everyone agreed.
y.B: No one knew who had picked it mixes up unanimous with anonymous, which means without a name.
y.D: A coin toss broke the tie between songs is how a split choir might settle it, the opposite of a choice everyone agreed on.

vr.q: Interest in the town's Friday night square dances began to wane, and each year ____.
c: the town built a bigger hall
fewer couples showed up to dance
vr.e: To wane is to grow smaller or weaker little by little. As interest waned, fewer couples came each year.

y.A: Just as many couples came means interest stayed the same, but to wane is to grow smaller.
y.B: The town built a bigger hall is what a town would do if interest were growing, the opposite of waning.
y.C: The fiddler learned new tunes says nothing about how many people still came.

vr.q: The director wanted a whimsical set for the spring play, so Ulla painted ____.
c: a purple tree with polka dots
a perfect copy of the town hall
a dark, gloomy castle with no windows
vr.e: Whimsical means playful and fanciful. A purple tree with polka dots is the kind of silly, imaginative touch a whimsical set has.

y.A: A plain gray wall is dull and serious, the opposite of playful.
y.C: A perfect copy of the town hall is realistic, while whimsical means fanciful and full of imagination.
y.D: A dark, gloomy castle with no windows is grim, but whimsical means light and playful.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: At halftime, the marching band moved in a compact formation, so ____.
c: they spread out across the whole field
vr.e: Compact means packed closely together into a small space. In a compact formation, the players marched close together.

y.A: Every player faced north mixes up compact with compass; compact means packed closely together.
y.B: They all wore red jackets is about the uniforms, not about how closely the band marched.
y.D: They spread out across the whole field is the opposite of compact.

vr.q: Valentina gave her consent for the town to use her painting of the harbor on the festival poster, so the committee ____.
c: asked her if they could use it
waited for every artist in town to agree
vr.e: Consent is permission given by one person. With Valentina's consent, the committee could put her painting on the poster.

y.B: Chose a different picture is what the committee would do if she said no, the opposite of giving consent.
y.C: Asked her if they could use it misses that consent is permission, and she had already given it.
y.D: Waited for every artist in town to agree confuses consent with consensus; consent comes from one person, and hers was the one that counted.

vr.q: Arriving at the piano recital, Wade felt conspicuous, so he ____.
c: slipped into a seat in the back
wondered whether anyone had seen him
vr.e: To feel conspicuous is to feel that you stand out and everyone can see you, often when you would rather not. Wade wanted to sit where fewer people would notice him.

y.A: Liked the second piece best says nothing about how much he stood out.
y.B: Signed autographs in the lobby confuses conspicuous with prominent, which means famous or important.
y.D: Wondered whether anyone had seen him is how someone who felt unnoticed would feel, the opposite of conspicuous.

vr.q: Xiomara declined her uncle's offer to help with her quilt for the town fair, so she ____.
c: finished it in half the time
declared it the finest quilt there
vr.e: To decline an offer is to politely say no to it. Having turned down her uncle's help, Xiomara sewed the quilt by herself.

y.A: Showed it at the fair would happen either way, so it does not follow from turning down the help.
y.C: Finished it in half the time is what an extra pair of hands would make possible, but she had turned his help down.
y.D: Declared it the finest quilt there mixes up declined with declared, which means announced.

vr.q: When his art teacher asked Vihaan to elaborate on how he made his clay owl, he ____.
c: made the owl twice as big
said owls were his favorite bird
vr.e: To elaborate is to add more detail. Asked to elaborate, Vihaan described each step of making his owl.

y.A: Answered in just one word gives less detail, the opposite of elaborating.
y.B: Made the owl twice as big changes the owl's size, but his teacher asked him to say more about how he made it.
y.D: Said owls were his favorite bird is about owls in general, not about how he made his clay one.

vr.q: Yesenia implied that the band was too loud by ____.
c: asking what the band was called
saying so out loud to the drummer
covering her ears during every song
noticing that other people had left early
vr.e: To imply is to suggest something without saying it outright. Covering her ears during every song hinted that the band was too loud.

y.A: Asking what the band was called says nothing about how loud it was.
y.B: Saying so out loud to the drummer states it directly, while to imply is to hint without saying it.
y.D: Noticing that other people had left early is gathering clues, which is inferring; the one who implies is the one giving the hint.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Because the volunteers at the town's spring cleanup were so industrious, ____.
c: they cleaned the riverbank as well
the mayor had to hire a cleaning crew
a new factory went up beside the park
they spent the day polishing one bench
vr.e: Industrious means hard-working and busy, getting a lot done. The volunteers got so much done that they cleaned the riverbank as well as the park.

y.B: The mayor had to hire a cleaning crew is what would happen if the volunteers were lazy, the opposite of industrious.
y.C: A new factory went up beside the park mixes up industrious with industry, the word for factories and making goods.
y.D: They spent the day polishing one bench is careful, slow work; industrious means busy and getting a lot done.

vr.q: When the director told the cast to break a leg, Zeno took her words in their literal sense, so he ____.
c: forgot every one of his lines
thanked her for the good luck
picked up litter in the aisles
vr.e: Literal means taking words in their exact, word-for-word meaning. Actors say break a leg to mean good luck, but taken literally it sounds like a wish to get hurt.

y.B: Forgot every one of his lines does not follow from how he understood her words.
y.C: Thanked her for the good luck takes the words the way the saying is meant, which is the opposite of taking them literally.
y.D: Picked up litter in the aisles mixes up literal with litter.

vr.q: The town wanted an objective answer to whether the new crosswalk made Main Street safer, so it ____.
c: counted the crashes before and after
asked people whether the street felt safer
vr.e: Objective means based on facts that can be checked, not on feelings or opinions. Counting crashes before and after gives a fact anyone can check.

y.A: Objected to building the crosswalk mixes up objective with object, as in to object to something.
y.B: Painted the crosswalk bright yellow changes the street but answers nothing about whether it is safer.
y.D: Asked people whether the street felt safer collects feelings, which is subjective; objective means based on facts that can be checked.

vr.q: Xander's prejudice against country music meant that, when a country band came to the town fair, he ____.
c: was asked to judge the band
said it was dull before it played
cheered loudest for his cousin's band
bought a ticket to hear it for himself
vr.e: A prejudice is an unfair opinion formed before you know the facts. Xander decided the band was dull before he had heard a note.

y.A: Was asked to judge the band hears the word judge in prejudice, but prejudice means judging too early and unfairly, not being chosen as a judge.
y.C: Cheered loudest for his cousin's band is favoring someone close to him, which is being biased, and it has nothing to do with country music.
y.D: Bought a ticket to hear it for himself is keeping an open mind, the opposite of prejudice, which decides before knowing.

vr.q: On Friday, the director rendered her decision about who would play each part, so that afternoon the students ____.
c: asked the director when she would decide
vr.e: To render a decision is to give it or make it known. Once the director rendered hers, the students could see the cast list.

y.B: Gave up and went home mixes up render with surrender; to render a decision is to give it.
y.C: Auditioned for the parts is out of order, since the auditions had to come before the director could decide.
y.D: Asked the director when she would decide is what they would do if she held her decision back, the opposite of rendering it.

vr.q: The arms of Winnie's new puppet were so rigid that ____.
c: they felt as cold as ice
they could not bend at all
vr.e: Rigid means stiff and unable to bend. Rigid puppet arms could not bend at all.

y.A: They felt as cold as ice mixes up rigid with frigid, which means very cold.
y.C: She tested every stitch twice is being rigorous, which means very thorough; rigid means stiff.
y.D: They flopped around like noodles describes floppy arms, the opposite of rigid.

vr.q: When her little brother announced that the town play had been canceled, Yuna was skeptical, so she ____.
c: cried that her part was gone
vr.e: Skeptical means not easily convinced, so a skeptical person wants proof. Instead of believing her brother, Yuna checked with the director.

y.A: Fed the cat its dinner has nothing to do with whether she believed her brother.
y.B: Stayed home that evening means she believed him right away, the opposite of skeptical.
y.D: Cried that her part was gone also takes his word for it; a skeptical person wants proof before believing news like that.

vr.q: Although the brass band's song list had been static for twenty summers, ____.
c: fans heard new songs every week
the players knew every tune by heart
vr.e: Static means not changing over time. Although sets up a surprise: the songs never changed, yet crowds still came.

y.A: The band wore gold jackets says nothing about the songs, so there is nothing surprising for although to point to.
y.B: Fans heard new songs every week cannot be true of a static list, which stayed the same.
y.D: The players knew every tune by heart is just what you would expect after playing the same songs for years, so it ignores although, which promises a surprise.

vr.q: Because Warren is a subordinate of the town's fire chief, he ____.
c: reports to the chief every day
decides who works on each truck
is not as skilled as the chief is
vr.e: A subordinate is a person lower in rank who works under someone else and reports to them. As the chief's subordinate, Warren reports to the chief.

y.A: Rides on the fire truck is true of firefighters of every rank, so it does not follow from being a subordinate.
y.C: Decides who works on each truck is a choice for whoever is in charge, and a subordinate is the one who is told, not the one who decides.
y.D: Is not as skilled as the chief is confuses subordinate with inferior, which means lower in quality; subordinate is about rank.

vr.q: The artist suspended her glass fish in the gallery's front hall, so visitors ____.
c: waited in suspense for the show
bought their tickets at the door
stepped around them on the floor
vr.e: To suspend something is to hang it from above. Fish hanging over the hall were above the visitors' heads, so they looked up.

y.B: Waited in suspense for the show mixes up suspend with suspense; to suspend the fish is to hang them.
y.C: Bought their tickets at the door would be true wherever the fish were, so it does not follow from hanging them.
y.D: Stepped around them on the floor would be true if the fish had been set down, but suspended means hung from above.

vr.q: Una always abides by the library's quiet rule, so in the reading room she ____.
c: checks out a stack of books
complains that the rule is unfair
vr.e: To abide by a rule is to follow it. Following the quiet rule means speaking only in a whisper.

y.B: Checks out a stack of books is something anyone at a library might do and says nothing about keeping the quiet rule.
y.C: Chats loudly with her friends breaks the rule, the opposite of abiding by it.
y.D: Complains that the rule is unfair argues about the rule instead of following it.

vr.q: Between songs, Yaw told the audience an anecdote, which was ____.
c: a cure for his sore throat
a list of his favorite chords
a short, funny story from his life
a long, invented legend about dragons
vr.e: An anecdote is a short, often funny story about something that really happened. A funny story from Yaw's own life is one.

y.A: A cure for his sore throat mixes up anecdote with antidote, a medicine that works against a poison.
y.B: A list of his favorite chords is not a story at all, and an anecdote is a story.
y.D: A long, invented legend about dragons is a tale, but an anecdote is short and true.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Zelda is Vito's apprentice in his violin shop, so she ____.
c: learns the trade by helping him
tells him how to carve each violin
owns half of the music shop with him
vr.e: An apprentice is a beginner who learns a trade by working for an expert. Zelda learns to make violins by helping Vito.

y.A: Buys her violins from him makes her a customer, while an apprentice works in the shop to learn the trade.
y.C: Tells him how to carve each violin makes her the expert, the opposite of an apprentice.
y.D: Owns half of the music shop with him makes her a partner, but an apprentice is a beginner still learning.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The raccoon in the children's play at the community center is crafty, so to get the bears' picnic basket, it ____.
c: makes a basket out of twigs
shoves the bears out of the way
tricks the bears into looking away
vr.e: Crafty means clever in a sneaky way. A crafty raccoon would trick the bears instead of asking or fighting.

y.A: Makes a basket out of twigs mixes up crafty with crafts, the things you make in art class.
y.B: Asks politely for a sandwich is honest and plain, the opposite of crafty.
y.C: Shoves the bears out of the way is rough, not clever; crafty means sneaky and clever.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Although Vivek craved silence when the noisy rehearsals for the town musical ended, on Sunday he ____.
c: read alone in the quiet park
vr.e: To crave something is to want it very much. Although sets up a surprise: Vivek wanted quiet, yet he spent Sunday drumming at a noisy party.

y.B: Carved a little wooden duck mixes up crave with carve, which has the same letters in a different order.
y.C: Read alone in the quiet park is just what someone craving silence would do, so it ignores although, which promises a surprise.
y.D: Wore his favorite red sweater says nothing about noise or quiet, so there is no surprise for although to point to.

vr.q: In the play at the town hall, the baker defies the king's order to stop giving bread to the poor by ____.
c: baking bread in a stone oven
asking the king to change the law
posting the king's order on the door
vr.e: To defy an order is to openly refuse to obey it. The baker kept handing out bread even though the king had forbidden it.

y.B: Baking bread in a stone oven is what a baker does either way, so it says nothing about the order.
y.C: Asking the king to change the law is a polite request; to defy an order is to openly refuse to follow it.
y.D: Posting the king's order on the door spreads the order and goes along with it, the opposite of defying it.

vr.q: Ziggy's stage fright diminished with every rehearsal, so by opening night he ____.
c: felt calm in front of the crowd
vr.e: To diminish is to become smaller or less. As Ziggy's stage fright shrank, he grew calm enough to face the crowd.

y.A: Begged for a smaller part is what he would do if his stage fright grew, the opposite of diminishing.
y.B: Wore a blue velvet costume says nothing about how his fear changed.
y.C: Asked for dimmer stage lights picks up the dim at the start of diminish, but the word means get smaller, not darker.

vr.q: Violet eagerly awaited her first rehearsal with the youth choir, so that morning she ____.
c: slept late and nearly forgot it
vr.e: Eagerly means in a way that shows you can hardly wait. Violet was so excited that she could hardly sit still.

y.B: Wished it would be canceled is what someone dreading the rehearsal would feel, the opposite of eagerly.
y.C: Ate pancakes with her brother could happen on any morning and shows nothing about how she felt.
y.D: Slept late and nearly forgot it shows she hardly cared, while eagerly means she could hardly wait.

vr.q: When rain began to fall at the outdoor concert, Wes, who was always gallant, ____.
c: looked up at the dark clouds
gave his umbrella to an old man
grabbed the last dry seat for himself
vr.e: Gallant means brave and noble, or very polite and kind to others. Giving his umbrella to an old man was a gallant thing to do.

y.A: Galloped off to his car mixes up gallant with gallop, and running off helps no one.
y.B: Looked up at the dark clouds is what anyone might do in the rain and shows nothing brave or kind.
y.D: Grabbed the last dry seat for himself is selfish, the opposite of gallant.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: To keep the town hall's spring art contest impartial, the judges ____.
c: hid the names of the artists
looked at only part of each painting
rushed through every painting in a minute
vr.e: Impartial means fair to all sides, favoring no one. Hiding the artists' names kept the judges from favoring people they knew.

y.B: Looked at only part of each painting reads the part inside impartial; the word means fair to everyone, not partly.
y.C: Picked their own children's paintings favors one side, the opposite of impartial.
y.D: Rushed through every painting in a minute mixes up impartial with impatient.

vr.q: The crowds along Front Street impeded the parade, so the marching band ____.
c: marched along at a quick pace
vr.e: To impede is to slow something down or get in its way. With the crowds in its way, the band could barely get through.

y.A: Ran wildly down the street mixes up impede with stampede, a wild rush.
y.C: Marched along at a quick pace means nothing was in the way, the opposite of being impeded.
y.D: Wore brand new purple uniforms is about how the band looked, not about the crowds getting in its way.

vr.q: Although Winona was the most intrepid reporter at the town paper, she ____.
c: was afraid of the mayor's tiny dog
climbed the bell tower to get a photo
carried a notebook everywhere she went
vr.e: Intrepid means fearless and adventurous. Although sets up a surprise: a fearless reporter who is afraid of a tiny dog.

y.A: Tripped over her camera bag is a clumsy slip, not fear; intrepid is about courage, so there is nothing for although to turn against.
y.C: Climbed the bell tower to get a photo is just what an intrepid reporter would do, so it ignores although, which promises a surprise.
y.D: Carried a notebook everywhere she went is what any reporter does and says nothing about fear, so there is no surprise for although to point to.

vr.q: The orchestra mourned its oldest violinist, so its summer concert ____.
c: began at nine in the morning
began with a bright, happy march
began with a slow, sad piece for her
vr.e: To mourn is to feel and show deep sadness after a loss. A slow, sad piece played for the violinist showed the orchestra's sadness.

y.A: Sold out a week early tells how popular the concert was, not how the orchestra felt about its loss.
y.B: Began at nine in the morning mixes up mourn with morning, which only sounds the same.
y.C: Began with a bright, happy march is cheerful, the opposite of mourning.

vr.q: Uri's new shadow-puppet screen turned out to be opaque, so the audience in front of it ____.
c: saw no shadows on it at all
clapped when the show was over
saw their own reflections in it
vr.e: Opaque means not letting any light through. A shadow-puppet show needs light to shine through the screen, so an opaque screen showed no shadows.

y.B: Clapped when the show was over happens at most shows and does not follow from a screen that blocks light.
y.C: Saw their own reflections in it treats opaque as shiny like a mirror, but opaque means no light gets through.
y.D: Saw the puppeteers' hands clearly would need a see-through screen, the opposite of opaque.

vr.q: In her plea at the end of the spring concert, Yvonne, the band leader, ____.
c: praised the band for working hard
promised a bigger show in the fall
begged families to donate old instruments
vr.e: A plea is an urgent, heartfelt request. Yvonne's plea begged families to donate old instruments.

y.A: Ordered everyone to clap louder is a command, but a plea is a heartfelt request.
y.B: Praised the band for working hard gives compliments, and a plea asks for something.
y.C: Promised a bigger show in the fall is a promise, not a request for help.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: To rectify the spelling mistake on the banner for the town's book fair, Zaid ____.
c: hung it up just as it was
repainted the word the right way
pointed the mistake out to his friends
trimmed the banner into a neat rectangle
vr.e: To rectify a mistake is to fix it or put it right. Repainting the word correctly fixed the banner.

y.A: Hung it up just as it was leaves the mistake in place, the opposite of fixing it.
y.C: Pointed the mistake out to his friends only notices it, while to rectify a mistake is to fix it.
y.D: Trimmed the banner into a neat rectangle picks up the rect at the start of rectify, but the word means put right, not cut into a shape.

vr.q: Among the relics on display at the town museum is ____.
c: a fiddle played two centuries ago
a plastic copy of a famous old drum
vr.e: A relic is an object that has survived from long ago. A fiddle played two hundred years ago is a relic.

y.A: A jar of pickle relish mixes up relic with relish, a pickle topping that has nothing to do with long ago.
y.B: A guitar built last week is brand new, the opposite of a relic from long ago.
y.D: A plastic copy of a famous old drum is a replica made recently; a relic is the real old object that has survived.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: The crowd at the Tuesday afternoon play was sparse: ____.
c: only a few seats were taken
not one seat had anyone in it
vr.e: Sparse means thinly spread, with only a few here and there. A sparse crowd fills only a few seats.

y.A: Every seat was filled describes a packed house, the opposite of sparse.
y.C: Not one seat had anyone in it means no crowd at all, but sparse means a few here and there, not none.
y.D: The costumes sparkled brightly mixes up sparse with sparkle and says nothing about the crowd.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: Uzma tenaciously pursued her dream of playing cello in the town orchestra, so after being turned down twice, she ____.
c: signed up to try out again
bought a shiny new cello case
vr.e: Tenaciously means holding on firmly and not giving up. After two turn-downs, Uzma signed up to try out again.

y.A: Took up tennis instead picks up the ten at the start of tenaciously and gives up on the cello, the opposite of holding on.
y.C: Practiced only on rainy days is a half-hearted effort, the opposite of holding on firmly.
y.D: Bought a shiny new cello case does not say whether she kept trying to join the orchestra.

vr.q: In the town's history play, the young drummer showed great valor when he ____.
c: heard that his side had won
sold his drum for a good price
kept drumming as the cannons boomed
vr.e: Valor is great courage, especially in battle. Drumming on while cannons boomed showed the drummer's valor.

y.A: Dropped his drum and fled is running away in fear, the opposite of valor.
y.B: Heard that his side had won is news of a victory, and valor means courage, not winning.
y.C: Sold his drum for a good price mixes up valor with value.

vr.ss: phrase completion — what the word describes

vr.q: PLEA most nearly means:
vr.e: A plea is an urgent request, asking for something you badly want or need: the lost hikers made a plea for help over the radio.

y.A: Pleasure begins with plea, which is the trap, but pleasure is a feeling of happiness or enjoyment.
y.B: Promise is something you say you will do for someone; a plea goes the other way, asking someone to do something for you.
y.D: Warning tells someone about danger ahead; a plea asks someone, often begging, for help or mercy.

vr.q: DEFY most nearly means:
vr.e: To defy is to openly resist or refuse to obey: the girl in the story defied the king's order and told the truth.

y.A: Complain means to grumble that something is unfair; a person who complains may still do as they are told, but one who defies refuses.
y.B: Deny looks almost like defy, which is the trap; to deny is to say that something is not true, while to defy is to refuse to obey.
y.C: Obey is the opposite: to obey a rule is to follow it, and to defy it is to openly refuse.

vr.q: RECTIFY most nearly means:
vr.e: To rectify is to fix something that is wrong, to make it right: the store rectified its mistake and gave us our money back.

y.B: Notice is the step before: you have to notice a mistake before you can rectify it, which means fixing it.
y.C: Repeat starts with the same two letters, but to repeat is to say or do something again, which would not fix anything.
y.D: Terrify ends with the same sound as rectify, which is the trap; to terrify is to frighten someone badly.

vr.q: MOURN most nearly means:
vr.e: To mourn is to feel and show deep sadness because someone has died or something is lost: the whole town mourned the old fire chief.

y.A: Celebrate is the opposite: people celebrate happy events, and they mourn sad losses.
y.C: Warn rhymes with mourn, which is the trap; to warn is to tell someone about danger ahead.
y.D: Worry is an uneasy feeling about what might happen; mourning is sorrow for something that has already been lost.

vr.q: IMPEDE most nearly means:
vr.e: To impede something is to hinder it, to slow it down or get in its way: deep snow impeded the school bus, so we were late.

y.A: Assist is the opposite: to assist is to help something along, and to impede is to get in its way.
y.C: Hurry goes the other way too: hurrying speeds things up, and impeding slows them down.
y.D: Stampede rhymes with impede, but it means to rush wildly in a big crowd, like frightened cattle.

vr.q: DIMINISH most nearly means:
vr.e: To diminish is to make something smaller or less, or to become smaller: the pile of firewood diminished as the cold night went on.

y.A: Divide means to split something into parts; each part is smaller, which is the trap, but all of the thing is still there, while diminishing leaves less of it.
y.B: Erase means to rub something out completely; to diminish is to make it smaller or weaker, and some of it is still there.
y.C: Finish rhymes with the end of diminish, but to finish is to come to the end of something.

vr.q: CRAVE most nearly means:
vr.e: To crave something is to want it very badly, to desire it: after the long, hot hike, I craved a cold glass of lemonade.

y.A: Carve has the same letters as crave in a different order, which is the trap; to carve is to cut wood or meat into shape.
y.C: Hate is the opposite: you crave the things you want most, and you hate the things you cannot stand.
y.D: Taste is a near miss, since people often crave a food, but to taste is to try it in your mouth; you can crave a food you have not tasted for months.

vr.q: SPARSE most nearly means:
vr.e: Sparse means thinly scattered, with only a few things spread far apart: grass was sparse on the dry, rocky hill, just a tuft here and there.

y.A: Crowded is the opposite: a crowded place is packed full, and a sparse one has only a few things, spread far apart.
y.B: Empty means nothing at all is there; sparse means a few things are there, just spread thin.
y.D: Sparkly starts like sparse, which is the trap; sparkly means glittering with tiny flashes of light.

vr.q: OPAQUE most nearly means:
vr.e: Opaque means not clear enough to see through, because light cannot pass through it: a wooden door is opaque, but a window is not. Words can be opaque too: an opaque explanation is unclear, hard to understand.

y.A: Shiny means reflecting light brightly, like a new coin; opaque is about whether light can pass through, and a shiny coin is opaque too.
y.B: Transparent is the opposite: you can see right through something transparent, like a clean window, and you cannot see through something opaque.
y.D: Unique ends in -que, just like opaque, which is the trap; unique means one of a kind.

vr.q: IMPARTIAL most nearly means:
vr.e: Impartial means fair, not favoring one side over another: a good referee stays impartial, even when her own school is playing.

y.A: Biased is the opposite: a biased judge favors one side, and an impartial judge treats both sides the same.
y.B: Complete is a guess from reading impartial as not partial, as if it meant not in part; but impartial means not taking sides.
y.D: Impatient looks a lot like impartial, which is the trap; impatient means unable to wait calmly.

vr.q: GALLANT most nearly means:
vr.e: Gallant means brave and noble, like a hero in an old story: the gallant knight rode out alone to face the dragon.

y.B: Fast is a guess from gallop, which looks like gallant; knights in stories do both, but gallant means brave and noble, not quick.
y.C: Loyal means always standing by a friend or a leader; a gallant knight may be loyal too, but gallant means brave and noble.
y.D: Wealthy means rich; the gallant heroes of old stories are often rich lords, but gallant describes courage, not money.

vr.q: CRAFTY most nearly means:
vr.e: Crafty means clever at tricking people to get what you want: the crafty pirate hid the real map and let his rivals steal a fake one.

y.A: Drafty rhymes with crafty, but it describes a room where cold air blows in through cracks.
y.B: Mean means unkind; a crafty person may be mean too, but crafty is about clever tricks, and a crafty plan can be harmless fun.
y.D: Truthful is the opposite: a truthful person says what is so, and a crafty one plays tricks.

vr.q: VALOR most nearly means:
vr.e: Valor is great courage, especially in danger or in battle: the firefighter won a medal for valor after carrying a child out of the burning house.

y.B: Glory is the fame and praise a hero may win; valor is the courage itself, and many brave acts are never praised at all.
y.C: Valley starts with the same letters as valor, which is the trap; a valley is the low land between hills.
y.D: Victory is winning; valor can help win a battle, but valor is the courage itself, and a brave soldier can show valor and still lose.

vr.q: RELIC most nearly means:
vr.e: A relic is an object that has lasted from long ago: the rusty sword in the museum is a relic of a battle fought hundreds of years ago.

y.B: Invention is nearly the opposite: an invention is something new that someone has just created, and a relic is something left from long ago.
y.C: Relish looks like relic, which is the trap; relish is a chopped pickle sauce for hot dogs, or great enjoyment.
y.D: Replica is a copy made to look like something old, the kind a museum gift shop sells; a relic is the real object that has lasted from long ago.

vr.q: ANECDOTE most nearly means:
vr.e: An anecdote is a short, interesting story about something that really happened: Grandpa told an anecdote about the day his cow got loose in town.

y.A: Antidote looks and sounds like anecdote, which is the trap; an antidote is a medicine that stops a poison from working.
y.B: Poem is a piece of writing with rhythm and often rhyme; an anecdote is a short true story, usually told out loud.
y.C: Riddle is a puzzling question you try to guess the answer to; an anecdote is a short true story, with nothing to guess.

vr.q: EAGERLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Eagerly means excitedly, really wanting something to happen: the puppy waited eagerly by the door for its walk.

y.A: Easily starts and ends like eagerly, which is the trap; easily means without trouble or effort.
y.C: Nervously also describes how someone might wait, but nervous waiting is worried, and eager waiting is excited and happy.
y.D: Patiently is close to the opposite: a patient person waits calmly, while someone waiting eagerly can hardly wait at all.

vr.q: ABRUPTLY most nearly means:
vr.e: Abruptly means suddenly and without warning: the music stopped abruptly, right in the middle of the song.

y.A: Absolutely starts with the same letters as abruptly, which is the trap; absolutely means completely, as in absolutely sure.
y.B: Early means before the usual time; something can end early but slowly, while abruptly means all at once, with no warning.
y.C: Loudly is about noise; a car that stops abruptly may screech loudly, but abruptly means suddenly, and a quiet thing can end abruptly too.

vr.q: Uncle Vince loves almost every kind of food, but he cannot ____ olives; he picks every last one off his pizza and leaves them on his plate.
vr.e: But turns from loving almost every food to one he cannot stand, and picking every olive off his pizza shows it. To abide something is to put up with it, so cannot abide means cannot stand.

y.B: Afford means to have enough money for something, but picking olives off a pizza is about disliking them, not about cost.
y.C: Find does not fit: he spots every last olive on his pizza, so he has no trouble finding them.
y.D: Resist would make it mean he loves olives too much to turn them down, but but says olives are the exception to the foods he loves.

vr.q: Unlike her timid older brother, who would not even try the low diving board, Zola was ____ and leaped from the highest platform on her very first visit.
vr.e: Unlike sets Zola against her timid brother, and leaping from the highest platform on her first visit shows how. Intrepid means fearless and bold.

y.A: Clumsy means awkward and likely to stumble, which says nothing about courage; unlike sets Zola against a brother too timid to try even the low board.
y.B: Graceful is about how smoothly someone moves, but unlike sets Zola against a timid brother, so the blank is about courage.
y.D: Timid is the sentence's own word for her brother, and unlike tells you Zola was different from him.

vr.q: Benjamin Franklin became a printer by starting out as his older brother's ____: from the age of twelve, he worked in his brother's Boston print shop and learned the trade from him.
vr.e: The words after the colon define the blank: someone who works for a skilled worker in order to learn a trade from him. An apprentice is a person learning a trade from an expert.

y.B: Customer is someone who buys things from a shop, but a customer does not work there or learn the trade, and Benjamin did both.
y.C: Master is the skilled worker who teaches the trade, and that was his brother; Benjamin, at twelve, was the one learning it.
y.D: Partner is someone who owns a share of a business as an equal, but a twelve-year-old still learning the trade from his brother was not his equal.

vr.q: Each spring, the town council chooses one citizen to receive the Golden Key, the highest honor the town can ____.
vr.e: The citizen receives the Golden Key, so the town is the one giving it. Bestow means to give an honor or a gift.

y.A: Auction means to sell something to whoever offers the most money, but an honor is given as a reward, not sold to the highest bidder.
y.C: Earn is what the citizen does to deserve the Golden Key; the blank is what the town does when it hands the honor over.
y.D: Inherit means to receive something from someone who has died, but the town is not receiving the Golden Key; it is the one giving it.

vr.q: A barnacle is a ____ little animal: once it cements itself to a rock or a ship's hull, it stays stuck there for the rest of its life.
vr.e: The colon gives the example: once stuck, it never lets go. Tenacious means holding on tightly and not giving up.

y.A: Delicate means easily broken or harmed, but this animal glues itself down for life.
y.B: Playful means full of fun, and the colon is about how tightly the barnacle holds on, not how it behaves.
y.C: Restless means unable to keep still, but this animal stays in one spot for the rest of its life.

vr.q: Everyone laughed, because they knew Zane's threat to trade his little sister for a puppy was only a ____.
vr.e: Because gives the reason they laughed: they knew he did not mean it. A jest is a joke, something said for fun.

y.B: Promise would mean he really planned to do it, and nobody laughs at a promise to trade away a sister if they believe it.
y.C: Secret means something hidden, but he said it out loud to everyone, which is why they laughed.
y.D: Warning means telling someone about danger ahead, and people do not laugh at a warning they believe.

vr.q: Although her classmates laughed at the idea, Zainab continued to ____ that a tomato is a fruit, and she brought in a book about plants to prove it.
vr.e: Although tells you she kept on even though others laughed, and bringing a book to prove it shows she said it firmly. Assert means to state something firmly.

y.B: Doubt means to be unsure, but she brought a book to prove her point, which is the opposite of doubting.
y.C: Forget does not fit continued to: you cannot keep forgetting something while you bring a book to prove it.
y.D: Regret means to feel sorry about something, and she was not sorry; she was proving she was right.

vr.q: Marie Curie, the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes, was one of the most ____ scientists of her time.
vr.e: The example tells you: two Nobel Prizes, a first in history, made her famous and respected. Eminent means famous and respected in your field.

y.B: Imminent sounds almost the same but means about to happen, like an imminent storm; it cannot describe a scientist.
y.C: Obscure means little known, but the first person to win two Nobel Prizes is famous.
y.D: Ordinary means nothing special, and winning two Nobel Prizes, a first in history, is far from ordinary.

vr.q: Rather than the whole clay pot they had hoped to find, the archaeologists dug up only a single ____ no bigger than a coin.
vr.e: Rather than the whole pot, they found only a piece no bigger than a coin: a small broken part. Fragment means a small piece broken off something.

y.A: Boulder is a huge rock, and the find was no bigger than a coin.
y.C: Original means the real thing rather than a copy, but the sentence is about size: rather than the whole pot, they found a piece no bigger than a coin.
y.D: Replica is a copy made later, but archaeologists dig up old, real things, and this was a piece of the pot itself.

vr.q: Because they found fossils of sea creatures near the top of Mount Everest, scientists were able to ____ that its rock had once been at the bottom of an ocean.
vr.e: Because tells you the fossils were evidence, and the scientists reasoned from that evidence to a conclusion. Deduce means to figure something out from the facts.

y.A: Conceal means to hide, and finding fossils does not help anyone hide a fact; it helps them prove it.
y.C: Imagine means to picture something in your mind, which needs no evidence at all; because says the fossils let them work it out.
y.D: Pretend means to act as if something were true when it is not, but the fossils showed it really was true.

vr.q: Uncle Vito's speech at the reunion was hardly ____; he read a long list of thank-yous for twenty minutes, and two cousins fell asleep.
vr.e: Hardly means almost not. A twenty-minute list that put two cousins to sleep was not clever or funny. Witty means clever and funny.

y.A: Dull describes the speech exactly, which is the trap: hardly means the blank is what the speech was not.
y.B: Lengthy fits a list read for twenty minutes, but hardly flips it; a twenty-minute speech cannot be hardly lengthy.
y.C: Solemn means grave and serious, but the second half shows how boring the speech was, not how serious, so it gives no reason for hardly solemn.

vr.q: The 1906 earthquake was a ____ for San Francisco: fires burned for four days, and more than 80 percent of the city was destroyed.
vr.e: The colon gives the evidence: fires for four days and most of the city destroyed. A catastrophe is a sudden, terrible disaster.

y.B: Mystery means something nobody can explain, but the colon does not puzzle over the earthquake; it lists the damage it did.
y.C: Nuisance means a small annoyance, like a buzzing fly; fires that destroyed most of a city were far worse than that.
y.D: Rehearsal is a practice before the real thing, but the earthquake and fires were real.

vr.q: After Wendy lost her earring at the beach, her whole family helped ____ the sand, sifting through it inch by inch until they found it.
vr.e: The words after the comma define the blank: sifting through the sand inch by inch is a careful, complete search. Scour means to search a place thoroughly.

y.A: Flatten means to press smooth and level, which would bury an earring deeper, not find it.
y.B: Measure borrows inch by inch from the sentence, but measuring sand would not turn up an earring; until they found it shows they were searching.
y.D: Sculpt means to shape something, like a sandcastle, but shaping the sand would not find an earring; sifting through it until they found it is a search.

vr.q: The deer in the city park have grown used to people and are hardly ____ at all; some will walk right up to a picnic blanket to sniff the sandwiches.
vr.e: Hardly means almost not. Deer that walk right up to people's picnics are not on guard at all. Wary means cautious and watchful for danger.

y.A: Graceful is about how smoothly deer move, and nothing after the semicolon is about movement; it is about how unafraid they are.
y.B: Hungry fits sniffing the sandwiches, which is the trap: deer that come to sniff the sandwiches are hungry, so hardly hungry contradicts the second half.
y.C: Tame is exactly what these deer are, and hardly means the blank is what they are not.

vr.q: Because land downtown was crowded and expensive, the new zoo was built on the ____ of the city, where open fields were cheap.
vr.e: Because gives the reason: downtown was crowded and costly, so the zoo went to the edge of the city, where land was open and cheap. Outskirts means the outer edges of a town or city.

y.A: Harbor is the place where ships dock, at the water's edge, not a spread of open fields.
y.C: Rooftops are the tops of buildings, and a zoo with open fields cannot be built on top of buildings.
y.D: Streets are the roads between buildings, and a zoo is not built on roads; the sentence says it went where open fields were cheap.

vr.q: Although the conductor never said a single word during the concert, the musicians ____.
c: had no idea when to begin
followed the motions of her hands
vr.e: Although sets up a surprise: with no words from the conductor, you might expect the musicians to be lost, yet they followed her hands, which is how an orchestra follows a conductor.

y.A: Had no idea when to begin goes along with her silence instead of against it, and although needs a surprise.
y.B: Listened to her long speech contradicts the first half: she never said a single word.
y.C: Wore black suits and dresses tells what they had on, which has nothing to do with whether the conductor spoke.

vr.q: Since the foxes were wary of people, the wildlife photographer ____.
c: walked right up to pet them
hid quietly behind a fallen log
called loudly to get their attention
vr.e: Since gives the reason: wary animals keep away from people, so the photographer had to stay out of sight, hiding quietly behind a fallen log.

y.A: Fed them from her hand would need foxes that come close to people, and wary ones keep away.
y.B: Walked right up to pet them is just what wary animals would run from.
y.D: Called loudly to get their attention would warn wary foxes that a person was near, and they would run.

vr.q: Now that the old bridge was no longer safe to cross, the farmers ____.
c: painted the barn a new color
vr.e: No longer safe to cross means the farmers could not use the bridge, so they had to go another way: the long way around.

y.B: Crossed it twice a day reads no longer safe as if it said safe; an unsafe bridge is one you stop crossing.
y.C: Raced their trucks over it would be even more dangerous on a bridge that is no longer safe.
y.D: Painted the barn a new color has nothing to do with the bridge, so it does not follow from the first half.

vr.q: Unless it stops raining by noon, the school picnic ____.
c: will have more food than ever
will be held on the sunny lawn
vr.e: Unless means if not. If the rain does not stop by noon, the picnic cannot stay outside, so it will move into the gym.

y.B: Will start an hour early is about the time, but unless is about the rain, and an earlier start does not keep anyone dry.
y.C: Will have more food than ever has nothing to do with whether it keeps raining, so unless has nothing to connect it to.
y.D: Will be held on the sunny lawn is what would happen if the rain did stop; unless says what happens if it does not.

vr.q: Unlike paper money, which tears and wears out within a few years, coins ____.
c: can last for hundreds of years
vr.e: Unlike sets coins against paper money, which wears out in a few years, so coins must last a long time; many coins have lasted for hundreds of years.

y.A: Burn easily in a fire is a weakness of paper money, not a difference from it, and metal coins do not burn.
y.B: Are used to buy things is true of paper money too, so it is not a way coins are unlike it.
y.C: Fold neatly into a wallet describes paper money; a metal coin does not fold.

qr.q: A garden club plants 28 bulbs, and 3/4 of them bloom. How many bulbs bloom?
qr.e: Find 3/4 of 28: 28÷4=7, and 7×3=21 bulbs.

y.A: 24 is 28 − 4, taking off the 4 from the bottom of the fraction rather than a quarter of the bulbs. A quarter of 28 is 7, so three quarters is 7 × 3 = 21.
y.B: 18 is three short of the answer. A quarter of 28 is 7, and three of those quarters is 7 × 3 = 21.
y.D: 25 is 28 − 3, three bulbs taken off the total. Three quarters means 7 × 3 = 21.

qr.q: Two runners complete 5/6 and 7/9 of a relay. Which runner completed more?
qr.e: Use eighteenths: 5/6=15/18 and 7/9=14/18, so the 5/6 runner completed more.

y.A: Equal would mean the same share, but over eighteenths 5/6 is 15/18 and 7/9 is 14/18 — one eighteenth apart.
y.C: There is enough here: give both fractions the same bottom number. 5/6 becomes 15/18 and 7/9 becomes 14/18, so the 5/6 runner did more.
y.D: 7/9 has the bigger numbers, but bigger numbers do not mean a bigger share. In eighteenths it is 14/18, just under 5/6 at 15/18.

qr.q: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for 8 muffins. At the same rate, how many cups are needed for 20 muffins?

y.A: 7 is half a cup short — the 7 1/2 rounded down to a whole cup. 20 muffins is 2 1/2 lots of 8, and 3 × 2 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups.
y.B: 8 is the number of muffins in the recipe, not a number of cups. 20 muffins is 2 1/2 times as many, so it takes 3 × 2 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups.
y.C: 6 is 3 × 2, enough flour for 16 muffins. Twenty muffins is 2 1/2 lots of 8, so 3 × 2 1/2 = 7 1/2 cups.

qr.q: Four notebooks cost $10. What is the cost per notebook?

y.C: 4 is 10 ÷ 2.5, the number of notebooks rather than the price of one. Divide the money by the notebooks instead: 10 ÷ 4 = $2.50.
y.A: 2.25 would make four notebooks $9.00; $10 ÷ 4 is $2.50.
y.D: 2.0 would make four notebooks $8.00, leaving $2 unaccounted for.

qr.q: 3/5 of a class is 18 students. How many students are in the whole class?
qr.e: 18 is 3 parts, so 1 part is 6; 5 parts = 30.

y.D: 36 is 18 × 2, the eighteen students doubled. Those 18 make up three of the five parts, so one part is 6 and all five parts come to 30.
y.A: 45 would make 3/5 of the class 27 students, not 18.
y.B: 24 would make 3/5 of the class 14.4, which is not a whole number of students.

qr.ss: finding the whole from a fraction of it

qr.q: The ratio of red to blue marbles is 2:3. If there are 25 marbles total, how many are red?
qr.e: There are 5 equal parts; 25 ÷ 5 = 5, and 2 parts = 10.

y.A: 8 is 2 × 4. The ratio makes 5 parts, each 25 ÷ 5 = 5 marbles, so red is 2 × 5 = 10.
y.B: 12 is 3 × 4, using the blue number. Red is 2 parts of 5 marbles: 10.
y.C: 15 is the blue share, 3 parts of 5. Red is the other 2 parts: 10.

qr.ss: a part from the total and a ratio

qr.q: Mia read 2/3 of a 60-page book, then read half of the pages that remained. How many pages are still unread?
qr.e: She read 40 pages, then 10 more of the 20 remaining, leaving 10.

y.A: 20 is 60 ÷ 3, the pages left over after the first two thirds were read. Half of those 20 were then read as well, so 10 are still unread.
y.B: 30 is 60 ÷ 2, half of the whole book. The halving only applies to the 20 pages left after the first two thirds: half of 20 leaves 10 unread.
y.D: 15 is what half of 60, halved again, would leave. She read 2/3 first, which is 40 pages, and half of the 20 remaining is 10.

qr.ss: a fraction of what is left

qr.q: A car travels 180 miles in 3 hours at a constant speed. What is its speed?

y.B: 90 is 180 ÷ 2, the miles shared over two hours rather than the three hours the car took. Divide by 3 instead: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 miles per hour.
y.C: 50 mph over 3 hours covers 150 miles, not 180.
y.D: 45 mph over 3 hours covers 135 miles.

qr.q: A trail is 2/3 paved and 1/4 gravel, with no overlap. What fraction of the trail is paved or gravel?

y.A: 3/7 is what you get by adding the tops and the bottoms straight across: 2 + 1 on top, 3 + 4 underneath. The bottoms have to match before you add — 2/3 is 8/12 and 1/4 is 3/12, so together they make 11/12.
y.C: 7/12 is 4/12 + 3/12, and 2/3 is not 4/12 — the 4 is what you multiply by, not the new top number. Multiply both parts by 4: 2/3 is 8/12, so 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
y.D: 3/4 is what is left when the 1/4 of gravel is taken off the whole trail. Here the two parts are added instead: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

qr.q: A 5 1/2-yard ribbon loses 2 3/4 yards. How much ribbon remains?
qr.e: Rename 5 1/2 as 5 2/4, regroup, and subtract 2 3/4 to get 2 3/4 yards.

y.B: 2 1/4 comes from 5 − 2 = 3 and then taking the whole 3/4 off, with the half yard dropped on the way. Borrow instead: 5 1/2 is 4 and 6/4, and 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4, so 2 3/4 yards.
y.C: 2 1/2 comes from 5 1/2 − 3, with the 2 3/4 rounded up to 3. Keep the quarters: 5 1/2 is 4 and 6/4, and 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4, leaving 2 3/4 yards.
y.D: 3 1/4 turns the fraction round, taking 1/2 from 3/4 because the half looked too small to take from. Borrow instead: 5 1/2 is 4 and 6/4, and 6/4 − 3/4 = 3/4, so 2 3/4 yards.

qr.q: How many 1/8-cup servings are in 3/4 cup?
qr.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six 1/8-cup servings.

y.B: 8 is the 8 out of one-eighth, not a count of servings. Written as eighths, 3/4 is 6/8 — six of them.
y.C: 4 is the 4 out of three-quarters. Rename it in eighths: 6/8, so six servings.
y.D: 5 is 8 − 3, the two bottom numbers subtracted. Rename 3/4 as 6/8 and count: six.

qr.ss: dividing a fraction by a fraction (beyond Lower Level)

qr.q: A paint recipe mixes yellow and blue in a 4:5 ratio. Which batch keeps the same ratio?
qr.e: Multiply both parts of 4:5 by 3 to get the equivalent ratio 12:15.

y.A: 16:25 times each part by itself, 4 × 4 and 5 × 5. An equal ratio needs both parts times the same number: 4 × 3 = 12 and 5 × 3 = 15.
y.C: 10:12 halves down to 5:6, which keeps the gap of one but not the mix. Both parts of 4:5 times 3 gives 12:15.
y.B: 8:12 reduces to 2:3, not 4:5; doubling 4:5 gives 8:10.

qr.q: Museum tickets cost $6 each. A family spends $24 on x tickets. How many tickets does the family buy?
qr.e: The equation is 6x=24. Divide both sides by 6 to get x=4 tickets.

y.A: 6 is the price of one ticket, not how many were bought. Divide instead: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.
y.B: 3 is 6 ÷ 2. The spend divides by the price: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 tickets.
y.D: 18 is 24 − 6, one ticket taken off the money. Each ticket costs 6, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

qr.ss: solving a one-step equation from a story

qr.q: A baker needs the fraction of a pie that is closest to one whole pie. Which amount is closest to 1?
qr.e: Compare each gap from 1. The gap for 9/10 is only 1/10, smaller than the other gaps.

y.A: 2/3 is a whole third away from one, the biggest gap of the four. 9/10 is short by only 1/10.
y.B: 3/4 is 1/4 away from a whole pie, and a quarter is bigger than a tenth. 9/10 misses by just 1/10.
y.D: 7/10 is 3/10 away from a whole pie — three times as far as 9/10, which misses by 1/10.

qr.ss: the fraction closest to 1/2 or to 1

qr.q: Five pens cost $7.50. At the same rate, how much do 8 pens cost?

y.A: 10.5 is $7.50 with $3 put on because there are 3 more pens — but a pen costs $1.50, not $1. Three more pens add 3 × $1.50 = $4.50, so eight pens come to $12.
y.C: 4.5 is what the three extra pens cost, not what all eight cost. A pen is $7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50, so eight of them come to 8 × $1.50 = $12.
y.D: 10 is 8 × 1.25, and $1.25 is $7.50 shared six ways rather than five. Share it five ways: 7.50 ÷ 5 = $1.50, so eight pens cost $12.

qr.q: 2/5 of the students are boys. If 18 students are girls, how many students are in the class?
qr.e: Girls are 3/5 of the class. If 3/5 = 18, then the whole is 30.

y.C: 36 is 18 × 2, the eighteen girls doubled. The girls make up three of the five parts, so one part is 6 and the whole class comes to 30.
y.A: 45 would make the 18 girls 2/5 of the class, and the girls are the other 3/5.
y.D: 24 would make 3/5 of the class 14.4, not 18.

qr.ss: finding the whole from a fraction of it

qr.q: A 48-seat bus has 25% of its seats reserved. How many seats are reserved?
qr.e: Twenty-five percent is one fourth, and 48÷4=12 reserved seats.

y.B: 16 is 48 ÷ 3, a third of the seats instead of a quarter. 25% is one quarter, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
y.C: 36 is how many seats are not reserved — the other three quarters of the bus. The question asks for the quarter that is reserved: 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
y.D: 10 is a quarter of 40, with the 48 rounded down first. A quarter of 48 itself is 48 ÷ 4 = 12.

qr.q: A 6/8-mile route is shortened to an equivalent fraction on a map label. Which label matches the route?
qr.e: Divide numerator and denominator by 2: 6/8=3/4 mile.

y.A: 3/8 mile halves the top of the fraction and leaves the bottom as it was. Both parts have to be halved: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 6/8 is 3/4.
y.B: 6/4 mile halves the bottom of the fraction and leaves the top as it was. Both parts have to be halved: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 6/8 is 3/4.
y.C: 2/3 is 4/6, which is 2 taken off the top and the bottom instead of both being halved. Halving gives 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 3/4.

qr.q: A school has 18 violins and 12 cellos. What is the ratio of violins to cellos in simplest form?
qr.e: 18:12 simplifies by dividing both numbers by 6 to 3:2.

y.A: 6:4 is 18:12 with both parts divided by 3, and it will still simplify — 6 and 4 both halve. Dividing by 6 in one go gives 3:2.
y.B: 2:3 is cellos to violins, the right pair the wrong way round. Violins come first here, so 18:12 becomes 3:2.
y.D: 3:4 divides 18 by 6 but 12 by 3. Both parts have to be divided by the same number: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so 3:2.

qr.q: A tank is 3/4 full and contains 18 gallons. How many gallons does it hold when full?
qr.e: 18 ÷ 3 × 4 = 24 gallons.

y.B: 21 is 18 + 3. One quarter of the tank is 18 ÷ 3 = 6 gallons, so the full tank is 6 × 4 = 24.
y.C: 22 is 18 + 4. Three quarters is 18 gallons, so a quarter is 6 and the whole tank is 24.
y.D: 27 is 24 + 3, the answer with three more added on. The tank holds 24.

qr.ss: finding the whole from a fraction of it

qr.q: Store A sells 6 markers for $9. Store B sells 10 markers for $14. Which store has the lower cost per marker?
qr.e: Store A is $1.50 each; Store B is $1.40 each.

y.A: The two are not the same once you price one marker: 9 ÷ 6 = $1.50 at the first store and 14 ÷ 10 = $1.40 at the second.
y.B: There is enough here — divide each price by the number of markers it buys: 9 ÷ 6 = $1.50 and 14 ÷ 10 = $1.40.
y.D: Store A has the smaller bill, but it also hands over fewer markers. Per marker it is 9 ÷ 6 = $1.50, against 14 ÷ 10 = $1.40 at Store B.

qr.q: A tile pattern has 2, 6, 18, and 54 tiles, tripling each time. How many tiles are in the next design?
qr.e: The rule is multiply by 3, so 54×3=162 tiles.

y.B: 216 is 54 × 4, the last design multiplied by 4 rather than by 3. The pattern triples each time: 54 × 3 = 162.
y.C: 108 is 54 × 2, the last design doubled. Each design is three times the one before, so 54 × 3 = 162.
y.D: 126 is not 54 × 3; tripling 54 gives 162.

qr.q: Three quiz scores are 8, 10, and 15. What is their average?
qr.e: Add the scores to get 33, then divide by 3: 33÷3=11.

y.B: 11 1/2 is halfway between the lowest and highest scores, 8 and 15 — the middle score left out altogether. An average uses all three: 8 + 10 + 15 = 33, and 33 ÷ 3 = 11.
y.C: 11 1/3 comes from dividing 34 by 3, one too many in the total. The three scores come to 8 + 10 + 15 = 33, and 33 ÷ 3 = 11 exactly.
y.D: 10 is the middle score, not the average of all three. Add them first: 8 + 10 + 15 = 33, and 33 ÷ 3 = 11.

qr.q: The ratio of cats to dogs is 7:3. If there are 50 animals total, how many are cats?
qr.e: There are 10 equal parts; 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so cats = 7 × 5 = 35.

y.A: 21 is 7 × 3, the two ratio numbers multiplied together. Those numbers count parts, not animals: 50 animals make 10 parts of 5, and the cats have 7 parts, so 7 × 5 = 35.
y.C: 15 is 50 − 35, the animals left once the cats are counted — the dogs rather than the cats. The cats are 7 of the 10 parts: 7 × 5 = 35.
y.B: 30 is not 7 parts of 5; 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so the cats are 7 × 5 = 35.

qr.ss: a part from the total and a ratio

qr.q: A recipe uses 4/5 cup of milk and 1/2 cup less water. How much water does it use?

y.A: 1/2 is how much less the water is, not how much water there is. Take it off the milk: 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10 cup.
y.B: 1/10 comes from writing 4/5 as 4/10, doubling only the bottom — that leaves just a tenth between 4/10 and 5/10. 4/5 is really 8/10, and 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10 cup.
y.C: 2/5 is half of 4/5, as if the water were half as much. It is half a cup less, not half as much: 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10 cup.

qr.q: A 2 1/4-liter jug is used to fill 3/4-liter bottles. How many full bottles can it fill?
qr.e: Rename 2 1/4 as 9/4. Then (9/4)÷(3/4)=3 full bottles.

y.A: 3 1/4 counts the last quarter as left over, but nothing is left over — that quarter goes into the third bottle. 2 1/4 is 9/4, and 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 3 exactly.
y.C: 2 is the whole-number part of 2 1/4, not how many 3/4s fit inside it. Three fit: 3/4 + 3/4 + 3/4 = 2 1/4.
y.D: 9 counts the quarter-liters in the jug, not the bottles. 2 1/4 liters is 9 quarters, and each bottle takes three of them, so the jug fills 9 ÷ 3 = 3 bottles.

qr.ss: dividing a fraction by a fraction (beyond Lower Level)

qr.q: On a map, 1 inch represents 6 miles. Two towns are 3.5 inches apart. How far apart are they?

y.A: 20 is 21 − 1, one mile short of the full distance. Each inch on the map stands for 6 miles, so 3.5 × 6 = 21 miles.
y.C: 24 is 6 × 4, four inches' worth of map rather than three and a half inches' worth. The towns are 3.5 inches apart, so 3.5 × 6 = 21 miles.
y.D: 18 is 3 × 6, dropping the half inch; 3.5 × 6 = 21.

qr.ss: map and model scale in words

qr.q: A 7-by-7 photo display uses one tile per space. How many tiles are needed?
qr.e: A photo display has 7 rows of 7 tiles, so 7×7=49.

y.A: 56 is 49 + 7, the display with one more row added. Seven rows of seven is 7 × 7 = 49.
y.C: 28 is 7 × 4, four rows. There are seven: 7 × 7 = 49.
y.D: 14 is 7 + 7, two rows added rather than seven rows multiplied: 7 × 7 = 49.

qr.q: An 81-square-inch mosaic is a square. How long is one side?
qr.e: A square with area 81 has side √81=9.

y.A: 10 would need 10 × 10 = 100 square inches, more than the mosaic has. 9 × 9 = 81, so the side is 9 in.
y.B: 8 gives 8 × 8 = 64 square inches, short of 81. The side that fills 81 is 9, because 9 × 9 = 81.
y.D: 7 gives 7 × 7 = 49 square inches, far short of 81. 9 × 9 = 81, so each side is 9 in.

qr.ss: the side of a square from its area

qr.q: A square game board uses 64 small tiles. How many tiles are in each row?
qr.e: The side length is √64=8 tiles.

y.D: 16 is 8 × 2, two rows of tiles rather than one. A row is the number that multiplies by itself to make 64: 8 × 8 = 64.
y.B: 7 rows of 7 make 49 tiles, not 64.
y.C: 6 rows of 6 make 36 tiles.

qr.ss: the side of a square from its area

qr.q: A square flower bed covers 50 square feet. Between which whole-number side lengths is its side?
qr.e: 7²=49 and 8²=64, so √50 lies between 7 and 8.

y.A: 6 and 7 square to 36 and 49, and 49 is still under 50 — so the side is more than 7, not less.
y.C: 8 and 9 square to 64 and 81, both past 50. The pair that traps 50 is 7 and 8, since 49 is under it and 64 is over it.
y.D: 5 and 6 square to 25 and 36, and 25 is only half of 50 — the side is not half the area. 7 × 7 = 49 sits just under 50, so the side is between 7 and 8.

qr.ss: estimating a square root between whole numbers

qr.q: Which patio tile count can be arranged as a perfect square array?
qr.e: 36 makes a 6-by-6 array; the other counts do not make equal rows and columns.

y.A: 32 makes rows like 4 by 8, never the same number each way. 36 does it, because 6 × 6 = 36.
y.B: 40 makes 5 by 8 or 4 by 10, but never equal rows and columns. 6 × 6 = 36 is the square one.
y.C: 30 makes 5 by 6, one row short of a square. The count that works is 36, since 6 × 6 = 36.

qr.q: A square has side length 12 cm. What is its area?
qr.e: Area of a square is side × side: 12×12=144 cm².

y.C: 48 is 12 × 4, the distance all the way round the square, not the space inside it. Area is side times side: 12 × 12 = 144 cm².
y.D: 24 is 12 × 2, two of the sides added together. Area comes from multiplying a side by a side: 12 × 12 = 144 cm².
y.A: 124 is not 12 × 12, which comes to 144.

qr.ss: area of a rectangle or square

qr.q: A square has area 81 square inches. What is its perimeter?
qr.e: The side is √81=9; perimeter =4×9=36 in.

y.B: 27 is 81 ÷ 3. The side is the number that multiplies by ITSELF to make 81, which is 9.
y.C: 32 is 4 × 8, so the side was taken as 8 — but 8 × 8 is 64, not 81.
y.D: 18 is two sides. A square has four.

qr.ss: perimeter of a rectangle or square

qr.q: Corner tiles in a growing display number 1, 4, 9, 16, ... . What is the next count?
qr.e: The counts are square arrays 1²,2²,3²,4²; next is 5²=25.

y.A: 24 is 25 − 1, one short. The counts are square arrays, and after 4 × 4 = 16 comes 5 × 5 = 25.
y.B: 20 is 4 + 16, two of the earlier counts added. Each count is a square number: next is 5 × 5 = 25.
y.C: 36 is 6 × 6, one square too far. The one straight after 16 is 5 × 5 = 25.

qr.q: Choosing one odd bead and one even bead gives a total that is always:
qr.e: Odd + even is always odd.

y.A: Even totals come from two odd beads or two even ones. One of each always leaves a single bead over, so the total is odd: 3 + 4 = 7.
y.B: Primes do turn up, as 3 + 4 = 7, but 3 + 6 = 9 is not prime. The part that is always true is that odd + even is odd.
y.D: Multiples of 4 are all even, and one odd bead with one even bead always leaves a single bead over — 3 + 4 = 7, 5 + 2 = 7. The total is odd every time.

qr.ss: odd and even sums and products

qr.q: A theater sells 234 tickets. Is that number divisible by 3?
c: No; it does not end in 3
qr.e: A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is divisible by 3. 2+3+4=9.

y.A: 3 does not have to be the last digit — 234 ÷ 3 = 78 with nothing left over. The test for 3 is the digit sum: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.
y.B: Being even is the test for dividing by 2, not by 3. For 3 you add the digits: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, and 9 divides by 3.
y.C: 2 + 3 + 4 comes to 9, not 8. Nine divides by 3, so 234 does too.

qr.q: 53 supplies are packed in boxes of 6. How many supplies are left over?
qr.e: 6×8=48, leaving 5 supplies.

y.B: 3 is 6 ÷ 2, half of a box rather than what is left after the full boxes. Take the full boxes off the total: 6 × 8 = 48, and 53 − 48 = 5.
y.A: 4 is one short; 6 × 8 = 48, and 53 − 48 = 5.
y.D: 6 cannot be left over when packing in sixes — another full box would fit.

qr.q: 42 flags are placed in equal rows. Which row size works with no flags left over?
qr.e: 42÷6=7, so rows of 6 work exactly.

y.B: 8 leaves 2 flags over: 8 × 5 = 40, and there are 42. Rows of 6 fit exactly, since 6 × 7 = 42.
y.C: 9 leaves 6 over: 9 × 4 = 36, six short of 42. Rows of 6 work, because 6 × 7 = 42.
y.D: 5 leaves 2 over: 5 × 8 = 40, not 42. Six goes in exactly — 6 × 7 = 42.

qr.q: A 100-square mural is arranged in a square. How many squares are on one side?
qr.e: √100=10, so a 10-by-10 mural has 100 squares.

y.D: 20 is 10 × 2, two sides' worth of squares rather than one side. One side is the number that multiplies by itself to make 100: 10 × 10 = 100.
y.A: 9 rows of 9 make 81 squares, not 100.
y.B: 8 rows of 8 make 64 squares.

qr.ss: the side of a square from its area

qr.q: A square seating section holds 121 seats in equal rows. How many seats are in each row?
