qr.q: Each of the 8 members of Imelda's science club needs 2/5 meter of string for an experiment. The store sells string only in whole meters. What is the fewest meters of string the club must buy?
qr.e: 8 members × 2/5 meter = 16/5 meters = 3 1/5 meters. Only whole meters are sold, and 3 meters is not enough, so the club must buy 4 meters.

y.A: 3 meters is 3 1/5 rounded down; 3 meters would leave some members without enough string.
y.B: 3 1/5 meters is exactly what the members need, but the store sells only whole meters.
y.D: 16 meters is 8 × 2, the number of fifths; 16 fifths of a meter is only 3 1/5 meters.

qr.ss: a fraction times a whole number

qr.q: Giselle has 1/2 hour to practice the piano before dinner. She splits the time equally among 3 songs. What fraction of an hour does she spend on each song?
qr.e: Splitting 1/2 hour into 3 equal parts gives 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6 hour for each song, because 6 such parts make a whole hour. (That is 10 minutes.)

y.B: 1/5 hour adds 2 + 3 for the denominator; splitting each half hour into 3 parts makes 6 parts in the hour.
y.C: 1/3 hour is each song's share of the half hour, not of a whole hour.
y.D: 1 1/2 hours is 1/2 × 3: the time was multiplied by 3 instead of split into 3 parts.

qr.ss: dividing a unit fraction by a whole number

qr.q: Hattie wrote down what fraction of the seats were full on four morning buses. Which of her fractions is closest to 1/2?
qr.e: Compare each with 1/2: 1/3 is 1/6 below it, 2/5 is 1/10 below, 7/12 is 1/12 above, and 11/24 is only 1/24 below (12/24 is a half). So 11/24 is closest.

y.A: 1/3 has a 1 on top like 1/2, but it is 1/6 away from 1/2, much farther than 11/24.
y.B: 2/5 treats 2 as half of 5, but half of 5 is 2 1/2, so 2/5 is 1/10 below 1/2.
y.D: 7/12 is one twelfth more than 6/12, while 11/24 is only one twenty-fourth less than 12/24, and a twenty-fourth is smaller.

qr.ss: the fraction closest to 1/2 or to 1

qr.q: Harold's school marching band has 53 members. They march in rows of 8, and the director wants every row to be completely full. What is the fewest new members who must join the band?
qr.e: 6 full rows hold 6 × 8 = 48 members, so the other 5 members stand in a 7th row that is not full. That row needs 8 − 5 = 3 more, so at least 3 new members must join (then 56 = 7 × 8).

y.B: 5 is the number of members in the last row now (53 − 48); that row still has 3 empty places.
y.C: 7 is the number of rows the band needs, not the number of new members.
y.D: 56 is how many members the band will have when every row is full, not how many must join.

qr.ss: how many more to fill the last group

qr.q: At the end of the farmers market, Ivana gives her 4 helpers 7 leftover pies to share equally. How much pie does each helper get?
qr.e: 7 ÷ 4 = 1 R 3: each helper gets 1 whole pie, and the 3 leftover pies are cut and shared by the 4 helpers, which gives each of them 3/4 of a pie more: 1 3/4 pies.

y.A: 4/7 pie is 4 ÷ 7, the helpers divided by the pies; the pies are shared among the helpers, 7 ÷ 4.
y.B: 1 pie drops the 3 pies left over; those 3 pies are shared too.
y.C: 1 3/7 pies puts the 3 leftover pies over 7, the number of pies; the 3 pies are shared by 4 helpers, so each gets 3/4 more.

qr.ss: sharing the remainder as a fraction

qr.q: The picture shows how Irma arranged her stamps in equal rows. She wants to rearrange all of them into a different number of equal rows, with no stamps left over. Which number of rows could she NOT use?
qr.e: The picture has 4 rows of 6, so 24 stamps. A number of rows works only if it divides 24: 2, 3 and 8 do (24 = 2 × 12 = 3 × 8 = 8 × 3), but 24 ÷ 5 = 4 R 4, so 5 rows would leave 4 stamps over.

y.A: 2 rows works: 2 rows of 12 use all 24 stamps.
y.B: 3 rows works: 3 rows of 8 use all 24 stamps.
y.D: 8 rows works even though 8 is more than 6: 8 rows of 3 use all 24 stamps.

qr.q: The table shows how often Jessie has each of her music lessons. On Monday she had all three lessons. How many days later will she next have all three lessons on the same day?
qr.e: The day must be a multiple of 2, 3 and 4. Singing falls on days 4, 8, 12, …; day 4 and day 8 are not multiples of 3, but 12 is a multiple of 2, 3 and 4. So all three lessons meet again 12 days later.

y.A: 6 days later she has piano and violin, but singing comes every 4 days (days 4, 8, 12), not on day 6.
y.B: 9 is 2 + 3 + 4; on day 9 she has only violin.
y.D: 24 is 2 × 3 × 4, a day when all three do fall together, but they already met on day 12.

qr.q: In Jerome's card game, a card wins a point if the number on it is a prime number. Which card does NOT win a point?
qr.e: A prime number has only 1 and itself as factors. 51 looks prime, but 5 + 1 = 6, so 51 is a multiple of 3: 51 = 3 × 17. It does not win a point.

y.A: 23 is prime even though it ends in 3: its only factors are 1 and 23.
y.B: 29 is prime even though it ends in 9: no number except 1 and 29 divides it.
y.C: 47 is prime even though it ends in 7; it is 49, not 47, that is 7 × 7.

qr.q: Gary has a large stamp collection. When the number of stamps is rounded to the nearest hundred, it is 2,500. Which of these CANNOT be the number of stamps Gary has?
qr.e: Numbers from 2,450 up to 2,549 round to 2,500. 2,551 is past 2,549, so it rounds to 2,600 and CANNOT be the number.

y.A: 2,451 can be the number: its tens digit is 5, so it rounds up to 2,500, even though it is in the 2,400s.
y.B: 2,499 can be the number: it is only 1 less than 2,500, so it rounds to 2,500, not 2,400.
y.C: 2,549 can be the number even though it has a 5 in the hundreds place: its tens digit is 4, so it rounds down to 2,500.

qr.ss: rounding to the nearest ten or hundred

qr.q: Mr. Ito's science club wants to collect 5,000 bottle caps for an art project. The graph shows how many caps each grade has collected so far. Which is closest to the number of caps the club still needs?
qr.e: Each grade has collected about 1,000 caps, so about 3,000 in all. 5,000 − 3,000 = 2,000 more. (Exactly: 950 + 1,020 + 980 = 2,950 collected, and 2,050 still needed.)

y.B: 3,000 is about how many caps have been collected, not how many more are needed.
y.C: 4,000 takes only one grade's caps (about 1,000) from 5,000; all three grades have collected caps.
y.D: 8,000 adds the caps collected to the goal instead of taking them away.

qr.q: Inez typed 4,215 ÷ 5 into a calculator for the science club's report, but she may have pressed a wrong key. Which of these answers is reasonable?
qr.e: 4,215 is close to 4,000, and 4,000 ÷ 5 = 800, so the answer should be a little more than 800. Only 843 is close. Check: 843 × 5 = 4,215.

y.A: 83 is far too small: 5 × 83 is only 415, so a digit is missing.
y.C: 4,210 is 4,215 − 5, a subtraction, not a division.
y.D: 8,430 is ten times too big: 5 × 8,430 is 42,150.

qr.ss: judging whether an answer is reasonable

qr.q: In Joelle's science club experiment, a candle gets shorter by the same amount each hour as it burns. The graph shows the candle's height after each of the first 5 hours. If it keeps burning the same way, after how many hours of burning will the candle be 6 centimeters tall?
qr.e: The candle loses 3 cm each hour (27, 24, 21, …), so before it was lit it was 27 + 3 = 30 cm tall. To get down to 6 cm it must lose 30 − 6 = 24 cm, which takes 24 ÷ 3 = 8 hours. (Or keep going from 15 cm: 12 after 6 hours, 9 after 7, 6 after 8.)

y.A: 2 is 6 ÷ 3, the hours needed to burn 6 centimeters; the question asks when 6 centimeters are left.
y.B: 7 is 21 ÷ 3, which starts counting from the height after 1 hour; that first hour has to be added back.
y.D: 10 is 30 ÷ 3, the hours until the whole candle has burned away, not until 6 centimeters are left.

qr.ss: input/output rules: from an output back to the input

qr.q: Gwyneth's drum exercise repeats the same pattern: 2 drum hits, then 3 claps, then 1 cymbal crash. She plays 44 sounds in all. How many of the sounds are claps?
qr.e: One pattern has 6 sounds with 3 claps. 44 sounds are 7 whole patterns (42 sounds) and 2 more. The 7 patterns have 7 × 3 = 21 claps, and the next 2 sounds are drum hits, so there are 21 claps.

y.B: 22 is half of 44: 3 claps in every 6 sounds is half, but the last 2 sounds are drum hits, not claps.
y.C: 23 counts the last 2 sounds as claps; each pattern starts with 2 drum hits.
y.D: 24 is 8 × 3, as if she played 8 whole patterns; 44 sounds are 7 whole patterns and 2 more sounds.

qr.q: Heath and his brother each had the same number of shells, n. At the beach they each found 5 more. Now they have 36 shells together. Which equation could be used to find n?
qr.e: After the beach each brother has n + 5 shells. The two of them together have 2 × (n + 5), and that is 36: 2 × (n + 5) = 36. (So each had 13 shells at first.)

y.A: n + 5 = 36 gives one brother's shells, but 36 is the total for both of them.
y.B: 2 × n + 5 = 36 adds only one set of 5 new shells; each of them found 5, so 10 new shells in all.
y.C: (n + 5) ÷ 2 = 36 splits one brother's shells in half, but the 36 is both brothers' shells added together.

qr.ss: writing a two-step equation from a story

qr.q: The table shows Hamza's results on a science club quiz. Every question he answered was either right or wrong. How many questions did he get right?
qr.e: The questions he did not get right are the 4 wrong ones and the 2 blank ones: 6 in all. So he got 30 − 6 = 24 right.

y.A: 6 is the number of questions he did not get right (4 wrong + 2 blank); the question asks how many he got right.
y.C: 26 is 30 − 4: it takes away the wrong answers but not the 2 blank questions.
y.D: 28 is 30 − 2: it takes away the blank questions but not the 4 wrong answers.

qr.ss: the other part: how many were right

qr.q: The table shows the egg prices at Horace's farm stand. Joanna needs 60 eggs. How much money does she save if she buys boxes of 30 instead of dozens?

y.A: $1.50 is the saving on just 30 eggs ($10.50 by the dozen against $9.00); she needs 60 eggs.
y.C: $4.80 is $9.00 − $4.20, a box of 30 against a single dozen, which holds fewer eggs.
y.D: $18.00 is what 2 boxes of 30 cost, not how much she saves.

qr.q: Hilda's farm stand sells only red and green apples. In the bar, the shaded parts stand for red apples and the other parts for green apples, in the same ratio as the apples at the stand. The stand has 40 apples. How many are green?
qr.e: The bar has 5 equal parts: 3 shaded for red and 2 not shaded for green. 40 apples ÷ 5 parts = 8 apples in each part, so there are 2 × 8 = 16 green apples.

y.A: 8 is 40 ÷ 5, the apples in one part of the bar; green has 2 parts.
y.C: 20 is half of 40, as if there were as many green apples as red; the bar has more shaded parts.
y.D: 24 is the number of red apples, the 3 shaded parts; the question asks for green.

qr.ss: a part from the total and a ratio

qr.q: The figure shows a triangular flower bed at a corner of the playground, with its perimeter. How long is the side that is not labeled?
qr.e: The three sides add up to the 24-meter perimeter. The two labeled sides make 8 + 6 = 14 meters, so the third side is 24 − 14 = 10 meters.

y.B: 14 meters adds the two labeled sides, 8 + 6, which is part of the perimeter, not the missing side.
y.C: 18 meters is 24 − 6; it takes away only one of the two labeled sides.
y.D: 48 meters is 8 × 6, but the sides are added to make the perimeter, not multiplied.

qr.q: The table shows the side lengths of four triangles Leah cut out for a mobile. Which triangle is scalene?
qr.e: Scalene means no two sides are the same length. Only Triangle S, with sides of 3, 4 and 5 cm, has three different lengths.

y.A: Triangle P has all three sides equal; that is equilateral, the opposite of scalene.
y.B: Triangle Q has a different third side, but its first two sides are both 6 cm, so it is isosceles.
y.C: Triangle R's two 7 cm sides are not next to each other in the table, but they are still equal, so R is isosceles.

qr.q: Koa drew a rectangular camp flag on a grid with three dashed fold lines. Which fold does NOT make the two halves of the flag match?
c: Every fold makes the halves match.
qr.e: Folding up the middle or across the middle puts one half exactly on the other. The fold from corner to corner makes two equal triangles, but when one is folded over, its corners stick out past the other, so that fold is NOT a line of symmetry.

y.A: The fold through P runs straight up the middle, and the left half lands exactly on the right half, so this fold does match.
y.B: The fold through Q runs straight across the middle, and the top half lands exactly on the bottom half, so this fold does match.
y.D: Every fold makes the halves match is the common mistake: the corner-to-corner fold cuts the flag into two equal triangles, but folded over they do not line up.

qr.q: The figure shows half of a paper cutout for the camp sign. The dashed side is the fold. When the paper is unfolded, how many sides does the whole cutout have?
qr.e: Unfolded, the bottom edge and its mirror image make one straight side, and so do the top edge and its mirror image. The right edge and the slanted edge each get a mirror copy. That is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 sides.

y.A: 5 counts the sides of the half that is drawn, with the fold counted as a side.
y.C: 8 doubles the 4 sides that are not the fold, but the bottom side and the top side each join their mirror image to make one long side.
y.D: 10 doubles all 5 sides of the half, including the fold, which disappears when the paper is opened.

qr.ss: folding a shape along a line

qr.q: The map of the campsite is drawn on a coordinate grid. Which place is at (6, 2)?
qr.e: Start at 0, go 6 across and then 2 up. The trailhead is at that point.

y.A: Campfire is at (5, 1), one line short each way; it counts the 0 line as 1.
y.B: Lake is at (6, 3), one line too high; it starts at the line marked 1 and counts 2 more lines up from there, instead of starting from 0.
y.C: Tent is at (2, 6), the same two numbers the other way round; the number across comes first.

qr.q: Kellan cut a sign for the camp kitchen out of cardboard: a rectangle with a triangle on top, as the figure shows. The dashed line shows where the rectangle and the triangle meet, and the two slanted sides are the same length. What is the perimeter of the sign?
qr.e: Go around the outside only: 8 + 12 + 8 along the rectangle and 10 + 10 along the slanted sides make 48 inches. The dashed line is inside the sign, so it is not part of the perimeter.

y.A: 30 inches adds only the three labeled sides; the right side and the other slanted side count too.
y.B: 40 inches goes around the rectangle alone: it counts the dashed line and leaves out the two slanted sides.
y.D: 60 inches counts the dashed line, which is inside the sign, as part of its edge.

qr.q: Lia drew a birdhouse for the playground on a grid of 1-inch squares, as the figure shows. What is the area of the birdhouse drawing?
qr.e: There are 14 whole squares and 4 half squares. Two halves make a whole, so the halves add 2 more: 14 + 2 = 16 square inches.

y.A: 14 square inches counts the whole squares and leaves out the 4 half squares under the roof.
y.C: 18 square inches counts each of the 4 half squares as a whole square.
y.D: 20 square inches is 4 × 5, the rectangle around the whole drawing, including the empty corners beside the roof.

qr.q: Milan built the block shown from identical small cubes, with no gaps and no hidden holes. Then he painted all six outside faces of the block. How many of the small cubes have no paint on them at all?
qr.e: A cube with no paint touches none of the six outside faces, so it sits inside, away from every face: 2 across, 2 deep and 1 high. 2 × 2 × 1 = 4 cubes.

y.A: 0 assumes every small cube touches the outside, but the cubes in the middle of the block touch no outside face.
y.B: 2 counts the cubes in the middle of the front face, but those cubes are on the front, so they are painted.
y.D: 18 counts every cube hidden from view in the drawing, but most of those still touch the back, the bottom or the left side, which are painted too.

qr.q: The table shows some units of capacity. Leona fills her family's 3-gallon fish tank with a pitcher that holds 2 pints. How many pitchers of water does she need to fill the tank?
qr.e: 3 gallons is 3 × 4 = 12 quarts, and each quart is 2 pints, so the tank holds 24 pints. Each pitcher holds 2 pints: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 pitchers.

y.A: 3 is the number of gallons; it still has to be changed into pitchers.
y.B: 6 is 3 × 2, the gallons times the pitcher's 2 pints, skipping the quarts in between.
y.D: 24 is the number of pints in 3 gallons, but each pitcher holds 2 pints.

qr.ss: converting units of weight and capacity

qr.q: The table shows how many minutes Kane practiced soccer on the sports field each day. How long did he practice in all?
qr.e: Add the four days: 40 + 25 + 45 + 35 = 145 minutes. Two hours is 120 minutes, and 145 − 120 = 25, so he practiced 2 hours 25 minutes.

y.A: 1 hour 45 minutes reads 145 minutes as 1 hundred and 45, as if an hour had 100 minutes; an hour has 60.
y.C: 2 hours 45 minutes gets the 2 hours right but copies the 45 from 145 instead of finding the 25 minutes left after 120.
y.D: 145 hours keeps the number of minutes and only changes the unit.

qr.q: The table shows the distances on a camping map between the stops on a trip. On the map, 1 inch stands for 4 miles. How many real miles is it from the camp to the falls, going by the bridge?
qr.e: On the map, camp to bridge to falls is 2 + 1 1/2 = 3 1/2 inches. Each inch stands for 4 miles: 3 inches is 12 miles and the half inch is 2 more, so 14 miles.

y.A: 6 miles is only the bridge-to-falls part, 1 1/2 inches; the trip starts at the camp.
y.B: 8 miles is only the camp-to-bridge part, 2 × 4.
y.C: 12 miles leaves out the half inch: 3 × 4 instead of 3 1/2 × 4.

qr.ss: scale read off a map, plan or ruler

qr.q: Mrs. Maddox's class voted for a field trip. The graph shows the votes. Which statement is NOT true?
c: The zoo got 2 more votes than the farm.
The farm got half as many votes as the aquarium.
The aquarium got 4 times as many votes as the museum.
qr.e: The aquarium has 12 votes and the museum has 4, and 12 = 3 × 4, so the aquarium got 3 times as many votes, not 4 times. The other three statements all match the graph.

y.A: 30 students voted in all is true: 12 + 8 + 4 + 6 = 30. Missing a bar while adding makes it look false.
y.B: The zoo got 2 more votes than the farm is true: 8 − 6 = 2. Comparing the zoo with the museum instead gives 4 and makes it look false.
y.C: The farm got half as many votes as the aquarium is true: 6 is half of 12. Reading the museum's bar for the farm's makes it look false.

qr.q: The graph shows how many people visited the aquarium each hour one Saturday. How many more people visited at 1 p.m. than at 10 a.m.?
qr.e: At 1 p.m. the line is at 60, and at 10 a.m. it is at 35. 60 − 35 = 25 more people.

y.B: 35 is the number of people at 10 a.m., not how many more came at 1 p.m.
y.C: 60 is the number of people at 1 p.m., not how many more than at 10 a.m.
y.D: 95 is 60 + 35, the two readings added instead of compared.

qr.q: The pictograph shows how many laps four friends swam at the camp lake. What is the mean number of laps they swam?
qr.e: Each symbol is 4 laps, so Kya swam 12, Lev 6, Macy 18 and Kade 8. The total is 44 laps, and shared equally among the 4 friends that is 44 ÷ 4 = 11 laps each.

y.A: 10 is the median, halfway between the two middle values, 8 and 12, not the mean.
y.C: 12 is the range, 18 − 6, how far apart the most and the fewest laps are.
y.D: 44 is the total number of laps, before it is shared equally among the 4 friends.

qr.ss: mean read off a graph or table

qr.q: Mr. Lund asked the 28 students in his class whether they visited the aquarium or the zoo this summer. The Venn diagram shows the answers, but the number of students who visited both has been left out. Students outside the circles visited neither. How many students visited both?
qr.e: All 28 students are somewhere in the diagram. The numbers shown add up to 9 + 8 + 6 = 23, so the missing middle part is 28 − 23 = 5 students.

y.B: 11 is 28 − 9 − 8; it forgets the 6 students outside the circles, who visited neither place.
y.C: 17 adds the two numbers inside the circles, 9 + 8, students who visited only one place.
y.D: 23 adds every number shown, 9 + 8 + 6, which is everyone except the students who visited both.

qr.q: The table shows the marbles in four bags at the camp game booth. Maisie will pick one marble without looking from one of the bags. From which bag is she most likely to pick a red marble?
qr.e: Compare the part of each bag that is red: P 1 out of 2, Q 8 out of 15, R 5 out of 16, S 6 out of 8. Bag S is three quarters red, the greatest part, so red is most likely from Bag S.

y.A: Bag P has the fewest blue marbles, but it has only 1 red too, so red is 1 out of 2, a half.
y.B: Bag Q has the most red marbles, but it has almost as many blue: 8 out of 15 is only a little more than half.
y.C: Bag R has the most marbles in all, but most of them are blue: red is 5 out of 16, less than a third.

qr.q: Kody spins the arrow on the number spinner once. All 8 parts are the same size. What is the probability that it lands on a number greater than 5?
qr.e: The 8 parts are equally likely. The numbers greater than 5 are 6, 7 and 8, which is 3 out of 8, or 3/8.

y.B: 1/2 counts 5 as greater than 5, making 5, 6, 7 and 8 four of the 8 parts.
y.C: 3/5 compares the 3 numbers greater than 5 with the 5 numbers that are not, instead of with all 8.
y.D: 5/8 is the chance of landing on 5 or less, the opposite of what is asked.

qr.q: The Venn diagram shows how many campers chose each mix of activities at summer camp. How many campers chose soccer but NOT tennis?
qr.e: Inside the soccer circle and outside the tennis circle are two parts: soccer only (6) and soccer with swimming (5). 6 + 5 = 11 campers.

y.A: 6 counts the soccer-only part and leaves out the 5 campers in soccer and swimming, who are also outside the tennis circle.
y.C: 13 adds the part where soccer and tennis overlap, but those 2 campers chose tennis.
y.D: 15 is everyone inside the soccer circle, including the 4 who are inside the tennis circle too.

qr.q: The table shows how many goals five players on the school soccer team scored this season. What is the median number of goals?
qr.e: The median is the middle value once the values are in order: 2, 3, 5, 6, 8. The middle of the five is 5.

y.B: 6 is the range, 8 − 2, the spread between the most and the fewest goals.
y.C: 8 is in the middle row of the table, but the goals must be put in order before the middle one is found.
y.D: 24 is the total of all the goals, not a middle value.

qr.ss: median read off a graph or table

qr.q: What is the smallest number greater than 100 that is a multiple of both 4 and 15?
qr.e: A number both 4 and 15 divide is a multiple of 4 × 15 = 60, because 4 and 15 share no factor bigger than 1. The multiples of 60 are 60, 120, 180, and the first one past 100 is 120. With two conditions, list the common multiples first and then check which one clears the extra condition.

y.B: 60 is 4 × 15, the smallest number both 4 and 15 divide — but the question wants one greater than 100. The next common multiple is 60 × 2 = 120.
y.C: 105 is 15 × 7, the first multiple of 15 past 100, but 4 does not divide it. The number has to be a multiple of both, and that is 120.
y.D: 104 is 4 × 26, the first multiple of 4 past 100, but 15 does not divide it. The first number past 100 that both divide is 120.

qr.q: A list of four numbers is 18, 25, 31 and 22. One more number is added and the range does not change. Which of these numbers could the new one be?
qr.e: The range is 31 − 18 = 13, and it only changes if the new number falls outside 18 and 31. Of these four, only 27 lands between them, so both ends stay where they are and the range is still 13. When a value joins a list, ask one question only: does it beat either end?

y.A: 10 is below 18, the lowest number already in the list, so it would become the new lowest and stretch the range to 31 − 10 = 21. Only a number between the two ends leaves the range alone.
y.C: 33 is above 31, the highest number already in the list, so the top end moves and the range grows to 33 − 18 = 15. Only a number from 18 up to 31 keeps the range unchanged.
y.D: 13 is the range itself, not one of the numbers. It is below 18, so adding it would stretch the range to 31 − 13 = 18. A number between the two ends, such as 27, leaves it alone.

qr.q: A photograph is 4 inches wide and 6 inches tall. It is enlarged to 12 inches wide, keeping the same shape. How tall is the enlarged photograph?
qr.e: The width goes from 4 inches to 12 inches, which is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times as wide, so the height is 6 × 3 = 18 inches. Find the number the sides are multiplied by first, then use it on the side you want.

y.A: 14 is 6 + 8, the same 8 inches added to the height as were added to the width. An enlargement multiplies instead: the width grew 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times, so the height is 6 × 3 = 18 inches.
y.C: 24 is 6 × 4, the height multiplied by the old width. The number to multiply by is 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so the height becomes 6 × 3 = 18 inches.
y.D: 9 is 6 + 3, the 3 added to the height instead of multiplied by it. Three times as wide means three times as tall: 6 × 3 = 18 inches.

qr.ss: enlarging lengths by a scale factor

qr.q: A door mat is a rectangle 90 cm long and 60 cm wide. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
qr.e: A rectangle whose sides are not all equal matches along the fold down its middle and the fold across its middle, so it has 2 lines of symmetry. The diagonals only work when all four sides are the same length, which is what makes a square's answer 4 and a rectangle's 2.

y.B: 4 is the number a square has, counting both diagonals as folds. Fold this mat along a diagonal and a long side lands on a short one, so only 2 folds match.
y.C: 1 counts the fold down the middle and stops there. The mat also folds across the middle the other way, so there are 2 lines.
y.D: 0 would mean no fold matches. Folding the mat end to end brings the two halves exactly together, so it has 2 lines.

qr.q: A box holds exactly 36 one-centimetre cubes. A second box is twice as long, twice as wide and twice as tall. How many of the same cubes does it hold?
qr.e: Doubling the length, the width and the height each multiplies the number of cubes by 2, so the second box holds 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes. A box grows in three directions at once, so one doubling counts three times over.

y.A: 72 is 36 × 2, one doubling counted and the other two forgotten. All three measurements double, so the box holds 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes.
y.C: 144 is 36 × 4, two of the three doublings counted. The third one counts as well: 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes.
y.D: 108 is 36 × 3, the three doublings turned into a single multiplication by 3. Each doubling multiplies on its own: 36 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 288 cubes.

qr.ss: how volume changes when edges change (beyond Lower Level)

qr.q: A bus route ran 6 trips on Monday carrying an average of 24 riders on each trip, and 4 trips on Tuesday carrying an average of 34 riders on each trip. What was the average number of riders per trip over the two days?
qr.e: Monday's 6 trips carried 6 × 24 = 144 riders and Tuesday's 4 trips carried 4 × 34 = 136, which is 280 riders across 10 trips, so 280 ÷ 10 = 28 riders per trip. Two averages cannot simply be averaged when the groups are different sizes — turn each one back into a total, add the totals, and divide once at the end.

y.B: 29 riders is 58 ÷ 2, the two averages averaged as though each day had the same number of trips. Monday carried 6 × 24 = 144 riders and Tuesday 4 × 34 = 136, so 280 ÷ 10 = 28.
y.C: 58 riders is 24 + 34, the two averages added instead of the riders counted. Each day's riders come first: 144 + 136 = 280, and 280 ÷ 10 = 28.
y.D: 280 riders is everyone who rode over the two days, before they are shared among the trips. There were 10 trips in all: 280 ÷ 10 = 28.

qr.q: A hall is set out with 2⁴ rows of chairs and 5² chairs in each row. How many chairs are there altogether?
qr.e: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 rows and 5² = 5 × 5 = 25 chairs in each row, so the hall holds 16 × 25 = 400 chairs. Turn each power into an ordinary number first, and what is left is a plain multiplication.

y.B: 200 is 8 × 25, with the rows worked out as 2 × 4 instead of four twos multiplied. 2⁴ = 16, so 16 × 25 = 400.
y.C: 160 is 16 × 10, with the chairs in a row worked out as 5 × 2. Squaring gives 5 × 5 = 25, so 16 × 25 = 400.
y.D: 41 is 16 + 25, the rows added to the chairs in a row instead of multiplied. Every row holds 25 chairs: 16 × 25 = 400.

qr.ss: powers of a number (beyond Lower Level)

qr.q: A tray holds 14 tomatoes. A market stall has t full trays and 5 loose tomatoes. Which expression gives the total number of tomatoes?
qr.e: Each tray brings 14 tomatoes, so t trays bring 14t, and the 5 loose ones are added once: 14t+5. Ask which part repeats and which part happens only once — the repeating part is the one that gets the letter.

y.A: 14+5t is one tray plus five tomatoes for every tray, the two numbers swapped round. It is the trays that repeat: 14t+5.
y.B: 14t-5 takes the five loose tomatoes away instead of adding them on. They are extra tomatoes: 14t+5.
y.C: 19t is 14 + 5 multiplied by every tray, which puts five loose tomatoes into each one. There are only five altogether: 14t+5.

qr.q: A garden path is made from 6 stone slabs laid end to end, each 80 centimeters long. How long is the path in meters?
qr.e: The six slabs come to 6 × 80 = 480 centimeters, and 480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 meters. Two-step measuring is safest done in the small unit all the way through and changed to the big unit at the very end — and a quick check helps: six slabs a little under a meter each should come out near five meters.

y.A: 480 meters is the path measured in centimeters with the word meters put after it. 480 centimeters is 480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 meters.
y.B: 48 meters is 6 × 8, the zero dropped from the 80. Six slabs of 80 come to 480 centimeters, which is 4.8 meters.
y.D: 0.48 meters is 480 ÷ 1,000, shorter than a single slab. There are 100 centimeters in a meter: 480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 meters.

qr.q: A garden show charges $3 for an adult and $2 for a child. A group of 4 adults and 7 children go in together. What does the group pay altogether?
qr.e: The adults pay 4 × 3 = 12 dollars and the children pay 7 × 2 = 14 dollars, so the group pays 12 + 14 = 26 dollars. Price each group on its own first — a single multiplication can never cover two different prices.

y.A: 22 is 11 × 2, all eleven visitors charged the child's price. The adults pay 4 × 3 = 12 and the children pay 7 × 2 = 14, so the total is 12 + 14 = 26.
y.C: 33 is 11 × 3, everyone charged the adult's price. Only the 4 adults pay 3 each: 4 × 3 = 12, and 7 × 2 = 14 for the children, giving 12 + 14 = 26.
y.D: 29 is 4 × 2 + 7 × 3, the two prices swapped round. Adults pay the larger one, so it is 4 × 3 = 12 and 7 × 2 = 14, and 12 + 14 = 26.

qr.q: A garden flag is made three times as long and three times as wide. How much cloth does the new flag need?
qr.e: Tripling the length multiplies the cloth by 3 and tripling the width multiplies it by 3 again, so the new flag needs 3 × 3 = 9 times as much. Count how many measurements changed, then multiply the changes together.

y.A: 3 times as much counts only one of the two triplings. The length is tripled and so is the width, so the cloth grows 3 × 3 = 9 times.
y.C: 6 times as much comes from adding the two triplings as 3 + 3 = 6. They multiply instead: 3 × 3 = 9 times as much cloth.
y.D: 27 times as much is 3 × 3 × 3, a tripling counted three times over. A flat piece of cloth has only a length and a width: 3 × 3 = 9.

qr.ss: how area changes when sides change (beyond Lower Level)

qr.q: A sign painter cuts capital letters from card and folds each one to test it. Which letter matches both when it is folded down the middle and when it is folded straight across?
qr.e: The letter H matches when it is folded down the middle and again when it is folded straight across, so it has both lines of symmetry. Test the two folds one at a time and keep only the letter that survives both.

y.A: The letter T matches when it is folded down the middle, but folded straight across the crossbar at the top has nothing to meet at the bottom. The letter H matches both ways.
y.B: The letter E matches when it is folded across, the top arm landing on the bottom arm, but its upright spine sits on the left only, so the fold down the middle fails. The letter H matches both ways.
y.D: The letter M matches when it is folded down the middle, but folded straight across the points along the bottom have nothing to meet above them. Only the letter H matches both ways.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 4,150.

y.A: 3,150 is the sum with the carried thousand left behind. The 400 and the 750 make 1,150, so that thousand joins the others: 2,400 + 1,750 = 4,150.
y.B: 4,050 is a hundred short. The 400 and the 750 make 1,150, and it is easy to carry the thousand and leave the extra hundred behind: put it back and 2,400 + 1,750 = 4,150.
y.D: 4,250 is a hundred too many, one carry counted twice. The 400 and the 750 make 1,150, so 2,400 + 1,750 = 4,150.

ma.q: What is 315 ÷ 7?

y.C: 47 keeps the 7 you were dividing by in the ones place. Seven fives make 35, so the last digit is a 5: 315 ÷ 7 = 45.
y.A: 39 is too small: 7 × 39 = 273, which is 42 short of 315.
y.D: 51 overshoots: 7 × 51 = 357.

ma.ss: dividing a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number

ma.q: Of 36 theater seats, two thirds are filled. How many seats are filled?

y.C: 18 is 36 ÷ 2, half the seats rather than two thirds of them. Split the 36 into three first: 36 ÷ 3 = 12, then 12 × 2 = 24.
y.A: 20 is not two thirds of 36; a third of 36 is 12, so two thirds is 24.
y.B: 27 comes from taking 3/4 of 36 rather than 2/3.

ma.q: Three quarters of a gallon fills how many one-eighth-gallon jars?
ma.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six eighths.

y.A: 4 is the 4 from "three quarters" — the number of parts a gallon splits into, not a number of jars. Three quarters is the same as 6/8, so it fills 6 jars.
y.C: 8 is how many eighth-gallon jars a whole gallon fills. Only three quarters of a gallon is being poured, and 3/4 is 6/8, so it fills 6 jars.
y.D: 3 is the 3 from "three quarters", the number of quarter-gallons. Each quarter fills two of the eighth-gallon jars, so 3 × 2 = 6 jars.

ma.q: What is 6.4 × 0.5?
ma.e: Multiplying by 0.5 means taking half.

y.A: 12.8 is 6.4 ÷ 0.5, the 6.4 divided by the half rather than multiplied by it. Multiplying by 0.5 takes half, and half of the 6.4 comes to 3.2.
y.B: 0.32 is a tenth of the answer; half of 6.4 is 3.2.
y.D: 32 is ten times too big — multiplying by 0.5 makes a number smaller, not larger.

ma.q: An $8.75 fare is reduced by a $3.90 coupon. What is the new fare?

y.A: 4.75 is 8.75 − 4, the coupon rounded up to a whole $4. That takes off 10 cents too much, so add them back: 4.75 + 0.10 = 4.85.
y.B: 5.15 takes the cents the other way round, 90 − 75 = 15, because 75 looked too small to take 90 from. Borrow a whole dollar from the 8 instead: 8.75 − 3.90 = 4.85.
y.C: 5.85 keeps all 8 dollars after a dollar has been borrowed from them. After the borrow there are 7 dollars: 7 − 3 = 4, so the fare is $4.85.

ma.q: Thirty percent of 90 campers choose chess. How many campers choose chess?

y.A: 9 is 90 ÷ 10, one tenth of the campers with the other two tenths never added on. Thirty percent means three tenths: 9 × 3 = 27.
y.B: 63 is 90 − 27, the campers who did not choose chess rather than the ones who did. Three tenths chose it: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.
y.D: 60 is 90 − 30, the thirty taken off the ninety rather than used as a percentage. Thirty percent means three tenths: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.

ma.q: What is 40% of 70?

y.B: 30 is 70 − 40, the forty taken off the seventy rather than used as a percentage. Forty percent means four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.C: 42 is 70 − 28, the part left behind rather than the part asked for. Forty percent means four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.D: 7 is 70 ÷ 10, one tenth found and the other three tenths never added on. Four tenths means 7 × 4 = 28.

ma.q: What is 7 + 3 × 9?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 34.

y.A: 37 is 34 + 3, with the 3 counted once on its own and again in the 3 × 9. The 3 is only there to multiply: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 + 7 = 34.
y.C: 90 is 10 × 9, from adding the 7 and the 3 first. Multiplying comes first: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 + 7 = 34.
y.D: 25 is 34 − 9, one nine short — only two of the three nines added on. There are three: 3 × 9 = 27, then 27 + 7 = 34.

ma.q: What is 5/6 - 1/3?
ma.e: 1/3 = 2/6; the difference is 3/6 = 1/2.

y.B: 2/3 is 4/6, from taking 5 − 1 on the tops while the bottoms were still different. Make them match first: 1/3 is 2/6, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.C: 1/3 is what is left when 1/3 is changed to 3/6 instead of 2/6 — the 3 is the bottom you are changing, not the new top. Two sixths make a third, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.D: 4/3 comes from working the tops and the bottoms separately, 5 − 1 = 4 and 6 − 3 = 3. Only the tops get subtracted, once the bottoms match: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, or 1/2.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 6,350.

y.B: 6,450 puts a 4 in the hundreds, but that column is 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, so a 3 goes there and the total is 6,350.
y.C: 6,250 leaves out the hundred carried over from the tens, where 7 + 8 = 15, so the hundreds come to 12 instead of 13. With the carry, 3,770 + 2,580 = 6,350.
y.D: 6,360 puts a 6 in the tens, but 7 + 8 = 15, so a 5 goes in the tens and a hundred carries over: 3,770 + 2,580 = 6,350.

ma.q: What is 750 ÷ 10?

y.A: 7.5 is 750 ÷ 100, the point moved two places instead of one. Dividing by 10 moves each digit one place to the right: 10 × 75 = 750, so 750 ÷ 10 = 75.
y.B: 70 is 700 ÷ 10, with the 50 of the 750 never shared out. Those 50 make five more tens, because 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so 750 ÷ 10 = 75.
y.C: 740 is 750 − 10, the 10 taken away rather than shared out. Sharing 750 into 10 equal parts gives 750 ÷ 10 = 75.

ma.q: What is 3/8 + 1/4?
ma.e: 1/4 = 2/8, so the sum is 5/8.

y.A: 4/12 comes from adding the tops and the bottoms, 3 + 1 = 4 and 8 + 4 = 12. The bottoms are made to match instead: 1/4 is 2/8, so 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.
y.B: 1/2 is 4/8, from adding 3 + 1 on the tops and keeping the 8 underneath. Once 1/4 becomes 2/8 it is 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.
y.C: 7/8 is 3/8 + 4/8, with the 4 from 1/4 copied up as the new top. Two eighths make a quarter, so 1/4 is 2/8: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.

ma.q: An 8.75 m ribbon loses 3.9 m of trim. What length remains?

y.B: 4.75 is 8.75 − 4, the trim rounded up to a whole 4 m. That takes off 10 cm too much, so add them back: 4.75 + 0.10 = 4.85.
y.C: 5.15 takes the hundredths the other way round, 90 − 75 = 15, because 75 looked too small to take 90 from. Borrow from the 8 instead: 8.75 − 3.90 = 4.85.
y.D: 5.85 keeps all 8 whole meters after one of them has been borrowed. After the borrow there are 7: 7 − 3 = 4, so 4.85 m remains.

ma.q: Thirty percent of 90 badges are blue. How many badges are blue?

y.A: 63 is 90 − 27, the badges that are not blue rather than the blue ones. Three tenths are blue: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.
y.C: 9 is 90 ÷ 10, one tenth of the badges with the other two tenths never added on. Thirty percent means three tenths: 9 × 3 = 27.
y.D: 60 is 90 − 30, the thirty taken off the ninety rather than used as a percentage. Thirty percent means three tenths: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27.

ma.e: Add by place value to get 7,450.

y.A: 7,350 leaves out the hundred carried over from the tens, where 5 + 9 + 1 = 15, so the hundreds come to 13 instead of 14. With the carry, 4,455 + 2,995 = 7,450.
y.C: 7,460 rounds 2,995 up to 3,000 and then adds the extra five on instead of taking it back off. 4,455 + 3,000 = 7,455, and 7,455 − 5 = 7,450.
y.D: 7,550 puts a 5 in the hundreds, but that column is 4 + 9 + 1 = 14, so a 4 goes there and the total is 7,450.

ma.q: What is 720 ÷ 8?

y.A: 9 is 72 ÷ 8, the 720 read as 72 and its zero left out of the answer. Put the zero back: 8 × 90 = 720, so 720 ÷ 8 = 90.
y.B: 72 is 720 with a zero crossed off, which shares it into 10 rather than into 8 — that shortcut only works when the dividing is by 10. Eight nines make 72, so eight nineties make 720: 720 ÷ 8 = 90.
y.C: 80 is 720 ÷ 9, the fact remembered the wrong way round — 72 ÷ 9 = 8 in place of 72 ÷ 8 = 9. Here the 8 is the one doing the sharing: 8 × 90 = 720, so 720 ÷ 8 = 90.

ma.ss: dividing a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number

ma.q: What is 6 + 4 × 8?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 38.

y.A: 80 is 10 × 8, from adding the 6 and the 4 first. Multiplying comes first: 4 × 8 = 32, then 32 + 6 = 38.
y.B: 42 is 38 + 4, with the 4 counted once on its own and again in the 4 × 8. The 4 is only there to multiply: 4 × 8 = 32, then 32 + 6 = 38.
y.D: 30 is 38 − 8, one eight short — only three of the four eights added on. There are four: 4 × 8 = 32, then 32 + 6 = 38.

ma.q: A 36-card deck has two thirds picture cards. How many picture cards are there?

y.D: 18 is 36 ÷ 2, half the deck rather than two thirds of it. Split the 36 into three first: 36 ÷ 3 = 12, then 12 × 2 = 24.
y.A: 20 is not two thirds of 36; a third of 36 is 12, so two thirds is 24.
y.B: 27 comes from taking 3/4 of 36 rather than 2/3.

ma.q: What is 7.2 ÷ 0.6?
ma.e: Multiply both numbers by 10: 72 ÷ 6 = 12.

y.B: 1.2 is 7.2 ÷ 6, dividing by 6 instead of by 0.6. Make both numbers ten times bigger first: 72 ÷ 6 = 12.
y.C: 10 would mean 0.6 × 10 = 6, not 7.2.
y.D: 120 is ten times too big; 72 ÷ 6 = 12.

ma.q: What is 20% of 80?

y.D: 60 is 80 − 20, the twenty taken off the eighty rather than used as a percentage. Twenty percent means two tenths: 80 ÷ 10 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16.
y.A: 12 is 15% of 80; 20% is a fifth, which is 16.
y.C: 21 is over a quarter of 80, and a fifth is 16.

ma.q: What is 630 ÷ 6?

y.A: 15 is 105 with the 0 in the middle left out. Six will not go into the 3, and that step puts a 0 in the answer rather than nothing at all: 6 × 105 = 630.
y.B: 100 is 600 ÷ 6, with the 30 of the 630 never shared out. The 30 gives another 5, because 6 × 5 = 30, so 630 ÷ 6 = 105.
y.C: 315 is 630 ÷ 2, halved and then not shared any further. Dividing by 6 is halving and then sharing into 3: 315 ÷ 3 = 105.

ma.ss: dividing a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number

ma.e: Add by place value to get 8,990.

y.A: 9,000 is 5,400 + 3,600, both numbers rounded to the nearest hundred. Added exactly, 5,414 + 3,576 = 8,990.
y.D: 8,890 puts an 8 in the hundreds, but that column is 4 + 5 = 9, so the total is 8,990.
y.B: 9,090 carries a thousand that is not there; the hundreds make 4 + 5 = 9 with no carry, so the thousands are 5 + 3 = 8.

ma.q: Three quarters of a yard makes how many one-eighth-yard strips?
ma.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six eighths.

y.B: 3 is the 3 from "three quarters", the number of quarter-yards. Each quarter makes two eighth-yard strips, so 3 × 2 = 6.
y.C: 4 is the 4 from "three quarters" — the number of parts a yard splits into, not a number of strips. Three quarters is the same as 6/8, so it makes 6 strips.
y.D: 8 is how many eighth-yard strips a whole yard makes. Only three quarters of a yard is used, and 3/4 is 6/8, so it makes 6 strips.

ma.q: A garden is 6 m by 3 m. What fencing length goes around it?
ma.e: Perimeter = 2(6+3) = 18 m.

y.A: 9 is 6 + 3 — one long side and one short one. The fence goes round all four.
y.B: 12 is 6 + 6, the two long sides, with the short ones missing.
y.D: 15 is 6 + 6 + 3 — one short side left out.

ma.ss: perimeter of a rectangle or square

ma.q: A triangular flag has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. What is its area?

y.B: 60 is 10 × 6, the base times the height — the whole rectangle around the triangle. The triangle fills half of it: 60 ÷ 2 = 30.
y.D: 16 is 10 + 6, the base and the height added rather than multiplied. Multiply them and take half: 10 × 6 = 60, then 60 ÷ 2 = 30.
y.C: 38 is not half of 10 × 6; 10 × 6 = 60, and half of that is 30.

ma.q: A roof triangle has angles 45° and 60°. What is its third angle?
ma.e: Triangle angles total 180°: the third angle is 75°.

y.B: 120 is 180 − 60, with the 45° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 45 − 60 = 75.
y.C: 105 is 45 + 60, the two known angles added together instead of taken away from 180. The three angles make 180, so 180 − 105 = 75.
y.D: 135 is 180 − 45, with the 60° angle never taken off. Both known angles come off the 180: 180 − 45 − 60 = 75.

ma.ss: angles of a triangle add to 180°

ma.q: A square patio has side length 10 units. What is its area?

y.A: 110 is 100 + 10 — the area with one more side added on the end. The area is just 10 × 10.
y.B: 40 is 10 × 4, the perimeter: the distance all the way round the patio, not the space inside it.
y.C: 20 is 10 × 2, two sides. Area covers the whole patio, so it is 10 × 10.

ma.q: A banner is 10 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?

y.D: 23 is 10 + 10 + 3 — one short side left out.

y.B: 18 is 10 + 8. Area multiplies the base and the height, it never adds them.

ma.q: A roof triangle has angles 45° and 75°. What is its third angle?

ma.q: A square game board has side length 4 units. What is its area?

y.B: 12 is 16 − 4. Nothing is taken off an area: 4 × 4 = 16.
y.C: 8 is 4 × 2, two sides. A square has four, and its area is 4 × 4.

ma.q: A $100 item is 75% off. What is its sale price?

y.A: 75 is three quarters of the $100, which is the money that comes off — not the price paid. The sale price is what is left: 100 − 75 = 25.
y.B: 175 is 100 + 75, the discount added on instead of taken off. A sale makes the price smaller: 100 − 75 = 25.
y.C: 12.50 is 100 ÷ 8, one halving too many — 100 halves to 50, then to 25, then to 12.50. A quarter of the price is left, not an eighth: 100 − 75 = 25.

ma.q: What is 5.5÷0.1?
ma.e: Dividing by 0.1 makes the number ten times as large: 55.

y.A: 0.55 is 5.5 × 0.1, the tenth multiplied in rather than divided into. Dividing asks how many tenths are in 5.5, and there are 55 of them.
y.B: 5.5 is 5.5 ÷ 1, the 0.1 read as a whole 1. A tenth goes in ten times as often as a 1 does: 5.5 ÷ 0.1 = 55.
y.D: 550 is 5.5 ÷ 0.01, the point moved two places instead of one. Dividing by 0.1 makes a number ten times bigger, not a hundred times: 5.5 ÷ 0.1 = 55.

ma.q: Solve 3x+5=83.
ma.e: Subtract 5, then divide by 3: x=26.

y.B: 27 is what 83 ÷ 3 comes to with the remainder dropped — the sharing done before the 5 came off, since 3 × 27 = 81 leaves 2 over. The 5 comes off first: 83 − 5 = 78, then 78 ÷ 3 = 26.

y.D: 75 is 78 − 3, the 3 taken away as well as the 5. The 3 is multiplying x, and dividing is what undoes that: 78 ÷ 3 = 26.

ma.q: Four tenths of 70 teams earn a badge. How many teams earn a badge?

y.A: 7 is 70 ÷ 10, one tenth of the teams with the other three tenths never added on. Four tenths means 7 × 4 = 28.
y.B: 56 is four fifths of 70, from halving the bottom of 4/10 and leaving the top alone. Four tenths means 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.D: 66 is 70 − 4, the four taken off the seventy rather than used as four tenths of it. A tenth of 70 is 7, so four tenths is 7 × 4 = 28.

ma.q: What is 25% of 88?

y.A: 11 is 88 ÷ 8, one eighth of the 88 rather than one quarter — one halving too many. A quarter is two halvings: 88 ÷ 2 = 44, then 44 ÷ 2 = 22.
y.B: 44 is 88 ÷ 2, the first halving done and the second one forgotten. A quarter is two halvings: 44 ÷ 2 = 22.
y.D: 63 is 88 − 25, the twenty-five taken off the eighty-eight rather than used as a percentage. A quarter of 88 is 88 ÷ 4 = 22.

ma.q: What is 7×6?

y.A: 49 is 7 × 7, seven sevens counted rather than six. Take one seven off: 49 − 7 = 42.
y.C: 84 is 7 × 12, twelve sevens rather than six — the six doubled. Halve it back: 84 ÷ 2 = 42.
y.D: 13 is 7 + 6, the two numbers added rather than multiplied. Six sevens: 7 × 6 = 42.

ma.q: What is 3/4 of 48?

y.A: 24 is 48 ÷ 2, half of the forty-eight rather than three quarters of it. Quarter it first: 48 ÷ 4 = 12, then 12 × 3 = 36.
y.D: 12 is 48 ÷ 4, one quarter of the forty-eight rather than three quarters of it. Three quarters means three of those quarters: 12 × 3 = 36.
y.C: 42 is not three quarters of 48; a quarter of 48 is 12, so three quarters is 36.

ma.q: What is 5×13?

y.A: 55 is 50 + 5, one five added on to the ten fives instead of three. Ten fives make 50 and three more make 15, so 50 + 15 = 65.
y.C: 75 is 50 + 25 — after 5 × 10 = 50, the next step multiplied by 5 again instead of by 3. Three fives make 15, so 50 + 15 = 65.
y.B: 120 is not 5 × 13, which comes to 65.

ma.q: 2.5 feet equals how many inches?

y.A: 24 is 2 × 12, the half foot never turned into inches. Half a foot is 6 inches, so 24 + 6 = 30.
y.C: 14.5 is 12 + 2.5, the twelve added on rather than multiplied by. Each foot is 12 inches: 2.5 × 12 = 30.
y.D: 25 is 2.5 × 10, counted as if a foot were ten inches. A foot is twelve inches: 2.5 × 12 = 30.

ma.q: What is 7×8?

y.B: 64 is 8 × 8, eight eights rather than seven. Take one eight away: 64 − 8 = 56.
y.A: 112 doubles the product; 7 × 8 is 56.
y.C: 22 is not 7 × 8; adding 7 and 8 gives 15, and multiplying gives 56.

ma.q: A storage box measures 6×2×2. What is its volume?

y.A: 56 is the area of the six outside faces added together — the paper to wrap the box, not the space inside it. The space inside is 6 × 2 × 2 = 24.
y.C: 14 is 6 × 2 + 2, two sides multiplied and the third one added on. All three multiply: 6 × 2 = 12, then 12 × 2 = 24.
y.D: 10 is 6 + 2 + 2, the three sides added instead of multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24.

ma.q: A poster is 3 feet long. How many inches is that?

ma.q: What is the mean of daily readings 54, 58, and 62?
ma.e: The sum is 174; divide by 3 to get 58.

y.A: 56 is the middle of 54 and 58 on their own, with the 62 left out. All three readings count: 54 + 58 + 62 = 174, and 174 ÷ 3 = 58.
y.B: 60 is the middle of 58 and 62, with the 54 left out. Add all three, then share: 174 ÷ 3 = 58.
y.D: 174 is the three readings added up — the total, not the mean. Share it between the three days: 174 ÷ 3 = 58.

ma.q: What is the median of 53,56,59,62,66?

y.B: 13 is 66 − 53, the biggest take away the smallest — the spread of the numbers, not the middle one. With five numbers in order, the middle is the third: 59.
y.C: 62 is the fourth number in order, one step past the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 59.
y.D: 56 is the second number in order, one step short of the middle. With five numbers, the middle is the third one: 59.

y.B: 56 is the smallest number in the list, and it appears only once. The mode is the one that turns up most often: 59 is there twice.
y.C: 61 appears just once, the same as 56 and 64. Only 59 is repeated, so 59 is the mode.
y.D: 64 is the biggest number here, not the most common one. 59 is the one written twice.

y.B: 4/9 is the blue share — 4 blue out of the 9 marbles. The reds are the other 5: 5/9.
y.C: 1/9 is the chance of one particular marble out of the nine. Any of the 5 reds counts, so it is 5/9.
y.D: 5/4 sets the reds against the blues. A chance is out of every marble, and there are 9 altogether: 5/9.

ma.q: A sheet of paper is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: Perimeter is the whole way round: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm.

y.A: 13 is 9 + 4 — that is only two of the four sides.
y.C: 36 is 9 × 4, which is the area. Area is the space inside the paper; perimeter is the walk around its edge.
y.D: 18 is 9 + 9, the two long sides, with both short ones left out.

ma.ss: perimeter of a rectangle or square

ma.q: A rug is 7 feet long and 3 feet wide. A ribbon is sewn all the way around its edge. How long is the ribbon?
ma.e: "All the way around" is the perimeter: 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 feet.

y.A: 10 is 7 + 3 — one long side and one short one. The ribbon goes round all four.
y.B: 14 is 7 + 7, the two long sides only.
y.C: 21 is 7 × 3, the area — how much floor the rug covers, not how far it is round the edge.

ma.ss: perimeter of a rectangle or square

ma.q: A square tile has sides of 6 inches. What is its perimeter?
ma.e: Four equal sides: 6 × 4 = 24 inches.

y.B: 12 is two sides. A square has four.
y.C: 18 is three sides — one is still missing.
y.D: 36 is 6 × 6, the area of the tile, not the distance round it.

ma.ss: perimeter of a rectangle or square

ma.q: A rectangular garden has an area of 24 square metres. It is 4 metres wide. How long is it?
ma.e: Area = length × width, so length = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 m.

y.A: 5 is one short. Count the fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 — that is six of them.
y.B: 12 is half of 24. Halving only gives the answer when the other side is 2.
y.D: 20 is 24 − 4. The two sides were multiplied to make the area, so divide to get one back.

ma.ss: missing side of a rectangle from its area

ma.q: A card has an area of 18 square centimetres and is 3 centimetres wide. How tall is it?

y.A: 5 is one short: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 is six threes.
y.B: 9 is half of 18 — right only if the card were 2 cm wide.
y.C: 15 is 18 − 3. Area comes from multiplying, so divide to undo it.

ma.ss: missing side of a rectangle from its area

ma.q: A doormat covers 8 square feet. It is 4 feet long. How wide is it?
ma.e: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 feet.

y.A: 1 is one short: 4, then 4 again, makes 8 — two fours fit, not one.
y.C: 4 is 8 − 4. Undo a multiplication by dividing, not subtracting.
y.D: 32 is 8 × 4, which multiplies the area again instead of splitting it.

ma.ss: missing side of a rectangle from its area

ma.q: A rectangular photo has a perimeter of 18 inches. It is 6 inches long. How wide is it?
ma.e: Two lengths take 12, leaving 18 − 12 = 6 for the two widths, so each width is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 inches.

y.A: 6 is what is left once both lengths are taken off — but that 6 is TWO widths. Halve it.
y.B: 12 is 18 − 6, which takes off one length when the photo has two.
y.D: 9 is half the perimeter, which is one length plus one width. The 6 still has to come off.

ma.ss: missing side of a rectangle from its perimeter

ma.q: A flowerbed is edged with 22 metres of brick. The bed is 7 metres long. How wide is it?
ma.e: Two lengths take 14, leaving 22 − 14 = 8 for the two widths, so each width is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 m.

y.B: 8 is both widths together. One width is half of it.
y.C: 11 is half of 22 — one length plus one width. The 7 still has to come off.
y.D: 15 is 22 − 7, taking off one length when the brick runs along two.

ma.ss: missing side of a rectangle from its perimeter

ma.q: If 3x + 7 = 19, what is x?
ma.e: Subtract 7, then divide by 3: x = 4.

y.D: 16 is 19 − 3, the total with the 3 taken off instead of the 7. The 7 comes off first: 19 − 7 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
y.A: 3 does not check: 3 × 3 + 7 = 16, not 19.

ma.q: Which bus route number is divisible by both 2 and 3?
ma.e: 24 is even and its digit sum is 6, so it is divisible by 6.

y.A: 164 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 6 + 4 = 11, which is not in the 3 times table. The digits of 24 add to 6, and 6 is a multiple of 3.
y.B: 166 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 6 + 6 = 13, so 3 will not divide it. The digits of 24 add to 6, and 6 is a multiple of 3.
y.C: 170 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 7 + 0 = 8, so it is not a multiple of 3. The digits of 24 add to 6, and 6 is a multiple of 3.

ma.q: A game starts with 8 base points and adds 5 packs of 10 points. What is the total?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 58.

y.A: 48 is 58 − 10, the total with ten taken off it — one pack of points short. All five packs count: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.C: 63 is 58 + 5, the total with the 5 counted a second time. The 5 is the number of packs, not points of its own: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.B: 130 adds the 8 first and then multiplies, (8 + 5) × 10; the five packs are multiplied before the base points go on.

ma.q: Three quarters of a cup makes how many one-eighth-cup samples?
ma.e: 3/4 = 6/8, so there are six eighths.

y.A: 3 is the 3 from three quarters, the top number read straight off. Turn 3/4 into eighths first: 3/4 = 6/8, which is six samples.
y.C: 4 is the 4 from three quarters, the bottom number read straight off. It is the size of the pieces, not how many: 3/4 = 6/8, so six samples.
y.D: 8 is how many eighths fit in a whole cup. Only three quarters of a cup is being shared out, and 3/4 = 6/8, so six.

ma.q: A 6.4-meter ribbon is cut in half. How long is each piece?
ma.e: Cutting in half means multiply by 0.5: 3.2 meters.

y.D: 12.8 is 6.4 × 2, the ribbon doubled rather than halved. Cutting in half means 6.4 ÷ 2 = 3.2 meters for each piece.
y.A: 0.32 is a tenth of half of 6.4, which is 3.2.
y.B: 32 is ten times too long; half of 6.4 meters is 3.2.

ma.ss: dividing a decimal by a whole number

ma.q: What is 25% of 64?

y.C: 39 is 64 − 25, the 25 taken away as a plain number rather than used as a percent. Twenty-five percent means a quarter: 64 ÷ 4 = 16.
y.B: 21 is about a third of 64, and a quarter is 16.
y.D: 12 is under a fifth of 64; 64 ÷ 4 = 16.

ma.q: A square has side length 5 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area = 5² = 25.

y.B: 20 is 5 × 4, the perimeter — the way round the edge, not the space inside.
y.C: 10 is 5 × 2, two sides. Area is 5 × 5.
y.D: 30 is 25 + 5, the area with a side added on. 5 × 5 = 25 is the answer.

ma.ss: area of a rectangle or square

ma.q: What is the volume of a 7 × 5 × 3 rectangular prism?

y.A: 15 is 5 × 3, two of the three sides multiplied — one face of the box, not the space inside it. The 7 still has to come in: 15 × 7 = 105.
y.B: 38 is not 7 × 5 × 3, which comes to 105.
y.C: 142 is not the product; 7 × 5 = 35, and 35 × 3 = 105.

ma.ss: volume of a box (length × width × height)

ma.q: What is the mean of 84, 88, and 92?
ma.e: The sum is 264; divide by 3 to get 88.

y.A: 264 is 84 + 88 + 92, the total before it is shared out. Divide by the three numbers: 264 ÷ 3 = 88.
y.C: 86 is the average of just 84 and 88, with the 92 left out. All three numbers count: 84 + 88 + 92 = 264, and 264 ÷ 3 = 88.
y.D: 90 is the average of just 88 and 92, with the 84 left out. All three numbers count: 84 + 88 + 92 = 264, and 264 ÷ 3 = 88.

ma.q: If 4x + 6 = 26, what is x?
ma.e: Subtract 6, then divide by 4: x = 5.

y.B: 22 is 26 − 4, the total with the 4 taken off instead of the 6. The 6 comes off first: 26 − 6 = 20, then 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
y.A: 4 does not check: 4 × 4 + 6 = 22, not 26.

ma.q: Which locker code has digits that add to 6 and is even?
ma.e: 24 is even and 2+4=6.

y.A: 184 is even, but that is only half of what the code needs: its digits add to 1 + 8 + 4 = 13, not 6. Only 24 does both — even, with 2 + 4 = 6.
y.C: 182 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 8 + 2 = 11. The code has to pass both tests, and 24 is even with 2 + 4 = 6.
y.D: 188 is even, but its digits add to 1 + 8 + 8 = 17, well past 6. Only 24 is even and has digits adding to 6.

ma.q: What is 7 + 6 × 9?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 61.

y.C: 67 is 61 + 6, the total with the 6 counted a second time. The 6 is only multiplied: 6 × 9 = 54, then 54 + 7 = 61.
y.D: 52 is 61 − 9, the total one nine short. There are six nines to add on: 6 × 9 = 54, then 54 + 7 = 61.
y.B: 117 adds first and then multiplies, (7 + 6) × 9; multiplication comes before addition.

ma.q: If 3x + 9 = 33, what is x?
ma.e: Subtract 9, then divide by 3: x = 8.

y.A: 30 is 33 − 3, the total with the 3 taken off instead of the 9. The 9 comes off first: 33 − 9 = 24, then 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

ma.q: Five sixths of a path is paved. One third of the whole path is closed for repairs, and all of the closed stretch lies within the paved part. What fraction of the path is paved and open?

y.B: 2/3 is 4/6, which comes from taking the 1 off the 5 and keeping the sixths. One third is really 2/6, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.C: 1/3 is the closed part of the path, not the part that is paved and open. Take it off the paved part: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.
y.D: 4/3 takes the tops away from each other, 5 − 1 = 4, and the bottoms too, 6 − 3 = 3. Bottoms never subtract: match them first and 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2.

ma.q: What is 2.4 × 0.3?
ma.e: 24 × 3 = 72, then place two decimal digits.

y.B: 8 is 2.4 ÷ 0.3, the two numbers divided rather than multiplied. Multiplying gives 24 × 3 = 72, then two decimal places: 0.72.
y.C: 0.072 has three decimal places; 2.4 and 0.3 carry two between them, so 72 becomes 0.72.
y.D: 7.2 has only one decimal place, and the two factors carry two.

ma.q: Forty percent of 70 seedlings sprout. How many seedlings sprout?

y.A: 30 is 70 − 40, the forty taken off the seventy rather than used as a percentage. Forty percent means four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, then 7 × 4 = 28.
y.C: 7 is one tenth of 70, the first step done and then left there. Forty percent is four of those tenths: 7 × 4 = 28.
y.D: 42 is 70 − 28, the seedlings that did not sprout rather than the ones that did. Forty percent is four tenths: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, and 7 × 4 = 28.

ma.q: A square has side length 8 units. What is its area?
ma.e: Area = 8² = 64.

y.A: 16 is 8 × 2, two sides. Area is 8 × 8.
y.B: 32 is 8 × 4, the perimeter — round the edge, not the space inside.
y.D: 72 is 64 + 8, the area with one more side added on.

ma.ss: area of a rectangle or square

ma.q: What is the volume of a 7 × 3 × 4 rectangular prism?

y.A: 25 is 7 × 3 + 4, two of the sides multiplied and the third one added on. Volume multiplies all three: 7 × 3 = 21, then 21 × 4 = 84.
y.B: 122 is how much paper would cover all six faces, not the space inside the box. Volume multiplies the three sides: 7 × 3 = 21, then 21 × 4 = 84.
y.D: 14 is 7 + 3 + 4, the three sides added rather than multiplied. Volume multiplies them: 7 × 3 = 21, then 21 × 4 = 84.

ma.ss: volume of a box (length × width × height)

ma.q: How many inches are in 9 feet?
ma.e: 9 × 12 = 108 inches.

y.A: 27 is 9 × 3, as if a foot were 3 inches — 3 is the number of feet in a yard. A foot is 12 inches, so 9 × 12 = 108.
y.B: 90 is 9 × 10, as if a foot were ten inches. A foot is twelve, so 9 × 12 = 108.
y.C: 21 is 9 + 12, the feet and the twelve added rather than multiplied. Each of the 9 feet holds 12 inches: 9 × 12 = 108.

ma.q: What is the mode of 95, 98, 98, 100, 103?
ma.e: 98 occurs most often.

y.B: 95 is the lowest number on the list. The mode is the one that turns up most often, and 98 is there twice.
y.C: 103 is the highest number on the list. The mode is the one that turns up most often, and only 98 appears twice.
y.A: 100 appears once, and 98 appears twice.

ma.q: A bag has 2 red and 5 blue marbles. What is the probability of red?
ma.e: There are 7 marbles and 2 are red: 2/7.

y.B: 1/7 is one marble out of the seven, but 2 of them are red. Two out of seven is 2/7.
y.C: 5/7 is the chance of a blue marble, the other color in the bag. Two of the 7 marbles are red, so 2/7.
y.D: 2/5 sets the 2 red marbles against the 5 blue ones. A chance counts them against every marble in the bag: 2 + 5 = 7, so 2/7.

ma.q: Which number is divisible by 6?
ma.e: 204 is even and its digits sum to 6, so it is divisible by 6.

y.A: 215 is odd, and every multiple of 6 is even. The 6s land on 210 and then 216, stepping straight over 215.
y.C: 211 is odd, so no number of 6s can land on it. They go 204, 210, 216 — and 211 is not among them.
y.D: 206 is even, but a multiple of 6 also has to be in the 3 times table, and its digits add to 8, which is not. 6 × 34 = 204, two short of 206.

ma.q: A price is written as 8+5×10. What is its value?
ma.e: Multiply first, then add, to get 58.

y.A: 48 is 58 − 10, the value with ten taken off it — one ten short of the whole. All five tens count: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.C: 63 is 58 + 5, the value with the 5 counted a second time. The 5 only multiplies the 10: 5 × 10 = 50, then 50 + 8 = 58.
y.B: 130 adds first and then multiplies, (8 + 5) × 10; multiplication comes first.

ma.q: What is the mean of 99, 103, and 107?
ma.e: The sum is 309; divide by 3 to get 103.

y.A: 101 is the average of just 99 and 103, with the 107 left out. All three numbers count: 99 + 103 + 107 = 309, and 309 ÷ 3 = 103.
y.C: 105 is the average of just 103 and 107, with the 99 left out. All three numbers count: 99 + 103 + 107 = 309, and 309 ÷ 3 = 103.
y.D: 309 is 99 + 103 + 107, the total before it is shared out. Divide by the three numbers: 309 ÷ 3 = 103.

ma.q: Which improper fraction is equal to 3 2/5?
ma.e: A mixed number converts as (3 × 5) + 2 = 17 fifths, so 3 2/5 = 17/5.

y.A: 32/5 writes the 3 and the 2 side by side on the top. The 3 wholes are 3 × 5 = 15 fifths, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.
y.C: 11/5 gets its 11 from 3 × 2 = 6 and then + 5, the right steps done on the wrong two numbers. The whole multiplies the bottom: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.
y.D: 13/5 is 2 3/5, the 3 and the 2 swapped round. The 3 is the whole part here: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 17/5.

ma.q: What is 2/3 + 1/4?
ma.e: Rewrite both with denominator 12: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

y.A: 5/12 is 2/12 + 3/12, with 2/3 turned into 2/12 by multiplying only the bottom. Both numbers multiply by 4, so 2/3 is 8/12 and 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
y.C: 7/12 is 4/12 + 3/12, and 2/3 is not 4/12 — the 4 is what you multiply by, not the new top number. Multiply both parts by 4: 2/3 is 8/12, so 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
y.D: 3/7 adds the tops, 2 + 1 = 3, and the bottoms, 3 + 4 = 7. Bottoms never add: put both fractions in twelfths first, then 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

ma.q: What is 7/8 − 2/3?
ma.e: Rewrite with denominator 24: 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.

y.A: 5/11 takes 7 − 2 = 5 on the top, then adds the bottoms out of habit, 8 + 3 = 11. The bottoms are made to match, not added: 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.
y.B: 13/24 is what adding gives: 21/24 + 16/24 = 37/24, which is 1 and 13/24. This one takes away: 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.
y.D: 1/6 is 4/24, one twenty-fourth under the difference; 21/24 − 16/24 = 5/24.

ma.q: What is 3/4 × 2/5?
ma.e: Multiply across: (3 × 2)/(4 × 5) = 6/20, which simplifies to 3/10.

y.A: 6/9 multiplies the tops, 3 × 2 = 6, but adds the bottoms, 4 + 5 = 9. The bottoms multiply too: 4 × 5 = 20, and 6/20 is 3/10.
y.B: 1 7/8 is 3/4 ÷ 2/5, the second fraction flipped over — that is how you divide, not how you multiply. Multiplying needs no flip: 6 over 20, which is 3/10.
y.C: 5/9 adds where it should multiply: 3 + 2 = 5 on the top and 4 + 5 = 9 underneath. Multiply straight across instead: 6 over 20, which is 3/10.

ma.q: What is 5/8 ÷ 1/4?
ma.e: Dividing by 1/4 means multiplying by 4: 5/8 × 4 = 20/8 = 2 1/2.

y.B: 2 is the whole-number part of 20/8, the leftover thrown away. Eight goes into 20 twice with 4 over, and those 4 eighths are half of one more: 5/8 ÷ 1/4 = 2 1/2.
y.C: 2/5 is 8/5 × 1/4, the flip landing on the wrong fraction. It is the second fraction, the one you are dividing by, that turns over: 5/8 × 4 = 20/8 = 2 1/2.
y.D: 5/32 is 5/8 × 1/4, the two fractions multiplied instead of divided. Dividing by 1/4 asks how many quarters fit inside 5/8: 5/8 × 4 = 20/8, which is 2 1/2.

ma.ss: dividing a fraction by a fraction (beyond Lower Level)

ma.e: Change to improper fractions: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.

y.A: 2 3/10 multiplies the wholes on their own, 2 × 1 = 2, and the fractions on their own, 1/2 × 3/5 = 3/10. Turn both into improper fractions instead: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.
y.B: 3 1/5 is 2 × 1 3/5, the half of the 2 1/2 left out of the multiplying. Both parts of it have to be used: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.
y.C: 4 1/10 is 2 1/2 + 1 3/5, the two mixed numbers added instead of multiplied — 1/2 + 3/5 = 11/10, which is 1 1/10 on top of the 3. Multiplying wants improper fractions: 5/2 × 8/5 = 40/10 = 4.

ma.q: What is 0.6 × 0.07?
ma.e: 6 × 7 = 42, and the factors have 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places, so the answer is 0.042.

y.A: 4.2 is 0.6 × 7, with the 0.07 read as a whole 7. Count the places: 0.6 has one and 0.07 has two, so 6 × 7 = 42 becomes 0.042.
y.B: 0.42 is 0.6 × 0.7, one decimal place short, because 0.07 is much smaller than 0.7. There are three places in all, so the answer is 0.042.
y.C: 0.0042 counts four decimal places instead of three. There are three, one in the 0.6 and two in the 0.07, so 6 × 7 = 42 becomes 0.042.

ma.q: What is 4.05 ÷ 0.9?
ma.e: Multiply both numbers by 10: 40.5 ÷ 9 = 4.5. Check: 0.9 × 4.5 = 4.05.

y.B: 45 is 40.5 ÷ 0.9, the point moved in the 4.05 but not in the 0.9. Move it in both: 40.5 ÷ 9 = 4.5.
y.C: 0.45 is 4.05 ÷ 9, the point moved in the 0.9 but not in the 4.05. Move it in both: 40.5 ÷ 9 = 4.5.
y.D: 5.4 has the digits swapped: 0.9 × 4.5 = 4.05, while 0.9 × 5.4 = 4.86.

ma.q: What is 7.3 − 2.85?
ma.e: Line up the points and write 7.3 as 7.30: 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.

y.A: 4.5 is 7.3 − 2.8, with the last digit of the 2.85 dropped. Write 7.3 as 7.30 and take all of it: 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.
y.B: 5.45 borrows a ten for the tenths but leaves the 7 untouched. Borrowing turns that 7 into a 6, so 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.
y.D: 4.55 reads the last column backwards, doing 5 − 0 instead of taking 5 from 0. Borrow for that column instead: 7.30 − 2.85 = 4.45.

ma.q: Which decimal is equal to 3/8?

y.A: 0.125 is 1/8, one eighth where the question asks for three. The 3 on top counts how many eighths there are: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
y.B: 0.625 is 5/8, the five eighths left over rather than the three you were asked for. Divide the 3 by the 8: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
y.D: 0.83 puts the 8 before the 3, the bottom number of the fraction written first. The line in 3/8 means divide, and it is the 3 being shared out: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

ma.q: Written as a percent, 0.045 is equal to which of the following?
ma.e: Move the decimal point two places right: 0.045 = 4.5%.

y.A: 450% is the point moved four places instead of two, which is × 100 done twice. Percent is exactly two places: 0.045 becomes 4.5%.
y.C: 0.45% moves the point one place, not two. Two places from 0.045 gives 4.5%.
y.D: 45% is what 0.45 would be as a percent, and 0.045 is ten times smaller than that. Two places from 0.045 gives 4.5%.

ma.ss: percent as another way to write a fraction or decimal

ma.q: What is 12.5% of 96?

y.A: 8 is 96 ÷ 12, the 96 split into twelve parts instead. Twelve and a half percent means an eighth of it: 96 ÷ 8 = 12.
y.B: 16 is 96 ÷ 6; 12.5% is an eighth, so it is 96 ÷ 8.
y.C: 10.5 is not 96 ÷ 8, which comes to 12.

ma.q: A muffin recipe uses 2 3/4 cups of flour for one batch. How many cups of flour are needed for 2 batches?

y.A: 4 3/4 comes from adding the 2 batches on rather than doubling: 2 3/4 + 2 = 4 3/4. Two batches means twice as much: 2 3/4 + 2 3/4 = 5 1/2 cups.
y.B: 5 3/4 turns the 6/4 into 1 3/4 by keeping the 3 you started with. Six quarters is one whole and 2/4, so 4 + 1 1/2 = 5 1/2 cups.
y.C: 3 1/2 is 2 + 1 1/2, the 3/4 doubled but the 2 whole cups left as one batch's worth. Both parts double: 2 3/4 + 2 3/4 = 4 + 1 1/2 = 5 1/2 cups.

ma.ss: a fraction times a whole number

ma.q: A pancake recipe calls for 2/3 cup of milk. To make only half of the recipe, how many cups of milk are needed?
ma.e: Half of 2/3 is 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/6, and 2/6 simplifies to 1/3 cup.

y.A: 1/6 halves the 2 on top and doubles the 3 underneath, which halves it twice over. Either one on its own is enough: half of 2/3 is 1/3 cup.
y.B: 1/2 is the half from the question, not half of the milk. Half of the 2/3 cup is 1/3 cup.
y.D: 1 1/3 is 2/3 × 2, the recipe doubled rather than halved. Half of 2/3 is 2/6, which is 1/3 cup.

ma.q: A pitcher holds 3 1/3 cups of juice. If 5/6 cup is poured out, how many cups of juice remain?

y.B: 2 1/3 is 3 1/3 − 1, the 5/6 rounded up to a whole cup. Five sixths is a little less than one: 20/6 − 5/6 = 15/6, which is 2 1/2 cups.
y.C: 3 1/6 is 3 1/3 − 1/6, the sixth left in the cup taken off rather than the 5/6 poured out. Take all five sixths: 20/6 − 5/6 = 15/6, which is 2 1/2 cups.
y.D: 2 5/6 takes 1/2 away rather than 5/6; over sixths, 20/6 − 5/6 = 15/6.

ma.q: A ribbon 4 1/2 feet long is cut into pieces that are each 3/4 foot long. How many pieces are there?

y.A: 3 3/8 comes from multiplying by 3/4 instead of dividing by it: 4 1/2 × 3/4 = 3 3/8. Asking how many 3/4-foot pieces fit is a division: 9/2 ÷ 3/4 = 9/2 × 4/3 = 6.
y.C: 1 1/2 comes from dividing by the 3 alone and leaving its quarters out: 4 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1 1/2. The pieces are 3/4 of a foot, not 3 feet: 9/2 ÷ 3/4 = 9/2 × 4/3 = 6.
y.D: 18 is the number of quarter-feet in the ribbon, since 4 1/2 feet is 18/4 — but each piece takes three of those quarters. One more step finishes it: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 pieces.

ma.ss: dividing a fraction by a fraction (beyond Lower Level)

ma.q: Apples cost $1.35 per pound. What is the cost of 2.4 pounds of apples?

y.B: $2.70 is 1.35 × 2, the 0.4 of a pound never paid for. That last 0.4 pound costs 1.35 × 0.4 = 0.54, and 2.70 + 0.54 = $3.24.
y.C: $32.40 is the right digits with the point one place too far over. 1.35 and 2.4 have three decimal places between them, so 135 × 24 = 3240 becomes 3.240, which is $3.24.
y.D: $3.42 is the answer with its last two digits swapped round. 1.35 × 2 = 2.70 and 1.35 × 0.4 = 0.54, and 2.70 + 0.54 = 3.24.

ma.q: Ben buys 3 notebooks that cost $2.45 each and pays with a $10 bill. How much change should he receive?

y.D: 7.35 is 3 × 2.45, what the three notebooks cost, not the change. The change is what is left of the $10: 10 − 7.35 = 2.65.
y.A: 2.55 would follow if the notebooks came to $7.45, and 3 × $2.45 is $7.35.
y.B: 3.65 would follow if they came to $6.35; three at $2.45 is $7.35.

ma.q: A coat is on sale for 30% off its regular price. Rosa pays the sale price of $42. What was the regular price of the coat?
ma.e: The sale price is 100% − 30% = 70% of the regular price, so 10% of the regular price is $42 ÷ 7 = $6, and the whole price is 10 × $6 = $60.

y.D: 72 is 42 + 30, the sale price with the 30 added on as dollars rather than counted as a percent. Taking 30 percent off leaves seven tenths of the price, so 42 ÷ 7 = 6 and 6 × 10 = 60.
y.B: 140 divides $42 by 0.3 instead of 0.7; the $42 is the 70% Rosa actually paid.
y.C: 54.60 adds 30% to the $42, but the discount came off a larger price, so it is $42 ÷ 0.7.

ma.ss: discounts, percent change and reverse percents (beyond Lower Level)

ma.q: A store raises the price of a $28 board game by 25%. What is the new price?

y.B: 53 is 28 + 25, the 25 added on as dollars rather than counted as a percent. A quarter of the 28 goes on top: 28 ÷ 4 = 7, then 28 + 7 = 35.
y.A: 21 takes 25% off instead of adding it on.
y.D: 32 adds about 14%; 25% of $28 is $7, which gives $35.

ma.ss: discounts, percent change and reverse percents (beyond Lower Level)

ma.q: A choir has 40 members, and 15 of them play an instrument. What percent of the choir members play an instrument?

y.A: 15% is the 15 who play read straight off as a percent, as if the choir had 100 people in it. Out of 40 it is 15/40 = 0.375, which is 37.5%.
y.C: 62.5% is the share who do not play an instrument — the other 25 of the 40. The 15 who do play are 15 out of 40, and 15/40 = 0.375, or 37.5%.
y.D: 75% is 15 + 60, the 40 pushed up to 100 by adding 60 and that same 60 added to the 15. Scaling to 100 multiplies instead: 40 × 2.5 = 100, so 15 × 2.5 = 37.5, which is 37.5%.

ma.ss: writing a part of a whole as a percent

ma.q: A bicycle is marked down from $200 to $150. What is the percent decrease in the price?
ma.e: The drop is $50, and 50/200 = 1/4, so the price decreased by 25%.

y.C: 50 is 200 − 150, the dollars the price fell by, not the percent it fell by. The drop is measured against the starting price: 50 ÷ 200 gives a quarter, or 25 percent.
y.B: 75% is what remains of the price, not how far it fell.
y.D: 33 1/3% compares the $50 drop with the new $150; percent decrease measures against the original $200.

ma.ss: discounts, percent change and reverse percents (beyond Lower Level)

ma.q: Which of these values is the greatest?
ma.e: Written as decimals, 3/5 = 0.6, 5/8 = 0.625 and 58% = 0.58, and 0.625 is more than 0.61, so 5/8 is the greatest value.

y.A: 3/5 works out at 0.6, a hundredth under 0.61 and less than 5/8. Dividing 5 by 8 gives 0.625, the biggest of the four.
y.C: 58% looks like the biggest number here, but a percent counts hundredths: 58% is 0.58, the smallest of the four. 5/8 is 0.625.
y.D: 0.61 beats 0.6 and 0.58, so it wins if 5/8 is left as a fraction. As a decimal, 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, which is bigger still.

ma.q: A tank holds 12.5 liters of water. If 3/5 of the water is used, how many liters remain?
ma.e: The part left is 2/5 of 12.5, and 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5, so 2 × 2.5 = 5 liters.

y.A: 6.25 is 12.5 ÷ 2, half of the tank. Two fifths of it is what remains: 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5, then 2 × 2.5 = 5.
y.B: 7.5 is 12.5 − 5, the water that was used. The question asks for what is left in the tank: 12.5 − 7.5 = 5 liters.
y.C: 4.5 is not two fifths of 12.5; a fifth of 12.5 is 2.5, so two fifths is 5.

ma.q: Alma cut a tray of granola bars into equal bars, as shown. The shaded bars were eaten at lunch. After school, her brother ate 3 more bars. What fraction of the tray has been eaten in all?
ma.e: The shaded part is 4 of the 10 bars, 4/10. Three more bars are 3/10, and 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10: when the denominators match, add only the numerators.

y.A: 3/10 counts only the 3 bars eaten after school and leaves out the 4 shaded bars eaten at lunch.
y.B: 7/20 adds the denominators too (10 + 10); the bars are still tenths of one tray, so only the numerators add.
y.C: 2/5 is 4/10, the shaded lunch bars alone, before the 3 bars eaten after school.

ma.q: Bryn read 1/4 of her library book on Saturday and 1/8 of it on Sunday. What fraction of the book does she still have left to read?
ma.e: Change 1/4 into 2/8. She has read 2/8 + 1/8 = 3/8 of the book, so 8/8 − 3/8 = 5/8 is left.

y.A: 3/8 is the part she has read, 2/8 + 1/8; the question asks for the part still left to read.
y.C: 3/4 is 1 − 1/4, which leaves out the 1/8 she read on Sunday; it is also what is left if 1/4 + 1/8 is added as 2/8, keeping eighths without changing 1/4 into 2/8.
y.D: 5/6 adds the numerators and the denominators, 2/12 = 1/6, and takes that from 1; fourths and eighths must be made the same size first.

ma.q: Andre is making burgers for a family cookout. He has 3 pounds of ground beef, and each burger uses 1/4 pound. How many burgers can he make?
ma.e: Each pound holds four 1/4-pound burgers, so 3 pounds make 3 × 4 = 12 burgers. Dividing by 1/4 counts how many quarters there are.

y.A: 3/4 is 3 × 1/4, the beef that 3 burgers use, not the number of burgers 3 pounds make.
y.B: 4 is the number of burgers one pound makes; Andre has 3 pounds.
y.C: 7 is 3 + 4, the two numbers added instead of counting 4 burgers in each of 3 pounds.

ma.ss: a whole number divided by a unit fraction

ma.q: Four friends are reading the same library book. The table shows what part of the book each friend has read so far. Which friend has read more than half of the book?
ma.e: A fraction is more than 1/2 when its numerator is more than half of its denominator. Half of 8 is 4, and 5 is more than 4, so Bao's 5/8 is more than half.

y.A: Amir has read 7/16, which has the biggest numbers in the table, but half of 16 is 8 and 7 is less than 8.
y.B: Avery has read 5/12, and half of 12 is 6, so 5/12 is less than half.
y.D: Cassie has read 2/5, the fraction with the smallest denominator, but half of 5 is 2 1/2 and 2 is less than that.

ma.q: Callum's class collected 32 books for a library book swap. Three eighths of the books are picture books. How many of the books are NOT picture books?
ma.e: One eighth of 32 is 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so three eighths is 3 × 4 = 12 picture books. The other 32 − 12 = 20 books are NOT picture books.

y.A: 4 is one eighth of 32, the size of one group, not the number of books that are not picture books.
y.B: 5 is the number of eighths that are not picture books (8 − 3); each eighth is 4 books, so that is 5 × 4 = 20 books.
y.C: 12 is 3 × 4, the picture books; the question asks for the books that are NOT picture books.
