rc.e: The comparison sits right next to the word and tells you what it means: something that starts and then does not reach its end. Strategy: when a comparison follows a hard word, read the comparison first and let it define the word.

y.A: Stalling can mean delaying on purpose, but Rafi is trying his best, and the word here is about hands that will not go on.
y.C: Nothing speeds up here; the word names the moment the movement runs out.
y.D: The story never says his hands were tired, and the comparison beside the word is about something unfinished, not something weak.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — an unfamiliar word's meaning from clues

rc.q: Why does the story show what Rafi's hands did before it says he was left-handed?
c: So the reader meets the trouble before its cause.
So the reader learns the three steps of the knot.
So the reader sees that Nina had taught herself.
So the reader sees that Nina's steps were right.
rc.e: Hands that go the other way are a puzzle until one short sentence solves it, and the story hands over the puzzle first so that the solving lands where Nina's does. Strategy: when two sentences sit side by side, ask what the first one makes the second one worth.

y.B: The three steps are given earlier, in the sentence about going through it slowly.
y.C: The opening sentence already says that, and it is there to explain her confidence, not his hands.
y.D: Hands that go the other way every time do suggest the steps were not at fault, but that says nothing about why this part comes before the short sentence that names the cause.

rc.ss: organization/logic — why things are told in this order

rc.q: In the last sentence, the word “only” before *watched* mainly suggests that
c: Nina had lost interest in the lesson.
Rafi did not need showing any more.
Nina was checking his work closely.
Rafi wanted to finish by himself.
rc.e: Up to this sentence Nina has been doing something at every step: sitting, showing, getting up, moving. In the last sentence she does nothing but watch, and that one small word is what says so, which means the showing is over because it is no longer needed. Strategy: when a small word is tucked into a sentence, take it out and read the sentence again; whatever changes is the work that word was doing.

y.A: A teacher who merely watches can look bored, but Nina has just got the lesson working, and the story gives no sign she stopped caring.
y.C: Watching can mean inspecting, but the small word says she did nothing except watch, which is the opposite of leaning in to check.
y.D: The story gives what Rafi managed, not what he wished for; it never says anything about what he wanted.

rc.ss: style — the effect of a word or phrase

rc.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
c: Desert rain follows a regular yearly pattern that seeds can match.
Seeds use dormancy and quick growth to survive uncertain desert conditions.
Tough seed coats are the only reason desert plants survive dry spells.
Heat from the desert sun is what finally wakes the sleeping seeds.
rc.e: Dormancy, substantial rain, rapid growth, and survival are all central. Strategy: select the choice that explains both the pattern and its purpose.

y.A: The passage calls the desert unpredictable, which is the opposite of rain arriving in a pattern a seed could match.
y.C: The tough coats do help, but they are only one part: the passage also gives the long wait beneath dry soil and the quick growth after a storm.
y.D: In this passage it is a storm soaking the ground that gets the seeds going; the sun's heat is never given that job.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: What helps prevent seeds from sprouting after only a little moisture?
rc.e: The passage directly names the coats and their function. Strategy: separate the seed-stage feature from later plant features.

y.B: Flowers do appear in the passage, but only after the seeds have sprouted, so they cannot be what holds the sprouting back.
y.C: Leaves come later, once the plant is growing; the part that protects the waiting seed is its tough outer coat.
y.D: Stems are never mentioned in the passage, and the question asks what keeps a seed from sprouting too soon.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: Why could sprouting after every small drizzle be risky?
c: The sprout would be washed away by the next storm that soaked the soil.
Nearby seeds would then be left with too little water for their own growth.
The plant might use energy before enough water was available for full growth.
The soil would dry out more quickly once many seeds had begun to grow.
rc.e: The last sentence states this cause and risk. Strategy: use an explicit warning to explain a cause-and-effect question.

y.A: The passage treats a soaking storm as the seed's chance to grow, and never mentions anything being washed away.
y.B: The passage never has seeds sharing or competing for water; the risk it names belongs to the one seed that sprouts too early.
y.D: The soil does dry again in the passage, but nothing there says growing seeds are what dries it.

rc.ss: inference — a cause the passage implies

rc.q: As used in the passage, *dormant* most nearly means
c: growing slowly beneath the dry soil.
hidden underground and no longer alive.
ready to sprout after a light drizzle.
inactive but able to become active later.
rc.e: The seeds wait beneath dry soil, then germinate after a storm. Strategy: use what happens before and after the word's condition.

y.A: The passage saves the growing for after a storm soaks the ground, and calls it quick; a dormant seed has not started growing.
y.B: The seeds do lie beneath the soil, but they germinate once a storm soaks the ground, so they were alive the whole time they waited.
y.C: The passage says the tough coats stop the seeds sprouting after only a trace of moisture, so this is the opposite.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — an unfamiliar word's meaning from clues

rc.q: Why does the author end with the example of a small drizzle?
c: To explain why waiting for substantial rain is useful.
To show how quickly flowers appear after rain.
To argue that seeds dislike water.
To show that all storms are harmful.
rc.e: The closing sentence says a seed that sprouted after every small drizzle “would risk using its stored energy before conditions could support a full plant.” That is the cost of not waiting, so the example is there to back up the earlier claim that the waiting “is an active survival strategy.” Strategy: ask which earlier claim a final example supports.

y.B: Flowers really do appear quickly, but that is after a soaking storm, earlier in the passage. The last sentence is about rain that is too small to help.
y.C: The seeds in the passage are waiting for water rather than avoiding it — a soaking storm is exactly what they need.
y.D: The substantial storm in the passage is the helpful one; the closing example is about too little rain, not too much.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a sentence or detail

rc.q: Calling dormancy an “active survival strategy” shows that the author views waiting as
c: a sign that the seed is dead.
rc.e: The phrase directly rejects the idea that waiting is mere inactivity. Strategy: notice when the author redefines an everyday idea.

y.A: Calling the wait active is how the author rules this out, right after admitting it may seem like waiting.
y.C: The word strategy gives the waiting a purpose, and the last sentence says what a seed avoids by doing it.
y.D: The seeds go on to germinate, flower and make new seeds, so waiting is not a sign of a dead seed.

rc.ss: tone — the author's attitude

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the passage's main idea?
c: The council's week-long trial proved the lunch change would work for all.
The council gave the athletes what they wanted and ignored the music students.
A school council used evidence and revision to reach a better compromise.
Voting quickly is the fairest way for a council to settle a disagreement.
rc.e: The passage follows disagreement, trial, evidence, adjustment, and compromise. Strategy: choose the full decision-making process, not one group's opinion.

y.A: The trial did happen, but it also turned up music groups losing setup time, and the passage says the disagreement was not erased.
y.B: The council moved a rehearsal period on two days to deal with the music groups' lost setup time, so they were not ignored.
y.D: The passage credits the council for not voting immediately, and for gathering evidence first.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: What concern did music students raise?
rc.e: The passage states it outright: “Music students worried that the new schedule would shorten rehearsal.” Strategy: match the group named in the question to its stated reason.

y.A: The council was considering moving lunch later, not earlier — and that was the proposal itself, not anyone's worry about it. What the music students raised was about their rehearsal time.
y.C: Practice is in the passage as the reason the athletes got hungry early, and the question asks what the music students were worried about.
y.D: The interviews went the other way round — the council interviewed the teachers — and nobody worried about them stopping.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: Why did the council move one rehearsal period on two days?
c: To respond to the setup-time problem found during the trial.
To keep the cafeteria lines from growing during the trial week.
To end the disagreement between athletes and music students for good.
To give teachers more time for the interviews the council held.
rc.e: The adjustment follows the finding that groups lost setup time. Strategy: trace an action back to the result that prompted it.

y.B: The trial found the lines stayed manageable, so they were not the problem the council had to fix.
y.C: The passage says the disagreement was not erased, and the question asks what the council was answering — the setup time the music groups lost during the trial.
y.D: The council did interview teachers, but that was part of gathering evidence, and the passage never links it to moving a rehearsal.

rc.ss: inference — a cause the passage implies

rc.q: In the passage, *manageable* most nearly means
rc.e: Cafeteria lines remained workable during the trial. Strategy: use the situation's outcome to choose the word's practical meaning.

y.A: This is the opposite: lines staying manageable was the good news the trial week turned up.
y.B: The word here is about the lines being workable, not about them being interesting to watch.
y.C: Saying the lines stayed manageable means they could be handled, not that anyone could look past them.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — an unfamiliar word's meaning from clues

rc.q: What is the role of the sentence beginning “The trial showed”?
c: It repeats the athletes' complaint that they grow hungry early.
It provides results that lead directly to the council's adjustment.
It compares this school's lunch with lunches at other schools.
It shows that the disagreement had been completely settled.
rc.e: The results reveal both a success and a problem, then the next sentence adjusts the plan. Strategy: look for evidence → response links.

y.A: The athletes' early hunger is in the passage, but before the trial; this sentence reports what the week of testing found.
y.C: No other school is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
y.D: This sentence reports a new problem with setup time, and the passage later says the disagreement was not erased.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a sentence or detail

rc.q: The phrase “replace guesses with evidence” reflects a tone that is
rc.e: The phrase praises a process that tests claims before deciding. Strategy: identify whether the author's key phrase praises, criticizes, or neutrally describes.

y.A: The passage describes what the students said and did straight, with no teasing in it.
y.B: The same sentence says the process led to a compromise that dealt with more than one group's concern, which is said with approval.
y.D: Nothing in the passage sounds cross; lunch is simply the thing the council was deciding about.

rc.ss: tone — the author's attitude

rc.q: What is the passage mainly about?
c: Water turned to steam bursts the shell and puffs the kernel.
A popcorn kernel's shell is the hardest part of the plant.
The starch inside a kernel softens into a thick paste.
Old kernels should be thrown away once they no longer pop.
rc.e: Every sentence is a step in one chain: water becomes steam, the shell holds it in, pressure rises, the shell bursts, and the paste expands. The choice about water and steam is the only one that names that chain, and the whole passage exists to explain it. Strategy: a main-idea answer should cover the passage from its first sentence to its last, not one true detail taken out of the middle.

y.B: The passage does call the shell hard, but it never compares it with any other part of the plant, and a passage's main idea has to be something it actually says.
y.C: This one is stated in so many words, which is what makes it tempting, but the softening starch is a single step in the chain rather than the chain itself, so it is too narrow to be what the whole passage is about.
y.D: The passage never tells anyone what to do with an old kernel.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, what happens to the starch inside a kernel as it heats?
c: It turns into steam and escapes.
It sets hard before the shell breaks.
It leaks out through the hard shell.
It softens into a hot, thick paste.
rc.e: The sentence about pressure ends by saying the starch softens into a hot, thick paste, which answers the question in the passage's own words. The other choices each take something the passage really says and attach it to the wrong substance or the wrong moment. Strategy: find the sentence that names the thing the question asks about, and read that sentence to its end before choosing.

y.A: That is what the water does, not the starch; the passage keeps the two apart and only the water is described as becoming steam.
y.B: The setting does happen, but only after the shell bursts and the paste has expanded, so this choice has the order backwards.
y.C: The passage has the shell holding the steam in until it bursts, and nothing at all is described as leaking out of it.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: Based on the passage, when a kernel with a small hole in its shell is heated, it would most likely
c: pop sooner than an unbroken kernel would.
lose its steam before pressure builds.
hold on to its water while it sits.
expand into a much larger piece of foam.
rc.e: The passage gives the shell a job: it holds the steam in, and the held-in steam is the reason pressure climbs. Put a hole in the shell and the cause named in that sentence is gone, so the steam slips out quietly instead of building. Strategy: when a passage explains why something happens, you can often work out what a break in that chain would do by removing one link and reading the sentence again.

y.A: It sounds reasonable that a damaged shell would break sooner, but the passage makes the sealed shell the reason pressure rises at all, so an opening works against the popping rather than hurrying it.
y.C: A hole in the shell lets things out rather than keeping them in, which is the opposite of what this choice claims.
y.D: The passage ties the expanding foam to the sudden release of trapped steam, so a kernel that had been leaking would have less pushing outward, not more.

rc.ss: inference — applying the passage to a new case

rc.q: As used in the passage, *climbs* most nearly means
rc.e: Nothing inside the kernel is going up a hill or a ladder, so the everyday meaning cannot be the one at work. The sentence is about how much pressure there is: it rises while the starch softens, and it rises until the shell can no longer hold. Strategy: try each meaning in the sentence, and if the ordinary one needs hands or feet that the subject does not have, look for the meaning about amount instead.

y.A: That is the everyday meaning of the word, used about a person on a ladder or a rock, and pressure inside a sealed kernel has nothing to hold on to.
y.B: This reads the word as though it said climbs out, but the sentence before it says the shell holds the steam in, so nothing is getting out yet.
y.D: The sentence builds toward a shell that finally gives way, which only happens if the pressure has been going up rather than dropping.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: Why does the author mention that the shell holds the steam in before mentioning the rising pressure?
c: To show that the trapping is why pressure rises.
To show that the shell is stronger than the steam.
To explain why a kernel must be heated slowly.
To show that steam is hotter than the starch.
rc.e: The sentence puts the trapping first and then the word so, which is the passage's way of saying that one thing causes the other: the steam cannot get out, and that is why pressure rises. Turn the two around and the pressure would look like the reason the steam stays in, which is not what the passage claims. Strategy: when two facts sit on either side of so or because, the one in front is usually the cause the author wants you to see.

y.B: The shell does hold and then break, but the passage never measures one against the other; the order of the sentence is doing something else.
y.C: No advice about heating appears anywhere in the passage; it explains what happens inside a kernel, not how anyone should cook.
y.D: The steam and the paste are both hot here, but their temperatures are never compared, and heat is not what the order of the sentence is arranging.

rc.ss: organization/logic — why things are told in this order

rc.q: The phrase “the water was the whole engine” suggests that the water
c: was pushed along by a machine of some kind.
did all the work that made the kernel pop.
was the only thing inside the hard shell.
did its work only after the shell broke.
rc.e: An engine is the part of a machine that supplies the power, so calling the water the whole engine says that the popping happened because of the water and that nothing else would have driven it. Placing the phrase right after a kernel that has lost its water and stopped popping makes that reading the only one the passage supports. Strategy: when an author compares one thing to another, ask what job the second thing is known for, because that job is what the author is claiming for the first.

y.A: This takes the word engine literally; there is no machine in the passage, and the water is called the engine rather than something an engine acts on.
y.C: The passage puts starch in there too, so the phrase is about which ingredient does the work, not about which ingredients are present.
y.D: The water is already working before the break: the steam it becomes is what makes the pressure climb while the shell is still whole.

rc.ss: figurative language — a metaphor or figurative phrase

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Warm air near the ground rises and then spreads out and cools.
Cloud bottoms line up flat because vapor condenses at one height.
Invisible water vapor turns into droplets as air cools.
The tops of puffy clouds heap and tumble as a cloud grows.
rc.e: Every sentence is building toward the flat bottoms: rising air, cooling, one height where the vapor condenses, and every parcel reaching that height together. The choice about rising air and the choice about vapor turning into droplets are both true, and both are single steps inside that chain. The choice about heaping tops takes a contrast from the final sentence and treats it as the subject. Strategy: when several choices are true, pick the one the other true ones are working for.

y.A: This is a true step in the explanation, but it is only the first step - the passage keeps going until it reaches the flat bottoms.
y.C: This is a true step in the chain, and the passage does say it - but it is the middle of the explanation, not the point the explanation is heading toward.
y.D: The tops are mentioned only in the last sentence, and they are there to set off the bottoms, which are what the passage is really about.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, what happens to rising air as it climbs into thinner air?
c: It speeds up and grows warmer.
It sinks back toward the ground.
rc.e: The second sentence answers this in its own words: the climbing air spreads out and cools. Growing warmer contradicts that sentence directly. Sinking is never described anywhere. And the vapor does not leave the air - it turns into droplets, which is why a cloud becomes visible at all. Strategy: find the sentence that uses the question's own words, and read it to the end before choosing.

y.A: The passage says the opposite about temperature - the whole explanation depends on the rising air getting cooler, not warmer.
y.B: The air in this passage only goes up; nothing in it ever comes back down.
y.C: The vapor is still there - it changes into droplets at a certain height, which is not the same as the air stopping carrying it.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: What does the passage suggest about the clear air just below a cloud's flat bottom?
c: It carries water vapor that has not yet condensed.
It has no water in it until the cloud drifts over.
It is cooler than the air inside the cloud above.
It already holds droplets too small to see.
rc.e: Two statements have to be joined. The rising air carries water vapor that is invisible, and the vapor only condenses once the air reaches a particular height. So the air below that height is carrying the same vapor, still uncondensed - which is exactly why you cannot see a cloud there. The choice about air with no water in it is the picture most people start with, and the passage quietly corrects it. The choice about droplets already being there goes wrong in the other direction, since the passage puts the first droplets at the condensation height and not below it. Strategy: when a passage says something is invisible, do not let invisible slide into absent.

y.B: The passage says the rising air is carrying vapor the whole way up, and that vapor is invisible, so empty-looking air is not the same as dry air.
y.C: This turns the passage upside down - air cools as it climbs, so the air lower down is the warmer air, not the cooler.
y.D: Droplets are where a lot of readers' instinct goes, but the passage puts the first droplets at the height where the vapor condenses, so below that height none have formed yet.

rc.ss: inference — a conclusion the facts support

rc.q: As used in the passage, *parcels* most nearly means
c: drops of water in a cloud.
rc.e: The phrase is parcels of air, and the sentence says each one rises, cools and reaches a temperature - so the word is naming separate portions or bodies of the air itself. The mail meaning and the farmland meaning are both real meanings of the word, which is what makes them tempting. The droplets belong to a different stage of the process. Strategy: put each meaning back into the sentence and ask whether it can do what the sentence says it does.

y.A: This is the everyday meaning of the word, which is why it is offered - but a package cannot rise from warm ground and cool as it climbs.
y.C: This is a genuine meaning of the word, and the wrong one here, since the passage is describing something moving upward through the sky.
y.D: Droplets do appear in the passage, but they form later and higher up; these parcels are still rising and still invisible when they are named.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: How is the passage arranged?
c: It begins with what a reader can see, then explains why.
It lists kinds of clouds in order from lowest to highest.
It compares a summer sky with the sky on a winter day.
It gives the reasons for and against one idea about air.
rc.e: The first sentence is a picture anybody could look up and check - clouds resting on an invisible shelf. The very next sentence starts the causes, and everything after it works backward from that picture: rising air, cooling, condensing, one height. Nothing is compared, listed by kind, or argued against. Strategy: ask what the first sentence is doing, then ask what job the rest of the passage does for it.

y.B: Only one kind of cloud appears, and no list of kinds is ever given.
y.C: Summer is mentioned once to set the scene, and winter is never mentioned at all, so there is no comparison being made.
y.D: The passage never argues two sides; it explains a single process from beginning to end.

rc.ss: organization/logic — how the whole passage is arranged

rc.q: The phrase "drawn by one rule" suggests that the flat bottoms
c: were sketched by someone with a ruler.
follow a law that people agreed on.
are produced by the same single cause.
are flat because the ground below is level.
rc.e: The word rule is doing double work. It brings in the straight edge of a ruler, which is why the bottoms look so level, and it brings in the idea of one principle acting everywhere, which is the reason the passage has just given: every parcel of air begins alike, cools the same way, and condenses at nearly the same height. The literal sketching reading grabs one ordinary meaning and stops, and the people-made-law reading grabs the other. The choice about level ground borrows the flatness but puts the cause in the wrong place. Strategy: when a final phrase sounds like a picture, check it against the explanation the passage just finished giving.

y.A: The phrase sounds like drawing with a ruler on purpose, but clouds are not sketched by anyone, so the words are doing something other than describing a hand.
y.B: A rule can mean something people decide on, and here it means something nature does the same way every time, with nobody deciding anything.
y.D: The parcels do rise from the same ground, but the passage never calls that ground level, and it puts the flatness down to the height where the vapor condenses.

rc.ss: figurative language — a metaphor or figurative phrase

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Barnacles are the toughest animals to be found anywhere along a rocky shore at low tide.
Tide pool animals are built to survive swings in heat and salt that the open sea never brings.
Tide pools are calm, protected places where small sea creatures stay safe from the harsh ocean.
Sudden rainstorms are the most serious threat facing ocean animals nearly everywhere in the world.
rc.e: The passage lists the pools' fast swings in temperature and salt, shows the animals' equipment for meeting them, and ends by calling them “specialists in a kind of hardship.” The choice calling the pools calm and protected is exactly the comfortable idea the third paragraph exists to correct, and the choice about barnacles offers one animal as the whole point. Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole passage, not one example.

y.A: The barnacle is one of three animals the passage uses as an example, and it never says one shore animal is tougher than another; the question asks what the whole passage is about.
y.C: The pools only look peaceful from a distance, and the last paragraph says plainly that the pool is the harsher place.
y.D: A rainstorm is one of the fast swings a pool animal has to meet, and the passage says nothing in the open ocean changes that quickly.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, how do sea stars avoid the worst of the sun?
c: They swim out into deeper water and wait there until the tide returns.
They travel back to a shallow groove worn into the rock.
They pull a set of hard plates shut over their soft bodies.
They slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach.
rc.e: The second paragraph states that when the sun is high, sea stars slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach. Pulling hard plates shut belongs to the barnacle, and travelling back to a worn groove belongs to the limpet. Strategy: check that the detail belongs to the animal the question names.

y.A: No pool animal leaves for deeper water in this passage; the fish from twenty meters down is the one carried in, and it would not last an afternoon.
y.B: Traveling back to a worn groove is what the limpet does, and the question asks about the sea stars.
y.C: The hard plates belong to the barnacle, which shuts them to trap a little seawater; the question asks how the sea stars get out of the sun.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: The passage suggests that a limpet travels back to its own groove before the water leaves because
c: other limpets are unable to reach that part of the rock at all.
the rock inside the groove stays cooler than any other place on the shore.
its shell seals tightly against the worn stone and keeps water in.
the groove holds bits of food that the limpet has stored there for later.
rc.e: The paragraph is about equipment for staying wet — the barnacle traps a reserve of seawater — and it says the limpet's shell fits the worn stone tightly, which is what the return trip buys. The choice about cooler rock borrows the sea star's shade, which the passage never connects to the groove. Strategy: combine two nearby facts rather than making a leap.

y.A: The passage never has limpets competing for space on the rock; what matters about the groove is that this limpet's own shell fits it.
y.B: Shade is how the sea stars escape the high sun, and the passage never says the groove is any cooler than the rock around it.
y.D: Months of feeding are how the groove got worn, but the passage never says the limpet keeps food there; it returns because its shell fits the worn stone tightly.

rc.ss: inference — a cause the passage implies

rc.q: In the second paragraph, *reserve* most nearly means
c: a store kept back for later use.
a quiet, shy way of behaving around others.
an order for a seat placed ahead of time.
a wild area set aside to protect animals.
rc.e: The barnacle traps seawater “enough to keep its body damp until the ocean comes back,” so the reserve is a store saved for later. The protected-area meaning is a real sense of the word and the one a nature passage invites, but a barnacle's shell is not a wildlife preserve. Strategy: test each dictionary meaning inside the actual sentence.

y.B: That is a real meaning of the word, but what the barnacle traps inside its plates is seawater, and water is a thing rather than a way of behaving.
y.C: That is the meaning you get from booking a seat ahead of time; here the barnacle is keeping enough seawater to stay damp until the ocean comes back.
y.D: That is a nature reserve, the meaning a passage about sea animals invites; here the reserve is the small amount of seawater a barnacle traps inside its plates.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The third paragraph mainly serves to
c: correct a comfortable idea about tide pools and say what the pools really demand.
offer one more example of the special equipment a shore animal carries.
explain how fish from deep water are collected and studied by scientists.
describe how the pools look to someone standing at a distance from the shore.
rc.e: It opens “It would be a mistake to picture a tide pool as a gentler ocean” and ends by calling the pool the harsher place. The choices about another animal's equipment and about the view from a distance describe the two paragraphs before it, not this one. Strategy: ask what a paragraph does to the ones around it, not only what it mentions.

y.B: The animals' equipment is the paragraph before this one; here the passage stops adding examples and tells you what kind of place the pool really is.
y.C: The fish from twenty meters down is mentioned only to show it would not last an afternoon in a pool, and nobody in the passage collects or studies it.
y.D: That is the opening, where the pools look peaceful from a distance, and the third paragraph exists to correct that first impression.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a paragraph

rc.q: The author's attitude toward the animals of the tide pool is best described as
c: amused by how small and helpless the pool creatures are.
worried that the pools along the rocky shore will soon disappear.
doubtful that they truly survive the changes described.
respectful of how well suited they are to a difficult place.
rc.e: “Equipment, not luck” and “specialists in a kind of hardship” credit the animals with skill instead of pitying them, which rules out the amused reading. Strategy: judge attitude from the author's word choices about the subject, not from the topic alone.

y.A: The passage credits the animals with “equipment, not luck” and calls them specialists, which is the opposite of small and helpless.
y.B: The passage never says the pools are in any danger of disappearing; it is about what the animals living in them can withstand.
y.C: The animals do come through it here, like the barnacle staying damp until the ocean returns, and the author never doubts that.

rc.ss: tone — the author's attitude

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Home delivery of mail to farmhouses was the most important change of the 1890s.
Bicycles could travel over deep, muddy roads more easily than heavy wagons could.
Farmers in the 1880s did not care at all what condition their dirt roads were in.
A campaign by bicycle riders prepared the roads automobiles would later use.
rc.e: The passage follows one thread from the riders' Good Roads campaign to the surveys, road departments, and public money that were “already in place” when cars arrived. The choice about mail delivery takes a single step in that chain and inflates it into the whole story. Strategy: a main idea has to account for the final paragraph too.

y.A: Mail coming to farmhouses is the step that changed the counties' minds, and the passage does say so. The question asks what the whole passage is about, and it runs from the riders' campaign to the roads cars later used.
y.B: It is the other way round in the passage: the new machines were “almost useless on a rutted road,” while the heavy wagons could grind through whatever the weather left.
y.C: The first paragraph says farmers complained about the ruts; what they resisted was paying for paving out of everyone's taxes.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, what did the Post Office require before it would carry letters to a farmhouse?
c: That a local cycling club map and inspect the route first.
That the route be one a mail wagon could travel all year.
That each farm family pay a small yearly fee for the service.
That the road be paved with stone from end to end.
rc.e: The third paragraph says the Post Office “would only serve routes a mail wagon could travel all year.” The choice about a cycling club mapping the route takes a real detail about the clubs, which mapped the worst stretches, and attaches it to the wrong group. Strategy: match the requirement to the group that actually set it.

y.A: Mapping the worst stretches is what the riders' clubs did in their campaign, and the question asks what the Post Office required.
y.C: The passage never has families paying anything for delivery; the one condition named is about the road the mail wagon had to travel.
y.D: The Post Office asked only for a route a mail wagon could travel all year, which is not the same as stone paving from end to end.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: Why did counties that had refused to spend a dollar begin to build roads?
c: A bad road had begun to cost farm families something they wanted.
Automobiles had already worn the county's dirt roads down past repair.
Farmers had stopped using the heavy wagons that cut ruts in the roads.
The cycling clubs had offered to pay for all of the work themselves.
rc.e: Once a good road was “the difference between getting the mail and not getting it,” paving stopped being a favor to visiting riders and became a local need. The choice about automobiles reverses the passage's order, since cars became common only after these changes. Strategy: look at the sentence just before a result to find its cause.

y.B: The cars come later in the passage: by the time they were common, the surveys and county road departments were already in place.
y.C: The passage never says the heavy wagons stopped; what had to get through all year was the mail wagon.
y.D: The clubs asked state legislatures for the money, which is the very thing the farmers objected to paying for.

rc.ss: inference — a cause the passage implies

rc.q: In the second paragraph, *mounted* most nearly means
c: fastened onto a board or a wall.
rc.e: The clubs “mounted a campaign they called Good Roads,” and the next sentence lists the doing of it: printing pamphlets, mapping stretches, asking legislatures for money. Climbing up onto something is the meaning a reader expects in a passage full of bicycles, but no one climbs onto a campaign. Strategy: let the sentence after the word show which meaning is at work.

y.A: Things can mount in that sense, but here the clubs mounted the campaign themselves, and the next sentence lists the doing of it: pamphlets, maps, requests for money.
y.B: That is the meaning for mounting a picture; a campaign of pamphlets and requests to legislatures is not fastened to anything.
y.D: Riders do climb onto bicycles, which is why this meaning feels right in a passage full of them, but nobody climbs onto a campaign.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The sentence “The argument changed when the mail changed” mainly serves to
c: list all of the printed pamphlets and route maps that the cycling clubs produced.
repeat the farmers' objection about taxes and city sportsmen in different words.
explain the way the mail had been carried to farm families in earlier centuries.
mark the point after which paving was no longer dismissed as a favor to city riders.
rc.e: It stands between the farmers' complaint about city sportsmen and the counties that suddenly began to build, so it announces a switch in reasons. The choice about repeating the objection misses that the sentence overturns the complaint rather than restating it. Strategy: a short sentence set between longer passages usually marks a turn.

y.A: The pamphlets and the maps are listed in the paragraph before; this sentence announces a change rather than adding to that list.
y.B: The objection about taxes and city sportsmen comes just before, and this sentence turns it over instead of saying it again.
y.C: The sentence after this one does say families used to travel to town for their letters, but this short sentence marks the turn in the argument, which is what the question asks about.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a sentence or detail

rc.q: In the last sentence, saying that drivers “owed a debt to people who had been pedaling” means that
c: the author wishes that automobiles had never replaced bicycles at all.
drivers benefited from work that cyclists had done for reasons of their own.
drivers should have repaid the old cycling clubs with money of their own.
the people who had been pedaling owed a debt to the later drivers.
rc.e: The debt is figurative — nobody ever pays the riders back. The clubs campaigned so that bicycles would have smooth roads, and by the time cars were common the surveys, the county road departments and the public money for highways were “already in place.” Strategy: ask what an image stands for before accepting its literal sense.

y.A: The passage never wishes the automobiles away; it says the drivers owed something to the riders who came first.
y.C: Nobody in the passage ever pays the riders back. The debt is a way of saying drivers got the benefit of work other people had already done.
y.D: The sentence runs the other way: it is the drivers who owed something, to the riders whose campaign got the roads built first.

rc.ss: figurative language — a metaphor or figurative phrase

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A bird's color depends on the food that the bird eats.
A feather's color disappears once the feather is crushed.
Each branch of a feather holds a layer of keratin.
A jay's blue comes from structure, not from a pigment.
rc.e: The passage opens by showing that grinding a jay's feather takes the blue away, explains that the color comes from the spacing of air pockets, and closes by saying the jay makes its blue rather than carrying it. Saying a bird's color comes from its food describes only the cardinal, which the passage brings in to contrast with the jay. Strategy: the main idea has to hold true for the beginning and the ending, not just one example in the middle.

y.A: That is how the cardinal's red is made, and the passage offers it as the opposite case to the jay, not as the rule for both birds.
y.B: The red feather ground to powder leaves red dust, so crushing a feather does not take every color away — only a color that depends on an arrangement can be crushed out of one.
y.C: The passage does say this, which is why it feels familiar, but it is one small piece of the explanation rather than the point the whole passage is making.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, what happens when a red feather is ground into powder?
c: The dust turns a dull brown, as the jay's did.
The dust left in the palm is still red.
The dust keeps a faint trace of pink.
The dust looks red at certain angles.
rc.e: The third paragraph states that a red feather ground to powder leaves red dust in the palm, because the color is a pigment and a pigment is a thing you can hold. The dull brown dust belongs to the jay's feather in the first paragraph. Strategy: check which bird the detail belongs to before you pick it.

y.A: Dull brown dust is what the jay's feather leaves behind, and the passage brings the red feather in precisely because it behaves differently.
y.C: The passage calls the dust red, with nothing to suggest the color weakens when the feather is ground.
y.D: No angle is mentioned for the dust; the passage's second test is about light coming through from behind, not about where a viewer stands.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: A feather from an unfamiliar bird is ground to powder, and the powder is still orange. The passage best supports concluding that
c: the feather held air pockets arranged inside it.
the orange came from a pigment in the feather.
the bird eats the same food a cardinal eats.
light from behind would turn the feather brown.
rc.e: The passage sets up a test: a color made by an arrangement disappears when the arrangement is crushed, while a color made by pigment survives, as the red dust does. Orange powder that keeps its color therefore behaves like the cardinal's red and must be a pigment. Strategy: when a question gives you a new case, apply the rule the passage demonstrated rather than looking for the new case in the text.

y.A: Arranged air pockets make a color that lasts only as long as the arrangement does, so a color that survives grinding points away from this answer.
y.C: The passage says a bird builds a pigment from what it eats, but it never says that one pigment means one particular diet.
y.D: Turning brown in light from behind is the jay's result, and this feather has just behaved like the cardinal's, which stays its own color when it is lit that way.

rc.ss: inference — applying the passage to a new case

rc.q: In the second paragraph, *swallows* most nearly means
c: darts and dives like a small bird.
swiftly eats a bite of food.
takes it in and absorbs it.
sends it straight back to the eye.
rc.e: The sentence before says the red and yellow light travels deeper into the feather, and it never comes back out, so the dark pigment takes it in. The bird meaning is planted by the subject matter, which is exactly why it is worth testing inside the sentence. Strategy: read the sentence before the word to see what the word is actually doing there.

y.A: A swallow is a bird, and the word is planted in a passage about birds, but here it names what a layer of dark pigment does, and a layer of pigment is not a creature.
y.B: This is the everyday meaning, and a layer of pigment does not eat anything; what reaches it is light.
y.D: Sending light back toward the eye is what the air pockets do with blue, and it is the opposite of what happens to the light that travels deeper in.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The paragraph beginning "A cardinal's red works the other way" mainly serves to
c: set a true pigment beside the jay's kind of blue.
give one more example of color made by structure.
explain why the cardinal's red is the brighter color.
teach a reader how to test a feather at home.
rc.e: The paragraph begins by saying the cardinal's red works the other way, then describes two tests that come out differently for a pigment and for an arrangement. Its job is comparison, which is why the word other is doing so much work in its first sentence. Strategy: watch the opening sentence of a paragraph for a signal about what the paragraph is for.

y.B: The cardinal's red is a pigment, which is the other kind of color entirely, so this paragraph adds a contrast rather than another example.
y.C: The passage never compares how bright the two colors are; it compares how each one is made.
y.D: Two tests are described, but they are there to show that the two colors behave differently, not to hand a reader a procedure to carry out.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a paragraph

rc.q: In the last two sentences, saying that the jay does not carry its blue but makes it suggests that
c: the color happens when light meets the structure.
the jay can change its feathers' color at will.
the feather works to keep its blue from fading.
the feather would be blue even in the dark.
rc.e: The closing lines draw a line between having a color, the way the cardinal has a pigment you can hold, and making one, which happens only when light strikes the arranged pockets and comes back. Reading makes as effort or as choice turns a figure of speech into a literal claim the passage does not make. Strategy: ask what an author's phrase is contrasted with before deciding what it means.

y.B: The bird is not choosing anything here; makes describes the feather's structure at work, not a decision the jay takes.
y.C: This takes makes to mean effort, and no fading and no effort appear anywhere in the passage.
y.D: The sentence says the blue arrives with the light, and the paragraph before says the blue depends on light bouncing back off a structure.

rc.ss: figurative language — a metaphor or figurative phrase

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A tree's rings record each year's weather, and that record can date old wood.
Counting a tree's rings is the surest way to learn how old the tree really is.
Trees growing in warm, wet places are of little use to researchers.
A wide ring proves that one tree was healthier than the trees near it.
rc.e: The passage grants that counting rings gives an age, calls that the least interesting thing they can tell you, and then spends two paragraphs on what the widths record and how that record dates a beam from an old roof. The choice about counting for age stops where the first paragraph stops. Strategy: when a passage calls an idea the least interesting thing, the main idea is what comes after it.

y.B: Counting for age is the one use the passage grants and then sets aside as the least interesting thing the rings can tell you, and the last paragraph shows a count can even be off by a year.
y.C: Those trees are one limit named near the end, not what the passage as a whole is about.
y.D: A wide ring is tied to a wet, mild year, not to one tree doing better than its neighbors.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, the ring a reader sees is the line between
c: the pale spring wood and the dark wood of that year.
one year's dark wood and next spring's pale wood.
the bark of the tree and the new wood beneath it.
the wood of a wet year and the wood of a dry year.
rc.e: The second paragraph names the line outright: the ring you see is where one year's dark wood stops and next spring's pale wood begins. The pale-and-dark pair inside one year is a real boundary but not the one the passage points at, and the new layer of wood goes beneath the bark rather than on it. Strategy: find the sentence that defines the thing and read it exactly.

y.A: Those two do sit side by side within a single year, but the passage points at the other edge — where one year's dark wood stops and the next spring's pale wood begins.
y.C: The tree adds its new layer of wood beneath the bark, so the bark is not the edge being described.
y.D: Wet and dry years give wide and narrow rings, but the line itself is a change from dark wood to pale wood, not a border between two kinds of year.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: The passage suggests that the researcher could not date the beam without
c: a mark left on the beam by whoever built the roof.
a count of how many rings the beam still holds.
rings from trees whose years are already known.
a sample taken from the same roof's other beams.
rc.e: A living tree's outermost ring is this year's, so its rings can be counted back to real years; the beam is dated by sliding its own pattern along that record until the wide and narrow years line up. Without a set of rings whose years are already settled, the beam's pattern is just a pattern with nowhere to sit. Strategy: ask what a method borrows from outside the object it is examining.

y.A: The passage says the beam is dated though nobody wrote a date on it, so a written mark is exactly what is missing.
y.B: Counting tells you how many years the wood grew, not which years those were.
y.D: The pattern is slid along the record kept by living trees, and other beams from the same roof would carry no known years of their own.

rc.ss: inference — a conclusion the facts support

rc.q: In the third paragraph, *agreement* most nearly means
c: a promise made between two people.
the same weather from year to year.
a rule about matching word forms.
rc.e: The sentence just before says the bands run in step, so the agreement named next is that matching between trees. The everyday promise-between-people meaning is the trap, and the weather choice lifts a true phrase from the sentence before and attaches the word to the wrong thing — what runs in step is the patterns. Strategy: put your choice into the sentence in place of the word and check that it still describes the same thing.

y.A: That is the word's everyday meaning, but nobody here is promising anything — what is happening is that bands are matching.
y.B: The sentence before does say trees in one region live through the same weather, but that agreement points back at the patterns running in step, and the passage's whole point is that the weather differs from year to year.
y.C: Agreement does mean that in a grammar lesson, where a subject and a verb must match, but this sentence is about bands of wood rather than words.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The last paragraph mainly serves to
c: set out the limits of a method the passage has explained.
explain again how a tree lays down wood each spring.
argue that ring patterns are too unreliable to use.
explain how one beam is matched against the living record.
rc.e: The paragraph announces that the limits are the ordinary kind and then names them — no clear band where it is warm and wet all year, a skipped year, a doubled one — before closing with the safeguard of checking many trees. Saying ring patterns are too unreliable to use goes further than a paragraph that ends by explaining how researchers work around the trouble, and the matching of a beam to the living record has already happened a paragraph earlier. Strategy: a paragraph that names limits and then a safeguard is qualifying a method, not throwing it out.

y.B: That was settled in the second paragraph; the last one turns to where the method runs into trouble.
y.C: The paragraph raises problems and then closes with the safeguard of checking many trees, which is a caution rather than a rejection.
y.D: Matching a beam against the living record is the third paragraph's job; the last one is about where that matching cannot be trusted.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a paragraph

rc.q: The comparison in “the rings are a row of entries, one for every year the tree stood” suggests that the rings
c: are written by hand onto the wood.
keep a record, one year at a time.
are all exactly the same width.
grow larger each year of a tree's life.
rc.e: An entry is a line written in a record, and the passage sets the rings in order with one for every year the tree stood, so the comparison turns the trunk into a year-by-year log. Taking the picture literally, as writing on the wood, misses that a comparison borrows a quality rather than stating a fact. Strategy: with a comparison, ask which quality is being borrowed, not whether the picture is literally true.

y.A: The rings are compared to written entries, but nothing in the passage says anyone writes on the wood.
y.C: The passage says the opposite — wide in a wet, mild year and narrow in a dry, hard one.
y.D: Ring width depends on the weather of that year, not on how old the tree has become.

rc.ss: figurative language — a metaphor or figurative phrase

rc.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the fourth paragraph (lines 19–25)?
c: Other bees follow the dancer closely in the darkness of the hive.
The farther away the flowers are, the longer the waggle run lasts.
The straight run's angle shows the flowers' direction from the sun.
Flowers directly away from the sun are shown by a run pointing down.
rc.e: Every sentence in lines 19–25 explains how the angle of the straight run stands for a direction measured from the sun: up for toward it, down for away from it, tilted for left or right. The main idea is the sentence that covers all of them, not one example.

y.A: Following the dancer in the dark comes from the last paragraph (lines 30–31), not from lines 19–25.
y.B: A longer waggle run for faraway flowers is the point of the fifth paragraph, which is about distance; lines 19–25 are about direction.
y.D: Pointing down for flowers away from the sun is one example inside lines 19–25; it is true, but it leaves out up, left and right, so it is too small to be the main idea.

rc.ss: main idea — the main idea of one paragraph

rc.q: According to lines 8–12, what does a round dance tell the other bees?
c: that food is near, but not which way to fly
which direction the bees should fly to reach it
that the flowers are more than a mile and a half away
how far the sun has moved across the sky since morning
rc.e: Lines 10–12 say the round dance “tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not which way to fly.”

y.B: Which direction to fly is exactly what lines 11–12 say the round dance does not tell; that is the waggle dance's job.
y.C: More than a mile and a half away is the distance in the waggle-dance example (lines 28–29); the round dance is for food very close to the hive.
y.D: How far the sun has moved comes from the last paragraph, about a waggle dance later in the day.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact on a cited line

rc.q: As it is used in lines 20–21, “stand for” means
rc.e: To stand for something is to represent it, the way a symbol on a map stands for a place. On the upright comb, straight up represents the direction of the sun.

y.A: Favor is the meaning in “what a club stands for,” what it believes in; the dancer is not taking the sun's side, she is using “up” as a sign for it.
y.C: Rise borrows “stands upright” from the start of the same sentence; the comb stands up, but “stand for” is about what straight up means.
y.D: Tolerate is the meaning in “I won't stand for that”; nothing in the sentence is being put up with.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: A bee dances at noon for a patch of flowers and dances again for the same flowers late in the afternoon. Based on the passage, which part of her dance would most likely be different?
c: how long each waggle run lasts
whether she does a round dance
the figure-eight shape of her path
the direction her straight run points
rc.e: Lines 31–34 say a bee dancing for the same flowers later in the day changes the angle of her run, because the sun has moved. The flowers have stayed put, so the distance, and the length of the waggle, stay the same.

y.A: How long each waggle run lasts reports distance (lines 26–27), and the flowers have not moved, so the distance has not changed.
y.B: Whether she does a round dance depends on how close the food is (lines 8–9), and the flowers are just as near or far as they were at noon.
y.C: The figure-eight shape belongs to every waggle dance (lines 16–18); nothing says it changes with the time of day.

rc.ss: inference — applying the passage to a new case

rc.q: Which of these questions can be answered from the passage?
c: How does a bee show how far away food is?
How many bees usually live together in a single hive?
Why do bees visit some kinds of flowers and not others?
How do honeybees turn the nectar they collect into honey?
rc.e: Lines 26–29 answer it: the farther away the flowers are, the longer each waggle run lasts. The passage never takes up the other three questions.

y.B: How many bees live in a hive is never given; the passage counts seconds and miles, not bees.
y.C: Why bees choose some flowers is never discussed; the passage only says a bee may find a plentiful patch.
y.D: Turning nectar into honey is never described; the passage follows the bees only as far as flying out to the flowers.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the question the passage answers

rc.q: Which word best describes the author's attitude toward the bees' dance?
rc.e: The author sets up a hard problem (no map, no way to point) and then shows the dance solving it exactly, even turning to keep up with the sun. That is the attitude of someone impressed.

y.A: Critical would mean finding fault, but the author never says anything is wrong with the dance.
y.B: Doubtful would mean questioning whether the dance works, yet the author says the other bees fly “directly toward the flowers.”
y.D: Sorrowful has nothing to attach to; nothing in the passage is sad or lost.

rc.ss: tone — the author's attitude

rc.q: The passage says that Wilson Bentley did all of the following EXCEPT
c: teach at a school in Vermont
make hundreds of sketches of snow
rc.e: The question asks for the one thing the passage does not say Bentley did. It was his mother who had once been a teacher (line 2); Bentley himself is never said to have taught.

y.A: Measuring raindrops is in line 27, so the passage does say he did it.
y.B: Photographing frost and dew is in lines 26–27, so it is something he did, not the exception.
y.D: Making several hundred sketches is in lines 9–10, so it is not the exception.

rc.ss: supporting detail — EXCEPT: the one detail the passage does not give

rc.q: In line 21, Bentley “nudged” a crystal into position. This means that he
rc.e: To nudge something is to give it a small, gentle push. With the feather, Bentley pushed the crystal a little at a time until it sat where he wanted it.

y.A: Breathed on it is exactly what lines 22–23 say he was careful never to do, because his breath could melt the crystal.
y.B: Lifted it high is the straw's job in lines 20–21; the feather came next, to move the crystal into place.
y.C: Melted it slowly names the danger he was guarding against, not what he did with the feather.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — an unfamiliar word's meaning from clues

rc.q: Bentley's two years of failed photographs most likely show that he
c: did not know how to use his microscope
agreed with his father about the camera
kept trying even when the work went badly
rc.e: Two years of failures did not stop him. He kept going until, on January 15, 1885, he made the first photograph of a single snow crystal, which shows he kept trying when the work went badly.

y.A: Selling his pictures is never mentioned; the passage gives no sign that money was what kept him going.
y.B: Not knowing how to use his microscope does not fit someone who had been using one since he was fifteen (lines 3–4).
y.C: Agreeing with his father would mean deciding snowflakes were a waste of time, yet Bentley kept going until he succeeded.

rc.ss: inference — what a character's actions show

rc.q: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?
c: It tells his life story in time order.
It compares snow crystals with frost and dew.
It explains how snow crystals form in clouds.
rc.e: The passage begins with his birth in 1865 and moves through the microscope at fifteen, the camera, the first photograph in 1885 and his later work, to his death in 1931: the events of his life in the order they happened.

y.A: Arguing for photographing snow is not what the passage does; it reports what Bentley did and never tells the reader to photograph snow.
y.C: Comparing snow crystals with frost and dew would take more than the one sentence (lines 26–27) that mentions frost and dew.
y.D: How snow crystals form is never explained; the passage is about the man who photographed them.

rc.ss: organization/logic — how the whole passage is arranged

rc.q: How does the author seem to feel about Bentley's work?
c: respectful of its care and patience
doubtful that his photograph came first
rc.e: The author lingers on his care (the black tray, the straw, the feather, never breathing on a crystal) and on more than 5,000 photographs. That is respect for patient work, not amusement or doubt.

y.A: Sorry it took so long reads regret into the passage; the author reports the years of work as patience, not as a loss.
y.B: Amused by an odd hobby borrows his father's view in lines 13–14; the author never makes fun of the work.
y.D: Doubtful that his photograph came first goes against lines 17–18, which state plainly that he made the first photograph of a single snow crystal.

rc.ss: tone — the author's attitude

rc.q: Which statement best expresses what the passage shows about Wilson Bentley?
c: He patiently photographed snow crystals for decades.
He proved that snow crystals form in six-sided shapes.
He was the first scientist to study raindrops closely.
His father taught him to use a camera and a microscope.
rc.e: From the microscope at fifteen to the book of photographs in 1931, every paragraph follows his long, careful work photographing snow crystals.

y.B: Six-sided shapes are never mentioned; the passage reports only that he never found two crystals alike.
y.C: Studying raindrops gets one mention (line 27), and the passage never calls him the first to do it.
y.D: His father thought fussing with snowflakes a waste of time (lines 13–14), and it was his mother who gave him the microscope; the passage never says anyone taught him to use either one.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: When Otis first reads the cast list, he most likely feels
rc.e: He reads the list twice “to be certain,” and he notes he is not Ancient Tree or Wise Old Tree but “simply Tree,” with no lines at all. He hoped for more, so he is disappointed.

y.B: Frightened mistakes reading the list twice for nerves; what he dwells on is how small his part is, not fear of the stage.
y.C: Grateful would need a sign that he wanted this part, but he notes it is not even Wise Old Tree, just Tree.
y.D: Proud has nothing to rest on: lines 5–8 stress that his part has no lines and that he will say absolutely nothing.

rc.ss: inference — a character's feeling

rc.q: Which of these events happens before the night of the performance?
c: Otis learns every line in the play.
Otis whispers the missing line to Nico.
Families surround the queen and the woodcutter.
Ms. Pruitt runs the lights from the back of the gym.
rc.e: During rehearsals, by the third week, Otis “could have recited every line in the entire play” (lines 15–17). The other three events happen on the night of the show or after it.

y.B: Whispering the missing line happens on the night, in the third scene (lines 26–28).
y.C: Families surround the actors afterward, once the show is over (lines 33–34).
y.D: Running the lights happens on the night of the performance (lines 18–20).

rc.ss: supporting detail — the order of events

rc.q: In line 15, the word “prompted” is closest in meaning to
c: gave him a topic to write about
rc.e: In a play, to prompt an actor is to say the forgotten words so the actor can go on. Each time Nico forgot his line, Ms. Pruitt reminded him of it from the front row.

y.A: Caused him to ask uses “prompt” in the sense of leading someone to do something, but Nico asks nothing; he has forgotten his line.
y.B: Made him move faster comes from prompt meaning quick or on time; Ms. Pruitt was helping Nico remember, not hurrying him.
y.D: Gave him a topic to write about is a writing prompt from class, but this is a play rehearsal and Nico needed his line.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: Which word best describes the mood of the scene in lines 20–25?
rc.e: Nico freezes, the silence stretches “like a rubber band about to snap,” someone coughs, and Nico stares at the floor. Everyone is uneasy and waiting, so the mood is tense.

y.A: Cheerful does not fit a scene in which nothing comes out of Nico's mouth and he stares at the floor.
y.B: Peaceful mistakes the silence for calm, but this silence stretches “like a rubber band about to snap.”
y.C: Sleepy does not fit an audience that is waiting, wide awake, to see what Nico will do.

rc.ss: tone — the mood of a scene

rc.q: Which event is the turning point of the story?
c: Otis reads the cast list on the door.
Otis whispers the forgotten line to Nico.
Ms. Pruitt says the tree had the most important part.
rc.e: Everything before the whisper builds toward it (the silent part, the listening, Nico frozen on stage), and everything after follows from it: Nico says his line and the play goes on.

y.A: Families surrounding the actors comes after the play, once the trouble is already over.
y.B: Reading the cast list is how the story begins; it sets up his small part but does not change anything yet.
y.D: Ms. Pruitt's remark at the party looks back on the turning point; it is not the moment things change.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the turning point of a story

rc.q: The story is mainly about a boy who
c: learns to run the lights in the gym
wants a bigger part in the next play
forgets his line on the night of the play
saves the play with what he heard at rehearsals
rc.e: The story follows Otis from a part with no lines, through weeks of listening, to the moment he whispers the line Nico has forgotten. What he heard is what saves the show.

y.A: Running the lights is Ms. Pruitt's job on the night; Otis is on stage the whole time.
y.B: A bigger part next year is never mentioned; the story ends at this year's cast party.
y.C: Forgetting a line on the night happens to Nico, not to Otis, the boy the story follows.

rc.ss: main idea — what a story is mainly about

rc.q: Why did the author most likely write this passage?
c: to describe a program where children read to a dog
to explain how a dog is trained to become a therapy dog
to persuade families to buy a dog for a child who reads
to tell the history of the public library in Salt Lake City
rc.e: Most of the passage shows one Saturday program (Oatmeal, Pam, the readers, Paloma) and explains why reading to a dog helps, with one paragraph on where the idea began.

y.B: How a dog is trained is never explained; line 7 says only that Oatmeal is a registered therapy dog.
y.C: Buying a dog is never suggested; Oatmeal belongs to Pam and comes to the library.
y.D: The Salt Lake City library fills one paragraph (lines 19–24), which shows where the idea began; it is not the subject of the whole passage.

rc.ss: main idea — the author's purpose

rc.q: In line 17, “puts it more simply” tells us that Paloma
c: writes it down in her notebook
places her book on a lower shelf
reads the hard words more slowly
says the same idea in plainer words
rc.e: To put something simply is to say it in plain, easy words. Paloma sums up the whole paragraph in one short sentence: “He never says, ‘Sound it out.’”

y.A: Writing it down turns speaking into writing; Paloma says her words aloud, and the passage quotes them.
y.B: Placing her book on a shelf takes “puts” in its everyday sense of setting something down.
y.C: Reading the hard words more slowly is about reading aloud, but “puts it” is about how Paloma says something.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a figurative or idiomatic phrase

rc.q: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that children need not worry about mistakes when they read to Oatmeal?
c: Paloma signs up for the following Saturday.
A dog never interrupts, corrects, or laughs at a reader.
Oatmeal listens patiently and rests his chin on a sneaker.
More than one hundred children came to the Salt Lake City program.
rc.e: The idea is about mistakes, and lines 15–16 speak to exactly that: a dog “never corrects a mistake or laughs when a word comes out wrong.” The other details are true, but they are about other things.

y.A: Signing up for the following Saturday shows Paloma enjoyed the visit, but it says nothing about how a mistake is treated.
y.C: Listening patiently and resting his chin on a sneaker show that Oatmeal is calm and friendly, but they do not show what happens when a reader makes a mistake.
y.D: More than one hundred children coming shows the Salt Lake City program was popular, not that mistakes were safe.

rc.ss: supporting detail — the detail that supports a claim

rc.q: Why does the author include the fourth paragraph (lines 19–24)?
c: to show where the idea began and how it spread
to describe the books that children bring to read
to explain why Oatmeal was chosen as a therapy dog
to argue that every library in the country should have a dog
rc.e: Lines 19–24 go back to a 1999 program in Salt Lake City, then say that libraries across the country have started similar ones: where the idea began and how it spread.

y.B: The books children bring are described in the second paragraph (lines 9–11).
y.C: Why Oatmeal was chosen is never explained anywhere in the passage.
y.D: Every library having a dog is never argued; lines 22–24 report only that many libraries have started similar programs.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a paragraph

rc.q: The author would most likely agree with which statement?
c: Dogs understand most of the words that children read.
A listener who never corrects can help a nervous reader.
Children should read only to animals and never to people.
Reading to a dog is a new idea that few libraries have tried.
rc.e: The passage says many children feel nervous reading aloud to people, and that a dog never interrupts, corrects, or laughs. So the author would agree that a listener who never corrects can help a nervous reader.

y.A: Dogs understanding the words is not claimed; Pam's question in lines 26–27 is a way to let the child explain, not proof that Oatmeal understands.
y.C: Reading only to animals goes far beyond the passage, which says some children feel nervous reading to people, not that they should stop.
y.D: A new idea that few have tried contradicts lines 19–24: the passage says the idea is not new, and libraries across the country have started similar programs.

rc.ss: inference — what the author would most likely say

rc.q: The passage is most like
c: a set of rules for dog owners
a folktale that explains why dogs wag
a letter asking the library for money
a news article about a library program
rc.e: The passage reports on a real kind of program, with a scene from one Saturday, a quotation from a child, and facts about where the idea began. That is how a news article reads.

y.A: A set of rules would tell the reader what to do; this passage describes what happens on Saturdays.
y.B: A folktale would be made up and set long ago; this passage reports a real kind of program happening now, with a date and a city.
y.C: A letter would be addressed to someone and ask for something; this passage asks for nothing.

rc.ss: style — what kind of writing the passage is

rc.q: What does the scene mainly show about Theo?
c: He realizes that his grandmother left him more work than he could manage.
He discovers that he is not suited to selling fruit at a busy market stall.
He gives up a rehearsed sales line and lets customers judge the fruit themselves.
He learns that neat handwriting matters far more than he had ever thought.
rc.e: Theo breaks off his practiced sentence, hands over a cherry instead of a description, and by four o’clock the crate is empty. The choice about neat handwriting reverses the ending, in which the hastily written, messier line is the one that works. Strategy: let the final sentence test your choice.

y.A: Theo minds the stall for two hours and has time to straighten every plum stem, so the amount of work is not what gets in his way.
y.B: By four o'clock the whole crate of cherries is gone, so the scene ends with him selling them, just not in the way he had practiced.
y.D: Nobody touched the cherries while the neat card was propped up, and the crate emptied after he rewrote a line in handwriting that was not nearly as neat.

rc.ss: main idea — what a story is mainly about

rc.q: What does Theo do to his price card after the woman buys the cherries?
c: He crosses out a line and adds new words in messier handwriting.
He writes the prices on it in his neatest handwriting.
He throws the card away and writes out a new one from scratch.
He props it up against the crate of plums at the end of the table.
rc.e: The last paragraph says he crossed out one line on his careful card and wrote underneath, “in handwriting that was not nearly as neat.” Strategy: watch where in the scene each detail happens.

y.B: He did write the prices in his neatest handwriting, but that was before the market opened. The question asks what he does to the card after the woman buys.
y.C: He keeps the card he made. He crosses out one line and writes underneath it.
y.D: He does prop the card up, but against the scale at the start of the morning, and the question asks what he does to it after the woman buys.

rc.ss: supporting detail — what a character says or does

rc.q: The bowl under the table was most likely put there so that
c: Theo could keep count of how many cherries he had sold.
Theo’s grandmother would have something to eat later on.
bruised cherries could be kept out of the customers’ sight.
customers could taste a cherry before buying.
rc.e: Theo assumes the bowl is her lunch, but it does its work the instant he offers a cherry to the woman, and he then sets it on the table “where people could reach it.” The lunch choice is what the character guesses, not what the scene shows. Strategy: trust what happens in a scene over what a character assumes.

y.A: Nothing in the scene uses the bowl for keeping count, and the cherries in it are the ones people get to taste.
y.B: That is what Theo assumes, and the passage adds that his grandmother never ate anything at the market; watch what the bowl actually does when the woman stops.
y.C: The passage never calls any of the cherries bruised; the ones in the bowl are the same cherries as the ones in the crate.

rc.ss: inference — a character's reason for acting

rc.q: In the first paragraph, *mind* most nearly means
rc.e: His grandmother leaves and “for two hours the stall was his to mind,” so he is the one looking after it. Being bothered by something is the meaning most readers meet first, as in “I don’t mind,” but a stall cannot be bothered by anybody. Strategy: substitute each choice into the sentence and hear which one survives.

y.A: That is the meaning when you say you do not mind something, but a fruit stall cannot be bothered by anything; the stall was his to look after.
y.C: Theo did memorize the prices, which makes this meaning feel close, but the thing that was his for two hours was the stall itself.
y.D: The word can mean obeying a person, and here what he minds is a stall, which nobody obeys.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The dash in “They’re excellent for—” marks the point at which
c: Theo abandons the sentence he practiced and changes his approach.
Theo’s grandmother comes back to the stall with the change.
the woman in the yellow coat interrupts Theo with another question.
Theo forgets the prices he had memorized before the market opened.
rc.e: The narrator says he stopped “because he could hear how it sounded: like a boy repeating something,” and from there he shows the fruit instead of describing it. The choice about an interruption gives the woman credit for a decision Theo makes on his own. Strategy: punctuation that breaks a sentence often marks the turn of a scene.

y.B: His grandmother has gone to find change and does not come back anywhere in the scene; Theo is the one who stops the sentence.
y.C: The woman had already asked her question, and the passage says he stopped because he could hear how it sounded.
y.D: The prices are not the trouble. He stops because the practiced sentence sounded “like a boy repeating something.”

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a sentence or detail

rc.q: The last sentence, about the empty crate and the beautifully arranged plums, is best described as
c: wistful and sad about the end of a long day at the market.
quietly amused, setting what looked good beside what actually sold.
excited and boastful about how much money Theo managed to earn.
sharply critical of the mistakes Theo made over the course of the day.
rc.e: The plums are called “arranged so beautifully” at the exact moment we learn they did not sell, a small joke the narrator makes without scolding Theo. Reading the line as sharp criticism mistakes gentle humor for blame. Strategy: notice when a detail from the opening returns with its meaning changed.

y.A: Nothing in the sentence sounds sorry, and an empty crate is good news at a market stall.
y.C: No money and no total appear at the end, and the sentence is quiet rather than boastful.
y.D: The narrator is gentle here: the joke is that the beautifully arranged plums are the ones still sitting there, and it is not aimed at Theo.

rc.ss: style — the effect of an ending

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: A damper is the only device that keeps a very tall tower standing up.
Strong wind is the greatest danger that any tall building will ever face.
A building that moves at all in the wind has been built incorrectly.
A tall building is built to sway a little and then stop quickly.
rc.e: The passage first explains why a frame is given room to bend and then why engineers work to make the motion fade fast, ending with what they actually measure.
