c: shows that the shelf had its own kind of order
suggests that Grandpa has forgotten where his books are
shows that Grandpa is angry at Raina for moving his books
tells the reader that Grandpa wants to go back to the lake
rc.e: Grandpa asks for a summer, not a book, because his books stood in the order he read them. The question leads him to explain the shelf's real order, which changes how Raina sees the "mess."

y.B: Forgetting where his books are takes the question too literally; Grandpa knows exactly which books he means and finds all three (lines 21–24).
y.C: Being angry at Raina does not fit: he asks quietly (line 20), explains the shelf, and offers to fix it with her (line 32).
y.D: Wanting to go back to the lake treats the question as a wish for a trip; “the summer we drove to the lake” names the summer he read three of the books (lines 24–26).

rc.ss: organization/logic — the turning point of a story

rc.q: Which best states what the story is mainly about?
c: A grandfather remembers a summer he spent at a lake.
A girl shows her grandfather how a library sorts books.
A girl discovers the hidden order of her grandfather's shelf.
A grandfather is upset when his granddaughter moves his books.
rc.e: Raina thinks the shelf is a mess and sorts it the library way, then learns from Grandpa that the books stood in the order he read them, and together they put it back.

y.A: A summer at a lake is one memory the shelf holds (line 19), not what the whole story is about.
y.B: Showing her grandfather how a library sorts books gets the story backward: Raina sorts them the library way (lines 8–10), and it is Grandpa who shows her something new.
y.D: Being upset when she moves his books is only the middle of the story (lines 14–16); the story goes on to what Raina learns and how the two of them rebuild the shelf.

rc.ss: main idea — what a story is mainly about

rc.q: At the end of the story, Grandpa most likely holds out his hand for Raina's novel because he wants to
c: give her visit a place on his shelf
take it back to the school library for her
see whether she has finished reading it yet
file it under the author's last name, the library way
rc.e: Grandpa's shelf is in the order he lived it, and he clears a space at the very end, where the newest books belong. Putting Raina's novel there makes her visit part of the shelf's story.

y.B: Taking it back to the school library is never suggested; the librarian appears only as the model for Raina's sorting (lines 9–10), and Grandpa is making room on his own shelf.
y.C: Seeing whether she has finished it misses why he first cleared a narrow space at the end of the shelf (lines 34–36), just before he asked for the book.
y.D: Filing it under the author's last name is Raina's library way (lines 8–10); Grandpa's shelf runs in the order he lived, and the new space is at the far end.

rc.ss: inference — a character's reason for acting

rc.q: When Mom says that Saffron's trotting off was “exactly what we raised her to do” (line 31), she most likely means that
c: the family would soon get Saffron back again
the family had already taught Saffron to guide
Saffron was ready to go calmly with someone new
Saffron had never really loved the family at all
rc.e: The family's job was to make Saffron comfortable anywhere and with anyone, so her trotting off calmly with a new trainer, without looking back, shows that the raising worked.

y.A: Getting Saffron back soon is not suggested; she is staying at the school for about four months of training to guide (lines 25–27).
y.B: Teaching her to guide was not the family's job: an instructor will spend about four months teaching her to guide (lines 26–27), while the family taught manners and socializing.
y.D: Never having loved the family takes “without looking back” (line 29) as a lack of love; Mom means that a calm, confident puppy is what all the socializing was for.

rc.ss: inference — what a character's words mean

rc.q: The author's main purpose in the passage is to
c: explain how instructors teach dogs to guide
tell how a puppy learned to walk through doors
persuade readers to adopt a dog from a shelter
describe what raising a guide dog puppy is like
rc.e: The narrator tells what the family did with Saffron, from the day she arrived to the day they handed her back, and explains why a guide dog puppy is raised that way.

y.A: How instructors teach dogs to guide is mentioned only once (lines 26–27); the passage is about the family's part, before that training begins.
y.B: Walking through automatic doors is one example of socializing (lines 20–23), not the purpose of the whole passage.
y.C: Adopting a dog from a shelter is never mentioned; Saffron belonged to a guide dog school, and the family was only raising her.

rc.ss: main idea — the author's main purpose

rc.q: The passage is told from the point of view of
c: a child whose family raised Saffron
the instructor who will train Saffron
a blind person who will someday use Saffron
rc.e: The narrator says “our puppy,” mentions “my math textbook” and “my soccer practice,” and writes “My mom squeezed my shoulder,” so the teller is a child in the family raising Saffron.

y.A: Saffron herself is the one being told about, not the teller; the narrator calls her “she” and “her” (lines 3–4).
y.C: The instructor who will train her appears only at the end (lines 26–27); the “I” is the one who hands the leash over to the trainer (lines 27–29).
y.D: A blind person who will use Saffron never speaks in the passage; the person she will guide is not even named.

rc.ss: style — who is telling the passage (point of view)

rc.q: Which detail from the passage best shows that socializing Saffron worked?
c: She rode in the car to soccer practice.
Later, she walked right through the doors.
She stopped and stared at the automatic doors.
She arrived with a green leash and a bag of food.
rc.e: Socializing means taking a puppy to new places until nothing surprises her. Saffron first stopped and stared at the automatic doors, but by the fifth trip she walked through them as if she had always done it (lines 20–23).

y.A: Riding in the car to soccer practice is part of the socializing itself (lines 18–19), one of the places she went, not proof that it worked.
y.C: Stopping and staring at the automatic doors is how she reacted the first time (lines 20–22), before the socializing had worked.
y.D: Arriving with a green leash and a bag of food describes her first day (lines 1–2), before any socializing had begun.

rc.ss: supporting detail — the detail that best supports an idea

rc.q: In line 13, “socializing” most nearly means
c: keeping a puppy safe at home
teaching a puppy to sit and stay
chatting with friends at a party
rc.e: Right after naming it, the passage explains socializing: taking a puppy to crowded, noisy places again and again until nothing surprises her. It means getting her used to new places.

y.B: Keeping a puppy safe at home is the opposite of what lines 15–17 describe: the puppy is taken out to busy places again and again.
y.C: Teaching a puppy to sit and stay is house manners and obedience (lines 10–11), which the passage names as a different part of the job.
y.D: Chatting with friends at a party is what socializing means for people; for a guide dog puppy, the school means getting used to new places (lines 15–17).

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — an unfamiliar word's meaning from clues

rc.q: The passage provides information to answer which question?
c: How many puppies does the school train each year?
What is the name of the person Saffron will guide?
What happens to puppies that do not become guides?
At what age do puppies go to their volunteer families?
rc.e: Lines 8–9 say puppies like Saffron go to volunteer families when they are seven or eight weeks old. The passage never gives the school's numbers, the name of the person she will guide, or what happens to puppies that do not become guides.

y.A: How many puppies the school trains each year is never stated; the passage tells about only one puppy, Saffron.
y.B: The name of the person Saffron will guide is never given; the passage ends as she trots off with her trainer (lines 28–29).
y.C: What happens to puppies that do not become guides is not explained; the passage ends as Saffron begins her training (lines 25–29).

rc.ss: organization/logic — which question the passage answers

rc.q: The passage is mainly about
c: a grandmother who teaches her granddaughter to swim across a lake.
a girl who gets thoroughly soaked during an early morning on a lake.
a girl who becomes strong enough to row after an hour of hard practice.
a girl who discovers that skill, not raw force, is what moves a boat.
rc.e: The last lines say plainly that Nadia “was not stronger than she had been an hour before” but “had simply stopped fighting the thing she was trying to move.” The choice about growing strong enough is tempting because it is what usually happens in practice stories, but the passage denies it in so many words. Strategy: when a story ends by correcting an expectation, that correction is the main idea.

y.A: The grandmother really is teaching her, but she is teaching her to row, and nobody swims anywhere in this story.
y.B: The spray does soak her knees, but that is one moment of the first hard stroke; the question asks what the whole passage is about.
y.C: The ending says the opposite in so many words: she "was not stronger than she had been an hour before."

rc.ss: main idea — what a story is mainly about

rc.q: What happens the first time Nadia pulls with all her weight?
c: The boat slides forward without a sound and the ripples spread behind in even rings.
The blades slap the surface, spray soaks her knees, and the boat barely moves.
The heron on the shore is startled by the noise and flies off quickly.
One of the wooden oars snaps in half and drops into the cold water.
rc.e: The second paragraph states that the boat barely moved, the blades slapped the surface, and the spray soaked her knees. The silent forward glide describes the later, corrected stroke, and the startled heron reverses the bird, which watches her and then lifts away “without hurrying.” Strategy: check that a detail belongs to the part of the story the question asks about.

y.A: That is a real sentence from the story, but it describes the later stroke, after her grandmother tells her to let the blade bite first.
y.C: The heron does leave, but it watches her first and then lifts away "without hurrying" — the passage never says it was startled.
y.D: The handles do jump out of her grip twice, but no oar breaks.

rc.ss: supporting detail — what a character says or does

rc.q: The grandmother most likely says nothing at first because she
c: is annoyed with her granddaughter and has decided not to speak to her again.
does not know how to row a boat and so has nothing useful to offer.
has quietly fallen asleep in the stern of the boat while Nadia works.
wants Nadia to feel the problem herself before she is told how to fix it.
rc.e: Her silence is called “her way of teaching,” and she speaks only after Nadia's hard pulling has failed, giving three exact instructions. The choice about not knowing how to row is impossible given how expert that advice turns out to be, and her folded hands and watchful stillness rule out sleep. Strategy: when a story labels a behavior, use that label to explain the character's purpose.

y.A: Her silence is called "her way of teaching," and she does speak — three exact instructions that work at once.
y.B: The advice she gives works the moment Nadia follows it, so she plainly knows how to row.
y.C: She sits in the back of the boat with her hands folded, and she speaks at exactly the right moment, after the hard pulling fails — she could not do that asleep.

rc.ss: inference — a character's reason for acting

rc.q: When the grandmother says, “Let it bite,” she means that the blade should
c: drop all the way to the lake bottom.
sting the hands sharply and painfully.
take firm hold of the water.
cut into something with sharp teeth.
rc.e: The next paragraph shows exactly what she meant: Nadia lowers the blade and feels “the water take hold of it, a firm and surprising grip.” Cutting with teeth is the everyday meaning of the word and has nothing to do with an oar. Strategy: when a word is used oddly, read on — a story often shows you the meaning a sentence later.

y.A: The lines just after show the water taking hold of the blade; nothing in the story reaches for the bottom of the lake.
y.B: Her shoulders do burn and the handles do jump from her grip, but this instruction is about what the blade does in the water.
y.D: That is the everyday meaning of the word, but an oar has no teeth — the story shows the water gripping the blade like a hand closing round it.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — the meaning of a phrase

rc.q: The paragraph that begins with the grandmother's instruction is the turning point of the passage because it
c: replaces Nadia's effort with a method, and the boat's behavior changes at once.
returns to the heron on the shore in order to slow the whole story down.
explains why the lake lies so calm and still early on a summer morning.
introduces a new character who takes over the rowing from Nadia herself.
rc.e: Before it, the boat barely moves and the handles jump from her grip; right after the instruction, the boat “slid forward without a sound” and the ripples spread in even rings. The choice about a new character is false, since the grandmother never rows. Strategy: to find a turning point, compare what is true just before it with what is true just after.

y.B: The heron belongs to the paragraph before, and it never comes back.
y.C: The still lake is in the first sentence, but no part of the passage explains why it is calm.
y.D: The grandmother is in the boat from the first paragraph, and Nadia still has the oars at the end, half way across the lake.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the turning point of a story

rc.q: The phrase “the oars quarreled with the water, arguing over every stroke” suggests that
c: the oars were old and creaked loudly in their worn metal locks.
the lake was rough and choppy that morning and full of waves.
Nadia was muttering complaints to herself the whole time she rowed.
Nadia's strokes and the water were working against each other.
rc.e: Giving the oars a quarrel is a way of picturing effort that fights the water instead of using it, which is why the boat barely moves. The rough-lake choice is contradicted by the opening description of a lake “perfectly still.” Strategy: ask what the figure of speech is describing in plain terms before choosing.

y.A: The oars do jump out of her hands, but the passage never says they were old or that they creaked.
y.B: The lake is "perfectly still" in the opening sentence, so the trouble is coming from her strokes rather than the water.
y.C: The quarrel is between the oars and the water, and it is a picture of her strokes; Nadia never says a word in this story.

rc.ss: figurative language — personification

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Road salt is the only substance that is able to clear ice from a winter road surface.
Sand is spread on the roads in very cold places because it helps tires grip the icy surface.
Winter storms across the country have become far more dangerous over the last thirty years.
Salt keeps water from freezing on roads, but within limits and at a cost, so crews now use less.
rc.e: The passage explains how salt works, states the temperature limit, describes the harm meltwater carries into soil and streams, and ends with brine spraying that “uses far less salt.” The sand choice is one detail from the second paragraph, and the claim that salt is the only ice remover is contradicted by the sand crews use in the coldest places. Strategy: a main idea has to cover the turn as well as the opening.

y.A: The passage never claims salt is the only thing crews use, and it goes on to give a temperature past which salt stops working at all.
y.B: This is true and the passage says it, but it is one detail about the coldest places; the question asks for the idea that covers the whole passage.
y.C: Thirty winters are mentioned, but as thirty years of salt building up on the same road, not as storms getting worse.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, why do trucks spread salt before the snow begins to fall?
c: Because salt melts ice much faster while the pavement is still dry and clear.
To keep a thin film of water from freezing onto the pavement in the first place.
Because the trucks cannot drive safely on a road once the snow has covered it over.
Because salt loses all of its melting power once the crystals become wet.
rc.e: The first paragraph says the salt “is not there only to melt ice that has already formed” but to stop a film of water from freezing onto the pavement to begin with. The choice about salt losing its power when wet is contradicted by the last paragraph, where crews deliberately dissolve salt into brine before spraying it. Strategy: read the sentence that follows a “not only” — it usually carries the real answer.

y.A: The passage says the early salt is there to stop a film of water from freezing at all, and it never compares how fast salt works on dry or wet pavement.
y.C: That sounds likely in real life, but the passage never gives it as a reason for going out early.
y.D: The last paragraph has crews dissolving salt into a brine on purpose, so wet salt has not lost its power.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a reason stated in the passage

rc.q: Based on the passage, in which situation would a crew be most likely to choose sand instead of salt?
c: A week when the crew's main goal is to lower the freezing point of water on the pavement.
A wet afternoon in early spring when the temperature stays near fifty degrees.
A night when the temperature is expected to fall to twenty below zero.
A storm arriving at thirty degrees, when the crew wants to stop ice from forming at all.
rc.e: Salted water stays liquid only down to about six degrees below zero; colder than that the salt is “simply cold grit,” which is why the coldest places use sand. The choice about lowering the freezing point is ruled out by the flat statement that “sand cannot lower a freezing point at all.” Strategy: apply the limit the passage gives to the numbers in each choice.

y.A: Sand is the wrong tool for that job: the passage says sand "cannot lower a freezing point at all."
y.B: Plain water freezes at thirty-two degrees, so at about fifty there is no ice for either salt or sand to deal with.
y.D: Thirty degrees is well inside the range where salt still works, and stopping ice from forming is exactly the job the passage gives salt.

rc.ss: inference — applying the passage to a new case

rc.q: As used in the first paragraph, “solution” most nearly means
c: a liquid with something dissolved in it.
a hard crust of salt and ice on the road.
an answer to a difficult problem or puzzle.
a plan that a city government agrees to follow.
rc.e: The sentence describes what forms when salt particles dissolve in water and then stay liquid below freezing, so the word names the salty liquid itself. The answer-to-a-problem sense is the word's everyday meaning and is especially tempting because the passage is about solving a winter problem. Strategy: prefer the scientific sense when the sentence is describing what a substance is, not what someone decided.

y.B: The sentence says what forms "stays liquid" below freezing, so it is not a crust of anything.
y.C: That is the meaning you meet most often, and a passage about a winter problem makes it very tempting; here the word names the salty liquid itself.
y.D: City trucks are in the passage, but this sentence describes what happens when salt dissolves in water, not a decision anyone made.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: What is the purpose of the short sentence “There is a limit.”?
c: It explains why many crews now spray brine on the pavement before a storm.
It simply repeats the main point of the first paragraph in fewer words.
It marks a turn from how salt works to the conditions in which it stops working.
It introduces the harm that meltwater does to roadside trees and to streams.
rc.e: Everything before it explains why salted water stays liquid; everything after it gives the freezing point, the minus-six limit, and the switch to sand. The meltwater harm and the brine spraying are real parts of the passage, but they come later, in the third and fourth paragraphs. Strategy: a short sentence set on its own is usually a hinge — read what changes right after it.

y.A: The brine is real, but it comes at the very end, and the passage ties it to using less salt because of the harm, not to this limit.
y.B: The first paragraph explains how salt works; what follows this sentence is where it stops working, so the sentence adds something instead of repeating it.
y.D: That harm is genuinely in the passage, but a paragraph later — what comes right after this sentence is the freezing point, the six-below cut-off, and the sand.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a sentence or detail

rc.q: The closing sentences — “The chemistry has not changed. What has changed is how carefully it is spent.” — suggest that the author sees the switch to brine as
c: a change in everyday practice, not a new scientific discovery.
a sign that scientists no longer agree about how water freezes.
proof that road salt has stopped working the way it once did.
a warning that brine harms the streams more than dry salt does.
rc.e: The pair of sentences separates the science, which is unchanged, from the habit of using less of it, which is what crews have altered. The choice calling brine more harmful is contradicted by the same paragraph, which says brine “uses far less salt.” Strategy: when an author sets two short sentences against each other, the second one carries the point.

y.B: The line says the chemistry "has not changed," which is the opposite of scientists disagreeing, and the passage never mentions scientists.
y.C: Salt still works exactly as it did; what the author says changed is how carefully crews spend it.
y.D: The same paragraph says brine "uses far less salt," so the author offers it as the gentler choice, not the more harmful one.

rc.ss: style — the effect of an ending

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: The Moon does not spin at all, which is why one face always points at us.
The Moon's far side was first photographed by a spacecraft that flew behind it.
The half we never see is permanently dark, unlike the half that faces Earth.
Earth's pull settled the Moon into a spin that matches its orbit.
rc.e: The passage sets up a puzzle in the first paragraph (the Moon must turn once per lap to keep one face toward us) and spends the third paragraph explaining what put it into that rhythm. The choice about the 1959 spacecraft is true but is a single closing detail, and the choice about a permanently dark half is contradicted in the last paragraph. Strategy: the main idea has to cover the whole passage, not one sentence of it.

y.A: This is the exact guess the first paragraph calls the reverse of the truth, so it is the idea the passage sets out to correct.
y.B: That happens in the very last sentence, and one closing fact is far too small to be what the whole passage is about.
y.C: The passage says outright that the hidden half gets as much sunlight as the half we know.

rc.ss: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage

rc.q: According to the passage, what is happening on the far side of the Moon when the Moon looks full to us?
c: It is dark there for all time.
It is going through its night.
It is turned toward the Sun.
It is warmer than the near side.
rc.e: The last paragraph states it directly: when the Moon looks full to us, the far side is in night. The choice about lasting darkness borrows the name people use for that half, which is the very name the paragraph calls wrong. Strategy: for a detail question, find the sentence that mentions the thing the question names, and read it all the way to the end.

y.A: This is the dark-side idea the paragraph is written to correct, since the far side gets as much sunlight as the half we know.
y.C: A full Moon means our side is the lit one, so the far side is the side facing away from the sunlight just then.
y.D: The passage never compares the two halves for warmth. It says only which one is in night.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: The passage suggests that if the Moon's orbit were a perfect circle,
c: the Moon would stop turning on its axis.
the far side would get sunlight of its own.
observers would have less of the Moon to chart.
the Moon would need much longer to finish a lap.
rc.e: The thin strip of the far side that observers managed to chart comes from the rocking, and the rocking comes from the Moon hurrying and lagging in an orbit that is not a true circle. Take the uneven orbit away and that strip goes with it, so there would be less of the Moon to map than the little-more-than-half they reached. Strategy: when a question removes a cause, follow the chain the passage already built and ask which effect shrinks.

y.A: Nothing in the passage ties the shape of the orbit to whether the Moon turns. The spin was settled long ago by the bulge.
y.B: The far side already gets as much sunlight as the near side, so a rounder orbit would change nothing about that.
y.D: The passage says the orbit's shape makes the Moon hurry and lag along the way, not that it changes how long a lap takes.

rc.ss: inference — applying the passage to a new case

rc.q: In the third paragraph, *faint* most nearly means
c: so slight it is hard to notice.
weak and about to fall over.
too quiet to be heard clearly.
rc.e: The bulge is the small stretch that Earth's slightly stronger pull produces, so faint here means barely there, hardly noticeable. The dizzy and the quiet-sound meanings are both genuine senses of the word, which is what makes them tempting, but neither fits a shape in rock. Strategy: read each meaning back into the actual sentence and keep the one that still makes sense.

y.B: That is a real meaning of the word, but rock does not feel dizzy, and the sentence is describing a shape.
y.C: A bulge is something you could see or measure, not something that makes a sound.
y.D: This meaning turns up in words like faint-hearted, and nothing in a stretched piece of rock is being called cowardly.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The second paragraph mainly serves to
c: let the reader act out the Moon's once-per-lap turn.
introduce the gravity explained in the paragraph after it.
prove that a chair and a moon obey the same laws.
show that the Moon's motion is too odd to picture.
rc.e: The first paragraph makes a claim that sounds wrong at first hearing, and the chair paragraph hands the reader a way to perform that same turn and feel that it is true. It introduces no new cause and it argues nothing about laws. Strategy: ask what a short paragraph does for the paragraph before it, not just what objects it mentions.

y.B: Gravity does not appear anywhere in the chair paragraph; it arrives fresh at the start of the next one.
y.C: The paragraph asks the reader to walk one circle, and nothing more. It never claims that a chair and a moon are governed by the same laws, which would be a far larger claim than this passage makes anywhere.
y.D: The paragraph does the opposite, making the motion easy to picture by putting the reader inside it.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a paragraph

rc.q: In saying that the same dark patches *stare back*, the author suggests that
c: the Moon is keeping watch over Earth.
the same view meets us each time.
the dark patches slowly change shape.
the patches are hard to see clearly.
rc.e: Patches of rock cannot stare, so the phrase has to mean something else, and the two words before it say what: tonight, and again next month, the same ones. It is a way of saying the view never changes. Strategy: when a writer gives an object a human action, ask what the action is standing in for, and look at the words around it for the answer.

y.A: This takes the staring literally. The patches are markings, and the author is describing what we see, not something the Moon is doing on purpose.
y.C: The whole point of the sentence is that the patches do not change, which is what makes the rest of the passage surprising.
y.D: The patches are the part that is easy to see; the passage never says anything about how hard they are to make out.

rc.ss: figurative language — personification

rc.q: The author's main purpose in this passage is to
c: explain why the grade of Hill Street is gentler at the park gate than at the top.
argue that Hill Street needs benches back and that the town must keep them up.
describe how one neighbor has done her shopping on foot for the past fifty years.
persuade neighbors to take turns driving Ruth up the hill to the grocery store.
rc.e: The first paragraph makes the request — benches back on Hill Street, spaced so that nobody climbs a whole block without a stop — and the third paragraph adds the other half of it, that the washing and the painting come out of the same budget as the benches. Everything else supports that request: the slope sets it up, Ruth shows what a bench does, the ending says what is at stake. Strategy: the main idea has to account for the whole argument, including the part about upkeep.

y.A: The slope is described in the opening lines, but it is the setting for the argument rather than the thing the author is asking the town to do.
y.C: Ruth is one example used to support the request, and a main idea has to cover the whole passage, not a single person inside it.
y.D: The car does appear in the passage, but the author is addressing the town and asking for benches, not organizing rides for anybody.

rc.ss: main idea — the author's main purpose

rc.q: According to the passage, what did Ruth do while the bench outside the bakery was still there?
c: She had her groceries brought to her by car on Tuesdays.
She walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down.
She waited at the bench for someone to drive her up the hill.
She carried her shopping up the hill and walked back down.
rc.e: One sentence in the second paragraph answers this directly: while the bench stood outside the bakery, she walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down. The sentence after it describes the present arrangement, groceries arriving by car, and one choice turns her trip around so that the shopping goes uphill. Strategy: when a passage describes a before and an after, put your finger on which one the question asks about, then check the direction of travel.

y.A: That is what happens now that the bench is gone, so this choice puts the after-picture into the before-slot.
y.C: Nobody in the passage waits at the bench for a ride; the bench is a place to stop partway through her own climb.
y.D: Every piece of this is in the sentence, but the trip runs the other way: she walked up and carried the shopping down.

rc.ss: supporting detail — a fact stated in the passage

rc.q: Suppose the town offered to install twelve benches but would not pay to wash or repaint them. Based on the passage, the author would most likely
c: prefer six benches the town has promised to look after.
accept the twelve, since more places to stop is the goal.
ask that the money go toward widening the sidewalk instead.
agree, if neighbors themselves did the washing and painting.
rc.e: The author has already faced this exact trade. There is room on Hill Street for twelve, and the author asks for six anyway, on the grounds that benches nobody looks after splinter before long — so a smaller number with the upkeep attached is the deal the author chose once cost was the objection. Strategy: when a question invents a new situation, look for the place where the author has already made the same choice.

y.B: More benches sounds like more of what the author wants, but the author says plainly that the ask is six with upkeep, even though twelve would fit on the street.
y.C: A wider sidewalk was the town's own answer last time, and the second paragraph exists to say that a bench does what widening cannot.
y.D: The author asks for the upkeep to come out of the town's budget, and nowhere offers to take that work on.

rc.ss: inference — what the author would likely think

rc.q: In the first paragraph, *grade* most nearly means
c: a mark given on a piece of schoolwork.
a level of school, such as fifth year.
the quality or rank of a material.
the slope of a rising road.
rc.e: The sentence sets the word between gentle and steep and attaches it to a street that earns the name Hill, so it has to mean the slope itself — how sharply the road rises. The two school meanings are real meanings of the word, which is exactly why they are offered here. Strategy: read the whole sentence with each meaning slotted in and keep the one that still makes sense.

y.A: This is the meaning you meet most often at school, but a park gate cannot be given a mark.
y.B: A street does not have school years, and the sentence is comparing the bottom of the hill with the top.
y.C: The word can describe how good a material is, but here gentle and steep are describing a slope, not a quality.

rc.ss: vocabulary in context — a word with two meanings

rc.q: The last two sentences of the passage mainly serve to
c: restate the cost of upkeep that the third paragraph accepts.
recall how Ruth used the bench outside the bakery.
admit what benches cannot do and name what they decide.
predict how many people will sit on the benches each week.
rc.e: Having said what a bench does, the author closes by giving one thing up and claiming another: the hill will stay exactly as steep as it was, and the benches will settle who is able to walk up it. Neither sentence goes back to the money, and neither counts anybody. Strategy: a closing line often concedes something small in order to hold on to something large — read the ending for that trade.

y.A: The cost of keeping benches up is granted in the paragraph before this one, and the closing lines never return to it.
y.B: Ruth's Tuesdays belong to the second paragraph, and the ending does not go back to her.
y.D: The author never counts users; the last line is about who is able to climb the hill, not how many will sit down.

rc.ss: organization/logic — the purpose of a sentence or detail

rc.q: In the last paragraph the author calls a sidewalk with benches “a room” in order to suggest that
c: benches turn a place people pass through into a place they stay.
benches take up as much space as the walls of a small building.
the town should build a shelter over the sidewalk on Hill Street.
a bench can make a public sidewalk feel like part of a home.
rc.e: A corridor is somewhere you walk through on your way elsewhere, and the author sets it against a room, then says straight out that people stay in rooms and offers two small pictures of staying. The figure is about what the sidewalk becomes for the people on it, not about the size of a bench or about turning a public place into a private one. Strategy: when an author makes a comparison, read the sentence just after it, which usually tells you what the comparison is for.

y.B: The passage does compare a bench to a small building, but that comparison is about upkeep, not about how much room a bench fills.
y.C: Nobody is asking for a roof here; the room is a way of describing the sidewalk, not a thing to be built on top of it.
y.D: A room does suggest a house, but the contrast the author draws is corridor against room — passing through against staying — not public against private.

rc.ss: figurative language — a metaphor or figurative phrase

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
c: Water hollows out caves and then builds stone shapes in them.
Rainwater carries the same acid that gives soda pop its fizz.
Cave visitors are asked never to touch the stone shapes they see.
A soda straw becomes a stalactite when its hollow inside gets blocked.
rc.e: The passage explains how acidic water dissolves rock to make caves and how dripping water then leaves calcite, ring by ring, to build soda straws, stalactites, stalagmites and columns.

y.B: Rainwater carrying the soda-pop acid is one step at the start (lines 6–9), part of how caves form, not the idea the whole passage builds.

explain how fast the riders could travel
show that the riders were paid very little
introduce the telegraph line across the land

y.B: Rooms where artists work are studios; Seurat's studies were things he painted (line 19), not places.

rc.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

Seurat painted with dots of color that mix in the viewer's eye.
The painting shows a crowded Sunday on the banks of the River Seine.

the same as it does in the museum today

Storms do more damage than long periods of calm.

Whoever claims to own something must also accept its troubles.

keep a record on the mill door

rc.q: Tamsin most likely made a chalk mark on the mill door each evening in order to

count the sacks she owed the lord

The storm happens because of the long summer calm.

rc.q: Which best describes the kind of writing in this passage?
rc.e: The story begins “Long ago,” takes place in an unnamed valley, has a clever hero who outwits a greedy lord, and ends by telling what people there still do “to this day,” all marks of a folktale.

y.B: A biography tells the true life of a real person; Tamsin and the lord are characters in a tale set “long ago” in an unnamed valley (line 1).
y.C: A news report tells real, recent events with dates and places; this story happens “long ago” and ends with a custom that lasts “to this day” (line 37).

RC-SEP-W1-S1-P.x: A vacant city lot had collected litter for years. When neighbors proposed a community garden, some residents doubted that vegetables could grow beside tall buildings. Volunteers tested the soil, built raised beds, and placed barrels beneath roof drains to collect rainwater. By midsummer, tomatoes climbed wooden supports and bees visited bright flowers. The garden produced food, but its larger success was social: people who had barely nodded to one another began trading recipes, sharing tools, and planning Saturday lessons for children. The lot had not simply become greener. It had become a place where neighbors had a reason to work together.

RC-SEP-W1-S2-P.x: Before radio, ships relied on flags, bells, lamps, and careful observation. A flag could communicate a standard message during daylight, while lamps extended signaling into darkness. Fog, heavy rain, and long distances could still interrupt communication. To reduce confusion, crews learned codes in which a small pattern of colors or flashes carried a particular meaning. A captain who saw a certain lamp pattern did not need to guess; both ships had agreed in advance on what the pattern meant. Modern satellite communication is much faster, yet it depends on the same basic rule: a sender and a receiver must share a system for turning signals into information.

RC-SEP-W2-S1-P.x: An owl approaching prey makes remarkably little noise. The leading edges of its wing feathers have soft fringes that break moving air into smaller currents. A velvety surface absorbs some sound as the wings move. Quiet flight gives the owl two advantages: it can hear faint rustling below, and its prey receives less warning. This adaptation has a tradeoff. The specialized feathers help the owl move silently, but they are not designed for the high-speed flight of a falcon. In nature, a feature that is helpful in one situation may limit an animal in another.

RC-SEP-W2-S2-P.x: A map may look like a finished picture of a place, but it represents many choices. Cartographers decide what to include, what to simplify, and how to show a curved Earth on a flat surface. Every projection changes something: shape, area, distance, or direction. That fact does not make maps useless. It means that a useful map depends on its purpose. A subway map may bend a route or leave out streets so passengers can follow stations easily. A navigation chart, in contrast, gives careful attention to position, water depth, and hazards. Readers should not ask whether a map is perfectly exact in every way; they should ask whether it helps them do the job for which it was made.

RC-SEP-W3-S1-P.x: After a storm damaged the town library, volunteers moved wet books into a dry school gym. They separated pages with absorbent paper, labeled boxes, and recorded each title before deciding what could be saved. Some books were too damaged to return, but the inventory helped the library identify essential works to replace. Months later, the repaired building had higher shelves and waterproof storage bins. The library's director called these changes “memory with a purpose.” The phrase meant that the town had not forgotten the storm; it had used what it learned to prepare for future trouble. Recovery, the passage suggests, is more than restoring what was lost. It can also mean building a wiser version of what remains.

RC-SEP-W3-S2-P.x: Mara expected her model bridge to hold ten kilograms, but it bent under six. Instead of hiding the result, she measured where the supports had shifted and compared the two sides. One joint had been glued at a slight angle. Mara changed that joint and tested a second bridge. It held eleven kilograms. Her first trial did not prove that her idea was useless; it revealed which part of the design needed attention. By treating an unexpected result as information, Mara turned a disappointment into a better experiment.

RC-SEP-W4-S1-P.x: Some desert plants complete most of their life cycle soon after rain. Their seeds may remain dormant for months or years beneath dry soil. Tough outer coats help protect the seeds and prevent them from sprouting after only a trace of moisture. When a substantial storm soaks the ground, the seeds germinate quickly. Leaves and flowers appear, and new seeds form before the soil dries again. This schedule may seem like waiting, but it is an active survival strategy shaped by an unpredictable environment. A seed that sprouted after every small drizzle would risk using its stored energy before conditions could support a full plant.

RC-SEP-W4-S2-P.x: The student council considered moving lunch twenty minutes later. Athletes supported the change because early practice often made them hungry before noon. Music students worried that the new schedule would shorten rehearsal. Rather than vote immediately, the council collected attendance data, interviewed teachers, and tested the proposed schedule for one week. The trial showed that cafeteria lines stayed manageable, but several music groups lost needed setup time. The council then adjusted the plan by moving one rehearsal period on two days. The process did not erase disagreement. It did, however, replace guesses with evidence and led to a compromise that addressed more than one group's concern.

RC-SEP-W1-S3-P.x: A canal that climbs a hill sounds impossible, since water will not flow uphill. A lock solves the problem without lifting the boat at all. The boat enters a walled chamber, and heavy gates close behind it. Valves then open, and water from the higher stretch of canal runs downhill into the chamber. As the water rises, the floating boat rises with it. When the level inside matches the level ahead, the forward gates open and the boat goes on its way. Gravity does the lifting, so most locks need no pump to do it. The chamber does not raise the boat. It raises the water, and lets the boat do what a boat already does.

RC-SEP-W1-S4-P.x: Bread dough rises because something inside it is alive. Yeast is a tiny fungus, and when it is mixed with flour and water it feeds on sugars in the dough and releases carbon dioxide gas. Stretchy strands of protein form and grow stronger as the dough is kneaded, and they hold the bubbles in place, so the whole lump swells. Heat finishes the work. In a hot oven the trapped gas expands, and the dough puffs a little higher. Then the yeast stops working, and the structure hardens around the bubbles the yeast made. The holes in a slice of bread are not decoration. They are a record of what the yeast was doing.

RC-SEP-W2-S3-P.x: The third-grade class needed a photograph for the school newsletter, and Amara had offered to take it. Twenty-six children squeezed onto the front steps. She pressed the button and turned the little screen around: in the front row, four pairs of eyes were shut. The second try came out worse. Amara stood and thought about it while the back row grumbled. “Everybody close your eyes,” she said at last. “Open them when I say three.” Twenty-six faces went dark at once, like a street when the lights cut out. She counted slowly. The eyes came up together, and this time the camera caught every one of them open. It is the picture that hangs outside the office now.

RC-SEP-W2-S4-P.x: A zipper looks like two rows of teeth that hook together on their own, but they cannot. All the work belongs to the slider. Inside the slider, two narrow channels meet in a Y. Pulled one way, the slider guides the rows together at an angle, so the top of each tooth settles into the hollow beneath the tooth opposite it. Pulled the other way, the slider drives a wedge between the rows and pries the teeth apart. This explains a familiar annoyance. If the slider's channels spread even slightly, the teeth pass through without seating, and the zipper opens again behind it. The teeth are usually fine. What wears out is the small part that was doing everything.

RC-SEP-W3-S3-P.x: Outside on a cold morning, the skin of your arm rises into tiny bumps. Each bump sits where a hair grows, because a hair starts in a small pocket in the skin, and a tiny muscle is attached to that pocket. When you are cold, the muscle tightens, pulls the hair upright, and gathers the skin into a little mound. In a furry animal, a raised coat traps a thicker blanket of air, holding warmth in. Human hair is too short and too fine to hold much, so the bumps warm almost nothing. Almost nobody can raise them on purpose. Goosebumps are an old instruction the body still follows, carried out by muscles with almost nothing left to lift.

RC-SEP-W3-S4-P.x: Nina had taught herself to tie her shoes when she was five, certain she could teach Rafi in one afternoon. She sat beside him, on his left, the way she always sat, and went through it slowly: cross, tuck, pull. Rafi's hands went the other way every time and stalled halfway, like a word he could not finish. She was about to tell him he wasn't watching when she saw which hand was holding the lace. Rafi was left-handed. Nina was not. She got up and sat down facing him, so that everything she did reached him backward, which, for him, was forward. He copied it once, then twice, and then tied the other shoe while Nina only watched.

RC-SEP-W4-S3-P.x: A popcorn kernel is not hollow. Inside its hard shell sits a packet of starch with a small amount of water held within it. Heat turns that water to steam, but the shell holds the steam in, so pressure climbs inside the kernel while the starch softens into a hot, thick paste. The shell finally gives way all at once. The steam rushes out, the paste expands into a foam many times the kernel's size, and it sets in that shape almost instantly. This is why a kernel left too long on a shelf often refuses to pop. It has quietly lost its water, and the water was the whole engine.

RC-SEP-W4-S4-P.x: On a summer afternoon puffy clouds seem to rest on the same invisible shelf. Warm air near the ground rises, and as it climbs into thinner air it spreads out and cools. That air carries invisible water vapor, and cooling lowers how much can stay in vapor form. At one height the air has cooled to the temperature where some of the vapor condenses into droplets too small to fall quickly. That height is where a cloud begins. Parcels of air rising from the same warm ground begin alike and cool at the same rate, so each reaches that temperature at nearly the same height. The tops may heap and tumble, but the bottoms were all drawn by one rule.

RC-W5-S1-P.t: The Pools the Tide Leaves Behind
RC-W5-S1-P.x:
Twice a day the ocean pulls back from a rocky shore and leaves behind dozens of shallow pools. From a distance the pools look peaceful, like small aquariums set into stone. For the animals inside them, though, the next six hours are the hardest of the day. Sunlight warms the trapped water until it is far warmer than the sea. Some of that water evaporates, and the salt left behind grows more concentrated. A sudden rainstorm can do the opposite, thinning the water until it is almost fresh. Nothing in the open ocean changes that quickly.

The animals that live there meet these swings with equipment, not luck. As the tide drops, a barnacle closes its hard plates and traps a small reserve of seawater inside, enough to keep its body damp until the ocean comes back. A limpet wears a shallow groove into the rock over months of feeding, and it travels back to that exact groove before the water leaves, because its shell fits the worn stone tightly. When the sun is high, sea stars slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach.

It would be a mistake to picture a tide pool as a gentler ocean, a nursery for creatures too delicate for deep water. A fish carried in from twenty meters down would not last an afternoon in one. The pool is the harsher place, and the animals crowded into it are not the leftovers of the sea. They are specialists in a kind of hardship most ocean animals never have to face.

RC-W5-S2-P.x:
In the 1880s most American roads outside of towns were simply dirt. Wagon wheels cut deep ruts into them, and a week of rain could turn a stretch of road into mud deep enough to swallow a boot. Farmers complained, but they had managed for a century, and their heavy wagons could grind through whatever the weather left behind.

Then came the bicycle. The new machines were light, quick, and almost useless on a rutted road. Riders formed clubs, and in the 1880s and 1890s those clubs mounted a campaign they called Good Roads. They printed pamphlets, mapped the worst stretches, and asked state legislatures for money to build smooth surfaces. Many farmers resisted. Paving, they argued, would be paid for with everyone's taxes so that city sportsmen could enjoy a pleasant Sunday ride.

The argument changed when the mail changed. The Post Office began carrying letters directly to farmhouses instead of making families travel to town for them, and it would only serve routes a mail wagon could travel all year. Suddenly a good road was not a luxury for visitors. It was the difference between getting the mail and not getting it, and counties that had refused to spend a dollar began to build.

By the time automobiles were common, the surveys, the county road departments, and the habit of paying for highways out of public money were already in place. The drivers who sped along those smooth surfaces owed a debt to people who had been pedaling.

RC-W6-S1-P.x:
Theo had memorized the prices before the market opened. He wrote them on a card in his neatest handwriting, propped it against the scale, and when his grandmother left to find change he was almost glad. For two hours the stall was his to mind. He straightened the plums until every stem pointed the same way.

The trouble was the sour cherries. They sat in a flat crate at the end of the table, small and dark and beautiful, and nobody touched them. A woman in a yellow coat finally stopped and asked whether they were sweet. Theo began the sentence he had practiced. “They’re excellent for—” he said, and then he stopped, because he could hear how it sounded: like a boy repeating something.

He looked down. Under the table, where his grandmother had set it before she left, was a small bowl of the same cherries with a folded napkin beside it. He had assumed it was her lunch, though she never ate anything at the market. He lifted one out and held it toward the woman without saying anything at all.

She ate it. Her whole face pinched, and then she laughed, and then she bought two pints for a pie. After that Theo set the bowl on the table where people could reach it. He crossed out one line on his careful card and wrote underneath, in handwriting that was not nearly as neat, that the cherries were too sour to eat and perfect for baking. By four o’clock the crate was empty, and the plums, arranged so beautifully, were not.

RC-W6-S2-P.t: Buildings That Are Meant to Move
RC-W6-S2-P.x:
A person standing on the top floor of a very tall building on a windy day may feel the floor lean, pause, and lean back. The movement is small, a few centimeters at most, but it is real, and it is not a flaw. Engineers planned it.

A tower could be built so stiff that it barely moved, but stiffness carries a hidden cost. Wind pressing on a rigid wall has nowhere to send its force, so the material itself must absorb all of it. Over years of storms, something inside that material will crack. A steel frame designed with a measured amount of give behaves differently. It bends a little, sheds the energy of the gust, and returns to where it started, the way a tall tree does in an open field.

The harder problem is not the leaning but the lingering. A building that keeps swaying long after the wind has died feels alarming to the people inside it, even when it is perfectly safe. Some towers answer this with a damper: an enormous weight, sometimes hundreds of tons, hung high in the building on cables or resting on a slick steel surface. Because such a weight is slow to start moving, it always lags a little behind the floors. It pulls backward while they swing forward, and the sway fades in seconds instead of minutes.

In a wind tunnel, engineers do not test a model to learn whether it will move. They already know it will. They measure how quickly it stops.

RC-W7-S1-P.t: The Case for the Repair Bench
RC-W7-S1-P.x:
Every school in our district teaches students to build something — a birdhouse in third grade, a model bridge in fifth. Almost none teaches students to fix something. I believe that is backwards, and that every school should set aside one bench, one box of tools, and one period a week for repair.

Start with the objection I hear most often: repairing is slower than replacing, and school hours are precious. That is true, and I will not pretend otherwise. But the objection mistakes what the period is for. The point of the hour is not to save the school money on chairs; it is to teach a habit of looking. A student handed a wobbling chair must decide, before touching a single tool, which part has actually failed. A chair with one loose leg is still sound in every other part, and noticing that is the whole lesson.

Consider Fenwick Middle School, which began a Thursday repair table two years ago. In its first term the table brought back forty-one items: eleven lamps, nine backpacks, six umbrellas, and fifteen library books with broken spines. The number worth watching, though, is not forty-one. It is four — the four students who joined in September and were still at the table in June, showing newcomers how to seat a screw.

Machines will keep getting harder to open, and some objects truly cannot be mended. That does not weaken the case; it sharpens it. The fewer things we are able to repair, the more it matters that we can tell which ones we can.

RC-W7-S2-P.t: The Kite That Crossed the Gorge
RC-W7-S2-P.x:
In the winter of 1848 the Niagara Gorge was a problem nobody had solved. Engineers wanted to hang a bridge across it, but the river below ran too fast and too crowded with ice for a boat to carry anything over. The rocky walls stood eight hundred feet apart. Before a bridge could be built, one thin thread had to reach the far side. So the engineer in charge announced a five-dollar prize. Whoever could fly a kite across the gorge and tie his string down on the opposite rim would win it.

Homan Walsh, a boy of about fifteen who lived nearby, understood something the adults seem to have overlooked. The wind in the gorge blew steadily from the Canadian side toward the American side. A kite launched from the American rim would be carried away from the crossing rather than across it. Homan took a ferry to the Canadian side and waited for a January evening when the wind held. He let his kite, which he had named Union, climb until his line lay across the whole gorge.

Then the line snapped on the ice below and the kite came down on the far bank. Ice choked the river for eight days, so he could not cross to fetch it. When the river cleared at last, Homan found the kite, mended it, and flew it again. This time the string held.

That string could not have held anything heavier than itself. But workers tied it to a stronger cord. They tied the cord to a rope, and the rope to a wire cable — until a bridge stood where a boy's kite string had gone first.

RC-W8-S1-P.x:
At five in the morning the lake lay like a sheet of hammered tin, gray and perfectly still, and Nadia was certain she could beat it. Her grandmother sat in the stern with her hands folded, saying nothing, which was her way of teaching. Nadia took the oars, leaned back with all her weight, and pulled.

The boat barely moved. The blades slapped the surface and threw up a spray that soaked her knees, and the oars quarreled with the water, arguing over every stroke. Twice the handles jumped out of her grip. A heron on the shore watched her the way a teacher watches a student who has not read the assignment, then lifted away without hurrying. Nadia's shoulders burned. The far bank looked no closer than it had ten minutes before.

“Stop rowing,” her grandmother said. “Put the blade in first. Let it bite. Then pull.” Nadia let the oars rest until the boat went quiet. She lowered one blade and felt the water take hold of it, a firm and surprising grip, like a hand closing around the wood, and she pulled slowly. The boat slid forward without a sound. She did it again, and the ripples spread behind her in long, even rings. Nothing about the second stroke was harder than the first. It was, if anything, easier.

By the time the sun cleared the trees the mist had let go of the shore and Nadia had crossed half the lake. She was not stronger than she had been an hour before. She had simply stopped fighting the thing she was trying to move.

RC-W8-S2-P.x:
When a winter storm is forecast, city trucks spread salt on the roads before the first flakes fall. The salt is not there only to melt ice that has already formed, though it can do that. It is there to keep a thin film of water from freezing onto the pavement in the first place. Water turns to ice by locking together in an orderly pattern, and dissolved salt particles get in the way of that pattern. What forms instead is a solution that stays liquid at temperatures far below the point at which plain water would harden.

There is a limit. Plain water freezes at thirty-two degrees Fahrenheit, and salted water can stay liquid down to roughly six degrees below zero. Colder than that, the salt lying on the road is simply cold grit. This is why crews in the coldest places often spread sand instead. Sand cannot lower a freezing point at all; it only gives tires something to grip.

Salt does not disappear when the snow does, either. Meltwater carries it off the pavement into soil, streams, and wells, where it can injure roadside trees and change the water that fish live in. One winter of salt does little harm by itself. Thirty winters of it on the same road is a different matter.

For that reason many crews now mix a brine before a storm and spray a thin coat on the pavement, which uses far less salt than scattering dry crystals that bounce into the ditch. The chemistry has not changed. What has changed is how carefully it is spent.

RC-W5-S3-P.t: The Feather With No Blue in It
RC-W5-S3-P.x:
A blue jay's feather lying in the grass looks like nothing much. Held up to the sun, it burns a clean, hard blue. Ground into powder, though, that same feather loses its blue completely. What is left in the palm is dull brown dust. Nothing leaked out and nothing was washed away. The blue was never a substance in the feather at all.

Inside each of the feather's thin branches lies a layer of keratin, the material fingernails are made of, riddled with air pockets too small to see. The pockets are spaced so that they scatter blue light back toward the eye, while red and yellow light, whose waves are longer, travels deeper into the feather. Deeper in, a layer of dark pigment swallows it. What comes back is blue, and it comes back only because those pockets sit where they do. The color lasts only as long as the arrangement does.

A cardinal's red works the other way. Red feathers carry a real pigment, built by the bird from what it eats, and a pigment is a thing you can hold. Ground to powder, a red feather leaves red dust in the palm. There is a second test, gentler than the first. Lit from behind, so that light passes through it, the red feather stays red. The jay's feather lit the same way turns brown, because its blue depends on light bouncing back off a structure rather than passing through a substance.

A soap bubble makes color out of structure too, with no pigment in it at all. The jay does not carry its blue. It makes it, every time the light arrives.

RC-W5-S4-P.x:
Cut across an old oak and you will find rings, one inside the next, and someone will tell you to count them for its age. That is true as far as it goes. It is also the least interesting thing they can tell you.

Where there is a clear growing season, a tree adds a layer of wood beneath its bark each year. Its spring wood is pale and full of open pores; the wood at season's end is darker and denser. The ring you see is the line where one year's dark wood stops and next spring's pale wood begins. A wet, mild year usually leaves a wide ring; a dry, hard year a narrow one. Read in order, the rings are a row of entries, one for every year the tree stood.

Trees in one region live through the same weather, so their patterns of wide and narrow bands run in step. That agreement makes the rings useful far from the tree that grew them. A living tree's outermost ring is this year's, so its rings can be dated. A beam from an old roof carries a pattern of its own, and a researcher slides it along that record until the wide and narrow years line up. The beam is dated, though nobody wrote a date on it.

The limits are the ordinary kind. A tree where it is warm and wet all year may lay down no clear band. Even a tree that normally does can skip a hard year, or lay down two bands in one. So no single trunk is trusted alone; patterns are checked against many trees before a band is called a year.

RC-W6-S3-P.x:
A family that wanted cold lemonade in July once depended on work done in January. When the ice on a pond would hold a horse and a loaded sled, crews went out with saws, cut the ice into heavy squares, and hauled the blocks to a windowless building called an icehouse. Some of that ice was still solid in August.

An icehouse made no cold of its own. It was built to slow heat down, and nothing else. Its walls were doubled and the gap between them packed with sawdust. Its door was small and kept shut. Some were dug into a shaded hillside so the sun rarely struck the walls. Sawdust is not cold. It is simply a poor path for heat, and heat that cannot get in cannot melt anything.

The shape of the stack mattered too. Ice melts at its surface, so the amount of exposed surface sets the pace. A single large block has less surface, for the amount of ice in it, than the same ice chopped into pieces. Workers therefore cut the blocks large, stacked them tight, and filled the seams so little was left in the open. The floor was sloped, because meltwater standing against the pile would carry heat into it faster than still air could.

Ships carried blocks cut from northern ponds to harbors in hot countries. Some of every load melted on the way, and the traders expected it. Nobody believed the melting had been stopped. It had only been slowed enough for the ice to arrive. An icehouse was never a machine for making cold. It was a machine for making winter last.

RC-W6-S4-P.x:
Ines had agreed to run the photographs for her aunt's talk because it sounded like the easiest job in the hall. You sat at a small table. You pressed a button. Nobody looked at you.

She understood her mistake about four minutes in.

Rosa did not stop between pictures. Each photograph had to arrive on the sentence that needed it. Ines had planned to listen for the words just before each change; by the time she heard them, they had gone past.

Rosa kept a finger under the line she was reading. Ines had the same pages on her knee, so a place on Rosa's copy was a place on hers. The typed words meant almost nothing to her, but the shapes did: black clusters where the paragraphs were busy, white space where they thinned out. She found the next red slash her aunt had drawn, counted back two lines, and put her thumb there. When Rosa's finger reached the spot her thumb held, Ines got ready. When it reached the slash, she pressed.

The photograph arrived on the word it belonged to. Rosa did not glance over, which Ines decided was the highest compliment available.

She stopped following the talk the way the room did. She watched the way a person crossing a street watches, ahead of herself, two lines early, her thumb already where she would need it next. Twice her copy tried to curl shut, and twice she flattened it without looking down.

At the end the room clapped and Rosa gathered her pages. Ines folded her own copy in half. Her thumb had pressed a crease down the middle of it, and her hand ached.

RC-W7-S3-P.t: The Stick That Was Never Carved
RC-W7-S3-P.x:
Nothing inside a pencil is lead. The gray core is graphite, a soft form of carbon, and the name is left over from a time when people took it for a kind of lead.

Graphite on its own is too crumbly to hold a fine point. So it is ground to powder and mixed with water and clay, which binds it into a smooth paste. The paste is squeezed through a small round opening, the way toothpaste leaves a tube, and the strand that emerges is cut into lengths, dried, and fired in a kiln. The baked cores still drag a little, so they are soaked in warm wax, which is why a pencil slides instead of scratching.

The clay does a second job. More clay bakes into a harder core that leaves a fainter line; more graphite makes a softer, darker core that wears away quickly. The grade mark stamped near the end of a pencil — HB, 2B, 4H — is simply a report of that mixture.

The wood is the surprising part. You might expect a hole to be drilled down the middle of a finished stick, but a drill that long will wander, and a core sitting off center would snap at the first sharpening. So the pencil is built open instead. Two flat boards of soft, straight-grained cedar are sawn, and shallow grooves are cut along each. The cores are laid into the grooves of the lower board, glue is spread, and the second board is pressed on top. Only then is the sandwich cut apart into pencils and shaped round or six-sided.

The stick in your hand was never carved. It was closed.

RC-W7-S4-P.x:
Dalia had watched her cousin Neel juggle at the bus stop the way people watch weather — as something that happened, not something a person did. On Tuesday he handed her three beanbags and said to start with one.

One was easy. She tossed it from her right hand into her left, which was already waiting. Neel made her do it forty times, then forty the other way.

Two bags were the trouble. Dalia threw the first, watched it up, then moved the second across into her empty hand like someone passing a note. Neel called that handing, not throwing. They practiced in his room, over the bed, because bending to pick things off a carpet is how people quit.

On Thursday Neel explained nothing. He threw one bag, threw the second when the first was at the top, and stood with his hands open while both landed on the quilt. “Like that,” he said. “Sixty times.”

It felt like being told to fail. Dalia threw, threw, and stood with her hands open while two beanbags thumped onto the quilt. Sixty times. Somewhere in all that throwing, the second throw stopped being a decision and became something her hand did while she watched the first. By the end her hands had begun closing on the bags again.

On Saturday Neel put a third bag in her hand and told her nothing new. There was nothing new to tell. Up went the first, the second, the third, and for eleven throws the pattern hung in the air like something she was reading rather than making. Then it came apart. She laughed. She did not count the drop. She counted the eleven.

RC-W8-S3-P.t: The Face That Never Turns Away
RC-W8-S3-P.x:
Look up at the Moon tonight, and again next month, and the same dark patches stare back. It is tempting to decide the Moon does not spin at all. The truth is the reverse. A moon that never turned would show us every side of itself during one trip around Earth. To keep one face pointed at us, the Moon must turn once on its axis each lap, and it does, in a little over twenty-seven days.

Try it with a chair. Walk a full circle around it, keeping your eyes on it. The chair sees only your front, but you have faced every wall in the room. You turned once.

The cause is gravity and time. Earth pulls a little harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, drawing its rock into a faint bulge. Long ago the Moon spun faster, and each rotation dragged that bulge out of line. The flexing worked like a brake. The turning never stopped; it slowed until the bulge pointed at Earth and stayed there.

People call the hidden half the dark side, which is wrong twice over. It gets as much sunlight as the half we know; when the Moon looks full to us, the far side is in night. Nor is it perfectly hidden. The Moon's orbit is not a true circle, so the Moon hurries and lags while its spin holds steady. It appears to rock, tipping a thin strip of the far side into view. Patient observers charted a little more than half that way. The rest stayed unseen until 1959, when a spacecraft flew behind it and sent back the first pictures.

RC-W8-S4-P.t: Who Gets to Climb Hill Street
RC-W8-S4-P.x:
Hill Street earns its name. The grade is gentle at the park gate and steep by the grocery at the top. Four years ago the last two benches were taken out, and we are asking the town to put benches back, spaced so that nobody climbs a whole block without somewhere to stop. The town's answer last time was a wider sidewalk.

Here is what a bench does that a wider sidewalk cannot. Our neighbor Ruth is eighty-one and has shopped on foot for fifty years. She can climb Hill Street in three stages; she cannot climb it in one. While the bench outside the bakery stood there, she walked up on Tuesdays and carried her shopping down. Now the groceries come by car, and Tuesday is no longer hers.

Now the objection, and it is a real one: a bench is not free. Somebody has to wash it, clear the snow off it in February, and repaint it when the paint lifts. A bench is a small building the town agrees to look after, and benches nobody looks after splinter before long. There is room on Hill Street for twelve. We are asking for six, with the washing and the painting written into the same budget that pays for the benches. The upkeep is part of the proposal, not an afterthought.

A sidewalk you cannot stop on is a corridor. A sidewalk with benches is a room, and people stay in rooms: a child sits to tie a shoelace, two neighbors talk longer than they meant to. None of that will make Hill Street less steep. It will decide who gets to climb it.

RC-W5-XP1.x:
A honeybee that discovers a plentiful patch of flowers
faces a problem. She cannot draw a map, and she has no
way to point. Yet soon after she returns to the hive,
other bees are flying directly toward the flowers. She
has given them directions by dancing.

The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent years
decoding these dances, work that earned him a Nobel
Prize in 1973. He found that when food is very close to
the hive, a bee performs a round dance. She runs in
small circles, suddenly reversing direction. This dance
tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not which
way to fly.

For flowers farther away, a bee performs the waggle
dance on the upright comb inside the dark hive. She runs
straight ahead a short way, waggling as she goes, then
circles back to where she began. She repeats the
straight run and circles back on the opposite side, so
her path traces a figure eight.

The straight run carries the directions. Because the
comb stands upright, the dancer lets straight up stand
for the direction of the sun. If the flowers lie toward
the sun, her straight run points straight up. If they
lie directly away from the sun, it points straight down.
Flowers to the left or right of the sun are shown by a
run tilted the same amount to the left or right.

The waggling itself reports the distance. The farther
away the flowers are, the longer each waggle run lasts.
A run of about two and a half seconds sends the bees to
flowers more than a mile and a half away.

In the darkness, other bees crowd close to the dancer
and follow her movements before they fly out. Later in
the day, a bee dancing for the same flowers changes the
angle of her run, because the sun has moved across the
sky. The flowers stay where they are, but the dance
turns to keep up with the sun.

RC-W5-XP2.x:
Wilson Bentley was born in 1865 on a farm in Jericho,
Vermont. His mother, who had once been a teacher,
educated him at home, and when he was fifteen she gave
him an old microscope. It was snowing that day, and his
first look at a snowflake through the lens began a
fascination that never left him.

Under the microscope, an ordinary snowflake turned out
to be a tiny crystal full of intricate detail. Wilson
tried to draw what he observed, and by his seventeenth
birthday he had made several hundred sketches. But snow
crystals do not last long, even in freezing air. At
seventeen, he asked his parents for a camera.

His father considered fussing with snowflakes a waste of
time. Nevertheless, the camera was purchased, and Wilson
attached it to his microscope. For about two years his
photographs failed. Then, on January 15, 1885, a few
weeks before his twentieth birthday, he succeeded in
making the first photograph of a single snow crystal.

His method required patience. He caught falling snow on
a tray painted black, and, working quickly, he lifted a
single crystal with a thin straw from a broom and nudged
it into position with a feather. He was careful never to
breathe on it, because his warm breath could melt it.

For the rest of his life he continued this work. He
photographed more than 5,000 snow crystals and never
found two that were identical. He also photographed
frost and dew and measured the sizes of raindrops. In
1925 he described snowflakes under the microscope as
"miracles of beauty."

In November 1931, a book of his work called Snow
Crystals was published, containing more than two
thousand of his photographs. Soon afterward, Bentley
walked six miles home through a snowstorm and became ill
with pneumonia. He died on December 23, 1931, at the age
of sixty-six. His book is still in print, and people
still call him "Snowflake" Bentley.

RC-W5-XP3.x:
When the cast list for the fourth-grade play appeared on
the classroom door, Otis read it twice to be certain.
Priya would play the queen, and Nico would play the
woodcutter. Otis would play Tree, not Ancient Tree or
Wise Old Tree, but simply Tree. His part had no lines at
all, which meant he would stand at the edge of the stage
with his arms raised from the first scene to the last,
saying absolutely nothing.

During rehearsals, the others practiced their speeches
while Otis stood with his arms in the air. With nothing
else to do, he listened to everyone. He heard Priya
rehearse the queen's long speech until it was perfect,
and he heard Nico forget the same line every afternoon:
"The crown is at the bottom of the well." Each time, Ms.
Pruitt prompted him from the front row. By the third
week, Otis could have recited every line in the entire
play, although nobody had asked him to.

On the night of the performance, the gym was crowded
with relatives and neighbors, and Ms. Pruitt was at the
back, operating the lights. In the third scene, Nico
stepped to the center of the stage, opened his mouth,
and nothing came out. The silence stretched like a
rubber band about to snap. Somebody in the audience
coughed, and Nico stared at the floor as though the
words might be printed there.

Trees do not move, so Otis remained perfectly still. A
tree, he decided, might whisper, however, so he breathed
the missing line without moving his lips. Nico's eyes
flicked toward him. A moment later, Nico announced that
the crown was at the bottom of the well, and the
performance continued as if nothing unusual had
happened.

Afterward, families surrounded the queen and the
woodcutter. At the cast party, Ms. Pruitt announced that
the tree had played the most important part in the
entire performance. Otis was fairly sure she was joking,
but he was not completely sure.

RC-W5-XP4.x:
Every Saturday at ten o'clock, a large gray dog named
Oatmeal settles onto a blanket in the children's room of
the public library. One at a time, children sit beside
him and read aloud from a book they have chosen. Oatmeal
listens patiently, and now and then he rests his chin on
a reader's sneaker.

Oatmeal is a registered therapy dog, and his owner, Pam,
sits nearby during every visit. Each reader receives
fifteen minutes. Some children bring picture books,
while others arrive with chapter books and a bookmark
already halfway through.

Why would anyone read to a dog? Reading aloud can be
difficult for children who are still learning, and many
of them feel nervous when an adult or a classmate is
listening. A dog does not interrupt. It never corrects a
mistake or laughs when a word comes out wrong. Paloma,
who is eight, puts it more simply: "He never says,
'Sound it out.'"

The idea is not new. In 1999, the public library in Salt
Lake City, Utah, held a program called "Dog Day
Afternoons," in which children read to therapy dogs, and
more than one hundred children attended. Since then,
libraries across the country have started similar
programs.

Pam has a technique of her own. When a reader reaches a
difficult word, Pam sometimes says, "I don't think
Oatmeal knows that one. Could you explain it to him?" At
that moment, the child, and not the adult, becomes the
teacher.

At a quarter past ten, Paloma closed her book, and
Oatmeal thumped his tail twice against the floor. Before
she left the library, Paloma signed up for the following
Saturday.

RC-W6-XP1.x:
A flash brightens the sky, and you begin counting: one,
two, three, four. Somewhere past fifteen, the thunder
finally arrives as a long, low rumble. Without realizing
it, you have just measured how far away the lightning
was.

Thunder is the sound that lightning produces. A bolt of
lightning heats the air along its path almost instantly,
