to temperatures as high as 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit,
which is about five times hotter than the surface of the
sun. The heated air expands suddenly, then cools and
squeezes back together. That rapid push and pull sends
out the sound wave we hear as thunder.

The flash and the sound begin together, but they do not
travel at the same speed. Light reaches your eyes almost
immediately, while sound moves much more slowly: thunder
takes about five seconds to travel one mile. To estimate
how far away the lightning struck, count the seconds
between the flash and the thunder, and then divide by
five. Fifteen seconds means the lightning was about
three miles away.

The sound itself contains clues. A sharp crack or click
usually means that the lightning passed close by, while
a rumble means that it was at least several miles away.

One more number is worth remembering. Thunder can
usually be heard only about ten miles from the place
where the lightning struck. Therefore, if you can hear
thunder at all, you are probably close enough to be
struck by the next flash. The count tells you where the
last bolt landed; it cannot promise anything about the
next one.

RC-W6-XP2.x:
Before 1883, Americans could not agree on what time it
was. Each town set its clocks by the sun, calling it
noon at the moment the sun reached its highest point in
the sky. Because the sun does not reach that point
everywhere at once, one town's noon came a few minutes
earlier or later than the next town's.

The differences were real. When it was noon by the sun
in Chicago, it was 11:50 in St. Louis, Missouri, and
only 11:27 in Omaha, Nebraska. In Indianapolis, Indiana,
it was already 12:07. For people who stayed in one town,
the differences hardly mattered, because everyone nearby
followed the same clock.

Railroads changed that. A train traveling east or west
passed through town after town, each keeping its own
time. The railroad companies kept separate times as
well, and by the early 1880s there were dozens of them.
Timetables were confusing, and a traveler's watch might
disagree with the clock at almost every station.

Eventually the railroads made a plan of their own. At
noon on November 18, 1883, they began using four time
zones across the country: Eastern, Central, Mountain,
and Pacific. Every clock inside a zone would show the
same time, and each zone was one hour apart from the
next.

In several cities, the clocks struck noon twice that
day, once by the old local time and once by the new
standard time, so people called it the Day of Two Noons.
Most cities adopted the new time immediately, and many
more switched within a year.

The railroads, not the government, had made the change.
Congress did not make standard time the law until 1918,
and by then much of the country had been living on
railroad time for thirty-five years.

RC-W6-XP3.x:
A steel pan looks like the bottom of an old barrel with
a few dents in it. In a way, that is exactly what it is.
Yet when a player strikes it with rubber-tipped sticks,
it rings with clear musical notes.

The steel pan developed in Trinidad and Tobago during
the 1930s and 1940s, and its story begins with a ban. In
the 1880s, drumming was banned at Carnival. Musicians
beat bamboo sticks together instead, in what came to be
called tamboo bamboo bands. Those bands were banned in
turn. By the mid-1930s, players were also striking
metal: frying pans, trash can lids, cookie tins, and
paint cans.

Players discovered that a dented tin could ring with its
own particular note. A raised part of the metal also
sounded different from a flat part. Young musicians
began experimenting with discarded oil drums, and they
learned to pound many notes into the bottom of a single
drum.

Making a pan is loud, careful work. First, the maker
pounds the bottom of the drum with a heavy hammer until
it sinks into a deep bowl. Next, the notes are marked
out and shaped in the bowl. The side of the drum, called
the skirt, is cut to a length that depends on the kind
of pan. The metal is then heated over a fire. Last comes
the tuning, as the maker carefully taps each note with a
hammer until it sounds exactly right. The maker does not
add music to the drum; the music is hammered out of the
metal itself.

The size of each note decides its sound: the larger the
oval of metal, the lower the note. A bass pan may use a
whole drum for only three low notes, so one bass player
may play six drums.

Today the steel pan is the national instrument of
Trinidad and Tobago. In 2023, the United Nations named
August 11 World Steelpan Day. That is quite a career for
a barrel that somebody once threw away.

RC-W6-XP4.t: Why the Mockingbird Sings Every Song
RC-W6-XP4.x:
Long ago, only one bird could sing. Every morning the
mockingbird sang from the top of the tallest pine, and
her melody was so long that it lasted until noon. It had
a section for rain, a section for wind, and many more.
The other birds could only chirp, and they listened
admiringly from the branches below.

One morning the owl flew up beside her. "Your song is
too long for one bird," said the owl. "Could you spare a
small piece of it for me? The nights are terribly
quiet." The mockingbird was proud of her melody, but she
was also generous. She gave the owl a slow, low section
that sounded like wind in an empty barn, and the owl
carried it into the night.

The next day the oriole arrived, hoping for something
bright for the treetops, and the day after that the
nuthatch appeared, wanting only something short and
quick. All spring the birds kept coming, and the
mockingbird never sent anyone away.

Then one morning she opened her beak to sing, and
nothing came out, because she had given away the final
piece without noticing. Her heart sank. She did not
blame the other birds, since every piece had been hers
to give. Still, the top of the pine felt dreadfully
quiet, and she sat there all day with her head tucked
low.

That evening the owl began calling in the woods, the
oriole answered from the treetops, and the nuthatch
chattered from a branch. The mockingbird listened, and
slowly she lifted her head. She recognized every one of
those melodies, because she had created them. So she
sang the owl's song back, then the oriole's, then the
nuthatch's, repeating each one to be sure she had it
right.

That is why, to this day, the mockingbird imitates the
songs of many other birds, repeating each one several
times. It is also why she occasionally sings on moonlit
nights: she is still keeping track of every song she
gave away.

RC-W7-XP1.x:
Alaska is home to three kinds of frogs and toads, and
two of them spend the winter hiding from the ice. The
western toad spends the winter in a burrow below the
frost line, where the soil does not freeze. The Columbia
spotted frog buries itself in the mud at the bottom of a
pond that is too deep to freeze solid. The wood frog
does something stranger. In the fall, it settles into a
shallow hollow on the forest floor, beneath a blanket of
fallen leaves, and waits for the cold to find it.

The cold always does. The wood frog is North America's
only amphibian north of the Arctic Circle, where winter
temperatures of fifty degrees below zero are not
unusual. A layer of snow on top of the leaves adds extra
protection. Still, as the first ice forms in the frog's
toes and eyes, its liver begins to produce large amounts
of glucose, a kind of sugar. The sugar travels through
the frog's blood into every cell in its body.

Within a few hours, ice fills the frog's belly and wraps
around its organs. Flat crystals of ice spread between
its skin and its muscles, and its eyes turn white.
Nearly seventy percent of the water in its body becomes
ice. Its heart stops beating, and it stops breathing.
Inside each cell, though, the thick, syrupy sugar keeps
the water from freezing, and the cell survives. The frog
can remain frozen solid this way for as long as eight
months.

In the spring, the frog thaws from the inside out. First
its heart starts beating again. Then its brain wakes up,
and finally its legs begin to move. Within hours, the
males are hopping toward shallow ponds and calling to
the females with a sound like ducks quacking.

RC-W7-XP2.t: The Fastest Woman in the World
RC-W7-XP2.x:
When Wilma Rudolph was a little girl in Tennessee in the
1940s, few people would have guessed that she would one
day race in the Olympics. She was the twentieth of
twenty-two children, and she was sick much of the time.
She survived pneumonia, scarlet fever, and polio, a
disease that can leave a person's arms or legs weak or
unable to move. She lost the use of her left leg and was
given a metal brace to wear.

Her family refused to give up on that leg. Again and
again, they took off the brace and rubbed the weak leg
to help it heal. Slowly it grew stronger. By the time
she reached high school, Wilma had left the brace far
behind and had become a star on her school's basketball
team.

In 1955, a college track coach named Ed Temple came to
Clarksville to referee a basketball game. He saw the
skinny fourteen-year-old play and invited her to his
summer camp. The next year, at sixteen, she was the
youngest member of the United States track team at the
Olympics in Australia. She came home with a bronze medal
from a relay race.

Four years later, at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, Italy,
she won gold medals in the 100-meter dash, the 200-meter
dash, and a relay race. No American woman had ever won
three gold medals in track and field at a single
Olympics. Soon she was being called the fastest woman in
the world.

Her hometown of Clarksville planned to welcome her back,
but it planned two separate celebrations, one for its
white residents and one for its Black residents. Rudolph
refused to take part. Because she insisted, the town
held one parade for everyone. It was the first event in
Clarksville's history that was open to Black and white
residents together.

RC-W7-XP3.x:
On her third day at her grandfather's house, Raina
decided to organize his bookshelf. It stretched along
the entire hallway, and it was a mess. Thin paperbacks
leaned against enormous atlases, a cookbook was wedged
between two mysteries, and a bird guide lay sideways
across a row of history books.

While Grandpa was at the hardware store, Raina carried
every book into the living room. She arranged them
alphabetically by the authors' last names, exactly the
way the school librarian did, and returned them to the
shelf one at a time. When she finished, the shelf looked
as orderly as a row of piano keys, and she sat down to
wait.

Grandpa came in whistling, set down his paper bag,
noticed the shelf, and stopped whistling. For a long
moment he said nothing at all. Then he slowly ran one
finger along the spines, the way a person might trace a
map of a town he used to live in.

"Where's the summer we drove to the lake?" he asked
quietly.

Raina did not understand, so he showed her. He located
the bird guide near the beginning of the shelf, the
cookbook near the end, and a paperback with a cracked
cover somewhere in the middle. Those three books had
always stood together, he explained, because he had read
them the same summer, the year he learned to make soup
and tell a heron from an egret. The shelf had never been
a mess. It had been arranged in the order he had lived
it.

Raina's face went hot. "I can put them back," she
offered, although she had no idea how.

"We'll do it together," Grandpa answered. "You hand me
the books, and I'll tell you where each one belongs."

It took them three evenings. When the last book was in
place, Grandpa cleared a narrow space at the far end of
the bottom shelf. Then he held out his hand for the
novel Raina had been reading all week.

RC-W7-XP4.t: The Puppy Who Was Not Ours
RC-W7-XP4.x:
Our puppy arrived on a Saturday in March with a green
leash, a bag of food, and a rule book thicker than my
math textbook. Her name was Saffron, and she was not
really ours. She belonged to a school that trains guide
dogs for people who are blind. My family had volunteered
to raise her until she was old enough to begin her real
training.

Puppies like Saffron go to volunteer families when they
are seven or eight weeks old. For about a year, the
family teaches the puppy house manners and basic
obedience: sit, stay, come, and do not chew the couch.
An important part of the job, though, is something the
school calls socializing. Someday a guide dog may have
to lead its owner through a crowded store or a noisy
airport without being frightened. So the family takes
the puppy to places like that while she is young, again
and again, until nothing surprises her.

Saffron went everywhere with us. She rode in the car to
my soccer practice. She napped under the table at my
cousin's birthday dinner. At the grocery store, she
stopped and stared the first time the automatic doors
slid open. By our fifth trip, she walked through them as
if she had been doing it all her life.

The rule book never said how hard the last day would be.
When Saffron was fifteen months old, we drove her back
to the school, where an instructor would spend about
four months teaching her to guide. I held the leash
until the very end. Then I handed it over, and Saffron
trotted off beside her new trainer without looking back.
My mom squeezed my shoulder. "That," she said, "is
exactly what we raised her to do."

RC-W8-XP1.x:
Deep inside a limestone cave, stone seems to drip from
the ceiling. Thin tubes and long, pointed shapes hang
overhead like icicles, and rounded mounds rise from the
floor beneath them. Nobody carved these shapes. They
were built one drop of water at a time.

The story begins above ground. As rain soaks through the
soil, it picks up a small amount of acid from rotting
leaves. This acid, called carbonic acid, is the same
thing that gives soda pop its fizz. The acidic water
seeps into small cracks in the rock below and slowly
dissolves the rock it touches. Over a very long time,
the moving water widens the cracks into passages and
rooms.

The water carries some of the dissolved rock along with
it. When a drop oozes out of a cave's ceiling, it meets
the cave's air and gives off carbon dioxide gas, the
same way an opened bottle of soda pop loses its fizz.
Without that gas, the water cannot hold on to all of its
dissolved mineral, which is called calcite. So before
the drop falls, it leaves behind a tiny ring of calcite.
The next drop adds another ring, and the next adds
another. Ring by ring, a hollow tube called a soda straw
grows down from the ceiling. A soda straw often takes a
hundred years to grow a single inch.

If the inside of a soda straw gets blocked, water begins
to run down its outside instead, coating it with calcite
and making it thicker. The straw has become a
stalactite. Meanwhile, drops that splash onto the floor
leave calcite there too, building a mound called a
stalagmite. Given enough time, a stalactite and the
stalagmite below it can meet and join into a column.

Cave visitors are asked never to touch these formations.
The oils on human skin leave stains, and they can also
waterproof the stone so that it stops growing.

RC-W8-XP2.x:
In 1860, the railroad and the telegraph reached only as
far west as St. Joseph, Missouri. Beyond that town lay a
vast land of deserts and mountains, and California was
nearly two thousand miles away. A letter sent across
that land by stagecoach took weeks. Many people believed
that no one could carry mail across it all year round.

Three businessmen were determined to prove them wrong.
On April 3, 1860, they started the Pony Express, a relay
of riders on horseback. Stations stood every ten to
fifteen miles along the trail, and at each one a fresh
horse was waiting. A rider would leap down, throw his
mochila, a saddle cover with four pockets for mail, onto
the new horse, and gallop on. On average, a rider covered
75 to 100 miles a day. The first mail from St. Joseph
reached Sacramento, California, in just ten days.

Speed was costly, though. Sending a letter by Pony
Express could cost as much as five dollars for half an
ounce. At the time, ordinary postage cost no more than
ten cents. Even with prices that high, the company never
earned enough to pay its expenses, and it sank deep into
debt.

Meanwhile, another kind of messenger was on its way.
About ten weeks after the first riders set out, Congress
approved money to help build a telegraph line across the
continent. As crews strung wire westward from the
Missouri River and eastward from California, the riders
carried telegrams across the shrinking gap between the
two ends. On October 26, 1861, the telegraph finally
joined San Francisco to New York City. On that same day,
the Pony Express officially came to an end. It had
lasted only eighteen months.

RC-W8-XP3.x:
Walk up close to a large painting by Georges Seurat, and
the people in it seem to fall apart. Faces, clothes, and
even the grass under their feet break into thousands of
tiny dots and dashes of color. Step back a few paces,
and the dots come together again into a sunny Sunday on
the banks of the River Seine, crowded with people of
every age.

Seurat, a French artist, began the painting in 1884.
Today it is known as A Sunday on La Grande Jatte.
Painters usually mixed their colors on a palette before
brushing them onto the canvas, but Seurat tried
something different. He set small touches of pure,
unmixed color side by side and left the mixing to the
eyes of the people looking. He believed that colors
blended by the eye would make a more striking picture
than paint stirred together on a palette. His way of
painting with tiny dots came to be called pointillism.

The work was slow. Seurat made many smaller drawings and
painted studies first, working out where each figure
should go. Later he returned to the big canvas, made the
outlines of some figures stronger, and added new ones,
including a monkey on a leash. The finished painting was
shown in Paris in 1886. It is nearly seven feet tall and
about ten feet wide.

Sadly, not every color has lasted. For the sunlit grass,
Seurat used a bright paint called zinc yellow. By 1892,
people had noticed that it was turning a dull brown.
Today the painting hangs in the Art Institute of
Chicago, darker in places than the day it was finished.
Visitors still step close and then step back, watching
the dots turn into people.

RC-W8-XP4.x:
Long ago, in a valley crowded with windmills, there
lived a lord named Rendal who believed that everything
in sight belonged to him. He owned the castle, the road,
and every field the road touched. One spring morning,
watching the sails of the mills turn, he announced a new
rule. The wind blew across his land, he declared, so the
wind was his property. Every miller who used it would
pay him a sack of flour each week.

The millers complained bitterly, but they paid. Tamsin,
whose family operated the mill at the far end of the
valley, paid too and said nothing. Every evening,
however, she made a chalk mark on the mill door: a
straight line for a windy day and a circle for a still
one.

That summer brought a long, hot calm. For three weeks
the air hung over the valley like a damp blanket, and
not a single sail turned. When the lord's servant came
for the flour, Tamsin handed him an empty sack and
pointed to the row of circles on the door. "Your wind
did not come to work," she explained, "so there is no
flour to share."

The lord frowned at the empty sack, but he could hardly
argue.

That autumn, a storm roared down the valley, tore the
sails from Tamsin's mill, and flattened her barn. The
next morning, she climbed the hill to the castle
carrying a long sheet of paper.

"Here is the bill for the repairs, my lord," she said
politely. "Your wind caused this damage, and since the
wind belongs to you, so does the bill."

Red in the face, the lord shouted that nobody could be
blamed for the wind, because it went wherever it
pleased.

"Then it is a strange thing to own," Tamsin replied.

Before evening, the lord's messengers galloped through
the valley announcing that the wind belonged to no one.
To this day, if a traveler there asks who owns the wind,
the children point at the turning sails and laugh.

DGN-RC-P01.x: Engineers often search for ideas in places that do not look like laboratories. One team studied barnacles, small sea animals that fasten themselves to rocks and ship hulls. A barnacle must make its bond while surrounded by moving salt water—a setting in which ordinary glue performs poorly. Researchers studying the animal's natural cement found that it first releases an oily substance that pushes water away from the surface, and only then do its sticky proteins form the bond. The team did not simply collect barnacle cement. Instead, it designed a new material that copied this useful action. In tests, the material joined wet surfaces more effectively than common household adhesives. A future version might help doctors close a wound without using as many stitches. The work illustrates biomimicry: studying a successful feature in nature and adapting its underlying principle to solve a human problem.

DGN-RC-P02.x: Every afternoon, Nia swept the floor of her uncle's clock-repair shop. She loved the rows of tiny gears but was allowed only to sort screws and polish cases. One rainy day, a customer returned a clock that chimed thirteen times at noon. Nia's uncle listened, frowned, and began opening the case. Nia noticed a thin lever brushing a wheel after each turn. She almost stayed silent; after all, she was only the helper. Then she pointed to a bright scratch on the lever. Her uncle adjusted it, and the clock chimed twelve times. He did not hand Nia a difficult repair. Instead, he placed a broken alarm clock beside her and asked her to describe what each part might do before touching anything. Nia understood that careful noticing had earned her a new kind of task—and that guessing quickly would not keep it.

DGN-RC-P03.x: Centuries ago, books were copied by hand and could take months to complete. The main text usually received careful attention, but the empty margins sometimes became places for a different kind of record. A reader might correct a copying error, define an unfamiliar word, or argue with an author's claim. Later readers could respond, creating a slow conversation across years. Modern historians value these notes because they reveal not only what people read but also how they reacted. A stain beside a recipe may suggest frequent use, while repeated symbols near one paragraph may show special interest. Such evidence must be interpreted cautiously: a note's writer may be unknown, and a mark may have several explanations. Even so, the margins can turn a surviving book from a container of old words into evidence of many individual encounters with those words.

DGN-RC-P04.x: On a sunny afternoon, a dark roof can become far hotter than the air around it. It absorbs much of the sunlight that strikes it and later releases that energy as heat. Across many buildings, this process contributes to an “urban heat island,” an area where streets and structures keep a neighborhood warmer than nearby land. Some cities are testing pale roof coatings that reflect more sunlight. In one trial, coated buildings required less air-conditioning during the hottest hours. Yet cool roofs are not a complete solution. Trees can shade sidewalks, parks can replace heat-absorbing pavement, and well-designed ventilation can reduce indoor heat. Climate, roof shape, maintenance, and winter heating needs also affect whether a coating is useful. The best plan therefore combines local measurements with several methods rather than treating one bright layer of paint as a universal answer.

DGN-RC-P05.x: During rehearsal, the youth orchestra repeatedly lost its place in a new piece. The loudest section was not the problem. Confusion began in a measure containing three beats of silence. Several players treated the rest as a chance to stop counting, so they entered at slightly different moments. The conductor asked everyone to tap the beat while no notes sounded. At first the tapping seemed unnecessary, but the next entrance was exact. She explained that silence in music is measured, not empty. A rest can build expectation, separate two ideas, or give a melody room to breathe. The students practiced the quiet measure as carefully as the fast passages. By the end, the audience would hear no tapping, of course. What listeners would hear was the result: a confident entrance made possible by musicians who had learned to perform the silence together.

M01-RC-P01.t: The Long Flight of the Monarchs
M01-RC-P01.x:
Every fall, something strange happens in the fields and
backyards of eastern North America. Monarch butterflies
that have spent the summer drifting from flower to
flower suddenly change. They turn south, and they keep
flying for weeks.

A monarch weighs less than a gram. Yet some of these
insects travel as far as 3,000 miles to reach their
winter home. They can cover 50 to 100 miles in a single
day, and the whole trip may take up to two months.
Monarchs from the eastern part of the continent gather
in the mountains of central Mexico. There they settle on
the branches of oyamel fir trees, high up where the air
stays cool. Tens of thousands of butterflies can cluster
on a single tree, so thickly that the branches look as
if they have grown orange leaves. Monarchs from the West
spend the winter on the California coast instead,
resting in groves of pine, cypress, and eucalyptus
trees.

The butterflies that make this journey are not ordinary
monarchs. A monarch born in early summer lives only two
to five weeks. The last generation of the year is
different. It can live as long as nine months, long
enough to fly south, wait out the winter, and start
north again in spring. Scientists think these
butterflies use the position of the sun and the changing
weather to know when it is time to leave.

No single butterfly makes the whole round trip. When
warm days return, the monarchs leave Mexico and fly
north, laying eggs on milkweed plants along the way. The
caterpillars that hatch feed on milkweed leaves, grow
into butterflies, fly a little farther north, and lay
eggs of their own. It takes three or four generations to
reach the northern United States and Canada. By late
summer the fields of the North are full of monarchs
again, and a new generation is getting ready to fly
3,000 miles to trees it has never seen.

M01-RC-P02.t: The Fossil Hunter of Lyme Regis
M01-RC-P02.x:
Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a town on
the south coast of England. The cliffs beside the town
are packed with fossils of sea creatures from the time
of the dinosaurs. Today that shore is known as the
Jurassic Coast.

Mary's father, Richard, was a cabinetmaker who collected
fossils. He taught Mary how to spot them on the beach
and how to clean them, and he sold them from his shop.
Fossil collecting was a fashionable hobby then, and
people paid for curiosities to display at home. Richard
died in 1810, leaving his family poor and in debt.
Mary's mother encouraged her to keep selling what she
found.

In the autumn of 1811, when Mary was twelve, her brother
Joseph found a strange fossil skull. About a year later
Mary found the rest of the animal and carefully dug out
its skeleton, five meters long. It was an ichthyosaur, a
sea reptile whose name means "fish lizard." In 1823 she
found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur,
another sea reptile. A French scientist who studied a
drawing of it doubted that it was real. Once he realized
it was genuine, Mary and her family were treated as true
experts. In 1828 she uncovered a jumble of bones that
turned out to be a pterosaur, a flying reptile. It was
the first ever found outside Germany.

Mary had little schooling, but she could read, and she
taught herself geology and anatomy. One visitor wrote in
her diary in 1824 that the moment Mary found a bone, she
knew what animal it came from. Yet the scientists who
bought her fossils and wrote about them often left her
name out. The Geological Society of London did not allow
women to join until 1908. Mary died in 1847, at the age
of forty-seven. In 2022, after a campaign led by an
eleven-year-old girl, a statue of Mary and her dog was
unveiled in Lyme Regis.

M01-RC-P03.x:
When you watch a movie, the crunch of footsteps on
gravel or the creak of a door seems to come from the
picture itself. Most of the time, however, it does not.
"Nearly every small sound you hear in a film was made
later, by a person in a room like this one," the sound
artist Ms. Castellano told the fifth graders visiting
her studio last spring.

The studio looked like an extremely messy garage. There
were trays of gravel and sand on the floor, a rack of
shoes in every size, a bathtub, and shelves crowded with
objects that seemed to have nothing in common: coconut
shells, a leather glove, a bag of cornstarch, celery, a
broken umbrella.

Ms. Castellano played a short film clip with the sound
turned off. A woman walked down a snowy lane, stopped,
and snapped a branch from a tree. Then the clip played
again, and this time Ms. Castellano made every sound
herself while she watched the screen. For the footsteps
in snow she squeezed a bag of cornstarch in her fists,
and the crunch was so real that several students glanced
down at their own feet. For the branch she snapped a
stalk of celery beside the microphone. "Your ears
believe whatever your eyes tell them," she said.

Then the students took their turns at the microphone.
One boy galloped two coconut shells across a tray of
dirt to make a horse, and another flapped the leather
glove to make a bird taking off. The hardest sound
turned out to be the simplest one. No one could produce
a convincing footstep until Ms. Castellano pointed out
that real people do not walk like a ticking clock. They
slow down, hesitate, and shift their weight. When Mina
finally got it right, stepping in place on a plank with
her eyes fixed on the screen, the whole room went quiet.
For a moment it sounded exactly as if someone were
crossing a wooden porch at night.

M01-RC-P04.x:
At a quarter to eight on Wednesday mornings, a bus pulls
up at the corner of Maple and Third. It has no engine,
no doors, and no driver. It is a bike bus: a long
procession of children on bicycles, riding to school
together behind a parent who leads the way.

The idea is simple. A grown-up leader rides at the
front, following the same route every week and stopping
at the same corners, just as a real bus does. Children
wait at the "stops" with their bikes and helmets and
join the line as it passes. Another adult rides at the
very back and is called the caboose. In between, the
line can stretch for a whole block. A speaker strapped
to the leader's bike plays music, so the group can be
heard coming before it can be seen.

This bike bus started small. On the first morning only
four riders showed up, and one of them was the leader's
own son. He made the ride anyway, music playing, waving
at people on their porches. By the end of the fall there
were nineteen riders, and in the spring the line grew to
more than thirty. Drivers along the route learned to
anticipate it. Some now wait at the corners with their
windows down to listen.

Riding in a group changes what a child is allowed to do.
A nine-year-old who would never be permitted to bike
alone across a busy street can cross it with twenty
others and two adults. The rules are strict: helmets on,
a hand signal before every turn, and no passing the
leader. A rider who misses a stop can usually catch up
at the next one, because the bus rolls slowly enough for
the youngest legs.

On rainy days the bus still runs. The riders arrive at
school with wet socks and red cheeks, and the bike rack,
which once held three or four bikes, is full before the
first bell.

M01-RC-P05.x:
Mrs. Dombrowski was away for three days, and Wren had
the responsibility of looking after her six hens. The
instructions were on an index card taped inside the coop
door: fill the water, scatter the feed, collect the
eggs, and shut the door at dusk. "The door is the
important part," Mrs. Dombrowski had explained.
"Whatever comes into a yard at night is not coming for
the eggs."

On the first evening, five hens filed up the ramp
without any encouragement as the daylight faded, and
settled on the perch inside. The sixth, a speckled brown
hen called Pepper, remained in the middle of the yard.
She regarded Wren as if Wren were the one who was late.

Wren approached cautiously with her arms outstretched.
Pepper trotted left, so Wren followed. Pepper went
right, then under the lilac bush, then behind the rain
barrel, where she scratched at the dirt as though
nothing unusual had happened. By the time Wren had
chased her twice around the yard, her hair was tangled
with lilac leaves and the sky had faded from pink to
gray. She collapsed on the back step to recover her
breath. Pepper walked calmly up the ramp and disappeared
inside.

On the second evening Wren rattled a handful of corn in
a tin cup, and five hens came hurrying. Pepper observed
from the fence post until the corn was gone, then
returned to her scratching. Wren waited patiently
without moving. When the first star appeared, Pepper
went in.

On the third evening Wren brought a book and settled on
the step before the sun had even reached the rooftops.
The hens pecked around her shoes while she read one
chapter, then another, and she never once glanced at the
speckled hen. The yard turned blue, then gray, and there
was a gentle thump on the ramp. Wren counted six shadowy
shapes on the perch and slid the latch home. Above the
coop, the first star was out, exactly where it had been
the night before.

M02-RC-P01.x:
By February, the lost-and-found box outside our school
gym had turned into a mountain. It held jackets and
sweatshirts, a lunchbox nobody dared to open, one purple
rain boot, and enough mittens to fill a laundry basket.
Every Monday, our principal reminded everyone over the
loudspeaker to check the box. Every Monday, the mountain
grew a little taller.

Then our art teacher, Mr. Ferreira, had an idea. "Nobody
looks at a pile," he told our class. "But everybody
watches a show." He asked the principal if the fifth
grade could put on a fashion show at the Friday
assembly, with every outfit borrowed from the
lost-and-found.

Twelve of us volunteered to be models. On Thursday we
sorted the pile into outfits, which was harder than it
sounds. A striped scarf went with a green raincoat that
was much too big for any of us. The rain boot had no
partner, so Ruben wore it with one of his own sneakers.

On Friday, the gym lights dimmed and music thumped from
the speakers. A row of blue tumbling mats made a runway
down the middle of the floor. One by one, we strutted to
the end, turned, and posed while Mr. Ferreira described
each outfit like a television host. "Here we have a cozy
gray hoodie," he announced, "with half a granola bar
still in the pocket."

The first shout came from the third row: "That's mine!"
A second grader raced down to collect her hoodie, and
the whole gym cheered as if she had won a prize. After
that, hands shot up all over the room. A kindergartner
claimed a jacket that hung down to his knees; it
belonged to his big brother, who had been searching for
it since December.

By the end of the assembly, forty-one items had been
claimed. The rest were washed, folded, and given to a
clothing drive downtown. Only the purple rain boot was
left, and it now stands on the windowsill of the front
office, holding a bunch of paper flowers.

M02-RC-P02.x:
A sea otter usually eats while floating on its back at
the surface of the ocean, using its own chest as a
table. When it naps, it often wraps itself in a long
strand of kelp so that it will not drift away. A group
of otters resting together is called a raft.

Unlike seals, sea otters have no thick layer of blubber
to keep them warm. Instead, they rely on the densest fur
of any animal. A single square inch of an otter's skin
can hold as many as a million hairs. The fur traps tiny
bubbles of air, which keep the cold water away from the
otter's skin. To keep its coat waterproof, an otter
spends hours every day cleaning and fluffing it.

Staying warm also uses an enormous amount of energy. To
keep up, a sea otter must eat about a quarter of its own
weight in food every day. It dives to the bottom for
crabs, clams, mussels, and sea urchins, and it tucks
what it catches into a loose pocket of skin under its
front leg. Back at the surface, it may crack open a hard
shell by pounding it against a rock, which some otters
even carry in that same pocket.

Those spiny sea urchins are more important than they
look. Urchins feed on kelp, a giant seaweed that can
grow 100 feet tall and forms thick forests under the
water. Thousands of tiny animals live among the kelp.
Where there are plenty of otters, they keep the urchins
in check. Where the otters disappear, the urchins can
multiply and chew through a kelp forest until the sea
floor is nearly bare. Scientists call such a place an
urchin barren.

For more than a hundred years, hunters killed sea otters
for their thick, soft fur. By 1900, only one or two
thousand were left in the whole world. In 1911, a treaty
between nations finally protected them, and during the
twentieth century their numbers recovered.

M02-RC-P03.x:
Hattie and her cousin Quinn had begged all week to sleep
in the backyard, and on Friday evening Aunt Lou finally
dragged the old tent out of the garage. They set it up
beside the fence, lined up their sneakers just inside
the entrance, and told ghost stories until the beam of
their flashlight began to fade.

Then the noise began. It was a high, sharp chirp,
repeated over and over, as regular as a ticking clock.
Hattie sat up suddenly in her sleeping bag. "Do you hear
that?" she whispered.

Quinn was already listening. "It's probably a bird," he
said, but he did not sound certain. Birds did not
usually sing in the middle of the night. Stranger still,
the sound seemed to come from everywhere at once: from
the fence, from the grass, from the dark row of tomato
plants beside the porch.

They decided to investigate. Quinn shook the flashlight
until it produced a weak yellow glow, and the two of
them crept out of the tent in their socks. The grass was
icy and soaking wet. Every time they tiptoed toward the
fence, the chirping seemed to slip around behind them,
back toward the tent. They searched underneath the porch
steps and inside an empty flowerpot. Hattie even lifted
the lid of the sandbox, half expecting some creature to
leap out at her.

After twenty minutes they gave up and crawled back
inside, shivering. The moment Quinn zipped the door
shut, the chirping grew louder than ever. Hattie pointed
the dim flashlight at the row of sneakers. Very slowly,
Quinn lifted his left one. Sitting inside the toe was a
small brown cricket, its back legs folded and ready to
spring.

Quinn carried the sneaker outside and tipped it gently
over the grass. For a while the yard was completely
silent. Then, from somewhere near the fence, the
chirping started again, softer now and farther away, and
the two cousins were asleep before it stopped.

M02-RC-P04.x:
Louis Braille was born in 1809 in Coupvray, a village
near Paris, France. His father was a harness maker who
made leather gear for horses. One day, when Louis was
three, he was playing in the workshop with one of his
father's sharp tools, and he injured his eye. An
infection set in and spread to his other eye, and by the
age of five he was completely blind. Even so, he went on
to attend the village school for three years.

When Louis was ten, he won a scholarship to the Royal
Institute for Blind Youth, a school in Paris. The school
owned only a handful of books, printed in large raised
letters that students read by running their fingers over
them. Telling the curved letters apart was slow work.

In 1821, when Louis was twelve, an army captain named
Charles Barbier visited the school. Barbier had invented
a code called night writing, which allowed soldiers to
pass messages in the dark without speaking. Instead of
letters, it used raised dots, and Louis recognized that
dots could be the answer for blind readers. Yet
Barbier's code had problems. Its signs stood for sounds
rather than letters, and a single sign could need as
many as twelve dots, a shape too tall to feel all at
once.

Louis spent the next three years improving the code. He
reduced the number of dots to six, arranged in two
columns of three, and he made each pattern stand for a
letter. By 1824, when he was fifteen, his system was
finished. Six dots can be arranged in sixty-four
different ways, enough for letters, numbers, punctuation
marks, and even musical notes.

At seventeen, Louis became a teacher at the school, and
he also played the organ in churches around Paris. In
1829 he published a book that explained his system. He
died of tuberculosis in 1852, when he was forty-three
years old. Two years after his death, France officially
adopted his code of raised dots.

M02-RC-P05.x:
One of the most famous pictures in the world is only
about ten inches tall and fifteen inches wide. It shows
a giant wave curling over a few sleek boats. The rowers
huddle low and cling to their oars. Far in the distance,
beneath the curl of the wave, sits Mount Fuji, looking
tiny.

The picture is known as The Great Wave. The Japanese
artist Katsushika Hokusai designed it for a series of
views of Mount Fuji. He began the series in 1830, when
he was seventy years old, and it helped make landscape
prints popular, as they still are today. Each picture
shows the mountain from a different direction, near or
far, in a different season or kind of weather. The boats
in The Great Wave were swift boats that carried fresh
fish to the markets of Edo, the city now called Tokyo.

Hokusai did not print the picture himself. Like other
artists of his time, he made only the design, a drawing
in lines with notes about the colors. A carver pasted
the drawing face down on a block of cherry wood and then
carved away everything except the lines. That first
block printed the outline of the picture. Next, the
carver cut a separate block for each color. He also cut
small marks at the edges so that the printer could line
up every color exactly.

The printer brushed color onto one block and laid a
sheet of paper on top. Then he rubbed the back of the
paper with a pad called a baren. He did the same with
the next block, and the next. For the sea and the sky,
Hokusai chose Berlin blue. This deep blue coloring had
only recently become cheap enough for printers to use.

Because the blocks could be inked again and again, the
same picture could be printed many times. The Art
Institute of Chicago owns three impressions of The Great
Wave. The National Gallery of Victoria, in Melbourne,
Australia, owns another.

M03-RC-P01.t: The Plant That Counts to Two
M03-RC-P01.x:
The leaf of a Venus flytrap looks like a small open
mouth. Each trap has two halves joined by a hinge, and a
row of bristles runs along their edges like teeth. The
famous scientist Charles Darwin called it "one of the
most wonderful plants in the world."

Venus flytraps grow wild in only one small corner of the
world. They live within about 75 miles of Wilmington,
North Carolina, in wet, sunny grasslands dotted with
tall longleaf pines. Fires often sweep through these
grasslands. Without the fires, trees and shrubs would
gradually spread and shade the little plants from the
sunlight they need.

Like other plants, a flytrap makes most of its food from
sunlight. The soggy soil where it grows, however, is
poor in nutrients, the substances a plant needs to grow
and stay healthy. Insects and other small creatures
supply what the soil cannot.

Catching them requires a clever trap. Near the hinge, on
the inside of the trap, grow a few tiny hairs. A single
touch does nothing at all. But if an ant or a spider
trips two of the hairs, one after the other, within a
few seconds, the trap snaps shut in as little as half a
second. This way, a raindrop or a scrap of blowing leaf
does not fool the plant into closing for no reason. Once
the trap is shut, its meal cannot squeeze out between
the bristles. The leaf then releases special juices that
slowly break the animal down, and the trap may stay
closed for three to twenty days while the plant absorbs
its meal. After about three meals, the trap turns black
and dies.

For a plant called a flytrap, it catches surprisingly
few flies. When scientists studied what the traps
actually capture, they found that most of the meals are
creatures that crawl rather than fly. About a third are
ants, and almost as many are spiders. Fewer than one
meal in twenty is a flying insect.

M03-RC-P02.x:
Nellie Bly, who was born in Pennsylvania in 1864, was a
young reporter for a New York newspaper called the
World. One day she sat down beside her editor's desk and
told him her idea. "I want to go around the world!" In a
popular novel by Jules Verne, a character named Phileas
Fogg makes that trip in eighty days. Bly believed that
she could do it faster.

Her editor liked the idea, so they took it to the
newspaper's business manager. "It is impossible for you
to do it," he said. "In the first place you are a woman
and would need a protector." He added that she would
carry so much baggage that it would slow her down. Bly
was angry. If the newspaper sent a man instead, she told
him, she would start the same day for another newspaper
and beat him. "I believe you would," he said slowly.

A year later, her editor asked if she could leave in two
days. "I can start this minute," she answered. She
bought a single hand-bag and fit everything she needed
inside it.

On November 14, 1889, Bly sailed from Hoboken, New
Jersey, on a steamship called the Augusta Victoria.
Jules Verne had asked to meet her, so after reaching
England she traveled day and night to Amiens, France, to
see him. Then trains and ships carried her through Italy
and Egypt and across Asia. At a ticket office in Hong
Kong, she heard surprising news. A magazine had sent
another reporter, Elizabeth Bisland, to beat her.

Back home, newspaper readers eagerly followed Bly's
progress. She crossed the Pacific Ocean to San
Francisco, and a special train rushed her across the
United States while Bisland fell far behind. On January
25, 1890, the train pulled into Jersey City, New Jersey,
where a large crowd was waiting. Cannons boomed, and
timekeepers stopped their watches. Nellie Bly had
circled the globe in 72 days, 6 hours, 11 minutes, and
14 seconds.

M03-RC-P03.x:
Most sculptures stand perfectly still. A statue carved
from marble looks the same today as it did a hundred
years ago, no matter who walks past it. The American
artist Alexander Calder, who was born in 1898, wanted to
change that. "Why must art be static?" he once asked.
"The next step in sculpture is motion."

Calder grew up in a family of artists. His mother was a
painter, and his father and grandfather were sculptors.
Yet Calder first trained as a mechanical engineer, and
as a young man living in Europe he began building a tiny
circus out of wire, cloth, cork, and other everyday
materials. Then he performed it for audiences himself.
He moved the little figures by hand, told the story in
English and French, and supplied the music.

In 1930, Calder visited the studio of the Dutch painter
Piet Mondrian. Mondrian's paintings were made of black
lines and rectangles of bright color on a white
background, and on one wall of his studio he had tacked
up rectangles of colored cardboard. Calder suggested
that it might be fun to make the rectangles swing back
and forth. Mondrian looked very serious. "No, it is not
necessary, my painting is already very fast," he
answered.

The visit stayed with Calder. "This one visit gave me a
shock that started things," he later recalled. He
stopped making figures of people and animals and began
building sculptures out of simple shapes. At first he
used motors and hand cranks to make the shapes move. In
1931 his friend Marcel Duchamp, another artist, gave
these sculptures a name. He called them mobiles, a
French word that can mean both "motion" and "motive."
Soon Calder discovered that the air alone could do the
job of a motor.

Calder kept making mobiles, using little more than
shears, pliers, wire, and painted sheet metal. He
balanced each piece so carefully that a passing breath
of air can set the whole sculpture slowly turning.

M03-RC-P04.x:
My grandfather lives on the other side of the world,
where it is already tomorrow morning while I am eating
dinner. For years we talked on the telephone every
Sunday. His voice always sounded small and crackly, and
I had to imagine the expression on his face.

Last spring my mother mailed him a tablet so that we
could see each other when we talked. The first video
call was a disaster. The screen showed his ear, then the
ceiling fan, then a close-up of one bushy gray eyebrow.
He was pressing the tablet against the side of his head
like a telephone and shouting hello over and over,
wondering why nobody answered.

I decided to teach him, one Sunday at a time. I showed
him how to hold the tablet in front of his face, like a
mirror. I explained that the tiny picture in the corner
was what I could see. The red button gave us the most
trouble. Every time he leaned forward to wave goodbye,
his thumb landed on it, and the call ended before he
could finish. Finally he copied my directions into a
notebook in big block letters and kept it open beside
the tablet.

By summer our conversations looked completely different.
My grandfather carried the tablet into his garden to
show me his tomato plants, which were taller than he
was. He taught me to fold a paper boat, and I taught him
a card trick. Once he called in the middle of the week,
just to show me a rainbow over the rooftops on his
street.

Now his breakfast and my dinner happen at the same
table, in a way. On Sunday evenings I prop our tablet
against the fruit bowl, and he props his against the
teapot. He raises his cup of tea, and I raise my glass
of milk. When it is time to say goodbye, he leans in so
close that the whole screen fills up with one bushy gray
eyebrow.

M03-RC-P05.x:
That fall, half the fourth grade at Sadie's school
seemed to own the same green backpack, the one with
orange zippers. Every afternoon the backpacks hung in a
crowded row of hooks in the fourth-grade hallway, and
every afternoon Sadie grabbed hers without looking and
hurried off to catch the bus.

On Thursday, when she sat down at the kitchen table to
start her homework, she unzipped her backpack and found
a stranger's things inside. There was a pencil case
shaped like a fish, a spotted banana, and a thick
sketchbook. On the inside cover, someone had printed
WYATT, ROOM 11 in neat capital letters.

Sadie only meant to look for a phone number. Instead she
found a comic. Page after page, a raccoon in a
detective's coat followed a trail of muddy footprints
through a city of tall, crooked buildings. Every picture
was drawn in pencil, with careful shading, and the
raccoon's eyes narrowed a little more with each new
clue. On the last page, the footprints stopped at the
edge of a bridge. Underneath, in tiny letters, were the
words TO BE CONTINUED.

Sadie read the comic three times before dinner. Only
then did she remember her math worksheet, which was
sitting in her own backpack, wherever that was.

The next morning a boy was waiting outside Room 9,
holding her backpack at arm's length, as if it might
bite him. "Your yogurt leaked," he said.

Sadie held out the sketchbook. "What happens to the
raccoon?"

The boy stared at her for a long moment. Then he opened
the sketchbook to the last page. He began to explain the
plot, faster and faster, waving his hands at the bridge,
the footprints, and a stolen trumpet that nobody in the
city had missed yet.

A week later, Sadie's backpack had a strip of red tape
wrapped around its handle. Wyatt's sketchbook had a new
page, and the words on it were written in two kinds of
handwriting.

words.task: Explain in your own words + give 1 synonym.
words.meaning: harmless, gentle, kind, mild
words.example: Despite his gruff appearance, the old soldier was benign and always gave the girls candy.
words.usage: often paired with "nature" or "influence." In ISEE sample #2, BENIGN means HARMLESS (not cunning, graceful, or sensible).

words.task: Explain the meaning and how it relates to skeptical.
words.meaning: doubtful, skeptical, uncertain, unsure, suspicious
words.example: Jo was dubious about Amy's plan to bake a cake all by herself, since Amy had never even cracked an egg before.
words.usage: often followed by about (e.g., dubious about the plan) or that (e.g., It is dubious that he will come); can also describe something of questionable quality (e.g., a dubious reputation)
words.connotation: neutral to negative (shows lack of trust)

words.task: Explain why this is stronger than simply remove.
words.meaning: destroy, eliminate, remove, erase, annihilate, extinguish, wipe out
words.example: Jo wished she could eradicate her quick temper completely, but she knew it was a habit that would take years of practice to overcome.
words.usage: always followed by a direct object (eradicate poverty, eradicate disease); noun: eradication; stronger than "destroy" – implies it can never come back
words.connotation: neutral to positive (if destroying something harmful) – implies total permanence

words.task: Give the meaning + write one natural sentence.
words.meaning: spirited, lively, plucky, scrappy, gutsy, tenacious
words.example: Even though she was the smallest of the sisters, Amy could be quite feisty when she felt she was being treated unfairly, standing up to Jo with surprising boldness.
words.usage: usually describes people or animals (a feisty puppy, a feisty old lady); often implies a bit of stubbornness but in an admirable way
words.connotation: positive – a compliment suggesting boldness and spunk

words.task: Give the meaning + use it correctly with about.
words.meaning: recall, remember, reflect, look back, dwell on the past
words.example: The sisters would often reminisce about their childhood Christmases, laughing at how they used to put on plays and pretend to be knights and princesses.
words.usage: often used with "about" (reminisce about old times); does not take a direct object (you don't "reminisce a memory")
words.connotation: positive or neutral – usually a pleasant, sentimental activity

words.task: Give a synonym + an opposite.
words.meaning: noticeable, obvious, clear, prominent, visible
words.example: Jo's long chestnut mane was conspicuous among the other girls, making her easy to spot in the crowd.
words.usage: often used with "in" (conspicuous in the crowd); opposite: inconspicuous (hard to notice)
words.connotation: neutral (can be positive or negative depending on context)

words.task: Explain the meaning and give a real-life situation where discretion matters.
words.meaning: prudence, tact, caution, judgment
words.example: Jo used great discretion when sharing her stories, never revealing which sisters were the models for her characters.
words.usage: often used with "with" (discretion with secrets) or "at" (use your discretion); adjective: discreet (not discrete)

words.task: Give one literal meaning and one figurative meaning.
words.meaning: grow, develop, nurture, farm, foster
words.example: The March sisters learned to cultivate their individual talents – Jo her writing, Amy her art, Beth her music, and Meg her homemaking skills.
words.usage: can be literal (cultivate a garden) or figurative (cultivate a friendship); noun: cultivation
words.connotation: positive – shows effort, patience, and care

words.task: Explain in your own words + give 1 synonym.
words.meaning: dilemma, trouble, difficulty, plight, bind
words.example: Jo found herself in a predicament when both Laurie and his tutor asked her to the same dance—she liked both, but could not say yes to one without hurting the other.
words.usage: often used with "in" (in a predicament) or "of" (the predicament of choosing); implies a need for a difficult decision

words.task: Explain the meaning + write a sentence using retaliate against or retaliate by.
words.meaning: fight back, get revenge, take revenge, strike back, counterattack
words.example: When Amy burned Jo's manuscript, Jo wanted to retaliate by destroying Amy's drawings—but she stopped herself, knowing that two wrongs would never make a right.
words.usage: often used with "against" (retaliate against her enemy) or "by" (retaliate by ignoring her); noun: retaliation

words.task: Give the meaning + 1 synonym.
words.meaning: determined, steadfast, unwavering
words.example: She remained resolute even after the first experiment failed.
words.usage: Stronger than determined; suggests firmness that does not change easily.

words.task: Give a literal meaning and a figurative meaning.
words.meaning: refuge, haven, safe place
words.example: The injured birds were taken to a wildlife sanctuary.
words.usage: Can mean a safe place, a protected area, or a sacred part of a church.

words.task: Explain two common meanings.
words.meaning: suppress, smother, restrain
words.example: She tried to stifle a laugh during the serious presentation.
words.usage: Can mean prevent breathing or suppress an emotion, sound, idea, or growth.

words.task: Explain lower in rank and give the opposite.
words.meaning: lower-ranking, secondary; place below
words.example: The assistant held a subordinate position in the organization.
words.usage: Can be a person lower in rank, an adjective meaning lower-ranked, or a verb meaning make less important.

words.task: Explain precisely what right this word refers to.
words.meaning: right to vote, voting rights
words.example: The women's suffrage movement fought for women's right to vote.
words.usage: Do not confuse with suffering. Suffrage specifically means the right to vote.

words.task: Explain the meaning + contrast with intangible.
words.meaning: touchable, concrete, real
words.example: The project produced tangible results that everyone could measure.
words.usage: Literal: able to be touched. Figurative: clear, real, or measurable. Opposite: intangible.

words.task: Give both common senses: place/condition and person/behavior.
words.meaning: dangerous, deceptive, disloyal
words.example: The icy mountain path was treacherous after the storm.
words.usage: Can describe dangerous conditions or a person who betrays trust.

words.task: Explain why unanimous is stronger than majority.
words.meaning: united, agreed, harmonious, like-minded, undivided
words.example: The sisters reached a unanimous decision to give their Christmas breakfast to the Hummel family, as each one of them felt it was the right thing to do.
words.usage: often used with "in" (unanimous in their opinion) or "on" (unanimous on the decision); noun: unanimity; adverb: unanimously

words.task: Explain the connotation + give a natural example.
words.meaning: playful, fanciful, quirky
words.example: The illustrator filled the page with whimsical animals wearing tiny hats.
words.usage: Suggests playful imagination and unusual charm, not randomness without purpose.

words.task: Explain the meaning + give the opposite verb.
words.meaning: decrease, diminish, fade
words.example: Her excitement began to wane after several hours of waiting.
words.usage: Opposite of wax in the traditional phrase 'wax and wane.' Often used for strength, interest, influence, or the moon.

words.task: Explain the difference. Who sends the hint? Who draws the conclusion?
words.meaning: IMPLY = to suggest something without saying it directly (the speaker or writer sends the hint). INFER = to work out what is meant from clues (the listener or reader draws the conclusion).
words.example: When Mom said 'It's getting late,' she implied we should leave; I inferred from her hint that it was time to go.
words.usage: The sender implies; the receiver infers. The classic mix-up is saying 'Are you inferring that…?' when you mean 'Are you implying that…?'

words.task: Explain the contrast and give one example of each.
words.meaning: OBJECTIVE = based on facts that can be checked, not on feelings or opinions. SUBJECTIVE = based on personal feelings, taste, or opinion.
words.example: 'The pool is 25 meters long' is objective; 'the pool is too cold' is subjective.
words.usage: A judge tries to be objective; a review of a movie is subjective. Objective can also be a noun meaning a goal.

words.task: Explain why these are not synonyms.
words.meaning: RIGID = stiff and unbending, either physically or in rules and attitudes (not flexible). RIGOROUS = extremely careful, thorough, and demanding.
words.example: The rigid schedule allowed no changes; the rigorous training tested every skill.
words.usage: Rigid is often negative (too strict); rigorous is usually positive (high standards, careful work).

words.task: Give the precise meaning of each and one example.
words.meaning: STABLE = steady, not likely to fall, change, or collapse. STATIONARY = not moving, staying in one place. STATIC = not changing or developing over time; showing no movement or progress.
words.example: The ladder was stable; the bus stayed stationary at the stop; the town's population stayed static for years.
words.usage: Stable is about balance and reliability; stationary is about position; static is about lack of change. Do not confuse stationary with stationery (paper).

words.task: Explain the ranking relationship among all three.
words.meaning: SUPERIOR = higher in quality, rank, or importance; as a noun, a person above you. INFERIOR = lower in quality or rank. SUBORDINATE = lower in rank and under someone's authority; as a noun, a person who reports to another.
words.example: The captain is the sailor's superior; a cheap copy is inferior to the original; a subordinate follows the manager's orders.
words.usage: Superior/inferior compare quality or rank; subordinate is specifically about the chain of command.

words.task: Explain literal meaning and contrast it with figurative language.
words.meaning: exact, word-for-word, actual
words.example: Jo meant her praise in the literal sense – Amy's drawing really was beautiful, not just pretty for a child.
words.usage: often paired with "meaning" or "sense"; opposite: figurative; adverb: literally (often misused)

words.task: Explain how they overlap and how they differ.
words.meaning: ELABORATE = worked out in great detail, with many parts (as a verb, to add more detail). INTRICATE = very complicated, with many small, carefully connected parts.
words.example: She built an elaborate model of the city; the clock's intricate gears fit together perfectly.
words.usage: Both mean detailed; intricate stresses fine, tangled complexity, while elaborate stresses effort and richness. Only elaborate is also a verb ('please elaborate').

words.task: Explain the difference between individual permission and group agreement.
words.meaning: CONSENT = permission or agreement given by one person (also a verb: to agree). CONSENSUS = general agreement reached by a whole group.
words.example: A parent must give consent for the field trip; the class reached a consensus on the theme.
words.usage: Consent is one person's yes; consensus is everyone's shared yes.

words.task: Explain the difference between noticeable and important/notable.
words.meaning: CONSPICUOUS = easily seen or noticed, standing out (sometimes in an unwanted way). PROMINENT = important, well-known, or standing out because of size or position.
words.example: The red hat was conspicuous in the gray crowd; a prominent scientist spoke at the museum.
words.usage: Conspicuous is about being noticeable; prominent adds importance or status. Opposite of conspicuous: inconspicuous.

words.task: Compare the three. Which emphasizes care? Which emphasizes steady hard work?
words.meaning: PAINSTAKING = done with great care and attention to every detail. DILIGENT = working hard and carefully, steadily and persistently. INDUSTRIOUS = hard-working and busy, getting a lot done.
words.example: Restoring the painting was painstaking work; a diligent student checks every answer; the industrious ants filled the hill by noon.
words.usage: Painstaking usually describes the work itself (careful, detailed); diligent and industrious usually describe the worker (steady, hard-working).

words.task: Explain the overlap and give a natural sentence with each.
words.meaning: SKEPTICAL = not easily convinced; having doubts and wanting proof. DUBIOUS = doubtful or uncertain (about something), or, of a thing, of questionable quality or honesty.
words.example: I was skeptical of the magic trick; the salesman's dubious promise made everyone uneasy.
words.usage: A person is skeptical; a claim, plan, or honor can be dubious ('a dubious excuse'). Dubious can also describe the person who doubts.

words.task: Explain the noun/adjective relationship and the idea of unfair judgment.
words.meaning: PREJUDICE (noun) = an unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts, often against a group of people. BIASED (adjective) = unfairly favoring one side or view over another.
words.example: Prejudice kept them from listening to the new student; a biased referee favored the home team.
words.usage: Prejudice is the unfair opinion; biased describes a person, judgment, or report that leans unfairly.

words.task: Give two meanings: formal document/license and hire/rent a vehicle.

words.task: Give two meanings: self-control/training and a field of study.
words.meaning: (noun) self-control, order, training; (verb) train, correct, punish

words.task: Give the verb meaning and the noun meaning. Explain why connotation changes.

words.task: Give one literal meaning and one figurative meaning.
words.meaning: grow, develop, nurture, farm, foster

words.usage: can be literal (cultivate a garden) or figurative (cultivate a friendship); noun: cultivation

words.task: Explain the noun and verb meanings, then give one sentence where two accounts conflict.

words.task: Explain both meanings: a safe/refuge place and a protected place.

words.task: Explain the meaning and give one natural phrase using strive for.
words.meaning: endeavor, work hard, struggle toward
words.example: She continued to strive for a clearer and more precise essay.
words.usage: Usually followed by 'to' + verb or 'for' + noun: strive to improve; strive for excellence.

words.task: Explain lower in rank and contrast it with superior.
words.meaning: lower-ranking, secondary; place below
words.example: The assistant held a subordinate position in the organization.
words.usage: Can be a person lower in rank, an adjective meaning lower-ranked, or a verb meaning make less important.

words.task: Give the verb meaning and explain why suspect is weaker than know.
words.meaning: suppose, distrust; person believed guilty
words.example: The detective suspected that the missing key was important.
words.usage: As a verb, believe without full proof. As a noun, a person thought to be involved in wrongdoing.

words.task: Explain not moving/changing and contrast with stationary.
words.meaning: unchanging, motionless; electrical charge
words.example: The population remained static for several years.
words.usage: Can mean not changing, not moving, or electrical static. Compare stationary: physically not moving.

words.task: Explain the precise difference among the three.
words.meaning: STABLE = steady, not likely to fall, change, or collapse. STATIONARY = not moving, staying in one place. STATIC = not changing or developing over time; showing no movement or progress.
words.example: The ladder was stable; the bus stayed stationary at the stop; the town's population stayed static for years.
words.usage: Stable is about balance and reliability; stationary is about position; static is about lack of change. Do not confuse stationary with stationery (paper).

words.task: Explain why these are not synonyms.
words.meaning: RIGID = stiff and unbending, either physically or in rules and attitudes (not flexible). RIGOROUS = extremely careful, thorough, and demanding.
words.example: The rigid schedule allowed no changes; the rigorous training tested every skill.
words.usage: Rigid is often negative (too strict); rigorous is usually positive (high standards, careful work).

words.task: Explain the ranking relationship and give an example.
words.meaning: SUPERIOR = higher in rank, quality, or importance; as a noun, the person above you. SUBORDINATE = lower in rank and under someone's authority; as a noun, a person who reports to another.
words.example: A lieutenant is subordinate to a captain; the captain is the lieutenant's superior.
words.usage: The two words describe the same relationship from opposite ends.

words.task: Explain why unanimous is stronger than majority.
words.meaning: united, agreed, harmonious, like-minded, undivided
words.example: The sisters reached a unanimous decision to give their Christmas breakfast to the Hummel family, as each one of them felt it was the right thing to do.
words.usage: often used with "in" (unanimous in their opinion) or "on" (unanimous on the decision); noun: unanimity; adverb: unanimously

words.task: Explain the meaning and contrast with intangible.

words.usage: Literal: able to be touched. Figurative: clear, real, or measurable. Opposite: intangible.

words.task: Give both common senses: dangerous conditions and disloyal behavior.
words.meaning: dangerous, deceptive, disloyal

words.task: Explain who gives the hint and who draws the conclusion.
words.meaning: IMPLY = to suggest something without saying it directly (the speaker or writer sends the hint). INFER = to work out what is meant from clues (the listener or reader draws the conclusion).
words.example: When Mom said 'It's getting late,' she implied we should leave; I inferred from her hint that it was time to go.
words.usage: The sender implies; the receiver infers. The classic mix-up is saying 'Are you inferring that…?' when you mean 'Are you implying that…?'

words.task: Explain in your own words + use it in a sentence about a conversation.
words.meaning: honest and direct, saying what you really think; frank, open, truthful
words.example: Her candid answer was that the cake tasted burnt.

words.task: Give a synonym + an opposite. Then name a job that demands it.
words.meaning: complete and careful, leaving nothing out; detailed, meticulous
words.example: A thorough search of the room finally turned up the keys.
words.usage: Opposite: careless, superficial. A surgeon or an editor needs to be thorough.

words.task: Explain what makes an excuse plausible + use it in a sentence.
words.meaning: seeming likely to be true or reasonable; believable, credible
words.example: His excuse was plausible, so the teacher accepted it.
words.usage: Plausible means it could be true, not that it is proven. Opposite: implausible, far-fetched.

words.task: Explain the connotation — is it positive, negative, or neutral? Say how you know.

words.task: Use it in a sentence about a disagreement, then give a synonym.
words.meaning: (noun) argument, disagreement; (verb) challenge, contest
words.example: There was a constant dispute between Jo and Amy over who had the best taste in fashion.
words.usage: often used with "over" (dispute over the land) or "about" (dispute about the rules); adjective: disputable

words.task: Give one literal meaning and one figurative meaning.
words.meaning: only on the surface; not deep or thorough; shallow

words.usage: Can be physical (a superficial cut) or about thinking (a superficial answer). Opposite: deep, thorough.

words.task: Rank worst to best: mediocre, excellent, poor. Explain your order.
words.meaning: of only average or slightly below-average quality; ordinary, unremarkable, so-so
words.example: The pizza was mediocre—not bad, but nothing special.
words.usage: Mildly negative. Opposite: excellent, outstanding.

words.task: Give a synonym + an opposite, then describe a lenient rule in one sentence.

words.usage: From admire. Opposite: shameful, contemptible.

words.task: Explain in your own words + write a sentence where being skeptical is smart.
words.meaning: doubtful, dubious, questioning, unconvinced, suspicious

words.usage: often followed by about (e.g., skeptical about the plan) or of (e.g., skeptical of his excuses); American spelling uses "k" (British: sceptical); noun forms are skeptic and skepticism
words.connotation: neutral to cautious (can become negative if overly distrustful)

words.task: Explain two common meanings and use each one in a sentence.

words.usage: Concede a point, concede defeat, concede the election. Noun: concession.

words.task: Give a synonym + an opposite, then use it in a sentence about a coach.
words.meaning: praise, applaud, compliment, approve, recommend
words.example: Marmee commended Jo for her honest writing, even when the subject was difficult to discuss.
words.usage: often used with "for" (commended her for her bravery) or "as" (commended as a great leader); noun: commendation

words.task: Explain what a neutral judge does + give one opposite.
words.meaning: impartial, unbiased, unaligned, non-partisan, indifferent (in this sense)
words.example: When Jo and Amy argued over who should get the last piece of cake, Marmee stayed neutral—she listened to both sides and then suggested they share it, rather than choosing a favorite.
words.usage: often used with "in" (neutral in the argument) or "between" (neutral between the two sides); can also mean a color (gray, beige) but the "no side" meaning is key for ISEE

words.task: Explain in your own words + give an example of a hasty decision.

words.usage: often paired with "decision", "departure", or "judgment"; adverb: hastily; noun: haste

words.task: Explain what a fair critique includes + give a synonym.

words.task: Explain the difference between sincere praise and polite praise.

words.usage: Opposite: insincere, fake. Noun: sincerity.

words.task: Explain in your own words + use it in a sentence about a game.

words.usage: often used with "make" (make a blunder) or as a verb (blundered through the test); suggests clumsiness

words.task: Give a synonym + an opposite. Then name something worth scrutinizing.

words.task: Explain two common meanings and which is more common on a test.
