RC.e: The passage shows a class learning how a sound artist makes the everyday sounds in a film, from footsteps in snow to a horse, by hand in a studio.

y.A: A messy garage is only what the studio looked like (line 8); the visit was about the sounds made inside it.
y.B: A girl learning to make a footstep is how the passage ends (lines 31–33), one example of what the students tried, not the subject of the whole visit.
y.D: Celery and coconut shells are two of the objects used for sounds (lines 21–22 and 25–26); the passage is about the sounds, not the objects.

RC.q: When Ms. Castellano says, “Your ears believe whatever your eyes tell them” (lines 22–23), she means that
c: people hear better when they can also see
pictures matter more than sounds in a film
a sound seems real when it matches the picture
the students should watch the screen while they work
RC.e: She says it right after a bag of cornstarch sounded like snow and celery sounded like a branch: when a sound fits what the viewer sees, the viewer accepts it as real.

y.A: Hearing better reads the sentence as being about how sharp our ears are; it is about being fooled, since cornstarch passed for snow once the picture showed snow.
y.B: Pictures mattering more takes the sentence as ranking the two; it is about how the two work together, with the picture making the sound believable.
y.D: Watching the screen is what Mina does later (lines 32–33); the sentence is about an audience's ears and eyes, not instructions for the students.

RC.q: According to the passage, Ms. Castellano made the sound of footsteps in snow by
c: walking in place on a plank
galloping two coconut shells in a tray
squeezing a bag of cornstarch in her fists
RC.e: Lines 18–20 say that for the footsteps in snow she squeezed a bag of cornstarch in her fists, and the crunch sounded real.

y.A: Snapping celery was for the branch the woman broke from the tree (lines 21–22), not for her footsteps.
y.B: Walking in place on a plank is how Mina finally made a footstep on wood at the end (lines 31–33), not how the snow was done.
y.C: Galloping two coconut shells in a tray was a boy's way of making a horse (lines 25–26).

RC.q: In line 33, “fixed” most nearly means
RC.e: Mina kept her eyes on the screen without looking away while she stepped, so her eyes were fixed on it, held steady in one place.

y.A: Closed is the opposite of what Mina was doing; she had to watch the woman's steps on the screen to match them.
y.B: Open describes eyes that are simply awake; fixed says more, that they stayed on one spot, the screen, without moving away.
y.C: Repaired is the everyday meaning of fixed, as in fixing a bike, but eyes are not broken; here fixed means held steady on something.

RC.q: Several students glanced down at their own feet (lines 20–21) most likely because
c: they were choosing shoes from the rack
the crunch seemed to come from under them
they were about to try the sound themselves
Ms. Castellano had told them to watch their steps
RC.e: The crunch was “so real” (line 20) that for a moment the students checked whether the sound of snow had come from their own shoes.

y.A: Choosing shoes from the rack mixes in the rack of shoes in every size from the description of the studio (lines 9–10); nobody is said to pick out shoes.
y.C: Trying the sound themselves comes next, in the fourth paragraph (line 24); at this moment they were still watching the artist.
y.D: Watching their steps is advice Ms. Castellano gives later about how real people walk (lines 29–31), after the students had tried footsteps.

RC.q: The passage provides information to answer which question?
c: Who started the first bike bus?
How long does the ride to school take?
How many riders came on the first morning?
What time does the bike bus reach the school?
RC.e: Lines 15–17 say that on the first morning only four riders showed up; the passage never says who started the first bike bus, how long the ride takes, or when it reaches the school.

y.A: Who started the first bike bus is tempting because a parent leads this one (line 5), but the passage never names a founder or says where the idea began.
y.B: How long the ride takes is not given; the passage says the bus rolls slowly (lines 29–30) but gives no time for the trip.
y.D: What time it reaches the school is not stated; a quarter to eight (line 1) is when the bus pulls up at one corner, not when it arrives at school.

RC.q: According to the second paragraph (lines 6–14), the speaker on the leader's bike plays music so that
c: the riders keep a steady pace
the riders know when to make a turn
drivers will roll their windows down
RC.e: Lines 12–14 say the speaker plays music so the group can be heard coming before it can be seen.

y.B: The riders keeping a steady pace comes from the bus rolling slowly for the youngest legs (lines 29–30), which is the leader's doing, not the music's.
y.C: The riders knowing when to turn is the job of the hand signal before every turn (lines 26–27), not the music.
y.D: Drivers rolling their windows down (lines 21–22) is something they do to listen, in the third paragraph; the second paragraph says the music is there so the group can be heard coming.

RC.q: The author mentions the bike rack (lines 32–34) most likely to show that
c: the bus runs even on rainy mornings
many more children now bike to school
the riders arrive before the first bell
the school should buy a bigger bike rack
RC.e: A rack that once held three or four bikes and is now full before the first bell shows how many children ride to school since the bike bus began.

y.A: Running on rainy mornings is said in line 31, but the rack is brought in after that to show the number of riders, not the weather.
y.C: Arriving before the first bell is when the rack fills (lines 33–34); the point of the sentence is that it fills at all, when it once held three or four bikes.
y.D: A bigger bike rack is a conclusion the passage never draws; the author compares the rack then and now to show the change in riders, not to ask for a new one.

RC.q: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
c: A bike bus follows the same rules as a real bus does.
A speaker on the leader's bike makes the group easy to hear.
Children should not be allowed to bike alone across busy streets.
A bike bus is a safe way for children to ride to school together.
RC.e: Every paragraph describes the bike bus, how it works, how it grew, and why riding together lets children do what they could not do alone, so the passage is about the bike bus as a safe way to get to school.

y.A: Following the rules of a real bus stretches the comparison in lines 6–8, where the leader keeps a route and stops like a bus; the passage is about the children riding, not bus rules.
y.B: The speaker making the group easy to hear is one detail from the second paragraph (lines 12–14), not the idea the whole passage builds.
y.C: Children not biking alone across busy streets comes from lines 24–26, which explain one thing the group makes possible; it is a reason the bike bus helps, not the main idea.

RC.q: The author's attitude toward the bike bus is best described as
RC.e: The author describes the bus warmly, with the waving leader, the growing line, drivers who roll their windows down to listen, and the full bike rack, and points out what it lets children do safely.

y.A: Amused picks up the playful details, like a bus with no engine and wet socks, but the author treats the bike bus as a serious, good idea rather than a joke.
y.C: Doubtful would need the author to question whether the bus works; instead the passage shows it growing from four riders to more than thirty.
y.D: Worried comes from the busy street and the strict rules (lines 24–27), but those are given to show how the group keeps children safe, not to raise alarm.

RC.q: In line 9, “filed” most nearly means
RC.e: The five hens went up the ramp one after another in a line, so filed means marched in single file.

y.A: Cut is what a file does to a fingernail or a piece of metal, but the hens are moving up a ramp, not being shaped.
y.C: Sorted comes from filing papers into folders; the sentence is about hens walking, one behind the other.
y.D: Stored comes from putting papers away in a file; the hens are going up a ramp in a line, not being put away.

RC.q: It can be inferred that Wren brought a book on the third evening because she
c: wanted Pepper to come and sit near her
had finished the chores on the index card
needed to look up how the hens should be cared for
had decided to wait for dark instead of chasing Pepper
RC.e: On the first evening chasing failed and on the second the corn failed, but both times Pepper went in once it was dark; on the third evening Wren settles down early with a book and does not look at the hen, so she has chosen to wait.

y.A: Wanting Pepper near her comes from the hens pecking around her shoes (line 32), but Wren never once glanced at Pepper (lines 33–34); she was not trying to attract her.
y.B: Finishing the chores may well be true, but it does not explain the book; she sat down before the sun had even reached the rooftops (lines 30–31), to pass the time until dark.
y.C: Looking up how to care for hens would send her to the index card (lines 3–5), not a book of chapters; she reads one chapter, then another (lines 32–33).

RC.q: According to the passage, what did Wren use on the second evening to bring the hens in?
RC.e: Lines 24–25 say that on the second evening Wren rattled a handful of corn in a tin cup, and five hens came hurrying.

y.A: The lilac bush is where Pepper hid on the first evening (line 16); Wren did not use it to call the hens.
y.C: The index card held the instructions for the chores (lines 3–5); it had nothing to do with calling the hens in.
y.D: A chapter book is what Wren brought on the third evening (lines 30–33), and she brought it to wait, not to bring the hens in.

RC.q: The main purpose of the first paragraph (lines 1–8) is to
c: show how the other five hens behaved
warn that something might get in at night
explain the responsibility Wren has taken on
RC.e: The first paragraph sets up the story: Mrs. Dombrowski is away, Wren is looking after the hens, and the index card and the warning explain why shutting the door at dusk matters.

y.A: What Pepper looks like, a speckled brown hen, comes in the second paragraph (lines 11–12), after the job has been explained.
y.B: How the other five hens behaved, filing up the ramp on their own, is in the second paragraph (lines 9–11), and it is there to make Pepper stand out.
y.C: The warning about the night is one sentence in the paragraph (lines 7–8), there to show why the door matters; the paragraph as a whole is about Wren's job.

RC.q: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
c: Hens go inside as soon as the sun goes down.
Wren finds that waiting works where chasing failed.
Looking after six hens is too much work for one child.
Pepper is a hen that enjoys being chased around the yard.
RC.e: Chasing Pepper on the first evening and tempting her with corn on the second both fail, yet each night she goes in once it is dark; on the third evening Wren simply waits, and the latch slides home.

y.A: Hens going in as soon as the sun goes down is contradicted by Pepper, who stays out until the first star each evening (lines 28 and 36–38).
y.C: Too much work for one child overstates the trouble; five hens go in by themselves, and Wren manages the sixth by the third evening.
y.D: Enjoying being chased is a guess about Pepper from the first evening (lines 15–18); on the second and third evenings nobody chases her and she still goes in at dark.

MA.q: In the number 473,582, what is the value of the digit 7?
MA.e: Reading from the right, the places are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands. The 7 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 7 × 10,000 = 70,000.

y.A: 7 is the digit itself; the question asks what that digit is worth in its place, and its place is ten thousands.
y.B: 700 is what a 7 is worth in the hundreds place, which is where it lands if the places are counted from the left instead of from the right.
y.C: 7,000 is a 7 in the thousands place, one place to the right of where this 7 sits.

MA.q: The population of Marisol's county was listed in words as three hundred thousand, five hundred eight. How is this number written in standard form?
MA.e: Three hundred thousand is 300,000 and five hundred eight is 508. Together they make 300,508, with a zero holding the tens place because there are no tens.

y.A: 30,508 has only two zeros after the 3, so it says thirty thousand, not three hundred thousand.
y.B: 300,058 puts 58 at the end, as if the number ended in fifty-eight instead of five hundred eight.
y.D: 300,580 ends in five hundred eighty; the 8 belongs in the ones place, with a zero in the tens.

MA.q: The table shows how many cans each grade collected for the food drive. How many cans did the three grades collect in all?

y.A: 4,622 is 2,935 + 1,687, the total with Grade 3's cans left out.
y.B: 5,900 comes from forgetting the 2 carried out of the tens column: the hundreds then add to 19 instead of 21.
y.C: 6,000 is an estimate, 1,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 with each amount rounded to the nearest thousand, not the exact total.

MA.q: A parking garage has 4,000 spaces. One morning 2,358 of the spaces were filled. How many spaces were still empty?
MA.e: Subtract 2,358 from 4,000. Regroup 4,000 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, and 10 ones; then 10 − 8 = 2, 9 − 5 = 4, 9 − 3 = 6, and 3 − 2 = 1, which gives 1,642.

y.B: 1,652 takes 5 from 10 in the tens column instead of from 9, forgetting that the tens had already lent a ten to the ones.
y.C: 1,752 lends a 10 to every column without taking 1 away from the column to its left, so the tens and the hundreds both come out one too big.
y.D: 2,642 keeps all 4 thousands, forgetting that one of them was broken up into hundreds, tens, and ones for the regrouping.

MA.q: A school orders 24 boxes of markers for the art room. Each box holds 36 markers. How many markers does the school order?
MA.e: Multiply 24 × 36. One way: 24 × 30 = 720 and 24 × 6 = 144, and 720 + 144 = 864 markers.

y.A: 60 is 24 + 36, the two numbers added when the question needs 24 groups of 36.
y.B: 216 is 144 + 72: the row for the 3 tens was written straight under the row for the 6 ones instead of being moved one place to the left.
y.C: 744 is 720 + 24, multiplying 20 by 36 and 4 by 6 but never 4 by 30.

MA.q: A print shop has 2,448 flyers to tie into bundles of 24. How many bundles can it make?
MA.e: Divide 2,448 by 24. 24 goes into 24 once, into 4 zero times, and into 48 twice, so the quotient is 102. Check: 24 × 102 = 2,448.

y.A: 12 is the quotient with its middle digit missing: 24 goes into 4 zero times, and that 0 has to be written down before the 8 is brought down.
y.C: 112 writes a 1 in the tens place, but 24 does not go into 4 even once, so that digit is 0.
y.D: 120 puts the zero at the end instead of in the middle, where the 4 came up short; 24 × 120 would be 2,880.

MA.sk: fractions, decimals and percents—fraction of a shaded model
MA.q: The grid is divided into equal squares. What fraction of the grid is shaded?
MA.e: There are 12 equal squares and 9 of them are shaded, so 9/12 of the grid is shaded. Dividing the top and the bottom by 3 gives 3/4.

y.A: 1/4 is the unshaded part: 3 of the 12 squares are white, not shaded.
y.B: 1/3 compares the 3 white squares with the 9 shaded ones instead of with all 12 squares.
y.C: 2/3 counts rows: two rows are fully shaded out of three, but the third row has a shaded square in it as well.

MA.sk: fractions, decimals and percents—mixed numbers on a number line
MA.q: Use the number line to answer the question. What number does point P show?
MA.e: The space between 1 and 2 is cut into 4 equal parts, so each tick mark is 1/4. Point P is 3 ticks past 1, which is 1 3/4.

y.A: 1 1/4 is one tick past 1; point P is three ticks past 1, one tick before 2.
y.B: 1 1/2 is the tick halfway between 1 and 2; point P is one tick further along.
y.C: 1 3/5 comes from counting the 5 tick marks from 1 to 2 and calling each part a fifth; it is the 4 spaces between them that matter, so each part is a fourth.

MA.sk: fractions, decimals and percents—money from a price list
MA.q: The table shows the prices at the school snack stand. Farah buys two muffins and a juice and pays with a $5 bill. How much change should she get?
MA.e: Two muffins cost 2 × $1.35 = $2.70, and with the juice the total is $2.70 + $1.60 = $4.30. From $5.00 that leaves $5.00 − $4.30 = $0.70.

y.B: $1.70 is the change from $3.30, which is what $2.70 + $1.60 comes to if the carry from the tenths is dropped.
y.C: $2.05 is the change after one muffin and a juice, $2.95; the second muffin was left out.
y.D: $4.30 is the cost of the three items, not the change she gets back from $5.

MA.q: Noor's granola recipe uses 2/3 cup of oats and 3/4 cup of nuts. How many cups of oats and nuts does the recipe use altogether?
MA.e: Rewrite both fractions with twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Then 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12, which is 1 5/12 cups.

y.A: 5/12 is the part of 17/12 left after one whole cup is taken out, but the whole cup counts too.
y.B: 1/2 is 2/3 × 3/4, the two amounts multiplied instead of added.
y.C: 5/7 is 2 + 3 over 3 + 4, the tops added and the bottoms added, but fractions can only be added once they have the same bottom number.

MA.q: Elena has 3.5 meters of yarn. She uses 1.85 meters of it to make a scarf. How many meters of yarn does she have left?
MA.e: Write 3.5 as 3.50 so the decimal points line up, then subtract: 3.50 − 1.85 = 1.65 meters.

y.A: 1.20 is 3.05 − 1.85, with the 5 of 3.5 pushed into the hundredths place; 3.5 means 3 and 5 tenths, so it is 3.50.
y.C: 2.35 takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column, 5 from 8 and 0 from 5, instead of regrouping.
y.D: 2.65 regroups a one into the tenths but leaves the 3 whole, as if nothing had been borrowed from the ones.

MA.sk: fractions, decimals and percents—percent from a graph
MA.q: The graph shows how the students in Mr. Okafor's class get to school. What percent of the class rides the bus?
MA.e: Add the bars to find the whole class: 7 + 5 + 6 + 2 = 20 students. The bus bar is 5 of those 20, and 5/20 = 1/4 = 25%.

y.A: 5% is the number of bus riders read as a percent; 5 students out of 20 is a quarter of the class, which is 25%.
y.B: 20% is the size of the whole class written as a percent, not the share of it that rides the bus.
y.D: 35% is the walk bar's share: 7 out of 20 is 35%, but the question asks about the bus.

MA.sk: fractions, decimals and percents—multiplying a decimal
MA.q: A bottle of juice holds 0.6 liter. How many liters of juice are in 8 of these bottles?
MA.e: Multiply 0.6 × 8. Since 6 × 8 = 48 and 0.6 has one decimal place, the product is 4.8 liters.

y.A: 0.48 puts the decimal point two places in, but 0.6 has only one decimal place, so the answer has one too.
y.C: 8.6 is 8 + 0.6, one bottle added to the number of bottles instead of 8 bottles multiplied.
y.D: 48 is 6 × 8 with the decimal point dropped; each bottle holds less than 1 liter, so 8 bottles hold less than 8 liters.

MA.sk: fractions, decimals and percents—fraction to decimal
MA.q: Anika made 7 of her 20 free throws at basketball practice. Which decimal shows the fraction of her free throws that she made?
MA.e: 7 out of 20 is 7/20. Multiply the top and the bottom by 5 to get 35/100, which is 0.35.

y.A: 0.07 is 7 hundredths, as if there had been 100 free throws; 7 out of 20 is 35 out of 100.
y.C: 0.7 is 7 tenths, as if there had been 10 free throws; 7 out of 20 is only 35 hundredths.
y.D: 3.5 is 7 ÷ 2, dividing by 2 instead of 20 and dropping the zero.

MA.q: The number machine uses the same rule on every input number. The table shows some inputs and their outputs. What output does the machine give for an input of 12?
MA.e: Each output is 4 times the input plus 1: 4 × 1 + 1 = 5, 4 × 4 + 1 = 17, and so on. For an input of 12, that is 4 × 12 + 1 = 49.

y.A: 45 is 33 + 12, adding the last jump in the output column again; but the input jumps by 4 this time, from 8 to 12, not by 3 as it did from 5 to 8.
y.B: 48 is 4 × 12, the multiplying step with the 1 at the end forgotten.
y.D: 52 is 13 × 4: the 1 was added to the input before multiplying instead of to the result afterward.

MA.q: Paulo had a bag of marbles. He gave 15 marbles to his sister and had 27 marbles left. If m stands for the number of marbles Paulo started with, which equation could be used to find m?
MA.e: Paulo started with m marbles and gave 15 away, so m − 15 is what he had left, and that was 27. The equation is m − 15 = 27, and m is 42.

y.A: m + 15 = 27 says Paulo gained 15 marbles, but he gave 15 away, so the 15 is taken from m, not added to it.
y.C: 15 − m = 27 takes the starting number away from 15, but Paulo took 15 away from his starting number; and 15 minus anything cannot be 27.
y.D: m + 27 = 15 adds the 27 marbles he kept to the ones he started with, but 27 is part of m, not something added to it.

MA.q: The graph shows the height of Lucia's bean plant at the end of each week. If the plant keeps growing at the same rate, how tall will it be at the end of week 7?
MA.e: The plant grows 4 cm each week: 10, 14, 18, 22. Three more weeks after week 4 add 3 × 4 = 12 cm, so at the end of week 7 it is 22 + 12 = 34 cm tall.

y.A: 28 cm is 4 × 7, the weekly growth times the week number, which leaves out the height the plant already had in week 1.
y.B: 30 cm is the height at the end of week 6, one week short of the week asked about.
y.D: 38 cm is the height at the end of week 8, one week past the one asked about.

MA.q: If 48 ÷ □ = 6, what number does the box stand for?
MA.e: Ask: 48 divided by what number gives 6? Since 6 × 8 = 48, the box stands for 8.

y.B: 42 is 48 − 6, taking away instead of asking what number 48 is divided by.
y.C: 54 is 48 + 6, adding instead of dividing.
y.D: 288 is 48 × 6, multiplying the two numbers instead of dividing 48 by 6 to find the box.

MA.q: Use the coordinate grid to answer the question. What are the coordinates of point K?
MA.e: Start at 0, go 5 units to the right along the bottom and 2 units up. Coordinates are written (right, up), so point K is at (5, 2).

y.A: (2, 5) is point J, 2 to the right and 5 up; it is also what K becomes if the two numbers are written in the wrong order.
y.C: (5, 3) is one unit too high; K sits on the line for 2, not 3.
y.D: (6, 2) is one unit too far to the right; K is directly above the 5 on the bottom axis.

MA.q: The figure shows a rectangle. How many lines of symmetry does the rectangle have?
MA.e: A line of symmetry folds the shape exactly onto itself. A rectangle folds across its middle from side to side and from top to bottom, so it has 2 lines. Its diagonals do not work, because folding along one leaves the corners sticking out.

y.A: 0 would mean no fold matches the rectangle onto itself, but a fold through the middle of the long sides does, and so does a fold through the middle of the short sides.
y.B: 1 counts only the fold across the middle from side to side and misses the fold from top to bottom.
y.D: 4 adds the two diagonals, but a rectangle folded along a diagonal does not line up unless it is a square.

MA.q: The figure shows quadrilateral PQRS on a coordinate grid. Which name best describes PQRS?
MA.e: Side PQ runs along the grid from (1, 1) to (6, 1) and side SR runs from (3, 4) to (8, 4); both are flat and 5 units long, so they are parallel. Sides PS and QR both slant the same way, so they are parallel too. Two pairs of parallel sides and no square corners make a parallelogram.

y.B: rectangle needs four square corners, but the corners at P, Q, R, and S are slanted, not right angles.
y.C: rhombus needs four sides of the same length, but PQ is 5 units long and the slanted side QR is shorter.
y.D: trapezoid has only one pair of parallel sides; here PQ is parallel to SR and PS is also parallel to QR, so there are two pairs.

MA.q: A shoebox is shaped like a rectangular prism. How many faces does a rectangular prism have?
MA.e: A rectangular prism is a box shape. It has a top and a bottom, a front and a back, and a left side and a right side: 6 flat faces in all.

y.A: 4 counts only the four sides around the box and forgets the top and the bottom.
y.C: 8 is the number of corners, or vertices, on a box, not the number of flat faces.
y.D: 12 is the number of edges, the straight lines where two faces meet.

MA.q: The figure shows the shape of Owen's garden, with some of the side lengths labeled. Every side meets the next at a right angle. What is the perimeter of the garden?
MA.e: The two unlabeled sides can be worked out from the others: the short upright side is 6 − 3 = 3 m, and the top side is 8 − 3 = 5 m. Adding all six sides, 8 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 28 m.

y.A: 20 m is 8 + 3 + 3 + 6, the four labeled sides only; the two unlabeled sides are part of the perimeter too.
y.B: 25 m leaves out the unlabeled upright side, which is 6 − 3 = 3 m long.
y.D: 48 m is 8 × 6, the area of a full 8-by-6 rectangle, not the distance around this shape.

MA.q: The figure shows a block built from small cubes. Each small cube has edges 1 centimeter long. What is the volume of the block?
MA.e: The block is 4 cubes long, 2 cubes deep, and 3 cubes high. Each layer has 4 × 2 = 8 cubes and there are 3 layers, so 8 × 3 = 24 cubes, which is 24 cubic centimeters.

y.A: 9 cubic centimeters is 4 + 2 + 3, the three measurements added instead of multiplied.
y.B: 12 cubic centimeters counts only the 4 × 3 cubes on the front face and forgets the layer behind it.
y.D: 26 cubic centimeters counts every small square that can be seen, 12 on the front, 8 on top, and 6 on the side, but some cubes are counted twice that way and the hidden ones not at all.

MA.q: The clock shows the time Hana's swim practice started. Practice ended at 5:10 p.m. How long did the practice last?
MA.e: The clock shows 3:45. From 3:45 to 4:45 is 1 hour, and from 4:45 to 5:10 is 25 more minutes, so practice lasted 1 hour 25 minutes.

y.B: 1 hour 35 minutes takes an hour out of 5:10 but then finds 45 − 10 = 35 instead of 70 − 45 = 25.
y.C: 2 hours 25 minutes gets the 25 minutes right but counts 5 − 3 = 2 hours, forgetting that one of those hours was broken into minutes.
y.D: 2 hours 35 minutes is 5 − 3 hours and 45 − 10 minutes, each pair of numbers subtracted on its own with the smaller taken from the larger.

MA.q: A recipe calls for 1.5 liters of water. Jonah's measuring cup holds 250 milliliters. How many times must he fill the cup to measure out the water?
MA.e: 1 liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 1.5 liters is 1,500 milliliters. Then 1,500 ÷ 250 = 6, because 250 × 6 = 1,500.

y.A: 4 is 1,000 ÷ 250, the number of cups in 1 liter; the half liter still has to be measured.
y.C: 60 is 1,500 ÷ 25, with a zero dropped from the 250 milliliters the cup holds.
y.D: 375 is 1.5 × 250, multiplying when the question asks how many 250s fit into 1,500.

MA.q: The pictograph shows how many books four students read in March. How many books did the four students read in all?
MA.e: Each full circle stands for 4 books and a half circle for 2. Tomas read 14, Greta 8, Yusuf 16, and Clara 6, and 14 + 8 + 16 + 6 = 44 books.

y.A: 11 is the number of circles and half circles drawn, not the number of books; each full circle stands for 4 books.
y.B: 40 is 10 × 4, counting only the whole circles and leaving out the two half circles, which stand for 2 books each.
y.D: 48 is 12 × 4, counting each half circle as a whole one; a half circle is only 2 books.

MA.sk: data and probability—median from a table
MA.q: The table shows Ravi's scores on five spelling tests. What is the median of his scores?
MA.e: Put the scores in order: 15, 16, 19, 20, 20. The median is the middle score, which is 19.

y.A: 15 is the middle number of the list as it is printed; the scores have to be put in order first.
y.B: 18 is the mean: the five scores add to 90, and 90 ÷ 5 = 18. The median is the middle score once they are in order.
y.D: 20 is the mode, the score that appears most often, not the middle score.

MA.sk: data and probability—probability from a spinner
MA.q: The spinner is divided into equal sections. If the spinner is spun once, what is the probability that it lands on blue?
MA.e: There are 8 equal sections and 3 of them are blue, so the probability of blue is 3 out of 8, or 3/8.

y.A: 1/4 counts the four colors and treats blue as one of four equal chances, but the colors do not cover equal numbers of sections.
y.C: 3/5 compares the 3 blue sections with the 5 that are not blue instead of with all 8 sections.
y.D: 5/8 is the probability of not landing on blue: 5 of the 8 sections are other colors.

MA.sk: data and probability—range from a bar graph
MA.q: The graph shows how many goals each team scored this season. What is the range of the numbers of goals?
MA.e: The range is the greatest value minus the least. The Foxes scored the most, 16, and the Owls the fewest, 6, so the range is 16 − 6 = 10.

y.A: 6 is the fewest goals, the Owls' bar, not the gap between the highest and lowest bars.
y.C: 16 is the most goals, the Foxes' bar; the range is how far that is above the lowest bar.
y.D: 22 is 16 + 6, the highest and lowest bars added together instead of subtracted.

VR.e: To dangle is to hang loosely, swinging a little, the way a child’s legs dangle from a high chair or a key dangles from a string.

y.A: Drop means to let something fall; a thing that dangles has not fallen—it is still hanging from something.
y.B: Fasten means to attach something firmly so it stays put; a dangling thing is held only at the top and swings free below.
y.D: Tangle rhymes with dangle, which is the trap; to tangle is to twist string or hair into knots.

VR.e: A foe is an enemy—someone who fights or works against you. The heroes of old stories face their foes.

y.A: Ally is the opposite of a foe: an ally is a friend who is on your side.
y.C: Soldier comes from picturing a battle, where foes are found, but a soldier can just as well be fighting on your own side.
y.D: Stranger is someone you do not know; a stranger is not against you, only unfamiliar.

VR.e: Swiftly means quickly, at great speed. A swift river moves fast, and a fox can dart swiftly into the woods.

y.B: Smoothly describes a movement without bumps or jerks; a slow sled can glide smoothly, so the word says nothing about speed.
y.C: Softly means gently or quietly; a cat can walk softly and slowly at the same time.
y.D: Suddenly means all at once, without warning; it tells when something happens, not how fast it moves.

VR.e: To ascend is to go up or rise, as a hot-air balloon ascends into the sky. Numbers in ascending order go up from smallest to largest.

y.A: Attend sounds like ascend, but it means to be present at something, such as a class or a party.
y.B: Descend is the twin word with the opposite meaning: to go down, as you descend a staircase.
y.C: Hover means to stay in one place in the air, as a hummingbird does at a flower; ascending is moving upward.

VR.e: Absurd means so silly or unreasonable that it makes no sense—ridiculous. Wearing a winter coat to the beach in July would be absurd.

y.A: False means not true; an absurd idea is more than untrue—it is so unreasonable that no one can take it seriously.
y.B: Funny is how people may react to something absurd, since it can make them laugh, but plenty of funny jokes make perfect sense, and absurd means making no sense.
y.D: Rude means impolite; an absurd remark can be perfectly polite and still make no sense.

VR.e: To barter is to trade goods or services without using money—swapping a basket of eggs for a pair of shoes, for example.

y.A: Argue comes from picturing two people haggling over a swap; bartering can involve some back-and-forth, but the word names the exchange itself.
y.B: Buy means to get something by paying money for it, and bartering is trading without money.
y.C: Sell means to give something up in return for money—one half of a sale, not a swap of goods for goods.

VR.e: A feat is an achievement that takes great courage, strength, or skill, such as swimming across a wide lake or balancing a tower of a thousand blocks.

y.B: Effort is the hard work that goes into a feat; a person can make a great effort and still fail, while a feat is something actually done.
y.C: Feast looks like feat with one extra letter, but a feast is a large, rich meal.
y.D: Skill is the ability that makes a feat possible; a feat is the remarkable thing done with it.

VR.e: Arid means very dry, with little or no rain. Deserts are arid—and some of the most arid places on Earth, such as parts of Antarctica, are freezing cold.

y.B: Flat describes the shape of the land, and a desert can be flat, but arid is about how little rain falls.
y.C: Hot is how many deserts feel, which is the trap, but arid means dry: some of the most arid places on Earth are freezing cold.
y.D: Sandy describes what the ground is made of; many deserts are sandy, but a rocky or icy place can be just as arid.

VR.e: To ignite is to set something on fire or to catch fire: a spark can ignite dry leaves. To light a candle is to ignite its wick.

y.A: Explode means to burst apart with great force; a match ignites with a small flame, not a blast.
y.B: Glow means to give off a soft, steady light, like coals after a fire has burned down; it describes shining, not catching fire.
y.D: Melt is what heat does to ice or wax, turning it to liquid, not setting it on fire.

VR.e: A hunch is a guess or a feeling that something is true, without any proof. A detective may have a hunch about who took the jewels before finding a single clue.

y.A: Clue is a piece of evidence, the kind of thing a detective finds; a hunch comes before there is any evidence at all.
y.C: Proof is what shows for certain that something is true—the opposite of a hunch, which has none.
y.D: Rumor is a story passed from person to person; like a hunch it is unproven, but it is something you hear, not a feeling of your own.

VR.e: Eerie means strange in a way that makes you uneasy or a little afraid—creepy. An empty playground at night can feel eerie.

y.A: Airy sounds like eerie, but it means light and open, full of fresh air.
y.B: Chilly means a little cold; an eerie feeling can send a chill down your back, which is the trap, but eerie is about fear, not temperature.
y.D: Haunted means visited by a ghost; an eerie house may seem haunted, but eerie describes the uneasy feeling, not a ghost.

VR.e: To cherish something is to treasure it—to love it and hold it dear, as a person cherishes a letter from a grandparent.

y.A: Collect means to gather things into a group; a person can collect bottle caps without caring much about any of them.
y.B: Protect means to keep something safe; you may protect what you cherish, but cherishing is the love, and protecting is the guarding.
y.C: Remember means to keep something in mind; a person can cherish a memory, but simply remembering it is not holding it dear.

VR.e: To cease is to stop or come to an end. When the rain ceases, it has stopped falling.

y.A: Pause means to stop for a moment and then go on; when something ceases, it stops and does not pick up again.
y.B: Seize sounds almost exactly like cease, but it means to grab something suddenly and firmly.
y.C: Start is the opposite of cease—beginning instead of ending.

VR.e: A deluge is a flood or a downpour—a huge rush of water. The word can also mean a flood of anything, such as a deluge of letters.

y.A: Drizzle is light, fine rain—a rain word, but from the gentle end of the scale, where a deluge pours.
y.B: Drought is a long time with no rain at all, the opposite of a deluge.
y.D: Mist is a cloud of tiny water drops hanging in the air; it is water, but nothing like a rushing flood.

VR.e: Gaunt means very thin and bony, often from hunger or illness: a gaunt face has hollow cheeks.

y.A: Pale describes a washed-out skin color; a gaunt face may also be pale, but gaunt is about how bony it looks, not its color.
y.B: Tall comes from gaunt looking a little like giant, but gaunt has nothing to do with height; a short person can be gaunt.
y.D: Weak means lacking strength; a gaunt person may feel weak, but gaunt describes how thin the person looks.

VR.e: Evidently means clearly or obviously, as the evidence shows. The plate was empty and the dog was licking its lips; evidently, the dog had eaten the toast.

y.A: Eventually looks and sounds like evidently, but it means in the end, after some time has passed.
y.C: Possibly means maybe; evidently is much stronger—it means the evidence makes something plain.
y.D: Secretly means hidden from others, nearly the opposite of evidently, which describes what anyone can see.

VR.e: Stealthy means moving quietly and secretly so as not to be seen or heard—sneaky. A cat creeping up on a bird takes slow, stealthy steps.

y.A: Clumsy is the opposite of stealthy: a clumsy person bumps into things and makes noise.
y.B: Healthy rhymes with stealthy, which is the trap, but it means well and strong.
y.D: Speedy pictures the hunter’s final pounce; a stealthy approach is usually slow and careful, so being quick is not what the word means.

VR.q: A king or queen usually inherits the throne from a parent, but a president must be ____ by the voters.
VR.e: But sets a president against a king or queen who inherits power, so a president must get the job another way: by being chosen in a vote, which is what elected means.

y.A: Crowned is how a new king or queen takes the throne, so it carries the first half of the sentence straight past the but.
y.C: Feared is how people may feel about a ruler, not how a president comes to power, which is what the but sets against inheriting.
y.D: Obeyed is true of a king and a president alike, so it draws no contrast with inheriting the throne.

VR.q: The ____ was so loud and long that the singer came back on stage for one more song.
VR.e: So … that links the sound to its result: an audience calls a singer back for one more song by clapping loud and long, which is applause.

y.B: Chatter is people talking among themselves; it can be loud, but an audience chatting is not asking the singer for another song.
y.C: Laughter is loud too, but people laugh at something funny, and laughing is not how an audience calls a singer back.
y.D: Silence cannot be loud at all; it pictures a hushed audience and skips the words so loud.

VR.q: The porcupine’s quills, the skunk’s spray, and the turtle’s hard shell are all forms of ____.
VR.e: The three examples decide it: quills, a bad-smelling spray, and a hard shell each keep an enemy away, so all three are forms of defense.

y.A: Attack comes from the fact that quills and spray can hurt, but each one is used to drive an enemy away, not to hunt.
y.B: Camouflage is another way animals stay safe, by blending in, but a skunk’s spray does not hide it, so the word does not cover all three examples.
y.C: Decoration treats quills and a shell as parts that look nice, missing what each of the three is for.

VR.q: Although the storm knocked down two trees in our yard, the old maple beside the porch was ____.
VR.e: Although sets the maple against the two fallen trees, so the blank must say the storm did not hurt it: the maple was unharmed.

y.A: Blooming is a pleasant thing for a tree to be, but a tree in flower can still be blown down, so it does not answer the although.
y.B: Toppled means knocked over, which carries the storm’s damage straight onto the maple—the very thing although says did not happen.
y.D: Uprooted means torn out of the ground, roots and all, the same fate as the other two trees, when although calls for the opposite.

VR.q: A ____ is a short story, often about talking animals, that ends with a lesson about how to behave.
VR.e: The sentence gives the definition: a short story with talking animals and a lesson at the end is a fable, like the tale of the tortoise and the hare.

y.A: Biography is the true story of a real person’s life; it is a story, but not a made-up one with talking animals.
y.C: Myth is an old story about gods and heroes, often told to explain something in nature, such as where thunder comes from, rather than a short animal tale with a lesson.
y.D: Poem names writing set out in lines, often with rhythm or rhyme; a poem can tell a story, but the word does not mean a story that teaches a lesson.

VR.q: Since a cactus stores water in its thick stem, it can ____ many months without rain.
VR.e: Since gives the reason the cactus lasts: the water saved in its stem carries it through the dry months, so it can endure them—live through them without harm.

y.A: Avoid treats the cactus as if it could get away from the dry months, but a plant stays where it is and has to live through them.
y.C: Enjoy turns the stored water into a matter of liking dry weather, but since points to the water as what lets the cactus last, not what makes it happy.
y.D: Prevent means to stop something from happening, and no plant can stop the dry months from coming; it can only last through them.

VR.q: Unlike the sun, which makes its own light, the moon shines only because it ____ light from the sun.
VR.e: Unlike tells us the moon does not make light the way the sun does; it shines because sunlight bounces off its surface, which is what reflects means.

y.A: Absorbs is a science word for soaking light up; something that absorbs light looks dark, so absorbing cannot be what makes the moon shine.
y.B: Creates means makes, and making its own light is exactly what unlike says the sun does and the moon does not.
y.D: Stores is how a glow-in-the-dark toy works, saving light to give off later, but the moon does not save sunlight; it shines only while sunlight is falling on it.

VR.q: Because the pioneer family’s covered wagon could carry only so much food, they had to ____ it, eating small portions each day of the long trip west.
VR.e: Because gives the reason: with only a little food for a long trip, the family had to make it last by eating a set small amount each day, which is what ration means.

y.A: Cook is something the family did with their food, but cooking does not make a small supply last any longer.
y.B: Pack is how the food got into the wagon at the start of the trip; packing does not explain eating small portions each day.
y.D: Waste is the opposite of what a family short of food must do; choosing it means reading the sentence as if the wagon held more than enough.

VR.q: The kitchen drawer held all kinds of ____: a wooden spoon, a whisk, a pair of tongs, and a vegetable peeler.
VR.e: The list after the colon decides it: a spoon, a whisk, tongs, and a peeler are small hand tools for cooking and serving, which is what utensils means.

y.A: Appliances are kitchen machines that plug in, like a toaster or a blender; a wooden spoon and a pair of tongs are simple hand tools.
y.B: Ingredients are the foods that go into a dish, such as flour and eggs; the list names tools, not food.
y.C: Recipes are written directions for cooking, something else a cook uses, but a spoon and a whisk are tools, not directions.

VR.q: Because three new students did not yet speak English, the school found an ____ who could explain each lesson to them in Spanish.
VR.e: Because gives the reason the school needed help: students who do not yet speak English need someone to put each lesson into their own language, and that person is an interpreter.

y.A: Announcer is someone who speaks to a crowd, as at a ball game; an announcer talks, but in one language, and does not turn English into Spanish.
y.B: Editor is someone who checks and corrects writing; it is a job with words, but an editor does not change one language into another.
y.C: Inspector is an official who checks that a building or a kitchen follows the rules; a school might have one visit, but not to explain lessons.

VR.q: Most of the paintings in the gallery were bright and cheerful, but one corner held a row of ____ portraits painted in grays and browns.
VR.e: But sets the corner against the bright, cheerful paintings, and the grays and browns confirm it: the portraits were dull and colorless, which is what drab means.

y.A: Dazzling means so bright it almost blinds you; choosing it means reading past the but and keeping the bright, cheerful paintings.
y.C: Miniature means very small; tiny portraits could be bright or dull, so size does nothing to set the corner against the cheerful paintings.
y.D: Realistic means showing people as they really look; a realistic portrait can be full of color, so the word draws no contrast with bright and cheerful.

VR.q: The ____ of a river is the place where it begins, often a small spring or a patch of melting snow high in the mountains.
VR.e: The sentence defines the word: the place where a river begins is its source. The opposite end, where the river empties into a lake or the sea, is its mouth.

y.A: Bank is the land along a river’s side, which runs the river’s whole length rather than marking where it starts.
y.B: Delta is the fan of land that can build up at a river’s far end, where it spreads into the sea—the opposite end from where it begins.
y.C: Mouth sounds like a beginning, the way eating starts at your mouth, but a river’s mouth is where it ends, emptying into a lake or the sea.

c: have a beak and webbed feet
VR.e: Yet warns that what comes next goes against what we expect: wings usually mean flying, so the surprise is that penguins cannot fly—they use their wings to swim instead.

y.A: Lay eggs like other birds is true of penguins, but it shows how they are like other birds, when yet calls for something that goes against having wings.
y.C: Have a beak and webbed feet describes the penguin’s body without saying anything against its wings, so yet has nothing to turn on.
y.D: Are covered in thick feathers is one more way penguins match other birds; it agrees with having wings instead of going against it.

VR.q: Since the library would close in five minutes, Felipe ____.
c: sat down to start a long book
hurried to check out his books
asked when the library was built
admired the fish tank in the lobby
VR.e: Since gives the reason for what Felipe did: with only five minutes left before closing, he had to be quick, so he hurried to check out his books.

y.A: Sat down to start a long book ignores the five minutes; a long book takes hours, and the library was about to close.
y.C: Asked when the library was built is a question with nothing to do with the closing time, so it does not follow from since.
y.D: Admired the fish tank in the lobby is lingering, the reverse of what a library closing in five minutes calls for.

VR.q: Before the telephone was invented, people who lived far apart could not talk to each other directly; instead, they ____.
VR.e: Instead points to what people did in place of talking: with no telephone, the way to reach someone far away was to write, so they wrote letters to one another.

y.A: Sent emails back and forth pictures how people keep in touch today, but email came long after the telephone, so these people could not have had it.
y.C: Called one another every Sunday needs the very telephone the sentence says had not yet been invented.
y.D: Visited each other every evening forgets that these people lived far apart; a visit every night was impossible, which is why they needed another way.

VR.q: Although the play was a comedy, its final scene ____.
c: had the whole cast on stage
took place in a busy kitchen
made many in the audience cry
was the shortest one in the play
VR.e: Although sets up a surprise: a comedy is meant to make people laugh, so the last scene must go the other way—it made many in the audience cry.

y.A: Had the whole cast on stage tells who was in the scene, which a comedy could have just as easily, so there is nothing in it for although to work against.
y.B: Took place in a busy kitchen gives the setting, and a funny scene can happen in a kitchen as well as anywhere, so it draws no contrast with comedy.
y.D: Was the shortest one in the play describes the scene’s length, not its mood, so it does not go against the play being a comedy.

VR.q: Rather than guessing which paper towel would soak up the most water, the class ____.
c: chose the one that felt softest
voted on which brand looked best
measured the water each towel held
picked the towel that seemed thickest
VR.e: Rather than tells us the class did not guess, so the ending must be a real test: they measured how much water each towel held.

y.A: Chose the one that felt softest is still a guess: softness is how a towel feels, not a test of how much water it holds.
y.B: Voted on which brand looked best shows what the class thought, not what the towels could do; a vote is a guess made by many people at once.
y.D: Picked the towel that seemed thickest judges by how the towel looks, which is exactly the kind of guessing that rather than says the class did not do.

QR.q: The Pinewood School library has 3,958 books. It receives a gift of 100 new books. How many books does the library have now?
QR.e: Adding 100 adds 1 to the hundreds digit. The library has 9 hundreds, and 10 hundreds make a new thousand, so 3,958 + 100 = 4,058.

y.A: 3,058 changes the 9 hundreds to 0 but forgets to carry the new thousand into the thousands place.
y.B: 3,968 adds 10, one ten, instead of 100, one hundred.
y.D: 4,958 adds 1,000 by raising the thousands digit instead of the hundreds digit.

QR.q: The graph shows how many cups of lemonade Tobias sold at his stand each afternoon. How many more cups did he sell on Tuesday than on Thursday?
QR.e: Tuesday's bar reaches 14 and Thursday's bar reaches 6, and 14 − 6 = 8.

y.A: 2 is 14 − 12, comparing Tuesday with Monday, the bar just before it, instead of with Thursday.
y.B: 4 is 14 − 10, comparing Tuesday with Wednesday, the bar just after it, instead of with Thursday.
y.C: 6 is the height of Thursday's bar alone, not the difference between the two days.

QR.sk: Algebra—missing factor from a pictograph key
QR.q: The pictograph shows how many raffle tickets a class sold each day, but the number of tickets each symbol stands for is missing from the key. The class sold 36 tickets on Monday. How many tickets does each symbol stand for?
QR.e: Monday's row has 4 symbols for 36 tickets, so 4 × □ = 36. Since 4 × 9 = 36, each symbol stands for 9 tickets.

y.A: 4 is the number of symbols in Monday's row, not the number of tickets each one stands for.
y.C: 32 is 36 − 4, taking the 4 symbols away from the tickets instead of sharing the tickets among the symbols.
y.D: 144 is 36 × 4, multiplying the tickets by the symbols instead of dividing.

QR.q: The movie at the school's Friday movie night is 2 hours 15 minutes long. How many minutes long is the movie?
QR.e: Each hour is 60 minutes, so 2 hours is 120 minutes, and 120 + 15 = 135 minutes.

y.A: 75 minutes is 60 + 15, counting only one of the two hours.
y.B: 120 minutes is the 2 hours alone; the extra 15 minutes are left out.
y.D: 215 minutes writes the 2 hours and the 15 minutes side by side, as if an hour were 100 minutes.

QR.q: The circle shows a round rug made of equal sections. The shaded sections are blue. Which decimal names the part of the rug that is blue?
QR.e: The rug has 10 equal sections and 4 of them are shaded, so 4/10 of the rug is blue. Four tenths is written 0.4.

y.A: 0.04 is four hundredths; the rug has 10 equal sections, so 4 sections are four tenths.
y.C: 0.6 is the part of the rug that is not blue, 6 of the 10 sections.
y.D: 4 is the number of blue sections, not the part of the whole rug they make.

QR.q: Each ride at the county fair costs $6. Hiro has $45. What is the greatest number of rides he can pay for?
QR.e: 7 rides cost 7 × $6 = $42, and the $3 left over is not enough for another ride. So 7 rides is the most he can pay for.

y.A: 3 is the number of dollars left over after 7 rides, not the number of rides.
y.C: 8 rounds 45 ÷ 6, which is 7 with $3 left over, up to the next whole number, but the leftover $3 cannot pay for an eighth ride.
y.D: 39 is 45 − 6, the money left after one ride, not the number of rides.

QR.q: The Ruiz family saved 3,450 pennies in a jar. They stack the pennies in piles of 10. How many full piles can they make?
QR.e: Every 10 pennies make one pile, so the number of piles is the number of tens in 3,450, which is 345.

y.A: 5 is the digit in the tens place; it leaves out the tens that are inside the hundreds and thousands.
y.B: 34 is the number of hundreds in 3,450, the piles there would be if each pile held 100 pennies.
y.D: 3,440 is 3,450 − 10, taking away one pile instead of finding how many piles there are.

QR.q: The pictograph shows how many loaves of bread a bakery sold each day. How many more loaves were sold on Tuesday than on Monday?
QR.e: Monday has 2 whole symbols and a half symbol, which is 8 + 2 = 10 loaves. Tuesday has 6 symbols, which is 24 loaves. 24 − 10 = 14.

y.A: 12 counts Monday's half symbol as a whole one: Monday looks like 3 symbols, or 12 loaves, and 24 − 12 = 12.
y.C: 16 leaves out Monday's half symbol: Monday looks like 2 symbols, or 8 loaves, and 24 − 8 = 16.
y.D: 34 is 10 + 24, the loaves for Monday and Tuesday added together.

QR.q: Soren built the stack shown from identical cubes, with no gaps or hidden holes. He wants to build a second stack that is just as deep and just as tall but twice as wide. How many cubes will the second stack need?
QR.e: The stack shown is 5 cubes wide, 3 deep, and 2 tall, so it has 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cubes. Twice as wide is 10 cubes wide, and 10 × 3 × 2 = 60 cubes.

y.A: 20 is 10 × 2, only the cubes on the front face of the new stack; it is also 3 cubes deep.
y.B: 30 is the number of cubes in the stack shown, not in the stack that is twice as wide.
y.C: 35 adds just 5 cubes for the 5 extra cubes across the front, but each of those is a whole new column of 3 × 2 = 6 cubes.

QR.q: The bar shows a board 15 feet long cut into equal pieces. Rohan uses the shaded pieces to build a shelf. How many feet of the board does he use?
QR.e: The board is cut into 5 equal pieces, so each piece is 15 ÷ 5 = 3 feet. Rohan uses 3 pieces, and 3 × 3 = 9 feet.

y.A: 3 feet is the length of one piece, 15 ÷ 5; Rohan uses three pieces.
y.B: 5 feet is the number of pieces the board is cut into, not a length of board.
y.C: 6 feet is the part of the board that is not shaded, the 2 pieces Rohan does not use.

QR.q: The Venn diagram shows the sandwiches a deli made one morning: sandwiches with cheese, sandwiches with tomato, and sandwiches with both. Sandwiches outside the circles have neither. How many sandwiches had exactly one of the two fillings?
QR.e: A sandwich with exactly one filling is in one circle but not in the overlap: 6 have only cheese and 5 have only tomato, and 6 + 5 = 11.

y.A: 3 is the number in the overlap, the sandwiches with both cheese and tomato.
y.C: 14 is 6 + 3 + 5, every sandwich inside the circles, including the 3 with both fillings.
y.D: 18 is every sandwich in the diagram, including the 4 outside the circles with neither filling.

QR.q: The graph shows how many people visited a school book fair each day. On how many days were there more than 30 visitors?
QR.e: Tuesday (35), Thursday (40), and Friday (45) are above 30. Wednesday is exactly 30, which is not more than 30, so the answer is 3 days.

y.A: 1 counts the days with fewer than 30 visitors, which is only Monday.
y.B: 2 counts the days with 30 visitors or fewer, Monday and Wednesday.
y.D: 4 counts Wednesday too, but 30 visitors is not more than 30.

QR.q: A leaky faucet drips 3 drops every 10 seconds. At this rate, how many drops does it drip in 1 minute?
QR.e: One minute is 60 seconds, which is 6 groups of 10 seconds. Each group has 3 drops, so 6 × 3 = 18 drops.

y.A: 6 is the number of 10-second groups in a minute, not the number of drops.
y.C: 30 is 3 × 10, multiplying the two numbers in the question.
y.D: 180 is 3 × 60, as if the faucet dripped 3 drops every second instead of every 10 seconds.

QR.q: The clock shows the time Celia started walking her dog one afternoon. The walk lasted 25 minutes. At what time did the walk end?
QR.e: The clock shows 2:50. Ten minutes later it is 3:00, and 15 more minutes makes 3:15 p.m.

y.A: 2:15 p.m. gets the 15 minutes past the hour but keeps the hour at 2 instead of moving on to 3.
y.B: 2:35 p.m. reads the minute hand, which points at the 10, as 10 minutes, and 2:10 plus 25 minutes is 2:35.
y.D: 4:15 p.m. reads the short hand, which is nearly at the 3, as 3 o'clock, so the start looks like 3:50 instead of 2:50.

QR.q: The number line shows a ruler marked in inches. Tariq lays a crayon along the ruler from point S to point T. How long is the crayon?
QR.e: The crayon starts at 2 and ends at 5 1/2. From 2 to 5 is 3 inches, and the half inch from 5 to 5 1/2 makes 3 1/2 inches.

y.A: 3 inches counts the whole inches from 2 to 5 and drops the last half inch.
y.C: 5 1/2 inches is the mark where the crayon ends; the crayon starts at 2, not at 0.
y.D: 7 1/2 inches is 2 + 5 1/2, adding the two marks instead of finding the distance between them.

QR.q: A garden bed is drawn on the coordinate grid. Each unit on the grid stands for 1 meter. What is the perimeter of the garden bed?
QR.e: The bed runs from 2 to 7 across, which is 5 meters, and from 1 to 4 up, which is 3 meters. The perimeter is 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 meters.

y.A: 8 meters is 5 + 3, one length and one width; the perimeter goes around all four sides.
y.B: 15 meters is 5 × 3, the area in square meters, not the distance around the bed.
y.D: 22 meters doubles 7 + 4, the coordinates of the top right corner, instead of the side lengths 5 and 3.

QR.q: Leila knows that 15 × 12 = 180. She uses this fact to find 15 × 13. What is 15 × 13?
QR.e: 15 × 13 is one more group of 15 than 15 × 12, so it is 180 + 15 = 195.

y.A: 181 is 180 + 1, adding one instead of one more group of 15.
y.B: 192 is 180 + 12, adding the 12 from the known fact instead of another 15.
y.C: 193 is 180 + 13, adding 13 instead of one more group of 15.

QR.sk: Symmetry—completing a shape from its half
QR.q: The figure shows half of a paper cutout. The dashed side is the fold, which is the cutout's line of symmetry. What is the perimeter of the whole cutout?
QR.e: The other half is a mirror image, so every side except the fold appears twice: 2 × (9 + 5 + 6) = 40 cm. The fold is inside the whole cutout, so it is not part of the perimeter.

y.A: 20 cm is 9 + 5 + 6, the outside edges of the half that is drawn; the mirror half has the same edges again.
y.B: 24 cm is the perimeter of the half that is drawn, 9 + 5 + 6 + 4, which counts the fold as an edge.
y.D: 48 cm doubles 24, the perimeter of the drawn half, so the fold is counted twice, but the fold is inside the whole cutout.

QR.q: The table shows how many steps four friends walked on Saturday. Which is the best estimate of how many more steps Hector walked than Zoe?
QR.e: Round each number to the nearest thousand: 6,912 is about 7,000 and 3,105 is about 3,000, and 7,000 − 3,000 = 4,000.

y.A: 2,000 is 7,000 − 5,000, comparing Hector with Abel, whose 4,870 steps round to 5,000, instead of with Zoe.
y.B: 3,000 is 6,000 − 3,000, cutting 6,912 down to 6,000 instead of rounding it up to 7,000.
y.D: 10,000 is 7,000 + 3,000, adding the two amounts instead of finding the difference.

QR.q: The spinner has 7 equal sections. If the arrow is spun once, what is the probability that it will not land on red?
QR.e: 3 of the 7 equal sections are not red, 2 blue and 1 green, so the probability is 3 out of 7, or 3/7.

y.B: 4/7 is the probability of landing on red, the 4 red sections out of 7.
y.C: 2/3 counts colors instead of sections: 2 of the 3 colors are not red, but red has more sections than the other colors.
y.D: 3/4 compares the 3 sections that are not red with the 4 red sections instead of with all 7 sections.

QR.sk: Algebra—writing an equation from a story
QR.q: A school had 50 posters for its spring play. Volunteers put up the same number of posters, p, in each of 3 hallways, and 14 posters were left over. Which equation could be used to find p?
QR.e: Each of the 3 hallways got p posters, so 3 × p posters were put up. Taking them away from 50 leaves 14, so 50 − 3 × p = 14.

y.A: 50 − 14 = p finds all the posters that were put up, 36, but p is the number in just one of the 3 hallways.
y.B: 50 − 3 − p = 14 takes away 3 posters and then p more, but 3 hallways of p posters is 3 × p posters.
y.D: 50 + 3 × p = 14 adds the posters that were put up, but putting posters up takes them out of the pile.

QR.q: The map shows Ivy's home and the town pool on a grid. Each unit on the grid stands for 50 meters. Ivy walks in a straight line from her home to the pool. How far does she walk?
QR.e: Home is at 1 and the pool is at 7 along the same row, so they are 7 − 1 = 6 units apart. Each unit is 50 meters, and 6 × 50 = 300 meters.

y.A: 6 meters counts the grid units between home and the pool but leaves out the scale of 50 meters for each unit.
y.C: 350 meters is 7 × 50, using the pool's place on the grid, 7, as the distance, but Ivy starts at 1, not at 0.
y.D: 400 meters is 8 × 50, adding the two places, 1 + 7, instead of finding the distance between them.

QR.sk: Median—finding the median from a bar graph
QR.q: The graph shows how many puzzles Dario solved each day for five days. What is the median number of puzzles he solved?
QR.e: Put the numbers in order: 3, 5, 6, 9, 12. The median is the middle number, 6.

y.B: 7 is the mean, the 35 puzzles shared equally among the 5 days, not the middle value.
y.C: 9 is the range, the difference between the most puzzles, 12, and the fewest, 3.
y.D: 12 is the middle bar as the days are drawn, Wednesday; the median is the middle number after the numbers are put in order.

QR.q: Gabe folds a square sheet of paper in half, then in half again, and then in half a third time. He punches one hole through all the layers of the folded paper. When he unfolds the paper, how many holes will it have?
QR.e: Each fold doubles the layers: 2 layers after the first fold, 4 after the second, and 8 after the third. The punch goes through all 8 layers, so the paper has 8 holes.

y.A: 3 counts one hole for each fold, but the punch goes through every layer of the folded paper.
y.B: 4 counts the layers after only two folds; the third fold doubles the layers again.
y.C: 6 adds 2 layers for each of the 3 folds, but each fold doubles the layers: 2, then 4, then 8.

QR.q: Odette strings beads in a repeating pattern: red, blue, green, yellow, then red, blue, green, yellow again, and so on. What color is the 39th bead?
QR.e: The pattern repeats every 4 beads, so beads 4, 8, 12, and so on up to 36 are yellow. Then the pattern starts again: bead 37 is red, bead 38 is blue, and bead 39 is green.

y.A: blue is bead 38, one bead before the 39th.
y.C: red comes from using 9, the number of whole groups of 4 in 39, as the place in the pattern; the 9th bead is red, but the 39th is not.
y.D: yellow is bead 36, the last bead of the 9th whole group; bead 39 is three beads later.

QR.sk: Pattern—extending a pattern in a table
QR.q: Square tables are pushed together in a row for a class party. The table shows how many chairs fit around different numbers of tables. If the pattern continues, how many chairs fit around 9 tables?
QR.e: Each new table adds 2 chairs. From 4 tables with 10 chairs, 5 more tables add 5 × 2 = 10 chairs, so 9 tables have 20 chairs.

y.A: 18 is 2 × 9, two chairs for each table, which leaves out the chair at each end of the row.
y.C: 22 is the number of chairs for 10 tables; the count goes one table too far.
y.D: 36 is 4 × 9, as if every table stood alone with 4 chairs; tables pushed together lose the chairs between them.

QR.q: Kai is thinking of a number between 30 and 60. It is a multiple of 7, and its two digits add up to 8. What is Kai's number?
QR.e: The multiples of 7 between 30 and 60 are 35, 42, 49, and 56. Only 35 has digits that add up to 8, because 3 + 5 = 8.

y.B: 42 stops after the first two clues: it is a multiple of 7 between 30 and 60, but its digits add up to 6, not 8.
y.C: 44 has digits that add up to 8, but it is not a multiple of 7; it checks the digit clue and skips the other.
y.D: 56 is the largest multiple of 7 below 60, but its digits add up to 11, not 8.

QR.sk: Area—covering a rectangle with square tiles
QR.q: A hallway floor is a rectangle 8 feet long and 6 feet wide. It is covered with square tiles that are each 2 feet long and 2 feet wide. How many tiles cover the floor?
QR.e: Along the 8-foot side, 8 ÷ 2 = 4 tiles fit, and along the 6-foot side, 6 ÷ 2 = 3 tiles fit. That makes 4 rows of 3 tiles, and 4 × 3 = 12 tiles.

y.A: 3 is the number of tiles along the 6-foot side only, just one row of the floor.
y.B: 4 is the number of tiles along the 8-foot side only, just one row of the floor.
y.C: 7 is 4 + 3, adding the tiles along the two sides instead of multiplying them.

QR.sk: Percent—percent of a number as a fraction
QR.q: Yara's book has 80 pages. She has read 25% of the book. How many pages does she still have to read?
QR.e: 25% is the same as 1/4. One fourth of 80 pages is 20 pages read, so 80 − 20 = 60 pages are left.

y.A: 20 is the number of pages she has already read, 1/4 of 80, not the pages left.
y.B: 55 is 80 − 25, treating 25% as 25 pages instead of one fourth of the book.
y.D: 75 is the percent of the book still to read, 100 − 25, written as if it were a number of pages.

QR.q: A cup of hot cocoa costs $2. Bianca has $15, and she must keep $3 for the bus ride home. What is the greatest number of cups of cocoa she can buy?
QR.e: After keeping $3 for the bus, Bianca has $15 − $3 = $12 to spend. Each cup costs $2, and 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cups.

y.B: 7 spends all $15 on cocoa, 7 cups with $1 left, and forgets the $3 she must keep for the bus.
y.C: 9 is 18 ÷ 2, adding the $3 for the bus to her money instead of setting it aside.
y.D: 12 is the number of dollars she can spend, $15 − $3, not the number of cups.

QR.q: Vera saves money each week. She saves $3 the first week, $5 the second week, and $7 the third week, and she keeps saving $2 more each week than the week before. How much money will she have saved in all after 6 weeks?
QR.e: Week by week she saves $3, $5, $7, $9, $11, and $13. Altogether that is 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 = $48.

y.A: $13 is the amount she saves in the sixth week alone, not the total of all six weeks.
y.B: $18 is 6 × $3, as if she saved $3 every week instead of $2 more each week.
y.C: $35 is the total after 5 weeks, 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11; the sixth week's $13 is left out.

QR.sk: Fractions—equal jumps on a number line
QR.q: Kenji makes equal jumps along the number line, starting at 0. The points show where he lands after each of his first three jumps. If he keeps jumping the same distance, where will he land after his fifth jump?
QR.e: Each jump covers 3 of the quarter marks, so each jump is 3/4. Five jumps land at 5 × 3/4 = 15/4, which is 3 3/4.

y.A: 3 is where he lands after four jumps, 4 × 3/4; the question asks about the fifth jump.
y.C: 4 1/2 is where he lands after six jumps; one jump too many is counted.
y.D: 5 3/4 adds 5 and 3/4 instead of taking 5 jumps of 3/4 each.

QR.q: The figure shows a triangle with three equal sides. A square has the same perimeter as the triangle. How long is each side of the square?
QR.e: The triangle's perimeter is 3 × 20 = 60 cm. A square with a perimeter of 60 cm has four equal sides, each 60 ÷ 4 = 15 cm long.

y.B: 20 cm is the side of the triangle; the square has the same perimeter, not the same side length.
y.C: 60 cm is the perimeter of the triangle, the distance around the whole square, not one side.
y.D: 80 cm is 4 × 20, the perimeter of a square whose sides are as long as the triangle's, not the length of one side.

QR.q: The window in the figure is made of 9 square panes of glass, all the same size. How many squares of any size can be found in the window?
QR.e: There are 9 single panes, 4 squares made of 2 × 2 panes (they overlap), and 1 large square made of the whole window: 9 + 4 + 1 = 14.

y.A: 9 counts only the single panes, not the bigger squares made of several panes.
y.B: 10 counts the 9 single panes and the whole window but misses the 4 squares made of 2 × 2 panes.
y.C: 13 counts the single panes and the 4 squares made of 2 × 2 panes but leaves out the whole window, which is a square too.

QR.sk: Perimeter—perimeter from area and one side
QR.q: The figure shows a rectangle, one of its side lengths, and its area. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
QR.e: The other side is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 cm, because 8 × 5 = 40. The perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm.

y.A: 13 cm is 8 + 5, one length and one width; the perimeter goes around all four sides.
y.B: 16 cm is 8 + 8, the two long sides only; the two 5-cm sides are left out.
y.D: 40 cm is the area of the rectangle in square centimeters, not the distance around it.

QR.q: At a farm stand, one melon weighs the same as 4 apples. A melon and an apple together weigh 1,000 grams. How much does one apple weigh?
QR.e: A melon weighs the same as 4 apples, so a melon and an apple weigh the same as 5 apples. 5 apples weigh 1,000 grams, so one apple weighs 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 grams.

y.B: 250 grams is 1,000 ÷ 4, sharing the weight among 4 apples and forgetting the apple that is on the scale beside the melon.
y.C: 500 grams is 1,000 ÷ 2, splitting the weight evenly as if the melon and the apple weighed the same.
y.D: 800 grams is the weight of the melon, 4 apples of 200 grams, not of one apple.

QR.q: The points on the grid follow a pattern. If the pattern continues, what is the y-coordinate of the point whose x-coordinate is 6?
QR.e: Each time the x-coordinate goes up 1, the y-coordinate goes up 2. After (4, 9) come (5, 11) and (6, 13), so the y-coordinate is 13.

y.A: 8 is 6 + 2, an add-2 rule taken from the first point, (1, 3), that does not fit the other points.
y.B: 11 is the y-coordinate when x is 5, one point short of x = 6.
y.C: 12 is 2 × 6, doubling the x-coordinate but forgetting the 1 more that every point has.

QR.q: The table shows the balloons in a bag. Uma adds 1 more blue balloon to the bag. Then she pulls out one balloon without looking. What is the probability that she pulls out a blue balloon?
QR.e: After Uma adds the balloon, there are 3 + 1 = 4 blue balloons and 12 + 1 = 13 balloons in all, so the probability is 4 out of 13, or 4/13.

y.A: 3/13 counts the new balloon in the total but not as a blue balloon: 3 blue out of 13.
y.B: 1/4 is the chance before the balloon is added, 3 blue out of 12.
y.D: 1/3 counts the new balloon as blue but leaves the total at 12: 4 blue out of 12.

RC.q: What does Mr. Ferreira most likely mean when he says that “nobody looks at a pile” but “everybody watches a show” (lines 8–10)?
c: the lost-and-found box was too full to search
the loudspeaker reminders were too quiet to hear
students cared more about shows than about clothes
students would notice their things if each one was shown
RC.e: A pile is easy to walk past, but people watch a show closely; Mr. Ferreira expects students to spot their own things once each one is shown on the runway, and in lines 26–32 that is what happens.

y.A: Too full to search takes “nobody looks at a pile” to mean the box was hard to dig through; he means a pile is easy to ignore, and his answer is a show people will watch.
y.B: Reminders too quiet to hear comes from the Monday announcements in lines 5–6, but Mr. Ferreira is not talking about the announcements; he is comparing a pile with a show.
y.C: Caring more about shows than clothes reads his words as a complaint about students; he is explaining why showing the clothes one outfit at a time would make students look at them.

RC.q: According to the passage, what happened to most of the things that no one claimed?
c: They were given to a clothing drive.
They were kept on the office windowsill.
They were put back in the box by the gym.
They were sorted into outfits for the models.
RC.e: Lines 33–35 say that after the assembly the rest were washed, folded, and given to a clothing drive downtown; only the rain boot stayed behind.

y.B: Kept on the office windowsill is what happened to the purple rain boot alone (lines 35–37), the one thing left over; the rest went to the clothing drive.
y.C: Put back in the box by the gym is where the things had piled up before the show (lines 1–2); after the assembly the rest were washed, folded, and given away (lines 34–35).
y.D: Sorted into outfits is what the models did on Thursday, before the show (lines 14–16), not what happened to the leftovers afterward.

RC.q: In line 35, “drive” most nearly means
RC.e: The leftover clothes were washed, folded, and given to the clothing drive, so here drive means a collection of things gathered for people who need them.

y.B: Determination is the drive a person has to keep at something, but the sentence is about where the folded clothes were given, not about anyone's effort.
y.C: Road is a drive in a street name, and “downtown” makes a place seem right, but clothes are given to people collecting them, not to a road.
y.D: Trip is a drive in a car, and “downtown” suggests one, but you cannot give clothes to a trip; a clothing drive gathers clothes for people who need them.

RC.q: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
c: The fifth grade learned how to put outfits together.
A kindergartner found the jacket his brother had lost.
A fashion show helped students find things they had lost.
Students learned to take better care of the things they own.
RC.e: The passage begins with a mountain of lost things, follows the fashion show, and ends with forty-one items claimed, so it is about a show that got lost things back to their owners.

y.A: The fifth grade putting outfits together is what the models did on Thursday (lines 14–16), one step in getting ready for the show, not the idea of the whole passage.
y.B: A kindergartner finding his brother's jacket is one moment at the show (lines 29–32), an example of things being claimed, not the main idea.
y.D: Taking better care of their things is a lesson a reader might expect, but the passage never says anyone learned it; it ends with the boot on the windowsill, not with a lesson.

RC.q: Which word best describes how the author feels about the fashion show?
RC.e: The author describes the show with funny details, a cheering gym, and forty-one items claimed, and even jokes about the leftover boot, so the author is pleased with how it went.

y.A: Embarrassed picks up the raincoat that was much too big and the boot worn with a sneaker (lines 16–18), but the author tells those details as jokes, and the models strutted and posed (lines 21–22).
y.B: Impatient fits the first paragraph, where the mountain grew taller every Monday (lines 5–7), but that is about the pile before the show, not the show itself.
y.C: Nervous is how a model in front of the whole school might be expected to feel, but the author says they strutted to the end of the runway and posed (lines 21–22).

RC.q: In line 26, “check” most nearly means
RC.e: Where there are plenty of otters the urchins stay few, and where the otters disappear the urchins multiply (lines 25–27), so keeping the urchins in check means keeping them under control.

y.A: Bill is the check a waiter brings at a restaurant, but nobody is paying for anything; the sentence is about otters holding down the number of urchins.
y.C: Inspection is a check-up, the kind a doctor gives, but the otters do not look the urchins over; they eat them, so the urchins cannot multiply (lines 25–27).
y.D: Mark is the check made in a box on a list, which has nothing to do with otters and urchins under the sea.

RC.q: According to the passage, what keeps a sea otter warm?
c: air trapped in its thick fur
a strand of kelp wrapped around it
resting close to other otters in a raft
RC.e: Lines 6–11 say that sea otters have no blubber and instead rely on the densest fur of any animal, which traps tiny bubbles of air that keep the cold water away from their skin.

y.A: A thick layer of blubber is what keeps seals warm, and line 6 says sea otters have none, which is why they rely on their fur instead.
y.C: A strand of kelp keeps a napping otter from drifting away (lines 3–4), not from getting cold.
y.D: Resting close to other otters is what a raft is (lines 4–5), but the passage never says it keeps them warm; it gives that job to the air in the fur (lines 9–11).

RC.q: Based on the passage, what most likely happened to many kelp forests while hunters were killing most of the sea otters?
c: They were protected by the treaty of 1911.
They were safe, since urchins stay on the bottom.
They grew larger, because otters had eaten the kelp.
Urchins multiplied and chewed them down to bare sea floor.
RC.e: Lines 25–28 say that where otters disappear, urchins multiply and chew through the kelp; with hunters killing most of the otters (lines 30–32), the same thing would have happened to many kelp forests.

y.A: Protected by the treaty of 1911 stretches lines 32–33; the treaty protected the otters, not the kelp, and it came only after more than a hundred years of hunting.
y.B: Safe because urchins stay on the bottom comes from otters diving to the bottom for urchins (line 15), but lines 26–28 say urchins chew through a kelp forest when the otters disappear.
y.C: Grew larger because otters ate the kelp mixes up who eats what: otters eat urchins (lines 15–16) and only wrap themselves in kelp (lines 3–4), and it is the urchins that feed on kelp (line 22).

RC.q: The passage is mainly about
c: how sea otters use rocks to open shells
how sea otters live and why kelp forests need them
why hunters wanted the thick, soft fur of sea otters
how kelp forests can turn into bare patches of sea floor
RC.e: The passage describes how otters eat, rest, and stay warm, explains that by eating urchins they protect kelp forests, and ends with how they nearly disappeared and then recovered.

y.A: Using rocks to open shells is one detail of how an otter eats (lines 18–20), part of the third paragraph, not the subject of the whole passage.
y.C: Hunters wanting the fur is how the last paragraph begins (lines 30–31); it explains why otters nearly vanished, one part of their story.
y.D: Kelp forests turning into bare sea floor is what happens where otters disappear (lines 26–29); it shows why otters matter, but the passage is about the otters themselves.

RC.q: The passage provides information to answer which question?
c: How long does a sea otter live?
How deep does a sea otter dive for its food?
How much food does a sea otter need each day?
How many sea otters are alive in the world today?
RC.e: Lines 13–15 answer it: to keep up with the energy it uses, a sea otter must eat about a quarter of its own weight in food every day.

y.A: How long a sea otter lives is never stated; the passage gives numbers for its food, its fur, and the kelp, but not for its age.
y.B: How deep it dives is not given; line 15 says it dives to the bottom for crabs and clams but never says how far down the bottom is.
y.D: How many are alive today is not answered; lines 31–32 give the number left in 1900, and the passage says only that their numbers recovered after 1911.

RC.q: According to the story, where did Hattie and Quinn find the cricket?
c: in the dark row of tomato plants
RC.e: Lines 29–32 say that Quinn slowly lifted his left sneaker and a small brown cricket was sitting inside the toe.

y.A: Under the porch steps is one of the places they searched in the yard (lines 22–23), and they found nothing there.
