y.C: Inside an empty flowerpot is another place they searched (line 23) while the chirping seemed to slip around behind them.
y.D: In the tomato plants is one of the places the sound seemed to come from (lines 15–16), but the cricket turned up inside the tent (lines 29–32).

RC.q: In line 8, the author compares the chirp to “a ticking clock” to show that the chirp
c: repeated at a steady, even pace
was coming from inside the house
was getting louder each time it sounded
told them it was the middle of the night
RC.e: A ticking clock repeats the same sound at the same speed, and line 8 calls the chirp “repeated over and over, as regular as a ticking clock,” so the chirp kept coming at a steady, even pace.

y.B: Coming from inside the house treats the clock as a clue to where the sound was, but the clock is only what the chirp is compared to; the cricket turns out to be in the tent.
y.C: Getting louder each time mixes in a later moment, when the chirping grows louder after the door is zipped (lines 27–28); the comparison in line 8 is about the chirp repeating evenly.
y.D: Telling them it was the middle of the night treats the clock as telling the time; the lateness comes from line 13, and the comparison is about the chirp's even beat.

RC.q: The chirping grew louder when Quinn zipped the tent door shut (lines 27–28) most likely because
c: the tent walls made the sound echo
the cricket was in the tent with them
the yard outside had suddenly gone quiet
Hattie pointed the flashlight at the noise
RC.e: While they searched the yard, the chirping seemed to slip around behind them, back toward the tent (lines 20–22); once they were zipped inside it grew louder, because the cricket was sitting in Quinn's sneaker by the door.

y.A: The tent walls making the sound echo is never suggested; the chirp grows louder because the cricket is only a few feet away, in a sneaker by the door (lines 29–32).
y.C: The yard going quiet happens later, after Quinn tips the cricket onto the grass (lines 33–35); when the door was zipped, the chirping was coming from inside the tent.
y.D: Pointing the flashlight comes after the chirping grows louder (lines 28–29); Hattie aims it at the sneakers because of the noise, not the other way around.

RC.q: The first paragraph (lines 1–6) mainly serves to
c: show that the cousins were scared of ghosts
explain why Aunt Lou did not want them outside
describe the flashlight the cousins would need later
introduce the cousins and their campout in the backyard
RC.e: Lines 1–6 tell who the characters are, where they are sleeping, and how they set up the tent and told stories until the flashlight faded, which sets up the night before the chirping starts in line 7.

y.A: Scared of ghosts reads too much into the ghost stories in line 5; the cousins tell them for fun, and the paragraph is setting up their night outside.
y.B: Aunt Lou not wanting them outside stretches “begged all week” and “finally” in lines 1–2; she brings the tent out, and the paragraph never gives her reasons.
y.C: The flashlight beginning to fade is one detail at the end of the paragraph (lines 5–6); it matters later, but the paragraph as a whole introduces who is camping, and where.

RC.q: Which sentence best tells what the story is mainly about?
c: Aunt Lou lets two children sleep in the backyard.
Two cousins are too frightened to stay in their tent.
A chirp sounds louder inside a tent than out in a yard.
Two cousins hunt outside for a noise that was in their tent.
RC.e: The story follows Hattie and Quinn as they hear a chirp, search the yard for it, and then find the cricket in Quinn's sneaker inside the tent, where the sound had been the whole time.

y.A: Aunt Lou letting them sleep outside is how the story begins (lines 1–3), not what it is about; she does not appear again.
y.B: Too frightened to stay in their tent is contradicted by the ending; the cousins crawl back into the tent and fall asleep there (lines 26–27 and 37).
y.C: A chirp sounding louder inside a tent turns one moment (lines 27–28) into a rule; it grew louder because the cricket was in the tent, not because tents make sounds louder.

RC.q: The passage is mainly about
c: how soldiers sent messages in the dark
why a school for the blind had few books
how a blind boy created a new way to read
how Louis Braille became a teacher and organist
RC.e: The passage follows Louis Braille from the accident that blinded him, through the slow raised-letter books and Barbier's code, to the six-dot system he finished at fifteen.

y.A: Soldiers sending messages in the dark is what Barbier's night writing was for (lines 16–17), the idea Louis started from, not the subject of the passage.
y.B: A school with few books is a detail from the second paragraph (lines 10–11); it shows why blind readers needed a better way to read.
y.D: Becoming a teacher and an organist is in the last paragraph (lines 31–32), what Louis did later in life, not what the passage is mainly about.

RC.q: According to the passage, why were the books at the Royal Institute hard to read?
c: Their letters were too small to feel.
Each sign was too tall to feel in one touch.
Their curved letters were slow to tell apart.
Their signs stood for sounds instead of letters.
RC.e: Lines 11–13 say the books were printed in large raised letters that students read with their fingers, and telling the curved letters apart was slow work.

y.A: Too small to feel is the opposite of line 11, which says the books were printed in large raised letters.
y.B: Too tall to feel in one touch describes the twelve-dot signs of Barbier's code (lines 21–23), not the letters in the school's books.
y.D: Standing for sounds instead of letters was a problem with Barbier's code (lines 20–21); the school's books used ordinary letters, raised from the page.

RC.q: Based on the passage, Louis most likely used six dots in two columns of three so that
c: each sign could stand for a sound
each sign could be felt in one touch
soldiers could still read it at night
the dots would look like printed letters
RC.e: Barbier's signs could need twelve dots, too tall to feel all at once (lines 21–23); a sign of six dots in two short columns is small enough for a reader to feel in a single touch.

y.A: Standing for a sound is what Barbier's signs did (lines 20–21); lines 26–27 say Louis made each pattern stand for a letter instead.
y.C: Soldiers reading at night was the purpose of Barbier's night writing (lines 16–17); Louis was making a code for blind readers.
y.D: Looking like printed letters mixes the dots up with the school's raised letters (lines 11–13), which were slow to read; a pattern of dots is not shaped like a letter.

RC.q: According to the passage, what did Louis do when he was seventeen?
c: became a teacher at the school
finished his system of raised dots
published a book explaining his code
won a scholarship to a school in Paris
RC.e: Line 31 says that at seventeen, Louis became a teacher at the school.

y.B: Finishing his system happened in 1824, when he was fifteen (lines 27–28), two years before he turned seventeen.
y.C: Publishing a book came in 1829 (lines 32–33); Louis was born in 1809, so he was twenty, not seventeen.
y.D: Winning a scholarship happened when he was ten (lines 9–10), when he first went to the school in Paris.

RC.q: In line 36, “adopted” most nearly means
RC.e: Two years after Louis died, France officially took up his system of raised dots, so adopted means accepted.

y.B: Celebrated fits honoring Louis after his death, but the sentence says France took up his code to use, not that it held a celebration.
y.C: Copied is how adopt is used for picking up someone's habit or accent, but France did not copy the code; it made his code the official way to read.
y.D: Raised is in the same line, in “raised dots,” and adopting a child means raising it, but a code is not raised like a child; France accepted it.

RC.q: The third paragraph (lines 16–24) mainly describes
c: where the boats in the picture were going
how the printer rubbed each sheet of paper
why Hokusai chose Berlin blue for the sea and sky
how Hokusai's drawing was turned into carved blocks
RC.e: Lines 16–24 explain that Hokusai made only the drawing, and that a carver pasted it onto cherry wood, carved the outline block, and cut a separate block for each color.

y.A: Where the boats were going, to the fish markets of Edo, is told at the end of the second paragraph (lines 13–15), not in the third.
y.B: The printer rubbing each sheet with a baren comes in the fourth paragraph (lines 25–27), after the blocks have been carved.
y.C: Choosing Berlin blue for the sea and sky is in the fourth paragraph (lines 28–30); the third paragraph is about the carver's work.

RC.q: According to the passage, what did Hokusai himself make?
c: the marks for lining up colors
a drawing with notes about colors
the deep blue coloring for the sea
RC.e: Lines 16–18 say Hokusai did not print the picture himself; he made only the design, a drawing in lines with notes about the colors.

y.A: The blocks of cherry wood were cut by a carver (lines 18–22), not by Hokusai, who made only the design.
y.B: The marks for lining up colors were cut by the carver at the edges of each block (lines 22–24).
y.D: The deep blue coloring, Berlin blue, was something Hokusai chose for the sea and sky (lines 28–29); the passage says he chose it, not that he made it.

RC.q: In line 33, “impressions” most nearly means
RC.e: The sentence before says the same picture could be printed many times, so the three impressions the museum owns are three printed copies of The Great Wave.

y.B: Dents are impressions pressed into something soft, like a footprint in mud, but a museum does not collect dents; the sentence before is about printing.
y.C: Feelings is the meaning in “first impressions,” but a museum cannot own a feeling; the sentence counts pictures printed from the blocks.
y.D: Imitations is the meaning when someone does an impression of a famous voice, but these are prints from the real blocks, not imitations of the picture.

RC.q: It can be inferred that Hokusai's original drawing
c: was used again for each color block
was printed many times in Berlin blue
was cut up as the first block was carved
is now kept in a museum in Melbourne, Australia
RC.e: The carver pasted the drawing face down on the cherry wood and carved away everything except the lines (lines 18–20), so the paper drawing was cut up in the carving and only the block was left.

y.A: Used again for each color block is a natural guess, but the drawing was pasted onto the first block and carved away (lines 18–20), so it had already been cut up when the color blocks were made.
y.B: Printed many times describes the blocks (lines 31–32), not the drawing; the drawing was glued to the wood and carved.
y.D: Kept in Melbourne is said of one printed impression (lines 34–35), not of Hokusai's drawing, which was carved away.

RC.q: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
c: The Great Wave shows boats carrying fish to Edo.
Berlin blue became cheap enough for printers to use.
The Great Wave was made by a team and printed many times.
Museums in Chicago and Melbourne own copies of The Great Wave.
RC.e: Most of the passage explains how Hokusai's design was carved into blocks and printed by a carver and a printer, which let the same picture be printed many times.

y.A: Boats carrying fish to Edo is a detail about what the picture shows (lines 13–15), not what the passage as a whole explains.
y.B: Berlin blue becoming cheap is one detail from the fourth paragraph (lines 29–30), about a color Hokusai chose.
y.D: Museums in Chicago and Melbourne owning copies is how the passage ends (lines 32–35); it is a result of the printing, not the main idea.

MA.sk: Number sense—standard form from expanded form
MA.q: Quentin wrote a number in expanded form as 80,000 + 3,000 + 40 + 6. What is Quentin's number written in standard form?
MA.e: 80,000 + 3,000 is 83,000. There are no hundreds, so a 0 holds the hundreds place; then come 4 tens and 6 ones. The number is 83,046.

y.A: 8,346 puts the digits 8, 3, 4, and 6 side by side with no zeros, so the 8 stands for 8 thousands instead of 8 ten thousands.
y.B: 80,346 writes 80 and then the digits 3, 4, and 6, which puts the 3 in the hundreds place instead of the thousands place.
y.D: 83,406 puts the 4 in the hundreds place, but 40 is 4 tens; it is the hundreds place that is empty.

MA.sk: Estimation—rounding to the nearest ten thousand
MA.q: A newspaper reported that 46,382 people went to the county fair. What is this number rounded to the nearest ten thousand?
MA.e: The ten-thousands digit is 4. The digit to its right, in the thousands place, is 6, which is 5 or more, so round up: 46,382 is closer to 50,000 than to 40,000.

y.A: 40,000 rounds down, by dropping the other digits or by looking at the 3 in the hundreds place; the digit that decides is the 6 in the thousands place, which says round up.
y.B: 46,000 is the number rounded to the nearest thousand, one place short of the ten thousands.
y.C: 46,400 is the number rounded to the nearest hundred, not the nearest ten thousand.

MA.q: The table shows how many people visited a city aquarium in four months. How many more people visited in July than in May?
MA.e: July had 6,105 visitors and May had 3,478. Regroup to subtract: 6,105 − 3,478 = 2,627 more visitors in July.

y.B: 2,737 regroups the 0 in the tens place as 10 without first taking 1 from the hundreds, so the tens and the hundreds each come out one too big.
y.C: 3,245 is 6,105 − 2,860, the July visitors minus the April visitors; the question asks about May.
y.D: 3,373 takes the smaller digit from the larger in every column, 8 − 5, 7 − 0, 4 − 1, and 6 − 3, instead of regrouping.

MA.q: An apple orchard has 38 rows of trees, with 26 trees in each row. How many trees are in the orchard?
MA.e: Multiply 38 × 26 in two parts: 38 × 6 = 228 and 38 × 20 = 760. Then 228 + 760 = 988 trees.

y.A: 64 is 38 + 26, the two numbers added, when the orchard has 38 groups of 26 trees.
y.B: 304 is 228 + 76: the row for the 2 tens, 38 × 2 = 76, was not moved one place to the left, so it counts as 76 instead of 760.
y.C: 648 is 600 + 48, which multiplies 30 by 20 and 8 by 6 but leaves out 30 × 6 and 8 × 20.

MA.q: Jae's class used place-value blocks to build a number. They used 7 thousands blocks, 15 hundreds blocks, 3 tens blocks, and no ones blocks. What number did they build?
MA.e: 15 hundreds is 1,500, which is 1 thousand and 5 hundreds. So the blocks show 7,000 + 1,500 + 30 = 8,530.

y.A: 7,153 writes the counts 7, 15, and 3 side by side, without thinking about what each kind of block is worth.
y.B: 7,530 keeps only the 5 of the 15 hundreds; 15 hundreds is 1 thousand and 5 hundreds, and that extra thousand was left out.
y.D: 71,530 writes all of 15 in the hundreds column, which pushes the 7 into the ten-thousands place instead of regrouping 10 of the hundreds as 1 thousand.

MA.sk: Remainders—how many more to fill a group
MA.q: Mr. Halvorsen's class is making goody bags for the school fair. They have 140 stickers and put 6 stickers in each bag, filling as many bags as they can. How many more stickers would they need to fill one more bag?
MA.e: 140 ÷ 6 = 23 remainder 2, so 23 bags are filled and 2 stickers are left over. One more bag needs 6 stickers, so they need 6 − 2 = 4 more.

y.A: 2 is the number of stickers left over after 23 bags are filled, not the number still needed to fill another bag of 6.
y.C: 23 is the number of bags they can fill, 140 ÷ 6 with the remainder dropped; the question asks about stickers.
y.D: 24 rounds 23 remainder 2 up to the next whole bag, which counts bags, not the stickers still needed.

MA.sk: Fractions—simplest form from a shaded model
MA.q: Ayla's family ordered a pizza cut into equal slices. The shaded slices have mushrooms on them. What fraction of the pizza has mushrooms, in simplest form?
MA.e: 10 of the 12 equal slices are shaded, so 10/12 of the pizza has mushrooms. Dividing the top and the bottom by 2 gives 5/6.

y.A: 1/6 is the part without mushrooms: 2 of the 12 slices are not shaded.
y.B: 1/5 compares the 2 plain slices with the 10 mushroom slices instead of with all 12 slices.
y.C: 5/12 divides only the top of 10/12 by 2; the bottom has to be divided by 2 as well.

MA.q: Use the number line to answer the question. What decimal does point P show?
MA.e: From 1 to 2 there are 5 equal spaces, so each space is 0.2. Point P is 3 spaces past 1, so it shows 1 + 0.6 = 1.6.

y.A: 1.3 counts the 3 spaces from 1 to P as tenths, but the line from 1 to 2 has only 5 spaces, so each one is 0.2.
y.B: 1.4 counts the 2 spaces between P and 2 and adds them to 1, starting from the wrong end of the line.
y.D: 1.8 counts the 4 tick marks from 1 to P, including the one at 1, instead of the 3 spaces between them.

MA.q: The table shows prices at a craft store. Odile buys one sketchbook and three paintbrushes. How much does she spend in all?
MA.e: Three paintbrushes cost 3 × $0.95 = $2.85. Adding the sketchbook gives $2.85 + $3.65 = $6.50.

y.A: $2.85 is the cost of the three paintbrushes alone; the sketchbook was left out.
y.B: $4.60 is a sketchbook and only one paintbrush, $3.65 + $0.95, but Odile buys three paintbrushes.
y.C: $5.50 adds $2.85 and $3.65 but drops the 1 carried from the tenths into the ones.

MA.q: The table shows how far Bodhi hiked on three days. How many miles did he hike on Saturday and Sunday together?
MA.e: Write 1 1/2 as 1 2/4. Then 1 2/4 + 2 3/4 = 3 5/4. Since 5/4 is 1 1/4, the total is 4 1/4 miles.

y.A: 3 1/4 adds the fractions to get 5/4 but keeps only the 1/4, forgetting to add the whole mile inside 5/4.
y.B: 3 2/3 adds the tops and the bottoms of 1/2 and 3/4 to get 4/6, but fractions need the same bottom number before they are added.
y.D: 5 1/12 is Friday and Sunday added together; the question asks about Saturday and Sunday.

MA.q: Paz's rain gauge collected 1.75 inches of rain on Monday and 0.8 inch on Tuesday. How many inches of rain did it collect on the two days in all?
MA.e: Line up the decimal points and write 0.8 as 0.80. Then 1.75 + 0.80 = 2.55 inches.

y.A: 0.95 is 1.75 − 0.8, taking Tuesday's rain away instead of adding it.
y.B: 1.55 adds 7 tenths and 8 tenths to get 15 tenths but does not carry the 1 into the ones place.
y.C: 1.83 lines up the 8 under the 5, as if 0.8 were 0.08; 0.8 is 8 tenths, so the 8 belongs under the 7.

MA.q: A farm stand had 48 pumpkins on Saturday morning. By noon, 25% of the pumpkins had been sold. How many pumpkins had been sold by noon?
MA.e: 25% means 25 out of every 100, which is 1/4. One fourth of 48 is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 pumpkins.

y.B: 25 is the percent itself, read as if it were the number of pumpkins sold.
y.C: 36 is the number of pumpkins still at the stand, the 75% that had not been sold.
y.D: 192 is 48 × 4, multiplying by 4 when 25% means one fourth, which is dividing by 4.

MA.q: Kiri has finished 3/5 of her science project. Which decimal is equal to 3/5?
MA.e: Fifths can be changed to tenths: 3/5 = 6/10, and 6 tenths is written 0.6.

y.A: 0.06 changes 3/5 to 6/10 but then writes 6 tenths as 6 hundredths.
y.B: 0.3 treats fifths as if they were tenths, writing the 3 as 3 tenths.
y.C: 0.35 writes the 3 and the 5 side by side after the decimal point.

MA.sk: Fractions—multiplying a fraction by a whole number
MA.q: The walking path around Lakeview Park is 3/4 mile long. Mr. Abernathy walks all the way around the path 6 times. How many miles does he walk?
MA.e: 6 × 3/4 is 18 fourths. Every 4 fourths make 1 mile, so 16 fourths make 4 miles, and the 2 fourths left over are 1/2 mile: 4 1/2 miles in all.

y.A: 3/4 multiplies the top and the bottom by 6, giving 18/24, which is still 3/4; six trips of 3 fourths is 18 fourths, so only the top is multiplied.
y.C: 6 3/4 writes the 6 trips beside the 3/4 mile as a mixed number instead of multiplying them.
y.D: 18 is 6 × 3, the number of fourths of a mile, with the fourths forgotten; 18 fourths is 4 1/2.

MA.q: Pilar's number machine uses the same rule on every input. The table shows some inputs and their outputs. What input gives an output of 30?
MA.e: Each output is 2 times the input plus 4: 2 × 3 + 4 = 10 and 2 × 5 + 4 = 14. Work backward from 30: take away the 4 to get 26, then halve 26 to get 13.

y.B: 15 is half of 30, which undoes the doubling but not the 4 that was added afterward; 30 − 4 has to come first.
y.C: 23 uses an add-7 rule, which fits only the first row: 3 + 7 = 10, but 5 + 7 is 12, not 14.
y.D: 64 is 2 × 30 + 4, putting 30 into the machine as an input when 30 is the output.

MA.q: Mrs. Oyelaran bought 6 packs of juice boxes. Each pack holds the same number of juice boxes, and there are 54 juice boxes in all. Which equation could be used to find j, the number of juice boxes in each pack?
MA.e: There are 6 packs with j juice boxes in each, so 6 groups of j make 54: 6 × j = 54. That makes j = 9.

y.B: 6 + j = 54 adds the number of packs to the number in one pack; 6 packs of j juice boxes is 6 groups of j, which is 6 × j.
y.C: j ÷ 6 = 54 says one pack split into 6 parts makes 54, but it is the 6 packs together that make 54.
y.D: 54 × 6 = j multiplies the two numbers in the problem, but 54 is already the total, so j must be smaller than 54.

MA.q: A number pattern begins 3, 4, 7, 12, 19. If the pattern continues, what is the next number?
MA.e: The jumps between the numbers are 1, 3, 5, and 7, getting 2 bigger each time. The next jump is 9, so the next number is 19 + 9 = 28.

y.A: 26 adds 7 again, repeating the last jump, but the jumps grow by 2 each time, so the next one is 9.
y.C: 31 adds the two numbers before it, 12 + 19; that rule works for 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 + 12 = 19, but 4 + 7 is 11, not 12.
y.D: 38 doubles 19, but doubling does not fit the pattern: 7 doubled is 14, not 12.

MA.q: Mr. Lund wrote this number sentence on the board: 24 + 18 = □ + 20. What number goes in the box to make the number sentence true?
MA.e: The left side is 24 + 18 = 42, so the right side must also be 42. Since 22 + 20 = 42, the box stands for 22.

y.B: 26 moves the wrong way: 20 is 2 more than 18, so the box must be 2 less than 24, not 2 more.
y.C: 42 is 24 + 18, the left side worked out, as if the box were the answer; the box plus 20 has to make 42.
y.D: 62 is 24 + 18 + 20, all three numbers added together.

MA.sk: Coordinates—locating a point on a map grid
MA.q: The grid shows where four places are in a town park. Which place is at (3, 6)?
MA.e: Start at 0, go 3 units to the right, and then go 6 units up. The place at that point is the Pond.

y.A: Bandstand is at (6, 3), which is reached by going 6 across and 3 up, the two numbers used in the wrong order.
y.B: Fountain is at (3, 7), one line too high; the count up went one line past 6.
y.C: Garden is at (2, 5), where the count lands if the lines at 0 are counted as 1 on both axes.

MA.q: The figure shows the front of a birdhouse. How many lines of symmetry does the shape have?
MA.e: A line of symmetry folds a shape exactly onto itself. The birdhouse folds onto itself only along the up-and-down line from the tip of the roof to the middle of the bottom, so it has 1 line of symmetry.

y.A: 0 treats the slanted roof as spoiling every fold, but a fold from the tip of the roof straight down makes the two halves match.
y.C: 2 adds a side-to-side fold, as a rectangle has, but folding the birdhouse from top to bottom puts the pointed roof on the flat bottom.
y.D: 5 counts the sides of the shape; the number of sides is not the number of folds that make the halves match.

MA.sk: Coordinates—sliding a figure on a grid
MA.q: Triangle PQR is slid across the grid without turning, so that point P moves to point T. What are the new coordinates of point Q?
MA.e: Point P moves from (1, 2) to point T at (5, 3), which is 4 units right and 1 unit up. Every point of the triangle moves the same way, so Q moves from (4, 2) to (8, 3).

y.A: (4, 3) moves Q 1 unit up but not the 4 units right that P also moved.
y.B: (5, 3) is point T, where P lands; Q moves 4 right and 1 up from its own place.
y.C: (8, 2) moves Q 4 units right but not the 1 unit up that P also moved.

MA.q: A wooden ramp for toy cars is shaped like a triangular prism. How many faces does a triangular prism have?
MA.e: A triangular prism has 2 triangle faces, one at each end, and 3 rectangle faces joining them: 2 + 3 = 5 faces.

y.A: 3 counts only the rectangle faces around the sides and leaves out the triangles at the two ends.
y.C: 6 is the number of corners, or vertices, of a triangular prism, not the number of faces.
y.D: 9 is the number of edges, the lines where two faces meet.

MA.q: The figure shows the floor of Ms. Varga's art room, with some side lengths labeled. Every side meets the next at a right angle. What is the area of the floor?
MA.e: Split the floor into two rectangles. The bottom part is 9 × 3 = 27 square meters. The part above it is 5 m wide and 7 − 3 = 4 m tall, so it is 5 × 4 = 20 square meters. 27 + 20 = 47 square meters.

y.A: 24 square meters adds the four labeled sides, 9 + 7 + 5 + 3, which measures part of the way around the floor, not the space inside it.
y.B: 27 square meters is only the bottom part, 9 × 3; the part above it, 5 m wide and 4 m tall, is floor too.
y.D: 63 square meters is 9 × 7, a whole rectangle; the 4-by-4 corner cut out of that rectangle is not part of the floor.

MA.q: Ama built the block shown from 1-centimeter cubes. She wants to add cubes to make the block 7 cubes tall, keeping the same length and width. How many more cubes does she need?
MA.e: Each layer has 5 × 2 = 10 cubes. The block is 2 layers tall now, so she needs 5 more layers: 5 × 10 = 50 cubes.

y.A: 5 is the number of layers she needs to add, not the number of cubes in them.
y.B: 10 is the number of cubes in one layer, 5 × 2; she needs five more layers, not one.
y.D: 70 is 5 × 2 × 7, all the cubes in the finished block, including the 20 she already has.

MA.q: The clock shows the time Kofi got home from school. He practiced piano for 45 minutes, took a 20-minute snack break, and then read for 35 minutes. At what time did he finish reading?
MA.e: The clock shows 3:50. Kofi spent 45 + 20 + 35 = 100 minutes, which is 1 hour 40 minutes. One hour after 3:50 is 4:50, and 40 minutes after that is 5:30 p.m.

y.A: 4:50 p.m. treats 100 minutes as 1 hour, but an hour is 60 minutes, so 100 minutes is 1 hour 40 minutes.
y.B: 5:10 p.m. leaves out the 20-minute snack break and adds only the 80 minutes of piano and reading.
y.D: 6:30 p.m. reads the short hand as 4, because it is close to the 4, and starts the count at 4:50 instead of 3:50.

MA.q: A bag holds 2 kilograms of flour. Mr. Ashby uses 350 grams of the flour to bake bread. How many grams of flour are left in the bag?
MA.e: 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams, so 2 kilograms is 2,000 grams. Then 2,000 − 350 = 1,650 grams are left.

y.A: 348 is 350 − 2, which takes the 2 from the 350 without first changing 2 kilograms into 2,000 grams.
y.C: 1,750 regroups 2,000 but forgets that the hundreds gave 1 to the tens, so the hundreds column gives 10 − 3 = 7 instead of 9 − 3 = 6.
y.D: 2,350 adds the 350 grams to the 2,000 grams instead of taking them away.

MA.q: Liko counted the birds that visited his bird feeder on four days. The pictograph shows his counts. How many more birds visited on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
MA.e: Each symbol stands for 6 birds, so half a symbol stands for 3. Wednesday had 4 1/2 symbols, which is 24 + 3 = 27 birds, and Tuesday had 2 symbols, which is 12 birds. 27 − 12 = 15.

y.B: 18 counts Wednesday's half symbol as a whole one, 30 − 12, but half a symbol stands for only 3 birds.
y.C: 27 is the number of birds on Wednesday alone, not how many more than on Tuesday.
y.D: 39 is 27 + 12, the two days added together instead of compared.

MA.q: The graph shows how many laps five swimmers swam on Saturday. What is the mean number of laps?
MA.e: Add the laps: 6 + 9 + 4 + 8 + 8 = 35. Share the total equally among the 5 swimmers: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 laps.

y.A: 5 is the range, 9 − 4, the gap between the most laps and the fewest.
y.C: 8 is the median and also the mode: the middle number once the laps are in order, and the number that appears twice.
y.D: 35 is the total of all the laps, before it is shared equally among the 5 swimmers.

MA.sk: Probability—simple event from a bar graph
MA.q: The graph shows the colors of the marbles in a bag. Wes picks one marble without looking. What is the probability that the marble he picks is red?
MA.e: There are 7 + 5 + 3 = 15 marbles, and 7 of them are red. The probability of picking red is 7 out of 15, or 7/15.

y.A: 1/3 treats the three colors as three equal chances, but there are more red marbles than marbles of either other color.
y.C: 8/15 is the probability of not picking red: 5 blue and 3 yellow make 8 of the 15 marbles.
y.D: 7/8 compares the 7 red marbles with the 8 that are not red, instead of with all 15 marbles.

MA.q: The Venn diagram shows how many students in Ms. Delgado's class are in the chess club, the art club, both clubs, or neither club. How many students are in Ms. Delgado's class?
MA.e: Add every part of the diagram once: 9 in chess only, 4 in both clubs, 7 in art only, and 6 in neither. 9 + 4 + 7 + 6 = 26 students.

y.A: 20 is 9 + 4 + 7, the students in at least one club; the 6 students in neither club are in the class too.
y.B: 22 is 9 + 7 + 6, which leaves out the 4 students in the middle who are in both clubs.
y.D: 30 adds the whole chess circle, 13, and the whole art circle, 11, plus the 6 outside, so the 4 students in both clubs are counted twice.

VR.e: To inquire is to ask, especially to ask for information: a traveler inquires about the train times, and a curious student inquires why the sky is blue.

y.A: Answer is the other half of a question: picking it mixes up the person who replies with the person who inquires.
y.C: Shout tells how loudly someone speaks, not what the words do; a person can inquire loudly or softly, and either way she is asking.
y.D: Whisper tells how softly someone speaks; a person can whisper an answer as easily as a question, so whispering is not asking.

VR.e: Soggy means soaked through and heavy with water, like cereal left too long in milk or a lawn after days of rain.

y.A: Crunchy is the opposite: cereal is crunchy straight from the box and soggy after it sits in milk.
y.B: Moldy is a different way food goes bad, with fuzzy spots growing on it; soggy food is not spoiled, only soaked.
y.D: Wilted describes a leaf that has gone limp and droopy, which can look like soggy lettuce, but wilted means drooping, not full of water.

VR.e: An oath is a serious promise, often spoken aloud in front of others, such as the oath a witness takes to tell the truth.

y.A: Lie is the opposite of what an oath is for: a witness takes an oath to tell the truth, not to say something false.
y.C: Speech is any talk given out loud; an oath is spoken aloud too, which is the trap, but what makes it an oath is the promise.
y.D: Threat also tells what someone will do, the way a promise does, but it warns of harm; an oath is a serious promise to keep your word.

VR.e: To hurl is to throw something hard and fast, the way a giant in a fairy tale hurls boulders down a mountain.

y.A: Carry is another way to move something heavy, but a carried thing stays in your hands, while a hurled thing flies through the air.
y.B: Hurt starts with the same sound as hurl, and a hurled stone might hurt someone, but to hurt is to cause pain, not to throw.
y.C: Kick also sends a ball flying, but with your foot; to hurl is to throw something hard with your arm.

VR.e: To shatter is to break suddenly into many pieces, the way a glass shatters when it hits a stone floor.

y.A: Bend is what a spoon or a wire does when it changes shape and stays in one piece; a shattered thing comes apart.
y.C: Scatter rhymes with shatter and names what the pieces do after the break, flying in every direction; it is not the breaking itself.
y.D: Spill is what happens to the milk when a glass tips over; the glass can spill without breaking at all.

VR.e: To ponder is to think about something carefully and for a long time, as you might ponder a hard riddle or a big choice.

y.B: Decide is what comes after pondering: you ponder while you turn a choice over in your mind, and you decide when you finally make it.
y.C: Describe means to tell what something is like; you can ponder a question in silence without describing anything to anyone.
y.D: Rush is the opposite pace: to ponder is to take your time thinking something over, and to rush is to hurry.

VR.e: A stench is a strong, very bad smell, like the stench of a garbage can left out in the summer sun.

y.A: Flavor is how food tastes, not how something smells; picking it mixes up two of the senses.
y.B: Smoke is the gray cloud that rises from a fire; it can carry a stench, but smoke is something you see, not the smell itself.
y.C: Stain begins with the same sound as stench and is also unpleasant, but a stain is a mark on cloth that you see, not something you smell.

VR.e: Humane means kind and gentle toward people or animals who could be made to suffer: a humane farmer makes sure every animal has food, water, and shelter.

y.A: Cruel is the opposite: a humane person tries to spare others from suffering, and a cruel one causes it.
y.B: Human looks almost the same as humane, which is the trap; human means having to do with people, while humane means kind.
y.D: Tame describes an animal that is used to people instead of wild; humane is about how people treat animals and one another, which is kindly.

VR.e: Eternally means endlessly, without ever stopping: a person who is eternally grateful will never stop being thankful.

y.B: Gratefully comes from the phrase eternally grateful, which is the trap; the two words often go together, but eternally means without end, not thankfully.
y.C: Occasionally means once in a while; it tells how often something happens, while eternally says it never stops.
y.D: Recently means a short time ago; it tells when something happened, not that it goes on and on.

VR.e: To dwell is to live somewhere and make it your home: in fairy tales, giants dwell in castles and trolls dwell under bridges.

y.A: Arrive means to come to a place; to dwell is to stay and live there long after arriving.
y.B: Depart means to leave a place, nearly the opposite of dwelling there.
y.D: Visit means staying somewhere for a short time; a guest visits a house, but the family that lives there dwells in it.

VR.e: Hardy means tough and strong enough to survive hard conditions: hardy plants live through frost, wind, and dry summers.

y.A: Delicate is the opposite: a delicate flower needs care and shelter, while a hardy one lives through frost and drought.
y.B: Heavy is about weight; a hardy little weed can weigh almost nothing and still survive a cold winter.
y.C: Stiff comes from reading hardy as hard, the way a board is hard and will not bend; hardy is about surviving rough conditions, not about bending.

VR.e: Utterly means completely, with nothing held back: the surprise party left him utterly speechless.

y.A: Aloud comes from utter, the verb that means to say something out loud, but utterly is a different word that means completely.
y.C: Partly means only in part, the opposite of utterly, which means all the way.
y.D: Usually means most of the time; it tells how often something happens, while utterly tells how much, which is completely.

VR.e: To deceive is to trick someone into believing something that is not true, the way a magician deceives an audience into thinking a coin has disappeared.

y.A: Believe is what the person who is deceived ends up doing, believing something false; it is not what the deceiver does.
y.B: Confess is the opposite of deceiving: to confess is to tell the truth about something you did.
y.D: Steal is what some tricksters do after deceiving someone, but to steal is to take what is not yours; to deceive is to make someone believe something false.

VR.e: A sentry is a guard who stands watch at a gate or a wall to keep out anyone who should not come in.

y.A: Entry is hiding inside the word sentry, which is the trap; an entry is a way in, such as a door, though a sentry often stands beside one.
y.C: Prisoner is someone a guard might keep watch over, the other side of the job, not the person keeping watch.
y.D: Spy also watches, but in secret, to learn things for the other side; a sentry stands in plain sight to guard a place.

VR.e: Hospitable means friendly and generous to guests: a hospitable family welcomes visitors with a warm meal and a place to sleep.

y.A: Medical comes from spotting hospital inside hospitable; the two words look alike, but hospitable has nothing to do with doctors.
y.B: Selfish is the opposite: a selfish host keeps the best for herself, while a hospitable one shares it with guests.
y.C: Wealthy means rich; a hospitable family may have very little and still share it gladly with visitors.

VR.e: Havoc is wild destruction and disorder: a herd of goats loose in a vegetable garden can cause havoc in a single afternoon.

y.B: Earthquake names one thing that can cause havoc, but havoc is the destruction and disorder that follow, not the event that causes them.
y.C: Haven looks like havoc, which is the trap, but a haven is a safe, peaceful place, nearly the opposite.
y.D: Noise often comes along with havoc, but noise alone can be harmless, like a cheering crowd; havoc means wild destruction and disorder.

VR.e: Distraught means so upset and worried that you can hardly think straight, as a parent might be after losing sight of a child in a crowd. Distressed means the same thing.

y.A: Angry is a strong feeling too, but it is aimed at someone who did wrong; a distraught person is overcome with worry and sadness.
y.B: Disgusted begins much like distraught, but it means sickened by something unpleasant; a distraught person is worried and upset, not sickened.
y.D: Exhausted means extremely tired; a distraught person may end up exhausted, but the word names the upset, not the tiredness.

VR.q: Instead of ____ the crumbling old mill to make room for a parking lot, the town repaired the mill's walls and opened it as a museum.
VR.e: Instead of tells us the town did the opposite of the blank. The town kept and repaired the mill, so the blank is the plan it turned down: tearing the mill down to make room for parking, which is demolishing.

y.A: Decorating is something you might do to a building you plan to keep, but no one decorates a mill to clear space for a parking lot.
y.C: Photographing is what visitors might do at the new museum; taking pictures of the mill would never make room for a parking lot.
y.D: Preserving is what the town actually did by repairing the mill; choosing it skips over instead of, which says the blank is the plan the town did not follow.

VR.q: Because the card tucked into the flowers was not signed, the gift was ____, and the family spent all week guessing who had sent it.
VR.e: Because gives the reason the family had to guess: no one signed the card, so no one knew who sent the gift. A gift from an unknown giver is anonymous.

y.B: Cheap is about what the flowers cost; the unsigned card says nothing about price, only that no one knew who sent them.
y.C: Pricey is about cost too, the other end from cheap; neither one follows from a card with no name on it.
y.D: Unexpected sounds right because the family was surprised, but a surprise gift can come with a signed card; the missing name is what made the giver unknown.

VR.q: The children were told not to ____ the nesting birds: no shouting, no climbing the tree, and no peeking into the nest.
VR.e: The examples after the colon decide it: shouting, climbing, and peeking all bother the birds, so the children were told not to disturb them.

y.A: Count is a quiet thing a bird watcher might do from a distance; none of the three forbidden things is counting.
y.C: Feed is the rule people often hear at a duck pond, which is the trap; the list after the colon is about noise and coming too close, not food.
y.D: Sketch is a quiet thing to do from far away, nothing like the shouting, climbing, and peeking that the list forbids.

VR.q: Scientists who use powerful telescopes to study the stars and planets are called ____.
VR.e: The sentence gives the definition: scientists who study stars and planets through telescopes are astronomers. The word begins with astro, which means star.

y.A: Architects design buildings; the word only begins with a sound like astronomers, and nothing in the sentence is about buildings.
y.B: Astronauts travel into space, which is the trap; the sentence describes scientists who study space through telescopes, mostly from the ground.
y.D: Geologists are scientists too, but they study rocks and the ground under our feet, not the stars.

VR.q: The settlers' first winter on the prairie was harsh, but the second was ____, with little snow and an early spring.
VR.e: But sets the second winter against the harsh first one, and the details agree: little snow and an early spring make a gentle winter, which is what mild means.

y.A: Brutal means just as harsh as the first winter, so it ignores but, which tells us the second winter was different.
y.B: Endless clashes with the early spring the sentence describes; a winter that ended early was not endless.
y.D: Snowy clashes with the little snow the sentence describes; it pictures winter weather without reading the details.

VR.q: Because a rockslide had buried the only road into the village, the whole village was ____ for a week, and supplies had to be dropped in by helicopter.
VR.e: Because gives the cause: with its only road buried, the village was cut off from everywhere else. Cut off and alone is what isolated means.

y.A: Abandoned means the people left for good, but supplies were dropped to the village, so people were still living there.
y.B: Connected is the opposite: the rockslide had just cut the village off from its only road.
y.C: Evacuated means the people were moved out to safety; if they had been, there would have been no one to drop supplies to.

VR.q: A spider's silk is thinner than a human hair, yet it is remarkably ____: it can stretch a long way without snapping.
VR.e: Yet promises something surprising about so thin a thread, and the words after the colon define it: something that can stretch a long way without snapping is elastic.

y.A: Brittle means hard but easy to snap, like a dry twig; it is what you might expect of a thin thread, but yet and without snapping point the other way.
y.C: Shiny describes how silk catches the light; it has nothing to do with stretching, which is what the words after the colon describe.
y.D: Sticky is true of some spider threads, which is how a web catches insects, but the colon explains the blank as stretching without snapping, not holding on.

VR.q: The ____ section of the orchestra plays instruments that are struck or shaken, such as drums, cymbals, and the xylophone.
VR.e: The examples decide it: drums, cymbals, and the xylophone are all struck or shaken to make sound, and instruments played that way make up the percussion section.

y.A: Brass is the section of trumpets and tubas, which are played by buzzing the lips into a mouthpiece; none of the examples is blown.
y.C: String is the section of violins and cellos, which are played by bowing or plucking their strings, not by striking or shaking.
y.D: Woodwind is the section of flutes and clarinets, which are played by blowing; drums and cymbals are not blown.

VR.q: Since the tour guide's soft voice could not be heard over the roar of the waterfall, she carried a small speaker to ____ her voice.
VR.e: Since gives the problem: her voice was too quiet to hear over the waterfall. A speaker solves that by making the voice louder, which is what amplify means.

y.B: Disguise means to change a voice so that no one knows whose it is; that would not help anyone hear it over the waterfall.
y.C: Muffle is the opposite: it means to make a sound softer, and her voice was already too soft to hear.
y.D: Record means to save a sound to play back later; the guide needed to be heard right then, over the roar of the water.

VR.q: Long ago, many families on the grasslands lived as ____, packing up their tents every few weeks and moving their herds to fresh grass.
VR.e: The rest of the sentence defines the word: people with no fixed home who keep moving with their herds to find fresh grass are nomads.

y.A: Farmers stay on their land to plant and harvest; these families packed up their tents and moved every few weeks.
y.B: Hermits live alone, far from other people; the sentence describes whole families moving together.
y.C: Merchants travel too, which is the trap, but they travel to buy and sell goods; these families moved to find grass for their animals.

VR.q: Although the treaty was meant to bring a ____ peace to the two nations, they were at war again within a year.
VR.e: Although means the new war came as a surprise. A war within a year is only surprising if the treaty was meant to make the peace last for good, so the blank is permanent.

y.B: Secret is about who knew of the peace, which the sentence never mentions; it was picked without asking what although is surprised by.
y.C: Shaky describes how the peace turned out, not what the treaty was meant to bring; nobody writes a treaty hoping for a shaky peace.
y.D: Short is the opposite of what although needs: if the peace was only meant to be short, a war within a year would be no surprise.

VR.q: The old letter was written in plain English, but its ink had faded and its handwriting was cramped, so the historian needed hours to ____ a single page.
VR.e: So gives the result of the faded ink and cramped handwriting: the words were hard to read, and to work out writing that is hard to read is to decipher it.

y.B: Frame is something you might do to protect a precious letter, but faded ink and cramped writing would not make framing take hours.
y.C: Translate means to change words from one language into another, but this letter was already in plain English; picking it pictures a foreign language that is not there.
y.D: Underline is something you do to words you can already read; the historian's problem was reading them at all.

VR.q: A solid keeps its own shape, but a liquid ____.
c: has weight and takes up space
is made of very tiny particles
takes the shape of its container
holds its shape wherever it is put
VR.e: But signals a difference: a solid keeps its own shape, so a liquid must not. Pour water into a cup or a bowl, and it takes the shape of whatever holds it.

y.A: Has weight and takes up space is true of liquids, but it is true of solids as well, so it gives no difference for but to point to.
y.B: Is made of very tiny particles is true of solids too, so it draws no contrast between the two.
y.D: Holds its shape wherever it is put describes the solid in the first half of the sentence; choosing it ignores but, which says the liquid behaves differently.

VR.q: The storm knocked out the power on our whole street, so my family ____.
VR.e: So tells us the blank is a result of losing power. With no electricity, the family could not use lamps or machines, so they ate dinner by candlelight.

y.A: Watched a movie on TV is an ordinary evening plan, but a television needs the power the storm had just knocked out.
y.B: Ran the washing machine needs electricity too, so it cannot be a result of the power going out.
y.C: Turned on all the lamps is what a family does when the power works; with the power out, the lamps would stay dark.

VR.q: Even though the composer had lost nearly all of his hearing, he ____.
c: went on writing music for years
could not hear the orchestra play
lived with his nephew in the city
stopped playing the piano for crowds
VR.e: Even though sets up a surprise: losing your hearing would seem to end a life in music, so the ending must go against that. He went on writing music for years.

y.B: Could not hear the orchestra play is just what losing his hearing would mean, so it agrees with the first half instead of going against it.
y.C: Lived with his nephew in the city is a plain fact about where he lived; it has nothing to do with his hearing, so even though has nothing to work against.
y.D: Stopped playing the piano for crowds is what you would expect of someone who could no longer hear, the opposite of the surprise that even though calls for.

VR.q: Despite having grown up in a busy city, the new park ranger ____.
c: got lost on her very first hike
had never seen a bear in the wild
could name every tree in the forest
wore a green hat and a golden badge
VR.e: Despite sets up a surprise: someone who grew up in a busy city would not be expected to know the forest well, so the ending must show that she did. She could name every tree.

y.A: Got lost on her very first hike is what you might expect from someone raised in a city, so it agrees with the first half instead of going against it.
y.B: Had never seen a bear in the wild fits a city childhood, so it is no surprise, and despite calls for one.
y.D: Wore a green hat and a golden badge describes her uniform, which has nothing to do with where she grew up, so despite has nothing to work against.

VR.q: At the new sculpture exhibit, visitors are invited to touch the artwork rather than ____.
c: come as close as they like
buy a ticket at the front desk
only look at it from behind a rope
run their fingers along each carving
VR.e: Rather than names the thing visitors are not asked to do. They are invited to touch the artwork, so the ending must be the opposite of touching: only looking at it from behind a rope.

y.A: Come as close as they like goes along with touching instead of against it, since you have to come close to touch; rather than needs the thing visitors are not asked to do.
y.B: Buy a ticket at the front desk has nothing to do with touching or not touching the art; it is something visitors might do on the way in, not the other choice the sentence turns down.
y.D: Run their fingers along each carving is itself a way of touching, which is what visitors are invited to do; choosing it reads rather than as if it meant and also.

QR.q: The number line shows the mile markers along a highway. The point labeled Gas is a gas station, and the point labeled Camp is a campground. A rest stop will be built exactly halfway between them. At which mile marker will the rest stop be?
QR.e: Gas is at mile 5 and Camp is at mile 13, which are 8 miles apart. Halfway is 4 miles past the gas station, at mile 9.

y.A: 4 is half of the 8 miles between the points, but the rest stop is 4 miles past mile 5, not at mile 4.
y.B: 8 is the distance from Gas to Camp, 13 − 5, not the marker halfway between them.
y.D: 18 is 5 + 13, the two markers added together; halfway is half of that sum, which is 9.

QR.q: After a hike, Gus had 6 ounces of water left in his bottle. During the hike he drank 10 ounces in the morning and 8 ounces in the afternoon. How many ounces of water were in the bottle when the hike began?
QR.e: Add the water he drank back to the water that was left: 6 + 10 + 8 = 24 ounces.

y.A: 12 is 10 + 8 − 6, taking away the water that was left instead of adding it back.
y.B: 16 is 10 + 6, which leaves out the 8 ounces he drank in the afternoon.
y.C: 18 is 10 + 8, only the water he drank; the 6 ounces still in the bottle were in it at the start too.

QR.q: At a nature center, the tallest tree is 48 feet tall. It is 4 times as tall as the shortest tree there. How tall is the shortest tree?
QR.e: 4 times as tall means 48 feet is 4 copies of the shortest tree, so the shortest tree is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 feet tall.

y.B: 44 feet is 48 − 4, taking away 4 feet instead of finding a height that fits into 48 four times.
y.C: 52 feet is 48 + 4, which would make the shortest tree taller than the tallest one.
y.D: 192 feet is 48 × 4, multiplying instead of dividing; that would be a tree 4 times as tall as the tallest one.

QR.sk: Factors—two numbers from their product and sum
QR.q: Bea is thinking of two whole numbers for a riddle game. When she multiplies them she gets 24, and when she adds them she gets 11. What are Bea's two numbers?
QR.e: Pairs that multiply to 24 include 2 and 12, 3 and 8, and 4 and 6. Of these, only 3 and 8 also add to 11.

y.B: 4 and 6 checks only the product: they multiply to 24, but they add to 10.
y.C: 4 and 7 checks only the sum: they add to 11, but they multiply to 28.
y.D: 5 and 6 checks only the sum: they add to 11, but they multiply to 30.

QR.q: The figure shows how Arlo set up his dominoes, with one domino in each square. Daisy has the same number of dominoes, and she sets all of them up in 3 equal rows. How many dominoes are in each of Daisy's rows?
QR.e: Arlo has 4 rows of 6, which is 24 dominoes. Sharing 24 dominoes into 3 equal rows gives 24 ÷ 3 = 8 in each row.

y.A: 6 keeps Arlo's row length, but Daisy has fewer rows, so each of her rows must hold more dominoes.
y.C: 18 is 3 × 6, six dominoes in each of Daisy's 3 rows, which uses only 18 of the 24 dominoes.
y.D: 24 is the number of dominoes in all, not the number in one of Daisy's rows.

QR.q: Cleo found r smooth stones at the lake. Her friend Hugo found 3 times as many stones as Cleo. Which expression shows how many stones Hugo found?
QR.e: 3 times as many means 3 groups of Cleo's r stones, which is 3 × r.

y.B: r + 3 gives Hugo 3 more stones than Cleo, not 3 times as many.
y.C: r − 3 gives Hugo 3 fewer stones than Cleo, but he found more.
y.D: r ÷ 3 gives Hugo one third as many stones as Cleo, which is fewer, not more.

QR.sk: Algebra—writing an equation for a story
QR.q: Finn cut a rope into 4 pieces of equal length to tie down his tent. Each piece is 9 feet long. Which equation could be used to find n, the length of the whole rope in feet?
QR.e: Cutting the rope into 4 equal pieces divides its length by 4, and each piece is 9 feet, so n ÷ 4 = 9.

y.A: n − 4 = 9 takes 4 feet off the rope instead of cutting it into 4 equal pieces.
y.B: n × 4 = 9 multiplies the rope's length by 4, but cutting a rope into pieces makes each piece shorter than the rope.
y.C: 4 ÷ n = 9 divides in the wrong order: the rope's length is what gets divided by 4.

QR.q: The map of a nature park is drawn on a coordinate grid. Esme begins at the point labeled Start. She walks 4 units to the right and then 3 units up. Where does she end?
QR.e: Start is at (1, 2). Walking 4 units right reaches (5, 2), and walking 3 units up from there reaches (5, 5), where the Cabin is.

y.B: Dock is where she is after walking 4 units right; she still has to walk 3 units up.
y.C: Falls is at (4, 3), as if the walk began at 0 instead of at Start.
y.D: Lookout is 3 units right and 4 units up from Start; the two moves are switched.

QR.q: The figure shows the sail Hal drew for his toy boat on a grid of 1-inch squares. What is the area of the sail?
QR.e: The sail covers 15 whole squares and 6 half squares along its slanted side. Six halves make 3 whole squares, so the area is 15 + 3 = 18 square inches.

y.A: 15 square inches counts only the whole squares and leaves out the 6 half squares along the slanted side.
y.C: 21 square inches counts each of the 6 half squares as a whole square.
y.D: 36 square inches is 6 × 6, every square in the box around the sail, including the empty ones above the slanted side.

QR.q: The clock shows the time one afternoon when Calla arrives at a park. The park closes at 6:00 p.m. How much time does Calla have before the park closes?
QR.e: The clock shows 4:40. From 4:40 to 5:00 is 20 minutes, and from 5:00 to 6:00 is 1 hour, so she has 1 hour 20 minutes.

y.A: 20 minutes reads the short hand as 5 because it is most of the way from 4 to 5; the clock shows 4:40, not 5:40.
y.C: 1 hour 40 minutes uses the 40 minutes shown on the clock instead of the 20 minutes from 4:40 to 5:00.
y.D: 2 hours 20 minutes subtracts the hours, 6 − 4, and the minutes, 60 − 40, separately, but from 4:40 to 6:00 is less than 2 hours.

QR.q: Coach Gil paints a starting line on the practice field. The line is 15 yards long. How many feet long is the line?
QR.e: Each yard is 3 feet, so 15 yards is 15 × 3 = 45 feet.

y.A: 5 feet is 15 ÷ 3, dividing instead of multiplying; feet are shorter than yards, so there are more of them.
y.B: 18 feet is 15 + 3, adding the 3 feet in a yard just once instead of once for every yard.
y.D: 180 feet is 15 × 12, which uses the 12 inches in a foot instead of the 3 feet in a yard.

QR.sk: Unit rate—distance at a steady speed
QR.q: A tour bus travels at a steady speed of 50 miles each hour. How far does it travel in 2 1/2 hours?
QR.e: In 2 hours the bus goes 2 × 50 = 100 miles, and in the extra half hour it goes half of 50, or 25 miles, so 100 + 25 = 125 miles.

y.A: 25 miles is how far the bus goes in just the half hour; the 2 whole hours are left out.
y.B: 52 1/2 miles is 50 + 2 1/2, adding the hours to the miles instead of multiplying.
y.C: 100 miles is the distance for 2 hours; the extra half hour adds 25 miles more.

QR.q: The graph shows the number of rainy days in a town during four months. June has 30 days. On how many days in June did it not rain?
QR.e: June's bar reaches 8, so it rained on 8 of June's 30 days and did not rain on the other 30 − 8 = 22 days.

y.B: 25 is 30 − 5, which uses July's bar, the one just after June.
y.C: 30 is every day in June; the 8 rainy days still have to be taken away.
y.D: 38 is 30 + 8, adding the rainy days instead of taking them away.

QR.q: Ezra has a pile of pine cones. He can sort them into equal groups of 6 with none left over, or into equal groups of 9 with none left over. What is the smallest number of pine cones Ezra could have?
QR.e: The number must be a multiple of both 6 and 9. Counting by 9s gives 9 and then 18, and 18 is also 3 groups of 6, so 18 is the smallest.

y.B: 24 makes 4 equal groups of 6, but groups of 9 would leave 6 over; it checks only one group size.
y.C: 27 makes 3 equal groups of 9, but groups of 6 would leave 3 over; it checks only one group size.
y.D: 54 is 6 × 9, which works for both group sizes but is not the smallest number that does.

QR.sk: Number sense—greatest even number from digits
QR.q: In a card game, Della draws four number cards: 3, 8, 1, and 7. She must use all four cards to make the greatest even number she can. What number does she make?
QR.e: An even number ends in an even digit, and 8 is the only even card, so 8 goes last. The greatest way to order 7, 3, and 1 in front of it is 7, 3, 1, which makes 7,318.

y.A: 1,378 is the smallest even number the cards make; it puts the other cards in order from least to greatest instead of greatest to least.
y.B: 7,138 is even, but it puts the 1 ahead of the 3, so it is not the greatest even number.
y.D: 8,731 is the greatest number the cards can make, but it ends in 1, so it is odd.

QR.q: Five friends share 3 bags of sand equally to build sandcastles at the beach. What fraction of a bag of sand does each friend get?
QR.e: Each bag shared by 5 friends gives every friend 1/5 of a bag. With 3 bags, each friend gets 3 × 1/5 = 3/5 of a bag.

y.A: 1/5 is each friend's share of only one bag; there are 3 bags to share.
y.B: 1/3 writes 1 over the number of bags instead of sharing the 3 bags among the 5 friends.
y.D: 1 2/3 is 5 ÷ 3, dividing the friends by the bags; with fewer bags than friends, nobody can get a whole bag.

QR.sk: Fractions—reaching a fraction of a set
QR.q: The figure shows a wooden sign that Freya is building for a trail. It is made of equal squares, and the shaded squares are already painted. She wants 3/4 of the squares to be painted. How many more squares must she paint?
QR.e: The sign has 12 squares, and 3/4 of 12 is 9. She has painted 4, so she must paint 9 − 4 = 5 more.

y.A: 4 is the number of squares already painted, not how many more she must paint.
y.C: 8 is every square not yet painted; painting all of them would paint the whole sign, not 3/4 of it.
y.D: 9 is the number of squares that should be painted in all, 3/4 of the 12, but 4 of them are painted already.

QR.q: At a track meet, Ari's long jump measured 2.35 meters. Which point on the number line shows 2.35?
QR.e: Each mark on the number line is one tenth. 2.35 is 5 hundredths more than 2.3, which is exactly halfway between 2.3 and 2.4, where point Q is.

y.A: P is at 2.3; it leaves off the 5 hundredths.
y.C: R is at 2.4, which is 2.35 rounded to the nearest tenth, not 2.35 itself.
y.D: S is at 2.53, which switches the tenths digit and the hundredths digit.

QR.sk: Percent—percent of a group from a graph
QR.q: All 25 members of a hiking club voted for one place to visit on their next trip. The graph shows the votes. What percent of the members voted for either the lake or the beach?
QR.e: The lake got 5 votes and the beach got 4, so 9 of the 25 members chose one of them. Each member is 100% ÷ 25 = 4% of the club, so 9 members are 36%.

y.A: 9% writes the 9 votes as a percent, but there are 25 members, not 100.
y.B: 16% counts only the beach's 4 votes, 4 × 4%, and leaves out the lake.
y.C: 20% counts only the lake's 5 votes, 5 × 4%, and leaves out the beach.

QR.q: Basil stacks logs for a campfire, with one more log in each row than in the row above it. The table shows how many logs are in piles with different numbers of rows. How many logs are in a pile with 6 rows?
QR.e: Each new row has one more log than the row before: the 5th row adds 5 logs, making 15, and the 6th row adds 6 logs, making 21.

y.A: 12 is 2 × 6, doubling the 3-row pile; twice as many rows does not mean twice as many logs.
y.B: 15 is the number of logs in a pile with 5 rows; the 6th row still has to be added.
y.C: 18 keeps adding 4 logs for each new row, 10 + 4 + 4, but each new row has one more log than the row before.

QR.q: A frog hops along a row of stones in a pond. Starting on stone 0, it jumps forward 4 stones, then back 1 stone, then forward 4 stones, then back 1 stone, and keeps repeating. On which stone is the frog after its 10th jump?
QR.e: Each pair of jumps, forward 4 and back 1, moves the frog 3 stones ahead. Ten jumps are 5 pairs, so the frog is on stone 5 × 3 = 15.

y.B: 20 is 5 × 4, counting the 5 jumps forward but forgetting the 5 jumps back.
y.C: 30 is 10 × 3, as if every jump moved the frog 3 stones ahead; it takes two jumps to move 3 stones.
y.D: 40 is 10 × 4, as if all 10 jumps went forward 4 stones.

QR.q: Four runners entered a relay race. Each runner paid the same entry fee, f dollars, and the team also paid one $6 team fee. Altogether they paid $54. Which equation could be used to find f?
QR.e: Four runners paying f dollars each pay 4 × f dollars, and the $6 team fee is added once, so 4 × f + 6 = 54.

y.B: 4 × f − 6 = 54 takes the team fee away, but the $6 was paid on top of the runners' fees.
y.C: 4 + f + 6 = 54 adds the number of runners instead of multiplying the fee by 4.
y.D: 4 × (f + 6) = 54 charges the $6 team fee to each of the 4 runners instead of once.

QR.q: Gemma and Hollis start jumping rope at the same time. For every 3 jumps Gemma makes, Hollis makes 4 jumps. When Gemma has made 24 jumps, how many jumps has Hollis made?
QR.e: 24 jumps is 8 groups of Gemma's 3 jumps. Hollis makes 4 jumps for each group, so he has made 8 × 4 = 32 jumps.

y.A: 18 flips the comparison, giving Hollis 3 jumps for every 4 of Gemma's, but Hollis is the one who jumps more.
y.B: 25 is 24 + 1, keeping Hollis just 1 jump ahead, but he gains another jump for every 3 jumps Gemma makes.
y.D: 96 is 24 × 4, multiplying Gemma's jumps by 4 without first finding how many groups of 3 jumps she made.

QR.sk: Symmetry—lines of symmetry of a star
QR.q: The figure shows a star that Dina cut out of wood for a sign at a campground. All five points of the star are the same size and shape. How many lines of symmetry does the star have?
QR.e: A fold line through the tip of any point and the middle of the star makes the two halves match. There are 5 points, so there are 5 lines of symmetry.

y.A: 1 counts only the up-and-down fold through the top point; the fold through each of the other points works too.
y.B: 2 adds a side-to-side fold, but folding the star across its middle does not make the halves match.
y.D: 10 counts a line from each of the 10 corners, but each line runs from a tip to the inner corner across from it, so every line is counted twice.

QR.q: The figure shows the first two layers of a block Eli is building from small cubes, with no gaps or hidden holes. He keeps adding layers just like these until he has used 84 cubes in all. How many layers will the finished block have?
QR.e: Each layer is 4 cubes long and 3 cubes deep, so it holds 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. 84 cubes make 84 ÷ 12 = 7 layers.

y.A: 5 is the number of layers he still has to add after the 2 shown, not the number in the finished block.
y.C: 12 is the number of cubes in one layer, not the number of layers.
y.D: 42 is 84 ÷ 2, sharing the 84 cubes between the 2 layers shown instead of making layers of 12 cubes.

QR.q: The trail map is drawn on a coordinate grid. Each unit on the grid stands for 2 miles, and the trails follow the grid lines. Harper hikes from the Lodge to the Lake along the trails by the shortest route. How many miles does she hike?
QR.e: From the Lodge at (1, 1) to the Lake at (7, 5) is 6 units across and 4 units up, 10 units in all. Each unit is 2 miles, so she hikes 10 × 2 = 20 miles.

y.A: 8 miles counts only the 4 units up, 4 × 2, and leaves out the 6 units across.
y.B: 10 miles counts the 10 grid units but forgets that each unit stands for 2 miles.
y.C: 12 miles counts only the 6 units across, 6 × 2, and leaves out the 4 units up.

QR.q: The pictograph shows how many fish a fishing club caught each day, but the Sunday row has not been filled in yet. On Sunday the club caught 10 more fish than on Saturday. How many symbols should be drawn in the Sunday row?
QR.e: Saturday has 3 1/2 symbols, which is 12 + 2 = 14 fish. Sunday's catch is 14 + 10 = 24 fish, and 24 ÷ 4 = 6 symbols.

y.A: 5 1/2 leaves out Saturday's half symbol: 3 symbols is 12 fish, and 12 + 10 = 22 fish is 5 1/2 symbols.
y.C: 13 1/2 is 3 1/2 + 10, adding 10 symbols instead of 10 fish.
y.D: 24 is the number of fish caught on Sunday, not the number of symbols.

QR.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections. Gideon spins the arrow 80 times. About how many times should he expect it to land on blue?
QR.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are blue, so the arrow should land on blue about 3 out of every 8 spins. 80 spins is 10 groups of 8, so blue should come up about 3 × 10 = 30 times.

y.A: 3 is the number of blue sections on the spinner, not a number of spins.
y.B: 10 is 80 ÷ 8, the spins expected for just one section, but blue has 3 sections.
y.C: 20 is 80 ÷ 4, treating the 4 colors as equally likely, but blue covers more of the spinner than any other color.

QR.sk: Data reasoning—greatest change on a line graph
QR.q: The graph shows how many people were at a beach at different times one day. What was the greatest increase in the number of people from one hour to the next?
QR.e: Find each hour's change: 20 to 35 is 15, 35 to 45 is 10, 45 to 70 is 25, and 70 to 80 is 10. The greatest increase is 25, from 11 a.m. to noon.

y.A: 15 is the first increase, from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m., not the greatest one.
y.C: 60 is 80 − 20, the change from the first time to the last, not from one hour to the next.
y.D: 80 is the greatest number of people at the beach, at 1 p.m., not the greatest increase.

QR.q: The Venn diagram shows how many campers at a summer camp went canoeing, went hiking, or did both on Saturday. The campers outside the circles did neither. How many campers did not go canoeing?
QR.e: Everyone outside the canoeing circle did not go canoeing: the 12 who only hiked and the 3 who did neither, so 12 + 3 = 15.

y.A: 12 counts only the campers who hiked and did not canoe, leaving out the 3 who did neither.
y.B: 14 is 9 + 5, the campers who did go canoeing, not the ones who did not.
y.D: 17 is 12 + 5, the whole hiking circle, but the 5 campers in the overlap went canoeing too.

QR.sk: Number sense—counting numbers with a given digit
QR.q: A soccer league gives each player a jersey with a different number from 1 to 50. How many of the numbers from 1 to 50 have at least one digit 3?
QR.e: All ten numbers from 30 to 39 have a 3, and so do 3, 13, 23, and 43, which is 4 more. That makes 10 + 4 = 14, with 33 counted only once.

y.A: 5 counts only the numbers that end in 3 — 3, 13, 23, 33, and 43 — and leaves out the rest of the thirties.
y.B: 10 counts only the numbers from 30 to 39 and leaves out 3, 13, 23, and 43.
y.D: 15 counts 33 twice, once for ending in 3 and once for being in the thirties.

QR.q: In a basketball game, the Comets scored 18 more points than the Jets. Together the two teams scored 48 points. How many points did the Comets score?
QR.e: Take away the Comets' extra 18 points: 48 − 18 = 30, which splits into two equal shares of 15. The Jets scored 15, so the Comets scored 15 + 18 = 33.

y.A: 15 is the number of points the Jets scored, not the Comets.
y.B: 24 is half of 48, as if the two teams had scored the same number of points.
y.C: 30 is 48 − 18, the two equal shares together; it still has to be split before the 18 extra points are added back.

QR.q: The figure shows a rectangular corral. Ada is building a fence around it. She puts a post at each corner and then a post every 2 meters along each side, so the posts are 2 meters apart all the way around. How many posts does she need?
QR.e: The fence is 10 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 32 meters around. Posts 2 meters apart around a closed loop make 32 ÷ 2 = 16 posts, because the last gap ends at the corner post where she started.

y.B: 17 adds one extra post, as for a straight fence with a post at each end, but around a closed loop the last post is the first corner post.
y.C: 20 counts each side's posts separately, 6 on each long side and 4 on each short side, so the 4 corner posts are counted twice.
y.D: 32 is the number of meters around the corral, not the number of posts.

QR.q: The figure shows the outline of a dock at a lake, with some of the side lengths labeled. Every side meets the next at a right angle. What is the perimeter of the dock?
QR.e: The unlabeled sides are the bottom of the notch, 10 − 3 − 3 = 4 ft, its left side, 4 ft like its right side, and the left edge, 6 ft like the right edge. So the perimeter is 10 + 6 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 6 = 40 ft.

y.A: 26 ft adds only the five labeled sides; the three unlabeled sides add 4 + 4 + 6 = 14 ft more.
y.B: 32 ft is the perimeter of the 10-by-6 rectangle around the dock, which leaves out the two 4-foot sides that run down into the notch.
y.D: 44 ft is the area of the dock, 60 − 16 = 44 square feet, not the distance around it.

QR.sk: Measurement—comparing trip times in a schedule
QR.q: The table shows four morning trains from Cedar Junction to the coast. Which train has the shortest trip?
QR.e: Count from leaving to arriving: Red takes 70 minutes, Blue 50 minutes, Silver 40 minutes (35 minutes to 9:00 and 5 more), and Green 45 minutes. Silver's trip is the shortest.

y.A: Blue arrives first, at 8:45 a.m., but it leaves at 7:55 a.m., so its trip takes 50 minutes.
y.B: Green looks shortest when the times are subtracted like whole numbers, which makes Silver's trip 905 − 825 = 80; but an hour has 60 minutes, and 8:25 to 9:05 is only 40 minutes.
y.C: Red leaves first, at 7:40 a.m., but its trip takes 70 minutes, the longest of the four.

QR.q: The clock shows the time in Pine Harbor when Effie's plane takes off one morning. The flight lasts 3 hours. The clocks in Eastport are always 2 hours ahead of the clocks in Pine Harbor. What time is it in Eastport when the plane lands?
QR.e: The plane takes off at 10:20 a.m. Pine Harbor time and lands 3 hours later, at 1:20 p.m. Pine Harbor time. Eastport is 2 hours ahead, so it is 3:20 p.m. there.

y.A: 11:20 a.m. takes the 2 hours away instead of adding them: it is 1:20 p.m. in Pine Harbor minus 2 hours.
y.B: 12:20 p.m. adds only the 2-hour time difference to 10:20 a.m. and forgets the 3-hour flight.
y.C: 1:20 p.m. is the landing time on the Pine Harbor clocks, not on the Eastport clocks, which are 2 hours ahead.

QR.q: The graph shows Asher's scores on the first four holes of a mini golf course. After he played the fifth hole, the mean of his five scores was the same as the mean of his first four scores. What was his score on the fifth hole?
QR.e: The first four scores add to 2 + 5 + 1 + 8 = 16, so their mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4. A fifth score of 4 makes the total 20, and 20 ÷ 5 is still 4.

y.A: 0 seems to add nothing, but a score of 0 makes the five scores total 16, and 16 ÷ 5 is less than 4, so the mean would go down.
y.C: 16 is the total of the first four scores, not the score on one hole.
y.D: 20 is the total the five scores must have, 4 × 5, not the score on the fifth hole.

QR.sk: Mixed reasoning—counting the games in a tournament
QR.q: Four teams play in a soccer tournament. Each team plays every other team exactly once. How many games are played in all?
QR.e: Number the teams 1 to 4. Team 1 plays 3 games, team 2 has 2 more games against teams 3 and 4, and team 3 has 1 more game against team 4, so there are 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 games.

y.A: 4 gives each team only one game, but each team plays the 3 other teams.
y.C: 12 is 4 × 3, each team's 3 games, but every game has two teams in it, so each game is counted twice.
y.D: 16 is 4 × 4, as if each team also played itself.

RC.q: In line 21, “trips” most nearly means
RC.e: In lines 20–23, an ant or a spider that trips two of the hairs makes the trap snap shut, so trips means sets off, the way a touch on a wire can set off an alarm.

y.B: Falls over is what trips means when a person catches a foot and stumbles, but nothing in lines 20–23 falls down; the ant's touch on two hairs is what makes the trap snap shut.
y.C: Steps over would mean the ant misses the hairs, but the trap snaps shut only when two of the hairs are touched (lines 21–22), so the ant must touch them.
y.D: Travels to comes from a trip as a journey; the sentence is about what the ant's touch does to the hairs, which is to make the trap close, not about going somewhere (lines 20–23).

RC.q: According to the passage, where do Venus flytraps grow in the wild?
c: in rich soil that is full of nutrients
in places where fires cannot reach them
RC.e: Lines 6–8 say that Venus flytraps grow wild only within about 75 miles of Wilmington, North Carolina.

y.A: Thick, shady pine forests comes from the longleaf pines in line 9, but the grasslands are only dotted with pines and must stay sunny; if trees spread, they would shade the flytraps (lines 10–12).
y.C: Rich soil full of nutrients is the opposite of lines 14–15, which say the soil where flytraps grow is poor in nutrients; that is the reason they catch insects.
y.D: Places where fires cannot reach treats fire as a danger to the plants, but lines 9–12 say the fires are what keep their grasslands open and sunny.

RC.q: According to the passage, what makes a trap snap shut?
c: a raindrop landing inside the trap
a single touch on one of its hairs
two of its hairs touched within seconds
an insect touching the bristles on its edge
RC.e: Lines 19–23 say that a single touch does nothing, but when two of the hairs are touched one after the other within a few seconds, the trap snaps shut.

y.A: A raindrop landing inside is exactly what the trap is built to ignore; lines 23–24 say a raindrop does not fool the plant into closing for no reason.
y.B: A single touch on one hair is what lines 19–20 say does nothing at all; the trap waits until two hairs are touched, one after the other.
y.D: An insect touching the bristles mixes up two parts of the trap: the bristles are the teeth along the edges (lines 2–3), while the hairs that set it off grow inside, near the hinge (lines 18–19).

RC.q: It can be inferred from the last paragraph (lines 31–36) that the name “flytrap”
c: was given to the plant by Charles Darwin
does not fit what the plant usually catches
comes from the shape of the plant's open leaf
shows that flies are the plant's favorite meal
RC.e: The last paragraph says that a plant called a flytrap catches surprisingly few flies and that fewer than one meal in twenty is a flying insect, so the name does not match what it usually catches.

y.A: Given by Charles Darwin misreads lines 4–5: Darwin called the plant one of the most wonderful in the world, but the passage never says who named it.
y.C: The shape of the open leaf is described in line 1, where it looks like a mouth; the last paragraph is about what the plant catches, not how it looks.
y.D: Flies as its favorite meal is what the name seems to promise, but lines 31–36 say it catches surprisingly few flies; most of its meals are ants and spiders.

RC.q: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
c: Fires keep the flytrap's grassland open and sunny.
Most of its meals are ants and spiders, not flies.
Charles Darwin thought the flytrap was a wonderful plant.
A rare plant traps small animals to get what its soil lacks.
RC.e: The passage tells where the flytrap grows, why its poor soil makes it catch small animals, and how its trap catches and digests them; the other choices are single details.

y.A: Fires keeping the grassland open and sunny is one detail from the second paragraph (lines 9–12) about where the plant lives, not what the whole passage explains.
y.B: Most of its meals being ants and spiders is the closing fact (lines 33–36), one part of how the plant feeds, not the idea the whole passage builds.
y.C: Charles Darwin's opinion is one sentence near the start (lines 4–5) that makes the plant sound special; the rest of the passage explains how it lives and hunts.

RC.q: The passage is mainly about
c: a visit Bly made to Jules Verne
how Bly packed for a long journey
a magazine's plan to beat Nellie Bly
how Nellie Bly raced around the world
RC.e: The passage follows Bly from her idea of beating the eighty days in the novel, through her travels, to her arrival 72 days later; the other choices are single details of that trip.

y.A: A visit to Jules Verne is one stop along the way (lines 22–24); the passage follows the whole journey, from the idea to the arrival.
y.B: How Bly packed is one detail (lines 18–19), part of getting ready to leave, not what the whole passage is about.
y.C: A magazine's plan to beat her comes up in just two places (lines 26–27 and line 31); the passage follows Bly, not the magazine's reporter.

RC.q: According to the passage, the business manager said the trip was impossible partly because he thought Bly
c: was too young to travel alone
wanted to work for a rival paper
would need a protector on the trip
would be beaten by another reporter
RC.e: In lines 9–12 the business manager says that as a woman Bly would need a protector, and that her baggage would slow her down.

y.A: Too young comes from “a young reporter” in line 2, but the business manager never mentions her age; he says that as a woman she would need a protector (lines 10–11).
y.B: Working for a rival paper is what Bly threatened to do after he said no (lines 13–15), not a reason he gave for saying no.
y.D: Being beaten by another reporter comes from the news Bly heard in Hong Kong (lines 25–27), on the trip itself a year later; the business manager gave no such reason.

RC.q: In line 28, “followed” most nearly means
RC.e: Readers back home could not travel with Bly; they kept up with her progress in the newspapers, so followed means watched, or kept track of.
